units.la: QUemadmodum non solùm Magistratus virum indicat, sed etiam magistratum vir, vt laudatissimus ille Thebanorum dux Epaminondas olim dicebat: ita non tàtum Disputatio erudita virum eruditum ostendit, uerum etiā Disputatorem subtilem, Disputationem, cuius finis est ueri cognitio. Quod enim de Gubernatoris Politici animo cognoscendo, Sophocles in sua Antigone prudenter uereq; monuit:
units.tr: Just as a magistrate reveals not only the man but also the man reveals the magistrate, as that most praised Theban commander Epaminondas once used to say, so a learned disputation shows not only a learned man but also a subtle disputant, and a disputation whose aim is the knowledge of truth. For concerning the knowing of a political ruler's mind, Sophocles in his Antigone warned wisely and truly:

units.la: ἀμήχανον δ' ἐκ τοῦ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἐκμαθεῖν [?] ψυχήν τε καὶ φρόνημα, καὶ γνώμην, πρὶν ἂν [?] ἀρχάς τε καὶ νόμους ἴδῃ φανείς [?]
units.tr: "It is impossible to learn from any man his soul, his mind and his judgment before he has been seen to display rule and laws" [ἀμήχανον δ' ἐκ τοῦ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἐκμαθεῖν ψυχήν τε καὶ φρόνημα, καὶ γνώμην, πρὶν ἂν ἀρχάς τε καὶ νόμους ἴδῃ φανείς].

units.la: id nos de homine, opinione nostrā, seueriore quadam & solida doctrina prāstāte, & ad eruditā placidāq; de vtilibus rebus συμφιλοσόφων egregiè instructo, quando calculi cognitionem prauertere non debet, prius testari nō possumus, quā multis & illustribus speciminibus exhibitis σεαυτὸν διαλεγεσθαι, vt Plato dicere solebat, reipsa coprobauerit.
units.tr: The same we cannot testify to beforehand about this man, who, in our opinion, excels in a rather severe and solid learning, and who is well instructed in the calm and learned discussion of useful matters with fellow philosophers (συμφιλοσόφων), since a knowledge of computation ought not to be turned aside. Only when, by many and illustrious specimens put on display, he has proved in practice that he "converses with himself" (σεαυτὸν διαλεγεσθαι), as Plato used to say, will we be able to vouch for him.

units.la: Tantisper enim, donec eius ordinis hominibus visum est φιλοσοφίας σιωπᾶν [?] & ingenij vires & opes modestè dissimulare, cū ὁ λόγος Βίω-σας, à vita ratione ad studiorū institutum reuocent: de ea quae pollent disserendi in vtramq; partem facultate, deq; eorum γνῶσι in rerum diiudicatione & æstimatione, spectatores non magis quàm de abscôdito thesauro diuinando pronunciare possunt.
units.tr: For, so long as the men of that order think it fitting to keep silent about philosophy and to modestly conceal the powers and resources of their talent, while reason (ὁ λόγος) calls them back from a life of reason to the pursuit of study, spectators can no more pronounce on their ability to argue on either side, and on their knowledge (γνῶσις) in judging and weighing things, than they can divine a hidden treasure.

units.la: At vbi, propter rerum varietatem, hominum q; imperitorum καὶ αὐτιλογικῶν turbam, veri falsiq; censura, palaestra & olei rem esse, ac disputatione, tanquā veritatis cribro (sententia nobilissimi generis & doctrina viri Ioan. Pici) sibi vtilandā, & ab opinionum commentitiarū quisquiliis purgandā persuasum habentes, in theatrū et phrontisterium praesidijs eruditae doctrinae velut armis instructi, progrediuntur, veritatisq; inuestigandae & tuendae studio, primas hastas argumentorum probabilium initio iaciant, respondentis tentandi causa: sermone interim tam ζητητικὸν q; ἀποδεικτικοῦ prudenter instituunt, sic vt oratio cum rebus ipsis crescat & consentiat, nihil habens ἐξαγγελτικὸν καὶ ἀσυνάρτητον: deinde demonstrationum signis in medium agmen opinionum illatis, adhibitisq; κριτηρίοις minimè fallentibus, illas fundunt & in fugam vertunt, vt solae victrici veritati locus sit: deniq; cū, iux-
units.tr: But when, because of the variety of things and the crowd of unskilled and contentious people (καὶ αὐτιλογικῶν), the judgment of true and false becomes a matter for the wrestling-ground and the oil, and for disputation, which they believe to be a sieve of truth (an opinion of the most noble kind, and of the learning of the man Giovanni Pico), and which they are persuaded must sift and purge things of the trifles of invented opinions, they advance into the theatre and the school of thought, armed as it were with the defences of learned doctrine. In zeal for seeking and defending the truth, they first hurl the opening spears of probable arguments, to test the respondent. Meanwhile they prudently arrange their discourse so that it is both inquiring (ζητητικόν) and demonstrative (ἀποδεικτικοῦ), so that the speech grows with the things themselves and agrees with them, having nothing incoherent or disconnected (ἐξαγγελτικὸν καὶ ἀσυνάρτητον). Then, bringing the signs of demonstrations into the midst of the army of opinions, and applying criteria that scarcely ever deceive, they scatter them and put them to flight, so that only victorious truth has room. Finally, when,

units.la: PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: ta proverbiū, adsciscut ad extremum scientiam & eas artes, ad quas confugiendum est, cū veritas periclitatur, eoq; extremis ingenij viribus utendum, tum demum, quae ipsorum in disserendo virtus & dexteritas sit, res ipsa docet: secundum illud Pindari in Nemeis dictum: ἐν δ' ἐπραξῖ τέλος διαφαίνεται, ὧν τις ἐξοχότερος γνώσται.
units.tr: As the proverb has it, they finally call in knowledge and those arts to which one must flee when the truth is in danger, and when the utmost strength of mind must be used. Only then does the matter itself show what their skill and dexterity in disputation amount to, in line with Pindar's saying in the Nemean odes: "In action the end becomes clear, by which one will know who is the more outstanding" [ἐν δ' ἐπραξῖ τέλος διαφαίνεται, ὧν τις ἐξοχότερος γνώσται].

units.la: In tanta autem seculi nostri licentia, opinionum confusione, & altercationū de rebus sacris & profanis turba, saepenumero animū meū subijt cogitatio, de Stentorum quorundā [illegible, ~10 letters] risu ne illa nobis, an vero gemitu planctuq; prosequendae sint?
units.tr: Yet in this age of ours, with its great licence, its confusion of opinions and its uproar of disputes over sacred and profane matters, I have often wondered whether we should answer the laughter of certain Stentors with laughter, or with groaning and lamentation.

units.la: Cū enim [illegible, ~12 letters] isti verè [illegible, ~10 letters], ut Arist. scribit, vel sint [illegible, ~8 letters], vel [illegible, ~6 letters], utrinq; suam fabulam sic salīt [?] in proscenio publico, ut non possit non in mentem venire spectatoribus eruditis illud Horatianum:
units.tr: For since [illegible] these men are truly [illegible], as Aristotle writes, either [illegible] or [illegible], each side struts out its own farce on the public stage in such a way that it cannot fail to bring to mind for learned spectators that line of Horace:

units.la: Spectatum admissi risum teneatis amici.
units.tr: Having been admitted to watch, can you hold back your laughter, friends?

units.la: Vtriq; enim Moria fascino occaecati, se solos sapere, ceteros autem oēs umbrarū more circumvolitare opinantur. Priores illi, opinionū suarum τερατισμάτα, haud secus ac simiae turpissimos suos catulos, mirantur, aliys ostentant & obtrudunt, ab omnibus velut è tripode prolata in pretio haberi volunt: eos qui ea [illegible, ~6 letters] expendunt, tanquam unguēs in vulcere auersantur: cōtradicentes, cane peius et angue oderūt. Posteriores, canina facundia & Sophistica armati, ut cū eruditis paria facere videātur, Logica quedā instrumēta adhibere conātur, ut, si Deo placet, disputatores subtiles & exercitati uideantur. Vtriq; panoplie abusu, imperitia videlicet sua τεχνικῷ [?] sese doctis deridedos propinant. Ad disputandū enim perinde instructi accedunt, ut Thersitem aliquem, armorū quae ὅπλοθήκας [?] καὶ φυλακτήρια Graeci vocant, vsum confundentem, parmam à tergo gestātem, thoracem capiti, ensem iugulo, cheirothecas tibijs adhibentem, & in lancea aduersus hostem tanquam in arundine longa equitantem, repraesentēt, & ut [illegible, ~6 letters] rerum imperitos videantur.
units.tr: For both sides, blinded by the spell of Folly, think that they alone are wise and that all others flit about like shades. The first group, like apes with their ugliest little ones, marvel at their own prodigies of opinion, display them to others, and press them on everyone, wanting them to be accepted as oracles delivered from the tripod. Those who weigh these things they shun as one shuns a thorn in a sore; contradicting them, they hate them worse than a dog or a snake. The second group, armed with a snarling eloquence and sophistry, try to use certain tools of logic so that they may appear to be on a level with the learned and, God willing, to look like subtle and practised disputants. Both, by misusing their panoply, offer themselves as a laughing-stock to the learned, through their own ignorance of the craft. They come to the dispute so equipped that they resemble some Thersites, muddling the use of the arms which the Greeks call armouries and amulets [ὅπλοθήκας καὶ φυλακτήρια]: carrying a shield on his back, a breastplate on his head, a sword at his throat, gloves on his shins, and riding against the enemy with a lance as if on a long reed, so that they appear ignorant of the things they handle.

units.la: Iam verò cum Panico apparatui, uelitationum & pugnae ratio respondet, lepidusq; Andabata, clausis quidem oculis, sed gladiatorio animo ad eum quem sibi oppugnandum duxit, viam affectat, & velut illud Homericum dicere videtur: [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐπὶ μ' ἐχολώσατε λίλω, [illegible, ~18 letters] μεγαίρω,
units.tr: Now, when the method of skirmishing and fighting matches the display of a Panic army, the witty Andabata, with his eyes indeed shut but with a gladiator's spirit, makes his way against the man he has chosen to attack, and seems to say the Homeric words: [illegible] "you have angered me with your [illegible], [illegible] I begrudge."

units.la: resq; ad summum venisse, & ut vulgo dicere solemus, in acie nouacula
units.tr: And things have come to the extreme, and, as we commonly say, to the razor's edge in battle.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: la, si[?] periclitari videtur, tum vero rationum & argumentorum perduelles, conuitiorum sputo, exprobrationum sordibus, dirarum imprecationum veneno, velut æstro quodam percitì, sic debacchatur in aduersarium, vt etiam theseos suæ obliti, palmarium facinus esse putent, sic pingere, immò verius deformare hominem, vt putetur esse monstrum, horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademtum, quotidie gnem spiret. Ex potestate tunc exisse illos non immeritò dicas, cum interim ipsi omnium plausu se dignos censeant.
units.tr: ...if he seems to be in danger, then indeed these enemies of argument and reason, goaded as if by some gadfly, rage against their opponent with spittle of insults, filth of reproaches and the poison of dire curses. They forget their own thesis and think it the crowning achievement to paint, or rather to distort, the man so that he appears a monster, horrible, misshapen, huge, with his light taken away, breathing out smoke every day. You may not unreasonably say that these men have got out of control, while they themselves think they deserve the applause of all.

units.la: Fortassis minus mali (si scandalū publicū et quidē nocentissimū excipias.) in eo fuerit, si cum Bitho Bachius congrediatur, habeant similes labra lactucas. Nam & Mandrabuli more res illis Mirmillonibus inter se rixantibus succedit, vt multa huius aetatis ὑομαχίαι[?] καὶ λογομαχίαι testentur, & bonis doctisq; viris, nonnihil respirandi, & ea [illegible, ~5 letters] in lucem producendi, & exponendi facultas interim conceditur. Sed enim illud modis omnibus dolendum et deplorandum est, Harmostas istos, secundum veterem versum:
units.tr: Perhaps it would be less harmful (unless you count the public scandal, and a most damaging one) if they went up against Bithus with Bacchius, and had lettuces for lips. For, in the manner of Mandrabulus, things go with these Mirmillones fighting among themselves, as the many squabbles and logomachies [ὑομαχίαι καὶ λογομαχίαι] of this age bear witness. Meanwhile good and learned men are granted some breathing space and the opportunity to bring such things into the light and to expose them. But it must by all means be lamented and deplored that these Harmostae, according to the old verse:

units.la: [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: [The verse is illegible in the scan.]

units.la: ut diligenter sibi ipsis, hoc est, ut tri[?] & culinæ suæ consulant, syncretismo iungi, & occupatis Midarum quorundam auribus & animis, summa cum impudentia & contentione bellum inferre viris doctis, quibus tamen hoc unum cordi est, vt in omni genere doctrinæ veritas quaeratur & illustretur. Quid autem in hac illorum ὑπομαχίαις καὶ [illegible, ~8 letters], istis qui pro tuenda veritate laborat, oppressis futurum sit, cordati homines non obscure animadvertunt: ipse equidem nolim male ominari.
units.tr: are busy looking after themselves, that is, their belly and their kitchen, joining in syncretism; and, with the ears and minds of certain Midases occupied, they make war on learned men with the greatest shamelessness and contentiousness, although these men care for this one thing only: that truth be sought and made clear in every branch of learning. What will become of those who labour for the defence of truth, once they have been crushed by these men's shouting, thoughtful people clearly see. I myself would rather not predict ill.

units.la: Verum omissis iis, qui pro Hierophantis Sycophantas agunt, nec nisi Cyclopum more omnia & facere et dicere consueuerunt, suaq; intemperie non solum barbariem, sed etiam Religionis veræ corruptelas, nisi Deus pro immensa sua bonitate auerterit ista mala, reuocaturi sunt: quantum iis debeamus, qui collatis argumentis placidè inquirunt veritatem, eamq; vt sunt candidæ Musarum ianuæ, publici boni ergo sic profitetur, vt sint ἀνδρῶν ἀγαθοὶ et duces boni, qui & comites reddunt bonos, sic vt gratos memoresq; decet ingenuè fateamur.
units.tr: But, leaving aside those who play the sycophant to the hierophants, who do and say everything in the manner of the Cyclopes and who, by their intemperance, will bring back not only barbarism but also corruptions of the true religion, unless God in his immense goodness turns these evils away: how much we owe to those who, by weighing arguments, quietly seek the truth and, as the doors of the Muses are open to all, so profess it for the public good that they are "good men and good leaders [ἀνδρῶν ἀγαθοὶ]", who also make their companions good. As is fitting, we should honestly confess ourselves grateful and mindful of them.

units.la: Qui in disputationibus seriis, utilia & necessaria argumenta sic tractat[?], vt [illegible, ~6 letters] λόγων perspicuè declaretur: nec quaerit victoriam multoq; minus applausum hominum, sed vt alicubi grauissimè monet Augustinus, bonum rectum, & verum duplici beneficio veritatis studiosos afficiit. Nam, & rerum pulcherrimarum & utilissimarum Methodicas expositiones subministrando, iudicium in multis studiosis hominibus informant, & eruditione augent & confirmant: & illustribus disputationum utilissimarum exemplis, usum Logices totius ostendunt, quaq; ratione & via alia res tractando velut e tenebris in lucem producenda, quo ordine, quo etiam orationis genere nobis utendum sit, ostendunt.
units.tr: Those who, in serious disputations, handle useful and necessary arguments in such a way that the matter is set out clearly and in order, and who seek neither victory nor, much less, the applause of men, but, as Augustine warns most weightily somewhere, benefit the lovers of the good, the right and the true with a twofold kindness of truth. For by supplying methodical expositions of the most beautiful and most useful things, they form the judgement of many studious men and strengthen and increase their learning; and by the illustrious examples of most useful disputations they show the use of logic as a whole, and by what method and way a matter is to be handled and brought out of darkness into light, and in what order and what kind of speech we ought to use.

units.la: Vt etiam in tota virorum bonorum vita virtutum pulcherrimarum vivae & expressae imagines, non liberali solùm voluptati, sed etiam magno usui sunt iis, qui amabili donorum Spiritus sancti spectaculo delectantur: sic in bonorum & doctorum disputationibus iucundum & utile est φιλαληθείας[?], candoris, modestiae, diligentiae & aliarum virtutum egregia documenta intueri, mirari, imitari.
units.tr: Just as in the whole life of good men there are living and vivid images of the most beautiful virtues, which give not only liberal pleasure but also great benefit to those who delight in the lovely spectacle of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so in the disputations of good and learned men it is pleasant and useful to behold, to admire and to imitate the outstanding examples of love of truth [φιλαληθείας], candour, modesty, diligence and other virtues.

units.la: Inter caeteras autem Disputatoris ingeniosi virtutes, neutiquam postremo loco illa, quae, ut citra contumeliam ab aliis in parte aliqua doctrinae communis dissentiamus, efficit, mihi numeranda videtur.
units.tr: Among the other virtues of a clever disputant, I think I should count, not at all in the last place, that virtue which makes it possible for us to dissent from others in some part of the common teaching without insult.

units.la: Etenim cum eius φιλαφωνίας[?] multae sint causae, eaq; partim genio & ingenio, partem institutioni, partim aliis causis acceptae ferendae sint: aequissimum fuerit aeterni sapientissimiq; Numinis exemplo, τροποφορεῖν[?] & hominum infirmitati nonnulla benignè tribuere. Is cuius ingenium σάσιμον[?] est, non poterit per omnia paria facere cum eo, cuius ἀυφυὲς[?] ingenium est. Videmus quosdam minimo fere negocio res apprehendere, dijudicare, ad usum transferre, memoria non item excellere. Alios contrà magno studio aegrè parta, fideliter retinere. Et cum intelligamus res, perinde ut successione temporis fiant, hoc est, non simul omneis, sed unam post aliam: ne mirum videatur, si proportione quadam institutio nostra intelligentia respondeat.
units.tr: For since there are many causes of his disagreement, and these are to be ascribed partly to temperament and talent, partly to upbringing and partly to other causes, it would be most fair, after the example of the eternal and most wise Deity, to bear with human weakness and to grant it some indulgence. One whose talent is unsteady cannot be made to agree in every point with one whose talent is naturally keen. We see some who grasp things with very little effort, judge them and apply them to use, yet do not excel in memory; others, on the contrary, with great effort retain faithfully what they have laboriously acquired. And since we understand that things come about in the course of time, that is, not all at once but one after another, it should not seem strange if our instruction corresponds in a certain proportion to our understanding.

units.la: Praeceptorum ingenijs, sic quidam (occulta ingeniorum conspiratione moti) delectantur, ut nunquam non illis satisfaciat illud Pythagoricum: αὐτὸς ἔφα. Et hac quidem in re tanto minus est periculi, quo magis aliena fuit ab omni fuco, sophistica & impostura Praeceptoris illius institutio. Humanitatis etiam fuerit, variè occupatis viris, ut maximè praecipuis solidae doctrinae praesidijs instructi sint, non eandem, quàm requirimus in ijs qui philosophico ocio abundant, ἀχείβαια[?], in omnibus doctrinae membris, exigere. Praecocia esse Melanchthonis scripta, M. Nizolium dicere solitum accepimus. Certum tamen est virum illum opt. & eruditissimum, in summa ocij penuria, ea doctrinae tum sacrae tum profanae capita exposuisse, quae si hic vel attigisset, aequior forsan illius studiis fuisset. Alias dissensionum causas, eo nomine non probo, quia culpa non vacant. Sunt qui praeiudicii, cuius fons est προσω-πολη̃ψια, fascino ita dementati sunt, ut nullum planè locum dent aliorum fideli admonitioni & posterioribus curis, quae tamen meliores sunt. Horum placitis si λόγου καὶ πείρας, indubitata sanè κριτήρια, cum Galeno opponas, cum nullo modo de opinionis semel conceptae possessione sese deijci patiantur, ne iacturam faciant doctrinae magno ut videtur labore partae, non magis profeceris, quam si hydropico aquam, si ebrioso vini usum potumq; dissuadeas. Alii natura ἐριστικοί, Sectarum studio delectantur, de quibus admodum scitè Galenus dicit: ὅτως ἄρα δ' ἀνόσα πότρεπτον τι κακοῦ ἔσχηκεν ἢ περὶ τὰς αἱρέσεις φιλοτιμία, καὶ δ' ἐν σ' ἐκνιπ' λον γὰρ τοῖς μέλλουσι [?] καὶ φύσεως ἀπάσης δ' σιατώτερον. Idem in opere de facultatib. naturalibus vere adfirmat: ὅτω ὁ μόνον ὁδ' ἐν ὑγιὲς ἴσασιν οἱ τὰς τοιαῦτας αἱρέσεις ἀσλδύοντες, ἀλλ' ὅδὲ μαθεῖν ἐθέλησι, τῇ λοιδορήσει προσέτι. Alii quasi iam ad eruditionis apice pervenerint, doctrina, quam sibi parasse videntur, citra omnem delectum contenti, subsistunt, surdi caecique ad ea omnia quae non didicerunt. De his praclarè idem Galenus scripsit: αἱ γὰρ ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ μόνον κωφὰς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τυφλὰς ἰσχάζον τὰ, τ' τοῖς ἄλλοις φαεργῶς ὁρωμένων.
units.tr: Some, moved by a hidden agreement of talents, delight in the talents of their teachers so much that the saying of Pythagoras, "He himself said it" [αὐτὸς ἔφα], never fails to satisfy them. And in this matter there is so much the less danger, the more that teacher's instruction was free from all paint, sophistry and imposture. It would also be humane, since men are busy with various things, not to demand in all branches of learning that the same solid doctrine, which we require of those who abound in philosophical leisure, be provided to those most especially engaged, who ought to be equipped, as far as possible, with the supports of sound learning [ἀχείβαια]. I have been told that M. Nizolius used to say that Melanchthon's writings were precocious. It is certain, however, that that excellent and most learned man, in the great scarcity of leisure, set out those heads of sacred and profane learning which, if he had touched on them here, would perhaps have been fairer to his studies. I do not approve of other causes of dissension on that account, because they are not free from fault. There are those who have been so maddened by the charm of prejudice, whose source is respect of persons [προσωπολημψία], that they give no place at all to the faithful admonition of others and to later considerations, which are nonetheless better. If you set against the opinions of such men "reason and experience" [λόγου καὶ πείρας], as Galen does, which are undoubted criteria, they will not allow themselves to be dislodged from the possession of an opinion once conceived, lest they lose the learning gained, as it seems, with great labour. You will achieve no more than if you should advise a dropsical man against water, or a drunkard against the use of wine. Others, being contentious by nature, delight in the zeal of sects, concerning whom Galen speaks very aptly: [Galen's Greek, as printed in the scan: ὅτως ἄρα δ' ἀνόσα πότρεπτον τι κακοῦ ἔσχηκεν ἢ περὶ τὰς αἱρέσεις φιλοτιμία, καὶ δ' ἐν σ' ἐκνιπ' λον γὰρ τοῖς μέλλουσι [?] καὶ φύσεως ἀπάσης δ' σιατώτερον.] In his work On the Natural Faculties he truly affirms: [Greek as printed: ὅτω ὁ μόνον ὁδ' ἐν ὑγιὲς ἴσασιν οἱ τὰς τοιαῦτας αἱρέσεις ἀσλδύοντες, ἀλλ' ὅδὲ μαθεῖν ἐθέλησι, τῇ λοιδορήσει προσέτι.] Others, as if they had already reached the summit of learning, rest content with whatever learning they seem to have acquired, without any discrimination, deaf and blind to all those things which they have not learned. Galen wrote of these men splendidly: [Greek as printed: αἱ γὰρ ψυχὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ μόνον κωφὰς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τυφλὰς ἰσχάζον τὰ, τ' τοῖς ἄλλοις φαεργῶς ὁρωμένων.]

units.la: Ego ut ingeniis fauendum, & de dissidētium sententiis mihi neutiquam temere pronunciandum, duco: sic viris praestantibus, etsi inter eos sit sententiarum aliqua discrepantia, venerationem & amorem me debere nunquā dubitavi. Et cum ut de religionis doctrina loquar cuiusq; hominis fidelis illuminationi ac huius gradibus, optimo providentiae divinae consilio, certa temporis momenta praestituta esse noverim, eam ergo alios humanitatem & ἐπιεικείαν mihi pro virili declarandam arbitror, qua velim alios erga me multiplici profecto infirmitate laborātem, uti. Delector sanè eam ob causam, patrui mei magni, Simonis Grynaei versiculis. Non eadem sentire bonis de rebus eisdem, Incolumi licuit semper amicitia.
units.tr: I think that one should be indulgent towards talents, and that I should never pronounce rashly on the opinions of those who disagree with me. So too, although there is some discrepancy of opinion among outstanding men, I have never doubted that I owe them reverence and love. And since, to speak of the doctrine of religion, I know that for every faithful man the stages of his enlightenment, and the moments at which it comes, have been fixed by the best counsel of divine providence, I think I should show to others, as far as I can, that humanity and forbearance [ἐπιείκεια] which I would wish others to show towards me, since I too am beset by manifold weakness. I take special delight in this for the sake of the verses of my great-uncle, Simon Grynaeus: "To hold different opinions about the same good things has always been allowed, while friendship remains unharmed."

units.la: Habet autem studiosi, in hisce de Astrologia divinatrice Epistolis, multa virtutum pulcerrimarum, quibus ingeniosum disputatorem instructum esse oportet, exempla: quae monet, nos quoq; τῆς μεθόδος, τῆς σαφηνείας καὶ φιλαληθείας in collatione erudita sententiarum & opinionum, amantes esse debere.
units.tr: In these Epistles on Divinatory Astrology, moreover, the studious reader will find many examples of the most beautiful virtues with which a clever disputant ought to be equipped. They advise us that we too should be lovers of method [τῆς μεθόδος], clarity [τῆς σαφηνείας] and love of truth [φιλαληθείας] in the learned comparison of opinions and views.

units.la: PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Non est autem mihi illud dissimulandum, quod res est, hasce videlicet Epistolas, meo quodam consilio editas esse, cum Epistolas, Viri clarissimi, & publicè de Re Medica, privatim etiam de me praclarè meriti, D. THOMAE ERASTI, à magni nominis Viris, ac imprimis à Generoso & illustri viro ANDREA DUDITHIO AB HOREHOVVIZA, Cæsareæ Maiestatis Oratore et Consiliario, desiderari, intellexissem. Etsi autem homini diligenti semper aliquid superest, auctore Ioanne Chrysostomo: eoque credibile est δευτέρας φρόντιδας, aliquid addere potuisse istis Epistolis iam olim scriptis, quas ante sedecim annos relegit, nec unquam postea inspexit D. Erastus, qui etiam cum absens de editione admonitus esset, quòd nondum excusas iudicaret, editionem differendam censuit: tamen cum viderem opere iam absolu-to, mira perspicuitate & evidentia argumentum hoc ab illo tractatum, & argumentis Antagonistarum satisfactum esse, ac futurum spe-rarem ut non solum non molesté ferret, se absente Epistolas hasce editas esse, sed etiam Aduersariarum Epistolarum copiam nobis aliquando faceret, studio publicæ utilitatis ductus, Typographum, cui eas dederam, in lucem eadem proferre passus sum.
units.tr: I must not conceal the fact that these Letters have been published by my own decision, since I had learned that the Letters of Thomas Erastus, a most distinguished man who has deserved well of the medical profession publicly and of me privately, were being sought after by men of great name, and above all by the noble and illustrious Andreas Dudithius of Horehowiza, Orator and Counsellor of His Imperial Majesty. Although, as John Chrysostom says, there is always something left for a diligent man, and it is therefore credible that Erastus might have added something of his own second thoughts to these Letters, written long ago, which he reread sixteen years ago and has never looked at since, and although when he was absent and was reminded about publication he judged that they were not yet fit to be issued and advised that publication be postponed, nevertheless, when I saw that the work was now finished, that this subject had been treated with remarkable clarity and evidence, and that the arguments of the opponents had been answered, and when I hoped that he would not take it badly that these Letters were published in his absence, and that he would one day give us a supply of the opposing letters, I was moved by zeal for the public good and allowed the printer, to whom I had given them, to bring them out into the light.

units.la: Scio nec nostrorum nec alienorum Scriptorum editionem præcipitandam esse, sed tamen, nisi me fallit iudicium, nonnunquam è re est videre etiam in summorum Artificum Libris, τὰς ποιήσεις[?] & progressiones in rerum maximarum intelligentia & explicatione. Prima enim aetatis ὠφελία[?] καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters], senilis prudentia & sapientia & eloquentia ubertatem & perfectionem mirificè commendat.
units.tr: I know that neither our own writings nor those of others should be published in haste; yet, unless my judgement deceives me, it is sometimes worthwhile to see, even in the books of the greatest craftsmen, the progress and development in the understanding and explanation of the greatest matters. For the early usefulness of youth and the mature prudence, wisdom and fullness and perfection of eloquence of old age commend one another wonderfully.

units.la: Est etiam humanitatis ea Scripta, quæ mediocrium ingeniorum viribus servire possant, eo nomine nō supprimere, quòd Dei dono ea sapientia & intelligentia ubertas et sublimitas alicui data sit, ut summis ingeniis satisfacere, immò etiam admirationi esse, captumq; inferiorum superare liceat. Dominus IESVS det ut ista omnia ipsius gloriæ serviant, Amen. Basi-
units.tr: Nor should writings of a humane kind, which can serve the powers of people of middling talent, be suppressed on the ground that a particular wisdom, understanding and sublimity has been given by the gift of God to someone else, so that it is permitted to satisfy the greatest minds and even to be a source of wonder, and to surpass the grasp of inferiors. May the Lord Jesus grant that all these things serve his glory. Amen. Basel, 1 April 1580.

units.la: leae Cal. Aprilis, M. D. LXXX.
units.tr: Basel, Calends of April, 1580.

units.la: THOMAS ERASTVS MEDICVS Pio & candido lectori, S. D.
units.tr: THOMAS ERASTUS, PHYSICIAN, to the pious and candid reader, greetings.

units.la: CUm me Principes Illustrissimi Hennenbergen-ses ex Italia Schlusingam vocassent, atq; apud eos Medicinam exercere incepissem, valde praeter opinionem accidit mihi, quod, sive pharmacum exhibere, sive venam secare, sive aliud agris remedium afferre tentarem, in quo signo Zodiaci Luna tunc esset, & quem positum ad alios Planetas haberet, plerq; percunctarentur. Etsi enim non nescirem Germanos pro Italis vanitati Astrologicae tribuere, tamen quia Italicis medicationibus assueveram, insolens mihi ea superstitio videbatur. Ante profectionem in Italiam saepe Ephemerides seu Calendaria videram, in quibus notati essent dies fausti & infausti ad stercorandum agros, ad ablactandum infantes, ad praecidendum ungues & capillos, ad scarificandum cucurbitulis, ad secandum venam, ad exhibendum vel potum purgatorium vel Electuarium, vel catapotia. Et quanquam scarificationes & venae sectiones iuxta Ephemeridum notas instituì scirem: non tamen ita superstitiose observari cum hac tum alia huius farina sciebam, ut Medico praescribenti non libenter parerent, tametsi non omni ex parte cum Ephemeridum notis consentiret. Caeterum cum ex tabella in iisdem Ephemeridibus descripta cernerem, multos etiam dies faustos vel infaustos eligere ad faciendum iter, ad induendum vestes novas, ad migrandum in alias aedes, ad mercandum, ad negociandum cum viris principibus, ad venandum, & denique ad quosdam auspicatò inchoandum dies certos ut faustos eligere, alios ut infaustos abijcere: non potui non imperitiam vulgi admirari, & infelicitatem miserari. Quis non graviter ferat, homines Christianos contra pietatem & manifestum Dei praeceptum, dies hoc modo observare? Dico hoc modo, ut illas temporum, electiones discernam à superstitiosa Astrologorum electione, quas rectè Agricolæ, Nautæ, Medici, & alij quidã observãt. Sanè Agricolæ certa tempora serendi, metendi, ligna cædendi, uites & arbores putandi, & reliqua opera rustica faciendi eligunt : non quia cælum aut huius signa felicitatem aut infelicitatem operi promittant, sed quia ab aeris tempe- rie res ita mutatæ sunt, ut eo ipso tempore uel facienda, uel omittenda sint, quæ faciunt omittuntq. Alia namq; hyeme, alia æstate, & alia aliis temporibus commodius fiunt. Sic Me- dici & Nautæ tempora obseruant, ac dies eligunt: non quia occultam certos dies habere maliciam bonitatemue possidere opinentur. Huc accedit , quòd persæpe contingit, occasionem rei alicuius bene gerenda, propter expectationem felicis diei, e- labi. Quod quàm frequenter & facilè Medicis accidat, nemo ignorat. Equidem timidè aliquando id egi, quod ratio facere iuberet, quod nonnunquam culpâ eorum, quæ uiolentia morbi secus euenissent quàm sperabatur, in pharmacum intempestiuè exhibitum relatam audiuissem. Et cum ex sententia cuncta accidissent, non defuère tamen ali quando, qui periculosam cu- randi rationem opinarentur, quotiens non inspecto Calenda- rio aliquid circa agrum Medici tentarent. Hinc factum vidi, ut aeger quidam ualde periclitaretur, quòd non ausus fuisset Medicus sanguinem mittere, propterea quòd Luna fuisset in Scorpione. Ego certè uocatus & sanguinem misi, & uanas esse eas obseruationes re & opere docens, persuadere tamen non po- tui, uanas esse. Quanquam vero adulari vetulis imperitisq; hominibus nunquam uolui, sæpe tamen ab initio quadam, ubi certò scirem ægro nihil inde mali accersitum iri, dissimulare ac inueteratæ superstitioni tribuere, seu potius concedere coactus sum. Postea maiore audacia deliria ista reprehendere, ac nulla in re cedere cœpi, valde absurdum pariter & iniquum uidebatur, ut artem quam per tot annos in Italia à præ- stantissimis, prudentissimis, & experientissimis uiris, curatio- nes eorum obseruando, & eosdem quantum ingenio & diligen- tia consequi potuissem, non sine optimo successu (Dei Opt.Max. ea laus esto.) imitando, magno labore ac studio didiceram, ad præscriptum Astrologorum & delirantium anuum aduer- sus rationem, certamq; experientiam exercere temperareq; iuherer. Hanc ob causam Hieronymi Savonarolæ viri sanctissimi & eruditissimi libellum, Italico sermone conscriptum, quem penes me habebam, in Germanicam linguam conuerti, atq; ad vulgi captum pro viribus attemperavi, quo vel aliquos ab ista vana superstitione retraherem. Hunc docti quidem valde approbarunt. Non pauciores, sed impense rudes & inerudi[?]ti, partim voce partim vero literis, nec non praefationibus in suas Ephemerides vel prognostica scriptis, eundem condemnarunt, & me una cum eo diris devouerunt. Conuicia & criminationes illorum, qui rationes sua opinionis nullas adferrent, ut canū latratus facile tunc contempsi, & nunc etiam contemno. Nolim enim, si qua maxime possim, hic victor evadere. Vinci hic prorsus malo, dum impietatem illi suam hoc pacto magis patefaciunt. Alij quidam argumentis ostendere conati, baud[?] recte me fecisse, qui Astrologiam oppugnare in animum induxissem, responsione digni visi sunt. Atq; hac occasione Epistolas in praeti[?] volumine comprehensas conscripsi, & praeter has alias complures, in quibus tamen eadem prope tractantur.
units.tr: When the most illustrious princes of Henneberg had called me from Italy to Schleusingen, and I had begun to practise medicine there, it happened quite unexpectedly to me that, whether I tried to give a medicine, or to open a vein, or to bring some other remedy to the sick, many people asked what sign of the zodiac the Moon was then in and what position it held relative to the other planets. For although I was not unaware that the Germans ascribe more to astrological vanity than the Italians do, nevertheless, since I had grown accustomed to Italian methods of treatment, that superstition seemed strange to me. Before my departure for Italy I had often seen almanacs or calendars in which were marked the days favourable and unfavourable for manuring the fields, for weaning infants, for cutting nails and hair, for scarifying with cupping-glasses, for opening a vein, and for giving a purgative drink, an electuary, or pills. And although I knew that scarifications and bloodlettings were performed according to the notes of the almanacs, I also knew that people of this sort and others like them did not observe these things so superstitiously that they would gladly obey a physician who prescribed otherwise, even though it did not wholly agree with the notes of the almanacs. Moreover, when I saw from the table described in the same almanacs that many days were chosen as fortunate or unfortunate for setting out on a journey, for putting on new clothes, for moving into other houses, for trading, for doing business with men of rank, for hunting, and finally for beginning certain undertakings under good auspices, choosing some days as lucky and rejecting others as unlucky, I could not but marvel at the ignorance of the common people and pity their unhappiness. Who would not bear it with grief that Christian men should observe days in this way, contrary to piety and the plain command of God? I say "in this way," so that I may distinguish those choices of times from the superstitious choice of the astrologers, which farmers, sailors, physicians and certain others rightly observe. Indeed farmers choose fixed times for sowing, reaping, cutting wood, pruning vines and trees, and doing the other rural tasks, not because the heavens or their signs promise good or bad fortune to the work, but because things are so altered by the temperature of the air that at that very time they should be done or left undone, which they do or leave undone. For some things are done more conveniently in winter, some in summer, and some at other seasons. So too physicians and sailors observe times and choose days, not because they think that certain days possess a hidden malice or goodness. To this is added that it very often happens that the opportunity of doing something well slips away on account of waiting for a fortunate day, and how often and how easily this happens to physicians no one is ignorant. Indeed I once acted timidly, doing what reason bade me do, and I heard that a remedy given at the wrong time had, through the fault of this, turned out otherwise than hoped, since the violence of the disease was such. And although everything had turned out as I wished, there were nevertheless times when some people thought the method of cure dangerous, whenever physicians attempted something with the sick without consulting the calendar. Hence I saw a certain sick man in very great danger because the physician had not dared to draw blood, on account of the Moon being in Scorpio. I, however, was called and drew blood, and by fact and deed showing that these observations were empty, I could not persuade them that they were empty. Yet although I never wished to flatter old women and unlearned men, I was often compelled, at the beginning, to dissemble in some matter, when I knew for certain that no harm would come to the patient from it, and to yield to an ingrained superstition, or rather to concede it. Afterwards I began to rebuke these delusions with greater boldness and to give way in nothing, since it seemed equally absurd and unjust that I should be ordered to practise, in accordance with the prescriptions of astrologers and of doting old women, and against reason and certain experience, an art which I had learned through many years in Italy, with great labour and zeal, from the most distinguished, most prudent and most experienced men, by observing their cures and imitating them as far as my talent and diligence could attain, not without the best success (to God, best and greatest, be that praise). For this reason I translated into German, adapting it as far as I could to the understanding of the common people, the little book of Girolamo Savonarola, a most holy and learned man, written in Italian, which I had in my possession, so that I might draw some people back from this vain superstition. Learned men indeed greatly approved of it. Not fewer, but very rude and unlearned men, partly by voice and partly in writing, and also in prefaces written to their almanacs or prognostications, condemned it, and together with it they cursed me with dreadful curses. The insults and accusations of those who offered no reasons for their opinion I then easily despised, like the barking of dogs, and I despise them still. For I would not, if I could possibly help it, emerge victorious here. I would much rather be utterly defeated here, since by this means they reveal their impiety all the more. Certain others, who tried to show by arguments that I had not acted rightly in resolving to attack astrology, seemed worthy of an answer. And on this occasion I wrote the letters contained in the present volume, and besides these several others, in which, however, almost the same matters are treated.

units.la: Editionis siue publicationis occasio haec est. Cum Christophorus Stathmion Medicus, me adscribendum provocauisset, atq; ego me ad eum unum scribere putarem, exempla ternarum apud me literarum nulla retinui. Nihil tunc minus cogitabam, quàm in publicum tales dare. Post aliquod tempus, ubi cum ex aliis, tum ex ipsomet Stathmione cognouissem, ipsum eas ad doctissimos viros Vvitebergam transmisisse, & tantum non publicasse, non immerito dolui. Non enim ea perscripta accuratione fuerant, qua elaborari decet, qua in conspectum doctorum hominum sunt uentura. Multa quoq; in ijsdem erant ad rem, de qua disputabatur inter nos, nihil attinentia, utpote qua ad nos duos solos pertinerent, quaq; alios scire minime utile erat. Attamen cum primum opera amicorum exempla superiorum literarum recepissem, ne parum iudicaret me causa confidere, dixi, me eas editurum esse, ut non aliqui solum, sed plurimi legere possent. Presi[?] autem hucusq; , quia grauioribus negocijs non occupatus modo, sed propemodum obrutus relegere, & quae ad rem & quaestionem nihil facerent, sed de aliis rebus scripta essent, resecare non potui. Ergo superiore hyeme, cum discie-
units.tr: The occasion of this edition or publication is as follows. When Christophorus Stathmion, a physician, had challenged me to a written dispute, and I thought I was writing only to him, I kept no copies of the three letters by me. I then had least thought of giving such things to the public. After some time, when I had learned from others, and from Stathmion himself, that he had sent them to the most learned men at Wittenberg and had almost published them, I grieved not without cause. For they had not been written with the care that ought to be taken over what is to come before the eyes of learned men. Moreover, there were many things in them not bearing on the matter we were disputing, being of concern only to the two of us, and it was in no way useful for others to know them. Nevertheless, as soon as I had received copies of the earlier letters through the efforts of friends, lest he should judge that I trusted my cause too little, I said that I would publish them, so that not just a few but very many might read them. But until now, because I was not only occupied with weightier business but almost overwhelmed by it, I could not reread them and cut out what did not bear on the subject and question, but had been written about other things. Therefore in the last winter, when I was about to...

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: Si propter pestem à schola & urbe exularemus, nec aliud facere eo tempore propter librorum absentiam, & loci extremam angustiam incommoditatem q; possem, prædictas epistolas recognovi, & inutilibus amputatis ea tantum suo manere loco suique ad rem controversam aliquo modo pertinere iudicavi. His alias etiam quasdam ad alios de re fermè eadem conscriptas addidi, illas videlicet, quæ aliquid operæpretij, hoc est, utilis alicuius rei quæstionisue decisionem vel explicationem continebant. Et horum quidem nomina non expressi ferè, propterea quòd parum constaret, an nominari hic vellent. Qui volent, aut seipsos nominabunt, aut alio loco & tempore à me, si Deo nõ secus visum est, nominari poterunt. Intellexi etiam non multo post, unum ex his quorum in his literis mentio fit, abreptum peste fuisse. Quocirca mox nomen expunxi, ne mortuos insectari velle viderer. Ac de Stathmione quidem alios malo iudicare. De cæteris quorum hic litera confutantur, non vereor affirmare doctrina eos & ingenio omnino plurimis antecellere. Etsi enim hanc causam frigidè egerunt, nihil tamen ex hoc laudi & existimationi eorum detrahitur. Quis enim quantalibet doctrina præditus, malam, imò pessimam causam docte & solide defendat? Quanquā iudico aliquos ex his, non tā oppugnare sententiam meam, quàm exercere me voluisse. Editionem verò literarum mearum ad ipsos, ideo non agrè ferent. Spero, quod veritatis studiosi hinc discere poterunt, quantum in utraq; causa insit roboris & certitudinis. De hisce lectorem admonendum putavi, ne factum meum aliquis sinistrè interpretetur. Vale.
units.tr: If, because of the plague, we had been driven out of the school and the city, and at that time could do nothing else because of the absence of books and the extreme narrowness and inconvenience of the place, I went over the aforementioned letters again, cut out what was superfluous, and judged that only those that belonged to their place and in some way pertained to the matter in dispute should remain. To these I have added certain others written to other people on nearly the same subject, namely those which contained something worthwhile, that is, something that helped to decide or explain a useful point or question. I have for the most part not named these people, because it was not clear whether they wished to be named here. Those who wish it will either name themselves, or, if it seems good to God, they may be named by me at another place and time. I also learned not long after that one of those mentioned in these letters had been carried off by the plague. For this reason I struck out the name at once, lest I seem to want to attack the dead. As for Stathmio, I prefer to leave the judgment to others. As for the rest, whose arguments are refuted in these letters, I do not hesitate to affirm that they far surpass most men in learning and talent. For although they have handled this cause feebly, nothing is taken from their praise and reputation on that account. For who, however well endowed with learning, could defend a bad, indeed the worst, cause learnedly and soundly? Yet I think some of them wanted to exercise me rather than really to oppose my opinion. They will not be displeased that my letters to them have been published. I hope that lovers of truth will be able to learn from this how much strength and certainty there is in either side of the cause. I thought the reader should be warned of this, so that no one may interpret my action unfavourably. Farewell.

units.la: Heidelbergæ, Calend. Nouemb. Anno 1564
units.tr: Heidelberg, 1 November, in the year 1564.

units.la: THOMAS ERASTUS D. CHRISTOPHORO Stathmioni, Medico Coburgensi S. D. Epistola I.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus to Christophorus Stathmion, physician of Coburg, greetings. Letter I.

units.la: LITERAS tuas, vir clarissime, quas prid. Calend. Augusti scripsisti, postridie accepi. Ais te gaudere, te occasionem nactum fuisse mecum conuersandi propter communia studia. Puto te id voluisse, gaudere te opportunitate tibi datam esse, mecum conferendi de rebus Astrologicis. Non enim unquam, dum istic essem, ad nos venire, tametsi vocatus fuisses, voluisti. In sententia me confirmat, quod mox addis, te intellexisse, me Astrologicae consideratione infestum esse. Quod me praeter rationem diuinatricem Astrologiam ridere putas, in eo non leuiter falleris. Ratio qua te commoueri ostendis, quia scilicet philosophus sim atque medicus, euanida est. Hoc enim docuerit potius, me si fidem Astrologiae habeam, neque philosophum neque medicum esse. Ego, mi Strathmion, hactenus cum in philosophia tum medicina mediocriter sum versatus, nec intelligere videreque aliud potui, quam vestra illa deliramenta & rationi & philosophiae principiis aduersari.
units.tr: Your letter, most distinguished sir, which you wrote on the day before the Kalends of August, I received the day after. You say you are glad to have had the chance of talking with me about our common studies. I think you wanted this: you are glad the opportunity has been given you to confer with me about astrological matters. For while I was there you never wanted to come to us, though you had been invited. What confirms me in this view is what you add soon after, that you have understood I am hostile to astrology in my thinking. You think I scorn divinatory astrology beyond reason, and in this you are not slightly mistaken. The reason by which you say you were moved, namely that I am a philosopher and a physician, has come to nothing. For it would rather show that if I held any belief in astrology, I would be neither a philosopher nor a physician. I, my Stathmion, have so far been moderately engaged in both philosophy and medicine, and I could neither understand nor see anything other than that those delusions of yours are opposed both to reason and to the principles of philosophy.

units.la: Philosophi munus esse veritatem indagare & amplecti, recte à te dictum est. Si philosophus ego essem, (contentum me esse in praesenti oportet, quod esse fieriq; cupio.) maiore utique industria & conatu contra philosophiae hostes, Astrologos, pugnem, cum praesertim multorum per Germaniam animos infatuatos ab illis non sine dolore perspiciam. A Galeni & Hippocratis placitis ut discedam tantum abest, ut eos maxime leues existimem, qui vel non ob iustam, vel ob leuem causam viros tatos [?] reprehendere solent. Apud Hippocratem nihil reperi, quod Astrologiae patrocinetur. Galenus vix unquam meminit, praeterquam in 3. de diebus decretoriis libro. Quid eum permouerit illa ut scriberet, ipsemet in 10. cap. satis declarauit. Deos aduocar testes, se ea non nisi paucis quibusdam amicis cogentibus scripsisse. Quod causæ quam ibidem tractavit parum consideret, ex eo potest intelligi, quòd cum omnes propemodum commentarios suos amicorum. hortatu scripserit ac ediderit, tali nunquam excusatione usus fuit. Sed non jam quid Galenus senserit quæritur. Illud in controversiam potius venire arbitror, utrum Galenus perfici-ente concludenteque ratione propositum confecerit.
units.tr: You rightly said that the task of the philosopher is to investigate and embrace the truth. If I were a philosopher (I ought to be content for the present with what I wish to be and to become), I would surely fight with greater diligence and effort against the enemies of philosophy, the astrologers, especially since I see with no little grief the minds of many throughout Germany bewitched by them. So far am I from departing from the opinions of Galen and Hippocrates that I think those least to be trusted are the ones who usually censure such men, whether without just cause or for a slight one. In Hippocrates I found nothing that supports astrology. Galen scarcely ever mentions it, except in the third book On Critical Days. What moved him to write that, he himself explained sufficiently in chapter 10. He calls the gods to witness that he wrote those things only at the urging of a few friends. That he gave little thought to the matter he treated there can be understood from this: since he wrote and published almost all his commentaries at the urging of friends, he never used such an excuse. But it is not now what Galen thought that is being asked. I think the question that should come into dispute is whether Galen carried out his proposal by a perfect and conclusive argument.

units.la: Credo te non ignorare, Galenicum' illum mensem, cuius gratia Astrologiæ ibi commeminit, fictitium esse, nullaque vel parum probabili ratione niti. Adde quod à Doctioribus medicis omnibus antiquis & recentioribus cō-temtus ac neglectus est. Astrologorum nostræ ætatis decretis minimè consentaneus existit. Neque facile eum approbaverint. Si otium mihi sit maius, non admodum difficile mihi fuerit ostendere, quæ Galenus in 3. decret. dierum de vi & efficientia siderum affert, vera & concessa philosophis esse, modò non perperam intelligantur. Nam si, ut Astrologi opinantur, interpretari aliquis velit, falsa pleraque sunt, & à philosophia maximè dissentanea. Quare non miraberis, si à Galeni sensu recedam in crassa illa philosophia, quam in suis scriptis aliis nec docuit nec probavit unquam. Hoc loco (jam enim ita eum sensisse po-no)ad probandum diem 20.non verò 21.decretorium esse. omnia talia proposuit. Quid hac de re alibi, post hos libros scripserit, tibi non incognitum arbitror.
units.tr: I believe you are not unaware that the Galenic month, for whose sake he there mentions astrology, is fictitious and rests on no reasoning, or on hardly any that is probable. Add that it has been despised and neglected by all the more learned physicians, ancient and modern. It does not agree with the decrees of the astrologers of our own age, and they would not readily approve it. If I had more leisure, it would not be very difficult for me to show that what Galen brings forward in the third book On Critical Days about the power and efficacy of the stars is true and conceded by the philosophers, provided it is not misunderstood. For if, as the astrologers think, someone wishes to interpret it, most of it is false and far removed from philosophy. So you will not be surprised if I depart from Galen's view in that crude philosophy, which he never taught or approved in his other writings. In this place (for I now suppose he thought so) he put forward all such things to prove that the day is the twentieth critical day, not the twenty-first. What he wrote about this elsewhere, after these books, I think is not unknown to you.

units.la: Cum porrò Hippocratem etiam studiosum Astrologiæ divinatricis fuisse scribis, pergravem seni optimo injuriam facis. Nisi si per Astrologiæ nomen Astronomiam aut æris qualitates intelligis. Id si est ita, de nomine litigas. Quod antiqui non uno modò semper hoc nomen usurparint, jam olim didici. Ergo si non divinatricem intelligis, causa excidisti: & cū Astrologiam te defendere putas, eiuscemodi adfers, quæ ad rem propositam nihil faciunt. Ego mehercle jam pridem sciui, Hippocrate & Galenū (alios raceo) aëris mutationes in prænoscendis, iudicandis & curandis morbis optima ratione observasse, nobisque observandas proposuisse. Novi illud etiam, Hippocratem anni temtempora per certorum siderum ortum & occasum inter-stinguere solitum fuisse. At hæc nihil Astrologiam iuvant, quod tute ipse nosti.
units.tr: Since you write that Hippocrates too was a devotee of divinatory astrology, you do a very grave injury to that excellent old man. Unless perhaps by the name astrology you mean astronomy or the qualities of the air. If that is so, you are quarrelling about a name. That the ancients did not always use this name in one sense I learned long ago. So if you do not mean divinatory astrology, you have fallen from your own cause; and while you think you are defending astrology, you bring forward things that have nothing to do with the matter at hand. By heaven, I have long known that Hippocrates and Galen (I say nothing of others) observed changes in the air, with the best reasoning, in foreknowing, judging and treating diseases, and proposed that we should observe them as well. I know too that Hippocrates was accustomed to mark the seasons of the year by the rising and setting of certain stars. But these things do not help astrology at all, as you yourself know.

units.la: Quæ ex Galeno verba adfers, ea sunt clarissimis quibus-que philosophis & astronomis concessa, vt rectè Galenus monuit. Si ita interpretari voles, vt philosophi ea intellexerint, perlibenter vera esse dabo. Quinetiam aliter non posse rem habere, si sit opus, probabo. At inde sequi, vt tu putas, Astrologiam certam esse, aut futura contingentia ex cælo præsagiri posse, id est quod pernego, falsumque esse contendo. Hoc si tu probaveris, facies quod Astrologiæ patronum decet.
units.tr: The words you bring from Galen are those conceded to the most distinguished philosophers and astronomers, as Galen rightly warned. If you wish to interpret them as the philosophers understood them, I will gladly grant that they are true, and if need be I will prove that the matter cannot be otherwise. But that it follows from this, as you think, that astrology is certain, or that future contingent events can be foretold from the heavens, that I flatly deny and maintain to be false. If you prove this, you will do what befits a patron of astrology.

units.la: Quod postremo loco Nautas & Agricolas de quibusdã rebus ex astris iudicare scribis, nihilo magis ad rem pertinet quàm superiora. Non enim ex siderum conversionibus, motibus & aspectibus vocatis tempestates futuras præsagiunt, sed ex aëris affectionibus præsentiunt, de quibus proprium habes apud Ptolemæum caput. Hæc si tu ad Astrologiam tuam refers, rursus de nominibus litigas. Talia namque ita fere indicant aëris mutationes, sicut vrinæ & alia excrementa facultatum naturalium actiones medicis ostendunt.
units.tr: As to your last point, that sailors and farmers judge certain things from the stars, this bears no more on the matter than what came before. For they do not foretell coming storms from the conjunctions, motions and aspects of the stars, as they are called; they perceive them from the condition of the air, about which you have a chapter of your own in Ptolemy. If you refer these things to your astrology, you are again quarrelling about names. For such signs indicate changes in the air in much the same way as urine and other excretions show physicians the actions of the natural faculties.

units.la: Quoties Astrologiam falsam esse aio, eam intelligo, quæ ex mutuis siderum aspectibus, conversionibus, retrocessionibus, exhalationibus, mansionibus & similibus futurorum præsensionem pollicetur. Hinc si vel Nautas vel Agricolas diuinare probaveris, aliquid certè dixisse videberis. Quod enim lunam interdum retusis cornibus, obscuram, rutilam, pallidam aliterue affectam videre videntur, ex quo aut ventos aut pluvias secuturas coniiciunt: hoc tu nō ad stellarum mutuos intuitus, sed ad meteora referre debes. Etenim à vaporibus sive exhalationibus in aëre talia perficiuntur. Habes ad omnia, quæ de Astrologia scripsisti, responsum certum minimeque ambiguum, tale scilicet, quale in maximis occupationibus scribere licuit.
units.tr: Whenever I say astrology is false, I mean that which promises foreknowledge of future things from the mutual aspects, conjunctions, retrogradations, exhalations, mansions of the stars and the like. So if you were to prove that sailors or farmers divine, you would seem at least to have said something. As for the moon sometimes appearing with its horns blunted, dark, reddish, pale or otherwise affected, from which they conjecture that winds or rains will follow, this you ought to refer not to the mutual gazes of the stars but to meteors. For such things are brought about in the air by vapours or exhalations. You have, for everything you wrote about astrology, a certain and by no means ambiguous answer, such as could be written amid the greatest occupations.

units.la: Cæterum non præter rem fuerit; omnia summatim repetere, vt quid ego negè clarius perspicias . Sic ergo scribis. Quamuis audieris me Astrologiæ infestum esse, credere tamen non potuisse, cum scias hominem Philosophum & Medicum damnare eam iure non posse. Me porrò inter hos (vtinam rectè) numeras. Ex quo confectum tibi censes, rectè fuisse te, qui persuaderi tibi hoc de me ante non fueris passus, quàm ex illis cognoueris, qui mecum in arce fuerant pransi. Summa hæc est, Philosophi & Medici non contemnunt Astrologiam. Ad hoc respondeo, Platonem, Aristotelem, Alexandrū, Auerroë, Hippocratem, Galenum, Auicennam, summos Philosophos & Medicos extitisse, & Astrologiam tamen vel despexisse vel improbasse. Certè pro ementitis fabulis plerique philosophorum habuerunt, quæ tanti æstimant Astrologi. De Medicis satis multa diximus.
units.tr: Moreover, it will not be beside the point to go over everything briefly, so that you may see more clearly what I deny. So you write thus: although you had heard that I am hostile to astrology, you could not believe it, since you know that a man who is a philosopher and a physician cannot rightly condemn it. Indeed you count me among these (would that I were rightly so). From this you conclude that you were right not to let yourself be persuaded of this about me until you had learned it from those who had dined with me in the citadel. The sum of it is: philosophers and physicians do not scorn astrology. To this I reply that Plato, Aristotle, Alexander, Averroes, Hippocrates, Galen and Avicenna, the greatest philosophers and physicians, existed, and yet they either despised or disapproved of astrology. Certainly most philosophers regarded as made-up fables the things that the astrologers esteem so highly. Concerning physicians, we have said enough.

units.la: Reliquum epistolæ tuæ ferè in eo probando consumitur, quod Hippocrates & Galenus in morborum curationibus Astrologiæ præcepta secuti sint, hoc est, quod more Astrologorum siderum oppositiones, coniunctiones, varios, multiplicesque rerum aspectus obseruarint. At falso te hoc illis attribuere iam dictum est. Quaquam enim Galenus causam adferre tentauit, cur 20.diem, non verò 21. Hippocrates decretorium statuerit, Medicis tamen eam obseruationem non iudicauit sequendam aut cognitu necessariam, quod partim ex 10. cap. partim ex peroratione, qua in hac materia visus est, apparet. Sed hæc res longiorē postulat orationem, si pro dignitate explicari debeat, apud eos præsertim, quibus nihil satis est.
units.tr: The rest of your letter is spent almost entirely in proving that Hippocrates and Galen followed the precepts of astrology in curing diseases, that is, that in the manner of the astrologers they observed oppositions and conjunctions of the stars and their various and manifold aspects. But it has already been said that you falsely attribute this to them. For although Galen tried to give a reason why Hippocrates set the twentieth day, not the twenty-first, as critical, nevertheless he did not judge that this observation ought to be followed by physicians or was necessary for them to know. This appears partly from chapter 10 and partly from the peroration with which he seemed to close this discussion. But this matter requires a longer discourse if it is to be explained as its importance deserves, especially before those for whom nothing is enough.

units.la: Hortaris me ad extremum, vt Hippocratem potius & Galenum quàm Manardum & Picum imitari velim, Manardum præstantem Medicum pariter & philosophum fuisse negare non audebis. Picum plurimis isdemque clarissimis philosophis plurimum antecelluisse cuncti intelligunt, qui scripta ipsius cum iudicio perlegerunt. Hi ab Hippocratis & Galeni sententia nunquam dissidere erunt, nisi quòd Astrologica Galeni, quæ in vnico illo 3.de diebus de-[illegible, ~8 letters] propter commemoratam causam scripsit, prore non potuerunt. Quod si Astrologum fuisse Galenum constaret, ac praeceptis Astrologicis omnes ipsius libri referti essent, & denique ipse decreta Astrologorum in curado obseruasse sciretur, haec inquam si omnia certa forent: & extaret aliquis qui non bene Galeni talia scripsisse certis argumentis demonstraret: an tu Galenum falsa docen-tē sequi malles, quam alium quemuis veritatem profitē-tem? Apud me certē nullius hominis authoritas est tanta, ut non maior sit veritatis. Ergo cum & Picum & alios cō-plures hoc effecisse constet, cur hac in re Galenum potius audiam, quam illos? Picum facile est reprehendere, ut alios omnes doctos. At confutare eius sententiam & argumenta dissoluere, hoc vero est difficillimum, imo impossibile. Qui hucusque tentarunt, ita tentarunt, ut ne ipsi quidem Astrologi probare possint. Tu quidem hic errasse eos affirmas, quod etiam antea in libello tuo fecisti, sed nihil pro-bas. Sine ratione quodlibet damnare quilibet quantum-uis rudis potest. Accipio nihilominus tuam adhorrationē[?] in bonam partem, atque animum, non rem ad quam me hortaris, specto.
units.tr: You urge me, in conclusion, that I should prefer to imitate Hippocrates and Galen rather than Manardus and Pico. You will not dare to deny that Manardus was an outstanding physician and likewise a philosopher. Everyone who has read Pico's writings with judgement understands that he far surpassed very many, and very distinguished, philosophers. These men would never have dissented from the opinion of Hippocrates and Galen, except that they could not approve of Galen's astrological writings, which he composed in that one book On Days, and which he wrote for the reason mentioned. But suppose it were established that Galen was an astrologer, that all his books were full of astrological precepts, and that he was known to have followed the astrologers' rules in treating the sick; suppose these things were all certain, and someone appeared who demonstrated by sure arguments that Galen had not written such things rightly. Would you rather follow Galen, teaching falsehood, than any other man professing the truth? For my part, certainly, no man's authority is so great that it outweighs the truth. Since it is established that Pico and very many others have done this, why should I listen to Galen rather than to them in this matter? It is easy to find fault with Pico, as with all the learned men. But to refute his opinion and dissolve his arguments is very difficult, indeed impossible. Those who have attempted it so far have attempted it in such a way that not even the astrologers themselves could approve. You indeed affirm that they erred here, as you also did before in your little book, but you prove nothing. Anyone, however rude, can condemn something without reason. Nevertheless I take your exhortation in good part, and I look to your intention, not to the matter to which you urge me.

units.la: Proinde ut ne ingratum me putes, te vicissim hortor ac oro, ut anilibus istis nugis relictis veritatem complectaris. Quod ut facere aptius possis, argumento unico falsitatem Astrologicae divinationis tibi declarabo. Utar autem argumento tali, quod nemo Christianus (iam enim philosophiam sepono) falsum aut elumbe iudicabit. Nulla quan-tumuis pura spiritualis & intelligens creatura futura contingentia novit, nisi si Deus peculiari inspiratione illis manifestarit, sed solus Deus hanc notitiam obtinuit. Atqui ita solus novit quid futurum sit Deus, (loquor semper de contingentibus) ut suam hanc esse gloriam velit: ut sibi soli tribuat: ut hoc argumento probet se unum Deum esse, praeterse Deum non esse. Dæmones hoc argumento Deos non esse efficaciter probat per prophetam[?] Esaiam, quia futura ignorent. Porrò Astrologos non Deos, sed mortales homines esse non negabis opinor. Quinetiam non ex inspiratione divina, sed ex arte futura praesentire posse videri volunt. Hinc necessariò duo sequuntur. Horum primum est, Astrologos non posse arte industriaue[?] vlla futura praecognoscere. Alterum est, ipsos illud sibi arrogare, quod sibi soli seruare Deus voluit. Hoc si non est cum Deo pugnare, quid Deum oppugnare sit nescio. Astra de coelo detrahere nos velle clamant Astrologi, quoties veritati contra figmenta ipsorum suffragamur. Multò sanè rectius de se ipsis hoc praedicauerint. Equidem Deus suum se honorem nolle alij tradere dixit. Quare cum scientia futurorum ad Deum pertineat, diligenter cauendū nobis erit, ne nobis hunc adscribamus honorem, & non astris duntaxat iniuriam faciamus, sed Deum quoque ipsum spoliare velle iudicemur.
units.tr: Therefore, so that you may not think me ungrateful, I in turn urge and beg you to leave aside those old wives' trifles and embrace the truth. So that you may be better able to do this, I will show you the falsity of astrological divination by a single argument. I will use an argument such that no Christian (I set philosophy aside) will judge it false or weak. No spiritual and intelligent creature, however pure, knows future contingent things, unless God has revealed them to it by a special inspiration; God alone has this knowledge. Now God alone knows what is to come (I am always speaking of contingent things), and he wishes this to be his glory: he wishes it to belong to him alone, and by this argument he proves that he is the one God and that there is no other God. By this argument, through the prophet Isaiah, God effectively proves that the demons are not gods, because they do not know the future. Moreover, I think you will not deny that astrologers are not gods but mortal men. Indeed, they want it to seem that they can foresee the future not by divine inspiration but by art. From this two things necessarily follow. The first is that astrologers cannot foreknow any future thing by art or industry. The second is that they claim for themselves what God wished to keep for himself alone. If this is not to fight against God, I do not know what it is to attack God. The astrologers cry out that we want to snatch the stars from heaven whenever we support the truth against their fictions. They would far more rightly say this about themselves. Indeed God said that he did not wish to give his honour to another. Therefore, since knowledge of the future belongs to God, we must take careful heed lest we assign this honour to ourselves, and we shall be judged not merely to do an injustice to the stars, but also to wish to despoil God himself.

units.la: Hæc ad tuas literas respondere volui, quas ob eam causam te scripsisse satis apparet, vt quid hac de re sentiam intelligeres. Quæ præterea hic de Medicis prædictionibus disputari solent, explicari hoc in loco non possunt. Neque est necesse apud te, quem nō ignorare arbitror, quantum inter Medicas & Astrologicas prædictiones sit discrimen.
units.tr: I have wished to answer your letter in this way; it is sufficiently clear that you wrote it for this reason, that you might understand what I think about this matter. As for what is commonly debated here about medical prognostications, these cannot be explained in this place. Nor is it necessary with you, whom I think is not ignorant of how great the difference is between medical and astrological prognostications.

units.la: Dabitur fortasse ocium ista copiose & cum methodo tractandi, id quod facere statui, propterea quod multos non satis perspicere video, quantum inter ipsas intersit. Vale. Masfeldiæ, 4. Nonas Augusti.
units.tr: Perhaps that subject will be given leisure to be treated fully and in an orderly method, which I have resolved to do, because I see that many do not sufficiently perceive how great the difference between them is. Farewell. Maasfeld, 4 Nones of August.

units.la: THOMAS ERASTVS D. CHRISTOPHORO Stathmioni Medico Coburgensi, S. D. Epistola II.
units.tr: THOMAS ERASTUS to Christopher Stathmio, physician of Coburg, greeting. Letter II.

units.la: Magna attentione tuas literas perlegi, quas 23. Augusti scripsisti, quod mihi persuasissem, te aliquid solidi scripturum fuisse. Verum pro argumentis, quibus Astrologica vanitas propugnari posse videretur, aceruum conuiciorum legi. Vocas me ἀμέθοδον, indoctum, amentem, & nescio quid non mihi tribuis. Praeterea λόγον τε ἀ λαλίαν [?] in mea narra-tione e requirere ais. Acerbè reprehendis, quod citra di-stinctionem praenotiones ex astris falsas, inanes, futiles dixe-rim. At parum bene, vt ne quid tuo iudicio dicam acerbi-us, hic me accusas. Etenim pro causa propositâ aptè satis omnia distinxi. Non puto te nescire, aliam esse rationem scribendi, cum alicui respondemus, & intentata crimina depellimus: aliam cum ipsi aliquid tractare instituimus. Nihil mihi probandum tractandumq; hactenus praecipuè sumsi, sed ad tuas tibi literas respondere tantum volui. Ad extremum, quia me adhortatus fueras ad complectendas nugas Astrologicas, admonendus mihi visus es, quanto cum periculo id esset coniunctum, quamq; pugnaret cum pietate Astrologica professio. Animum, non rem quam mihi laudabas, spectaui. Ideo officium officio compensa-re volui. Quam ergo Methodum hic aliam desiderabas? Species, ais, diuinationum non distinxisti. Cur hoc à me postules non video. Nam in tuis literis, quibus respondendum mihi erat, solius Astrologicae mentio facta fuit. Cuius cum esse partem credere videreris eam, qua Nautae atque Agricolae futuras praesentiunt aeris mutationes, quod inter eas discrimen esset, obiter solum indicaui.
units.tr: I read your letter, which you wrote on 23 August, with great attention, because I had persuaded myself that you would write something solid. But instead of arguments by which astrological vanity might seem to be defended, I found a heap of insults. You call me ἀμέθοδος [unmethodical], unlearned, mad, and you attribute to me I know not what else. You also say that my account lacks [λόγον τε ἀλαλίαν] reasoned discourse and is mere idle chatter. You bitterly rebuke me for calling astrological predictions false, empty and worthless without a distinction. Yet in this you blame me without good reason, since I made all the necessary distinctions suitably for the matter proposed. I do not think you are unaware that one way of writing is needed when we answer someone and refute charges brought against us, and another when we set out to treat a subject on our own. Up to now I have not undertaken to prove or treat anything in particular; I only wanted to answer your letter. Finally, since you had urged me to embrace astrological trifles, it seemed to me that I ought to warn you how great a danger that carries, and how far the profession of astrology conflicts with piety. I looked to your intention, not to the thing you praised to me; so I wished to repay a service with a service. What other method, then, did you want here? You say I did not distinguish the kinds of divination. I do not see why you demand this of me. In your letter, to which I had to reply, only astrology was mentioned. Since you seemed to believe that part of it was the one by which sailors and farmers foresee changes in the weather, I merely pointed out in passing what difference there is between them.

units.la: An non apertis verbis, de qua Astrologia intelligi vellè, exposui? Non de genere, sed de specie vnâ litem mihi mo-uisti. Ergo cum de sola diuinatrice Astrologia sermo no-bis esset, non de alia loquendum mihi duxi. Quinetiam si-dera vniuersali ratione terrena haec exornare, immutare, disponere,concedere me, licet obscurè, significaui . Tantum futura contingentia ex cœlo præcognosci posse negaui .Idem hoc iam repeto,ne iterum querare me indistinctè[?] sententiam meam tibi proposuisse. A ppello autem futura contingentia,quæ non magis fieri possunt,etiam quæ raro eueniunt, ac non euenire poterant . Horum ex astris præsensionem, quo modo Astrologi se præuidere dicitât, vanam & futilem esse,nullisq; vel naturæ vel rationis principijs niti dixi. Quare non est,vt naturalem esse hanc diuinationem me credere credas, quæ principijs naturalibus caret,ac falsis tantum nititur nugacium Chaldæorum Aegyptiorumq; opinionibus. Quod si non hoc modo in vnū quasi fasce collecta reperisti, colligere debebas, non tam acerbè reprehendere .
units.tr: Did I not state in plain words which astrology I wished to be understood? You have raised a dispute not about the genus but about a single species. So, since our discussion concerned only predictive astrology, I did not think I should speak of any other. Indeed, I did indicate, though obscurely, that I grant that the stars, by a general principle, adorn, alter and arrange these earthly things. I only denied that contingent future events can be foreknown from the heavens. I now repeat this, lest you complain again that I set out my opinion indistinctly. By contingent future events I mean those which cannot be more or less likely to happen, even those which happen rarely, or which might not have happened. I said that the foreknowledge of these from the stars, in the way the astrologers claim to foresee them, is empty and worthless, and rests on no principles either of nature or of reason. So you should not think I believe this divination to be natural, since it lacks natural principles and rests only on the false opinions of the trifling Chaldeans and Egyptians. If you have not found these points gathered together in this way as in one bundle, you ought to have gathered them yourself, rather than rebuke me so bitterly.

units.la: Cum nullius creaturæ,sed solius Dei esse dixi futura contingentia intelligere, debebas vtiq; ,me non admoncnte, hoc de talibus accipere,quorum causæ nondum agunt,vel agere non sciuntur . Caussas intelligo non remotas, vt Astrologi solent, sed definitas,proprias, & proximas .Etenim cum ita Deus per prophetam argumentatur, Dæmones in Idolis non sunt Dij,quoniam ignorant futura:nemo tam est iners,qui de talibus cum loqui intelligat,quæ iam fieri producíque incœperunt.Non enim nesciunt Dæmones,plumbum quod in ignem iectum est,nisi aut restinguatur ignis,aut rursum eximatur plumbum,mox esse dissoluendum . Norunt Medici, cum ex vrina alijsíue[?] excrementis,naturæ vires,actiones,opera perspiciunt, nihilque adesse quod eam impedire queat,intelligunt crisim certo quodam tempore futuram . Antea verò quàm à natura morbi materiam superari,(& quæ alia huc pertinent) cognouerint, de futura crisi percipere nihil possunt . Quis enim medicum doceat, quo modo morbus, qui nondum natus est, finiendus sit? Ex hisce haud difficulter intelligitur, Medicos non ante futurum aliquid præuidere, quàm esse iam incœperit, siue producià propinquis & proprijs caussis perspexerint . Hoc inter artificem & imperitum interest,quòd ille exilia principia videt,quæ huic nondum apparent. Itaq; cum artifex,quod iam esse fieriq; incoepit, at propter paruitatem cæteros adhuc latet,futurum præ-dicit,divinasse ipsis putatur.
units.tr: Since I said that only God, and no creature, understands future contingent events, you should, even without my reminding you, have taken this to refer to those whose causes are not yet acting, or are not known to be acting. I mean causes not remote, as the astrologers usually do, but defined, proper and proximate. Indeed, when God argues through the prophet that the demons in the idols are not gods because they do not know the future, no one is so dull as not to understand that this refers to things which have already begun to happen and to be produced. The demons do not fail to know that lead thrown into the fire will soon be melted, unless the fire is put out or the lead is taken out again. Physicians, when they perceive from the urine or other excretions the powers, actions and works of nature, and see that nothing is present that could hinder it, understand that a crisis will come at a certain time. But before they have recognised that the matter of the disease is being overcome by nature (and the other things that pertain to this), they can perceive nothing of the coming crisis. For who could teach a physician how a disease that is not yet born is to be ended?
