From this it is not hard to understand that physicians do not foresee anything in the future before it has begun to be, or before they have discerned it from its near and proper causes. The difference between the skilled and the unskilled is this: the former sees the slight beginnings which are not yet apparent to the latter. So when the skilled man predicts what has already begun to be and to happen, but which remains hidden from others because of its smallness, he is thought to have divined it.

units.la: Jam igitur argumentum, spero,intelliges. Futura con-tingentia solus Deus, non vlla creatura, nouit. Astrologi non Dij sunt,sed mortales homines. Quare futura contin-gentia ignorant. Addamus jam reliqua. Astrologicæ præ-dictiones versantur penè omnes circa futura contingen-tia. Ea igitur profitentur & pollicentur Astrologi,quæ præ-stare nulla creatura potest,nisi Deus peculiari modo pate-fecerit. Ubi nam à Methodo & à propositā nobis caussa aberrauí? Dicis alicubi ista perspicuè expositā esse vniuer-sa,vt non opus habeas τῷ θεολογίζειν[?] mecum.Ego verò cum nomen authoris taceas,non possum divinare(neque enim Astrologus sum)quid, quando, quomodo scripserit. Hoc tibi affirmem, ante hæc nostra tempora nullum probatæ eruditionis & vitæ Theologum extitisse, qui non vestras nugas, ea distinctione, quam nuper exposui adhibita,dam-narit ac repudiarit. Dixerim hoc amplius,nullum philoso-phum insignem fuisse,qui eadem probaret. Omnes enim aut neglexerunt, aut palàm lacerarunt. Ficinus principio aliquid huic vanitati tribuere visus est. Sed in epistolis ad Picum & Politianum omnino deridet. Quinetiam com-mentario quodam in Plotinum, philosophum Platonicum solidissimè vniuersam confutat: parum igitur rectè scripsi-sti, me pro mea sapientia præclarissimos Philosophos & Medicos,qui hæc studia coluerint,contenere. Ego, Strath-mion,si sapere est mendacijs Astrologorum non credere, plurimum hac in parte sapio. Etenim diuinationibus Astrologorum fidem nullam adhibeo, sed ut veritatis hostes vito. In cæteris rebus nemini me ipsum, non dicam prætulerim,sed temerè comparauerim.
units.tr: Now, I hope, you will understand my argument. Only God, and no creature, knows future contingent events. Astrologers are not gods but mortal men. Therefore they do not know future contingent events. Let us now add the rest. Almost all astrological predictions are concerned with future contingent events. So the astrologers profess and promise things which no creature can accomplish unless God has revealed them in a special way. Where, then, have I strayed from method and from the cause I proposed? You say somewhere that all these things have been set out so clearly that you have no need to discuss theology [τῷ θεολογίζειν] with me. But since you do not name the author, I cannot guess (for I am not an astrologer) what he wrote, when, or how. I will assert this to you: before our own times there has been no theologian of proven learning and life who did not condemn and reject your trifles, using the distinction I have just explained. I would add this further: no famous philosopher has approved of the same things. For they all either neglected them or openly tore them apart. Ficino at the start seemed to grant something to this vanity, but in his letters to Pico and Politian he mocks it entirely. Moreover, in a certain commentary on Plotinus he refutes the whole thing most solidly, as a Platonic philosopher. So you have written rather wrongly in saying that, by my own wisdom, I despise the most distinguished philosophers and physicians who cultivated these studies. Stathmio, if to be wise is not to believe the lies of the astrologers, then I am very wise in this respect. For I give no trust at all to the divinations of the astrologers, but avoid them as enemies of the truth. In other matters I would not place myself before anyone, let alone rashly compare myself to them.

units.la: Ad ea quæ de Pico scribis,nihil opus est respondere. Unū hoc scio,neminē veris argumentis confutaturum esse, quæ contra Astrologos scripsit.Ut enim quædam reprehedi possint,nō tamen hōn[?] pleraq; sunt vera. Ptolemæum insignem fuisse philosophum, neque tu neq; alius quisquam probabit, at Astronomum fuisse præstantissimum, facilè o-stenderis. Nolim hic mihi insultes, quasi Astronomiam à philosophia excludam. Ego namq; Ptolemæum naturalē philosophum fuisse alicuius nominis nego, Mathematicum extitisse summum libenter concedo. In huius libris Astrologicis (quos tu me sine delectu damnare putas) si quid inest veri & boni, id perexiguum est, atque ita fabulis & mendacijs conspurcatum, vt nō omnino auarus homo facilius ex stercore aurum colligat, quàm veram ex illis li-bris sententiam is excerpat, qui bonas horas non malè collocatas velit. Galenum me cum Pico nugatorem nomi-nasse scribis. Quam verè non attinet dicere. Quod si nugari eum hac in parte, in qua Astrologica tractat, dixerim non graviter, puto, peccauerim. Non sunt prorsus eadem, si aliquem nugas aliquot scripsisse dicam, & si absolutè nugatorem esse affirmem. Ego tamen ita me eum appellasse non recordor.
units.tr: As for what you write about Pico, there is no need to reply. I know this much: no one will refute with true arguments what he wrote against the astrologers. For although some things may be found fault with, most of them are true. That Ptolemy was a famous philosopher neither you nor anyone else will prove, but that he was an outstanding astronomer you will easily show. Do not wish me to insult you here, as if I were excluding astronomy from philosophy. For I deny that Ptolemy was a philosopher of any note as a natural philosopher, but I gladly grant that he was a supreme mathematician. In his astrological books (which you think I condemn without discrimination), if there is anything true and good in them, it is very little, and it is so defiled with fables and lies that a man as greedy as he who would rather gather gold from dung would more easily extract a true opinion from those books than one who wishes to spend his good hours well. You write that I have named Galen, together with Pico, a trifler. How falsely, it is not worth saying. If I had said that he trifled in that part where he treats of astrology, I think I would have erred only slightly. It is not at all the same to say that someone has written a few trifles and to affirm that he is an absolute trifler. Yet I do not remember having called him that.

units.la: Tandem sic ratiocinaris, si in certam formam reducantur quę confuse tu proponis. Quod manifesta probat ex-perientia, id nullis potest eludi rationibus. Atqui principia naturalia secundum lunæ, & astrorum circuitus mo-tusque alterari, mutari, disponi, manifesta probat experien-tia[?]. Nullis itaque rationibus refelli id poterit. Ego neque ἀνωμότος[?], neque truncus sum, neque cum Democrito nivem atram esse assero (Omnia ista pulchrius ac verius in Astrologos, quàm in me, quadrant, quibus à Ptolemæi Arabumq; Astrologorum mendacijs vel paulùm discedere maior est religio, quàm Pythagoreis fuit à sui magistri pla-citis dissentire) sed totam ratiocinationem vt veram ad-mitto. Quinimò veram esse firmissimis me rationibus de-monstrare posse confido. Astra certè horum sublunarium causæ sunt generales, ordinis & dispositionis effectrices causæ. Et prætera ita omnia hæc conseruant, ut si vim cœli nobis eripi, vel momento temporis cogitemus, om-nia sint collapsura. Non enim causa duntaxat cœlum est, ut apud nos hic omnia fiant, verum etiam actum dat singulis, ut unumquodque id agere possit, ad quod agendum à natunatura factum est. Sicut corporis nostri pars nulla viuit aut viuere potest, si non à corde vitam recipiat: ita sublunarium rerum nulla sine salutari vi coelitus infusa persistere, & pro sua natura agere valet. At hinc sequi, quod tu putas, illud est quod & nego, & falsum esse dico. Quis enim hanc putet ratiocinationem veram & efficacem esse? Coelum & astra sunt generales horum inferiorum causae, ergo ex ipsorum motus aspectuumque observatione possunt futurae particulares mutationes praecognosci. Nemo certè praeter Astrologos vitium siue falsitatem non videt. Si argumento illo Galenus fuit permotus, vt dierum de-cret causas in coelo quaereret, nihil ipse habuit, quod non omnes docti ante & post ipsum habuerint. Et nihilominus hi causam eorum in coelo non reperiri euidentibus & certis argumentis confecerunt. Exemplum quod ex Galeno adfers, ipse ex Aegyptiorum placitis se desumpsisse ostendit, quod tam est falsum, quàm tota Astrologica ariolatio falsa & mentita est. Si experientia vrgeas, negabo tibi vllam de his rebus experietiam habere posse, scilicet quòd à siderum positu haec fiant alia quàm vniuersali ratione. Neque debes à me hic probationem expectare, qui ad ea tantum respondeo, quae mihi tu proposuisti. Dabitur fortasse occasio ista probandi alio tempore.
units.tr: Finally you reason thus, if what you confusedly put forward is reduced to a fixed form: what experience plainly proves cannot be overturned by any arguments. But experience plainly proves that natural principles are altered, changed and arranged according to the circuits and motions of the moon and the stars. Therefore it cannot be refuted by any arguments. I am neither [ἀνώμοτος] unsworn nor a mutilated man, nor do I assert with Democritus that snow is black. (All those things fit the astrologers far better and more truly than me, for whom to depart even a little from the lies of Ptolemy and the Arab astrologers is a greater scruple than it was for the Pythagoreans to dissent from the tenets of their master.) But I admit the whole argument as true. Indeed, I am confident I can show by the firmest reasons that it is true. The stars are certainly general causes of these lower things, causes that produce order and arrangement. Moreover, they preserve all these things in such a way that, if we were to think for a moment that the power of heaven was taken from us, everything would collapse. For the heaven is not merely a cause for all things to happen here among us; it also gives action to each thing, so that each can do that to which it was made by nature. Just as no part of our body lives, or can live, unless it receives life from the heart, so none of the things beneath the moon can persist or act according to its nature without the saving power infused from heaven. But that what you think follows from this is something I both deny and say is false. For who would think this reasoning true and valid: the heavens and the stars are general causes of these lower things, therefore particular future changes can be foreknown from observing their motions and aspects? Certainly no one except the astrologers fails to see the fault or falsity in it. If Galen was moved by this argument to seek the causes of the days' fates in the heavens, he had nothing that all the learned before and after him did not have too. Yet they all showed, by evident and sure arguments, that their causes are not to be found in the heavens. The example you bring from Galen he himself shows he took from the opinions of the Egyptians, and that is as false as the whole astrological soothsaying is false and lying. If you press me with experience, I will deny that you can have any experience of these things, namely that they happen from the positions of the stars in any way other than by the general principle. Nor should you expect a proof from me here, since I am answering only the things you put to me. Perhaps this occasion of proving will be given at another time.

units.la: Valde miror te, dum sic scribis. Adde quod Galenus ipsemet ingenuè fateatur, se in accommodando lunae motu diebus Hippocratis, nullam discriminationem adferre, sed verisimilitudinem tantum. Haec sunt tua. Primum illud consideratione dignum est, quòd Galenum contendis nihil demonstrasse. Idem consuerunt in hoc negocio omnes docti, qui eum secuti sunt. At verò Galenus aliter sensisse iudicari potest. Sexto namq; cap. libri illius sophistas illos appellat, qui lunae tetragonas & diametras stationes non credunt in principijs bonis bonas facere alterationes, in malis malas. Affirmat etiam principio se vti omnibus confesso cap. ii. à sideribus terrena haec exornari disponiq; asserens. Quod si ex vero principio rectè conclusionem deducit, non verisimilis ea ratio dicenda erit, sed necessaria. Cæterùm istud jam sinamus, & quod ex dictis infers, secundo loco perpendamus. Galenica seu potius Astrologica non putas nugas vocari posse, quia Galenus non ne-cessaria, sed verisimili ratione pro illis asserendis usus sit. Ex ista tua ratiocinatione sequetur, nihil pro nugis habendum esse, nisi is qui dixit, demonstrasse se affirmarit puta-ritúe.
units.tr: I am very surprised that you write this. Add that Galen himself frankly admits that when he fits the motion of the moon to the days of Hippocrates, he brings no certain distinction but only probability. These are your words. First, it is worth considering that you claim Galen demonstrated nothing. All the learned men who have followed him have usually agreed on this point. Yet it can be judged that Galen thought otherwise. In the sixth chapter of that book he calls those sophists who do not believe that the square and opposition positions of the moon produce good changes in good beginnings and bad changes in bad ones. He also affirms that at the start of chapter 2 he is using a principle that everyone accepts, namely that these earthly things are adorned and disposed by the stars. If he draws his conclusion correctly from a true principle, that argument must be called not probable but necessary. But let us leave that aside and consider, in the second place, what you infer from what has been said. You think the Galenic, or rather the astrological, doctrines cannot be called trifles, because Galen used not necessary but probable reasoning to support them. By your reasoning it would follow that nothing should be regarded as trifling unless the person who proposed it has claimed to have demonstrated it.

units.la: Non multo post falli nos scribis, quod disputationem Galeni de causa dierum crisimorum ad artis opera exer-cenda minimè necessariam esse diximus, & quod non alia de causa ipsum scripsisse vniuersa illa affirmauimus, quàm vt 20. diem probaret decretorium esse. Ego vtrumque ex Galeno probari posse existimo. Et quod ad primum attinet, ex 10. cap. cognoscere quilibet poterit. Satis namque explicatè ostendit tertium illum librum Medico non esse necessarium. In 4. Aph. 36. tam clarè ab eo scriptum est, quæ in tertio libro de causis horum dierum disseruerit, nihil ad artis opera conferre, vt planius dici vix queat. Quibus addi potest, quod in nullo alio commentario horum mentionem facit, quàm in hoc loco. Et facere tamen sæpe debuerat, si vtilia iudicauerat. Quod verò præcipuè propter 20. diem opus illud scribere aggressus sit, argumento illud est, quod ex lunæ tetragona & diametra statione de die septima & in 14. probare aliquid conatus est. De reliquis diebus nihil propemodum dixit, quo pacto scilicet à lunæ motu efficiantur decretorij. Deinde in alijs com.vt in prognost. præcipuè 20. diei meminit. Quod si non placet, vt propter hunc diem præcipuè comm. illum scripsisse dicatur, non repugnabo. Facilè namque cessero cuiuis, quoties non firmis argumentis sententiam tueri possum. Hac igitur in re vicerit, & non magis propter 20. quàm omnes alios scripserit eum librum.
units.tr: Shortly afterwards you write that we are wrong when we said that Galen's discussion of the cause of the critical days is by no means necessary for practising the art, and when we claimed that he wrote that whole work for no other reason than to prove that the twentieth day is decisive. I think both points can be proved from Galen. As for the first, anyone can recognise it from chapter 10. There he shows quite clearly that the third book is not necessary for the physician. In the commentary on Aphorism 4.36 he states so plainly that what he discussed in the third book about the causes of these days contributes nothing to the practice of the art, and it could hardly be said more clearly. To this may be added that he mentions these matters in no other commentary except this one. Yet he would often have had to mention them if he had judged them useful. As for the fact that he undertook to write that work chiefly on account of the twentieth day, the evidence is that he tries to prove something about the seventh and fourteenth days from the square and opposition positions of the moon. He says almost nothing about the other days, namely how they are made decisive by the motion of the moon. Moreover, in his other commentaries, as in the Prognostics, he mentions chiefly the twentieth day. But if you do not like the view that he wrote that commentary chiefly because of this day, I will not object. I readily yield to anyone whenever I cannot defend my opinion with firm arguments. Let this point, then, be won by you: he wrote that book not more for the sake of the twentieth day than for all the others.

units.la: Jam tuam conclusiunculam inspiciemus. Breuiter ergo, cum reuera planetarum consideratio hoc commodi præstet, quod in ea morborum & naturæ vires nec non mutationes eorundem, augmenta item & decrementa antequam fiant perspiciantur, vnde commodius feliciusque tum dictæ tum pharmacorum modus & usus, gubernari potest,nō video semel quo pacto astrorum observatio vel Philosopho vel Medico indigna sit,&c. Hactenus tua.
units.tr: Now let us examine your little conclusion. Briefly, then: since the consideration of the planets offers this advantage, that in it the powers of diseases and of nature, and likewise their changes, increases and decreases, can be seen before they happen, so that the manner and use of diet and medicines can be governed more conveniently and happily, I do not at all see how the observation of the stars can be unworthy of a philosopher or a physician, and so on. So far your words.

units.la: Vehementer scire velim,ex quibus ista sequeretur con-clusio: Non poteris ex eo deducere, quod Galenus dierū decret.caussas ad lunæ motum retulit. Ipse enim hanc notitiam nihil adferre commodi Medicinam exercenti affir-mauit. Neque ex eo,quod sidera universales caussas horum inferiorum rectè ponit. Nam ex universali & remota caussa nihil certi de particularibus rebus cognosci potest. Sed & tu quoque ais,Galenum non motum lunæ diebus, sed dies motui accommodasse. Quibus hoc significare velle videris,non ex luna dies hoc habere, ut sint decretorij, vel non sint:sed Galenum in lunæ motum, ut potuerit reduxisse,quo caussam aliquam reddidisse iudicaretur. Ego certè non video,quomodo non æquè debeat ac possit motus lunæ diebus aptari,atque dies motui, siquidē ille caussa est,hi autem sunt effectus. Est enim mutua inter effectus atque caussas relatio.
units.tr: I should very much like to know from what premises that conclusion would follow: that you cannot deduce from the fact that Galen referred the causes of the critical days to the motion of the moon. For he himself affirmed that this knowledge brings no advantage to one who practises medicine. Nor can you deduce it from the fact that he rightly makes the stars the universal causes of these lower things. For from a universal and remote cause nothing certain can be known about particular things. But you also say that Galen did not adapt the days to the motion of the moon, but adapted the motion of the moon to the days. By this you seem to wish to signify that the days do not have their being critical from the moon, or not; rather, Galen bent the motion of the moon to fit them, as far as he could, so that it would be judged that he had given some cause. Truly I do not see why the motion of the moon should not be just as properly and as possibly fitted to the days as the days to the motion, since the one is the cause and the others are the effects. For there is a mutual relation between effects and causes.

units.la: Tot ferè occurrerūt quæ rescriberem ad tuas literas. Quòd si præter institutum atque officium meum probasse tibi videbor,Galenum dissertationem de caussis dierum decretoriorum neque utilem neque necessariam existimasse ad artis opera rectè exercenda:id eo me fecisse cogitarone posthac necessitatem huius vanitatis authoritate Galeni prædices.
units.tr: I have touched on almost as many points as I could answer in your letter. If I seem to you to have proved, beyond my purpose and office, that Galen did not think his dissertation on the causes of the critical days either useful or necessary for the sound practice of the art, I have done so in order that you may not henceforth proclaim the necessity of this vanity on Galen's authority.

units.la: Ergo ubi paucula hæc adiecero, finem scribendi faciam. Mensis Galeni figmentum falsum est tuo etiam testimonio. Sed nec probat 20.diem decretorium esse potius quā Neque ex lunæ motu probari potest decretorium ipsum esse vel alium quemuis,ut Galenus credidisse videtur. Etenim si lunæ motus efficiunt dies alij decernant, alij nō decernant,omnium erit caussa decretoriorum,ut scilicet decretorij sint,non quorundam tantum. Erit ergo & 3.& 5.& 11.& 17.& tandem 20. Si vero aliquorum & non omnium caussa existit, quæ erit excogitanda ratio aliorum? Aut quid habebunt? 7. & 14. dies, quod non omnes alij dies ha-beant? Si de indicibus & in utilibus dubites, saltem excretoriorum[?] ratio erit eadem omnium. Ego multò rectius Galenum causas reddidisse passim in suis commen-tarijs, cur hi, non vero alij morbos iudicent, puto, quàm in præsenti loco. Et in hoc ipso libro falsis veras causas per-miscuit. Non ex luna repetendæ videntur causæ, sed in ipsa agentis causæ natura, scilicet in humoris quantitate & qualitate, in corporis structura, in virtutis robore aut im-becillitate, in perpessi loci conditione, & in alijs talibus quærendam potius existimo, vbi etiam inueniri eam certò mihi persuadeo. Sed hæc quoque extra rem dixi. Feci verò ob eam causam, ut neque Galenum vobis, nec vos Galeno consentire cerneretis. Vale. Die 17. Augusti Masfeldiæ.
units.tr: Therefore, having added these few words, I will bring my writing to an end. Your own testimony shows that Galen's doctrine of the months is a false fiction. Nor does it prove that the twentieth day is decisive, any more than it can be proved from the motion of the moon that the day itself, or any other, is decisive, as Galen seems to have believed. For if the motions of the moon make some days decisive and others not, they would be the cause of all the decisive days, so that they are decisive, not only some of them. Then the third, fifth, eleventh and seventeenth days, and at last the twentieth, would also be decisive. But if the moon is the cause of some days and not all, what reason must be devised for the others? Or what will they have? Why do the seventh and fourteenth days have something that all the other days do not? If you doubt these matters as to the indicating days, at least the reason for the excretory days will be the same for all. I think Galen gave the causes far more correctly in various places in his commentaries, explaining why these days, and not others, judge diseases, than in the present passage. And in this very book he mixes true causes with false ones. I think the causes should not be sought in the motion of the moon, but in the nature of the acting cause itself: namely in the quantity and quality of the humour, in the structure of the body, in the strength or weakness of the power, in the condition of the affected part, and in other such things; and I am persuaded that the cause can certainly be found there. But I have said these things too beside the matter. I did so in order that you might see that neither Galen agrees with you, nor you with Galen. Farewell. Masfeld, 17 August.

units.la: THOM. ERASTVS D. CHRISTO-phoro Stathmioni Medico Coburg. S. D. Epistola III.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus to Christophorus Stathmion, physician of Coburg, greetings. Letter III.

units.la: CVM heri vesperi ex Thuringia domum revertissem, tuæ mihi redditæ sunt literæ. Quas cum longiusculas esse viderem, non mediocri voluptate affectus sum. Nam fructum aliquem ex illis me percepturum considebam. At cum legere incœpissem, antiquam recantilenam canere deprehendi. Etsi verò nihil propè sit, cui non antè responderim, placuit nihilominus iterum tibi respondere, non quidem ad convicia, sed ad ea quæ ad propositam nobis controversiam propius accedere videtur. Hoc modo in superioribus literis ratiocinatus fui: Solus Deus novit futura contingentia. Astrologi non sunt dij, sed homines, ut nos sumus, mortales. Nō possunt igitur arte aut industria in horum præsensionem pervenire. Dixi postea, ne qua relinqueretur in verbis obscuritas, me de illis loqui contingentibus, quorum causæ vel ignorarentur, vel nondum agerent: vel si agere incœpissent, nobis nondum innotuissent. Hæc si tu candidè inter-preterpretari voluisses, non tam absurda & aliena effutiuisses. Quamuis autem supra exemplo rem, breuiter licet, declaraui, non grauabor tamen eandem exemplis tum Medicorum, tum Nautarum iterum exponere.
units.tr: When I got home from Thuringia yesterday evening, your letter was handed to me. Seeing that it was rather long, I was not a little pleased, for I supposed I would gain some profit from it. But when I began to read, I found you singing the old refrain again. Although there is hardly anything you have raised that I have not already answered, I am nonetheless pleased to reply to you once more. I do this not to answer your abuse but to the matter that seems to bear more closely on the controversy we have before us. In my earlier letter I reasoned as follows: only God knows future contingent events; astrologers are not gods but men, mortal as we are; therefore they cannot reach a foreknowledge of these things by art or industry. I then added, so that no obscurity might remain in my words, that I was speaking of those contingent events whose causes are either unknown or have not yet begun to act, or, if they have begun to act, have not yet become known to us. If you had been willing to interpret this frankly, you would not have blurted out such absurd and irrelevant things. Although I explained the matter briefly with an example above, I will not hesitate to set it out again with examples from physicians and from sailors.

units.la: Medicus cum in vrinis videt naturam incoepisse iam morbi caussam euincere & concoquere, ac preterea quousque progressa sit perspicit, artificiosa coniectura colligit hoc vel illo tempore totam superatam iri, vt crisim expectare tum possit. Similiter etiam Nautae ex motu vaporis aut nubeculae in aere futurum ventum tempestatemque cognoscunt. Vtrique non ante intelligunt, quam effectus iam fieri, siue quam causas proximas iam agere incoepisse perspexerint. Ista caussarum actio quia ab initio pertenuis & obscura est, a peritis tantum & exercitatis in qualibet arte deprehenditur, vulgares & imperitos latet. Vt igitur nec Nautae futuram tempestatem serenitatem ue praescire, nec Medici morbi finem & euentum praeuidere possunt, quam vtrique propinquę & propriae caussae actionem incepisse cognouerint, ita omnes alij artifices futura praedicunt, in sua quilibet arte. Quod si proximam caussam ignorent, il-lud autē agere coepisse videant, quod illam excitare comouereque potest, ratio eadem omnino existit. Ex istis, nisi me prorsus fallit mea de re opinio, aperte perspicies quid per contingentia intellexerim, id quod hactenus intellexisse non videris. Sic enim ad supradictum argumentum respondes: Maiorem tuam nego, falsamq; esse pronuncio. Quid ita Stathmion? Quoniam, inquis, omnem praescientiam, non eam tantum quae ex astris sumitur, tollit. Quam erudita sit responsio ista tua videamus.
units.tr: When a physician sees in the urine that nature has begun to master and concoct the cause of the disease, and further perceives how far it has progressed, he infers by skilled conjecture that at this or that time the whole disease will be overcome, so that he can then expect the crisis. Likewise sailors learn from the movement of vapour or a little cloud in the air what wind and storm are coming. Each of them understands nothing until the effect is already coming about, or until they have seen the proximate causes already beginning to act. Since this action of causes is at first very faint and obscure, it is detected only by those skilled and practised in any art, and it escapes common and unskilled people. So just as neither sailors can foresee a coming storm or calm, nor physicians foresee the end and outcome of a disease, until they have recognised that the near and proper cause has begun to act, so all other craftsmen predict the future in their own arts. And if they do not know the proximate cause but see that something has begun to act which can stir up and set in motion that cause, the reasoning is exactly the same. From these examples, unless my opinion on this matter deceives me utterly, you will clearly see what I meant by contingent events, something you do not seem to have understood until now. For you answer the argument above like this: "I deny your major premise and declare it false." Why so, Stathmion? "Because," you say, "it removes all foreknowledge, not only that which is drawn from the stars." Let us see how learned that reply of yours is.

units.la: Non sequitur, si solus Deus norit futura contingetia, omniū propterea rerū praescientiam e medio tolli, sed contingentiam tantum, non autem necessariorum. Deinde non omnium contingentium, sed eorum duntaxat, quorum caussae vel non sunt notae nobis, vel nodum agunt, vel si agunt, non sciuntur a nobis agere. Sic quae de Medicis & Nautis adfers, quibus te deleuisse argumentum, quod recte indis-solubile vocaui, putabas, inefficacia & elumbia prorsus esse cernis. Utrique enim non de contingentibus illis vaticinantur, de quibus argumentum loquitur, sed de illis solis, quæ iam fieri producíque[?] vel in caussis vel aliter animad-verterunt. Equidem nullus reperietur Medicus, nisi ide forte sit etiam astrologus, qui se de certi alicuius hominis morbo aliquid pronunciare ante posse credat, quàm naturæ actionem in morbum, eiusdemque causam perdiderit, quanta sit, quousque progressa sit, quando incoeperit, & quæ his similia sunt. Quare minimè probasti falsam ef-se meam propositionem, quæ immota adhuc suo consistit loco, & ab omnibus omnium astrologorum machinis fa-cile tuta permanebit.
units.tr: It does not follow that, if God alone knows future contingent events, the foreknowledge of all things is therefore removed; only the foreknowledge of contingent events is removed, not that of necessary things. Further, it is not the foreknowledge of all contingent events but only of those whose causes are either unknown to us, or have not yet begun to act, or, if they have begun to act, are not known by us to be acting. So the examples you bring from physicians and sailors, with which you thought you had dissolved the argument that I rightly called insoluble, you can see are wholly ineffective and feeble. For they do not prophesy about those contingent events with which the argument deals, but only about those things which they have observed already coming into being and being produced, either in their causes or otherwise. Indeed no physician will be found (unless perhaps he is also an astrologer) who believes he can announce anything in advance about a particular person's illness before he has grasped the action of nature upon the disease, its cause, how great it is, how far it has progressed, when it began, and things like these. Therefore you have not at all proved that my proposition is false; it stands still in its place, and it will easily remain safe from all the engines of all the astrologers.

units.la: Quæ de certorum dierum obseruatione, quos Germa-ni loistag[?] nominant, scribis, magnam mihi admirationem attulerunt. Fieri potest, ut, cum tot sis iam annos natus, nec dū perdidiceris, vix unquam euenire (& si quandoque ita euenerit, casu fuisse factum) ut annus illis diebus respondeat. Non nescis, arbitror, multos etiam Astrologos confiteri, nullam hanc dierum obseruationem in natura causam habere. Alia est ratio temporis, quod in cædendis lignis obseruatur. Hoc enim certam habet euidentemq; causam. Similiter aëris mutatio sub exortum Pleiadum, Arcturi, & similium non sine ratione plerunque expectatur similis, quemadmodum etiam æstas & hyes, & ethesię & huius generis alia quædam. Hæc, inquam, partim ad ne-cessario euenientia (ut in natura necessitas consideratur) partim vero ad ea quorum causæ iam agere incoeperunt, referuntur. Quòd si sol moueretur aliquando, mox non moueretur, neque nobis motus ipsius natura & tempus non tam foret, nec æstatem[?] nec hyemē præuidere ante possemus, quàm perciperemus, aut certe quàm solem vel accedere ad nos, vel recedere à nobis incoepisse percognouissemus.
units.tr: What you write about the observance of certain days, which the Germans call loistag, has caused me great astonishment. It may be that, although you are already so many years old and have not yet learned better, it almost never happens that the year corresponds to those days (and if at some time it has so turned out, it happened by chance). I suppose you are not unaware that many astrologers themselves confess that this observance of days has no cause in nature. The reasoning about the time observed in felling timber is different, for that has a certain and evident cause. Similarly, a change in the air at the rising of the Pleiades, of Arcturus and of similar stars is commonly expected, not without reason, to be of a like kind, as are summer and winter, and the equinoxes, and some other things of this sort. These, I say, are referred partly to things that happen by necessity (since necessity is considered in nature) and partly to those whose causes have already begun to act. But if the sun were at some time to move and then soon not move, and if the nature and time of its motion were not such as they are, we could not foresee summer or winter until we perceived it, or at least until we had learned that the sun had begun to approach us or to recede from us.

units.la: Hinc vides nō tam esse me rudem & hebetem, ut propo-sitioni distinctionem addere nesciuerim, quod parum ve-re de me scribis. Utinam tam recte tu eam intellexisses, quàm bono ego consilio addidi, certè non tam absurdè fuisses interpretatus. Nō enim de contingentibus locutus sum, quæ caussis carent. Quis enim hoc apud se cogitet? Nihil absque causa fieri à qua producatur, notius est, quàm vt ignorare potuerim. De illis locutus sum, de quibus me iam satis multa disputasse existimo. Non ideo contingentia alia qua carent caussis, quia nos eas aut non nouimus, aut non ante nouimus, quàm effectum suum producere inceperint. Quamobrem plumbea, imò herbacea tela sunt, quæ in propositionem nostram contorquere tibi visus es.
units.tr: From this you see that I am not so crude and dull as not to know how to add a distinction to my proposition, which is what you write about me, and wrongly. Would that you had understood it as rightly as I added it with a good purpose; you would certainly not have interpreted it so absurdly. For I did not speak of contingent events that lack causes. Who would think that in his own mind? That nothing comes about without a cause by which it is produced is better known than that I could have been ignorant of it. I spoke of those events about which I think I have already disputed at sufficient length. I did not say that other contingent events lack causes merely because we either do not know them, or did not know them before they began to produce their effect. Therefore the weapons you seem to have turned against my proposition are made of lead, or rather of grass.

units.la: Est quòd gaudeam, quòd caussam mihi recitas, cur me a methodum in superioribus literis, stupidum & indoctū appellaueris, scilicet quia me Dialecticæ imperitum animaduerteris. Quantam tibi huius facultatis peritiam arroges, tuæ declarant literæ. Quàm turpiter te ipsum fallas, eædem docent. Vbi mox tua quædam examinare coepero, tuam in disserendo peritiam obiter attingemus. De Ptolemæo hîc nihil dicam, præsertim cum propter occupationes mihi festinandum sit. Si, quantus ille Philosophus fuerit,scire cupis, lege ipsius libros, non quidem vt Astrologus, (sic enim aurea esse omnia prædicabis) sed vt Philosophus, & tantus, quantus videri vis, Dialecticus. Specimen quoddam philosophiæ Ptolemæi in libello Hieronymi Sauonarolæ, viri nunquam satis laudati, à me conuerso & edito reperies, non vno tantum in loco. Quòd si tu probabis, quæ ibi rectè reprehenduntur, frustra sperem te de meis rebus rectè iudicaturum. Hactenus ad primam epistolæ tuæ partem responderim.
units.tr: I am glad that you recite the reason why you called me, in your earlier letter, a dull and unlearned man: namely, because you noticed that I am inexperienced in dialectic. How great a skill you claim for yourself in this discipline your letter shows; how shamefully you deceive yourself, the same letter teaches. When I soon begin to examine some of your statements, we will touch on your skill in disputation in passing. I will say nothing here about Ptolemy, especially since I must hurry because of my duties. If you wish to know how great a philosopher he was, read his books, not as an astrologer (for you will call everything in them golden in that case), but as a philosopher, and as the dialectician you wish to seem. You will find a specimen of Ptolemy's philosophy, translated and published by me, in the little book of Hieronymus Savonarola, a man never praised enough, and in more than one place. But if you approve what is rightly criticised there, I would be vainly hoping that you will judge my own work rightly. So far I have answered the first part of your letter.

units.la: In secunda parte acerbè me reprehendis, mendacijque accusas, quòd Galenum in curandis morbis Astrologica decreta non obseruasse scripsi. Deinde quòd nihil vtilitatis Medico ad opera artis rectè exercenda conferre dixi. Vtrumque verum esse per se patet. Sanè si aliquo in loco Galenum in curationibus Astrologicos siderum aspectus obseruasse docueris, errorem libenter confitebor. Si ad 3. de diebus decret. prouoces, ne ibi quidem reperies, quibus tuæ sententiam confirmes. Etenim Galenus ipse in eo libro apertè satis testificatur, disputationem illius libri nihil adferre commodi artem exercitanti. Quod hic obscurius dixisse videri potest, in 4. Aph. 36. explicatissime affirmat. Per ocium inquirere talia cum iussisset (idem alibi quoque fecit) tandem sic scripsit: [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters]. Quomodocunque interpretari ista conaris, semper tamen quod affirmavi verum esse comperies. Sed & ipsum libri propositum suis argumentum idem probat. Nihil enim de curationibus ibi docet, sed rationem duntaxat adferre studet, cur ex diebus alij quidem decernant, alij vero non decernant, & cur alij in iudicando alijs fortiores tutioresque existant. Has, inquit Galenus, rationes qui ignoraverit, (modo reliquorum nihil ignoret quae ab eo in alijs commentarijs expósita fuerunt) recte poterit aegrotos & cum gloria curare.
units.tr: In the second part you reproach me bitterly and accuse me of lying, because I wrote that Galen did not observe astrological decrees in treating diseases. Then you say I have said that the physician's art brings no advantage to the correct practice of medicine. That both of these are true is plain in itself. Certainly, if you show that Galen somewhere observed the astrological aspects of the stars in his cures, I will gladly confess my error. If you appeal to book 3 of On Critical Days, you will not find there anything to confirm your view. For Galen himself testifies quite plainly in that book that the discussion of that book brings no benefit to one practising the art. What may seem to have been said rather obscurely here, he states most explicitly in Aphorisms 4.36. When he had ordered such matters to be investigated at leisure (as he did elsewhere too), he finally wrote thus: [illegible] [illegible] [illegible]. However you try to interpret these words, you will always find that what I affirmed is true. But the very purpose of the book and its argument prove the same thing. For there he teaches nothing about cures; he only aims to give the reason why some physicians decide by days and others do not, and why some are stronger and safer in judging than others. Galen says that whoever is ignorant of these reasons (provided he is not ignorant of the rest that were set out by him in other commentaries) can cure the sick well and with credit.

units.la: Sed quid opus est probatione cum tumet tuis in literis idem affirmes? Sic enim tu met scribis. Verum hoc dicit (Galenus) quod 3. liber, si cui videatur difficilior propter disputationis subtilitatem, quae vulgo Medicorum non conuenit, sed eruditis & Arithmeticae Astronomiaeque peritis, bona ratione praeteriri queat, cum causarum inquisitio, cur dies decretorij sint, nihil ad curationes iuuet Medicos. Haec tua sunt. Quomodo ergo me, cum Galenum ista scripsisse affirmavi, mentitum esse ais, cū aliud in his scriperim, quàm quod tutemet Galeno tribuisti? Si vero tu de Galeno dicere hoc potuisti, cur ego non potui? Sed hoc omnibus pene accidit, qui veritatem oppugnant, vt, quod ipsi faciunt, in alijs damnent. Ergo cum Galenus nullibi legatur in morborum curatione Astrologica decreta Medicinae coniunxisse, & illam ipsam de astris dissertationem, quam in 3. illo libro legimus, minimè vtilem ac necessariam, ad artis opera recte exercenda Galenus tuo etiam iudicio affirmet, liquet vtrumque à me recte dictum fuisse.
units.tr: But why do we need proof, when you yourself affirm the same thing in your letter? For you write thus: "Galen says this: that the third book, if anyone finds it too difficult because of the subtlety of the disputation, which does not suit the common run of physicians but the learned and those skilled in arithmetic and astronomy, may reasonably be passed over, since the inquiry into the causes of why days are critical helps physicians nothing in treating patients." These are your words. How then, when I affirmed that Galen wrote these things, do you say I lied, since I wrote nothing about this except what you yourself attributed to Galen? And if you could say this about Galen, why could I not? But this happens to almost all who attack the truth: they condemn in others what they themselves do. Therefore, since Galen is nowhere read as joining astrological decrees to the treatment of diseases, and since he himself, by your own judgement, affirms that that very discussion of the stars which we read in that third book is least useful and necessary for rightly carrying out the work of the art, it is clear that both of my statements were rightly made.

units.la: Sed quid te deceperit video. Quando cum Galeno inquisitionem ac notitiam causæ dierum decretoriorum,
units.tr: But I see what has deceived you. When I wrote that, according to Galen, the inquiry into and knowledge of the cause of critical days is useless to one who is about to practise medicine,

units.la: ut à Galeno traditur, inutilem esse Medicinam facturo scripsi, tu me idem dixisse putas, ac si ad Medicinam inutilem esse affirmassem. Verumtamen multa nos ἐν τῇ θεωρίᾳ saepe inquirere constat, quae inter agendum nobis non sunt usui. Cum enim in scholis artem profitemur, multorum causas perquisitare tentamus, quorum in operibus artis τὸ ὂν [?] scire sufficit. Hinc Aristoteles recte affirmauit, ibi ele[?]gantem ordiri Medicum, vbi Philosophus desierit. Ostendit etiam Galenus multas in arte nostra iam olim quoque logicas quaestiones omnem artis usum excedentes agitatas fuisse. Haec tu tantus logicus quomodo non animaduerteris & distinxeris non parum admiror. Sed iam tempus est vt ad eam ratiocinationem descendamus, qua te efficaciter probasse opinaris, Astrologiam Medico necessariam esse.
units.tr: you think I said the same as if I had affirmed that medicine is useless. Yet it is certain that we often inquire into many things ἐν τῇ θεωρίᾳ [in theory], which are of no use to us in the doing. For when we profess the art in the schools, we try to investigate the causes of many things, of which it is enough to know the fact in the works of the art. Hence Aristotle rightly affirmed that the physician should begin his elegant work where the philosopher has stopped. Galen also shows that in our art, even in ancient times, many logical questions were debated which went beyond all use of the art. That you, being so great a logician, did not notice and distinguish these things, I do not a little wonder. But now it is time to come down to that reasoning by which you think you have effectively proved that astrology is necessary to the physician.

units.la: Si mihi concedas, inquit, Hippocratis ac Galeni doctrinam perfectissimam esse, & praecipuè Medico imitandam, ac vtrumque diligenter dies crisimos observandos praecepisse, vt qui magnum medentibus vsum praestent. Et [?] (praeterea dies) Galenum demonstrasse, causam horum dierum lunam existere, etiamsi te in omnes formas instar Prothei transmutes, tamen lunae cursum Medico observandum esse fateri cogeris ad intelligendas criseis videlicet menstruas. Hactenus tua recitaui. Si tibi dedero & concessero quicquid proponés, probabis perfacile quicquid voles. Hippocratis ac Galeni doctrinam libenter summoque studio amplector. Dies criticos Medico recte curaturo maximè observandos esse fateor. Sed non ideo non errasse Galenum, cum in luna veram eorum causam quaerit, concedo. Sed vt tuam incogitantiam planius perspicias, ecce dabo tibi in praesentia Galenum recte verèque demonstrasse causas dierum decret.ad lunae motum pertinere. An hinc efficietur Astrologiam Medico necessariam esse ad exercendam artem? Dico Astrologiam, propterea quòd per motum lunae te hanc intellexisse suspicor. Nisi enim haec fuerit mens tua, nihil ad rem dicis. Deinde cum mox aliorum quoque errantium siderum motus necesarios eidem esse scribas, facile quid senseris apparet. Ad rem redeo.
units.tr: "If you grant me," you say, "that the doctrine of Hippocrates and Galen is most perfect and especially to be imitated by the physician, and that both prescribed carefully observing the critical days, as those which are of great use to those who treat the sick; and (besides) that Galen demonstrated the cause of these days to be the moon, even if you transform yourself into every shape like Proteus, you will still be forced to confess that the physician must observe the course of the moon in order to understand the critical periods, namely the monthly ones." Thus far I have recited your words. If I grant you whatever you propose, you will very easily prove whatever you wish. I gladly and with the greatest zeal embrace the doctrine of Hippocrates and Galen. I admit that the critical days are above all to be observed by the physician who is to treat rightly. But I do not concede that Galen did not err when he sought the true cause of these days in the moon. Yet so that you may see your lack of thought more plainly, look: I will grant you for the present that Galen rightly and truly demonstrated that the causes of the critical days pertain to the motion of the moon. Will it follow from this that astrology is necessary to the physician for exercising the art? I say astrology, because I suspect that by the motion of the moon you have meant this. For unless this was your intention, you say nothing to the point. Then, since you soon write that the motions of the other wandering stars are also necessary to the same, it is easy to see what you meant. I return to the matter.

units.la: Etiamsi Galenus probasset lunæ motum veram & proximam criticorum dierum causam esse, non vniuersalem solum, non tamen necessaria futura fuisset illa motus lunæ consideratio artis opera exercenti, vt ex Galeno te ipso teste supra ostendi. Deinde si ad theoriam aliquid faceret, non necessario in opus referretur. Multa namque exqui-ri in theoria, quæ in vsum non veniunt, imò vsum transcendunt, ex supra dictis patet. Postremò constat illud etiam, Galenum talia inter curandum nunquam obseruasse. Hæc inquam si Galenus propositum validissimè probasset, cō-cedere nihilominus cogereris. Atque ex his tuam logicā disce. Cæterùm nihil probasse horum Galenum certum est. Quare multo minus obtinebis. Tu quidem, quia vocem ἀποδείξεως[?] vsurpauit, demonstrasse ipsum omnia putare videris. At falleris plurimuum si ita existimas. Nonenim in proprio semper significato hac dictio-ne vtitur.
units.tr: Even if Galen had proved that the motion of the moon is the true and proximate cause of critical days, not merely a universal one, that consideration of the motion of the moon would still not have been necessary to one who exercises the work of the art, as I have shown above from Galen himself as your witness. Next, even if it bore on theory, it would not necessarily be carried over into practice. For many things are sought in theory which are not put to use, indeed which go beyond use, as is plain from what was said above. Lastly, it is also certain that Galen never observed such things while treating patients. These things, I say, even if Galen had most strongly proved his proposition, you would nonetheless be forced to concede. Learn your logic from these points. For the rest, it is certain that Galen proved none of these things, and so you will gain far less. You indeed, because he used the word ἀπόδειξις [demonstration], seem to think he demonstrated everything. But you are greatly mistaken if you think so, for he does not always use this word in its proper meaning.

units.la: Argumenti quod pro Galeno, ex ipso maiore desumta struis, hæc est summa. Omne naturale principium iuxta lunæ & astrorum circuitus mutatur, alteratur, disponitur. Ad hoc probandum frustra tot verba quot sequuntur, fundis. Totum enim pro confesso tibi do, modo vniuersali ratione cœlum ista facere intelligas. Aliter enim vera non fuerit sententia. Adijcis deinde assumtionem, principium illud à quo morbi magis vno quàm alio die commouentur & iudicantur, est naturale. Ergo à motu lunæ & astrorum afficitur, mutatur, disponitur. Omnia sunt vera, sed tibi nihil prosunt. Quis nesciat aliter affici hominem à lu-na febre pituitosa laborantem, & aliter biliosa ægrotantē? Si igitur eodem tempore luna homines aut res diuersas, diuerso modo, quamlibet nimirum pro sua natura afficit, vniuersali ratione id, vel ob eam tantum rationem, fieri, à nemine sano dubitari negariue potest. Ergo cum demon-stratio per causam fiat proximam & propriam, Galenus autem remotissimam maximeque communem attulerit, necessario sequitur ipsius probationem non esse veram demonstrationem. [?]ides nihil te probasse, & recte à me dictum fuisse disceptat[?]ionem Astrologicam in 3. de diebus criticis nihil præstare commodi ei qui ægros recte curare studet. Equidem philosophus ille qui quadratum circulo æquale se demonstrare putabat, longe melius ex probabi-libus ratiocinabatur, hoc modo: Ubi potest maius & mi-nus inveniri, ibidem reperiatur etiam æquale. At in circu-lo quadrato reperitur maius & minus. Ergo æquale etiā inveniatur. Quid ad hæc Aristotelis? Ridet, ac nihil pro-batum esse affirmat non sine optima ratione, quia scilicet ex communibus constata esset ratio. Quid ad argumentū Galeni dicturum fuisse censes?
units.tr: The sum of the argument you build for Galen, drawn from the major premise itself, is this: every natural principle is changed, altered and disposed according to the circuits of the moon and the stars. You pour out so many words, as many as follow, to prove this in vain. For I grant it all to you as agreed, provided you understand that the heavens do these things in a universal manner; otherwise the opinion would not be true. You then add the assumption: the principle from which diseases are moved and judged more on one day than another is natural. Therefore it is affected, changed and disposed by the motion of the moon and the stars. All these things are true, but they do you no good. Who does not know that a man suffering from a phlegmatic fever is affected differently by the moon from one who is sick with a bilious fever? If, therefore, at the same time the moon affects different men or things in different ways, each according to its own nature, no sane person can doubt or deny that this happens in a universal way, or for that reason alone. Therefore, since demonstration is made through the proximate and proper cause, and Galen has brought forward the most remote and most common cause, it necessarily follows that his proof is not a true demonstration. Thus you see that you have proved nothing, and that I rightly said that the astrological discussion in the third book on critical days provides no advantage to one who seeks to treat the sick rightly. Indeed, that philosopher who thought he demonstrated that a square is equal to a circle reasoned far better from probabilities, in this way: where a greater and a lesser can be found, an equal is also to be found in the same place. But in a square circle a greater and a lesser are found. Therefore an equal is also found. What do you think Aristotle would have said to these things? He laughs, and affirms that nothing was proved, not without the best reason, because the argument was constructed from common matters. What do you think he would have said in reply to Galen's argument?

units.la: Age breviter repetatur. Mutationum naturalium om-nium astra causæ sunt. Morborum permutationes siue motiones sunt naturales quædam mutationes. Astra igi-tur harum causæ sunt. Vides in ipsis expressum verbis, ta-cite tamen, astra universales causas esse. Etenim si sunt rerum omnium causæ, etiam hominis, leonis, brutorum omnium, & herbarum & cæterarum rerum universarum atque earūdem motionum siue mutationum causæ sunt. At quis est tam iners, qui harum rerum ortum ad cœlum potius referat, quàm ad veras & univocas earum causas? Dicendum igitur est, astra ita esse criticorum dierum siue motionum naturæ, quæ illis fiunt diebus, causas, vti sunt rerum iam enumeratarum omnium causæ. At non sunt harum causæ aliter quàm modo generali. Proinde nihil hac ratione probas aliud, quā generales causas esse, quod ego nunquam, quod quidem meminisse queam, negaui. Addantur cætera.
units.tr: Let us briefly repeat it. The stars are the causes of all natural changes. The changes or motions of diseases are certain natural changes. Therefore the stars are their causes. You see that it is expressed in these words, though tacitly, that the stars are universal causes. For if they are the causes of all things, also of man, lion, all brute animals, herbs and all other universal things, and of their motions or changes, then who is so sluggish as to refer the origin of these things to the heavens rather than to their true and specific causes? It must therefore be said that the stars are causes of the critical days, or of the natural motions which occur on those days, just as they are causes of all the things already listed. But they are not causes of these in any way other than in a general manner. Therefore by this reasoning you prove nothing except that they are general causes, which I, so far as I can recall, never denied. Let the rest be added.

units.la: Inter astra maximè agunt sol & luna. Sed critici dies nō ad solem reduci possunt. Ad lunam ergo referri debebūt. At hæc septimo feré die est dichotomos siue quadrata, & decima quarta die plena. Ergo dies septimus & decimus-quartus potentiores sunt cæteris. Tunc enim cuidentius[?] luna agit. Hac eadem ratione, si pro verissimis ambæ propositiones admittantur utriusque, dico, syllogismi, aliud nihil probabitur, quàm illos dies cæteris felicius & efficacius iudicare, qui in lunam vel qua[?]am vel plenam inciduntpropterea quòd tum lumen[?] est efficacius, quàm ante. At hoc modo magis decernet 9. quàm septimus. Et 11. efficacior erit omnibus præcedentibus. Sed sufficiat indicasse, quomodo ista sint vera. Deinde quòd nihil patrocinentur Astrologis.
units.tr: Among the stars the sun and the moon act most. But critical days cannot be referred to the sun. They must therefore be referred to the moon. Now the moon is at the half, or quadrature, roughly on the seventh day, and full on the fourteenth day. Therefore the seventh and fourteenth days are more powerful than the others, for then the moon acts most evidently. By this same reasoning, if both premises are admitted as most true, I say that the syllogism will prove nothing else than that those days which fall on the moon's quarter or full judge more happily and effectively than the others, because then the light is more effective than before. But by this method the ninth day will decide more than the seventh, and the eleventh will be more effective than all those preceding. But it is enough to have indicated how these things are true, and then that they give no support to the astrologers.

units.la: Inscitè etiam improbas, quòd naturam crises efficere dixi pro humorum qualitate & quantitate, ac aliis circumstantijs. An tu nunquam legisti, Naturas morborum indicatrices ac medicatrices esse? Post hæc qua in parte Galeni demonstratio peccet, ostendi tibi cupis. Si quæ dicta mihi sunt hactenus recto iudicio examinare voles, abundè perspicies quid de argumento Galeni sentiam. Mox hæc addis.
units.tr: You also unskilfully find fault with my saying that nature produces the crisis according to the quality and quantity of the humours and other circumstances. Have you never read that the natures of diseases both indicate and heal? After this you want me to show where Galen's demonstration goes wrong. If you are willing to examine with sound judgement what I have said so far, you will see plainly what I think of Galen's argument. Then you add the following.

units.la: Tu ne igitur effectus astrorum in sublunaribus deprehendi posse negas? Experientia enim nihil aliud est, quàm sensuum confirmatio. Hæc tua sunt. Vires astrorum universales deprehendi posse, præcipuè solis ac lunæ sæpe dixi. Addidi ne momento quidem hunc inferiorem mundum, aut actiones ipsius consistere posse, nisi perpetuò à cœlo regatur. Exemplo cordis, quomodo intelligam, exposui. Hoc tu exemplum ieiunum esse scribis atque eiusmodi, quo memet ipse instar furiosi, proprio scilicet ense iugulē. Pro confirmatione addis: Hæc enim (cordis videlicet similitudine) sentiri, & evidentes esse astrorum effectus clarè concedis, quos tamen eosdem rursus velut attonitus quispiam nunc negas. Non ego Stathmion attonitus sum, sed tu potius, qui quod plane & aperte dico non aduertis. Nolo enim dicere non intelligis. Particulares illas astrorum actiones, de quibus Astrologi multa nugantur, esse ac deprehendi nego. Vniuersales sentiri non eo inficias, solis præsertim atque lunæ. An falsi aliquid tibi dixisse videor, cum fictitias illas astrorum vires siue actiones percipi à nemine posse asserui?
units.tr: Do you therefore deny that the effects of the stars can be detected in the sublunary world? For experience is nothing but the confirmation of the senses. These are your words. I have often said that the universal powers of the stars can be detected, especially those of the sun and moon. I added that not even for a moment can this lower world, or its actions, exist unless it is continually governed from heaven. I explained how I understand this by the example of the heart. You write that this example is feeble and of the kind by which a man, like a madman, cuts his own throat with his own sword. In support you add: For you clearly concede that these effects are perceived, and that the effects of the stars are evident (by the likeness of the heart, namely), and yet, like someone astonished, you now deny the same effects. It is not I, Stathmion, who am astonished, but rather you, who do not notice what I say plainly and openly. For I do not want to say that you do not understand. I deny that those particular actions of the stars, about which the astrologers chatter a great deal, exist or can be detected. I do not deny that the universal ones can be sensed, especially those of the sun and moon. Do I seem to have said anything false, when I maintain that those fictitious powers or actions of the stars cannot be perceived by anyone?

units.la: Nescio quid in mentem tibi venerit, aut quid tibi velis cum experientiam nil aliud esse asseueras, quàm sensuum confirmationem. Secus eam nobis Aristoteles, Galenus alij auctores describunt. Velim cum diceres Aristotelem & Galenum astra non pro vniuersalibus tantum caussis effectuum sublunarium (intelligo particularium) agnouisse, locum aliquem ex operibus eorum produxisses, quo sententiam tuam probasses. Ego certè nullum inuenire hucusque potui. Tu quoque tamersi longo tempore quæras, nullum inuenies. Non enim aliter locuti sunt, quàm vniuersales causas esse cœlos horum inferiorum siue terrenorum.
units.tr: I do not know what came into your head, or what you mean, when you assert that experience is nothing but the confirmation of the senses. Aristotle, Galen and other authors describe it otherwise. I would like you, when you say that Aristotle and Galen recognised the stars as not merely universal causes of sublunary effects (I mean particular effects), to have quoted some passage from their works to prove your view. For my part I have not been able to find any such passage so far. Nor, however long you search, will you find one. For they spoke in no other way than that the heavens are the universal causes of these lower, that is, earthly, things.

units.la: Quæ iam sequuntur in tuis literis fateor me non intelligere. Si enim interpretari velim iuxta verba, tam est absurda eorum sententia, vt te quidvis potius, quàm quod illis verbis significatur, cogitasse ac sensisse opiner. Repetā proximè dicta, vt sententia fiat planior. Ea sic habent. Has enim (cordis similitudine) sentiri & euidētes esse astrorū effectus clarè concedis, quos tamen eosdem rursus, velut attonitus quispiam nunc negas. Nisi forte per effectum alterationem intelligas, & dicas, alterationem dum afficimur ab astris, non sentiri aut deprehendi posse. At tute nosti ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ εἶναι αἴσθησιν, si non ex Aristotele, saltem ex Galeno. Quapropter alteratio nisi sensibilis fiat, effectus dici non potest. Donec enim effectus sensu non iudicatur, effectus dici nequit, nec est. Hæc tua sunt verba, quorum libenter sensum ex te ipso didicerim.
units.tr: I confess that I do not understand what follows in your letter. If I were to interpret it according to the words, its meaning is so absurd that I would think you had thought and felt anything rather than what those words signify. I will repeat what I said just now, so that the meaning becomes plainer. It reads thus: "For you clearly concede that these effects are perceived, and that the effects of the stars are evident (by the likeness of the heart), and yet, like someone astonished, you now deny the same effects." Unless perhaps by "effect" you mean alteration, and say that while we are affected by the stars the alteration cannot be sensed or detected. But you yourself know that alteration is not sensation [ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ εἶναι αἴσθησιν], if not from Aristotle, at least from Galen. Therefore, unless the alteration becomes sensible, it cannot be called an effect. For as long as an effect is not judged by the senses, it cannot be called an effect, and it is not one. These are your words, whose meaning I would gladly learn from yourself.

units.la: Mox, inquis, nihil referre siue vniuersali ratione siue particulari agant in hæc inferiora cœli. Si tua non refert, quod equidem credo, mea multum refert, qui non defendere nugas, sed veritatem inuestigare enitor. Quantum referat ex illis quæ hactenus disputata nobis sunt, præclarè cognosces, modò animum aduertas. Si nàque vniuersales duntaxat causæ sint astra, fluxa & inutilis est Galeni ratiocinatio, si id sensit, quod tu putas. Præterea est tota Astrologica vaticinario nil aliud quàm merum figmentum & ludibrium Sathanæ. Si res aliter habet, non prorsus erraueris. Tantum interest hoc ne an illo modo cœli agant. Quæ te non ignorare decebat, si tantus es, quantum te esse prædicas, logicus.
units.tr: Next, you say, it makes no difference whether the heavens act on these lower things in a universal or a particular way. If it makes no difference to you, which I indeed believe, it makes a great deal of difference to me, who strive not to defend trifles but to investigate the truth. You will clearly recognise how much it matters, from what has been disputed between us so far, provided you pay attention. For if the stars were only universal causes, Galen's reasoning would be weak and useless, if he thought what you suppose. Moreover, all astrological prophecy is nothing but a mere fiction and a plaything of Satan. If the matter stands otherwise, you will not be entirely wrong. The only difference lies in whether the heavens act in one way or the other. You ought not to be ignorant of this, if you are as great a logician as you proclaim yourself to be.

units.la: De mense Medicinali nihil admodum dicam in præsen-tia, propterea quòd cōmentum hoc ne peritioribus qui-dem Astrologis probare Galenus potuit. Nemo sanè do-ctus inde à Galeni usque temporibus inventus est, cui non hæc partitio displicuerit. Tu qui tantum tibi logices peri-tiam arrogas, rationem tecum Galeni studiosè expende, ut me nihil temerè dicere perspicias. Et ut facere commo-dius possis, pro mea tenuitate te adjuvabo.
units.tr: I will say very little for now about the medicinal month, because Galen could not prove this fiction even to the more skilled astrologers. Indeed, from Galen's time onwards no learned man has been found who has not disliked this division. You, who claim so much skill in logic for yourself, should weigh Galen's reasoning carefully with me, so that you may see that I do not speak rashly. And to help you do this more easily, I will assist you as far as my modest ability allows.

units.la: Mensis peragrationis, si cum apparitorio coniungatur, & summa per medium dividatur, atque medietas quadri-partito rursus secetur, atq; ex partibus quatuor hisce, tres tantum coniunctim sumantur, orientur dies 20. horæ 4. cum aliquot minutis. Hoc fundamentum est. Jam ratio-cinatio breviter hæc sit. Proximè dicta summa propin-quior est viginti, quàm viginti & uno diebus: ergo vigesi-mus, non autem vigesimus primus est decretorius. An ti-bi probabilis hæc ratiocinatio videtur? Mihi sanè non pro-batur, ut nec ullis aliis, qui non prorsus nihil hic vident. Cur puerili isto tibi argumento usus videtur? Respondes & quidem rectè, meo judicio, & Hippocratem ostenderet bene 20. diem, contra quàm alii quidam Clarissimi Medici fecissent, decretorium statuisse. Futura autem videbatur res credibilior, si alios etiam dies aliquot inde hoc accipe-re declararet. Hinc factum est, ut tertium illum librum si-bi scribendum duxerit. Hoc tu suprà negabas verum esse. Neque ego quamvis probabile sit, de eo cum quoquam contenderim, ut antè etiam monui. Parum etenim refert sive hoc, sive alio quopiam consilio eum librum conscri-ps![](# "placeholder") stm[?] est. Cæteris omnibus missis, tuam in disserendo peri-tiam considerare libet hoc etiam loco, cum ita argumenta-ris. Galenus non fecit fallendi causa, ergo non est nugatus. Quid nugationem vocent logici, non est opus hic pluribus exponere. In præsentia sufficiat monere, non eandem esse nugari & fallere. Potest enim quis infirma & frivola uti ratione, cum se firma admodum uti putat, nec aliter persuasus est. Non enim nugax ratio semper est sophistica sive captiosa, si animum eius, qui ea utitur, spectes. Sed frequenter pro infirma & lubrica minimeque momentanea, atque adeo pro ridicula ratione sumitur. Nugator itaque potest non esse, potest etiam esse sophista.
units.tr: Let the month of the course, when it is joined with the apparitional period, be taken in total and divided in the middle, and let the half be cut again into four parts, and let three of these four parts be taken together. There will result 20 days and 4 hours with some minutes. This is the foundation. Now the reasoning may be stated briefly. The sum just mentioned is nearer to twenty than to twenty-one days; therefore the twentieth, and not the twenty-first, is decisive. Does this reasoning seem plausible to you? It does not seem so to me, nor to anyone else who sees the matter at all. Why do you seem to have used that childish argument? You answer, and rightly in my judgement, that Hippocrates showed well that the twentieth day was decisive, unlike certain other very famous physicians, who had made it something else. The matter would, however, have seemed more credible if he had also shown that several other days follow from this. Hence it came about that he thought fit to write that third book. You denied above that this was true. Nor, although it is probable, have I contended about this with anyone, as I warned before. For it matters little whether he wrote that book for this purpose or for some other reason. Setting aside everything else, I should like to consider your skill in argument here too, since you argue thus: Galen did not do it for the sake of deceiving, therefore he did not talk nonsense. There is no need to explain at length here what the logicians call trifling. For the present it is enough to point out that to trifle and to deceive are not the same. For someone may use weak and frivolous reasoning while thinking he is using very firm reasoning, and being persuaded of nothing else. A trifling argument is not always sophistical or captious, if you look at the mind of the person who uses it. But it is often taken to mean a weak, slippery and almost worthless argument, and so a ridiculous one. Someone may therefore not be a trifler, and may yet be a sophist.

units.la: Quod necessariam me rationem à probabili non posse distinguere scriptitas, parum me movet, dum video, quàm aptè scitéque, si Diis placet, tu inter ipsas distinguas. Sophistam me immeritò appellas, cum fallere nunquam argumentris vel te vel alium quempiam propositum habuerim. Si quid tale in meis literis repereris, imprudenti utiq; excidit. admonitus non grauatè corrigam. At Galenus, inquies forte, ita te appellat. Scio quid Galenus dicat. Nec ignoro pleraque posse commodè exponi. Ubi res postulet, non sit admodum difficile ostendere, non continuò sophistam esse qui non credat, quæ illo in libro Galenus A-strologica scripsit.
units.tr: That you write that I cannot distinguish necessary reasoning from probable reasoning moves me little, since I see how neatly and cleverly, God willing, you distinguish between them. You call me a sophist unjustly, since I have never intended to deceive either you or anyone else by my arguments. If you find anything of the kind in my letters, it has slipped in through carelessness, and once I am warned I will gladly correct it. But Galen, you may perhaps say, calls him that. I know what Galen says. Nor am I unaware that most of it can be explained conveniently. Where the matter requires it, it would not be very difficult to show that a man is not necessarily a sophist if he does not believe what Galen wrote about astrology in that book.

units.la: Cæterum non cum Galeno, qui se defendere nequit, sed tecum in præsentiarum res mihi est. E-pistolæ tuæ satisfactum esse puto, quare finem facio.
units.tr: But for the present my business is not with Galen, who cannot defend himself, but with you. I think I have answered your letter, so I will make an end.

units.la: Die 5. No. Malfeldiæ.
units.tr: Given at Malfeldia, 5 November.

units.la: THOMAS ERASTVS D. CHRISTO-phoro Stathmioni, Medico Coburgensi S. D. Epistola IIII.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus to Christopher Stathmion, physician of Coburg, greetings. Letter IV.

units.la: ITERAE illæ tuæ, quas Cal. Ian. scripsisti, atq; ego ad septimum Id. accepi, paulò mihi æquiores visæ sunt quàm priores. Hoc præcipuè in te iam desidero, quòd non satis attentè mea legere, tuaque scribere videris. Quod si facere voluisses, nihil erat cur has scriberem. Sic enim quæ de Galeno adfers declarata & confutata mihi sunt in superioribus meis ad te literis, ut hæc omnia superuacanea censeri possint. Id ut dilucidius appareat, breuiter ea repetam. Dixi Astrologiam nihil artis opera exercēti commodare posse, etiamsi vera esse ponantur, quæ Gal. in 3. Decret. dierum proposuit. Hanc meam sententiam inde probari posse iudicaui, quòd Galenus in curando & prænoscendo ea nunquam usus fuisse reperiatur, neque nos, ut ea uteremur, iussisse alicubi legatur. Clarissimos quoque omnium ætatū post Galenum Medicos, quorum nomē est illustre & monumenta per Galliam, Italiam, Germaniam, extant plurima, summa cum gloria & felicitate sine Astrologiæ auxilio, quam & despexerunt & repudiarunt, medicinam exercuisse affirmaui. Quia verò te protinus videbam testimonium Galeni ex 3: decret. contra me productūrum, addidi suo loco, me non ignorare quòd illo in libro plus æquo huic ei fauisse viderētur, atque adeò sophistas illos appellasset, qui nō fidem adhibere suæ ibi disputationi voluissent. Quam autem non alij modò, sed etiam Astrologorum aliqui Galeni studium illud probarint, te non ignorare iam quoque existimo. Monui etiam Galenum amicè exponi atque excusari posse, præsertim quòd ad ea probanda, quæ illo in loco proposita habebat, Astrologiæ aliquid tribuere coactus videretur. Nam quòd aliter senserit, neque necessaria illa ad rectè medendum existimarit, cùm ex illo ipso libro, tum ex commentarijs in Aph. Hipp. patere posse docui. Etenim quæ usum aliquem conferre ad artis opera censuit, ea se vniuersa in prioribus duobus libris complexū fuisse scripsit, quæ vero in 3. docuit, ea per ocium legi posse putauit. Quòd si ad artem exercendam vel necessaria vel vtilia existimasset, nunquam id dixisset, præsertim cum indefessum vbique studium in talibus requirat. Præterea in illo ipso libro etiam indicia quædam inueniri scripsi, ex quibus intelligatur, eum sibi neque satisfecisse, neque causæ[?] sæ satis cōfidere potuisse. Per Deos immortales iurat, quòd alibi non solitus est facere, se inuitum & coactum ea planè paucis scripsisse amicis. Postea cum horum alibi meminit, non pro sua consuetudine confidenter asserit se ea demonstrasse, sed se tentasse ea probare aut inuenire tantum dicit. Locum ex Aph. produxi. Alter est in 3.Comment.in Prognost.Hippoc. Equidem quoties alibi hoc libros citat, quantum obseruare hactenus potui, propter priores duos citat, in quibus quæ docuit, vtilissima maximeque necessaria merito censentur. Hæc si[?]on ordine & deinceps, sed sparsim in prioribus posui, factum ob eā est causam, quòd tibi respondendum mihi memini. Ideo passim ea tuis solum opposui, quæ ad propositam mihi in quouis loco sententiam declarandam sufficere visa sunt. Quòd si tibi colligenda & examinanda duxisses, ex alijs Galeni libris testimonia conquisiuisses, non ex hoc tertio citasses, in quo ipsum Astrologica non aspernatum fuisse, iam ante confessus fueram.
units.tr: Your letters, which you wrote on the first day of January and which I received on the ninth of April, seemed to me somewhat more reasonable than your earlier ones. What I especially miss in you now is that you do not read my writings closely enough, and that your own writing seems to show the same carelessness. If you had been willing to do so, there would have been no reason for me to write these letters. What you cite from Galen has already been explained and refuted in my earlier letters to you, so that all of it could be judged superfluous. To make this clearer, I will briefly repeat the points. I said that Astrology can contribute nothing to the practice of the art, even if the things Galen proposed in the third book of his On Days of Decision were granted to be true. I judged that my view could be proved from this: Galen is never found to have used astrology in treating or in foretelling, nor is it anywhere read that he urged us to use it. I also affirmed that the most famous physicians of every age after Galen, whose names are illustrious and whose monuments survive in great number throughout France, Italy and Germany, practised medicine with the highest glory and success without the aid of astrology, which they both despised and rejected. But because I saw at once that you would bring forward Galen's testimony from the third book of On Decrees against me, I added in its place that I was not unaware that in that book he seemed to favour this doctrine more than was right, and indeed called those sophists who would not give credence to his disputation there. I think you are also not unaware how far not only others but even some of the astrologers have approved that enthusiasm of Galen's. I also warned that Galen could be kindly explained and excused, especially since, in order to prove what he had set out to prove in that place, he seemed compelled to grant something to astrology. For I showed that he thought otherwise, and that he did not consider those matters necessary for treating well, as can be seen both from that very book and from his commentaries on the Aphorisms of Hippocrates. For he wrote that he had comprehended in the first two books all that he judged to contribute some use to the practice of the art, while what he taught in the third he thought might be read at leisure. If he had judged them necessary or useful for practising the art, he would never have said this, especially since such a subject demands unflagging diligence everywhere. Moreover, I wrote that in that very book certain signs can be found from which it is understood that he could neither satisfy himself nor place sufficient trust in his argument. He swears by the immortal gods that he has written these things, which he does not usually do elsewhere, only briefly and under compulsion, and only to a few friends. Afterwards, when he mentions these matters elsewhere, he does not, as is his custom, confidently assert that he has demonstrated them, but says only that he has tried to prove or discover them. I cited a passage from the Aphorisms. The other is in the third Commentary on the Prognostics of Hippocrates. Indeed, as far as I have been able to observe so far, whenever he cites this book elsewhere, he cites the two former ones, in which what he taught is rightly judged most useful and especially necessary. I have set these points out not in order and one after another, but scattered through my earlier letters; this was because I remembered that I had to reply to you. So I have opposed to your statements only those points which seemed sufficient to explain the view I had put forward in each place. But if you had thought fit to gather and examine these things, you would have sought out testimonies from Galen's other books, and not cited this third book, in which I had already admitted beforehand that he did not disdain astrological matters.

units.la: Vt autem non querare posthac, age ex Galeno perspicuē valideque probabo, eum in curando & præsagiendo Astrologia nequaquam, sed sola arte Medica vsum fuisse. Conqueritur non vno in loco tantum Galenus, quòd pro uate habitus sit, & quòd, quæ prædixisset aliquando, diuinatricis alicuius artis ope præcognouisse creditus fuerit. Ne sim longior, vnicum ex tertio cap.libri de Præcognit. ad Posthumum testimonium huc adscribam, vbi de Martiano medico loquens ita scribit: At adeò non ex medica facultate, verùm ex diuinatricibus scientijs prædictiones meas fuisse mentiebatur, interrogatusq; à quibusdam, quasnam diuinatrices scientias diceret, interdum augurium, interdum extis spicium, nonnunquam coniectatricem, aliquando Mathema-ticam respondebat.
