At non explicatis hic verbis audis Galenum accusare Martianum Medicum mendacij, quia dixerit ipsum usum in prænotionibus mathematica siue Astrologia? Non puto pluribus opus esse, præsertim si addidero, Galenum multis in locis docere, quomodo futuri morborum euentus præuidendi sint, & in nullo tamen Astrologiç mentionem unquam fecisse. At si utilem aut necessariam ad hæc prænoscenda cognouisset, nunquam omisisset. Etenim aliorum nihil omittit, quamtumuis exiguum conferant, vbi ista ex professo tractat.
units.tr: But so that you may not complain hereafter, come, I will prove clearly and strongly from Galen that in treating and foretelling he never used astrology, but only the medical art alone. Galen complains in more than one place that he was regarded as a prophet, and that he was believed to have foreknown by the help of some divinatory art the things he had at some time predicted. Not to be too long, I will cite here one testimony alone, from the third chapter of the book On Prognosis, to Posthumus, where, speaking of the physician Martianus, he writes thus: "But he lied, saying that my predictions came not from medical skill but from divinatory sciences; and when some asked him what divinatory sciences he meant, he sometimes answered augury, sometimes inspection of entrails, sometimes conjecture, and sometimes mathematics." But do you hear, without the words being explained here, Galen accusing the physician Martianus of lying, because he said that he used mathematics or astrology in foreknowing outcomes? I do not think more is needed, especially if I add that Galen in many places teaches how the future outcomes of diseases are to be foreseen, and yet never once made mention of astrology. But if he had known it to be useful or necessary for this foreknowledge, he would never have omitted it. For he omits nothing else, however little it may contribute, when he treats these matters expressly.

units.la: Præterea quoties narrat quomodo in ęgris aliquando futura siue crises præsenserit, omnia ex quibus intelle-xerit enumerat, Astrologiç ne syllaba quidem una comme-minit. An non satis tibi hæc sint ad intelligendum, quòd nullibi ea sit in curationibus ipse usus, nec utendum ea nobis exis-timarit? Hæc si cū a[illegible, ~1 letter]è recensitis coniunxeris, haud difficulter videbis, quæ in 3. Decret. ex Astrologorum placitis protulit, minimè vel necessaria vel utilia ipsi visa fuisse ad ægrorum curationes. Quibus illud etiam addi potest, quod in illo tertio ipsi non fuit propositum docere, quomodo crises essent prænescendæ, vel ægri percurandi. Illud solum inuestigabat, an ratio aliqua inveniri posset qua probaretur, naturam uno die facilius & felicius decernere quàm alijs. Hoc enim experientia notum erat, sed cur ita usueniret, eo in loco indagare decreuerat. Ergo cum in prædictionibus Astrologia non sit usus Galenus, ut probatum est, ne in curationibus quidem ea usus credi ab homine sano poterit. Nam si usus aliquis ipsius sit, in prænotione futurorum esse oportet, vel ipsis Astrologis testibus. Quod si usus ipse non est, an nobis ea utendum putauit? Nihil minus credibile est. Iam, opinor, intelligis prudentissimè fecisse, atque etiam nunc facere, præstantissimos per Italiam & Galliam Medicos, cum Galenum imitantes, ex Medica arte, non ex astris de euentu morborum coniectāt ipsi, & coniectare nos præclarè docent. Horum ego auctoritate, & præterea falsitate impietateque Astrologicarum nugarum permotus, Astrologiam nihil ad curationes conferre bene, recte, vereque dixi. Iam ad tuas literas redeo.
units.tr: Moreover, whenever he relates how in sick people he at some time foresaw the future or the crises, he enumerates all the signs from which he understood them, and does not mention a single syllable of astrology. Are these facts not enough for you to understand that he nowhere used astrology in his treatments, nor judged that we should use it? If you join these things with what I have recalled, you will without difficulty see that the things he put forward from the opinions of the astrologers in the third book On Decrees did not seem to him at all necessary or useful for the treatment of the sick. To this can also be added that it was not his purpose in that third book to teach how crises were to be foreknown, or how the sick were to be treated. He was investigating only whether some reason could be found by which it might be proved that nature decides more easily and successfully on one day than on others. For this was known from experience, but he had resolved to inquire in that place why it so happened. Therefore, since Galen, as has been proved, did not use astrology in predictions, no one who is sane can believe that he used it in treatments either. For if he used it at all, it must have been in foretelling future events, as the astrologers themselves would witness. But if he did not use it even there, can it be thought that he judged we should use it? Nothing is less credible. Now, I think you understand that the most distinguished physicians throughout Italy and France acted most prudently, and still do, in imitating Galen: they conjecture the outcome of diseases themselves from the medical art and not from the stars, and they teach us excellently to conjecture likewise. Moved by their authority, and besides by the falsity and impiety of the astrological trifles, I have rightly, correctly and truly said that astrology contributes nothing well to treatments. Now I return to your letter.

units.la: Locum,quem ex 4.Aph.36.produxi,nihil ad rē facere ais; imò iugulare me eundem illum scribis. Quid tibi velis nescio. Ego Galenum eo in loco affirmare asserui, quòd quae ad opera artis utilia censeri debeant, in prioribus duobus libris persecutus sit, causas vero in 3. reddere tentarit, quas per ocium legi posse dixerit. Hic tu quid reprehendere possis, equidem non video. At experientiam, inquis, ne-gas. Nunquam ego negaui, imò ne dubitaui quidem aliquando, alios dies magis feliciusque decernere, quā alios. Nihilomnino improbo ex omnibus quae in praesenti loco Galenus asseuerauit. Sic sentio, Galenum, si, quę in 3.de diebus Decret. disputauit utilia ad exercēdam Medicinam cognouisset, non fuisse permissurum, imò praecepturum, ut per ocium talia exquireremus. Non enim quae necessa-rium in arte usum habent obiter addisci debent, sed summo studio cognoscenda sunt. Quod experientiam me ne-gare dicis, quomodo probaturus sis nequaquam intelligo. Quanquam si vere id de me dicere posses, non tamen hic recte argueres. Negas experientiam, ergo hic te locus iugu-lar. Egregia vero ratiocinatio. Sed de tua logica postea. Fortasse arbitratus es me experientiae aliquid detrahere, quia dixi particulares istas siderum effectiones, quas Astrologi somniant, nulla experientia ostendi atque cognosci posse. Etenim quod non est, cognosci nequit.
units.tr: You say that the passage I cited from the fourth Aphorism, number 36, has nothing to do with the matter; indeed you write that it destroys me. I do not know what you mean by this. I asserted that Galen in that place affirmed that he had pursued in the first two books what ought to be counted as useful for the works of the art, and had tried to give the causes in the third book, which, he said, might be read at leisure. Here I do not see what you could find to reproach. But you say I deny experience. I never denied it; indeed I never even doubted at any time that some days decide more happily and successfully than others. I utterly reject nothing of all that Galen has asserted in this place. My view is this: if Galen had known what he disputed in the third book On Days of Decision to be useful for practising medicine, he would not have allowed us to seek such things at leisure, but would rather have instructed us to do so. For things that have a necessary use in the art should not be learned by the way, but are to be known with the utmost diligence. As for your saying that I deny experience, I do not at all understand how you will prove it. Yet even if you could rightly say this of me, you would not argue correctly here. You deny experience; therefore this passage destroys you. An excellent piece of reasoning indeed. But I will speak of your logic later. Perhaps you thought I was detracting something from experience because I said that those particular effects of the stars which the astrologers dream up can be shown and known by no experience. For what does not exist cannot be known.

units.la: Proinde nihil habes, quo mihi hunc locum è manibus eripias, quo valide neruoseque probatur, Astrologicam Galeni dissertationem, quae in 3. Decret. continetur, nihil iuuare Medicas curationes. Adde quod Galenus primum se fuisse scribit, qui Decret. dierum causas in lunae motu quaesierit. Quod hinc etiam credibile fit, quia nullus est ex antiquioribus Galeno Medicis vel ab ipso, vel ab alio quopiam citatus, qui huc proprie pertineat. An tu ante Galenum neminem recte curasse ægros iudicas? Certe si neminem alium extitisse contendas, ipsum saltem Hippocratem mihi relinques. Quid igitur pro te excogitabis, ut Galeni illā Astrologiam usui nobis esse doceas ex Galenisententia‡ Locum adfers ex i.[?] cap.libri ad Posthumum, quem si aliquid hic probare existimas, in doctiores multò quàm ego putem.
units.tr: Therefore you have nothing with which to snatch this point out of my hands, the point which is strongly and firmly proved: Galen's astrological discourse, contained in the third book of the Decret., does nothing to help medical cures. Add that Galen writes that he was the first to seek the causes of the decretory days in the motion of the moon. This also makes it credible, because none of the physicians older than Galen is cited by him or by anyone else as bearing properly on this. Do you judge that no one before Galen cured the sick correctly? Certainly, if you contend that no one else existed, you will at least leave me Hippocrates himself. What then will you devise to show us that Galen's astrology is useful to us, according to Galen's own opinion? You cite a passage from the first chapter of the book to Posthumus, and if you think it proves anything here, you are far more learned than I suppose.

units.la: Quæ porrò ex libro peculiariter Astrologiæ dedicato (ita enim tu scribis) tanquam Galeni legitimo & genuino opere citas, responsione minimè digna sunt. Tres leuissimæ coniecturæ te impulerunt, ut contra omnium doctorum judicium Galeni esse legitimum credas. Stilus[?] est Galeni, ergo ipse autor est. Argumentum huius simile est ei quod in 3. Decret. tractatur, ergo idem utriusque operis est autor. Galenus citat Dioclem. Hic autor citat eundem, ergo Galenus autor fuit. Hæ sunt grauissimæ illæ tres causæ, ut tu loqueris, quæ tibi persuaserunt Galenum ista composuisse. Quisquis autor fuerit, parum Medicæ artis peritus fuit, quod omnes ij affirmabunt qui cum judicio perlegere volent. Ex ipso statim libri principio tum de eruditione, tum artis disserendi peritia coniecturam capere licet. Ita enim fere arguit, ut tu in tertia tua coniectura. Oro te considera quantus sis logicus, ut cautius posthac agas. Si quia Dioclem citat autor, Galenus tibi autor est, multos certè Galenus libros scripsit, quos nunquam vidit. Ex duabus aientibus in secunda figura nihil efficitur, nisi vera ca-su aliquando inde exoriatur conclusio. Arte talis collectio prorsus caret. Stilum Galeni esse nemo praeter te dicer faci le. Quo fit ut laboris me hic merito pigeat. Simile argumentum, hic & in 3. Decret. tractari quomodo sis probaturus, & quibus argumentis, libenter equidem videam. Ne prudentiores quidem Astrologi tibi hac in re assentiantur.
units.tr: Moreover, what you cite from the book devoted specially to astrology (for so you call it), as a genuine and authentic work of Galen, is in no way worthy of a reply. Three very slight conjectures have led you to believe, against the judgement of all learned men, that Galen is the legitimate author. (1) The style is Galen's, therefore he is the author. (2) The subject is similar to that treated in the third book of the Decret., therefore the same man wrote both works. (3) Galen cites Diocles; this author cites the same man, therefore Galen was the author. These, as you put it, are the very weighty three reasons which persuaded you that Galen composed these things. Whoever the author was, he had little skill in the medical art, as all those will affirm who read the book through with judgement. From the very beginning of the book one may draw a conjecture both of his learning and of his skill in reasoning. For he argues roughly as you do in your third conjecture. I beg you to consider how great a logician you are, so that you act more cautiously hereafter. If Galen is the author for you because the author cites Diocles, then Galen certainly wrote many books that he never saw. Nothing follows from two affirmative premises in the second figure, except that a true conclusion may occasionally arise from them by chance. Such a collection entirely lacks art. No one but you would easily say that the style is Galen's. Hence I am rightly weary of this labour. I would gladly see how you will prove the similar argument, treated here and in the third book of the Decret., and by what arguments you will do so. Not even the more prudent astrologers agree with you in this matter.

units.la: Ego quia petis, argumentis duobus hic longè firmissimè probabo non esse eum Galeni. Plura si quis cupiat, facile per se inveniet. Docti omnes Medici Galeno judignū, & ab ipsius doctrina prorsus alienum judicant. Negare nō poteris ita rem habere, nisi si quod testatum notumq; est cunctis, audacter negare velis. Addo alterum. Galenus in Catalogo suorum librorum huius non meminit, ergo non est autor. Si ergo nec Galenus pro suo eum agnouit, nec viri clarissimi eruditione Galeno dignum censu e-runt, miror quomodo plus tibi credas hac in parte, quàm vel Galeno vel summis ingenio, iudicio, eruditione viris. At Galeni catalogum, dices forte, mutilum esse. Verum id est, sed in ea tamen parte, in qua recensendus fuisset (fuisset autem inter prognosticos reponendus) mancus nō est.
units.tr: Since you ask, I will here prove, by two arguments, and very firmly, that it is not Galen's. If anyone wants more, he will easily find them for himself. All learned physicians judge it unworthy of Galen and wholly alien to his doctrine. You cannot deny that the matter stands thus, unless you wish to boldly deny what is attested and known to everyone. I add a second argument. Galen does not mention this book in his catalogue of his own books, therefore he is not the author. If, then, Galen did not acknowledge it as his own, and the most distinguished men of learning have not judged it worthy of Galen, I wonder how you can believe it in this matter more than either Galen or men most eminent in talent, judgement and learning. But you will perhaps say that Galen's catalogue is incomplete. That is true; yet in that part where the book should have been listed (it would have been placed among the prognostics), the catalogue is not defective.

units.la: Cum caussarum alias dico esse generales & remotas, alias verò particulares & propinquas, tu me nescio quid Erasistrati simile facere pronuncias. An ignoras non me ista excogitasse, sed caussarum istam distinctionem ab omnibus philosophis, qui vnquam extiterunt, agnitam, probatam, traditam fuisse? Si demonstrationem, vt tu opinaris, non intelligo, vix ex re discam. Illud mihi hoc loco satis est, quod nihil tu meorum falsum docere hucusque potui, cum ego penè omnia tua refutarim, falsaque esse, aut ad rem nihil pertinere docuerim. De experientia quam me iterum affirmas negare, & aliis huius generis pluribus nihil praeterea dicam. Nam aut respondi ad ea, aut extra rem propositam dicuntur.
units.tr: When I say that causes are on the one hand general and remote, and on the other particular and proximate, you pronounce that I am doing something like Erasistratus. Do you not know that I did not devise this? This distinction of causes has been recognised, proved and handed down by all the philosophers who have ever existed. If I do not understand the demonstration, as you suppose, I could scarcely learn it from the matter. For me it is enough at this point that you have so far been unable to show anything of mine to be false, since I have refuted nearly all your points and shown them either to be false or to have nothing to do with the question. About experience, which you again say I deny, and about the other points of this kind, I will say nothing further. For either I have already answered them, or they are raised beside the matter in hand.

units.la: Illorum verborum expositionem, quę nuper interpre-tari nolui, (ne, cum absurdam continerent sententiam, iniquè tecum agere dici credique possem) ita tu iam inter-pretaris, vt ego tum quoq; intelligenda fueram suspicatus. Facile iam praeterijssem, si non tu repetiuisses. Nō enim me mineram amplius. Nunc perpendere examinareque libet, vt non sine errore te esse opineris. Dixeram particulares siderum vires & earundem actionis effectus, de quibus A-strologi loquuntur, sentiri non posse. (Quis enim quod non est in rerum natura percipiat sensu?) generales posse. Et qualem esse putarem generalem istam vim coeli, exem-plo cordis expositui. Quod cum minus probè tu perpendis-ses, me, quod antè negassem, mox velut attonitum iterum affirmare scripsisti. Et cum suspicatus fuisses me responsurum, quod per effectus astrorum in hisce terrenis rebus alterationem intellexissem, omnem mihi elabendi occasio-nem praeclusurus, nullam alterationem, qua alteratio est, effectum esse dicíque posse scribis. Quid aliud volueris, excogitari non facile queat. Etenim si aliud voluisse rogi-teris, nihil ad rem dicis, nec probas aduersus me quicquā. Verba tua haec sunt: Sic confirmauit (Galenus, astra in haec inferiora agere) vt nihil opus sit quicquam tua similitudine cordis ieiuna, ad hoc probandum amplius, qua tamen tu te ipsum iugulas non secus quàm demens aliquis aut mentis impos proprio se ense confodit. Hoc enim sentiri & euidentes esse astrorum effectus clarè concedis, quos tamen eosdem rursus attonitus quispiam nunc negas. Nisi forte per effectum alterationem intelligas, & dicas, alterationem dum afficimur ab astris, non sentiri aut deprehendi posse. At tuae nostri ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ ἀναισθητον[?] si non ex Aristotele, saltē ex Galeno. Quapropter alteratio nisi sensibilis fiat, effectus dici nequit. Donec enim effectus sensu non iudicatur, effectus dici non potest nec est. Hactenus tua recitaui.
units.tr: I did not wish to interpret those words I spoke recently (lest, since they contained an absurd opinion, I might be said and believed to deal unfairly with you). Now you interpret them in such a way that I too was then suspected of being understood. I would have passed over it easily, had you not repeated it, for I no longer remember them. Now I am pleased to weigh and examine them, so that you may not think yourself free from error. I had said that the particular powers of the stars and the effects of their action, of which the astrologers speak, cannot be perceived by the senses (for who could perceive by sense what is not in the nature of things?), but that the general power can. And I set out, by the example of the heart, what sort of general power of the heaven I thought it to be. Since you weighed this rather poorly, you wrote that I, as if astonished, affirmed again what I had earlier denied. And since you suspected that I would reply that by the effects of the stars I had understood an alteration in these earthly things, you wished to close off every chance of escape for me, and you write that no alteration can be called an effect, in so far as it is an alteration. What else you meant is hard to imagine. For if you ask that I take you to have meant something else, you say nothing to the point, and you prove nothing against me. Your words are these: Thus he (Galen) confirmed that the stars act on these lower things, so that there is no need to add anything further to prove this, your similitude of the heart being barren; yet by it you cut your own throat no differently than some madman or someone out of his mind stabs himself with his own sword. For you clearly concede that this is felt and that the effects of the stars are plainly evident, which same effects someone astonished now denies. Unless perhaps by effect you mean alteration, and say that alteration, while we are affected by the stars, cannot be perceived or detected. But your phrase [ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ ἀναισθητον], if not from Aristotle, is at least from Galen. Wherefore, unless an alteration becomes sensible, it cannot be called an effect. For as long as an effect is not judged by sense, it cannot be called an effect, nor is it one. So far I have quoted your words.

units.la: Primùm non adduxi exemplum cordis ad probandum coelos inferiora ista permutare. Non sum enim tam rerum imperitus, vt nesciam exempla nihil probare, illud declarare exemplo eo volui, quomodo coelestia in haec terrena agere concederem. Quare non memet eo confutaui, aut mihi contradixi, multò minus me iugulaui. Aliud est cum dicitur, coelum vniuersalem causam esse permutationum huius mundi inferioris, & cum negatur esse particularis & propinqua seu proxima causa eorum, quae hic fiunt. Hanc posteriorem coeli vim cum esse nego, & experientia nulla astrui posse assero, tu me falli probaturus, duo tibi sumis non falsa modò, sed etiam ab omnium philosophia tum eruditione aliena. Horum alterum est, Nullam alterationem esse sensum. Alterum verò, Effectum non aut esse aut dici effectum posse, antequam sensibilis sit factus. Idem enim puto haec duo (sensibilem fieri, & sensu iudicari) significare. Sed praestiterit fortasse in syllogismos redigere, vt clariora omnia fiant.
units.tr: First, I did not adduce the example of the heart to prove that the heavens change these lower things. For I am not so ignorant of things as not to know that examples prove nothing; I wished to show by that example how I would allow that celestial things act on these earthly things. Therefore I did not refute myself by it, nor contradict myself, much less cut my own throat. It is one thing to say that the heaven is the universal cause of the changes in this lower world, and another to deny that it is the particular and proximate cause of the things that happen here. When I deny this latter power of the heaven, and assert that it cannot be established by any experience, you, wishing to prove me wrong, take to yourself two propositions that are not only false but also alien to the philosophy and learning of all. The first is that no alteration is perceived by sense. The second is that an effect neither is nor can be called an effect before it has become sensible. For I think these two mean the same thing (becoming sensible, and being judged by sense). But it would perhaps be better to reduce them to syllogisms, so that everything becomes clearer.

units.la: Cum probare statuisses alterationem nō esse effectum, sic ratiocinaris. Omnis effectus est sensibilis. Nulla alteratio est sensus. Nulla igitur alteratio est sensibilis. Si in prima figura videre mauis, reducetur per minoris transposi-tionem tionem & conuersionem hoc pacto. Nullus sensus est alteratio. At omnis effectus est sensibilis. Nullus ergo esse-ctus est alteratio. Et per conuersionem, Nulla ergo alteratio est effectus. Si libet formetur sic: Quod non est sensibile, non est effectus: Atqui alteratio non est sensus, ergo alteratio non est effectus. Vel sic, vt tu posuisti. Alteratio non est sensus, ergo alteratio nisi percipiatur sensu, non est effectus. In istis te tanquam in speculo contempleris licet. Et si feceris, recte sane facies. Sic enim quantus sis logicus pariter & philosophus discere incipies. Quomodocunq; ra-tionem formare coneris, si tuas sumtiones conseruare vo-les, quatuor semper terminos reperies. Deinde non minus veram esse hanc argumentationem intelliges. Cor non est oculus, ergo non est corporis pars aut membrum, nisi vi-deatur. Firmior certe haec est quam tua,
units.tr: Since you have resolved to prove that alteration is not an effect, you reason thus: Every effect is sensible. No alteration is sensed. Therefore no alteration is sensible. If you prefer to see it in the first figure, it will be reduced by transposing the minor premise and by conversion, thus: No sense is an alteration. But every effect is sensible. Therefore no effect is an alteration. And by conversion: Therefore no alteration is an effect. If you like, let it be formed thus: What is not sensible is not an effect; but alteration is not sense; therefore alteration is not an effect. Or thus, as you put it: Alteration is not sense; therefore alteration, unless it is perceived by sense, is not an effect. In these you may look at yourself as in a mirror, and if you do so you will do well indeed, for thus you will begin to learn how great a logician and likewise philosopher you are. However you try to frame the argument, if you wish to keep your premises, you will always find four terms. Then you will understand that this argument is no less true: The heart is not an eye; therefore it is not a part or member of the body, unless it is seen. Certainly this is firmer than yours,

units.la: Sed videamus quomodo probes omnē effectū esse sensibilē (Alteram propositionē tam putas esse veram, vt ab A-ristot. & Galeno probatam, & ab his discī posse putes. Tam es feliciter in his autoribus versatus.) Donec effectus non percipitur sensu, non est effectus, ergo omnis effectus sensu percipitur. Hoc pacto quiduis probaueris. Donec intelle-ctio non sentitur, non est intellectio, ergo intellectus actio sensu iudicatur. Donec coctiones, distributiones, nutrica-tiones, auctiones sensu no iudicantur, non sunt hoc ipsum quod esse perhibentur. Ergo sensu iudicantur. Sed & con-tra tuam positionem argumentabor, & probabo alteratio-nem omnem sensibilem esse. Donec alteratio non perci-pitur sensu, non est alteratio, ergo omnis alteratio sensu comprehenditur. Vel ita, ergo omnis alteratio sensus est. Non ego repente tuam perdidici logicam? Docilem me esse fareberis, scio, cum meam hanc in re imitando indu-striam perspexeris. Nolo hic logica examinare amplius. De ipsis aliquid rebus dicam.
units.tr: But let us see how you prove that every effect is sensible. (You think the other proposition is true, as proved by Aristotle and Galen, and you think you can learn it from them. You have been so happily versed in these authors.) Until an effect is perceived by the senses, it is not an effect; therefore every effect is perceived by the senses. In this way you could prove anything. Until an act of understanding is not sensed, it is not an act of understanding; therefore the action of the intellect is judged by the senses. Until concoctions, distributions, nutritions and growths are not judged by the senses, they are not what they are said to be; therefore they are judged by the senses. But I will also argue against your position and prove that every alteration is sensible. Until an alteration is not perceived by the senses, it is not an alteration; therefore every alteration is comprehended by the senses. Or thus: therefore every alteration belongs to the senses. Have I suddenly unlearned your logic? You will say I am teachable, I know, once you have seen how diligently I imitate you in this matter. I do not wish to examine logic any further here. I will say something about the things themselves.

units.la: Apud quem tu autorem legisti, effectum non esse quod dicitur, tantisper dum sensu percipi nequit? Effectus non cum sensu, sed cum efficiente sui causa confertur. Ab hac quatenus producitur, aut productus intelligitur, effectus st ac nominari effectus debet, siue in sensus cadat, siue nō cadat. Ratio docet, quòd ab aliquo efficitur, id eiusdem illius rei effectum esse oportere. Suspicor te pro opere dixisse effectum. Verum hic etiam te ipsum falleres. Etenim naturæ actiones docet Galenus naturæ opera etiam esse diciq̃e. Quid præterea diceres motiones illas esse, post quas opus nullum relinquitur, qualis est saltatio, cantio, & huiusmodi alia penè infinita? An non istæ omnes motiones, tametsi nihil quod permaneat efficiant, earum facultatum à quibus producuntur effectus sunt, atque etiam opera? Non nescio talia opera ab illis plurimum differre, quæ actione abeunte relinquuntur. Post scriptas literas, incidit mihi suspicio, te per effectum intellexisse affectum. Verum quidem est, Galenum rectè affirmare affectum, [?]ἀλλοίωσιν, ante non esse, quàm alteratio desierit in permanentem qualitatem, hoc est, qualitatem esse, quæ permanet: aut certè permanere, si naturam eius consideres, potest tum alteratio desijt. Sed hoc si dicere voluisti, neque contra me aliquid probasti (Nulla enim nobis hac de re lis est) neque verum est omnem affectum esse sensilem. Omnes etenim dispositiones siue affectus & habitus animi sensu nullo percipiuntur, vt de cæteris nihil dicam.
units.tr: Which author did you read saying that an effect is not an effect for as long as it cannot be perceived by the senses? An effect is not compared with the sense but with the efficient cause of which it is the effect. Insofar as it is produced by that cause, or is understood as produced, it is and ought to be called an effect, whether it falls under the senses or not. Reason teaches that what is brought about by something must be an effect of that same thing. I suspect you said "effect" when you meant "work." But even here you would be deceiving yourself. For Galen teaches that the actions of nature are also called its works. What would you say about those motions after which no work remains, such as dancing, singing and almost countless other things of this kind? Are not all these motions, although they produce nothing that remains, effects of the faculties by which they are produced, and indeed works? I am not unaware that such works differ greatly from those which are left behind when the action passes away. After writing my letter, it occurred to me that you may have understood "effect" to mean "affection." It is true that Galen rightly affirms that an affection [ἀλλοίωσιν] does not exist before the alteration has ceased into a permanent quality, that is, into a quality which remains, or at least, if you consider its nature, can remain; then the alteration has ceased. But if this is what you wished to say, you have proved nothing against me (for we have no dispute about this matter), nor is it true that every affection is sensible. For all dispositions or affections and habits of the mind are perceived by no sense at all, to say nothing of the rest.

units.la: Porrò ne alteram quidem tuam positionem verum esse declarabo. Tu Aristotelem & Galenum testes aduocas. At hi viri tam absurdæ & falsæ sententiæ testimonium nullum vnquam perhibebunt. At verò in proximis, inquis, probaui. Itaque videamus probationem æquum est. Ratio tua in hisce verbis consistit. Nemo enim vnquam se pinguescere aut macrescere, longum aut breuem fieri, aut in summa, augeri minuiue sentit, licet auctū, minutum, iam clarè deprehendat, &c. Argumentum hoc est. Nemo se sentit alterari, aut nemo alterationem percipit sensu, ergo alteratio non est sensus. Si antecedens verum sit, hoc sequeretur, alterationem non esse sensilem. At sensum non esse, quomodo ex positis consequatur, tu videris. Ego omnibus omissis cæteris, de tua positione duntaxat aliquid dicam.
units.tr: Nor will I show that your other proposition is true. You call Aristotle and Galen as witnesses. But these men will never bear witness to so absurd and false an opinion. But, you say, I proved it in the preceding words. Let us see whether the proof is fair. Your reasoning rests on these words: "No one ever feels himself to grow fat or lean, to become tall or short, or, in short, to be increased or diminished, although he clearly perceives that he has been enlarged or reduced, etc." The argument is this: no one feels himself altered, or no one perceives alteration by the senses; therefore alteration is not sensible. If the antecedent is true, it would follow that alteration is not sensible. But how it follows from what you have laid down that alteration is not a sense, you must see for yourself. I, leaving aside all the others, will say something only about your position.

units.la: Sensus apud philosophos tria significat, licet nomine ad tria ista notanda abutantur aliquantum, scilicet actionem sensus, ut visionem, instrumentum, ut oculum, & postremo facultatem, ut aspiciendi virtutem. Sic propositio tua, qua alterationem sensum negas, vera concedi poterit, si pro instrumento, vel pro ipsa met facultate posita sit. Non enim alteratio potest alterutrum duorum esse. Falsum nihilominus erit, nullam alterationem esse sensum. Etenim ipsa sensio est alteratio quaedam. At hęc aliquando sensus dicitur omnibus bonis autoribus. Sensus enim ex sententia Peripateticorum, quorum princeps est Aristotatque[?] Galenus (in eadem opinione Platonem fuisse vel ex ipso Galeno cognoscere promtum est) in quodam pati consistit. Et omnis sensio est passio, non quidem corrumpens, sed perficiens. Porro omnem passionem esse alterationem tumet, nisi plane nihil intelligas, confiteberis. Hinc sequitur, omnem sensionem esse alterationem: & per conversionem, quandam alterationem esse sensum. Falsa igitur tua est oratio, quae nullam alterationem sensum affirmat. Nunquid melius ipse tibi, quàm tu facias, quod volo perficere concludereque videor? Si propositionem maiorem converteris, quod volo in tertia figura aptissimè conficies.
units.tr: Among the philosophers "sense" has three meanings, although in naming these three things people use the word somewhat loosely: the act of sensing, as seeing; the instrument, as the eye; and finally the faculty, as the power of seeing. So your proposition, by which you deny that alteration is a sense, may be granted as true if it is taken to refer to the instrument or to the faculty itself. For alteration cannot be either of these two. Nevertheless it will be false that no alteration is a sense. For sensation itself is a certain alteration. And this is sometimes called "sense" by all good authors. For according to the opinion of the Peripatetics, whose prince is Aristotle and Galen (that Plato held the same opinion one may readily learn even from Galen himself), sense consists in a certain undergoing. And every sensation is a passion, not indeed destroying but perfecting. Further, you will confess that every passion is an alteration, unless you understand nothing at all. From this it follows that every sensation is an alteration, and conversely, that some alteration is a sense. Your statement, then, which denies that any alteration is a sense, is false. Does it not look better to you, when you do it yourself, than when you do what I want to accomplish and seem to conclude? If you convert the major proposition, you will very aptly accomplish, in the third figure, what I want.

units.la: Quòd si obiicias te non pro generali hanc posuisse orationem tuam, sed pro particulari, facilis est responsio. Tu eam simpliciter veram iudicasti, imò necessariam, quod ex tua probatione liquet. Quare pro generali posuisse videris. Deinde nisi ita tu senseris, nihil adversus mea attulisti. Hoc enim propositum tibi fuerat probare, nullam alterationem effectum dici posse. Caeterum cum particulares effectus astrorum nulla experientia cognosci posse dixi, quod scilicet vim habeant astra particulares effectus producendi, non de alterationibus solum id intellexi, sed de rebus cunctis quae & nascuntur & intereunt non necessario. Frustra igitur si quae attulisti vera maximè essent, illis me oppugnare tentasses. Sic ad interrogationem tibi responsum vides, qua quaeris quid absurdi, & à philosophia alieni in tuis verbis deprehenderim. Cuncta[?] namque cum à philosophia, tum à logica discordare perspicis.
units.tr: But if you object that you did not put forward your statement as a general one but as a particular one, the reply is easy. You judged it simply true, indeed necessary, as your proof makes clear. Therefore you seem to have put it forward as a general one. Furthermore, unless you thought so, you have brought nothing against my views. For you had proposed to prove that no alteration can be called an effect. Moreover, when I said that the particular effects of the stars cannot be known by any experience, because the stars have the power to produce particular effects, I understood this not only of alterations but of all things which come into being and perish not by necessity. Therefore, if what you brought forward were most true, you would have tried in vain to attack me with it. So you see that I have answered your question, in which you ask what absurd things, alien to philosophy, I have detected in your words. For you perceive that everything you say disagrees both with philosophy and with logic.

units.la: Rursus me trahis ad dissertationē de experientia. Succes-ses mihi propterea quòd me non probare sententiam tuā ostendi, quā nihil aliud quàm sensuum confirmationem esse asseuerabas. In hisce igitur idem illud pro tuo more erudite hoc modo probas. Cum enim sit rei eodem modo sæpius euenientis obseruatio experientia, illud non tam de visu, quàm de gustu, olfactu, & tactu intelligi debet & solet. Vnde etiam addo illud, quod qui negat experientiam, eum etiam sensus ipsos negare. Quid ergo culpas hic quoque, nisi forte nodum in scirpo quaeris? Hæc tua sunt. Quid culpem quæris? Omnia ferè culpanda sunt, sed ego hoc loco non extra propo-situm egrediar. Tu experientiam aliud nihil esse scribebas, quàm sensuum confirmationem. Iam scribis esse eiusdem rei eodem modo sæpius factæ obseruationem, vt à me doctus es. Quod si ergo prior tua sententia vera est, & posterior negari nequit, oportebit concedere duas istas tuas orationes idem significare. At hoc falsum est. Culpo præterea ratiocinationem tuam, est obseruatio rei eodem modo sæpe factæ, ergo est sensuum cōfirmatio. Culpo etiā quod sensuum confirmationem dixisti. Aut enim instrumenta, aut facultates aut actiones sensuum confirmabit. At horum nullum confirmare potest. Culpo quod nondum didicisse videris, ex sensionibus eiusdem in eodem modo euenientis, sæpè repetitis, gigni memoriam, ex quarum deinceps collectione seu obseruatione oriatur experien-tia. Culpo quod memoriam sensus confirmare putasti. Memoria est quasi quidam thesaurus simulachrorum per sensus ad animum ingressorum. Quæ licet à sensibus profecta sunt, ad sensus tamen non redeunt. Vnde patet memoriam per sensuum actiones fieri, & ab his tanquam à caussa, non tamen sine medio, procedere. Quomodo ergo sensus confirmabit, aut quomodo nil erit aliud, quàm confirmatio sensuum experientia, quæ ex multis memorijs, vt sic dicam, coalescit constatúe[?]? Culpo quod non considerasti obseruationem esse quandam veluti ratiocina-tionem, quæ neque est sensuum confirmatio, neque con-firmafirmationis eorum caussa. Opiniones quas de certis rebus habemus, per tales observationes confirmari non nescimus. At sensus quomodo confirment non intelligimus.
units.tr: Again you drag me into a discussion about experience. I have yielded on this point, because I showed that you do not prove your opinion, which you kept asserting was nothing other than a confirmation of the senses. In these matters, then, you prove the same thing, in your learned manner, in this way: For since experience is the observation of a thing which happens often in the same way, that is to be understood and commonly is understood not so much of sight as of taste, smell and touch. Hence I add also that whoever denies experience, denies the senses themselves. Why, then, do you find fault here too, unless perhaps you are looking for a knot in a bulrush? These are your words. What do you ask me to find fault with? Almost everything deserves blame, but at this point I will not go beyond the matter in hand. You wrote that experience is nothing other than a confirmation of the senses. Now you write that it is the observation of a thing done often in the same way, as you were taught by me. If, then, your former statement is true, and the latter cannot be denied, it must be conceded that these two statements of yours mean the same thing. But this is false. Further, I find fault with your reasoning: it is an observation of a thing often done in the same way, therefore it is a confirmation of the senses. I also find fault with your saying that it is a confirmation of the senses. For it will confirm either the instruments, or the faculties, or the actions of the senses. But it can confirm none of these. I find fault with the fact that you seem not yet to have learned that memory arises from repeated sensations of the same thing happening in the same way, and that experience arises from the collection or observation of these memories. I find fault with your thinking that memory confirms the sense. Memory is, as it were, a store of images that have entered the mind through the senses. Although they proceed from the senses, they do not return to the senses. Hence it is clear that memory comes about through the actions of the senses and proceeds from them as from a cause, yet not without an intermediary. How, then, will sense confirm it, or how will experience, which coalesces, so to speak, out of many memories and is composed of them, be nothing other than a confirmation of the senses? I find fault with your failing to consider that observation is a kind of reasoning, which is neither a confirmation of the senses nor a cause of their confirmation. We know that the opinions we hold about certain things are confirmed by such observations. But we do not understand how the senses confirm anything.

units.la: Suspicor te hoc dicere voluisse, experientia opiniones, quae per actiones sensuum ortae sunt, confirmari atque comprobari. Similiter fere supra quoque cum diceres ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ εἶναι αἴσθησιν[?], cogor cogitare te dicere voluisse, ἀλλοίωσιν[?] ὡς[?] non esse sensum. Hoc enim probationes additae significare posse videntur. Verumtamen sive haec sive alia quaedam utrobique intellexeris, aut te dicere putaris, non est cur divinare velim, cum praesertim artem vaticinandi nullam (nulla enim extat) didicerim. Tua ita exposui, ut tu ipse ea intelligi voluisti. Cum tibi per imprudentiam excidisse cogitarem, atque ideo ut corrigeres monerem, non modo nihil impetravi, sed calumniari propterea a te creditus sum. Iam opinor perspicis, quo animo tecum hactenus egerim.
units.tr: I suspect you meant to say that opinions which arise through the actions of the senses are confirmed and established by experience. Similarly, above too, when you said ἀλλοίωσιν οὐκ εἶναι αἴσθησιν[?], I am forced to think you meant to say that ἀλλοίωσιν[?] ὡς[?] is not sense. For the additional proofs seem to signify this. However, whether you understood this or something else on both points, or whether you think you said it, I have no reason to want to guess, especially since I have never learned the art of prophesying (for there is none). I have set out your words just as you wished them to be understood. When I thought you had let these things slip through carelessness, and so warned you to correct them, not only did I gain nothing, but I was thought by you to be slandering you for it. I think you now see in what spirit I have dealt with you until now.

units.la: Vale.8.Id. Ianuarij.Maffeldiæ[?].
units.tr: Farewell. Maffeldiae[?], 8 days before the Ides of January.

units.la: THOMAS ERASTUS D. CHRISTOPHORO Stathmioni, Medico Coburgensi S. D. Epistola V.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus to Christopher Stathmio, physician of Coburg, greetings. Letter V.

units.la: CUm heri domum revertissem, tuas reperi literas, in quibus tui similis es. Miror te ne duplici quidem responsione contentum esse posse, sed eadem identidem odiose repetere. Excidisse ne tibi credam qua de re controversia inter nos sit? Hoc quaerebatur, An Galenus in curando Astrologia usus fuisset. Ego nunquam ipsum adhibuisse multis ostendi, quae tu certe non labefecisti. Caeterum quia te ad 3. Decret. provocatarum praevidebam, firmis coniecturis & ipsusmet Galeni testimoniis probavi, Galenum illo in loco praeter suam & voluntatem & consuetudinem Astrologum fuisse. Non enim ignorabam te aliud nihil habiturum, si illum tibi locum extorsissem. Quod praeterea neque confiderit[?] satis caussæ, id quoque est declaratum. Tandem copiose demonstravi eum praeceptis illis Astrologicis in curandis morbis nunquam usum fuisse. Quæ cum ita habeant, libet jam videre, quo pacto refellere ea, quæ pro meæ sententiæ confirmationem attuli, tentaveris.
units.tr: Yesterday, when I had come home, I found your letter, and in it you are just like yourself. I am surprised that you cannot be content even with a double answer, but keep repeating the same objections tediously. Am I to believe you have forgotten what our controversy is about? The question was whether Galen used astrology in curing. I showed at length that he never employed it, and you have certainly not overturned that. Since I foresaw that you would appeal to the third book of the Decretoria, I proved by firm conjectures and by Galen's own testimonies that in that passage Galen was an astrologer against both his will and his custom. I knew you would have nothing else left if I wrested that passage from you. I have also shown that he had no sufficient grounds for confidence. Finally, I demonstrated at length that he never used those astrological precepts in curing diseases. Since this is so, I now want to see how you have tried to refute the arguments I brought forward to confirm my view.

units.la: Ad locum de Martiano Medico Romano respondes, non dixisse Galenum quòd falsò ab eo sit accusatus, aut quòd mentitus sit, cum ipsum dixit mathematica usum. Ait, inquis, Martianum criminatum & cavillatum esse quasi mathematicus esset. Διαβάλλει [?] enim scribitur in textu, non ἐψεύ-δετο. Et hæc prima est responsio. Addis alteram hoc modo. Patet hoc loco mathematica de non naturali divinatione intelligi, quod species enumeratæ Augurij, Extispicij, &c. declarant. Hic me contra meam voluntatem grammatica, quæ supra data opera aliquoties dissimulaui, tentare oportet. Cavillari Latinis duo fere significat, scilicet σκώπτειν aut χερτομεῖν [?], iocari aliquis dixerit, & σοφίζεσθαι, quam vocem cum Cicerone Latini omnes pene interpretantur verbo cavillari. Martianus ergo cum non luserit aut iocatus cum Galeno sit, quem propter invidiam pessimè oderat, cuiq; odium apud omnes conflare studebat, ergo in posteriore significato intelligi accipiique vox ea debebit. Unde sequitur tuam primam responsionem Astrologicam, hoc est, putridam, euanidam, falsam, ineptam esse. Quid quæso aliud græcis διαβάλλειν significat, quàm calumniari, seu falsa de aliquo spargere ei ut noceat? Siue igitur cavillari pro σοφίζεσθαι positum velis, siue pro calumniari, perinde erit. Sic rectè interpretem conuertisse confitebere, cum Martianum mentitum fuisse posuit. Tu si, quid criminari significet, & quid διαβάλλειν notet apud te considerasses, non hic sine ratione interpretem suggillasses. Constat hunc esse prædicti loci sensum, Martianum ut Galenum redderet invisum, & prædictiones ipsius convelleret per mendacia persuadere aliis conatum fuisse, ipsum non ut Medicum, sed divinatricis artis ope futura præsagire solitum fuisse. At Galenus id constanter negat, ac solam Medicam artem ista docere contendit.
units.tr: You reply to the passage about Martian, the Roman physician, that Galen did not say he was falsely accused by him, or that he lied, when he said that he practised mathematics. Martian, you say, slandered and mocked him as if he were a mathematician, since the text reads diaballei, not epseudeto. That is your first answer. You add a second: "It is clear that here mathematics means non-natural divination, as the enumerated species of augury, haruspicy, and so on show." Here I must, against my own wish, take up grammar, which I have deliberately passed over at times above. In Latin cavillari means roughly two things: either to jest or mock (skoptein or chertomein), or to quibble (sophizesthai), a word which nearly all Latin translators render with Cicero's verb cavillari. Since Martian did not jest or joke with Galen, whom out of envy he hated bitterly and whose hatred he strove to stir up among everyone, the word must be understood in the second sense. From this it follows that your first answer, the astrological one, is rotten, faded, false, and inept. What, I ask, does diaballein mean to the Greeks except to calumniate, or to spread falsehoods about someone so as to harm him? So whether you want cavillari taken as sophizesthai or as calumniari makes no difference. You will thus have to admit that the interpreter translated correctly when he put that Martian lied. If you had considered what criminari means and what diaballein signifies, you would not have hissed at the interpreter here without reason. The sense of the passage is agreed to be this: Martian, to make Galen hated and to overturn his predictions, tried by lies to persuade others that Galen did not foretell the future as a physician but was accustomed to do so by the help of divinatory art. Galen, however, constantly denies this and contends that only the medical art teaches those things.

units.la: Veniamus ad secundam responsionem. Dicis Galenum de non naturali Astrologia seu mathematica locutum esse. Vbi Galenus vel antiqui alij mathematicam diuinationem distribuerunt in naturalem ac non naturalem? Aut quid intellexit per non naturalem mathematicam Galenus? Certum est non naturalem eam esse, quae nullis nitatur rationibus naturae consentaneis. Talis illa est, quam tu profiteris, & de qua huc vsque contendimus inter nos. Aliam tu mihi nunquam probabis Galenum intellexisse. At, inquis, Auguria, Extispicia, &c. diuinationes sunt non naturales. Nego tibi Galenum minus naturales has diuinationis species quam Astrologiam existimasse. Qui commentarios ipsius volet legere, facile intelliget, ipsum Augurium & Extispicium non minus credidisse naturales quasdam artes esse, quam Astrologiam. Vtrobique enim abutuntur corporibus naturalibus, qui ex ipsis futura venantur. Galenus hic discrimen non facit, sed Martianum solitum dicere asserit, quod diuinatricis artis auxilio futura praecognosceret. Et cum interrogatus saepe fuisset, ait, qua nam arte vterer, modo vnam modo aliam respondit. Galenus in genere negat, se vlla diuinatrice arte adiutum fuisse ad praesagiendum, siue naturali siue non naturali, sed ex arte medica se omnia percepisse quae praedixerit euentura. Falsa igitur & puerilis & inepta est tua responsio.
units.tr: Let us come to your second answer. You say Galen spoke of non-natural astrology or mathematics. Where did Galen or the other ancients divide mathematical divination into natural and non-natural? Or what did Galen mean by non-natural mathematics? It is certain that that is non-natural which rests on no reasoning consistent with nature. Such is the astrology you profess, and about which we have been contending so far. You will never prove to me that Galen meant anything else. But, you say, augury, haruspicy and so on are non-natural divinations. I deny that Galen thought these species of divination less natural than astrology. Anyone who reads his commentaries will easily see that he believed augury and haruspicy to be no less natural arts than astrology. For both sorts of diviner abuse natural bodies to hunt out the future. Galen makes no distinction here, but states that Martian used to say he foreknew the future with the help of a divinatory art. When he was often asked which art he used, he sometimes named one and sometimes another. Galen, speaking generally, denies that he was aided by any divinatory art in foretelling, whether natural or non-natural; he says he perceived from the medical art everything he predicted would happen. Your answer is therefore false, puerile, and inept.

units.la: Tantundem valet quod de abusu artis affers, de quo Galenus nihil dicit. Nec Martianus id voluit, Galenum mathematica abuti, sed hoc illi crimen seu vitium falso intentabat, ipsum non ex facultate medica, sed alius artis praesidio futuros morborum euentus praeintelligere. Si potuisset crises Martianus, sicuri [?] Galenum posse videbat, praeuidere, nunquam eum ita fuisset calumniatus. Vbi Mathematica diuinatrix ars aliqua pro abusu Astrologiae posita sit ab antiquis, ipse videris. Ego non magni facio quae tu citra omnem probationem temere & inconsiderate dicis, vel potius effutis. Cauillatio est, nihil aliud, quicquid hic adfers, & argumentum meum non modo non obscurant, sed maxime illustrant, ac firmamentum ipsius quale sit declarant.
units.tr: What you bring forward about an abuse of the art is worth just as much, and Galen says nothing about it. Nor did Martian mean that Galen abused mathematics; he falsely charged him with this crime or fault, namely that Galen foreknew the outcomes of diseases not from medical skill but with the help of another art. If Martian could have foreseen the crises, as he saw that Galen could, he would never have slandered him in this way. Where the ancients put some mathematical divinatory art as an abuse of astrology, you yourself must see. I do not think much of what you rashly and carelessly say without any proof, or rather babble. Whatever you bring here is nothing but cavilling; it does not obscure my argument but greatly illuminates it, and shows how firm its support is.

units.la: Videris credere, me negasse illum locum, quem ex caps[?] libri ad Posthumum protulisti de diuinatrice Astrologia intelligi debere. At ego nunquam negaui, sed nihil ad eam rem, de qua nos agimus, facere dixi. Iterum dico, si eum huc facere putes, te multò esse opinione mea imperitiorē, vt ne quid asperius dicam. Nec loquitur ibi de Medicis Galenus, vt tu perperam interpretaris: sed diuites, ait, artes vtilitate metiri, ac quod in singulis inest pulchri & eruditi non vel minimum curare.
units.tr: You seem to think I denied that the passage you cited from the chapter of the book to Posthumus should be understood of divinatory astrology. But I never denied it; I said only that it has nothing to do with the matter we are discussing. I say again: if you think it bears on this, you are far less experienced than I supposed, not to say anything harsher. Nor does Galen there speak of physicians, as you wrongly interpret. He says that wealthy arts are measured by their usefulness and that one cares not the least for what is beautiful and learned in each.

units.la: Tale illud etiam est, quod asseris, Galenum in 3. Decret. cap. 10. tantopere sese excusasse propter caussam 20. diei. Verba ipsius probant eum de omnibus Astrologicis loqui. Qui iam disputationis huius, inquit, subtilitati succenset[?], ac difficilem eam existimat, hunc nemo ipsam addiscere cogit, verum primus huius operis liber ei sufficit. Quòd si non laboris fugitantior sit, secundum quoque adijciat, à tertio autem abstineat. Nos siquidem haec paucis plane, ijsque inuitò scripsisse affirmamus. Vos ô Dij immortales nouistis, vos in testimonium voco, hæc me amicorum quorundam precibus vehementer adactum scriptis mandasse. Ex his verbis tam clarè patet, eum de tertio libro toto, non de parte vna tantum loqui, vt cæcum esse oporteat qui videre nequit.
units.tr: Equally wrong is your assertion that Galen, in the third book of the Decretoria, chapter 10, excused himself so greatly on account of the cause of the twentieth day. His own words show that he is speaking of all astrological matters. "Whoever," he says, "is irritated by the subtlety of this discussion and thinks it difficult, no one compels him to learn it; the first book of this work is enough for him. But if he is not too averse to labour, let him add the second as well, but let him abstain from the third. For we affirm that we have written these things briefly and quite unwillingly." You immortal gods know, I call you to witness, that I was strongly driven to commit these things to writing by the entreaties of certain friends. From these words it is so clear that he speaks of the whole third book, not of only one part, that whoever cannot see it must be blind.

units.la: Ad locum ex Aphor. productum respondes, Galenum ibi solum de caussis dierum criticorum dicere inutiles eas esse ad exercitium artis Medicæ. At inde non efficitur, ais, Astrologiam inutilem esse. Age dabo tibi eum de solis criticorum dierum caussis loqui. Quid inde habebis vtilitatis? Ego enim hunc locum non ideo adduxi, vt Astrologiam inutilem docerem esse, sed vt Galenum in ea fuisse sententia demonstrarem, illa quæ in 3. Decretoriorum disputaset[?], non esse ei qui artem vellet[?] exercere necessaria, modò aliorum nihil ignoraret; quæ passim aliàs necessaria dixit esse. At verò si non est vtilis quatenus docet caussas dierum decretoriorum, vt iam apparuit, ad quam rem confert? Ad præsciendas crises? Malè ergo Galenus omisit, cum quomodo prænoscendæ sint docere nos voluit. Docuit autem multis in locis, atq; ex professo quidem in lib. de Crisibus. Hoc in loco omnia quæ ad hanc partem vtilia & necessaria iu- dicauit tractauit, sicut debuit. At Astrologiæ facta men- tio nulla ei fuit. Malè quoque Hippocrates, qui in suis Pro- gnosticis nunquam rei tam necessariæ, si tibi credendum sit, meminit. Ne hîc quidem igitur elabi potes.
units.tr: To the passage you quoted from the Aphorisms, you reply that Galen there says only that the causes of critical days are useless for the exercise of the medical art. But from this, you say, it does not follow that astrology is useless. Very well, I grant that he speaks there only of the causes of critical days. What advantage will you gain from that? I did not cite this passage to show that astrology is useless, but to show that Galen held the view that the matters he discussed in the third book of the Decretoria were not necessary for one who wished to practise the art, provided he did not ignore anything else; elsewhere he often says such things are necessary. But if astrology is not useful insofar as it teaches the causes of decretory days, as has now become clear, what does it contribute? To foreknowing crises? Then Galen wrongly left it out, since he wanted to teach us how crises are to be foreknown. He did teach this in many places, and expressly in his book On Crises. In this passage he treated everything he judged useful and necessary for this part, as he should have. But he made no mention of astrology. Hippocrates too was wrong, for in his Prognostics he never mentions a thing so necessary, if we are to believe you. So you cannot escape even here.

units.la: Si non tibi probaui librum Astrologicum de decubitu ægrorum ex mathematica scientia spurium esse, obie- cta te in eo quantum voles. Similes habent labra lactucas, non ineptè hîc dixerim. Video te nihil gustare posse & ad- mittere, quod non mendacia & lutum Astrologicum sapit oletque. Ego ad illius authoris testimonia tibi posthac ni- hil respondere statui.
units.tr: If I have not convinced you that the astrological book on the position of the sick, which is said to be Hippocrates' or Galen's, is spurious from the standpoint of mathematical science, then object to it as much as you like. Lettuces and lips, as they say, are a good match here. I see that you cannot taste or accept anything that does not smack of lies and astrological mud. From now on I have decided not to answer you on the testimonies of that author.

units.la: De contingentibus tam absurda adfers, vt quid consu- tem vix sciam. Ergo pauca quædam tantum attingam. Ga- lenum risurum putas fuisse, si dicentes nos audiuisset, A- strologiam circa contingentia solum versari. Tua si legis- set, sine stomacho & fastidio nunquam, credo, facere po- tuisset. Contingentia sunt, quæcunque cum non extant, ex- tare possunt: & cum extant, extare non etiam possunt, & contra necessaria distinguuntur. Huius quasi genera tria sunt. Aut enim in pluribus cernuntur, qualia ea sunt, quæ vel Natura vel Ars efficit. Aut æquè sunt ac non sunt, vt quorum voluntas est causa. Aut in paucioribus reperiun- tur raroque eueniunt, quæ casu accidisse dicimus, fortui- taque nominamus. Omnium ne tu horum causas igno- rari contendes? Non, respondebis, tantum posteriorum duorum generum causas ignorari dico. Hæc in literis tuis responsio videtur posita esse, non quidem his verbis, sed hac sententia. Ergo stulti & vani ac mendaces omnes fue- runt philosophi, qui secundi generis euentuum causam ef- festatuerunt[?] optimo iure προαίρεσιν voluntatemque. Vi- des quam habeam occasionem hîc te exagitandi? Memi- nisse te saltem decebat, artes omnes circa contingentia versari, & earum effectus esse contingentes.
units.tr: You bring such absurd claims about contingent things that I scarcely know how to stitch them together. So I will touch on only a few points. You think Galen would have laughed had he heard us say that astrology is concerned only with contingent things. If he had read your work, I believe he could never have done so without disgust and distaste. Things are contingent when, although they do not exist, they can exist, and when they exist, they can also not exist. They are distinguished from necessary things. There are roughly three kinds of contingent things. Some occur in most cases, such as the things produced by Nature or by Art. Others are equally likely to be and not to be, as are those whose cause is the will. Still others are found in few cases and happen rarely; we say these happen by chance and call them fortuitous. Will you insist that the causes of all these are unknown? No, you will reply, I say only that the causes of the last two kinds are unknown. This seems to be your answer in your letter, not in these words but in this sense. So all the philosophers were foolish, empty and liars who asserted that the cause of events of the second kind is choice [προαίρεσιν] and will, and rightly so. Do you see what an opportunity I have here to harass you? At least you should have remembered that all the arts are concerned with contingent things, and that their effects are contingent.

units.la: Crises præterea cum à corporum nostrorum natura tanquam proxima & propria causa perfici concedis, con- cedere te quoque oportebit, eas fieri quoque non posse. Sinegas,plane imperitè & inscitè facis. Si affirmas, ex contin-gentium numero rerum erunt. Quid igitur Pius & Ma-nardus peccassent, (quos tu viros conuicijs & maledictis impudenter laceras immeritò) se Astrologiam circa sola contingentia versari affirmassent? Mendacem & futilem atque adeò impiam esse demonstrarunt, tantum abest, vt aliquid ex ea de contingentibus recte præsciri censuerint,
units.tr: Furthermore, since you concede that crises are brought about by the nature of our bodies as their immediate and proper cause, you will have to concede that they also cannot be predicted. If you deny this, you act quite ignorantly and unskilfully. If you affirm it, they will belong to the class of contingent things. Then what sin did Pius and Manardus commit (whom you shamelessly and undeservedly tear apart with insults and abuse) when they asserted that astrology is concerned only with contingent things? They showed it to be false, trifling and even impious; so far were they from thinking that anything about contingent things could be rightly foreknown from it.

units.la: Fortuitorum causas à nobis ignorari quod dicis acci-pio,& quod arte comprehendi nulla posse concedis, simi-liter probo. Si iam addidero,pleraque eorum,quorum si-bi præscientiam inscitè arrogant Astrologi, fortuita esse, rectè me inde conclusurum non puto negabis,ipsos tenta-re quæ fieri nequeant. Sed hæc extra rem. Ad vniuersale descendo.
units.tr: I accept your statement that we do not know the causes of chance events, and I likewise approve your concession that they cannot be grasped by art. If I now add that most of the things which astrologers foolishly claim to foreknow are chance events, I do not think you will deny that I am right to conclude that they attempt what cannot be done. But this is beside the point. I now come to the universal.

units.la: Cum cœlos vniuersales causas & generali modo in hæc terrena agere dico,tu duobus id modis intelligi posse iudi-ces. Sic enim scribis: Aut enim illud vis,quod effectus astro-rum quiin inferioribus cernuntur à solis astris pendeant, quo-niam hæc vniuersalia sunt tantum. Aut illud, quod astro-rum facultates seu vires perpetuò inter se vniantur & co-eant, &c. Mox priorē partem confuturus dicis, In omni actione necessarium esse patiens, &c. Dispeream si credere vn-quam potui,talia mihi ab homine, qui doctus videri cu-piat,nec tamen deliret, obiectum iri. Tu ne contra libel-lum à me editum scribes,neque ex eo hactenus intelligere quiuisti, quomodo cum philosophis & doctis omnibus cœlestia vniuersales causas appellem, aut generali modo in hæc terrena agere intelligam? Si primo modo tuo, cœ-los dicere aut putare causas vniuersales esse( hoc est, si eò stupiditatis deuenirem) tu tamen non posses me erroris conuincere tuis putidulis ratiunculis. Dicerem, frustra te patientium rerum mentionem inijcere,cum mihi de cauf-sis efficientibus sermo foret. Cum cœlestia generali ratio-ne in hæc terrena agere dico,quis non me terrena pro pa-tientibus ponere, præter vnum te, perspicit? Quæ igitur te causa impulit,multa vt de patiente inaniter disputares?. Si aliquid vidisse videri volebas,hoc probare debebas, non solas cœlestes caussas hic efficere aliquid posse, sed alias praeterea intervenire efficientes caussas oportere. Hoc si fecisses, nihil quidem ad rem propositam protulisses, cum ego longè aliter cœlos generales caussas & universaliter huc agere docuerim, attamen: tuum propositum probasses, sicque venia minus indignus censeri potuisses. Sic autem clarè probas, te nec vera intelligere, nec quæ palam falsa sunt confutare scire. Hæc cum ita sint, nihilominus quæ verissima sunt te convellere argumentis posse impruden-ter equidem credis.
units.tr: When I say that the heavens act as universal causes, and in a general way upon these earthly things, you judge that this can be understood in two ways. For you write: Either you mean that the effects of the stars seen in lower things depend only on the stars, since these are merely universal; or that the powers or faculties of the stars are continually joined and combined with one another, etc. Then, about to refute the first part, you say: In every action it is necessary that there be a patient, etc. May I perish if I ever thought I would be charged with such things by a man who wishes to seem learned and yet is not delirious. Will you write against the little book I have published, and until now have you been unable to understand from it how I call the heavenly bodies universal causes, together with all philosophers and learned men, or how I understand them to act upon these earthly things in a general way? If in your first sense I were to say or think that the heavens are universal causes (that is, if I had sunk to such stupidity), you still could not convict me of error with your foul little arguments. I would say that you mention the patient in vain, since I am speaking of efficient causes. When I say that the heavenly bodies act upon these earthly things in a general manner, who, except you, does not see that I place earthly things as the patient? What cause, then, drove you to dispute at length about the patient to no purpose? If you wished to seem to have seen something, you ought to have proved not only that the heavenly causes alone can produce anything here, but that other efficient causes must also intervene. Had you done this, you would indeed have brought nothing to the matter at hand, since I have taught quite differently that the heavens act as general causes and act universally here; yet you would have proved your point, and so you might have been thought less unworthy of pardon. As it is, you clearly show that you neither understand the truth nor know how to refute what is plainly false. Since this is so, you are foolish indeed to believe that you can overturn with arguments even what is most true.

units.la: Pars altera, quam longissima oratione declaras, & quasi iam vicisses ex aggeras, te prorsus digna est. Si enim inter verum & falsum distinguere didicisses, aliter loquaris. At-tigit hoc argumentum Sauonarola in edito libello, sed longè aliter eo utitur ac tu putas. Ego, Strathmion, nec hoc nec illo modo cœlos universaliter huc agere unquam vel credidi vel somniavi, multò minus docui. Quare nihil huc faciunt ea universa. Unū in te demiror summopere, quòd non vides te tibi in paucissimis versibus manifestè contra-dicere. Etenim astra concedis causas esse universales, re-motas & communes rerum omnium, & nihilominus A-strologum ex vario eorum positu de particularibus euen-tibus horum inferiorum divinare artificiosè contendis.
units.tr: The second part, which you explain at great length and as if you had already won by piling up your heaps, is entirely worthy of you. If you had learned to distinguish true from false, you would speak otherwise. Savonarola touched on this argument in a published booklet, but he uses it quite differently from what you suppose. I, Stathmion, have never either believed or dreamed, much less taught, that the heavens act here universally in either this or that way. So those universal considerations have nothing to do with the matter. One thing in you I greatly marvel at: that you do not see that in a very few lines you plainly contradict yourself. For you concede that the stars are universal causes, remote and common to all things, and yet you contend that the astrologer can skilfully divine particular events of these lower things from the varying positions of the stars.

units.la: Dixeram clarissimos per Galliam & Italiam Medicos omnibus floruisse ætatibus, & hodie quoque florere, qui Astrologiam exemplo antiquorum nunquam adhibuissent, & felicissimè tamen suos ægros percurassent. Ad hæc tu, multos te sine astrologia, plures etiam sine pulsu curas-se scribis. Ut autem non sequitur, pulsum propterea inutilem esse: ita neque astrologiam sequi inutilem esse, quia multi multos sine astrologia curarint. Sic tibi argumen-tari licet, qui novam excogitasti logicam, qua quiduis de quovis vel approbes vel improbes. Non habet eandem cum arte medica cognationem astrologia, quam cum eadem pulsus habent. Nec tu ex eorum es numero, de quibus ego loquebar. Hos enim monumenta quæ extant do-ctissimos & optimos Medicos fuisse & esse, quos eorum nihil latet, quæ ad artem necessaria rectè iudicantur. Dein-de non illi aliquando quidem usi sunt astrologiæ benefi-cio, aliquando verò non sunt usi, sicuti te non semper non observasse pulsus suspicor, si modò aliquid hîc intelligis, sed nunquam sunt usi, nec ut voluerunt, quod falsam esse vanamque intelligerent. Tam multa sunt in tuo simili dis-similia quæ ad rem pertinent. Tu tuos, si libet, ut fortè etiam aliquando facis, etiam sine aliis rebus necessariis cu-rato. Illi de quibus ego loquor, nihil talium omiserunt, quantum ingenio, studio, iudicio, eruditione, usu, consilio, consequi potuerunt, quæ ad artem rectè exercendam vel necessaria vel utilia esse cognouerunt. Astrologiam autem despectui habuerunt ac riserunt, quoniam inutilem & va-nam esse perspexerunt, quod de pulsu dici nequit.
units.tr: I had said that the most distinguished physicians throughout France and Italy have flourished in every age, and flourish today too, who never employed astrology following the example of the ancients, and yet most happily cured their patients. To this you reply that you have cured many without astrology, and more still without the pulse. But just as it does not follow that the pulse is therefore useless, so it does not follow that astrology is useless because many have cured many without it. You may argue in this way, you who have devised a new logic by which you may either approve or disapprove of anything concerning anything. Astrology does not have the same kinship with the medical art that the pulse has. Nor are you one of those of whom I was speaking. For those who are extant in the records were, and are, most learned and excellent physicians, and nothing is hidden from them of what is rightly judged necessary for the art. Moreover, those men at some times did use astrology, and at other times did not use it, just as I suspect you do not always neglect the pulse, if indeed you understand anything here. But they never used it as they wished, since they understood it to be false and vain. Many things in your case are unlike those that pertain to the matter. You cure your patients, if you like, and perhaps sometimes you do, even without other necessary things. Those of whom I speak omitted none of these things, so far as they could attain them by talent, study, judgement, learning, experience and counsel, which they knew to be either necessary or useful for practising the art rightly. But they held astrology in contempt and laughed at it, because they saw that it was useless and vain, which cannot be said of the pulse.

units.la: Tandem controversiæ nostræ statum in hoc situm esse affirmas, ut doceam Galenum Astrologum non fuisse. Quā [?] bonus fuerit Astrologus, & quam bene de Astrologia in 3. Decret. disputarit, multi Astrologi iam ante docuerunt. Quæstio proprie non hæc est, sed, An Astrologiam in cura-do adhibuerit aliquando, nec ne. Si Astrologus est appellandus, quisquis Astrologicum aliquid quacunque de causa scribit, negare non possum quin fuerit Astrologus Galenus. At verò præter & contra suam voluntatem Astrologus, ut ipsemet Deos testes advocans docuit, fuit. Necessitate quadam non voluntate, ut iam sæpe diximus, in 3. Decret. Astrologica quædam tractauit. Quod illa ipsa non probarit, supra quoque ostensum recordor. Sanè si causam sententiæ nullam haberemus aliam præter hanc unam, quòd in tam multis libris, quos ante & post illos scripsit, & in quibus non tantum occasionem habebat de ea differendi: sed etiam cogebatur, si perfectam rei doctrinam, ut promittebat, tradere nobis volebat, nullam unquam ipsius mentionem fecit, quasi conferre medico aliquid posset non sine efficaci ratione ita sentiremus. Iam cum alias habeamus, & aperta ipsius proferre possimus testimonia, nō video quid desiderari queat amplius. Ex hoc illud etiam sequitur, in quo statu controversiæ nostræ existit, eum nō fuisse astrologia in curando usum. Nam si semel tantum, & contra suam volūtatem de ea disputauit, eademque omit-ti posse absque omni artis incommodo significauit, satis manifestum est, ipsum ea postea non fuisse usum. Haec pri-ma sit ratio, cui validiores iam alias adijciam.
units.tr: Finally, you assert that the state of our controversy lies in this: that I should prove Galen was not an astrologer. However good an astrologer he was, and however well he disputed about astrology in the third book of the Decrees, many astrologers have already shown this before. The question is properly not this, but whether he ever employed astrology in curing, or not. If anyone who writes something astrological for whatever reason is to be called an astrologer, I cannot deny that Galen was an astrologer. But he was an astrologer, as he himself taught, calling the gods to witness, against and contrary to his own will. By necessity, not by will, as we have often said, he treated certain astrological matters in the third book of the Decrees. I recall that I have also shown above that he did not approve of those matters himself. Indeed, if we had no other reason for our opinion than this one, namely that in so many books which he wrote before and after those, in which he not only had occasion to discuss astrology but was even compelled to do so if he wished to deliver to us, as he promised, a complete doctrine of the subject, he never once mentioned it at all, as if astrology could contribute nothing to the physician, we would rightly think so for a sound reason. Now, since we have other evidence and can produce his own plain testimonies, I do not see what more could be wanted. From this it also follows, in the state in which our controversy stands, that he did not use astrology in treating the sick. For if he disputed about it only once, and against his own will, and indicated that the same things could be omitted without any harm to the art, it is quite clear that he did not afterwards use it. Let this be the first reason, to which I shall add stronger ones in due course.

units.la: Ignominiam & iniuriam sibi fieri putauit, si quis eum Astrologia usum dixisset, non igitur ab ea adiutus est. Con-stat quod di[?]i verum esse, cum calumniam appellat, quod Martianus id de ipso affirmasset.
units.tr: He thought it an insult and an injury to himself if anyone said that he had used astrology, so he was not helped by it. It is clear that this is true, since he calls it a calumny that Martianus had asserted this about him.

units.la: .Idem fere testatur in eiusdem libri cap. 7. sic scribens. Hic ego ut pueri in brachio venam pulsantem attigi, sine febre quidem ipsum esse pronunciaui, me vero deludendi hisce, qui me Vatem appellarent, ansam dare. Excipies Boethus, & ego, inquit, in comparatione illorum soleo te reuera Vatem, ut scis, appellare, quoties aliquid praedicis, quod aemu-li tui negant, praecognosci Medica facultate posse. Atqui hactenus, subiunxi, ea omnia te docui Medica arte inveni-ri, priscosque aliquot Medicos hisce de rebus conscripsisse.
units.tr: He bears almost the same witness in chapter 7 of the same book, writing thus: "Here I touched the pulse in the arm, as with a boy, and pronounced that he had no fever, but that I gave occasion for mockery to these men who call me a seer." "You will object, Boethus, and I," he says, "in comparison with them, I usually call you a true seer, as you know, whenever you foretell something which your rivals deny can be known in advance by the medical art." "But so far," I added, "I have taught you that all these things are found by the medical art, and that certain ancient physicians have written about these matters."

units.la: Iterum in fine huius cap. affirmat Boethus iterum, se non mirari, quod ipsum quovis modo alio, quam Medica disciplina suas praedictiones facere divulgent.
units.tr: Again, at the end of this chapter, Boethus again affirms that he does not wonder that they make their predictions known in any way other than by the medical discipline.

units.la: Item cap. 10. ait, se, quomodo quis diem [?]criseos praenouisse debeat & possit, in libris de Crisibus docuisse. At nullam in his mentionem astrologiae fecit, ergo sine ipsa praenouit futuras crises.
units.tr: Likewise, in chapter 10 he says that he has taught in his books on Crises how a man ought and is able to foresee the day of the crisis. Yet he makes no mention of astrology in these, therefore he foresaw the future crises without it.

units.la: Paulo post addit, se suos ideo praedictiones non solere praedicare, ne delusorem & vatem se appellent, & huiusmodi alia de se obloquantur.
units.tr: A little later he adds that for this reason he is not in the habit of announcing his predictions, lest they call him a deceiver and a seer, and speak ill of him in similar ways.

units.la: Mox haec addit. Quanquam haec praedictio nihil quod mireris continet, si eorum es memor, quae tibi in commet[?]. quos in 1.Hipp.librum de Vulgar.morb. conscripsimus, & praeterea quae in libris de Crisibus docuimus, didicisti.
