units.tr: Soon he adds these words: "Although this prediction contains nothing that you should marvel at, if you remember those things which you learned from us in the commentaries which we wrote on the first book of Hippocrates' On Epidemic Diseases, and besides, those things which we taught in the books on Crises."

units.la: In 13. cap. cum riderent astantes, quod sanguinem ex na-re dextra fluxurum praedixisset, air: Ar, inquam, vel utrumque eveniat oportet, vel alterutrum me decipiat. Nam & quod sanguis fluxurus est, & quod e dextra nare venturus, arte Medica praesciri potest.
units.tr: In chapter 13, when those present laughed because he had predicted that blood would flow from the right nostril, he says: "Well, I say, either both must happen, or one of them must deceive me. For both that the blood is going to flow, and that it is going to come from the right nostril, can be known in advance by the medical art."

units.la: Ex his testimonijs quæ ex unico libro attuli, nec omnia tamen, satis arbitror patet, Galenum non ex cœli inspe-ctione, sed ex arte Medica crises omnes præuidisse. Si cum hisce argumentis superiorum literarum, quæ te non dissol-uisse non ignoras, modò nō prorsus cæcutiat animus tuus, coniunxeris, non ratione tantum, sed autoritate etiam pro positum me abundè probasse intelliges. Plura in præsentia addere non libet. Postrema verba literarum tuarum hæc sunt: Scito rem ad doctos arbitros peruenturam. Idem hoc nuper cum in arce pranderem istic ex nobilissimo viro arcis præfecto intellexi Literas à te sibi paulò ante missas legit, in quibus te Vuitebergā transmisisse exemplum scriptum erat. Ego ingenuè fateor, me putasse initio uni tibi à me scribi, quò factum est, ut priorum exemplum mihi nulla seruarim, quæ recepi tamen postea. Quod si publicandas cogitassem, accuratius quædam scripsissem. Nolim putes me doctorum hominum iudicium aspernari aut detrectare. Unam veritatem omnium hominum autoritati, gratiæ & commodis omnibus anteferendam præclarè intelligo. Neque ullum pro ea defendenda existimationis meæ periculum defugere certum est. Quamobrem [?]licet ita non scri-psi, ut qui pluribus scribere se cogitaret: facilè tamen, spero, doctis & æquis hominibus caussam meā probabo. Si igitur, quos tibi arbitros caussæ nostræ elegisti, te tuāq; amicitiam, pluris quàm veritatem, (quod minimè spero) fe-cerint, me nec veritati, nec caussæ meæ defuturum, idem perspicient. Et quoniam te id cupere video, plures ut no-stra hæc legant, cum primum ocium nactus à gra-uioribus negocijs fuero, efficiam ipsemet, tibi ut gratificer, ut omnino plurimi peruidere possint, quàm sis egre-gius Astrologiæ patronus.
units.tr: From these testimonies, which I have brought forward from a single book, though not all of them, I think it sufficiently plain that Galen foresaw all the crises not from inspection of the heavens but from the medical art. If you join these arguments to those of my earlier letters, which you are not unaware you have not dissolved, provided your mind is not utterly blinded, you will understand that I have proved what I proposed not only by reason but also by authority, and abundantly so. I do not wish to add more at present. The last words of your letter are these: Know that the matter will come before learned judges. I learned this recently when I was dining at the castle there, from a most noble man, the governor of the castle, who read me a letter sent to him a little while before by you, in which it was written that you had sent a copy of it to Wittenberg. I frankly confess that at first I thought I was writing to you alone, and so it happened that I kept no copy of my earlier letters, though I have received them since. But if I had intended them to be published, I would have written some parts more carefully. Do not think that I despise or disparage the judgment of learned men. I clearly understand that one truth must be preferred to the authority, favour and all the advantages of all men. Nor am I determined to shrink from any danger to my reputation in defending it. Wherefore, although I have not written as one who intended to write to many, I hope nevertheless to make my case acceptable to learned and fair-minded men. So if those whom you have chosen as judges of our case have valued you and your friendship more than the truth (which I very much hope is not so), they will see that I shall not fail either the truth or my cause. And since I see that you desire it, I myself will, as soon as I have leisure from weightier business, make it possible for you to be gratified, so that as many people as possible may see how distinguished a patron of astrology you are.

units.la: Vale 18. Febr. Mas-feldiæ.
units.tr: Farewell. 18 February, at Mansfeld.

units.la: Epistola VI. THOMAS ERASTVS D. CHRISTOPHORO Stathmioni Medico Coburgensi, S. D.
units.tr: Epistola VI. THOMAS ERASTVS to CHRISTOPHORVS STATHMIO, physician of Coburg, greetings.

units.la: Esi literæ quas Id. Martij accepi, nihil continet, cui non sit à me iam sæpe responsum: nihilominus tamen, quia te solam veritatem spectare in tota causa asseris [?], iterum respondere placuit, ut si sanabilis [?] es, remedium tibi denegatum non queraris.
units.tr: Your letter, which I received on the Ides of March, contains nothing to which I have not often replied already. Nevertheless, since you claim [?] to look only to the truth in the whole matter, I have decided to answer again, so that, if you are curable [?], you cannot complain that the remedy has been denied you.

units.la: Non in eo controversia nostra amplius versatur, An Gal. in 3. Decret. Astrologis fauere visus sit, (Hoc enim tibi non semel affirmaui) sed, An in exercenda arte medica, Astrologorum more cœlorum positus observarit; quærebatur. Ego ex nullo Galeni testimonio probari posse aio, nisi quæ in 3. Decret. dicta sunt, male huc aliquis detorquere conetur. Etenim non unum duntaxat extare locum in legitimis ipsius operibus, quibus diversum ostendi valeat. Tales in libro ad Posthumum scripto inveniri plures monui, & ex ijs aliquot produxi, quibus apertè testificatur Galenus, si non ex arte divinatrice aliqua (Astrologiæ inter has nominatim sub nomine mathematicæ commemini) sed ex sola Medica futuros morborum euentus præcognouisse, aliosque præcognoscere docuisse. Ex aliis libris nihil proferre volui, & ne nunc quidem volo, quod hæc abundè pro positum demonstrent. Repetam ergo breuiter, ut me nihil temere affirmare appareat.
units.tr: Our dispute no longer turns on whether Galen in the third book of the Decrees (3. Decret.) seemed to favour the astrologers (I have already told you more than once that I grant this), but on whether, in practising the medical art, he observed the positions of the heavens in the manner of the astrologers. I say that no testimony of Galen can prove this, except what is said in the third book of the Decrees, and even that someone may twist to this purpose in a bad way. For there is not just one passage in his genuine works from which the opposite can be shown. I have pointed out that several such passages are to be found in his book written to Posthumus, and from these I have quoted some which Galen plainly bears witness to: that he foresaw the future outcomes of diseases, and taught others to foresee them, not by any divinatory art (among these he mentions astrology by name, under the name of mathematics), but by medicine alone. I did not wish to bring forward anything from other books, and I do not wish to even now, since these are amply sufficient to demonstrate my point. I will therefore repeat briefly, so that it may appear that I affirm nothing rashly.

units.la: Ubicunque Galenus narrat, quomodo & ex quibus aliquem futurum in morbis euentum præcognouerit, tametsi plurima recitet, Astrologiæ tamen nunquam meminit, sed ex arte Medica sola se præuidisse affirmat. Ergo nō est in præsentiendo unquam usus Astrologia.
units.tr: Wherever Galen relates how and from what signs he foresaw the future outcome of a disease, although he recounts very many things, he never mentions astrology, but affirms that he foresaw it by the medical art alone. Therefore astrology was never used in foreseeing.

units.la: Ubicunque Galenus docet (siue obiter id faciat, siue ex professo eam rem tractet,) quomodo crises prænoscendæ sint: itemque quales & quando futuræ sint cognoscere docet, omniaq; se ad eam rem facientia persecutum asserit, Astrologiæ tamen non meminit. Ergo non necessariam aut utilem iudicauit.
units.tr: Wherever Galen teaches (whether he does so in passing or treats the matter professedly) how crises are to be foreknown, and teaches to know their kind and when they will occur, and asserts that he has pursued everything bearing on the matter, yet he makes no mention of astrology. Therefore he did not judge it necessary or useful.

units.la: Galenus asseuerat, artem prænoscendorum euentuum in morbis ab Hippocrate perfectè doctam, una doctrina de pulsibus excepta: neque Astrologiæ is unquam meminit, ergo ad præsagiendum non judicauit utilem. Quare ne usus quidem ea credi poterit.
units.tr: Galen asserts that the art of foretelling outcomes in diseases was perfectly taught by Hippocrates, with the single exception of the doctrine of pulses; and he never mentions astrology in this connection. Therefore he did not judge it useful for prognosis. Hence it cannot even be believed that he used it.

units.la: Galenus Astrologiæ auxilio se aliquid præsensisse negat, atque adeò illum qui hoc de ipso affirmasset calumniatū mentitumúe[?] ait. Ergo non est ea[illegible, ~2 letters]sus.
units.tr: Galen denies that he foresaw anything with the help of astrology, and says that anyone who asserted this about him would be a slanderer and a liar. Therefore he did not make use of it.

units.la: Vides, opinor, non ideò me negare quòd ea usus fuerit, quia in curationibus nominatim eius non meminerit (Quanquam non leue hoc etiam argumentum censeri debeat) Sed quod ea se usum diserte neget, quod cum ea enumerat, per quæ præuiderit omnia, Astrologiæ non meminerit, quod præsensiones nos docens & necessaria atq; utilia se omnia adferre asserens, nullam huius tamen vel unico verbulo mentionem faciat. Equidem ubi diem atq; adeò horam futuræ crisios cognoscere docet, quod tu Medica arte præsciri posse negas, & à Galeno eam rem doctos nos esse ignoras, huius vanitatis præcepta nulla enume-rat. Quòd si faciendam ipsius mentionem illis in locis neges, quis sis, te apertissimè prodas. Si tam obliuiosum fuisse censes, ut rei tam necessariæ tamque utilis tot in locis & libris ne semel quidem recordari potuerit, rursus quis sis ostendis. Non ignorabat Galenus, cum ex professo, non consequentiæ sermonis gratia, doctrinam de crisibus & pro-gnosticis tractaret, nihil sibi omittendum esse illorum omnium, quæ ad rem propositam vel necessaria vel utilia co-gnouisset. Jam quid ad hæc tu dicas consideremus. Ut Ara-bes inquis, nemo dixerit non usos Astrologia, quia in suis doctrinis prognosticis & curatiuis non meminerunt ipsius, ita ne de Galeno quidem sequitur.
units.tr: You see, I think, that I do not deny that he used it because he did not name it in his cures (though this too should not be counted a slight argument); rather, I deny it because he expressly denies using it when he lists the means by which he foresaw everything; because, while teaching foreknowledge and asserting that he brings forward all things necessary and useful, he makes not a single mention of it, not even in a word. Indeed, when he teaches how to know the day and even the hour of a future crisis, which you deny can be known by the medical art, and you are ignorant that Galen has taught us this, he enumerates no precepts of this vanity. But if you deny that he made any mention of it in those places, you betray yourself most plainly as to who you are. If you think he was so forgetful that in so many places and books he could not recall even once a thing so necessary and useful, again you show who you are. Galen was not unaware that, when he treated the doctrine of crises and prognostics professedly, and not merely for the sake of the flow of his discourse, he must omit nothing of all those things which he knew to be necessary or useful for the matter in hand. Now let us consider what you say in reply to this. As with the Arabs, you say, no one would say that they did not use astrology, because in their prognostic and curative doctrines they make no mention of it; so neither does it follow in the case of Galen.

units.la: Qui à simili argumentum vult ducere quomodo con-uenit, eum similia non dissimilia adferre decet. Quod cum hic tu non facias, non mirum est, si argumentum sit elum-be, nugax & puerile. Si mihi Arabem ostenderis qui id faciat, quod Galenus fecit, in historijs curationum & prædi-ctionum particularium, & eúdem tamen Astrologia usum fuisse ostenderis, tum quod debes perficeris quidem: at nequaquam mea refutabis ideo. Quid aliud obtenturus sis, quā mendacem illum esse, nescio. Etenim Galenus enumerat ex quibus & per quæ cognouerit & curarit. Deinde Medica arte se præsensisse dicit. Postea se in libris vbi de Astrologia altissimum est silentium, docuisse monet omnia, ex quibus talia possint prædicere. Postremò neque alia diuinatrice arte, neque Astrologia se adiutum asseuerat. Hæc si Arabem in particularibus suis curationibus & prædictionibus commemorante ostenderis, concludā ego ipsum Astrologia non vsum. Si contrarium tu probaueris, mendacissimum esse hominem argues, quod de Galeno tibi nemo concedat. Vides ne quàm ieiuna, inania & inconsiderata sint, quæ pro te & astrologia adfers? Qui ex Arabibus Astrologiam cum Medicina coniunxerint, vt nunquam eius meminerint, aut coniunxisse eam negent, tu videris. Ego nescio nec scire cupio. Hoc de talib. affirmare ausim, eos non modò non tacuisse, sed frequentissimè prædicasse. Etenim maiorem in modum tales nugatores sibi in suis nugis placent, nec prædicare satis possunt.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to draw an argument from a like case ought to bring forward like cases, not unlike ones. Since you do not do this here, it is no wonder if your argument is limp, trifling and childish. If you show me an Arab who does what Galen did, in the histories of particular cures and predictions, and yet show that the same man used astrology, you would indeed accomplish what you owe; but you would by no means thereby refute my claims. What else you could obtain by this, I do not know, except to make that man a liar. For Galen lists the signs by which and through which he knew and treated. Then he says that he foresaw by the medical art. Afterwards, in books where there is the deepest silence about astrology, he advises that he taught everything by which such things could be predicted. Finally, he affirms that he was helped neither by another divinatory art nor by astrology. If you show an Arab who, in his particular cures and predictions, mentions it, I shall conclude that he did not use astrology. If you prove the contrary, you will be arguing that the man was a most lying fellow, and no one would grant you this about Galen. Do you see how meagre, empty and ill-considered are the things you bring forward for yourself and for astrology? As for those Arabs who joined astrology with medicine, whether they never mentioned it or deny they joined it, that is for you to judge. I do not know, nor do I wish to know. This much I would venture to affirm about such men: they not only did not keep silent, but proclaimed it very frequently. For such triflers take the greatest pleasure in their trifles and cannot praise them enough.

units.la: Verum enimuero istos mittamus, & de Auicenna, qui omnium Medicorum Arabum facilè princeps fuit, aliquid dicamus. Hunc [?]tecum facere ostendere posses, Deum immortalem, quàm triumphares? quàm mihi insultares? quàm non dubiam tibi victoriam polliceri auderes? At damnasse eum vanitatem hanc clarissimi iam pridem viri monuerunt. Contrariam philosophiæ, partes ipsius omnes esse falsas, fieri non posse vt vera prædicant astrologi, nisi casu quodam interdum ita eueniat, scripsisse eum declararunt. Et quidem quæ hîc dicis, Astrologica, hoc est, vana & falsa omnia esse, si quid omnino vides, cernis. Quòd si iterum ad 3. Decret. tanquam ad sacrum asylum confugias, non est vt à me aliâ responsionem expectes. Coniecturis minimè leuibus docui, Galenum illa ipsa quæ partim ex Astrologorum sententia, partim vero ex sua ipsius opinione scripsit, non omnino probasse. Si voles tuum hoc argumentum vnicum cum meis conferre pluribus, & studio aliquo veritatis cognoscendæ teneris, perfacile tibi responsum esse cognosces.
units.tr: But indeed, let us leave those men aside, and say something about Avicenna, who was easily the prince of all the Arab physicians. Could you show that he did this with you, immortal God, how you would exult! How you would insult me! How boldly you would promise yourself a certain victory! But men most famous long ago have pointed out that he condemned this vanity. He wrote that it is contrary to philosophy, that all its parts are false, and that it cannot be that astrologers predict true things, except that sometimes by a certain chance it happens so. And indeed, whatever you say here as astrological, that is, empty and false, you see clearly if you look at all. But if you again flee to the third book of the Decrees as to a sacred refuge, you need not expect from me any other answer. By conjectures that are by no means slight, I have shown that Galen did not wholly approve those very things which he wrote partly in accordance with the opinion of the astrologers and partly out of his own opinion. If you wish to compare this single argument of yours with my many, and you are held by some zeal for knowing the truth, you will learn that a reply has been very easily given.

units.la: Maiorem in modum miratus sum te, cum in tuis legi, nullum post 3. Decret. librum Galeni extare (de legitimis loquor) & quo certiora argumenta promi queant ad probandum Galenum Astrologiam adhibuisse ad curationes, quàm ex eo, quem ad Posthumum scripsit. Nullus est ferè, ex quo plura suppeditentur nobis argumenta eandem expugnandi. Certè si nullo alio in loco meliora, aut æquè bona habes, in hoc autem omnia habes aduersa, quid aliud desperare præsidij poteris? Dicis cū ab initio statim queri, Astrologiam, vt & reliquas disciplinas, negligi. Debebas primum obseruasse, Galenum Astrologiæ nomen pro Astronomia vsurpasse. Deinde quod ait vsum artium duntaxat homines requirere, quod verò in singulis pulchrum est, ac demonstrationum certitudinem negligere. Hæc si obseruasses, Galeni hanc fuisse in præsenti loco mentem, percepisses etiam, scilicet Astrologiam diuinatricem propter vsum ab omnibus illis expeti, at Astronomiam quæ certis nitatur demonstrationibus, quia non vtilis æquè videatur, despici ac negligi. Quomodo ego sperem te desiderio aliquo veritatis teneri, qui aperta loca tam confidenter audes peruertere ad stabiliendas conceptu[?]s animo nugas? Miror non minus, quòd ea pro te imprudenter adfers, quæ tibi oculos eruunt, aut certè ostendunt te instar cæci obuium quodlibet arripuisse, delectum habere non potuisse.
units.tr: I have been greatly astonished at you, since I read in your writings that after the third book of the Decrees there is no book of Galen extant (I speak of genuine ones) from which more certain arguments can be drawn to prove that Galen employed astrology in his cures, than from the one he wrote to Posthumus. There is hardly any other from which more arguments are supplied for overthrowing the same thing. Certainly, if you have nowhere else better or equally good arguments, and in this one you have everything against you, what other help can you hope for? You say that from the very beginning you complain that astrology, like the other disciplines, is neglected. You ought first to have observed that Galen used the name of astrology in the sense of astronomy. Then, that he says only men seek the use of the arts, but neglect what is beautiful in each and the certainty of demonstrations. If you had observed these things, and perceived that this was Galen's intention in the present passage, you would also have understood that divinatory astrology is sought by all for its use, whereas astronomy, which rests on certain demonstrations, is despised and neglected because it does not seem equally useful. How could I hope that you are held by any desire for truth, when you dare so confidently to pervert plain passages in order to establish the trifles you have conceived in your mind? I am no less astonished that you bring forward, without judgement, things which put out your own eyes, or at least show that, like a blind man, you have seized upon whatever came to hand and were unable to make any choice.

units.la: Quæ de sexto in codē libro scribuntur, patrocinari tibi putasti, quia scilicet horâ atq; diē crisis prædixit, quod tu ex arte Medica cognosci posse negas. Sic enim scribis: Si tu vel quisquâ alius mihi probauerit, vlla vel via vel ratione in Medicina, horâ crisium sciri posse alia, quàm ex astrorum, maximè autē lunæ, crisiū[?] veluti rectricis, motu, cum illud neque pulsus, neque vrina, neque morbi, neque accessionis natura vel singula vel omnia simul, nisi verisimiliter & coniecturaliter, quomodo Gal. Sexto non prædixit, sed nominatim & certè secundam ei noctis horam diei 17. criticam præfiniuit, id Seuero Consuli, &c. Si tam fuisses in Galeni scriptis versatus, quod te Medicum in primis decebat facere, quàm in mendacijs Astrologicis te exercuisti, nunquam hæc scripsisses. Vel sola ista declarant & probant, qualis Medicus sis. Etenim Galenus docet, quomodo sola Medica arte crisis præcognoscenda sit, & quomodo nō dies modo, verum etiam hora præsciri valeat. Nec docuit tantum paucis verbis, sed fusè explicauit, explicandoque probauit. Quare non est huius rei vt vel à me vel ab alio probationem expectes, quam apud Galenum inuenire iam olim potuisti comprobatam & declaratam. Galenus in illo ipso loco negat, se ex Astrologia aut obseruatione motus lunæ præuidisse, sed ex illis quæ in 1.[?]Epidem. & in lib. de Crisibus docuit. Quæ si quis norit, nihil admiraturum scribit. Ro-go te captu illud iterum vt legas, quo tandem quàm in-consideratè pleraque scribas, perspicias. Vides iterum quā tuam socordiam prodas, nihil verò obtineas quocunque te vertas. Nolo iam singula examinare diligentius, ne occa-sionem captasse videri queam tuam negligentiam, ne di-cam imperitiam, in lucem protrahendi. Vnum certè hic dicere cogor, si quod sentio dicere debeo, me vehementer vereri, ne nullo veritatis studio ad hæc scribenda impul-sus fueris.
units.tr: You thought the passage in the sixth book that says the hour and day of the crisis were foretold supported you, since you deny that this can be known from the medical art. You write: "If you, or anyone else, can show me any way or method in medicine by which the hour of crises can be known other than from the motions of the stars, especially the moon, as the guide of crises, since neither the pulse, nor the urine, nor the nature of the disease or of its attacks, singly or all together, can tell it except probably and by conjecture, then how did Galen not foretell it in the Sixth [Epidemics], but named and fixed the second hour of the night on the seventeenth day as critical for Severus the consul, etc." If you had been as well versed in Galen's writings, as a physician above all should be, as you have been in Astrological falsehoods, you would never have written this. These points alone show what sort of physician you are. For Galen teaches how a crisis can be foreseen by the medical art alone, and that not only the day but the hour can be known beforehand. Nor did he teach it in a few words only, but explained it at length, and proved it by his explanation. So there is no need for you to expect proof of this from me or from anyone else, when you could long ago have found it proved and set out in Galen. In that very passage Galen says that he did not foresee it from astrology or from observing the motion of the moon, but from what he taught in the first book of the Epidemics and in the book On Crises. Anyone who knows these things will write that he is not surprised. I ask you to read that passage again, so that you may see how thoughtlessly you write most things. Again you reveal your carelessness, and you gain nothing whichever way you turn. I do not want to examine each point more closely now, lest I seem to have sought an occasion to bring your negligence, not to say your ignorance, into the light. Only this one thing I am bound to say, if I must say what I think: I greatly fear that you were driven to write these things by no zeal for the truth at all.

units.la: Cum dicis, Crises non esse ex numero illorum contin-gentium, quorum causæ incertæ vel nullæ habeantur, rur-sus te parum in Medicina iuxtà ac philosophia exercitatū declaras. Etenim crises particulares ex numero contin-gentium esse, nemo sanus vnquam aut Medicus aut philo-sophus negauit. Deinde causas eas habere extra omnem controuersiam est. Nihil enim fit sine causa ipsum efficiē-te, nisi aliquid seipsum facere dicatur, atque tum cum nō-dum est, se producere cogitetur, quæ fortasse facilè ab Astrologis sententia admittatur. Concedunt enim & docent, figurationes cœli sæpe multis post mensibus agere, primum incipere, quàm esse in rerum natura desierunt. Hoc dixi, causas crisium varias multiplicesque esse, & tamen inter se varie & diuersè concurrere, vt earum congressus ante sciri nequeat, quàm conuenerunt iam effectumque producere inchoarunt. Unde sequitur, particularem cri-sim nullam praesciri posse & praedici, nisi cum iam fieri producíq;[?] coepta est, ac impedimentum accessisse nullum cernitur. Hinc illud etiam liquet, male te credere, contin-gentia esse quae causas nullas habeant. Habent res omnes causas certas quidem, aliter enim fieri nunquam possent, at nobis non sunt semper cognitae etiam tum, cum effectū productum videmus. Multo minus nouimus eas, cum producturae adhuc sunt, nec tamen producere adhuc incoe-perunt, imo cum ne determinatae quidem adhuc sunt ad illum vel hunc effectum hoc vel illo modo producendam. Sed haec spinosiora esse putabis forte, quam ut tibi conue-niant.
units.tr: When you say that crises are not among those contingent events whose causes are uncertain or non-existent, you again show that you are not well practised in medicine or in philosophy. For no sane person, whether physician or philosopher, has ever denied that particular crises belong to the class of contingent events. Moreover, that they have causes is beyond all dispute. For nothing happens without a cause producing it, unless something is said to make itself, and is thought to produce itself even before it exists, which the Astrologers would perhaps readily admit. For they concede and teach that the configurations of the heavens often act many months after they have ceased to exist, and begin before they have begun to be in the nature of things. I have said that the causes of crises are various and manifold, and yet they come together in different and diverse ways, so that their meeting cannot be known before they have come together and have begun to produce the effect. From this it follows that no particular crisis can be foreknown or predicted, except when it is already coming about and beginning to be produced, and no hindrance is seen to have intervened. From this too it is clear that you are wrong to believe that those things are contingent which have no causes. All things have definite causes, for otherwise they could never come to be; but these causes are not always known to us, even when we see the effect produced. Much less do we know them while they are still about to produce something, and have not yet begun to produce it, indeed while they are not yet determined to produce this or that effect in this or that way. But perhaps you will think these matters too thorny to suit you.

units.la: • Suprà dictis haec addis. Neque vniuersali tantum ratione vel causa fiunt eadem, sed pro speciali & proprio solius Lunae motu, naturam, quae proxima crisium causa est, &[?] re vera certis intervallis ad sui exonerationem inuitante & iuuante. Hic alijs missis, ne essem longior sine causa, illud considerabā, quae nam tua esset in his verbis mens atque sententia. Ego sic intelligo, ac si dicere velis, Crises non à lunae solum motu, hoc est, ab vniuersali causa fieri, sed oportere etiam particularem & propriam causam, Naturam scilicet, à Lunae motu impulsam ad sui exonerationem accedere. Si igitur Lunam vt causam vniuersalem, Naturam, videlicet proximam causam, impellere censes, recte quidem sentis mecumque facis. Neque hac de re vlla posthac nobis lis futura est, si in sententia persistere voles. Ego namque multis alibi ostendi, (& exemplis quomodo intelligi velim expo-sui,) non Lunam modo, sed & alia astra omnia vniuersa-les, communes, remotas, indefinitas omnium rerum ter-renarū causas existere. Hoc autem omnem ex astris praedi-ctionem funditus euertit, vt intelligere omnes poterunt, qui rerum consequentias videre queunt. Quare aut non intelligis hoc consequi, aut aliter tua explanari voles.
units.tr: • In addition to what you said above, you add these words: "Crises happen not only by a general reason or cause, but by the special and proper motion of the moon alone, nature, which is the nearest cause of crises, being indeed invited and assisted at certain intervals by it to discharge itself." Setting aside the other matters, so as not to be longer than necessary, I considered here what your mind and meaning in these words was. I understand you thus, as if you wished to say that crises come about not only from the motion of the moon, that is, from a general cause, but that a particular and proper cause is also needed, namely nature, impelled by the motion of the moon to discharge itself. If, then, you think that the moon, as a general cause, impels nature, the nearest cause, you are indeed right and agree with me. Nor will there be any further dispute between us on this point, if you are willing to keep to this opinion. For I have shown in many other places (and explained, with examples, how I wish it to be understood) that not only the moon but all the other stars are universal, common, remote, and indefinite causes of all earthly things. This, however, utterly overturns all prediction from the stars, as all will be able to understand who can see the consequences of things. Therefore either you do not see that this follows, or you will want to explain your words differently.

units.la: Quod si ita est, hunc esse sensum tuum suspicor, Lunam speciatim magis hoc tempore quàm a'io, & hanc magis quàm aliam quamuis Naturam ad crisim mouere impel-lerecac. lereque[?]. At hæc sententia rationi, sensui, evidentiæ, experientiæ, omnium doctorum hominum iudicio aduersaria est, quippe quæ Lunam non sinit vniuersalem causam, sed particularem & definitam aliquo pacto statuit. Etenim quæcunque causa vnum quàm aliud magis minusue assi-cit, mutat, mouet, nec omnia, quantum in se est, ex æquo alterat, eadem omnibus, hoc est, communis & generalis omnium similiter causa dici atque esse nunquam poterit. Lunæ vero motus & facultas omnibus eadem est, omnia ex æquo, quantum in ipsa est situm, commouet alteratq;. Quo fit, vt vnius rei non possit magis minusue causa dici, quàm alius cuiuslibet. Dico quantum in ipsa est, propterea quòd pro naturæ eorum, quæ motum eius recipiunt, diuersitate, nihil prohibet, imò necesse est, effectus diuer-sissimos, & plane dispares atque adeò contrarios enasci. Quod enim recipit non pro dantis seu mouentis natura, sed pro sua propria recipit agentis actionem cuiuslibet. Ni si ita esset, posset[?] res quælibet in quodlibet transmutari. Quocirca diuersissima uno tempore efficit communis causa, modò non aliter in rem vnam, quàm in alias agat, sed vnum eúdemque effectum in singulis per se exerceat. Quæ hoc modo agit, rectè communis & vniuersalis caus-sa dicetur.
units.tr: But if it is so, I suspect that this is your meaning: that the moon, at this time rather than at another, and this rather than any other nature, moves and impels nature to crisis in particular. But this opinion is opposed to reason, to the senses, to evidence, to experience, and to the judgement of all learned men; for it does not allow the moon to be a universal cause, but establishes it in some way as particular and defined. For whatever cause affects, changes, or moves one thing more or less than another, and does not alter all things equally, so far as it is in itself, can never be called or be the same, that is, a common and general cause of all alike. But the motion and power of the moon are the same for all; so far as lies in itself, it moves and alters all things equally. Hence it cannot be called the cause of one thing more or less than of any other. I say "so far as lies in itself," because, owing to the diversity of the natures that receive its motion, nothing prevents, indeed it is necessary, that very diverse, and quite unlike and even contrary, effects should arise. For whatever receives an action does not receive it according to the nature of the one giving or moving it, but according to its own nature. If it were not so, any thing could be changed into any other. Therefore a common cause produces very diverse effects at one time, provided it does not act on one thing differently from others, but exerts one and the same effect on each thing by itself. Whatever acts in this way will rightly be called a common and universal cause.

units.la: Sol quia ex æquo lutum atq; ceram calefacit, non hanc magis quàm illud, & parem utrique calorem, quod in se est, impertit, rectè causa communis utriusque effectus, qui in utroque consecutus est calorem ab eo impressum, appellatur. Sed hæc satis hoc loco sunto. Non magnopere solicitus sum, cur ad mea respondere noluerit[?]: quinimò consilium laudo. Sic enim minus te cognoscendum nobis exhibes, minusque negocij facessis. Claris viris cum innotuisse controuersiam nostram per me scribis, quid dicas non intelligo. Te publicasse tua causa ex animo doleo. Mea tātum abest, vt ægrè feram, vt, quoniam te id velle video, publicaturus sim vltrò, quò vel sic plures habeas reconditæ & rarae tuae doctrinae laudatores, & Astrologi tibi multi pro frigida, (dicere volebam strenua) defensione gratulentur. Quàm eruditè ac neruosè Astrologiam asse-rueris, & quàm rectè ac validè Sauonarolæ argumenta dis-solueris, ex ea defensione, quam pro eo iam conscripsi, pro-pediem, Deo volente, perspicies. Vale. Massfeldiæ[?].17.Mart.
units.tr: The sun, because it warms clay and wax alike, and imparts to each, so far as it is in itself, an equal heat, and not more to one than to the other, is rightly called the common cause of each effect, since each receives the heat impressed on it by the sun. But let these things be enough for this place. I am not greatly troubled about why he has been unwilling to answer my remarks; indeed I commend his decision, for in this way he shows himself less for us to know, and gives us less trouble. When you write that our controversy has become known to learned men through me, I do not understand what you mean. I am heartily sorry that you have published it for your own cause. I am so far from being vexed that, since I see you wish it, I will publish it of my own accord, so that you may have more admirers of your recondite and rare learning, and so that many Astrologers may congratulate you on your cold (I was going to say vigorous) defence. How learnedly and vigorously you have asserted astrology, and how rightly and forcefully you have dissolved Savonarola's arguments, you will soon see, God willing, from the defence which I have already written against him. Farewell. Mossfeld, 17 March.

units.la: Epistola VII. THOMAS ERASTVS D. CHRISTO-phoro Stathmioni, Medico Coburgensi, S. D.
units.tr: Letter VII. Thomas Erastus to Christoph Stathmio, physician of Coburg, greetings.

units.la: VErissimè Galenum alicubi dixisse re ipsa compe-tio, falsas opiniones eos quorum occupant animos, surdos ac cæcos reddere, ut nec audire nec videre possint, quæ alij omnes tum audiunt tum vident. Nam si, quæ pro me protuli, non vidisti, merito te cæcum esse putem. Si vidisti, & à falsa opinione tua discedere noluisti tamen, haud persuadebis tu mihi, te veritatis indagendæ studio commoueri. Argumenta mea te refellere non posse, periculo facto, intelligis, nec tamen de sententia cedis. Quinetiam positiones, nescio quas, vltro citroque, ut audio, dimittis, scilicet, ut vel sic aliquibus probes, te bonam contra me causam defendere. Si ad me illas misisses, fortasse ad eas respondissem, sicut ad omnes meas literas tuas respondisse expertus es. Iam ut non tu modò, sed etiam alij, qui hæc nostra legent, liquidò cernant, me rectè verèque scripsisse, Galenum in artis operibus ab Astrologia subsidium nunquam petiuisse, pluribus hanc rē mihi tractandam duxi. Non iam ad te solum, ut in præcedentibus, sed ad alios multos respicio. Quam ob rem ea quoque proponam, quæ tu fortasse minus commodè fue-ras percepturus. Ac si me non fallit animus, ita meam sententiam argumentis communiam, ut qui veritatem amat, nihil præterea sit desideraturus. Demonstrationes materia proposita, in qua quid Galenus fecerit, quæritur, nullas quidem admittit. Argumentis talibus nihilominus proba-bo, quæ in proposito demonstrationum verissimarum vim prorsus habere ratione putentur optima.
units.tr: Galen said somewhere, and experience itself confirms it, that false opinions make those whose minds they hold deaf and blind, so that they can neither hear nor see what everyone else both hears and sees. If you have not seen the things I have put forward, I would rightly think you blind. If you have seen them and yet refuse to abandon your false opinion, you will not persuade me that you are moved by a zeal for searching out the truth. You know from trying that you cannot refute my arguments, yet you do not give up your view. Moreover, as I hear, you are sending various propositions back and forth, evidently so that you may show some people that you are defending a good cause. If you had sent them to me, perhaps I would have answered them, as you have found I answered all your letters. Now, so that not only you but also others who read what I have written may plainly see that I have written rightly and truly, and that Galen never sought help from astrology in the works of his art, I have thought the matter worth treating at greater length. I now have in view not only you, as in my previous letters, but many others. For this reason I will also set out points which you might have grasped less readily. If my judgement does not deceive me, I have supported my opinion with arguments such that anyone who loves the truth will want nothing more. Demonstrations are not admissible at all in a question like this, concerning what Galen did. Nevertheless, by arguments of the sort I will use, I will prove what, in this matter, is judged on the best reasoning to have the full force of true demonstrations.

units.la: Antea verò quàm ad ipsam rem accedam, scilicet ut omnia magis dilucida apertaque fiant, ostendere conabor, Hippocratem in medendo Astrologiam non adhibuisse vnquam. Vnde nam hoc probare incipiam? An inde, quòd in suis ille scriptis Astrologiæ (Loquor autem de sola diui natrice, quam iudiciariam nominant) nunquam meminit? Verum falli me vociferabis, & logices me imperitum di-ces, si, quia illius non meminerit, nunquam ea vsum putè. At verò si rectè artenteq; consideres, vel hac ipsa ratione, quod propositum est, me commodè effecturum esse planè ac certè videbis. Etenim si in curando vsus ea esse putetur, credere cogemur ipsum ea in præsentiendo vsum fuisse. Siquidem dici facile non potest, in qua parte Medicinæ vsum habeat, si ei parti, quæ futura præcognoscere docet, nihil vtilitatis conserit. Ipsimet Astrologi hactenus nullum ipsius vsum alium præcipuum indicare potuerunt. Quæ namque Bellantius atque alij omnes, quos ego vidi, de ipsius vtilitate commemorant, huc omnia referri aptissimè possunt. Ratio etiam futura eadem est, siue huc, siue alió referre malis. Consentaneum quoque est rationi, vt diuinandi ars, non nisi ea in parte, in qua præscientia futurorum tractatur, locum habere putetur. Dubitari ergo nō potest, quin Hippocrates, siquidem vsus Astrologia in curando concedatur, ad præsagiendos corporum motus morborumque euentus præuidendos eam adhibuerit. Hoc si falsum comprobetur, liquebit, Astrologiam eum cum Medicina non coniunxisse in ægrotorum curationibus. Sic igitur arguo.
units.tr: Before I come to the matter itself, and so that everything may be made clearer and plainer, I will try to show that Hippocrates never used astrology in medicine. How shall I begin to prove this? Shall I do so because in his writings he never mentions astrology (I mean only that divinatory astrology, which they call judicial)? You will cry out that I am mistaken, and you will call me unskilled in logic if I suppose he never used it merely because he does not mention it. But if you consider the matter carefully and attentively, you will see that I shall accomplish what I propose, even by this very reasoning. For if astrology is held to be used in curing, we shall be forced to believe that Hippocrates also used it in foreseeing. Indeed, it cannot easily be said in what part of medicine it has a use, if it contributes nothing to that part which teaches us to foreknow the future. The astrologers themselves have so far been unable to point out any other chief use of it. Whatever Bellantius and all the others I have read say about its usefulness can most fittingly be referred to this. The reasoning about the future is the same, whether you prefer to refer it here or elsewhere. It is also consistent with reason that the art of divination should be thought to have a place only in that part where foreknowledge of future events is treated. Therefore there can be no doubt that Hippocrates, if its use in curing is granted, would have employed it to foretell the movements of bodies and the outcomes of diseases. If this is shown to be false, it will be clear that he did not join astrology with medicine in curing the sick. So I argue as follows.

units.la: Vbi Hippocrates methodum ac rationem præcognoscendi futuros in morbis euentus siue successus exponit, Astrologiæ ne vno quidem verbo meminit. Astrologia igitur non est ipse in præcognoscendo vsus. Non, arbitror, dubitabit quisquam, quin vniuersam & absolutam nobis Hippocrates præsagiendi artem, (vna de pulsibus doctrina excepta) præscripserit, qua instructus ipse tanta omnium doctorum admiratione futura præuidit. Equidem Galenus præter pulsuum tractationem doctrinæ Hippocratis nihil addidit, & in præsagiendo omnes omnium ætatum Medicos post Hippocratem longo post se interuallo reliquit. Ex quo certè necessariò efficitur, eandem uobis artem in-tegrè perfectéque ab Hippocrate, quanquam obscurè & breuiter, traditam fuisse, si pulsus demas, quos obseruasse eum non constat. Quod autem non meminerunt Astrolo-giæ, manifestius multo est, quàm vt probari à me debeat. Cui satisfactum nondum est, is plura in sequentibus repe-riet, quæ hoc ipsum comprobent. Sic habet igitur argu-mentum: Hippocrates totam eam artem, quam ipse ad præintelligendas corporum morborumque permutatio-nes adhibuit, scripto nobis tradidit, Astrologiæ verò nus-quam mentionem fecit. Ergo Astrologia non est vsus. Ex indiciis atque signis quæ in corpore, non in cœlo, apparet, additis circunstantiis aliis præsensit ipsemet omnia, & præ-sentire nos quoque eadem docuit.
units.tr: Where Hippocrates sets out the method and reasoning for foreknowing the future outcomes or successes in diseases, he does not mention astrology even in a single word. Therefore astrology is not the means he used in foreknowing. I think no one will doubt that Hippocrates prescribed for us the whole and complete art of prognosis (apart from the one doctrine on the pulse), and that, instructed in it, he foresaw the future to the great admiration of all learned men. Indeed, Galen added nothing to the teaching of Hippocrates beyond the treatment of the pulse, and in prognosis he left all the physicians of every age after Hippocrates far behind him. From this it certainly follows necessarily that the same art was handed down by Hippocrates to us whole and complete, though obscurely and briefly, if you take away the pulse, which it is not established that he observed. That they do not mention astrology is far too plain to require proof from me. Whoever is not yet satisfied will find more in what follows that confirms this very point. The argument therefore stands thus: Hippocrates handed down to us in writing the whole art which he himself used to foresee changes in bodies and diseases, and he nowhere mentioned astrology. Therefore astrology is not a means he used. From the signs and indications which appear in the body, not in the heavens, together with other circumstances, he himself perceived everything, and he taught us also to perceive the same things.

units.la: Ad hanc rem cognoscendam, cui non hi libri sufficiunt, quos Galenus interpretatus est, alios etiam adiungat, ac quæ in 2.lib.Prædictionum narrat, expendat. Solus iste ve-ritatem amanti abundè satisfecerit. Nec mouere quem-quam debet, quod Hippoc. non legitimus esse creditur, in qua sententia Galenum quoque fuisse probè scimus. Siue Hipp. siue alium quempiam faciamus autorem, constat vi-rum fuisse antiquissimum ac doctissimum, & Hippocrati-cæ doctrinæ sectatorem diligentissimum, nec parum in ar-te exercitatum.
units.tr: To learn this matter, for which these books which Galen interpreted are not enough, let the reader take up others as well, and weigh what he relates in the second book of the Prognostics. That book alone will satisfy anyone who loves the truth. Nor should it trouble anyone that Hippocrates is not believed to be the author of the book, a view which we know Galen also held. Whether we make Hippocrates or some other person the author, it is established that he was a man of very great antiquity and learning, a most diligent follower of the Hippocratic doctrine, and not a little practised in the art.

units.la: Cui ne hoc quidem probatur, is ita secum cogitet, Hip-pocratem Astrologiam prorsus ignorasse, ideoque vti illa, si maximè voluisset, minimè potuisse. Non obscurè patet historias legentibus & considerantibus, post Hippocratis ætatem Astrologiam primum ex Aegypto in Græciā fuisse illaram[?]. Equidem non Astrologiæ modò Græci Hippocra-tis seculo ignari fuerunt, verum etiam Astronomiæ vix ele-menta adhuc cognouerant. Tempore Platonis primum ferè coeperunt aliquid certi, quodq; notatu sit dignum, in Astronomicis intelligere: id quod cùm ex alijs, tum ex Aristotele eiusdemque interpretibus conijcere licet. Hip-pocratem ætate Democrati non vixisse modò, sed etiam in tota Graecia celeberrimum fuisse propter incredibilem artis Medicae peritiam, vel una ista res probat, quod Abderas ad Democritum sanandum evocatus est, quemadmodum in suis ipsemet Hippocrates epistolis testificatur. Hoc tempore floruerunt etiam Heraclytus & Anaxagoras physici.
units.tr: If anyone does not even accept this, let him consider this: Hippocrates was entirely ignorant of astrology, and so, even had he very much wished to use it, he could not have done so at all. It is plain to those who read and consider the histories that after the time of Hippocrates astrology first passed from Egypt into Greece. Indeed, in the age of Hippocrates the Greeks were not only ignorant of astrology, but had hardly learned even the rudiments of astronomy. It was roughly in the time of Plato that they first began to understand anything certain and worth noting in astronomical matters, as may be inferred both from other sources and from Aristotle and his interpreters. That Hippocrates not only lived in the age of Democritus but was also most famous throughout Greece for his incredible skill in medicine is shown by this one fact: he was summoned to Abdera to cure Democritus, as Hippocrates himself attests in his own letters. At this same time the natural philosophers Heraclitus and Anaxagoras also flourished.

units.la: Hic primus inter Graecos causam Lunae luminis atque umbrae scriptis mandasse scribitur. Quam ob rem ab Arrhenensibus est in vincula coniectus, & vix Periclis precibus servatus. Non enim tutum erat illo tempore de coelestium motuum & affectionum causis disputare, propterea quod astra pro Diis tum colerentur habenturque, ut Plutarchus refert. ἃ γὰρ ἠνείχοντο, inquit, τὰς φυσικὰς καὶ μετεωρολέσχας τὸν καλουμένας, ὡς εἰς αἰτίας ἀλόγως καὶ δυνάμεις ἀπορουμένας [?] ἀπροσηθήσαντας [?] τὸ θεῖον [?]. Qui plura requirit, & apud eundem, & alios quoque autores facile reperiet, si modo quaeret.
units.tr: Anaxagoras is written to have been the first among the Greeks to commit to writing the cause of the light and shadow of the moon. For this reason he was thrown into prison by the men of Clazomenae, and was scarcely saved by the prayers of Pericles. For at that time it was not safe to dispute about the causes of the motions and affections of the heavenly bodies, because the stars were then, and are still, worshipped as gods, as Plutarch reports. For, he says, they tolerated those who were called physicists and talkers about the heavens only as men who were unreasonably puzzled about causes and powers, and who had not been brought to reverence the divine [?]. Anyone who wants more will easily find it in him and in other authors too, if only he looks for it. [ἃ γὰρ ἠνείχοντο, inquit, τὰς φυσικὰς καὶ μετεωρολέσχας τὸν καλουμένας, ὡς εἰς αἰτίας ἀλόγως καὶ δυνάμεις ἀπορουμένας [?] ἀπροσηθήσαντας [?] τὸ θεῖον [?].]

units.la: Annis plus minus octoginta post Anaxagoram, ita fuit adhuc vulgo eclipsis lunae causa incognita, ut Nicias dux Atheniensium vir clarissimus, propter huius rei ignorationem non parum in Sicilia Atheniensium opes affixerit. Etenim ab eclipsi, cuius causam nesciebat naturalem esse, territus, classem ex portu educere cum deberet, nō est ausus. Si quis Hippocratis testimonium flagitet, ne hoc quidem destituimur. In principio namque libri de Veteri Medicina, quem legitimum esse constat, aperte affirmat, Coelestium sive sublimium & subterraneorum rerum scientiam incertam esse, atque adeo nihil in his esse, cui quis in-nixus progredi longius valeat. Facile hinc perspicitur, Grae-cos tum rerum Astronomicarum non admodum peritos fuisse. Quod si aliquos coelestium rerum studiosos tum quoque per Graeciam fuisse contendas, nō repugnabo, sed vltro concedam. Satis habeo in praesentia ostendisse, Hippocratem Astrologiae ignarum fuisse, & qui ne Astrono-miae quidem valde peritus esse potuerit. Recte ergo asseueraui supra, Hippocratem in curationibus ab Astrologia subleuari non potuisse.
units.tr: About eighty years more or less after Anaxagoras, the cause of a lunar eclipse was still so commonly unknown that Nicias, the most distinguished commander of the Athenians, through ignorance of this matter greatly weakened the Athenian forces in Sicily. For, terrified by an eclipse whose natural cause he did not know, he did not dare to lead his fleet out of harbour when he ought to have. If anyone demands the testimony of Hippocrates, we are not left without it even here. For at the beginning of the book On Ancient Medicine, which is accepted as genuine, he plainly states that knowledge of the heavenly or lofty and of the subterranean things is uncertain, and that there is therefore nothing in them on which a man can rely to advance far. From this it is easily seen that the Greeks at that time were not very skilled in astronomical matters. But if you should contend that there were some men then throughout Greece who studied the heavenly things, I shall not object, but will readily concede it. For the present it is enough for me to have shown that Hippocrates was ignorant of astrology, and could not have been very skilled even in astronomy. I was therefore right to assert above that Hippocrates could not have been assisted by astrology in his cures.

units.la: Diceret hic forte Astrologus, quomodo verum esse possit, quod dico, cum ortus & occasus certorum siderum obseruare iusserit Hippocrates? Non nescio Astronomiam siderum ortus, occasus ac motus inquirere, ac docere. Hac de causa ad perdiscendam eam hortatur Medicinæ candidatos Hippocrates. Sed illo tempore nihil fere docebat hæc scientia aliud. Non ita erant cœlestium motus, vt hodie sunt, explorati. Vix inerrantium omnium motus, hoc est ortus & occasus tum sciebatur. Nec Hippocrates aliud præcepit, cum siderum certorum ortum & occasum inspicere cognoscereque imperat, quàm vt mutationes anni temporum, quæ ab illis sideribus orientibus occidentibus ue circunscribebantur & denominabantur, diligenter inter se distingueremus, & quæ cuiusque priuatim temperies esset, singulis annis & locis attentè obseruaremus. Ac vt non me ista fingere putes, Galenum legito in commen. quos in Aphor. & Epidem. libros Hipp. maximè in 1. conscripsit, nihilque me dicere perspicies, quod non ante Galenus explicatissimis verbis asseruerit.
units.tr: Perhaps the astrologer will object: how can what I say be true, when Hippocrates himself ordered the risings and settings of certain stars to be observed? I am not unaware that astronomy investigates and teaches the risings, settings and motions of the stars, and for this reason Hippocrates urges those who are to learn medicine to study it thoroughly. But in his time this science taught almost nothing beyond that. The motions of the heavenly bodies were not then as well understood as they are today, and hardly anyone knew the motions of all the fixed stars, that is, their risings and settings. Nor did Hippocrates prescribe anything more when he bade us watch and learn the risings and settings of certain stars than that we should carefully distinguish from one another the changes of the seasons of the year, which were marked and named by those stars as they rose or set, and should diligently observe, each year and in each place, what the temperament of each season was. And so that you may not think I am inventing this, read Galen's commentaries on the Aphorisms and Epidemics of Hippocrates, especially on the first book. You will see that I am saying nothing that Galen did not state earlier, in the plainest words.

units.la: Hoc magis aliquem mouerit, quod Galenus in 3. Decret. cap. 12. in hunc modum scripsit: A me itaque veritatem ipsam, quantum homini licet, inuentam ase[?] puto, quam quidem & Hipp. primus cognouerat, sicut & præscriptis verbis nobis indicauit: vulgare autem Medicorum genus præ segnitie eam subticuit. Item in 3.com.Prognost.com.1. Caterum, inquit, cognouit non primus solum, sed etiam maximè admirandus Hippocrates decretoriorum dierum naturam, atque etiam indicauit causam generationis eorum, quam nos quoque tractata[?] de diebus criticis docuimus. In duobus hisce locis aperte Galenus dicere videtur, Hippocratem cognouisse. Lunæ motum in causa esse, cur alij dies magis ac melius iudicent quàm alij. Ego verò, etsi hæc omnia concedam Astrologis, non video, quid contra dicta inde concludere possint. Nō enim sequitur, Hippocrates putauit Lunæ motum causam esse dierum Decretoriorum, ergo fuit Astrologiæ peritus. Sunt enim hodie permulti, qui hoc credunt, (perperam tamen) & sunt nihilominus Astronomiæ pariter & Astrologiæ imperitissimi. Quinimò certum est Hippocratis ætate Lunæ motum nequaquam cognitum fuisse. Iam enim monui, Anaxagoram sub illa tempora non sine suo periculo de ea re primum scripsisse. Constat multis post seculis, hanc rem demum perquisitam inventamque esse.
units.tr: This may move someone more, because Galen wrote in book 3 of the De decretoriis, chapter 12, in this manner: I therefore think I have discovered the truth itself, as far as it is permitted to man; Hippocrates was the first to know it, as he indicated to us in express words, but the common kind of physicians, through laziness, passed it over in silence. Likewise in book 3 of the commentary on the Prognostics, comment 1: But, he says, not only was the nature of the decisive days first recognised, but most admirable Hippocrates also indicated the cause of their generation, which we too have taught in our treatise on critical days. In these two passages Galen clearly seems to say that Hippocrates knew that the motion of the Moon is the cause why some days judge better and more reliably than others. For my part, although I grant all this to the astrologers, I do not see what they can conclude from it against what I have said. For it does not follow that Hippocrates thought the motion of the Moon was the cause of the decretory days, and therefore that he was skilled in astrology. There are today very many who believe this (though wrongly), and who are nonetheless wholly ignorant of astronomy as well as of astrology. Indeed, it is certain that in Hippocrates' age the motion of the Moon was not known at all. For I have already pointed out that Anaxagoras was the first to write on this matter, and not without danger to himself, in those times. It is established that this question was only investigated and discovered many centuries later.

units.la: Sed istis omissis, illud potius, quod ad rem propius acce-dit, expendamus, an Hippocrates crediderit, Lunam esse horum dierum caussam. Profecto nisi aliud adferatur, non probabitur. Atqui Galenus, dices, affirmat. Ego non quid affirmet hic specto iam, sed quid sit verum consídero. At probauit, respondebis. Hoc si sit, facilè cessero. Videamus igitur quo argumento probauerit. Hippocrates neque an-num neque menses docuit integris diebus numerari. Ergo putauit dierum Decret. caussam Lunam esse. Vel hoc mo-do, Ergo Hippocr. putauit menses ita miscendos esse, & ego miscui. Hæc aut similis est Galeni ratiocinatio, vt videre quisque poterit qui locum perpenderit. Præscriptis, in-quit, verbis indicauit. Ea in principio 9. capitis habentur. Non puto quenquam esse, qui aliquid à Galeno hic pro-batum existimet. Ego ne quidem voluisse hoc Galenum suspicor. Vix enim credo ipsum tale quid de Hippocrate credidisse. Hoc fortasse voluit ostendere, se in eo nihil præ-ter Hipp. mentem fecisse, quod non integris diebus septi-manas numerari dixit. Verùm siue hoc siue aliud volue-rit, nemo non videt, rectè à me dictum ac probatum suis-se, Hippocratem Astrologia non fuisse in curando vsum. Quinetiam monui supra, non posse eo Astrologos iuua-ri, si Hippocratem Lunæ motum dies Decret. efficere con-cedam existimasse, quod tamen probari nullis vnquam po-terit argumentis.
units.tr: But setting those points aside, let us weigh the point that bears more directly on the matter: did Hippocrates believe that the Moon is the cause of these days? Certainly, unless something else is brought forward, it will not be proved. Yet Galen, you will say, affirms it. I am not now looking at what he affirms, but at what is true. But he proved it, you will reply. If so, I will readily give way. Let us see, then, by what argument he proved it. Hippocrates taught that neither years nor months are to be counted by whole days. Therefore, Galen concludes, he thought the Moon was the cause of the decretory days. Or in this way: therefore Hippocrates thought that months ought to be reckoned in this way, and I have reckoned them so. Galen's reasoning is of one of these two kinds, as anyone who weighs the passage will see. He pointed it out, he says, in express words. These are found at the beginning of chapter 9. I do not think anyone exists who considers anything proved by Galen here. I do not even suspect that Galen wished this. For I scarcely believe that he himself thought any such thing of Hippocrates. Perhaps he wished only to show that in this he had done nothing beyond Hippocrates' intention, since Hippocrates said that weeks are not to be counted by whole days. But whether he meant this or something else, everyone sees that I was right to say, and to prove, that Hippocrates did not use astrology in treating the sick. Moreover, I have pointed out above that the astrologers cannot be helped even if I grant that Hippocrates thought the motion of the Moon produces the decretory days, which nevertheless can never be proved by any argument.

units.la: Quare cum Hippocrates Astrologiam prorsus ignora-rit, vt quæ Græcis nondum esset cognita, vti illa inter cu-randum non potuit. Plato certè & discipulus ipsius Eudo-xus Cnidius atque Callippus Cyzicenus primi fere Græ-cos Astronomica paulò fusius, luculentius & verius docue-runt, cum ante illa tempora vix amplius quàm elementa degustauisse non sine grauibus caussis credantur. Nō erat necesse, cur Plato, Eudoxus atque alij in Aegypto pro ijs addiscendis navigarent, siquidem domi aptos habere præceptores poterant. Hos secutus est Aristoteles, & eorum inventionibus addere aliquid conatus est, quem tamen ipsum quoque non peritissimum harum rerum fuisse constat. Quòd si totius Græciæ lumina illo tempore tam parum adhuc profecerant, quid de antiquioribus dicere nos oportebit? Vixit Aristot. annis fere 140. post Anaxagoram, cum quo Hippocratem floruisse clarissimumque fuisse supra indicavimus. Et hæc de Hippocrate satis.
units.tr: Therefore, since Hippocrates was entirely ignorant of astrology, as a science not yet known to the Greeks, he could not use it in treating patients. Plato certainly, and his pupil Eudoxus of Cnidus, and Callippus of Cyzicus, were almost the first Greeks to teach astronomical matters somewhat more fully, clearly and truly, although before those times the Greeks are believed, not without serious reasons, to have scarcely tasted more than the rudiments. There was no need for Plato, Eudoxus and the others to sail to Egypt to learn these things, if they could have had suitable teachers at home. Aristotle followed these men, and tried to add something to their discoveries, though he too is known not to have been very expert in these matters. But if the lights of all Greece had at that time advanced so little, what shall we need to say about earlier men? Aristotle lived about 140 years after Anaxagoras, with whom we have already indicated that Hippocrates flourished and was most famous. And this is enough about Hippocrates.

units.la: Iam verò quod & alij omnes post ætatem Hippocratis ad Galeni usque tempora Astrologiam vel ignoraverint, vel non usurparint, haud difficulter ostendatur. Equidem inter Græcos neminem scimus Astrologica serio tractasse ante Ptolemæum, quem cum Galeno vixisse notissimum est, quantumvis hic illius libros nō legisse videatur. Quod Eudoxus, cuius suprà memini, apud Aegyptios Astrologi-ca pariter cum Astronomicis hauserit, certum esse puto. Quomodo enim despectui habendam iudicasset, falsamq; affirmasset, si non gustum ipsius aliquem percepisset? Indicat Strabo locum in Ægypto esse specularum[?] Eudoxi nomen habens, quod huc duce Platone profectus, res coelestes ex æditiori loco observasset. An aliquis alius inter Græcos ante Ptolemæum huic vanitati opera aliquam navavit, mihi nondum innotuit, (hunc quia Græcè scripsit, quanquam Aegyptium fuisse natione minimè nesciam,) inter Græcos pono. Loquor de astrologia, ut in superioribus literis aliquoties ostendi, non aërea illa divinandi facultate, qua Nautæ & Rustici rectè utuntur, & de qua Aratus multa eruditissimè scripsit. Attigerunt eandem poetæ interdum. Rerum rusticarum quoque scriptores non raro præcepta quædam ipsius exposuerunt.
units.tr: Now, that all the others after Hippocrates' time down to the times of Galen either ignored astrology or did not practise it can be shown without much difficulty. Indeed, I know of no one among the Greeks who treated astrological matters seriously before Ptolemy, who is well known to have lived at the same time as Galen, although Galen does not seem to have read his books. That Eudoxus, whom I mentioned above, drew astrology from the Egyptians along with astronomy, I think is certain. For how else would he have judged it to be held in contempt, and called it false, unless he had had some taste of it? Strabo mentions a place in Egypt called the observatory of Eudoxus, where, having gone there under Plato's guidance, he observed the heavenly bodies from a rather elevated spot. Whether any other Greek before Ptolemy contributed some effort to this folly has not come to my knowledge; I count him among the Greeks, since he wrote in Greek, although I am well aware that he was by nation an Egyptian. I am speaking of astrology, as I have shown several times in my earlier letters, not of that aerial power of divination which sailors and farmers use rightly, and about which Aratus wrote much with great learning. Poets have sometimes touched on the same thing, and writers on rustic affairs have not infrequently set out certain rules of it.

units.la: Porrò, ut ad rem redeam, Ptolemæi libros Galenum nō vidisse, argumento esse videtur, quòd, cū de Lunæ motu & mensium interuallo disserit, Hipparchum citat: ubi ad Astrologica delabitur, autorem Græcum habet neminem, sed Aegyptios testes advocat. Valde verisimile est, si Græcum habuisset autorem, non fuisse eum Aegyptios pro testibus adducturum, quos pro deliris alibi habuit, Graecis vero semper plurimum fauit. Forte tum non erant Ptolemaei opera edita, aut ad ipsius manus non peruenerant, quod ij facile credent, qui norunt, quàm difficile esset ante inuentam artem typographicam exempla librorum ad multos peruenire. Quòd si legisse eum contendat aliquis, mea nō multum refert, praesertim cum negare talis nequeat, quin sit indignus Galeno visus, vt à se citaretur. Certè Aegyptiorum potius testimonio vti cum voluisse fatendum erit.
units.tr: Furthermore, to return to my point, the fact that Galen had not seen Ptolemy's books seems to be shown by this: when he discusses the motion of the Moon and the interval of the months, he cites Hipparchus; but when he slips into astrological matters, he has no Greek author, and calls on Egyptians as witnesses. It is very likely that, had he had a Greek author, he would not have brought forward Egyptians as witnesses, whom he elsewhere regarded as raving, while he always greatly favoured the Greeks. Perhaps Ptolemy's works had not then been published, or had not come into his hands; this will be readily believed by those who know how difficult it was, before the invention of printing, for copies of books to reach many people. But if someone insists that he did read them, it does not matter much to my argument, especially since no one can deny that such a work seemed unworthy to Galen of being cited by him. Certainly it must be admitted that he preferred to use the testimony of the Egyptians.

units.la: Haec in eum finem exposui verbofius, vt facilius intelligatur, Medicos qui Galenum praecesserunt, Astrologia non fuisse adiutos. Nō enim ita fuisset neglecta à Graecis omnibus, si tantum ipsius vsum percepissent. Ac quòd nullus ante Galenum Medicus Astrologica scripserit aut docuerit, illud primum probat, quòd nemo id de ipsis prodidit. Leue argumentum, dices, est hoc. Fateor & scio. At si quo pacto ego proponam peruideris, & caetera coniu-xeris, locum ei fortasse hic suum esse fines. Alterum est, quòd Galenus in omnibus penè artis nostrae dogmatibus priorum Medicorum sententias citare, opinionesque recensere solet, quò vel suam illorum authoritate comprobet, vel qua in re aberrauerint, demonstret, nusquam autem Astrologicarum rerum ipsos vel gnaros vel studiosos fuisse indicat. Sanè si quid illos tale vel scripsisse vel docuisse cognouisset, illorum potius quàm Aegyptiorum testimonio sua comprobasset. Huc addatur, quod affirmat, se primum fuisse, qui Decret.dierum caussam inuestigare tentarit, atque in Lunae motum deducere studuerit.
units.tr: I have set this out at some length for this purpose, so that it may be more easily understood that the physicians who preceded Galen were not aided by astrology. For it would not have been neglected by all the Greeks in that way if they had perceived any practical use of it. And that no physician before Galen wrote or taught astrological matters is first proved by the fact that no one has reported this about them. You will say this is a light argument. I grant it, and I know it. But if I should set forth the matter in some other way, and join the rest of the evidence, perhaps this point will find its proper place here. The second point is that Galen, in almost all the doctrines of our art, is accustomed to cite the opinions of the earlier physicians and to review their views, either to confirm his own by their authority or to show where they went wrong, yet nowhere does he indicate that they were either acquainted with or devoted to astrological matters. Certainly, had he learned that they had written or taught anything of that kind, he would have confirmed his own views by their testimony rather than by that of the Egyptians. Add to this that he affirms that he was the first to attempt to investigate the cause of the decretory days and to strive to trace it to the motion of the Moon.

units.la: Postremò nec Galenus nec alij eius aetatis Medici probri loco duxissent, si ex Astrologia praesentire morborum mutationes dicti fuissent, siquidem exemplo maiorum id facere se posse arbitrari fuissent. At Galenus, vt infrà compluribus ipsius testimonijs apertissimis demonstrabo, ignominiam sibi fieri & contumeliam putauit, quoties ab Astrologia in suis praedictionibus adiutus diceretur. Deinde ne Romanenses quidem Medici Galeno, cui propter eruditionem inuidebant,ac malè cupiebant, nunquam pro crimine ip- si obiecturi fuissent, si quid tale à superioris ætatis Medicis factum sciuissent. Equidem argumentum hinc quoq; mi- nimè leue nobis sese offert ad probandum, quòd Hippocra- tes non adhibuerit Astrologiam in curationibus ex Galeni sententia. Non enim Galenus pro calumnia & re turpi re- putaturus fuisset, si ea facere dictus fuisset, quæ ante Hippo- crates absque omnium reprehensione fecisset.
units.tr: Finally, neither Galen nor the other physicians of his age would have regarded it as a disgrace if it had been said that they foretold changes in disease from astrology, since they would have thought they could do so by the example of their predecessors. But Galen, as I will show below from several of his own most explicit testimonies, thought it a disgrace and an insult to himself whenever it was said that he was helped by astrology in his prognoses. Again, the Roman physicians, who envied Galen for his learning and wished him ill, would never have brought this charge against him had they known that any such thing had been done by physicians of an earlier age. Indeed, this is no small argument for us to prove that Hippocrates did not use astrology in his cures, according to Galen's judgment. For Galen would not have regarded it as a calumny and a disgraceful thing if he had been said to do what Hippocrates had done before him without anyone's reproof.

units.la: Non vereor, vt boni doctíque viri mihi hac in parte sint assensuri, & mecum confessuri, argumenta quæ proposui, satis efficaciter propositum probare, præsertim cum, qui contrarium sentit, pro sua sententia nihil æquè firmum sit allaturus. Nihil enim reperient, quod vel minimam habeat probabilitatem, nisi fortasse illius libri autorem Galeno superiorem antiquioremque suspiceris, cui titulus est, Prognostica ex mathematica de infirmorum decubitu, quem pro patrono supra quoque adducebas. Antiquior Galeno an fuerit, nec ne fuerit, in præsentia non possum certis vel argumentis vel scriptorum testimonijs affirma-re. At Galenum non esse autorem, supra satis ostendi. Argumento satis valido esse illud poterat, quòd præter aniles fabulas, & ineptissimas superstitiones atque nugas nihil continet. Deinde quod artu[?] nostræ maximè aduersatur: Demum quòd nugacis. & ineptis. homo fuisse præclarè conspicitur ab omnibus, qui cum iudicio illum librum legerit. Ex hos[?] ipso, si autoritate illius vti me non puderet, facilè probarem, Medicos ipsum nullos legisse, qui Astrologica tractarint aut probarint. Anxiè namque testimonia undique conquirit, vt suas nugas Medicis vriles esse prober. Sed frustra se fatigat. Hoc dici forte non malè potest, cum si apud Medicos Hippocrate posteriores aliquid præsidij reperisset, nunquam ex Hipp. ad rem nihil facientia producturum[?] potius fuisse, quàm certa ex alijs testimonia.
units.tr: I do not fear that good and learned men will agree with me on this point and admit that the arguments I have put forward prove my thesis well enough, especially since whoever holds the opposite view will have nothing as firm to bring forward for his opinion. For they will find nothing with even the slightest plausibility, unless perhaps you suspect that the author of that book entitled Prognostica ex mathematica de infirmorum decubitu, which you also cited above as your patron, was older than Galen. I cannot at present affirm with certain arguments or the testimony of writers whether he was older than Galen or not. But I have shown above well enough that Galen is not its author. This could have been a sufficiently strong argument in itself, since apart from old wives' tales and most foolish superstitions and trifles it contains nothing; furthermore, because it is most opposed to our art; and finally, because it is clearly seen by everyone who reads that book with judgment that its author was a silly and foolish man. From this very book, if I were not ashamed to use its authority, I could easily prove that no physicians had read it who treated or approved of astrological matters. For it anxiously seeks testimonies from everywhere to prove that its trifles are useful to physicians. But it tires itself in vain. This may perhaps be said not unfairly: if he had found any support among physicians later than Hippocrates, he would never have brought forward from Hippocrates things that have nothing to do with the matter, rather than certain testimonies from others.

units.la: Hactenus Hippocratem Astrologia non vsum fuisse, co-piosè valideque probatum à me est. Quinetiam plus præ-stiti, quàm initio pollicitus fui, quando ne alios quidem Hippocrate posteriores Medicos ipsam adhibuisse docui. Tempus iam esse videtur, ut, quod me in primis ostensu-rum recepi. Galenum scilicet in arte facienda nunquam Astrologicis observationibus sine præceptionibus usum fuisse. Maiore hic mihi conatu opus fore video, propterea quod in 3. Decret. non obscure Astrologiæ patrocinari videri potest. Hinc illa in multis superstitio nata est, ipsum in medendo & præsagiendo Astrologiæ opera usum fuisse.
units.tr: That Hippocrates did not use astrology I have proved at length and forcefully so far. Indeed I have done more than I promised at the outset, since I have also shown that not even the physicians after Hippocrates employed it. It now seems time to take up what I undertook to show first: that Galen, in practising his art, never used astrological observations without precepts. I see that this will require greater effort on my part, because in the third book of the Decretorum it can be seen to plead for astrology not obscurely. From this has arisen that superstition, widespread among many, that he used the work of astrology in healing and in foretelling.

units.la: Præsens quæstio hæc est, utrum in artis operibus exercendis Galenus solius artis Medicæ opera usus sit, an potius Astrologicas observationes Medicis præceptis coniunxerit. Tu utriusque beneficio ipsum futura præuidisse in ægris affirmas, ego nego, sed ex sola Medica arte præcognouisse omnia aio. Ratio, qua te moveri ostendis, hæc est, quod in 3. Decret. Galenus Astrologiæ visus sit fuisse, dum sophistas illos appellat, qui talia non crederent, qualia ex Aegyptiorum placitis promisisset. Ego vero hanc ratiunculam tuam imbellem, evanidam & lubricam esse probaui. Non enim recte sequitur, Galenus opinatus est causam dierum Decret. esse Lunæ motum. Ergo in exercenda arte Medica usus est etiam Astrologia. Suprà monui complures inve-niri, qui idem putant, non tamen Astrologia unquam uti in medendo, ut quam numquam didicerint. Imò ne hoc altero quipem[?] modo recte colligas, Galenus causam dierum Decret. censuit esse motum Lunæ sive lumen Lunæ. Ergo ista noritia utilitatem affert medenti talem, cuius causa Astrologiam addiscere debeat. Si, inquam, verum esset, pro mutatione luminis Lunæ mutationes istas in ægris accidere, non tamen sine Astrologia non possemus optimè exercere Medicinam. Tam enim est ista res iam nota, ut omnes idiotæ norint, & ex ephemeridibus annuis perfacilè videant. Sic hodie post exactam illam anni in suos menses distinctionem, quæ à C. Iulio Cæs. introdu-cta fuit, facilè nos carere Astronomia posse existimauit Ga-lenus. Etenim quæ tum ex ea scientia nos discere oportebat, per nos ipsos iam scimus, & veluti cum lacte materno imbibimus. Sed hæc extra rem.
units.tr: The present question is this: whether in carrying out the operations of his art Galen used only the work of the medical art, or whether he rather joined astrological observations to medical precepts. You assert that he foresaw the future in the sick by the benefit of both, whereas I deny it and maintain that he knew everything from the medical art alone. The reason by which you show yourself moved is this: that in the third book of the Decretorum Galen seems to have been an astrologer, since he calls those sophists who did not believe such things as he had promised from the opinions of the Egyptians. But I have shown that this little reasoning of yours is weak, empty and slippery. For it does not follow correctly that, because Galen thought the cause of the critical days was the motion of the Moon, therefore he used astrology also in practising the medical art. I have said above that many are found who think the same, yet they never used astrology in healing, since they never learned it. Indeed, you cannot correctly infer even in this other way that Galen judged the cause of the critical days to be the motion or light of the Moon. Therefore this knowledge brings the healer no such benefit that he ought to learn astrology for its sake. Even if it were true that these crises occur in the sick according to the light of the Moon, we could nonetheless practise medicine very well without astrology. For this matter is now so well known that all laymen know it, and they can see it very easily from the yearly ephemerides. Thus today, after that exact division of the year into its months, which was introduced by Gaius Julius Caesar, Galen thought we could easily dispense with astronomy. For what we ought to learn from that science we already know ourselves, and we have absorbed it, as it were, with our mother's milk. But these things are beside the point.

units.la: Naturam morborum medicatrices esse, eorūque causas certis temporum periodis concoquere, mox noxia ab utilibus separare, separata extra corpus propellere. Medi-cum sanè conuenit. Vtrum autem sola temperatura corporis, an alia in corpore substantia, anima scilicet, per temperaturam hæc efficiat, nihil prodest Medico scire, si Galeno credimus. In causa est, quòd hæc substantia siue anima nostra hæc operationes bene aut male, citò aut tardè, per temperaturam semper sine ea nunquam perficit. Ergo prout hæc est bene aut male affecta, fiunt istæ operationes quoq; vel temporius[?] vel tardius quomodocūque anima esse cogitet in corpore inesse. Eodem modo inutilis est in Medicina ista disceptatio de anima, quid sit & quomo-do corpus moueat. Item hæc, an anima congenitis sine à Deo sibi insitis viribus corpus moueat, an potius à Lu-næ motu impellatur.
