Quòd si ex ipsius animæ contempla-tione, quæ sine medio corpus mouet, sicut mouere animum est, intelligere non possumus quando fit concoctura, separatura, expulsura: quomodo quæso ex causæ externæ & præterea generalis siue communis consideratione horum aliquid intelligatur? Etenim cœlum multò magis corpus nostrum, prout aptum est, magis minusque mouet, quàm anima. Qui temperaturæ bonitatem nouit, & quomodo in morbum agat perspexit, crisim futuram præintelligit, etiamsi de anima, quæ tamen principium est morbo-rum omnium, nunquam cogitarit. Multò ergo magis qui hæc per-nouerit, crisim præuidebit, etiamsi cœlum esse nesciat, aut saltem harum rerum causas non esse, quomodo nō sunt, sciat. Hæc pluribus ideo exposui, vt cernerent omnes, me non temerè argumenta tua despicere & ridere, ac veluti inutilia & puerilia omni nervo carentia abijcere. Tu iam mea quæ afferre statui, considera, examina & pondera diligenter, & si quod vitium deprehenderis, similiter contem-ne & ride.
units.tr: That nature is the healer of diseases, that she digests their causes in fixed periods of time, then separates the harmful from the useful, and drives the separated matter outside the body: this certainly belongs to the physician. But whether the temperament of the body alone effects these things, or some other substance in the body, namely the soul, effects them through the temperament, it does the physician no good to know, if we believe Galen. The reason is that this substance or soul of ours never accomplishes these operations well or badly, quickly or slowly, except through the temperament, and never without it. Therefore, according to whether this is well or badly disposed, these operations occur either sooner or later, however the soul may think it dwells in the body. In the same way that dispute about the soul, what it is and how it moves the body, is useless in medicine. So too is the question whether the soul moves the body by powers innate and implanted in it by God, or rather is driven by the motion of the Moon. But if from the contemplation of the soul itself, which moves the body without an intermediary, just as it moves the mind, we cannot understand when concoction, separation or expulsion will occur, then how, I ask, can any of these things be understood from the consideration of an external cause and, moreover, of a general or common one? For the heaven moves our body, as it is suited to be moved, far more and less than the soul does. Whoever knows the goodness of the temperament and has observed how it acts in disease foresees the coming crisis beforehand, even if he has never thought about the soul, which nevertheless is the principle of all diseases. Much more, then, will one who has thoroughly known these things foresee the crisis, even if he does not know that the heaven exists, or at least that these things are not the causes of the crisis, as in fact they are not. I have set this out at length so that everyone might see that I do not rashly despise and laugh at your arguments, nor cast them aside as useless and childish and lacking all strength. Now consider, examine and weigh carefully the arguments I have decided to bring forward, and if you detect any flaw in them, despise and laugh at them in the same way.

units.la: Ratio prima, & quæ minus fortasse neruosa alicui conseri possit, non contentioso tamen abundè satisfacerit, hæc est. Galenus in curando & præsagiendo solam Hippocratieam[?] artem, vt nihil ei addiderit praeter doctrinam de pulsibus, est secutus. Ergo Astrologia non est visus. Quippe Hippocrates nec visus ea fuit, nec vti potuit. Ac si visum erigi-darem[?], Galenus imitari[?] tamen non potuisset, cum ipsius partem nullam Hippocrates docuerit, imo nec docere potuerit. Quis enim tam sit temerarius, qui Hippocratem in aliquo suorum operum loco Astrologica docuisse asseuerret? Equidem vbi praedictiones docet, nunquam Astrologicarum observationum meminit, quod tamen facere ipsum oportebat, si vtilem esse suspicabatur.
units.tr: My first argument, which perhaps can be set against anyone's as less forceful, but which will nonetheless amply satisfy an unargumentative reader, is this. In curing and foretelling, Galen followed only the Hippocratic art, so that he added nothing to it except the doctrine of the pulses. Therefore astrology was not seen by him. Indeed, Hippocrates neither saw it nor could he have used it. And even if I were to suppose that he had seen it, Galen could still not have imitated it, since Hippocrates taught no part of it, nor indeed could he have taught it. For who is so rash as to assert that Hippocrates taught astrological matters in any part of his works? Certainly, wherever he teaches prognoses, he never mentions astrological observations, which he ought to have done if he thought them useful.

units.la: Sed quia haec res est per se testata omnibus, nosque supra de ea plura disseruimus, illud potius comprobemus, non ex aliis Galenum, ex aliis rursus Hippocratem futura praesensisse. In libro Galeni ad Posthumum, in primo capite, affirmatur, Hippocratem sicut[?] aliorum bonorum omnium, ita etiam artis praesagiendi autorem esse.
units.tr: But since this matter is attested in itself to everyone, and we have discussed it at length above, let us rather prove this: that Galen foresaw the future from one set of signs and Hippocrates from another. In Galen's book to Posthumus, in the first chapter, it is affirmed that Hippocrates was the author of the art of prognosis, just as he was of all other good things.

units.la: Decimo deinde cap. haec legimus: Quanquam haec praedictio nil, quod mireris, continet, si eorum memor es, quae tibi in com. in 1. Hipp. Epidem. librum conscripsimus, & praeterea quae in libris de Crisibus docuimus didicisti, &c. Porro nihil docuit in illis libris Galenus, quod non ab Hippocrate se accepisse fateatur. Vnde cap. 13. eiusdem sic scribit: Ego vero tibi mearum rerum studioso, quo pacto id praesciuisem[?], idq; ex Hipp. monumentis exposui[?]. Et in 3. de Crisi cap. 8. Equidem haec omnia quae ad crisin attinent, vel futura praenoscere, vel iam praesentia dignoscere ex aliis principiis haud inueni, quam ex iis quae supposuit Hippocrates. Complures alij loci passim reperiuntur. Ego vnicum adhuc ex cap. 12. libri iam ante citati adscribam. Tu vero, inquit Galenus, mi Posthume, scis omnia me ab Hippocrate dicta monstrasse, quaecunque hisce de rebus conscripsi, & te vidente praedixi, praeter pulsuum scientiam nihil adiiciens, quam etiam solam Hippocrates non attigit. Non puto apertius aliquid dici posse. Neque necesse iudico esse, vt pluribus confirmare coner, ex isdem vtrunque praedixisse.
units.tr: Then in the tenth chapter we read these words: "Although this prediction contains nothing to be wondered at, if you remember those things which we wrote for you in our commentary on the first book of Hippocrates' Epidemics, and besides, what you learned from our teaching in the books on Crises, etc." Moreover, Galen taught nothing in those books that he does not confess he received from Hippocrates. Hence in chapter 13 of the same work he writes thus: "As for me, since you are a student of my work, I have explained how I came to know this, and I have set it out from the monuments of Hippocrates." And in the third book on Crises, chapter 8: "Indeed, I have found no other principles by which to foreknow all these things that pertain to the crisis, or to recognise things already present, than those which Hippocrates laid down." Many other passages are found here and there. I will add just one more, from chapter 12 of the book already cited above. "But you, my Posthumus," says Galen, "know that I have shown everything I have written on these matters to have been said by Hippocrates, and that I predicted, in your presence, nothing beyond the science of the pulses, which Hippocrates himself did not touch." I do not think anything can be said more plainly. Nor do I judge it necessary to try to confirm by many examples that both predicted from the same things.

units.la: Sic igitur argumentum, si paucis complecti omnia velimus, habet. Galenus non ex aliis vllis indiciis aut signis praedixit, quam ex illis, quae Hippocrates nobis obseruanda præscripsit in libris, quos hodie quoq; habemus, nec quic-quam illis adiecit præter doctrinam de pulsibus. Atque Hippocrates Astrologiæ non meminit, nec discedam eam nobis putauit, quin ipsemet ignorauit. Ergo ne Galenus quidem ab ea adiutus fuisse in suis prædictionibus censeri poterit. Argumentum efficax & validum foret, quod ad conclusum attinet, etiamsi concederem, Hippocratem Astrologia vsum fuisse, nobisque eam commendasse. Non enim desunt, qui inscitè locum suprà expositum, & præterea quod in prognosticis τὰ ὥρα[?] obseruandum imperauit, ad hoc probandum in medium adducere solent. De priore loco dixi, quomodo eum Galenus intellexerit, longè aliter nimirum quàm vellent Astrologi. Quod posteriorem quoque non de Astrologia intellexerit ac exposuerit, sed de aëris temperie accipi voluerit, ex ipsius commentario tam dilucidè patet, vt planius explicari à me non possit. Quare si Hippocratem aliquid Astrologici scripsisse concederem, quod falsum esse, atque adeò fieri ab eo non potuisse ostendi, nihilominus rectè conclusissem, Galenum ea non fuisse vsum. Etenim Hippocratis principia tantum, nihil illis præter pulsus adijciens, imitatus secutusque est, vt ipse intellexit. At quæ Astrologi suis fabulis stultè arbitrantur patrocinari, Galenus secus explanauit, atque intellexit. Quare perinde est, quod ad hanc rem attinet, siue vsus Hippocrates fuisse putetur, siue non vsus Astrologicis figmentis sciatur. Ex his apparet quibus nituntur fundamentis Astrologi, falsis scilicet, quæque, si concedas, nihil tamen eos iuuent. Raro etenim ex datis conclusio rectè ac necessariò sequitur. Sed hæc alio in loco, iam ad institutum redeundum videtur.
units.tr: So the argument, if we wish to embrace everything in a few words, runs thus. Galen predicted from no other indications or signs than those which Hippocrates prescribed for us to observe in the books that we still have today, and he added nothing to them except the doctrine of the pulses. And Hippocrates made no mention of astrology, nor did he think it was to be discarded by us, unless he himself was ignorant of it. Therefore Galen cannot even be judged to have been aided by it in his predictions. The argument would be strong and valid as far as the conclusion goes, even if I granted that Hippocrates used astrology and commended it to us. For there are no lack of those who clumsily bring forward into the midst the passage explained above, and also what he commanded to be observed in the Prognostics concerning the hours [τὰ ὥρα], to prove this point. I have said about the first passage how Galen understood it, certainly far differently from what the astrologers would wish. That he did not understand and expound the latter either as concerning astrology, but wished it to be taken of the temperature of the air, is so clearly evident from his commentary that it cannot be explained more plainly by me. Therefore, even if I were to grant that Hippocrates wrote something astrological, which is false and which I have shown could not have been done by him, I would nonetheless have rightly concluded that Galen did not use it. For he imitated and followed only the principles of Hippocrates, adding nothing to them except the pulses, as he himself understood. But what the astrologers foolishly think they can support with their fables, Galen explained and understood otherwise. Therefore, so far as this matter is concerned, it makes no difference whether Hippocrates is thought to have used astrology or is known not to have used astrological fictions. From these things it appears on what foundations the astrologers rest, namely false ones, which, even if you grant them, would still not help them. For rarely does a conclusion follow rightly and necessarily from the given premises. But these things belong to another place; now it seems we must return to our purpose.

units.la: Ratio altera hæc est. Galenus artem præcognoscendi omnes in morbis mutationes sæpe nos studiosè docuit, atque ita quidem docuit, sicut ipse eam per omnem vitam exercuit, Astrologiæ verò nullo in loco meminit. Ergo huius beneficio siue præsidio nihil vnquam præuidit. Non arbitror quemquam ita distorto esse animo & iudicio, qui ipsum aliquid nos celare voluisse sibi persuadeat, atq; aliquid eorum omisisse credat, quibus adiutus ipse in praesagiendo fuerit. Non hanc modo partem, sed vniuersam artem absolutè integreque docuit, nihil aut neglexit, aut omisit, quod praecipuum aliquem vsum habeat. Id vel ex eo vnusquisque perspiciat, quod ne hodie quidem aliquis melius se eam perfectiusque docere posse sperat, quam ipse docuerit. Porrò passim affirmat, se solius artis Medicae praesidio & curasse & praedixisse, nulla diuinandi facultate vsum fuisse. Ex quo certè efficitur, ipsum eadem illa praecepta in curando simul & praesagiendo obseruasse, quae nobis obseruanda praescripsit. Testimonia huius rei qui apud ipsum cupit videre, legat cap. 5. 7. 10. libri ad Posthumum, expositionem 17. sententiae in 3. com. lib. 1. Epidem. Quanquā vero verba, quae in fine 10. cap. ad Posthumum scripta sunt, homini moderato abundè probent perfectissimè ipsum nos praesagiendi artem docuisse, non grauabor tamen alijs quoque testimonijs idem illud plenius confirmare.
units.tr: The second reason is this. Galen taught us diligently the art of foreknowing all the changes in diseases, and he taught it in just the way he himself practised it throughout his whole life; but he makes no mention of astrology anywhere. Therefore he never foresaw anything by its benefit or aid. I do not think anyone is so twisted in mind and judgement as to persuade himself that Galen wished to hide anything from us, or to believe that he omitted any of those things by which he himself was aided in predicting. He taught this art not only in part but in its entirety, completely and perfectly; he neglected or omitted nothing that has any principal use. Anyone may see this from the fact that not even today does anyone hope he can teach it better or more perfectly than he himself taught it. Moreover, he affirms everywhere that he both treated and predicted by the aid of the medical art alone, and used no faculty of divination. From this it certainly follows that he observed in curing and in foreseeing those same precepts which he prescribed for us to observe. Whoever wishes to see the testimonies of this in him, let him read chapters 5, 7 and 10 of the book to Posthumus, and the exposition of the 17th aphorism in the third commentary on the first book of the Epidemics. Although the words written at the end of the 10th chapter to Posthumus amply prove to a moderate man that he taught us most perfectly the art of foreseeing, I will not hesitate to confirm the same thing more fully by other testimonies as well.

units.la: Praecognoscere nihil aliud esse, libro citato cap. 12. in fine scribitur, quàm exactam affectuum corporis notitiam obtinere. Quod si hoc est verum, is nos optimè praecognoscere docet, qui nos affectus corporis perfectissimè cognoscere docet. Atqui nemo Galeno melius nos docuit quomodo affectus corporum cognoscamus. Quare omnium ipse optimè nos docuit futurorum praesensionem, nec aliquid neglexisse dici poterit. In cap. 9. eiusdem libri haec habetur: Si perte[?] ipsum discere vis, qua disciplina praedixerim ea, quae in altero Quintilij filio praedixi, facile tibi & dilucidū erit, si libros de Crisi à me conscriptos leges. Porrò in libris de Crisibus omnes morborum mutationes docere se affirmat, quomodo scilicet cum praesentes dignoscendae, tum futurae praenoscendae sint. Huc illa etiam pertinent, quae 18. cap. de const. artis Medicae, & vlt. cap. libri primi ad Glauconem, & 4. de Praesag. ex pulsib. cap. 11. idem scripta reliquit. Non vero obijci nobis potest, illis nos libris, in quibus explicata haec sint, carere. Extant enim nunc omnes, neque vllam Astrologicarum fabularum mentionem continent.
units.tr: In the book cited, chapter 12, near the end, it is written that to foreknow is nothing other than to obtain an exact knowledge of the affections of the body. If this is true, then he who teaches us to know the affections of the body most perfectly teaches us best to foreknow. But no one has taught us better than Galen how we may know the affections of bodies. Therefore he himself taught us best of all the foreseeing of future things, and it cannot be said that he neglected anything. In chapter 9 of the same book this is found: "If you wish to learn from me by what method I predicted those things which I predicted in the case of the other son of Quintilius, it will be easy and clear to you if you read the books on Crises that I wrote." Moreover, in the books on Crises he affirms that he teaches all the changes of diseases, namely how both those present are to be recognised and those future are to be foreknown. To this also pertain those things which he left written in chapter 18 on the constitution of the medical art, and the last chapter of the first book to Glaucon, and in the fourth book on Prognosis from the pulses, chapter 11. Nor can it be objected to us that we lack those books in which these things are explained. For they all exist now, and none of them contains any mention of the fables of astrology.

units.la: Consídera hoc loco, quantæ ignauiæ & tarditatis Galc[?] num insimulent[?], qui absque Astrologia non facile eum aliquid prædixisse, imprudenter affirmant. Quis quæso tā fuit unquam iners & obliuiosus scriptor, qui artem aliquā ex professo docturus, eius partis, quæ in proposita disserta-tione si non primas, at secundas partes obtinet, nunquam meminerit? Mirum profecto sit, Galenum eius rei, sine qua pauca ipse præsagire prævidereque solitus esset, recor-dari nunquam potuisse, cum præsertim tam crebrò illa ipsi repetenda fuerit disputatio. Si libri, quos de Crisibus com-posuit, postremi fuissent, non tamen ex animo excidisse po-tuissent, quæ tam necessaria utiliaq; expertus ipse frequen-ter fuisset. Multò minus id nobis de eo nunc cogitare li-cet, cum tam multos post horum editionem conscripsisse ipsum videmus. Quòd si in illis oblitus fuisset, in his saltem indicasset. Quamuis verò semper asseueret, se omnia quæ utilia esse cognouerit docuisse, Astrologiæ tamen præce-pta nulla unquam tradidit, quæ obseruare nos iuberet. Quare ne hanc ignauiæ notam ei inurere velle putemur, (Quanquam non Galenum ignauum & obliuiosum, sed se ipsum stupidum, obstinatumque declarat, qui aliter sen-tit.) id quod res est fateamur potius, ipsum nihil omisisse, quibus est in præsagiendo vsus: sed summa nos fide cuncta docuisse, quæ ad futurorum in ægris præscientiam vel ra-tione perceperit utilia, vel experientia didicerit. Quòd si in tota illa doctrina nullam Astrologiæ mentionem fecit, ideo ab eo factum esse consectarium est, quia nec ratione nec experientia utilem esse inuenerit. Ex quibus omni-bus apparet, ipsum non aliter tum affectus ipsos corporū, tum eorundem permutationes præcognouisse, quàm in suis nos libris utrunque cognoscere præclarissimè docuit.
units.tr: Consider here how great a sloth and dullness those people charge Galen with, who rashly assert that without astrology he could not easily have predicted anything. Who, I ask, was ever so idle and forgetful a writer, who, about to teach an art professedly, never mentioned a part of it which holds, if not the first, at least the second place in the discourse proposed? It would indeed be strange if Galen could never have remembered that thing, without which he was accustomed to foresee and predict few things, especially since that discussion had to be repeated so often. If the books he wrote on Crises had been his last, still those things which he himself had often found so necessary and useful could not have slipped from his mind. Much less may we think this of him now, since we see him to have written so many after the publication of these. But if he had forgotten it in those, he would at least have indicated it in these. And although he always asserts that he taught everything that he knew to be useful, he never delivered any precepts of astrology which he bade us observe. Therefore, lest we seem to wish to brand him with this mark of sloth (although whoever thinks otherwise declares not Galen to be slothful and forgetful but himself stupid and obstinate), let us rather confess what is the truth: that he omitted nothing by which he made use of in predicting, but with the greatest faithfulness taught everything which he had perceived by reason to be useful for foreknowing the future in the sick, or had learned by experience. But if in all that teaching he made no mention of astrology, it follows that he did so because he found it useful neither by reason nor by experience. From all these things it appears that he foreknew both the affections of the bodies themselves and their changes in no other way than that by which he taught us in his books to know both most clearly.

units.la: Equidem qui mediocriter est in Galeni lectione versa-tus, non ignorat, ipsum, dum suas quasdam siue curationes siue prædictiones recitat, & ex quibus tum curarit tum prænouerit, percensét, illorum tantum meminisse, quæ suis in commentarijs antè expo[su]isset, Astrologiæ verò ne quidem unico verbulo recordari. Exempla si quis videre ac legere cupit, cap.2.& 3. ad Posthumum de Eudemo phi-losopho, losopho,& cap.ultimum 5.libri de Locis affect. de Medico Siculo inspiciat. In omnibus fere commentarijs,ne in cita-tis tantum locis tibi quærendum opineris,aliquid inveni-es,quo hæc nostra tum illustrentur tum confirmentur. Nos in re minimè dubia longiores esse nec volumus nec debemus,præsertim cum,quæ dicenda supersunt,præce-dentia semper magis corroborent. Sic enim inter se om-nia connexa esse,meminisse te velim,ut non minus præce-dentia sequentibus comprobari, quàm sequentia antece-dentibus confirmari & illustrari queant. Quare si Galenus ex sola Medica arte,quam nos perfectè docuit, præsagiuit, si exactam corporis affectuum notitiam nobis tradidit, si denique,cum suas prædictiones enarrat,ex ijsdem illis, nō aliis,se omnia præcognouisse asseueranter affirmat,ex quibus nos eadem præintelligere docuit: consectarium prior sus est,eadem ipsum ratione prospexisse futuras in morbis permutationes,quas nos prospicere docuit. At sine Astrologia nos omnia talia docuit. Sine igitur ipsa prævidit eiuscemodi omnia.
units.tr: Indeed, anyone who is moderately well read in Galen knows that when he recounts some of his cures or predictions, and the grounds on which he cured or foretold, he mentions only those things which he had set out earlier in his commentaries, and does not recall so much as a single word about astrology. If anyone wishes to see and read examples, let him consult chapters 2 and 3 of the book to Posthumus on the philosopher Eudemus, and the last chapter (5) of the book On the Affected Places, concerning the Sicilian physician. In almost all his commentaries you will find something, not only in the places cited, that illustrates and confirms what we say here, so you need not think you must search only the cited passages. In a matter that is not at all doubtful, we neither wish nor ought to be lengthy, especially since what remains to be said is always strengthened by what precedes. For I would have you remember that everything is so interconnected that what comes earlier can be proved by what follows no less than what follows can be confirmed and illustrated by what comes before. Therefore, if Galen foretold from the art of medicine alone, which he taught us thoroughly, if he gave us an exact knowledge of the affections of the body, and if finally, when he relates his predictions, he firmly asserts that he foreknew everything from those same things, and not from others, from which he taught us to foreknow the same things, then it follows that he foresaw in the same way the future changes in diseases which he taught us to foresee. But he taught us all such things without astrology. Therefore he foresaw all such things without it.

units.la: Neque est cur aliquis argumenta hæc effugere se posse sperer[?],si eodem modo Galenum futura prænovisse dicat, quo nos prænosse absque Astrologia docuit:multò tamen facilius ac melius hanc rem nos consecuturos esse, si ad Galeni præcepta Astrologiam adiungamus. Non enim id in hoc loco quærimus,an ars præsagiendi,quam Hippocra-tes primùm docuit,deinde Galenus illustrauit ac perfecit, ab Astrologia perfectior ac facilior reddi possit. Hoc quæ-rebatur,an artem,qua ipse præsagijsset nos perfectè do-cuisset,id quod satis ostensum jam arbitror. Cæterùm si rem accuratè examinemus,facilè intelligemus nihil ei posse addi. Et quod ab Astrologia nihil ipsi commodi perse-ctionisque accedere queat,nemo ignorat,qui mendacium veritatem perficere non nescit. Sed hic Medicè,quod dixi, probandum est.
units.tr: Nor is there any reason why anyone should hope to escape these arguments by saying that Galen foreknew the future in the same way that he taught us to foreknow it without astrology. Yet we shall attain this far more easily and better if we add astrology to Galen's precepts. For we are not asking here whether the art of prognosis, which Hippocrates first taught, and which Galen then illustrated and perfected, can be made more perfect and easier by astrology. The question was whether he had taught us thoroughly the art by which he himself foretold, and I think this has already been shown sufficiently. Moreover, if we examine the matter carefully, we shall easily understand that nothing can be added to it. And that nothing of advantage or perfection can accrue to it from astrology, no one can fail to know who is not ignorant that falsehood cannot perfect truth. But this must be proved from medicine, as I have said.

units.la: Hoc mihi ab omnibus concessum iri nihil dubito, Gale-num,post Hippocratem,talem ac tantam curandi ac præ-sagiendi facultatem atque peritiam adeptum fuisse,qua nemo ampliorem ac perfectiorem temerè expetat. Nemo certè post ipsum tanti ingenij tantæque eruditionis extitit, qui se in arte Medica ipsi parem, ne dicam superiorem esse profiteri auderet. Talis ac tantus præsagiendi artifex, cum solius Medicæ artis beneficio fuerit, frustra desideramus perfectionem hanc quam nobis Medicina præstat ampliorem. Nam si eam ita didicerimus, ut in prædicendo nunquam offendamus, sed omnes omnium morborū mutationes, quæ arte præsciri possunt, præterea diem & horam in qua futuræ sunt, cum Galeno præuideamus, nihil puto amplius desiderabimus. Dixi quæ præsciri possunt. Non enim omnes mutationes, sed illas tantum, quæ ui[?] morbi eueniunt, postquam causa ipsius certo in loco constitit, præsciri posse Galenus atque ratio probant. Cæterum quod in re nulla prædicenda Galenus offenderit, ipse de seipso grauiter restatur in exposit.17. sententiæ in 3. comm.libri 1. Epidem. & in interpretatione 20. sententiæ com.2. in lib. de humoribus Hippocr. Quod verò diem atq; horam prænouerit, notius est, quàm ut probationem eius hic à me aliquis expectet. Quod quomodo hæc omnia ipse cognorit, ac nos cognoscere possimus, planè copiosè aperte docuerit, controversia iam carere existimo. Cui ergo hæc doctrina imperfecta videtur, ei quid perfectum sit non video. Quamobrem frustra & inaniter perfectionem reddere Astrologi tentauerint.
units.tr: I have no doubt that everyone will grant me this: that Galen, after Hippocrates, attained such a great faculty and skill in curing and prognosis that no one would rashly aspire to a fuller and more perfect one. Certainly no one after him of such great talent and such great learning has arisen who would dare to profess himself his equal in the art of medicine, let alone his superior. Since so great a master of prognosis owed everything to the art of medicine alone, we vainly look for a fuller perfection than medicine itself provides. For if we have learned it in such a way that we never go wrong in predicting, but foresee with Galen all the changes of all diseases that can be known by art, together with the day and the hour in which they will occur, I think we shall desire nothing more. I have said "that can be known." For Galen and reason both prove that not all changes, but only those which arise from the disease itself, once its cause has settled in a certain place, can be foreknown. Moreover, that Galen never went wrong in predicting anything he himself bitterly confesses about himself in the explanation of the 17th aphorism of the third commentary on the first book of the Epidemics, and in the interpretation of the 20th aphorism of the second commentary on the book of Hippocrates On Humours. That he foretold the day and hour is too well known for anyone here to expect me to prove it. How he knew all these things, and how we too can know them, he has taught clearly and fully, so I think the controversy is over. Therefore, for anyone who finds this doctrine imperfect, I do not see what could be perfect. Hence the astrologers have tried in vain and to no purpose to add perfection.

units.la: Sed præstat hanc rem exactius tractare. Exactam corporis affectuum notitiam, non ex astris, sed ex illis indicijs, quæ in corporibus apparent, & quæ ars Medica docet, petendā & cognoscendam esse cuncti Medici intelligunt & concedunt. Quinimò non Medici tantum, sed omnes omnino homines sani verum esse vident. Atqui futurorum cognitio nil est aliud, teste Galeno in fine cap.12. ad Post humum, quàm exacta corporis affectuum cognitio. Ergo ex indicijs istis, quæ ars Medica docet, non ex astris desumendum & cognoscendum est, quid sit in morbis futurum. Ex istis clarè intelligitur, quòd nihil adfert cōmodi notitiæ affectuū corporis, præsensionem adiuuare, melioremque reddere nequanequaquam posse. Quomodo vero aliquid hic nos lunæ motus doceat, ne fingi quidem potest. Etenim in ipso corpore signa ista, non in coelo, tum morbum tum caussam eius consequentia apparent. De his Galenus in multis libris disputat, fontesque eorum omnes diligentissimè explicat. In i. comm. in librum Hipp. de humoribus, in declaratione ii. sententiæ inter alia sic scribit Galenus: Vult enim ip se, (intellige, Hippocrates) è morbis sumi rationem præsagiendi quid futurum sit, quod nos prolixo sermone, cum in lib. de Crisibus, tum verò etiam in comment. in Aphorismos editis explicauimus. Nolo ista pluribus exponere, ne quod nemo ignorare potest, probare velle videar.
units.tr: But it is better to treat this matter more exactly. That an exact knowledge of the affections of the body must be sought and known not from the stars, but from those signs which appear in bodies and which the art of medicine teaches, all physicians understand and grant; indeed not only physicians, but all sound men of every kind see that it is true. Yet, as Galen testifies at the end of chapter 12 of the book to Posthumus, knowledge of future things is nothing other than exact knowledge of the affections of the body. Therefore what is to come in diseases must be derived and known from those signs which the art of medicine teaches, and not from the stars. From this it is clearly understood that astrology can in no way help foreknowledge or make it better, since it adds nothing of advantage to knowledge of the affections of the body. But how the motion of the moon could teach us anything here cannot even be imagined. For in the body itself these signs appear, both the disease and its cause, and not in the heavens. Galen discusses these in many books and explains all their sources most diligently. In the first commentary on the book of Hippocrates On Humours, in the explanation of the second aphorism, Galen writes among other things as follows: For he himself wishes (understand, Hippocrates) that the rationale of foreseeing what will be is drawn from diseases, which we explained at length both in the book On Crises and in the commentary on the Aphorisms that has been published. I do not want to set these things out at greater length, lest I seem to wish to prove what no one can fail to know.

units.la: Omnes certè in ægris euentus & mutationes morborū, aut vi morbi, aut naturæ aut vtriusq; efficiuntur, vt à caussis proximis & propriis. Nemo arbitror tam est imperitus, vt Lunā vel astra hæc efficere in nobis credat, non interuenientibus iam dictis caussis. Nec moueri quidem has ab illis cogitabit aliter, quàm aptæ natæ sunt moueri. Quo fit, vt perfectionis nihil conferre notitia remotę istius caussæ prorsus rectè credatur. Non cuiusque rei perfectissima cognitio tunc solum habetur, cum causa effectus cuiuslibet propinquissima & immediata est exploratè cognita? Equidem quanto causa minus est propinqua & propria, tanto notitia effectus est incertior. Atque hoc est, quod philosophi omnes affirmarunt, confusam esse notitiam, quæ ex remota & vniuersali caussa orta sit. Confusissimam autem & ad nihil rectè intelligendum vtilem, eam esse, quam remotissima & maximè generalis parit caussa, quisque per se intelligat, etiamsi ab illis non fuisset dictum. Doctrinam Hippoc.ac Galeni non alia de caussa omnes omnibus ætatibus docti tanropere commendarunt, quàm quòd ex propriis caussis effectus quoslibet intelligere cognoscereque docet, non ad improprias communes remotas, quod Astrologia facit, lectorem dimittit. Quis negare poterit cœlestia corpora earum rerum, quæ hic apud nos fiunt, remotissimas generalissimasque caussas esse, ideoq; non nisi confusissimam earum notitiam in nobis gignere posse? Quamobrem Galenus, cum nos præsagiendi artè distinctè docere constituisset, ac ex proximis eâ proprijsq; caussis, non remotis & indefinitis, petendam præclarè intelligeret, ex affectibus & indicijs in corporibus apparentibus, tanquam certissimis & continuatis quasi caussis, futuros euentus prospicere docuit. Vnde quodam in loco sic scriptum reliquit: Nam futurorum præsagia ex præsentibus fumi[?], quamuis iam ante sæpe demonstrauimus, tamen omnia nunc etiam summatim necesse est ut percurramus, hinc indutô exordio de euentis qui expectantur, dignoscendis. Sed hæc mox pluribus exponentur, magisque confirmabuntur.
units.tr: Certainly all the outcomes and changes of diseases in the sick are brought about by the force of the disease, or of nature, or of both, as by their proximate and proper causes. I think no one is so unskilled as to believe that the Moon or these stars produce such things in us, without the causes already mentioned intervening. Nor will anyone think that these causes are moved by those stars otherwise than as they are naturally fitted to be moved. Hence it is rightly believed that knowledge of such a remote cause contributes nothing to perfection. Is not the most perfect knowledge of anything had only when the cause of any effect is known with certainty as the nearest and most immediate? Indeed, the less near and proper the cause, the more uncertain is the knowledge of the effect. And this is what all the philosophers have affirmed: that knowledge which arises from a remote and universal cause is confused. That knowledge is most confused and least useful for understanding anything correctly which is produced by a most remote and most general cause, anyone can understand for himself, even if it had not been said by them. The teaching of Hippocrates and Galen, which all learned men in every age have so highly commended, is commended for no other reason than that it teaches us to understand and know any effects from their proper causes, and does not leave the reader to improper, common and remote causes, as astrology does. Who could deny that the heavenly bodies are the most remote and most general causes of the things that happen here among us, and that therefore they can produce in us only the most confused knowledge of them? Therefore Galen, when he had resolved to teach us the art of prognosis distinctly, and clearly understood that it must be sought from the nearest causes, their proper ones and not remote and indefinite ones, taught us to foresee future outcomes from the affections and signs appearing in bodies, as from the most certain and, so to speak, continuous causes. Whence he left written in a certain place as follows: For the forecasts of future things are drawn from present things; although we have often demonstrated this before, it is nevertheless necessary now to run through all of them briefly, beginning from here, in distinguishing the events that are expected. But these things will soon be set out at greater length and confirmed more fully.

units.la: Hoc in loco vnicum adhuc monebo, Galenum non putasse per Astrologiam aut aliam diuinandi quamlibet facultatem, veri aliquid de ægris prædici potuisse. Romæ Vates tale[?] nihil potuisse discrètè affirmat, de aliarum vrbium Vatibus periculum se non fecisse dicens. Recitabuntur infrà verba Galeni hac de re. Quo in loco illud etiam probabitur, ipsum ex hoc numero Astrologos non exemisse, sed non minus de ipsis, quàm alijs quibuslibet, locutum fuisse. Ex istis quæ hactenus exposuimus liquidò patet, nihil addere Astrologiam perfectionis arti nostræ posse, ne ex Galeni quidem sententia. Ergo valide me conclusisse iam apparet, Quia Galenus per eandem methodum futura in ægris prædiuinarit, quàm nos perfectè, vt addi nihil possit, docuit, neque tamen Astrologiæ mentionem aliquam fecerit, ipsum Astrologiam minimè vsum, vel in curando vel præsagiendo fuisse. Has neque tu, neque alius Astrologus, scio-rationes dissoluet. Nihilominus tamen alias adhuc euidentiores etiam caussas adijciam, vt argumentis nos destitui non posse perspiciatis.
units.tr: Here I will give just one more warning: Galen did not think that by astrology, or by any other kind of divination, anything true could be predicted about the sick. He affirms that at Rome the seers could discern nothing of the kind, saying that he had not tested the seers of other cities. Galen's words on this matter will be quoted below. In that passage it will also be shown that he did not exclude astrologers from this number, but spoke of them no less than of any others. From what we have set out so far it is clear that astrology can add nothing of perfection to our art, not even by Galen's own judgment. So it now appears that I have validly concluded: since Galen foretold the future in the sick by the same method which we have been taught thoroughly, so that nothing can be added to it, and yet made no mention of astrology, it follows that he used astrology neither in curing nor in prognosis. Neither you nor any other astrologer, I know, will dissolve these reasons. Nevertheless, I will add other, still more evident grounds, so that you may see that we cannot be deprived of arguments.

units.la: Tertia ratio principalis hæc sit, Galenus, quem in medendo optimi quique omnibus post ipsum seculis secuti & imitati sunt, nihil vnquam circa ægros futurum prædixit, quod non iam præsens aliquo modo esse, ac fieri incœpisse cognouerit, hoc est, cuius non iam aliquid factum ex signis in corpore apparentibus perdidicerit. Quod quomodo intelligi debeat, accuratius exponere tentabo. Ita Galenus[?] futuras in ægrotis mutationes præuidit,ut Nautæ tempestates,Rustici fructuum copiam aut inopiam prospicere solent.Nautæ cum nubeculam,perpusillam licet,certo motu per aërem ferri cernunt,atque inde unde illa mouetur ventum exortum perspiciunt, eam paulò post oriturum tempestatem,quam ventus,qui spirare incœpit,secum tra-here consueuit,pronunciant . Imperiti harum rerum, qui minimas & vix apparentes ipsis motiones non obscruant, nec obseruare possunt,talia admirantur,atque pro mira-culo habent,ignorates scilicet illud ipsum,quòd futurum esse audierunt,jam tum cum euenturum diceretur fieri in-coepisse,se autem id latuisse. Simili ratione & modo Agri-colæ tempestates,ex aliis tamen indicijs, fructuum uberta-tem,& huius generis alia præcognoscunt. Galenus exem-plum arborum & plantarum proponit considerandum. Quod quia nō modò illustrat negocium propositum,sed etiam corroborat,adscribendum duxi. Sic igitur in princi-pio comm.in lib.Prorrhet.Hippocratis scribit: Nempe in il-lis rationi consentaneum esse videtur, non postea venturam præ-cognoscere nos accessionem, sed incipientem jam dignoscere ex-pulsuum permutatione. Quoniam vero nondum insignem acceperit magnitudinē, ut ægro quidem tanquam dicenda con-spicuè videatur,à nobis vero,ut tanquam jam facta cognosca-tur . Hæc res non aliter, quàm planta è terra orta dignoscitur. Quas Rusticus quidā, vel qui in herbis omnibus dignoscendis est peritus,confestim internoscit,cæteris vero incognita manet. Agros siquidè herbas germinatione similimas ferre cōspicimus, quas nos quidē non internoscimus,Rustici vero internouerunt, quid nā scilicet ex his herba sit,quid triticū nuper enatū, quid hordeū,quid zea,quid aliorū unūquodque. Ad hunc modum quoque res habet in arboribus,nepe & eas,cū sunt partibus suis omnibus absoluta universi cognoscimus. Cū vero enasci incipi-unt,omnino à paucis cognoscuntur. Sermone igitur hunc tan-quā admodū probabile commendare oportet. Eodem fere exē-plo utitur in 2.lib.de Crisibus,cap.2.Item lib.14. Meth.The-repeut.cap.9.
units.tr: The third main argument is this: Galen, whom all the best physicians after him have followed and imitated in healing, never predicted anything about the sick that he had not already recognised as present in some way and as having begun to happen; that is, he never learned that anything in the future had already been partly accomplished from signs appearing in the body. I shall try to explain more precisely how this must be understood. Galen foresaw changes that would occur in the sick in the same way that sailors foresee storms and farmers foresee a plentiful or poor harvest. When sailors see a little cloud, however small, moving through the air with a fixed motion, they observe that a wind has risen from the place it is moving from, and they announce that a storm will soon come, which the wind that has begun to blow is accustomed to bring with it. The inexperienced, who do not notice or cannot notice such very small and barely visible movements, marvel at these things and regard them as miracles, not realising that what they have heard is going to happen had already begun to happen when it was said to be about to happen, and that they themselves had simply failed to notice it. In a similar way farmers foresee the weather, and the abundance of crops and other things of this kind, from other signs. Galen offers the example of trees and plants for consideration. Because it not only illustrates the matter in hand but also confirms it, I have thought it worth quoting. Thus, at the beginning of his commentary on the Prorrhetic of Hippocrates, he writes: Indeed, in such cases it seems reasonable that we do not foreknow the paroxysm that will come later, but recognise it as it begins, from the change in the symptoms. But since it has not yet reached a conspicuous size, so that it is plainly visible to the patient as something to be spoken of, it is recognised by us as already done. This matter is recognised in no other way than a plant that has sprung up from the earth. Some farmer, or one skilled at recognising all herbs, at once distinguishes it, while it remains unknown to others. For we see fields bearing herbs very like one another as they sprout, which we indeed do not distinguish, but farmers do distinguish: what this herb is, whether it is newly sprouted wheat, or barley, or spelt, or each of the others. It is the same with trees, for we recognise them when they are complete in all their parts. But when they begin to sprout, they are recognised by very few. Therefore it is fitting to commend this account as very probable. He uses almost the same example in the second book of his work On Crises, chapter 2, and likewise in the fourteenth book of the Method, On Therapeutics, chapter 9.

units.la: Ita,inquit Galenus: Cognoscit Medicus futuras morborum mutationes, sicut Rusticus novit ex qua planta nuper ex terra orta aut quercus, aut ficus, aut hordeum aut aliud tale quippiā sit nasciturum. At Rusticus hic quercum, ubi ficum nascituram ex eo novit, quòd jam natas conspicatus est, atque propter experientiā usumq; novit inter pullulātes plantas distinguere, quas imperitus aliquis non internoscit, sed eiusdem esse omnis generis opinatur. Ex quo efficitur, Medicum quoque ex Galeni sententia hoc aut illud quodlibet eventurum prædicere, quia exortum jam sit, at propter paruitatem imperitos adhuc lateat.
units.tr: Thus Galen says: The physician recognises future changes in diseases just as the farmer knows from what plant that has recently sprung from the earth there will grow either an oak, or a fig, or barley, or something else of that sort. And this farmer knows that an oak, and not a fig, will grow from it because he has seen it already sprouted, and through experience and practice he has learned to distinguish among the sprouting plants, which an inexperienced person does not tell apart, but thinks are all of the same kind. From this it follows that, in Galen's view, the physician too foretells that this or that will happen, because it has already begun to arise, but remains hidden from the inexperienced on account of its smallness.

units.la: Et ne aut dubites hanc fuisse Galeni mentem atque sententiā, aut non de omnibus affectionibus mutationibusve intelligendam cogites, lege quæ in expos. 4. sententiæ in eodem comm. scripsit. Dixi autem & ante, ait Galenus, exordientis affectionis notas, prognostica signa esse eius quæ jam completa est. Adhuc clarius mox in declaratione .s. dictionis ita scribit: Primùm quidem promte assumunt illud, solos eos morbos, qui cum propriis magnitudinibus absoluti sunt, propriis nominibus appellari, confirmantes non parum eum sermonem, qui inter initia à nobis dictus est, nempe, quòd nullum futurum pathema à Medicis præsentiatur: verum eorum quæ jam principium quidem generationis habent, sed nondum propter paruitatem vulgò cognita sint, facta ab artificibus cognitio idiotis, pronunciata, præsensio apud illos existit, ita ut & Phre-niticiam ab artificibus cognoscantur, affectione in cerebro nuper consistente, &c. Idem fere invenies in 3. comm. in eundē librum in explanat. sententiæ 8.
units.tr: So that you may not doubt that this was Galen's mind and opinion, or think that it should not be understood of all affections or changes, read what he wrote in the exposition of the fourth aphorism in the same commentary: I said before, says Galen, that the signs of an affection beginning to arise are prognostic signs of what has already been completed. Still more clearly, shortly afterwards, in the explanation of the word s., he writes as follows: First, they readily assume that only those diseases which have been completed with their proper magnitudes are called by their proper names, thereby confirming to no small extent what we said at the beginning, namely, that no future disorder is foreseen by physicians. But for those things which already have the beginning of their generation, yet are not yet commonly known because of their smallness, the recognition made by the experts, announced to the laymen, is a foreknowledge that exists among them, so that even phrenitis is recognised by the experts when an affection has recently taken up its seat in the brain, and so on. You will find almost the same in the third commentary on the same book, in the explanation of the eighth aphorism.

units.la: Neq; in prædictis locis solū, quæ huc faciūt, sed sæpe aliàs in illis commentariis, sed nec in isto libro tantum ita sensit. Quod ut intelligatur planius, unū atq; alterū adhuc proferā. In fine 8. cap. libri 3. de difficultate respirationis hæc leguntur: Est autē bonorum Medicorum opus, non quæ idiotis jam apparēt prasagire, sed quæ ipsos latēt: & cum nihil æger mali habere putetur, apparent. Præclarè hanc rē illustrant & cōprobant quæ in interpret. 6. sententiæ in 3. Prognost. & cap. 18. de artis Medicæ constitutione scripsit, quæ huc transferre nimis longum foret. Hinc jam omnes intellecturos spero, quàm verè dixerim,Galenum nihil in ægris futurum ante prædixis-se,quàm fieri iam atque produci à proxima caussa cognoscuisset,siue esse iam perspexisset,idque ex signis,quæ non in cœlo,sed corporibus ægrorum apparuissent. Hoc postremum supra satis est ostensum,quando ab Astrologia nihil artì huic perfectionis accedere posse probaui. Qui plura desiderat expos.5.sent.in 1.Prognost.& quæ ex fine 12.cap ad Posthumum supra adduxi. Item cap.18.de art.Med.constitutione. Clarissimè vero in 4.de præsagio ex pulsibus cap.11. Hoc in loco tam apertè & disertè ostendit Galenus præsa-gia futurorum ex præsentibus in corpore affectibus sumi, vt qui præterea aliquid desideret,is merito carere iudicio dicatur atque communi sensu. Totum illud caput diligen-ter perlegat,cui nondum est satisfactum. Quinetiam qui rem per se ipsam cognoscere cupit,modo non prorsus iu-dicio priuatus sit,perfacile ita necessario habere eam,vt di-xi,oportere perspiciet. Hactenus liquet veritati,rationi, Galeni & Hippocr.doctrinæ,imprimis consonum esse, nega-riqué non posse,quin recte affirmauerim, Galenum nihil futurum prædixisse,nisi hoc ipsum quod iam aliquo mo-do[?] esse fieriqué explorasset,quantumuis imperiti perspicere propter exilitatem & paruitatem nondum possent. Hoc enim artifex maximè ab idiotis differt,vt in Prognost.loco paulò ante citato pulchrè exemplo inter se pugnantium declarauit Galenus.
units.tr: And he has thought in this way not only in the passages mentioned, which bear on this point, but often elsewhere in those commentaries, and not only in that book. So that this may be understood more plainly, I shall adduce one or two more. At the end of the eighth chapter of the third book, On Difficulty of Breathing, these words are read: It is the task of good physicians not to foretell what is already apparent to laymen, but what is hidden from them; and when the patient is thought to have no trouble, it becomes evident. The passages that he wrote in the interpretation of the sixth aphorism in the third book of the Prognostics, and in chapter 18, On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine, illustrate and confirm this admirably, but it would be too long to transfer them here. From this, I hope, everyone will now understand how truly I said that Galen never predicted anything in the sick before he had come to know, from the proximate cause, that it was already being done and brought forth, or had clearly seen that it already existed, and this from signs that appeared not in the heavens but in the bodies of the sick. This last point has been shown sufficiently above, when I proved that nothing that could add to the perfection of this art can come from astrology. Whoever wants more should consult the exposition of the fifth aphorism on the first book of the Prognostics, and what I cited above from the end of the twelfth chapter to Posthumus, likewise chapter 18 on the constitution of the art of medicine. Most clearly of all, however, in the fourth book, On Prognosis from the Pulses, chapter 11. In this passage Galen shows so openly and so plainly that prognoses of future things are drawn from affections already present in the body, that anyone who wants anything more is rightly said to lack judgement and common sense. Let him read carefully through that whole chapter, with which he is not yet satisfied. Indeed, anyone who wishes to know the matter for itself, provided he is not entirely deprived of judgement, will readily see that it must necessarily be so, as I have said. Thus it is clear that this agrees above all with truth, with reason, and with the doctrine of Galen and Hippocrates, and I cannot deny that I have rightly affirmed that Galen predicted nothing in the future unless he had first ascertained that it was already in some way being and coming to be, even though the inexperienced could not yet perceive it because of its slightness and smallness. For this is what most of all distinguishes the expert from the layman, as Galen clearly showed, with a fine example of opposing things, in the passage of the Prognostics cited shortly before.

units.la: Hunc locum diligenter vnà cum aliis ponderare & exa-minare illos velim,qui quomodo sæpe triduum vel quatriduum Galenus crisim prænorit,secum dubitant.Nō enim tum incœpisse dici potest,& paulatim aucta esse donec cōpleretur.Est enim subita quædam mutatio crisis. Qui ita, inquam,hæsitat,hunc & similes locos perpendat,facileque ex difficultate,quæ reuera nō magna est,se extricabit. Qui hoc modo,quæ futura in ægris essent, præsensit, poterit is ex Astrologia præuidisse? Neminem quantumuis stupidū affirmaturum censeo. Ergo cum Galenum haud secus prædixisse iam constet, velis nolis concedere omnino cogeris,cū Astrologia in exercēda arte Medica nō fuisse usum. Tribus huc usque argumentis praecipuis (Nam qui numerum magis, quàm robur spectat, is in vno facile plura inueniet) Galenum in curando & praesagiendo nō fuisse ab Astrologia adiutum neruosissimè perfeci conclusiqúe [?]. Primum huiusmodi fere est. Galenus ex ijsdem futuros morborū cuentus praeuidit, ex quibus Hippocrates eosdē praecognouit, ac praecognoscere alios docuit, nihil illis praeter pulsuum notitiam adiecit. Atqui non usum fuisse Hippocratem Astrologia, non ipsi tantum verè diximus, ac validis argumentis probauimus, sed ipse etiam Galenus credidit, ut est expositum. Galenus igitur nihil subsidij aut auxilij ad curandum ab Astrologia vel expectauit, vel percepit. Altera talis est ratio: Galenus autem ac methodum, qua instructus futura in morbis omnia praeuidit, nos integrè perfecteque docuit, Astrologiae vero non commemimit: Non est igitur ipsa unquam usus ipse, nec uti nos ea voluit. Equidem legimus aliquot narrationes, in quibus suas quasdam tum curationes tum praesensiones recitat, ac quibus & quomodo vel curarit, vel praeuiderit, universa percenset, nunquam tamen Astrologicis usum sese affirmat. Unde non rationibus tantum, sed etiam exemplis, (quibus causa nihilominus quam caeteris argumentis comprobetur) nostra confirmari undique omnes perspiciunt. Tertiae haec est: Galenus nihil praesciri praedicique posse censuit, cuius non iam aliquid factum, & quasi principium apparéret, aut cuius vera & propria causa non iam actu suo producere effectum incoepisset. Hinc nemo non videt, Astrologia eum uti non potuisse. Non ex coelo, sed ex indicijs, quae in corporibus extant, quorum dignotionem distinctionem, & significationem sola Medica ars docet, affectiones cognosci & distingui possunt. Ex his praesentibus futura coniciunt Medici, ut supra verbose satis declarauimus. Valde stultum esse oportet, imò prorsus insanum, qui cum iam aliquid fieri ac generari ante oculos suos videt, ex coelo hoc ipsum cognoscere velit. Neque enim res ulla, utrum sit, an non sit, melius ex alijs, quàm vel sua ipsius praesentia, vel immediatę causę actione cognosci potest. Has rationes tametsi certò scio neminem confuraturum[?] esse, utut obscurare & inuoluere eas Astrologi conentur, non tamen scribendi finem ante mihi faciendum hic duxi, quàm et iam quartam adderem, quae iam dictis adhuc euidentius & clarius propositum demonstrat.
units.tr: I should like those who, like me, hesitate over how Galen often foretold a crisis three or four days in advance to weigh and examine this passage carefully together with the others. For it cannot be said that it had then only begun and gradually increased until it was complete, since a crisis is a sudden change. I say that whoever hesitates in this way should weigh this and similar passages, and he will easily extricate himself from a difficulty that is in truth not great. Could anyone who foresaw in this way what would happen in the sick have foreseen it from astrology? I think no one, however dull, would maintain that. Therefore, since it is established that Galen made his predictions in no other way, you are compelled, willy-nilly, to concede altogether that astrology was not used in the practice of the medical art. I have most vigorously shown, by these three chief arguments (for whoever looks more to number than to strength will easily find more in one of them), that Galen was not aided by astrology in healing and in prognosis, and I have concluded this. The first is more or less this. Galen foresaw the future outcomes of diseases from the same things from which Hippocrates foreknew them and taught others to foreknow them, and he added nothing to them except the knowledge of the pulses. But we have truly said, and proved by strong arguments, that Hippocrates did not use astrology, and Galen himself believed this, as has been set out. Galen therefore neither expected nor obtained any support or help for healing from astrology. The second argument is of this kind: Galen has fully and perfectly taught us the method by which he foresaw all future events in diseases, but he made no mention of astrology. Therefore he never used it himself, nor wished us to use it. Indeed, we read several narratives in which he recounts certain cures and foreseeings of his own, and he surveys in full how and by what means he either healed or foresaw them, yet he never declares that he used astrological methods. From this, all can see that our position is confirmed on every side not only by arguments but also by examples, by which the cause is nonetheless proved as well as by the other arguments. The third is this: Galen held that nothing can be foreknown or predicted of which something has not already been done, and which does not already appear as if begun, or whose true and proper cause has not already begun to produce its effect by its own action. Hence no one fails to see that astrology could not have been used by him. Affections are recognised and distinguished not from the heavens, but from the signs that exist in bodies, the recognition, distinction and interpretation of which the medical art alone teaches. From these present things physicians conjecture future ones, as I have explained at sufficient length above. It must be very foolish, indeed utterly mad, for someone who sees before his own eyes that something is already happening and coming into being to want to know this from the heavens. For no thing can be known, whether it is or is not, better from other things than from its own presence or from the action of its immediate cause. Although I am certain that no one will be convinced by these arguments, however much the astrologers try to obscure and entangle them, I thought I should not make an end of writing here before adding a fourth, which demonstrates the point even more evidently and clearly than what has been said.

units.la: Galenus probri loco habuit, & pro calumnia atq; ignominia reputauit, si ope atque auxilio diuinatricis facultatis, inter quas Astrologiam etiam conumerari voluit, praedixisse aliquid dictus fuisset. Ergo solius Medicae artis beneficio absque Astrologia omnia circa aegros praevidit. Primùm, quod solius Medicae artis ope praedixerit, frequenter ab eo dictum est. In 7.cap.libri ad Posthumum, sic ait. Hic ego ut pueri venam pulsantem in brachio attigi, sine febre quidem esse pronunciaui, me vero deludendi hisce qui me vatem appellare consueuissent ansam dare. Excipiens Boëthus, & ego, inquit, in comparationem illorum soleo tecum vera vatem, ut scis, appellare, quoties aliquid praedicis, quod aemuli tui negant Medicae praecognosci facultate posse. Atqui hactenus, subiunxi, ea omnia te docui Medica arte inueniri, prisco[s]q; aliquot Medicos de hisce conscripsisse. Et sub cap. finem, Haec simul atq; Boëthus audiuit, per Deos, inquit, non miror, cum ita inuestiges[?], si nullus alius Medicus ista sciat? Perspicuum autem est eos nescire, cum ipsi quod tu facis nunquam efficiant, & te ista alio quouis modo potius quàm Medica arte facere diuulgant. In eodem lib.cap.5. Mihiq; perinde atque omni ex parte superati detrahebat, (Medici Romanenses) huc illuc per urbem venientes varia diuulgabant, Alius casu me quempiam fanasse, periculosoq; admodum curationis genere uti, alius diuinatrice peritia, non arte Medica quid in morbis futurum esset praedicere. Eandem sententiam reperies cap.10.eiusdem libri. De causis procatarct. cap.1. Secundo de febr.differ.cap.7. Prognost.3.in principio expositionis 7.sententiae. De Simpl.med.fac.10.cap.de sanguine Crocodili, ubi sic scribit: Et caveba. ne praestigiatura opinione merito referre, cum ita etiam improbi quidam Medici, ex diuinandi quapiam arte, non ex speculatione Medica, me in morbis solere praedicare calumniarentur.
units.tr: Galen regarded it as a reproach and a slander if he were said to have predicted something by the aid of divinatory skill, among which he wished Astrology also to be counted. Therefore he foresaw everything about his patients by the sole benefit of the art of medicine, without astrology. First, that he predicted by the sole power of the medical art, he often said. In the seventh chapter of his book to Posthumus he speaks thus: "Here I touched the pulse in the arm, as one does with a boy, and declared that there was no fever, but I gave to those who used to call me a seer an occasion to mock me. Boethus replied: 'And I, as you know, usually call you a true seer in comparison with them, whenever you predict something which your rivals deny can be foreknown by medical skill.' But so far, I answered, I have taught you that all these things are discovered by the medical art, and some ancient physicians have written about them." And near the end of the chapter: "As soon as Boethus heard this, 'By the gods,' he said, 'I am not surprised, since you investigate in this way, if no other physician knows these things? Clearly they do not know them, since they never accomplish what you do, and they proclaim that you do these things by some other means rather than by the medical art.'" In the same book, chapter 5: "And the Roman physicians, coming here and there through the city, spread abroad various things about me, who was, so to speak, entirely outdone by them: one said that by chance I had cured someone, and that I used a rather dangerous kind of treatment; another, that by divinatory skill, not by medical art, I foretold what would happen in diseases." You will find the same opinion in chapter 10 of the same book; in On the Causes of Progressive Illness, chapter 1; in On the Differences of Fevers, book 2, chapter 7; in the Prognostics, book 3, at the beginning of the exposition of the seventh sentence; and in On the Simple Medicines, book 10, in the chapter on crocodile blood, where he writes thus: "And I take care not to be reckoned, and rightly so, a trickster in opinion, since certain wicked physicians likewise slander me, saying that in diseases I am accustomed to predict not by medical speculation but by some art of divination."

units.la: Satis, nisi fallor, propositum demonstrauissem, nisi Astrologos mihi obiecturos suspicarer, Galenum nullam fecisse Astrologiæ nominatim mentionem, ideo non debere prę-dicta testimonia de eaintelligi [?]. Hos iubeo, vt cum alios hu-iusmodi locos, quorum capita notaui (omnes adscribere superuacaneum & longum nimis fuisset) tum postremum diligenter examinent. Id si fecerint, nullam excipi diuina-tricem facultatem, qualiscunque tandem ea sit intelliget, vna Medicina excepta. Ex sola arte Medica se prænouisse omnia asseuerat, artem diuinatricem nullam se adhibuis-se asserens. Sanè qui de omnibus loquitur nihil eximit. Inanis igitur est hæc Astrologorum excusatio. Quinetiam Vatem se esse negauit constanter, vt ex dictis dicendisque intelligi poterit. At omnis Astrologus, quatenus talis, Vates (μάντις) rectè appellatur, atque etiam existit. Ars etenim quam profitetur, & à qua denominatus est, ex genere est τῶν μαντικῶν. Malè ergo Galenus negasset, Vatem se esse, si Astrologica vaticinia coluisset vel cum vel sine Medicina. Futile ergo est hoc eorum effugium, & verè Astrologicũ.
units.tr: Unless I am mistaken, I would have sufficiently demonstrated my point, except that I suspect the astrologers will object that Galen never made any explicit mention of astrology, and that therefore the aforementioned testimonies should not be understood of it. I bid them carefully examine these, as well as the other passages of this kind whose chapters I have noted (it would have been superfluous and too long to write them all out), and especially the last one. If they do so, they will understand that no divinatory skill, whatever it may be, is excepted, apart from medicine alone. He asserts that he foresaw everything from the medical art alone, declaring that he used no divinatory art. Indeed, one who speaks of all things excludes nothing. This excuse of the astrologers, therefore, is empty. Moreover, he steadfastly denied that he was a seer, as can be understood from what he has said and will say. But every astrologer, as such, is rightly called, and indeed is, a seer (mantis) [μάντις]. For the art which he professes, and from which he takes his name, belongs to the class of divinatory arts [τῶν μαντικῶν]. Galen would therefore have spoken falsely in denying that he was a seer, if he had cultivated astrological prophecies, whether with or without medicine. This escape of theirs is therefore futile, and truly astrological.

units.la: Hæc quanquam sanis probant doctis ac moderatis veri-tatisque amantibus rem propositam, non tamen non fir-miora & planiora subijciam, atque ostendam Galenum nominatim etiã Astrologiæ fecisse mentionem, vt quo se recipiant, omnino non inueniant. Quo autem intelliga-tur res melius, ac verum simul perspiciatur, eum sub gene-re etiam speciem hanc complecti voluisse, duos locos de eodem casu atque ægro scriptos producam, in quorum al-tero generatim, in altero speciatim Astrologiæ cum alijs quibusdam Hariolandi modis commeminit. Prior est in 1. Epid. comm. 3. expositione 17. sententiæ: Ego verò hanc speculationem etiam cum apud Eudemum philosophum prædicerem, qui tribus tenebatur quartanis, primam de illis recessuram primum, quæ certis diebus inuadebat: & post totidem circuitus abhac depulsa alteram certo die: similiq; modo cum postea tertiam prænunciarem, ex diuinandi arte hac prædicere iactabant non ex Medica speculatione: tametsi Vates nunquam vidissent ve-ra Romæ de ægris prædicentes. Nam illorum qui aliis in urbi-bus fuerunt, nullum feci periculum. Nos, quod Deo approbante di-cam; eam[?], nullâ re unquam praedicenda offendimus. Atque si ea quae de iudiciis sunt exposita mediteris, Hippocrate eris arteq; di-gnus. Hactenus Galenus. Eandem istam historiam reperi-es in 2.com. in lib.de humoribus expositione 20. sententiae, ubi postremò haec etiam verba leguntur: Ac nos non modò in illo homine, sed etiam, quod Deo approbante dictum sit, in nulla unquam praedictione offendimus. Hunc locum Astrologos diligenter examinare maximè velim, quo tandem intelli-gere incipere nt diuinandi modos, vel Galeni experientia inutiles esse ad Medicas praesagitiones. Nunquam, (obserua quod ait, Nunquam) Romæ Vates, quicunque tandem illi essent, aut per quemcunq; modum vaticinarentur, vera de aegris praedixisse suo tempore visos. (Nam quod sub his etiam comprehendi Astrologos velit, partim exiam dictis, partim ex dicendis patebit.) Ergo Astrologi nunquam Romæ visi sunt vera de aegrotis praedicere. An in aliis urbibus vera praedixerint unquam, ignorare se fatetur, quod nullum fecerit periculum.
units.tr: Although these points prove the matter proposed to learned and moderate men who love the truth, I will nonetheless add firmer and plainer ones, and show that Galen also made explicit mention of astrology, so that they may find no way out at all. In order that the matter may be better understood and the truth seen at the same time, I will bring forward two passages written about the same case and the same patient, in one of which he mentions astrology along with certain other modes of soothsaying in general terms, and in the other specifically. The first is in the commentary on the first book of the Epidemics, book 3, the exposition of the seventeenth sentence: "But I, when I was predicting this, even to the philosopher Eudemus, who was held by a triple quartan fever, that the first fever would leave first, the one which attacked on fixed days, and after as many cycles the second would be driven off on a certain day, and in the same way when I afterwards foretold the third, they boasted that they predicted this by the art of divination, not by medical speculation, although the seers had never seen true things foretold about the sick in Rome." For I made no trial of those who were in the other cities. We have, God willing, I shall say, "encountered no failure in any prediction, nothing ever being foretold; and if you meditate on what has been set out concerning the crises, you will be worthy of Hippocrates and of his art." So far Galen. You will find this same story in the second commentary on the book On the Humours, exposition 20 of the sentence, where these words are also finally read: "And we have encountered no failure, not only in that man, but also, as may be said with God's approval, in any prediction at all." I would especially like the astrologers to examine this passage carefully, so that at last they may begin to understand that divinatory methods, by Galen's experience, are useless for medical prognoses. "Never" (observe what he says, never) "Romans, seers, whoever they might be, or by whatever method they prophesied, were seen to have foretold true things about the sick in their time." (For that he wishes astrologers also to be included under these, will be clear partly from what has been said, partly from what is to be said.) Therefore astrologers were never seen in Rome to foretell true things about the sick. Whether they ever predicted true things in other cities, he confesses he does not know, since he made no trial.

units.la: An non hinc liquet, ipsum nec Romæ nec alibi Astrologia usum, aut modum alium quemlibet diuinandi cum Medicina coniunxisse? Si nullum aliis in urbibus Vatum periculum fecit, ac Romæ semper mendaces deprehendit, quomodo quis utilem ab eo existimaram credat? Non ignauissimos Vates Romæ fuisse, ac in suo genere imperitissimos, sed omnino summos atque optimos nemo dubitat, qui urbis illius statum, qualis tunc esset, vel ex Gal. vel ex aliis autoribus nouit, ac considerat. Hos tamen omnes, nunquam veri aliquid de aegris ex artibus suis praescire potuisse asseuerat. Unde facile apparet, ne aliarū quidem urbium Horiolos aliquid hic praestare valuisse. Se vero, ait, nunquam errasse, cum ex arte Medica praesagiret. Nec uno tantum loco id affirmat, sed totidem pene verbis repetit alibi, ne excidisse ipsi aliquis existimare posset. Hac de causa in postremis verbis hortatur, ut, qui velit Hippocrate arteque dignus videri, hoc est, perfecte & absque errore omnes in morbis mutationes praeuidere, ea meditetur, nō quę de astrorum conuersionibus & aspectibus commentantur Astrologi, sed quæ in libris de Crisibus exposita ipsi sint. Ex quibus nemo tam iners est, qui non videat, nihil ac-cedere perfectionis artis prænoscendi nostræ, à diuinatricibus modis accedere, quippe quos mentiri semper, cum de ægris vaticinantur, obseruatum sit. Et me hercle qui sincero & incorrupto iudicio intendere hunc animum voleri, is certò deprehendet, nunquam non Astrologos in suis de morborum mutationibus mentiri, nisi forte casu aliquan-do quod dixerunt, aut simile quippiam, euenit, quod ad suas prædictiones ipsi postea accommodare tentant. Negare ne ipsi quidem possunt, ex Medicis indiciis omnia rectius ac certius (loquor ex ipsorum mente) prædiuinari & præsentiri, quàm ex siderum motibus. Hactenus de priore loco.
units.tr: Does it not clearly follow from this that he joined neither astrology nor any other mode of divination with medicine, either in Rome or elsewhere? If he made no trial of seers in other cities, and always found them lying in Rome, how could anyone believe that they were regarded by him as useful? No one who knows and considers the state of that city, as it then was, either from Galen or from other authors, doubts that the Roman seers were not feeble and wholly inexpert in their own kind, but altogether outstanding and of the highest quality. Yet he declares that all of these could never know anything true about the sick from their arts. Whence it readily appears that the soothsayers of the other cities could not have achieved anything here either. He says, however, that he himself never erred when he foretold from the medical art. He affirms this not in one place only, but repeats it in nearly the same words elsewhere, lest anyone might think it had slipped from him. For this reason, in the final words he urges that whoever wishes to seem worthy of Hippocrates and his art, that is, to foresee all changes in diseases perfectly and without error, should meditate not on the conjunctions and aspects of the stars with which the astrologers busy themselves, but on what has been set out in the books on Crises. No one is so dull that he cannot see from these that nothing of the perfection of our art of foreknowledge is gained from divinatory methods, since they have been observed always to lie when they prophesy about the sick. And indeed, by Hercules, whoever wishes to turn his mind to this with a sincere and uncorrupted judgment will certainly find that astrologers always lie in their accounts of the changes of diseases, unless perhaps by chance something they said, or something similar, turns out, which they then try to fit to their predictions. Not even they themselves can deny that everything is more correctly and certainly foreseen and perceived from medical signs (I speak in their own opinion) than from the motions of the stars. So much for the first passage.

units.la: Alter locus de eodem Eudemo tribus laborante quartanis, quo prædictus quasi exponitur in 3.capite libri ad Posthumum scriptus est hoc modo: Atque ideo non ex Medica facultate, verum ex diuinatricibus scientijs prædictiones meas fuisse mentiebatur, (De Martiano Medico loquitur) interrogatus à quibusdam, quasnam diuinatrices scientias diceret, interdum Augurium, interdum Exspicium, nonnunquam Coniectatricem, aliquando Mathematicam respondebat.
units.tr: The second passage, about the same Eudemus suffering from a triple quartan fever, by which he is as it were explained in the third chapter of the book to Posthumus, is written in this way: "And so he falsely claimed that his predictions were made not from the medical faculty, but from divinatory sciences," (he speaks of the physician Martianus) "when he was asked by certain people what divinatory sciences he meant, he sometimes answered augury, sometimes haruspicy, sometimes conjecture, sometimes astrology."

units.la: An non hic Galenus explicatè negat se ab Astrologia adiutum fuisse in prædicendo? Quinetiam contumelia se effectum à Martiano iudicauit, quòd de ipso talé quid mentitus fuisset. Legat qui volet quæ in sequenti capite sequuntur, vbi Galenus ait, se vidisse quidem, quæ in 2. Prædictionum libro Hipp. scripserit (aut quisquis libri autor est) nō tamen vaticinari. Hic vt multo plura Galenum respondisse perspicias, quàm verba obiter inspecta significare videntur, & hunc ipsum locum, & 2. librum Prædictionum attentè vt legas moneo. Quæ si diligenter tecum considerabis, intelliges etiam, ipsum, in genere cum loquitur de Vatibus, Astrologos non excludere. Nemo arbitror ignorat, Mathematicos illo tempore vocatos etiam Genethliacos, siue Astrologos, vt hodie fere loquimur, appellatos fuisse. Quo fit, vt negari nullo modo possit, quin per diuinationem Mathematicam, vocatam à nobis Astrologiam intel-lexerit.
units.tr: Does not Galen here explicitly deny that he was helped by astrology in foretelling? Indeed he judged that he had been wronged by Martianus, because he had lied about him in such a way. Let whoever wishes read what follows in the next chapter, where Galen says that he has indeed seen what Hippocrates (or whoever is the author of the book) wrote in the second book of the Prognostics, but that he does not prophesy. Here, so that you may see that Galen answered much more than the words, looked at in passing, seem to signify, I advise you to read carefully both this passage and the second book of the Prognostics. If you consider these things carefully with me, you will understand also that, when he speaks in general about prophets, he does not exclude the astrologers. I think no one is unaware that at that time mathematicians were also called genethliaci, or astrologers, as we nowadays commonly say. Hence it cannot in any way be denied that by "mathematical divination" he meant what we call astrology.

units.la: Ex istis manifestissimè liquet, ac necessaria consecutio-ne concluditur, Galenum, vbi suprà diuinatricium ab ipso vocatarum seu facultatum, seu artium, seu scientiarum me-minit generatim, Astrologiam quoque comprehendere voluisse. Cur verò sæpius in genere loquatur, quàm speciatim omnes enumeret, in causa fuit, quòd non de vna sem-ter vaticinandi facultate aduersarij ipsius loquerentur, sed modò de vna, modò de alia, vt ex proximè citato loco pulchrè apparet. Quare cum sigillatim semper enumerare omnes nec posset nec deberet, summatim eas complecti-tur, atque improbos Medicos mentitos de se fuisse calumniatosque asserit, quòd ex diuinatricibus artibus futuros morborum euentus præsagiret. Ita quòd suprà quoque, eū perfici non posse præsagendi[?] artem nostram ab Astrologia declararem, facturum me promisi, perspicuè ostendi, Galenum non minus Astrologiam, quàm vel Augurium vel Extispicium vel alium quemuis vaticinandi modum intellexisse, quoties ait Romanenses Medicos falso (detrahendi scilicet causa) dixisse, ipsum ope[?] diuinatricium artium futura præsentire. Si quem hæc non permouent, vt falsam illam opinionem, videlicet Galenum in medendo Astrologia vsum esse, abiiciat, huius ego morbum insanabilem esse verè ac certè affirmare possem. Neque enim certiora in præsenti dissertatione argumenta quisquam sanæ mentis homo postulauerit. Quamobrem nihil iam restare videtur amplius, quàm vt totam hanc disputationem concludam, finemque faciam. Puto enim me quod ab initio recepi liberaliter præstitisse.
units.tr: From these things it is most manifestly clear, and it is concluded by a necessary consequence, that Galen, when above he mentions generally the divinatory faculties, or arts, or sciences, which he himself called such, meant also to include astrology. Why he speaks more often in general than he enumerates them all one by one was because his opponents did not speak of only one manner of prophesying at a time, but now of one, now of another, as is evident beautifully from the passage cited just above. Therefore, since he could neither nor ought to enumerate them all individually, he embraces them summarily, and asserts that wicked physicians lied about him and slandered him, because he foretold the outcomes of diseases by divinatory arts. So, as I promised above, when I declared that our art of foretelling could not be perfected without astrology, I have clearly shown that Galen understood astrology no less than augury, or extispicy, or any other mode of prophesying, whenever he says that the Roman physicians falsely (namely, for the sake of slander) said that he foreknew future things by the aid of divinatory arts. If these things do not move anyone to abandon that false opinion, namely that Galen used astrology in healing, I could truly and certainly affirm that his disease is incurable. For no one of sound mind would demand more certain arguments in the present discussion. Wherefore nothing seems to remain now but that I conclude this whole disquisition and make an end. For I think I have done what I undertook at the beginning, and done it generously.
