units.la: Verùm enimuerò, quia re, cum aliud nihil habebis, ad sacrum tuum asylum, nimirum ad 3. Decret. nos relegaturum suspicor, non fuerit fortasse præter rem aliquid de eo quoque loco hic dixisse. Ergo totam illam disputationem ad artis opera faciendam inutilem esse dico. Etenim usum omnem transcendit, & planè Logica disceptatio est, vt Galenus alicubi appellauit. Non enim vt Medicus, sed vt Philosophus[?] Decret.dierum caussas ibidem investigare tentauit Galenus. Quod tam est consideranti apertum, ut dubitare nemo possit.Duos eundem aegrotum Medicos cura recogita, quorum alter quidem dies decretorios optime norit, causam eorum ignoret tamen: alter non hoc modo sciat, sed etiam Lunae motum causam eorum esse arbitretur. An hunc tu melius cogniturum putas, quando morbus sit soluendus, altero illo, qui in omnibus aliis aeque sit tum peritus tum exercitatus? Ego sane non credo. In causa quid sit quaeris? Quia uterque ex iisdem indicijs cogitur de futura solutione morbi coniecturam capere, ex signis, inquam, quae ars Medica docet in corpore & excrementis ac similibus obseruare. Deinde quia ex Astrologia aut motu Lunae de aegris nihil praedici potest, ut jam ex Galeno probatum est. Sed quoniam res haec nota est doctis omnibus, paucissimis hic me expediam, & rationes aliquot digitis quasi monstrabo solum, quibus tractatio illa probetur Logica & ad artem exercendam inutilis esse.
units.tr: But truly, since you will have nothing else, I suspect you will send us back to your sacred asylum, that is, to the third book of the Decretals; perhaps it was not beside the point to say something here also about that passage. Therefore I say that that whole disputation is useless for practising the art. For it goes beyond all use, and is plainly a logical debate, as Galen somewhere called it. For Galen there tried to investigate the causes of the decretory days not as a physician but as a philosopher. This is so evident to anyone who considers it that no one can doubt it. Think over the same sick man with two physicians: one of them knows the decretory days very well, but does not know their cause; the other not only knows this but also thinks that the motion of the Moon is their cause. Do you think the latter will know better, when the disease is to be resolved, than that other who is equally skilled and experienced in all other things? I certainly do not believe so. You ask what the reason is? Because each of them is compelled by the same indications to form a conjecture about the future resolution of the disease, namely from the signs, I say, which the medical art teaches us to observe in the body, the excretions, and similar things. Next, because nothing can be predicted about the sick from astrology or from the motion of the Moon, as has already been proved from Galen. But since this matter is known to all the learned, I shall deal with it very briefly, and merely point out, as it were with my fingers, a few reasons by which that treatment is shown to be logical and useless for the practice of the art.

units.la: Prima ratio haec sit, quod Hippocrates, & qui ipsum secuti sunt illustres Medici omnes, hanc dierum decretoriorum causam, quam Galenus confinxit, nesciuerunt, & suos nihilominus aegros rectissimè optimeque percurauerunt. Galenus primum se hoc tentasse scribit, alios ante se omnes ne dicere quidem aggressos unquam fuisse. Huc & illud facit, quod clarissimi praestantissimique nostrae aetatis Medici per Galliam atque Italiam in suis curationibus non obseruant. Calendarijs istis nugacibus carent, nec venam secaturi in scorpio aut piscibus Luna moueatur inspiciendum unquam iubent. Qui horum aliquid obseruat, quod tamen Astrologicum esse negari posset, operam dant, ne in coniunctione aut oppositione Solis & Lunae corpus aut venae sectione aut purgatione vacuent. Et ne hoc quidem facerent, nisi a vulgo quasi cogerentur interdum. Hisce terminis continetur omnis eorum Astrologia.
units.tr: The first reason is this: Hippocrates, and all the famous physicians who followed him, did not know this cause of the decretory days which Galen invented, and nevertheless they treated their sick most correctly and excellently. Galen writes that he was the first to attempt this, and that all others before him never even ventured to speak of it. To this also pertains the fact that the most distinguished and outstanding physicians of our age throughout France and Italy do not observe it in their cures. They have no need of those silly calendars, nor do they ever order that the Moon be looked at to see whether it is moving in Scorpio or Pisces before they open a vein. Whoever observes any of these things, which yet could be denied to be astrological, takes care not to empty the body by bloodletting or purging at the conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon. And they would not even do this, unless at times they were in a way forced by the common people. Their whole astrology is contained within these limits.

units.la: Deinde nemo est Medicus bonus, qui crisim bonam non sciat in statu aut declinationis initio, hoc est, post coctionem expectandam demum esse. Quae ante illud tempus accidunt crises, nec laudabiles sunt ac fidæ, nec arte à Medico præintelligi sicut veræ & bonæ possunt. In malis autem, quæ mortem exitiumque afferunt, contraria ratio locū habet. At verò ex Lunæ motu nō posse intelligi certissimum est, quando & quomodo Natura morbi causam cōcoquat, quando status futurus sit. Ad quod probandum non est cur hic aliquid adferam, cum per se notum sit, atqʒ; ipsis etiam prudentioribus minusque pertinacibus Astrologis confessum. Nihil igitur Lunæ motus ad præsciendā particularem crisim adiuuat.
units.tr: Next, there is no good physician who does not know that a good crisis is to be expected only at the beginning of the state or decline, that is, after concoction. Crises which occur before that time are neither praiseworthy nor trustworthy, nor can they be foreknown by the physician through his art as true and good ones can. In the bad cases, however, which bring death and ruin, the opposite reasoning holds. But it is most certain that from the motion of the Moon it cannot be understood when and how the nature of the disease will concoct its cause, when the state will be. There is no reason for me to bring forward anything here to prove this, since it is known in itself, and is acknowledged even by the more prudent and less obstinate astrologers. Therefore the motion of the Moon contributes nothing to foreknowing a particular crisis.

units.la: Tertiò notum illud est etiam, Auicennam autem[?] Medicam methodo tractauisse, & ex omnibus veteribus quicquid vtile cognouit in suum canonem collegisse. At hanc quæstionem tanquam inutilem & falsam reiecit, locumq; in opere suo habere non est passus. Ex quo satis perspicitur, nihil eā nobis conducere. Non enim tam imbecillo iudicio vir ille fuit, vt aut non videre vsum eius posset: aut tam imprudens, vt omittendam sibi putaret: aut tam obliuiosus, vt non recordaretur: aut tam tardus, vt non intelligeret. Astrologos certè longo post se interuallo omnes reliquit.
units.tr: Thirdly, this is also well known: Avicenna treated medicine by method, and from all the ancients gathered into his canon whatever he knew to be useful. But this question he rejected as useless and false, and did not allow it a place in his work. From this it is sufficiently clear that it is of no benefit to us. For that man was not of so feeble a judgment that he could not see its use; nor so imprudent that he thought it should be omitted; nor so forgetful that he did not remember it; nor so slow that he did not understand it. Certainly he left all the astrologers far behind him.

units.la: Quartò putauit Galenus, & rectè quidem, Lunam quælibet morbum ita mouere, vt moueri aptus est, pro natura corporis ægrotantis, morbi huius caussæ, facultaris[?] & similium. Talem verò notitiam qui inutilem ad artis opera nō intelligit, is morbos curare cum ratione nondum didicit.
units.tr: Fourthly, Galen thought, and rightly indeed, that the Moon moves any disease in the way that it is apt to be moved, according to the nature of the sick body, the cause of the disease, the faculty, and similar things. But whoever does not understand that such knowledge is useless for the practice of the art has not yet learned to cure diseases with reason.

units.la: Possum hoc loco illud etiam addere, Astrologiam Galeni falsam esse, atque ab eo ignoratam vel ipsis Astrologis testibus. Certissima ratione supra mihi confectum memini, Astrologiam perfectissimam, qualem hodie ipsam esse dictitant, arti præsagiendi nihil commodare posse, multò ergo minus Galenica illa falsa conferre ei possit.
units.tr: I can add here also this: that Galen's astrology is false, and ignored by him, even by the testimony of the astrologers themselves. I remember having shown above by a most certain reasoning that the most perfect astrology, such as they nowadays keep insisting it is, can contribute nothing to the art of foretelling; much less, therefore, can that false Galenic astrology contribute anything to it.

units.la: Huc & illud tanquam auctarium accedit, quod Galenus suæ illius disputationis vsum nullū indicare potuit, cū maximè cupere videretur. Qui non mihi fidē habet, vltimum illius libri ʒ.[?] caput legat, ac consequentiā orationis & argumentorum diligenter obseruet, quo me non decipi perspiciat.
units.tr: To this also is added, as a supplement, that Galen could show no use of his disputation, although he seemed to desire it most eagerly. Whoever does not trust me, let him read the last chapter of that book, the third, and carefully observe the sequence of the discourse and of the arguments, so that he may see that I am not deceived.

units.la: Postremò Galeni testimonijs probari potest, ipsummet in ea fuisse sententia, vt totam illam disputationem inutilem ad vsum artis censeret. Primùm quidem in ipso libri principio id ostendit: Deinde cap. 10.[?] multò apertius. Quo in loco tali vtitur excusatione, quali nullo in loco alio vsus legitur. (Tantum non Deos testatur, se, quæ ibi disputarit, minimè omnium credere.) Longè autem explicatissimè & apertissimè hoc fatetur in 4 Aph. 36. ad quem locum legendum & perpendendum mittendus est, quisquis nondum persuasus est.
units.tr: Finally, it can be proved from the testimonies of Galen that he himself was of the opinion that the whole disputation was useless for the use of the art. First he shows this at the very beginning of the book; then, in chapter 10, much more openly. In that place he uses an excuse such as is read nowhere else in his writings. (He calls on the gods, as it were, to witness that he least of all believes what he argued there.) But he confesses this at much greater length and most openly in Aphorisms 4, 36, to which passage whoever is not yet persuaded must be sent to read and weigh it.

units.la: Iam, nisi me fallunt cogitationes meæ omnes, occasionem ac materiam vberem habes te exercendi, & argumentum quod obiectare vnum soles ac potes Galenum in 3. Decret. Astrologis fauisse, cum hisce meis conferendi occasionem nactus es amplissimam. Satis ostensum esse arbitror, quicquid pro te adfers, planè Astrologicum esse, hoc est, euanidum, inutile, falsum, puerile, nugax. Quod verò ipse produco firmum, solidum, constans, verumque esse, quod me recte negare, nec interpretando lenire, aut contemnendo effugere queas. Vnusquisque quantum potest antiquos imitari studeat.
units.tr: Now, unless all my thoughts deceive me, you have an ample occasion and material for exercising yourself here, and you have a splendid opportunity to compare these views of mine with the argument you are accustomed to raise, and can raise, that Galen favoured the astrologers in his third book of Decretoria. I think I have sufficiently shown that whatever you bring forward on your side is wholly astrological, that is, empty, useless, false, childish and trifling. As for what I myself put forward, it is firm, solid, constant and true, so that you cannot rightly deny it, nor soften it by interpretation, nor escape it by contempt. Let each man strive as far as he can to imitate the ancients.

units.la: Si ætatis nostræ Medicos clarissimos consideres, omnes aut imperitos huius vanitatis esse, aut non adhibere eam comperies, atque his, vt antiquis omnia felicissimè succedere perspicies. Contrà verò, qui Astrologica auidissimè consectantur, ineptissimos esse ad præsagiendum & curandum inuenies. Hoc ego cum multis annis studiosè obseruassem, & dogmatis incredibilem absurditatem, & manifestam falsitatem percognouissem, mirari desij, cur antiqui illi Medici cum Galeno magna se affici iniuria putarent, si Astrologia in medendo vsi existimarentur. Vale.
units.tr: If you consider the most distinguished physicians of our own age, you will find that they are either ignorant of this vanity or do not employ it, and you will see that, as with the ancients, everything succeeds for them most happily. On the contrary, you will find that those who most eagerly pursue astrological practices are most inept at prognosis and at healing. Having studiously observed this for many years, and having come to know both the incredible absurdity of the doctrine and its manifest falsity, I have ceased to wonder why those ancient physicians, together with Galen, thought they would be greatly wronged if they were judged to have used astrology in medicine. Farewell.

units.la: Heidelbergæ.
units.tr: Heidelberg.

units.la: Epistola VIII. THOMAS ERASTVS D. H. M. MEDICO, amico & D. suo plurimum colendo.
units.tr: Letter VIII. THOMAS ERASTUS D. H. M. To the physician, my friend and most honoured Sir.

units.la: S. P. D.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: IUdicium tuum de postremis literis meis ad D. Stathmionē Medicum, uir præstantissime, perlibenter vidi ac legi. Neque grauatè tibi petenti respondebo, vt, quemadmodum cupere te ostendis, hac etiam in parte meam sententiam perspicias. Et ne sim longior, tuarum literarum summa hæc esse videtur. Primum præclarè me demonstrasse putas, neque Hippocratem neque Galenum in prædicendo Astrologiam vsurpasse. Inde tamen non sequi, quin vel alter vel vterque ea fuerit ad præuidendas tempestates vsus. Et de Hippocrate quidem minus, quàm de Galeno dubitare videris, propterea quòd ex Hippocrate certiora videaris tibi testimonia producere posse, quàm ex Galeno. Etenim Hippocratem cùm alibi, tum in libro de aëre, aquis & locis non semel præcipere, vt siderum exortus occasusque intueamur, vt sic qualia tempora anni futura, & per consequentiam, qui morbi in quolibet loco regnaturi sint, prænoscamus. Neque verò possunt, ais, hæc de Astronomia proprie dicta intelligi. Nam hæc scientia non considerat, quid in hæc terrena sidera efficiant. At in citato loco de siderum actio-ne Hippocrates loquitur. Ex Galeno sola verba illa, quæ in principio vltimi cap. libri 3. de dieb. decretorijs leguntur, profers. Et hæc in prima tuarum literarum parte haben-tur.
units.tr: I was very glad to see and read your judgement on my last letter to Dr. Strathmion, most excellent man. I will answer your request without reluctance, so that, as you show you wish, you may weigh my opinion on this point too. To be brief, the sum of your letter seems to be this. First, you think I have clearly shown that neither Hippocrates nor Galen used astrology in prognosis. But it does not follow that one or the other did not use it to foresee the weather. You seem to doubt this more for Hippocrates than for Galen, because you think you can produce surer testimonies from Hippocrates. For Hippocrates, both elsewhere and in the book On Airs, Waters and Places, more than once instructs us to observe the risings and settings of the stars, so that we may foreknow what kind of seasons of the year are coming and, by consequence, which diseases will prevail in any place. Nor, you say, can these things be understood of astronomy properly so called, since that science does not consider what the stars effect in these earthly things. But in the passage cited, Hippocrates speaks of the action of the stars. From Galen you bring forward only those words which are read at the beginning of the last chapter of the third book On Critical Days. These are the contents of the first part of your letter.

units.la: In altera parte ratione probare tentas, ex astrorum notitia temperiem aëris præuideri posse, etiamsi neque Hippocrates neque Galenus hoc intellexerint. Et particulares quidem euentus alios ex situ astrorum non præsciri posse concedis, ad tempestates autem præintelligendas horum considerationem utilem censes. Cum enim astra, inquis, in aërem ante, velut vicinorem agant, quàm in composita ex ele-mentis, haud absimile vero est, ea suas vires in elementa, præser-tim verò in aërem efficacius infundere, quàm in composita. Quamobrem siderum mixtiones recte videntur dici aërem pro sua natura permutare posse, licet ex omnibus 4. elementis composita non æquè citò & facilè permutare concedantur. Sol enim citius aërem quàm terram aut homines calefacit, ac facilius purum quàm impurum aërem illustrat. Qua de re tempestates producere sidera poterunt, etiamsi animalia non tam subitò alterare possint. Non verò soli Astrologi hoc senserunt, sed præter hos multi philosophi doctissimi superioris temporis idem dixerunt. Quid igitur prohibet, ex sideribus tempestates, ex his futuros morbos prædiuinare? Sic ad victus rationem rectè instituendam non parum utilis iudicanda erit. Hæc tua sunt, longiore à te oratione exposita. Nihil me puto omisisse, quod huc pertinere possit.
units.tr: In the second part you try to prove by reasoning that the temperature of the air can be foreseen from knowledge of the stars, even if neither Hippocrates nor Galen understood this. You concede that other particular events cannot be foreknown from the position of the stars, but you judge that the consideration of them is useful for foreseeing the weather. For since the stars, you say, act on the air first, as on something nearer, before they act on compounds made of the elements, it is not at all unlikely that they pour their powers into the elements, and especially into the air, more effectively than into compounds. Therefore the mixtures of the stars are rightly said to be able to change the air according to its nature, although compounds made of all four elements are not granted to change so quickly and easily. For the sun warms the air more quickly than the earth or men, and lights up pure air more easily than impure. Hence the stars will be able to produce weather, even if animals cannot be altered so suddenly. Nor did only the astrologers think this, but besides them many very learned philosophers of earlier times said the same. What, then, prevents us from foretelling weather from the stars, and future diseases from the weather? Thus it will be judged not a little useful for ordering a proper regimen of living. These are your points, set out by you in a rather long discourse. I think I have left out nothing that could bear on this.

units.la: Ego serio ne ista scripseris, an vt me tentares siue exercere potius, & quàm aptè responsurus sim experiaris, non facile dixero. Nisi te delectatum istis rebus aliquādo scire, non possem iudicare aliter, quàm te iocari nobiscum vel exercere nos hoc pacto voluisse. Non enim quæ tua est e-ruditio, hæc non optimè intelligis, vt mea tibi hac in re opera minimè sit opus. Huius rei causa vulgaria te ad du-cere noluisse scribis, quod quomodo aptissimè ac verissi-mè talia refelli queant, minimè ignores. Quoquo modo hæc habeant, ad proposita breviter respondere, cùm vt mi-himet, tum verò etiam vt tibi gratificer, constitui.
units.tr: I shall not easily say whether you wrote these things in earnest, or rather to test me or exercise me, and to find out how aptly I am going to reply. Unless you had at some time been delighted by these matters, I could judge no otherwise than that you wished to joke with us or to exercise us in this way. For your learning is such that you understand these things not poorly, so that my help is by no means needed by you in this matter. You write that you did not wish to lead me to commonplace arguments, because you are by no means ignorant of how such things can most aptly and truly be refuted. However these things stand, I have resolved to reply briefly to the points proposed, both for my own sake and also to oblige you.

units.la: Hippocratem ex astrorum inspectione, quo Astrologi modo solent, futuras prævidisse tempestates, ais. Hoc si probasses, rem mihi non parum gratam, & tua doctrina dignam fecisses. Ego in illis meis literis ad Strathmionem mihi vi-deor non inconcinnè nec etiam inualidè, si rei qualitas considerctur[?], probasse Hippocratè ne scire quidem Astrologiam potuisse. Deinde nullus extat locus vel apud ipsum Hippocratem, vel aliquem autorem alium antiquum, qui affirmet, eum ex motu siderum aëris temperiem præcognoscere studuisse. Huc Galeni testimonium accedit, qui, cum quomodo futuræ cognoscantur pluviæ, docet, simul-que rationes aliquot ex Hippocrate producit, nullam huius rei mentionem unquam fecit. At nihil Hippocrates dixit ad artem Medicam vtile,quod non in tam multis in ip-sius libros comment. commedarit, confirmarit, laudarit. Quinetiam quod probare nequiuit,aut ab Hippocrate pro-sectum ac legitimum negauit,aut certè interpretando leni-uit, & quatenus probari posset indicauit. Quàm sæpe de aeris mutationibus locutus sit Hippocrates, notum est. Quàm multos locos tales,& quàm diligenter Galenus in-terpretatus fuerit, nesciri non potest. At neque illum ta-le quippiam,quod huc detorqueri commodè queat, dixis-se,neque hunc dictorum aliquid secus,quàm in literis meis declaratum est,intellexisse, nullo labore probari poterit.
units.tr: You say Hippocrates foresaw future weather from observing the stars, in the way the astrologers usually do. If you had proved this, you would have done me a service not a little welcome, and one worthy of your learning. In those letters of mine to Strathmion I seem to myself, if the nature of the matter is considered, to have proved, not inelegantly nor weakly, that Hippocrates could not even know astrology. Then there is no passage, either in Hippocrates himself or in any other ancient author, which affirms that he sought to know the temperature of the air from the motion of the stars. To this is added the testimony of Galen, who, when he teaches how future rains may be known, and brings forward several reasons from Hippocrates, never made any mention of this matter. Yet Hippocrates said nothing useful to the medical art that Galen did not comment on, confirm and praise in so many of his books. Moreover, whatever he could not prove, he either rejected as not genuinely Hippocratic, or at least softened by interpretation, indicating how far it could be proved. How often Hippocrates spoke of changes of air is well known. How many such passages Galen interpreted, and how diligently, cannot be unknown. But it will by no means be proved that Hippocrates said anything of such a kind that could conveniently be twisted to this purpose, or that Galen understood any of these sayings otherwise than has been declared in my letters.

units.la: In præsentia vnum illum adscribam locum, quem in 3. com.in lib.Hippocr. de Humoribus nuper edito, ante bi-duum opportunè admodum legi, in 20.sententiæ enarra-tione. Pluuiæ autem futura, inquit, multis modis cognoscuntur, vt à Luna velut Aratus cecinisse videtur his ver-sibus:
units.tr: For the present I will cite that one passage which I happened to read very opportunely two days ago, in the third commentary on the book of Hippocrates On Humours, recently published, in the exposition of the twentieth aphorism. But future rain, he says, is known in many ways, as Aratus seems to have sung of it from the Moon in these verses:

units.la: Cum verò incedit sublimi Cynthia cornu, Tum segnes Borea campi spirante rigebunt: Sin prono, terris pluuium denunciat Austrum.
units.tr: When Cynthia advances with her horn raised high, then the sluggish fields will freeze in the blowing North wind; but if she lies prone, she announces rainy Auster to the lands.

units.la: Hippocrates verò ait, Arcturo exoriente pluuiam cum ventis frigidis plerunq; decidisse. Scribit verò etiam hæc, Pluuia, inquit, multa, continua, lenes, vt cum flat Auster. Hæc Galenus.
units.tr: Hippocrates indeed says, when Arcturus rises, rain generally falls with cold winds. He writes these things too: The rain, he says, is heavy, continuous, gentle, as when the South wind blows. So Galen.

units.la: Tres hic modos Galenus recitat,p[?] quos futuras pluuias nouisse possumus. Primum ex Arato mutuatus est, duos reliquos ex Hippocrate sumsit. Ac primum non pertinere ad Astrologos confessum omnibus puto, qui vel Aratum legerunt, vel Galenum non obiter solum inspexerunt. Etenim eadem, hæc in duobus alijs imò tribus locis, in Ga-leno legimus, ex Arati libro, de illis quæ in aere cōspiciun-tur, citata, nempe in 3. Decret. cap. 5. In princip. comm.in librum Hipp. prorrheticorum, & demum in I[?] com.in Prog-nost. in longa enarratione illa. In omnibus istis tribus lo-cis docet per hunc modum, Nautas & Rusticos pluuias præsagire solere. Porrò non esse hos Astrologiæ peritos, frustrà probare coner. Præsentiunt igitur ex Lunæ variata luce & imagine,non vt ex causa,sed vt ex signo,quod à vaporibus in aërem elevatis philosophi cuenire præclarè in-telligunt ac docent. Simili ferè modo ex auium atq; ani-malium quorundam gestibus, aëris mutationes, quas nō-dum persentiunt homines, animalia verò illa sentiunt, prædicimus, non vt ex caussis, sed vt ex signis, atq; adeò ex iam factæ mutationis effectibus. Huc pertinent omnes aëris affectiones reliquæ, quas enumerare hoc loco non est necesse. Neque probare me ista oportet, cum ipsa libri inscriptio id nobis indicet, atque rei natura ita sentire nos prorsus cogat. Non esse hæc ad Astrologiam referenda ali-bi diximus. Sed & ex iam dictis patet.
units.tr: Here Galen recites three ways by which we can know future rains. The first he borrowed from Aratus, the other two he took from Hippocrates. And first, I think everyone agrees that this does not belong to the astrologers, who have either read Aratus or have looked into Galen with some care. For we read these same things, quoted from the book of Aratus about the things seen in the air, in two or rather three other places in Galen, namely in the third book of On Critical Days, chapter 5; at the beginning of his commentary on the book of Hippocrates Prorrhetics; and finally in the long exposition of the Prognostics. In all three places he teaches in this way that sailors and countrymen are wont to foretell rains. Further, I try in vain to prove that these men are not skilled in astrology. They therefore perceive from the varying light and image of the Moon, not as from a cause but as from a sign, which the philosophers clearly understand and teach arises from vapours lifted into the air. In much the same way we predict changes of the air from the gestures of certain birds and animals, which men do not yet perceive but those animals do, not as from causes but as from signs, and so from the effects of a change already made. To this belong all the other affections of the air, which it is not necessary to enumerate here. Nor ought I to prove these things, since the very title of the book indicates them to us, and the nature of the thing compels us to think so entirely. We have said elsewhere that these matters are not to be referred to astrology, and this is also clear from what has already been said.

units.la: Alter modus, nempe, tertius in loco supra citato, sumi-tur à natura ventorum. Austro namque spirante nemo idiota non expectat pluuiam. At cum Boreas spirat, sereni-tatem futuram prædicimus. Et ne hunc quidem ad Astro-logos pertinere certum est.
units.tr: The second way, namely the third in the passage cited above, is taken from the nature of the winds. For when the South wind blows, no ignorant person does not expect rain. But when the North wind blows, we predict that fair weather will follow. It is certain that this too does not belong to the astrologers.

units.la: • Tertius sumitur à natura quatuor anni temporum. Etenim ab ortu Arcturi autumnus incipit, ac definit æstas, quo tempore sol ad Virginis medium, & vltra pertransijt. Hinc & frigus & pluuiæ in aëre sese rursus exerunt. Neque alia de caussa nos Hippocrates iussit siderum quorundam ortus occasusque obseruare, vt ex ipso tu citasti. Hoc enim tantum docere voluit, in quolibet loco Medicum obseruare debere, quomodo Arcturus oriatur, Pleiades oc-cidant atque oriantur: Quomodo solstitium vtrunq; habeat, hoc est, quomodo aërin loco quouis in Autunno, Hyeme, Vere, Æstate temperatus affectusúe sit. His enim sideribus, siue horum occasu & ortu anni tempora antiqui describebant, & circumscribebant. Porrò vt non aliam ob caussam Hippocratem nobis imperasse perspicias, quæ in productis à te locis iubet, diligenter lege: quæ Galenus hac de re scripsit in 1. Epid. com.1. expos. sententiæ primæ.
units.tr: • The third is taken from the nature of the four seasons of the year. For autumn begins at the rising of Arcturus, and summer ends, at which time the sun passes through the middle of Virgo and beyond. Hence cold and rains again show themselves in the air. Nor for any other reason did Hippocrates bid us observe the risings and settings of certain stars, as you quoted from him. For he wished only to teach that the physician ought to observe in any place how Arcturus rises, how the Pleiades set and rise, how the solstice takes place at either time, that is, how the air in any place is tempered and affected in autumn, winter, spring and summer. For the ancients described and marked off the seasons of the year by these stars, or by their setting and rising. Moreover, that you may see that Hippocrates ordered us for no other reason than that which he commands in the places you cited, read carefully what Galen wrote on this matter in the first commentary on the first exposition of the first aphorism of the Epidemics.

units.la: Atque hæc mihi, inquit, semel iam dicta sint quæ ad omnia, quæ sub hac[?] docemus, memoria velim teneri, quo promptius ad omnium nationum menses, qui aliis alij sunt transire queas. Nam si iidem sint apud omnes, nullam Hippocrates faceret ne-que Arcturi, neque Vergiliarum, neque Canis: nullam etiamaut æquinoctiorum aut solstitiorum mentionem, sed tantum di-ceret, In Macedonia, verbi gratia, initio Mensis quem Macedo-nes Dion appellant, eiusdemodi fuisse statum in temperamento aëris. Nunc quia Dion solis est Macedonibus clarum, contra ob-scurum Atheniensibus caterisq; mortalibus (volebat autem omni-bus nationibus iuxta prodesse Hippocrates) non potuit melius, quàm neglectis mensibus, solum scribere æquinoctium. Est enim æquinoctium universale, at menses singulis gentibus sui. Qui ergo Astronomiæ imperitus est, hunc celatum nolim, ipsum haud quaquam obsequi Hippocrati, ad illam ob prædictorum usum cohortanti. Hæc Galenus, & quæ antecedunt ac sequuntur plura.
units.tr: "And let these things," he says, "be said to you once and for all, so that I would like you to keep in memory everything we teach under this heading, so that you may more readily pass on to the months of all nations, which are different for different peoples. For if they were the same among all, Hippocrates would make no mention of Arcturus, nor of the Pleiades, nor of the Dog Star; nor would he make any mention of the equinoxes or solstices, but would simply say that in Macedonia, for example, at the beginning of the month which the Macedonians call Dius, the air's temperament was of such and such a kind. But since Dius is known only to the Macedonians, and obscure to the Athenians and other mortals (Hippocrates, however, wished to be of equal benefit to all nations), he could not do better than, leaving aside the months, to write only of the equinox. For the equinox is universal, whereas months belong to each people separately. Therefore I would not want one who is unskilled in astronomy to be kept in the dark, since he cannot by any means follow Hippocrates, who urges that science for the sake of its use in these predictions." These are Galen's words, and several more precede and follow them.

units.la: Non poterat apertius dicere Galenus, quàm dixit, Hip-pocratem scilicet ideo tempora per siderum ortus & occa-sus describere, quia menses non omnibus ijdem sint, ipse autem omnibus prodesse cupiuerit. Neque aliam ob causam Astronomiam discere Medicos iussit, quàm ut horum siderum ortu & occasu observato, tempora anni interstin-guere, & qualia in loco quolibet sint, inspicere valeant. Addit postea Galenus, si ita sint menses, ut apud Romanos, constituti, ut dies æquinoctiorum & solstitiorum certus nominari possit, non est opus observatione ista Hippocra-tica. Neque Hippocrates, ait, mentionem fecisset, si omnes Nationes menses habuissent recte similiterque constitu-tos. Hinc luce meridiana clarius patet, nihil ista Hippocra-tis testimonia Astrologis ad vaticiniorum suorum asser-tionem prodesse. Quòd si Galeni iudicio standum nobis censes, obiecta iam plane dissoluimus. Sin aliter sentis, de-siderari fortasse aliquid adhuc poterit. Quanquam non vi-deo, cur quisquam se melius mentem ac sententiam Hip-pocratis videre, quàm viderit Galenus, existimet. Ut enim concedam esse aliquem hodie, qui neque iudicio, neque studio & diligentia, neque doctrina Galeno cedat, id quod mihi non temerè persuadebit Astrologus, non tamen ille æquè commodè Hippocratis sententiam perspexerit arq; Galenus. Erenim si alia in re nulla, in hac saltem meliore est conditione usus, quòd plurimos & præstantissimos Hippocratis interpretes legere potuit, quorum vix nomina sola ad nos peruenerunt. Ab his quoties dissentit in re alicuius momenti, libenter commemorat. Facit quoque horum & similium tam frequenter mentionem, vt credi non possit, alios secus istos Hippocratis locos intellexisse, quàm interpretatos ab eo paulò ante audiuimus. Qui sapit, Galeno hac in re assentietur potius, naturæ & sententiæ Hippocratis consentanea afferenti, quàm nugacibus Astrologis diuersum affirmantibus. Longiore enim inter-vallo Galenum subsequuntur, quàm vt comparatio inter eos aliqua iniri tentarique debeat ac possit.
units.tr: Galen could not have said more plainly than he did: Hippocrates describes the times of the year by the risings and settings of the stars precisely because the months are not the same for everyone, and he wished to benefit everyone. Nor did he bid physicians learn astronomy for any other reason than that, by observing the rising and setting of these stars, they may be able to distinguish the seasons of the year and see what sort of weather prevails in any given place. Galen adds afterwards that if the months are so fixed, as among the Romans, that the days of the equinoxes and solstices can be named with certainty, then that Hippocratic observation is unnecessary; and Hippocrates, he says, would not have mentioned it if all nations had months rightly and similarly arranged. From this it is clearer than noonday light that these testimonies of Hippocrates are of no help to the Astrologers in establishing their prophecies. But if you think we should abide by Galen's judgment, we have plainly already resolved the objections; if you think otherwise, perhaps something may still be wanting. Yet I do not see why anyone should think he sees Hippocrates' mind and meaning better than Galen saw them. For even if I grant that there is someone today who yields to Galen neither in judgment, nor in zeal and diligence, nor in learning (which an Astrologer will not easily persuade me of), still he will not have perceived Hippocrates' meaning as conveniently as Galen did. For if in nothing else, Galen had the better position in this, that he could read very many and most excellent interpreters of Hippocrates, of whom scarcely the names alone have come down to us. Whenever he dissents from them on a matter of any importance, he readily mentions them. He also refers to these and similar writers so often that one cannot believe they understood those passages of Hippocrates otherwise than as he has just been heard to interpret them. Anyone of sense will agree with Galen in this matter, since he offers an explanation consonant with the nature and meaning of Hippocrates, rather than with the trifling Astrologers who assert the contrary. For they follow Galen at too great an interval for any comparison between them to be undertaken or attempted.

units.la: Quod si verò contentus esse nolis ista Galeni expositio-ne, ipsos locos diligenter vt introspicias hortor, & alterum locum per alterum (Bis enim in eodem libro aperte, sæpius obscure & implicite, vt vocant, idem dixit) exponas moneo. Sic enim ipse peruidebis, non aliam ipsius fuisse mentem, quàm eam, quæ dicta est. Equidem non dicit Hippocrates, ex sidcrum [?] ortu & occasu & ad cætera aspectu vario præsciri aëris futuram temperiem posse. Hoc ait. Obseruare Medicum debere, quomodo sidera jam sæpe nominata oriantur & occidant, vt sic temperiem omnium temporum notet. Qua cognita, facile ei fore, adhibitis cæteris coniecturis, de futuris morbis in qualibet vrbe recti aliquid præscire præsentireque. Quocirca cum eo ipso ostendat se de Astrologia vaticinatrice ex sideribus non loqui, quod neque omnibus annis similiter, neq; vno in omnibus locis modo sidera ista oriantur & occidant, satis esse hoc diligenti poterit lectori.
units.tr: But if you are unwilling to be content with this exposition of Galen, I urge you to examine the passages themselves carefully, and I advise you to explain one passage by another (for in the same book he has said the same thing twice, openly, and more often obscurely and implicitly, as they say). In this way you will yourself see clearly that his mind was none other than what has been stated. Indeed, Hippocrates does not say that the future temperament of the air can be foreknown from the rising and setting of the stars, and from their various aspects to other things. He says this: the physician ought to observe how the stars already often named rise and set, so that he may note the temperament of all seasons. Once this is known, it will be easy for him, with the other conjectures added, to foreknow and presage something right about future diseases in any city. Wherefore, since he himself shows that he is not speaking of a prophetic Astrology drawn from the stars, it will be enough for a diligent reader to note that these stars do not rise and set in the same way in every year, nor in one and the same way in all places.

units.la: Deinde est, quod ab eo dicitur, ac si hoc modo pronunciasset ea verba: Studiose obseruare in qualibet vrbe Medicus debet (si peregrinus sit) quæ sit autumni, hyemis, veris, æstatis, eo in loco temperies. Hoc intellecto, facilius de morbis qui nasciturí [?] videantur præsentiet. Non enim ratio eadem est horum temporum in locis omnibus. Sæpe nanque vicinas duas vrbes, propter situs diuersitatem, vt cum altera in montibus, altera in planitie posita ædifica-taque est, reperias plurimum habere discriminis hac in parte. In altera frequenter pluet, ac frigus aërem occupabit multo maius longioreque tempore, quàm in altera. Ventorum quoque alios omnibus communes, alios certæ regioni proprios & peculiares esse præter experientiam ipsemet Hipp.in principio libri à te citati affirmauit, vt Aristotelem & Theophrastum omittam.
units.tr: Next there is what he says, as though he had put it in these words: the physician ought to observe carefully, in any city (if he is a stranger), what the temperament of the place is in autumn, winter, spring and summer. Once this is understood, he will more easily foresee the diseases that seem likely to arise. For the reckoning of these seasons is not the same in all places. Often you will find two neighbouring cities differing greatly in this respect because of the diversity of their situation, for example when one is built on mountains and the other on a plain. In the one it will often rain, and cold will occupy the air much more greatly and for a longer time than in the other. Hippocrates himself, at the beginning of the book you cite, has also affirmed, apart from experience, that some winds are common to all and others are proper and peculiar to a certain region; I omit Aristotle and Theophrastus.

units.la: Ex istis, nisi fallor, manifestè liquet, non aliud Hippocratem, cum ad certorum siderum obseruationem nos adhortarur, voluisse, quàm quod Galenus eum voluisse censuit. Confirmat eandem sententiam illud etiam, quod nō nisi paucorum semper siderum meminit, scilicet illorum quibus anni tempora antiqui circunscribere ac denominare soliti erant. Quid contra hæc dici excogitarique possit non video, si modò qui contradicere volet, non indiligenter Hippocratis tempora consideret, & quàm tunc istæ Astrologorum ineptiæ non multis per Græciam notæ fuerint non ignoret. Qui indissimulanter[?] est malus & rixosus, (qualem esse neminem aliquando stultè[?] putaui,) is certa & incerta ex æquo despiciet, ridebitque. Sed dum ineptè ridet, à non stupidis quis sit facilius agnoscitur. Tibi me in præsentia satisfecisse, nihil prorsus ambigo.
units.tr: From these things, unless I am mistaken, it is clearly evident that Hippocrates, when he urges us to observe certain stars, wished nothing other than what Galen judged he wished. That same view is confirmed by the fact that he mentions only a few stars, namely those by which the ancients were accustomed to mark off and name the seasons of the year. I do not see what could be devised to say against this, if indeed one who wished to contradict would consider Hippocrates' times carefully and not be ignorant of how little these absurdities of the Astrologers were known throughout Greece in those days. Whoever is malicious and quarrelsome without disguise (as I have never foolishly thought anyone to be) will despise and laugh at the certain and the uncertain alike. But while he laughs foolishly, it is easily recognised by those who are not dull who he is. That I have satisfied you on these matters, I do not doubt at all.

units.la: Restat vt de Galeni loco aliquid attingam solum. Non enim alia refutatione indiget, quàm vt cum antegressis ac mox sequentibus conferatur. Hoc qui fecerit, ingenuè fatebitur, nihil eo probari posse. Deinde nullus extat in tam multis Galeni commentarijs locus, qui ipsum ex cœlo de futura aëris temperie iudicasse vel indicet solum. Quinimò in 3. Decret. vbi maximè conatus est Astrologus esse, nihil tale dixit. Quod de tempestatum prænotione in eo libro protulit, ex Arato desumsit. Et quidem ex eo libro, in quo, quid meteora in aëre apparentia significent, describitur. Supra etiam docui, quot modos venturæ pluuiæ prænoscendæ cognitos habuerit. Certè si plures norat, tacere illo in loco, & aliis compluribus, vbi de aëris temperie & qualitatibus loquitur, minimè debebat. Hic satis est declarasse, neque Hippocratem neque Galenum ex cœli sideribus more Astrologico de futura aëris temperie vnquam diuinasse,atque locos illos,quibus nituntur ad deliria sua com- probanda Astrologi,nec prodesse ipsis posse, nec à Gale- no ita intellectos & expositos esse,vt perperam ipsi intelli- gunt. Possem hoc loco disputationem abrumpere, & plu- ra me in illis literis non quærere voluisse,dicere. Sed ne ita quæstiones argumentaque tua soluere videar voluisse, vt Gordonis nodum Alexander Magnus,cum soluere nequi- ret aliter,nec insolutum sinere vellet tamen, secuisse legi- tur:illa quoque perpendemus breuiter, quæ in altera tua- rum literarum parte mihi proposita à te sunt.
units.tr: It remains for me to touch only briefly on Galen's passage. It needs no other refutation than to be compared with what goes before and what immediately follows. Whoever does this will frankly confess that nothing can be proved from it. Moreover, in so many commentaries of Galen there is no passage which even hints that he judged from the heavens the future temperament of the air. Indeed, in the third book of the Decrees, where the Astrologer has most tried to make a case, he said nothing of the kind. What he set forth there about the foreknowledge of weather he took from Aratus, and indeed from that book in which is described what the meteors appearing in the air signify. I have shown above, too, how many means of foreseeing approaching rain he knew. Certainly, if he knew more, he ought not by any means to have been silent about them in that place and in many others, where he speaks of the temperament and qualities of the air. It is enough here to have shown that neither Hippocrates nor Galen ever foretold the future temperament of the air from the heavenly bodies in the Astrological manner, and that those passages on which the Astrologers rely to confirm their delusions can neither help them, nor have been explained by Galen as they wrongly understand them. I could break off the discussion at this point and say that I did not wish to seek more in those letters. But lest I seem to have wished to solve your questions and arguments as Alexander the Great is read to have cut the Gordian knot, since he could not otherwise untie it and yet did not wish to leave it unsolved, we shall briefly weigh also those points which you have put to me in the other part of your letters.

units.la: Quòd siderum coitiones variasque radiorum mistio- nes non iudicas veras & propinquas causas euentuum, qui circa hominem accidunt particularium,libenter acci- pio & agnosco pro vero. Quod deinde Solis atque Lunæ (arbitror te de aliis quoque sideribus idem hoc dictum velle,) facultates primum & magis in aëre cerni ac depre- hendi affirmas, quàm in conflatis ex omnibus elemen- tis corporibus,id quoque rationi consonum est. Etenim quoties causa aliqua vna in duo agere apta est, semper in id, quod propinquius est,tum citius tum efficacius poten- tiusve agit. Aërem esse sideribus viciniorem nobis,aper- tum est. Aristoteles sententiam in Analysticis hanc posuit: Propter quod res quaelibet talis, id magis tale est. Hæc sem- piterne veritatis existit,cum rectè intelligitur. Intelligi au- tem eo pacto debet,sicut præclari in philosophia viri rectè docuerunt,ac ipsum,quod adfert,exemplum probat. Nem- pe cum affectio vna in duobus reperitur, atque in altero propter alterum inest,tum sequitur semper,magis illud ta- le esse,propter quod alterum tale factum est,quatenus ni- mirum tale existit propter aliud. Nisi hoc adijciatur,fallet interdum regula.
units.tr: That you do not judge the conjunctions of the stars and the various mixtures of their rays to be the true and proximate causes of the particular events that happen to man, I gladly accept and acknowledge as true. As to your claim that the powers of the Sun and Moon (I take it you mean the same of the other stars too) are seen first and more clearly in the air than in bodies compounded of all the elements, this also agrees with reason. For whenever a single cause is able to act upon two things, it always acts more quickly, more effectively and more powerfully on the one that is nearer. It is plain that the air is nearer to us than the stars are. Aristotle put forward this maxim in the Analytics: Whatever thing is of such a kind, that thing is more so because of which the other is such. This is an eternal truth when it is rightly understood. It must be understood, however, in the way that distinguished philosophers have correctly taught, and as the example he gives itself proves. Namely, when one quality is found in two things, and is present in one because of the other, it always follows that the thing because of which the other is such is more such, insofar as it is such because of something else. Unless this is added, the rule will sometimes fail.

units.la: In nostro proposito concessum est,elementis pariter ac ex his coalitis rebus hoc adesse, vt à cœlo mutari, alterari, perpetuè,possint. At hiisce id adest propter illa. Quicquid enim non ex elementis natum effectumque est, id mutationi siderum minimè subijcitur. Unde Astrologi quoq; fatentur, animos nostros verè ab actione siderum non pati aliquid posse, nisi quatenus mutatæ corporis temperaturæ ipsi consentiant. Ex quo patere potest, elementa tum celerius tum amplius & facilius ab omnium siderum actionibus permutari, quàm ex his conflata corpora. Est tamen in illis quoque discrimen. Facilius enim rarefit atque incalescit aër quàm aqua, & hac difficilius etiam rarescit terra. Hactenus ergo, cum nihil dictum à te videam, quod ab ipsa rerum natura alienum dissentaneumque putem, nihil etiam reprehendo.
units.tr: In our present matter it is granted that both the elements and the bodies compounded from them have this property, that they can be changed and altered continually by the heavens. But these bodies have it because of the elements. For whatever is not born and made from the elements is not subject to change by the stars at all. Hence the astrologers too admit that our souls can truly suffer nothing from the action of the stars, except insofar as they go along with the altered temperament of the body. From this it can be seen that the elements are changed both more quickly and more fully, and more easily, by the actions of all the stars than the bodies compounded from them. There is a difference even among the elements themselves: air is rarefied and heated more easily than water, and earth is rarefied with even more difficulty than water. So far, then, since I see nothing said by you that I think alien to, or at odds with, the nature of things, I find nothing to criticise either.

units.la: Cæterùm quod cum hisce mox connectis, id mihi neque verum, neque ex dictis consequi videtur. Sidera citius, facilius, potentius in aërem agunt, quàm in composita ex elementis corpora. Ergo ex notitia coitionum & positus siderum, futuræ tempestates aëris prædici queunt. Non requires à me hic, puto, verbosè, ut probem argumentum nihil concludere. Solem ego potentius ac facilius aërem calefacere quàm aquas, terras, corpora animalium, facile concedo. At hinc non sequitur aëris propterea qualitates me prædicturum hinc esse. Non enim iam calefacit, mox humectat Sol per se aërem: attamen iam siccitatis, mox pluuiarum causa existit, alia tamen ratione, intervenientibus scilicet aliis multis. Ratio eadem est Lunæ & siderum aliorum. Non semper eodem modo agunt, siue idem efficiunt in aëre, vt neque Sol eundem æqualiter semper calefacit. In ipsis certè diebus canicularibus sæpe admodum frigidum aërem experimur, in ipsa etiam meridie. Quod cum dico, non id intelligo, Solem, quod ad ipsum attinet, non simili semper modo agere. Causa & corpus naturale est, ideoque semper eodem modo agit, & quantum omnino potest, præsertim cum mutationi nulli subiiciatur. Quare semper aërem pro suis viribus calefacit. At non similiter hic semper calesit. In causa est, quòd modò purior, modò impurior per administrationem vaporum de terra eleuatorum existit. Idem de cæteris mihi dictum puta. Si igitur ne de Solis quidem viribus aliud prædici potest, quàm calefacturum ipsum aërem ac terram, quàtum pro affectione eorum possit, quomodo de aliis certi quippiam prædixeris, quorum actiones sunt exiles valdè, & im-pediri facilius multo possunt: Sed redeamus ad argumētū.
units.tr: But what you join to these points next seems to me neither true nor to follow from what has been said. The stars act upon the air more quickly, more easily and more powerfully than upon bodies compounded of the elements. Therefore the future weather of the air can be foretold from knowledge of the conjunctions and positions of the stars. You will not require me here, I think, to argue at length that this argument proves nothing. I readily grant that the Sun heats the air more powerfully and more easily than water, earth or the bodies of animals. But it does not follow from this that I shall therefore predict the qualities of the air from it. For the Sun does not at once heat and then moisten the air by itself; yet it is now the cause of dryness and now of rains, though by a different route, namely through the intervention of many other things. The reasoning is the same for the Moon and the other stars. They do not always act in the same way, nor do they always produce the same effect in the air, just as the Sun does not always heat it equally. Indeed, even in the very dog days we often experience quite cold air, even at midday. When I say this, I do not mean that the Sun, so far as it is concerned, does not always act in the same way. It is a natural cause and body, and so it always acts in the same way, and to the full extent of its power, especially since it is subject to no change. Hence it always heats the air to the full extent of its strength. But the air is not always heated equally here. The reason is that it is sometimes purer and sometimes less pure, owing to the mixing in of vapours raised from the earth. Consider that I have said the same of the other bodies too. If, then, nothing can be foretold even about the powers of the Sun except that it will heat the air and the earth as far as their condition allows, how could you state anything certain about the others, whose actions are very slight and much more easily impeded? But let us return to the argument.

units.la: Sidera magis mutant aërem quàm cætera, ergo pluuiæ ex eorum motibus prædici poterunt. Hoc tantum ad antecedens sequitur. Ergo aërem permutabunt tunc etiam, cum compositæ non sensibiliter permutata conspiciemus. At verò hoc ipsum volui, respondebis fortè, inferre. Rectè hoc sequi dixeris. At ne sic quidem propositum concluse-ris[?], nempe Tempestates indicari à cœlo. sic existimo, (ut ni-hil dissimulem) te voluisse argumentari. Sidera quædam naturali vi prædita sunt, pluuias aut ventos aut alia simi-lia efficiendi. Nec frustrantur sua actione, sed in aëre faci-le quod possunt perficiunt: ergo qui congressus[?] eorum tales obseruare didicerit, futuras aëris mutationes præintel-liget.
units.tr: The stars change the air more than other things do; therefore rains can be predicted from their motions. From this only the following: they will change the air even at times when we see no sensible change in compounded bodies. But perhaps you will reply that this is exactly what you wished to infer. You might say that this follows correctly. But even so you would not have concluded your proposition, namely that the weather is indicated by the heavens. This, I think (not to dissemble), is how you wished to argue: some stars are endowed by nature with the power of producing rains or winds or other such things; nor do they fail in their action, but easily accomplish in the air what they can do. Therefore whoever has learned to observe their conjunctions will foresee the future changes of the air.

units.la: At hic percunctari me oportet, quæ sit ista in sideribus vis suscitandi ventos, aut procreandi pluuias, scilicet, an hoc per se efficiant sidera, eo quòd aërem permutant, an verò vapores quos in aëre cogunt? Si prius affirmetur, necessarium est nil aliud esse pluuias & ventos, quàm aëris affectiones & qualitates, non autem substantias. Sic rectè antiqui aliqui, quos Aristoteles primùm, deinde etiam Galenus confutauit ac reprehendit, Ventum nihil aliud esse, quàm aërem motum dixerunt. Nisi, inquam, hæc sen-tentia vera sit, vera esse ista opinio de generatione Ven-torum nequit. Et vt de ventis id rectè dici contendat aliquis, de pluuia, niue, grandine, nubibus, defendi sententia tamen nequaquam poterit. Etenim iam enumerata, substantiæ sunt, non simplices ac nudæ qualitates. Ergo per coactionem vaporum ex aqua & terra in aërem elatorum pluuias generabunt, ac ventos sidera. Hoc posito, frustra illud positum est, sidera facilius aërem permutare. Non enim aëris, sed aquæ ac terræ permutatio necessaria erit, si generari pluuiæ debent.
units.tr: But here I must ask: what is this power in the stars of raising winds or bringing forth rains? Do the stars effect this by themselves, because they change the air, or do they do it through the vapours which they gather in the air? If the first is affirmed, it follows that rains and winds are nothing other than affections and qualities of the air, and not substances. This is why certain ancients, whom Aristotle first and then Galen refuted and criticised, said that wind is nothing other than air in motion. Unless, I say, this opinion is true, the opinion about the generation of winds cannot be true. And although someone might contend that this is rightly said of winds, it can by no means be defended of rain, snow, hail and clouds. For the things just listed are substances, not mere simple qualities. Therefore the stars generate rains through the gathering of vapours raised from water and earth into the air, and winds too. Given this, it is pointless to assume that the stars change the air more easily. For it will not be a change of the air, but of water and earth, that is necessary if rains are to be generated.

units.la: Sed hic quoque tuam sententiam de omnibus elemen-tis accipio & concedo. Non quidem quasi veram esse nihil dubitem, sed vt quid hinc effici queat animaduertam. Sic igitur argumentum instituendum est, si recte colligere velis: Sidera, quae vim habent insitam pluvias creandi, facilius vapores ex terra & aqua extrahunt, quàm composita ex elementis corpora sensibiliter permutent. Ergo cum ex talibus generentur pluviae, nives, grandines, &c. rectius ac certius tempestates ex sideribus praenoscuntur, quàm corporum permutationes, aliíque particulares effectus. Ut totum argumentum concedatur, inaniter tamen glorientur Astrologi. Nam si paulò etiam certius praenosci pluviæ & tempestates queant, quàm aliarum rerum permutationes, quid inde concludetur? Hæ nullo modo praevideri possunt, illæ[?] ergò paulò minus non cognoscuntur. Nihil hinc aliud concluseris, quàm incertam esse totam hanc praedicendi rationem, paucula quaedam tamen, eaque perobscurè posse conijci, quae tamen nullum habeat momentum notitia.
units.tr: But here too I accept and grant your view about all the elements; not that I doubt it is true, but so that I may consider what can be inferred from it. The argument must therefore be set out in this way, if you wish to draw the conclusion correctly: the stars, which have the power implanted in them of creating rains, draw up vapours from earth and water more easily than bodies compounded of the elements are sensibly changed. Therefore, since rains, snows, hail and so on are generated from such vapours, weather can be foreknown from the stars more correctly and more certainly than changes of bodies and other particular effects. Let the whole argument be granted, yet the astrologers would boast in vain. For even if rains and storms could be foreknown a little more certainly than changes in other things, what would follow? The latter cannot be foreseen at all, the former only a little less; so nothing else would follow from this than that the whole method of prediction is uncertain, and that a few things may be conjectured, and those very obscurely, yet that even these have no weight as knowledge.

units.la: Sed exactius perpendenda sunt. Qui siderum effectiones sive actiones facilius ab elementis recipi hoc modo, ut certus ex ea re consequatur effectus, concedunt, non illud etiam concedere coguntur, ex siderum inspectione futuras tempestates praevideri posse. Etenim non ita agunt in haec terrena sidera, ut statim evincat, sic dico evincant, ut particulares isti effectus consequantur. Actum dare ea omnibus, ut pro sua natura res singulae id agant, ad quod peragendum factae sunt, non negamus. At similes hinc in omnibus operationes & effectus prodire, id est quod negamus. Sol certè omnia, quod in se est, ex aequo calefacit, & calefaciendo etiam rarefacit, quae rarefieri possunt. Sed neque aequabiliter omnia calefiunt ac rarefiunt à Sole, nec duobus etiam diebus deinceps res eadem similiter à sole semper afficitur, aut similiter semper patitur. At huius facultas longè manifestissima & efficacissima est, si cum aliorum omnium astrorum viribus comparetur. Multò ergo minus alia sidera eosdem semper producent effectus.
units.tr: But these matters must be weighed more exactly. Those who concede that the effects or actions of the stars are received by the elements more easily, in such a way that a certain effect follows from them, are not thereby compelled to concede that future weather can be foreseen from observing the stars. For they do not act upon these earthly things in such a way as to bring about, as I put it, so as to produce these particular effects. We do not deny that they give all things the capacity to act, so that each thing acts according to its own nature for the purpose for which it was made. But that similar operations and effects follow from this in all things, that is what we deny. The Sun certainly heats everything in its reach equally, and by heating also rarefies whatever can be rarefied. But things are not heated and rarefied equally by the Sun, nor on two successive days is the same thing affected in the same way by the sun, or does it always suffer in the same way. Yet its power is by far the most evident and effective when compared with the powers of all the other stars. Much less, then, will the other stars always produce the same effects.

units.la: Quare ut verum sit, esse quaedam sidera quae peculiari vi ex terra excitare vapores valeant, non tamen eodem semper modo poterunt. Nam terra alias magis, alias minus apta erit ad excipiendas astrorum vires. Reddet vno tempore vapores inuitata à cœlo plures, quàm alio. Quod dum ignoratur, necesse est illud etiam ignorari, an sidera terram præparatam ad reddendos vapores repertura sint. Et quòd non semper similiter sit idonea, velipsis demon-strem astrologis testibus. Princeps eorum Ptolemæus hinc plurimum variari præsensiones ipsemet confitetur, & explicando docet. Cæteros libenter non nomino, quòd ineptiores multò sint. Frustra igitur sciet Astrologus, sider-rum quandam coitionem futuram, quæ aerem vapori-bus refercire possit, nisi hoc simul non ignoret, aptam esse futuram eo tempore terram, ut radijs illorum percusso vaporum copiam effundat.
units.tr: Therefore, even if it is true that certain stars are able to draw up vapours from the earth by a peculiar power, they will not always be able to do so in the same way. For the earth will be more or less apt at different times to receive the powers of the stars. At one time it will give off more vapours when summoned from the heavens than at another. While this is unknown, it must also be unknown whether the stars will find the earth prepared to give off vapours. And that it is not always equally suitable, I will show by the testimony of the astrologers themselves. Their prince, Ptolemy, himself admits and explains that the forecasts vary greatly for this reason. I willingly pass over the others, since they are much more foolish. The astrologer will therefore know in vain that some conjunction of the stars is going to come about which can fill the air with vapours, unless at the same time he also knows that the earth will then be fit to pour out a quantity of vapours when struck by their rays.

units.la: Si semper paratam esse dicas, & sola attractione opus esse in sublime, nugari videberis. Etenim hoc modo omnia sidera talia semper pluuiâ producent: At non semper, imò raro pluit, cum prædicunt astrologi pluuias, id quod negare nec possunt nec etiam solent, cum serio argumentis premuntur hoc in parte. Certum est, Solem, Lunam, aliaq; omnia astra, facultatem habere attrahêdi vapores sursum de terra. Si ergo satis magna semper eorum præparata est copia, semper tot attrahentur, quot suscitando vento ac pluuijs suffecerint. Quòd si non tâ multos suppetere cogitemus, educi eos ex terra oportebit & aqua. Sed hoc nõ fit, nisi calore rarefiant. At frigus resistit calori. Facilè ergo imbecillus & non sensilis astrorum calor eludetur irritus-que fiet, in frigidiorem incidens terram. Etenim ne Sol quidem calefacere eam semper poterit. Hyeme, exempli gratia, tametsi Sol sit infirmus apud nos, potentior tamen est alijs sideribus quæcunque tandem proponere libeat. At non posse tunc ab eo terræ frigus ita superari, ut in vaporem aut fumum soluta, in aërem ascendat, notius est quàm ut probationis egeat. Quanto ergo minus reliqua id sidera tum perficient? Taceo iam quod primo loco dictum oportuit, impossibile esse ut tam breui tempore, quâ Astrologici aspectus perdurant, mutatio aliqua notabilis vel in aqua vel in terra effici possit. Vix momento ocuí tales permanent. At Sol sæpe magna vi aquas calefacit, neque multis tamen horis in vapores convertit. Quo pa-cto igitur de aliis hoc credere poterimus, quorum actio à nobis distinctè nunquam deprehensa est?
units.tr: If you say that the earth is always ready, and that only attraction is needed to draw it upwards, you will seem to be talking nonsense. For in this way all such stars would always produce rain. But they do not always do so; indeed, it rains rarely, although astrologers predict rains, which they can neither deny nor are accustomed to deny when they are seriously pressed with arguments on this point. It is certain that the Sun, the Moon and all the other stars have the power of drawing vapours upwards from the earth. If, then, a sufficiently great supply of these is always prepared, the same amount would always be drawn up as would suffice for stirring up winds and rains. But if we suppose that there are not so many available, they will have to be drawn out of the earth and water. This does not happen, however, unless they are rarefied by heat. But cold resists heat. Therefore the weak and imperceptible heat of the stars will easily be eluded and rendered ineffective, falling upon a colder earth. Indeed, not even the Sun can always warm it. In winter, for example, although the Sun is weak with us, it is nevertheless more powerful than any other stars one might care to name. But that the earth's cold cannot then be so overcome by it that the earth, dissolved into vapour or smoke, rises into the air, is better known than that it needs proof. How much less, then, will the other stars accomplish at such a time? I pass over what ought to have been said first: it is impossible that any notable change should be effected in water or in earth in so short a time as that for which the astrological aspects endure. Such configurations last scarcely a moment of an eye. Yet the Sun often heats waters with great force, and yet does not turn them into vapours within many hours. How, then, can we believe this of the others, whose action has never been clearly observed by us?

units.la: Breuiter sic habet res: Astrorum figurationes Astrologicæ vix sunt momentaneæ. Et si longissimo etiam tempore perdurent, nullo prorsus modo Solis atque Lunæ vires æquare possunt. Quinimò nulla est eorum virtutis ad potentiam Solis comparatio. Cum igitur pluuias & ventos non nisi per vaporum suscitationem gignere queant, hi verò non nisi à calore rarefaciente suscitentur, manifestum est, vix unquam quod debebant effecturas. Etenim ut omnem repugnantiam sua potentia Sol hactenus superet, ut quatuor anni tempora producat, non tamen eiusdem hæc semper sunt temperamenti. Simili modo, ut aliquid agere ista concedantur sidera, non tamen eodem modo perficient perpetuò. Atque tanto consequetur minus effectus certus, quanto Sole imbecilliores obtinent vires. Quare aut rarissimè aut nunquam desideratum sibi finem consequuntur. Luna menstrua facit temporum discrimina. At non similiter hæc etiam eadem facit, cum cætera omnia astra similiter habent. Quid in causa est? Non aliud quâ quòd actio non pro natura agentis causæ, sed pro affectione varia & dissimili patientum varie dissimiliterque recipitur. Deinde quia sidera ista efficiunt ut universales causæ. Postremò quia per accidens ab ipsis talia efficiuntur. Interveniunt enim valde multæ aliæ causæ, quæ vel promouent atque adiuuant, vel impediunt siderum actionem generalem. Difficilius calefit à Sole terra perfrigerata & humectata, quàm si aliter affecta sit. Minus illustratur aër crassis nebulis refertus, quàm purus. Interdum à densioribus nubibus tantum non prorsus nobis lumen Solis eri-pitur. Idem aër crassior calefit tardius à Sole, at calefactus refrigeratur quoque difficilius. Exhalant sæpe plurimi ex loco aliquo terræ vapores siue spiritus, qui multis ante temporibus inde nunquam exire visi sunt. Qui sub terra metallis effodiendis operam dant, mirabilia narrant de subterraneis mutationib.quas inclusus in terra calor efficit tunc,cū in aere nostro omnia æquabiliter fiunt. Sic etiā sæ-pe in corporibus nostris non omnia omni tempore eodē modo habent, tametsi exterius nihil admodum sit mutatum. Non factum est nunquam, vt vapores in nubem coa-cti pluuiam nobis minitarentur, ac vento repente exorto ex loco aliquo, dissijcerentur[?] sine guttulæ casu. Ista exempli[?] gratia tantum recensui, vt quàm nihil hîc certi sit cernas.
units.tr: Briefly, the matter stands thus: the astrological configurations of the stars are scarcely momentary. And even if they last for a very long time, they can in no way equal the powers of the Sun and Moon. Indeed, there is no comparison of their power with the power of the Sun. Since, therefore, they can produce rains and winds only by raising vapours, and these vapours are raised only by heat that rarefies, it is evident that they will hardly ever bring about what they ought. For although the Sun by its power overcomes all resistance so far as to produce the four seasons of the year, these are nevertheless not always of the same temperature. In like manner, even if it is granted that these stars act at all, they will not always act in the same way. And the less powerful they are than the Sun, the less certain will be the effect. Therefore they will either very rarely or never attain the end desired of them. The Moon makes the divisions of time by months, but it does not do this in the same way, though all the other stars likewise have their own courses. What is the cause? Nothing other than that the action is received not according to the nature of the acting cause, but variously and dissimilarly according to the varied and dissimilar disposition of the things acted upon. Further, because these stars act as universal causes. Lastly, because such effects are produced by them only accidentally. For very many other causes intervene, which either promote and assist, or hinder the general action of the stars. Earth that is chilled and moistened is warmed by the Sun with more difficulty than if it were otherwise disposed. Air filled with thick mists is less illuminated than pure air. Sometimes the light of the Sun is almost entirely snatched from us by denser clouds. The same thicker air is warmed more slowly by the Sun, and when warmed is cooled with more difficulty. Often many vapours or exhalations rise from some place in the earth which were never seen to issue from there in many former times. Those who labour in digging out metals under the ground report marvels about the subterranean changes which heat enclosed in the earth then brings about, when in our air all things happen uniformly. So too in our bodies all things do not always stay in the same condition at all times, although outwardly nothing has much changed. Has it never happened that vapours gathered into a cloud threatened us with rain, and then, a wind suddenly rising from some place, they were scattered without a drop falling? I have recounted these instances only by way of example, so that you may see how little certainty there is here.

units.la: Iam verò sic cogita: Nihil certi est, vbi admittuntur pro veris quæ incertissima & prorsus controuersa sunt. Quid igitur efficere nos posse sperandum fuerit, si probare principia cogamur? De veritate huius sententiæ quæritur, scilicet, an certa sidera vel ex insita vi, vel propter positum & aspectum ad alia, peculiarem vim nanciscantur[?] pluuiàs po-tius quàm a'iud quippiam producendi. Hoc tu pro vero & certo ponebas, quod aliud nihil est, quàm principium petere, hoc est, quod probandum fuerat, tanquam probatum ponere. Ego concessi ea de causa, vt nihil tamen inde iuuari Astrologorum causam perspiceres. Iam si, vt probent ita rem habere, iubeantur, quo id sint facturi[?] modo ipsi viderint. Certè ratio nulla ab ipsis hactenus excogitata pro-ductaue est, quæ vel leuiter institutum defendat.
units.tr: Now think of it in this way: there is nothing certain where things that are most uncertain and wholly disputed are admitted as true. What, then, could we hope to accomplish if we were forced to prove our principles? The question concerns the truth of this opinion, namely, whether certain stars, either by an inborn power or by their position and aspect towards others, acquire a peculiar power of producing rains rather than anything else. You were assuming this as true and certain, which is nothing other than begging the question: that is, laying down as proved what was to be proved. I granted it for this reason, so that you might nevertheless see that the cause of the astrologers is helped by nothing from it. Now if they are ordered to prove that the matter is so, they must see for themselves by what means they will do it. Certainly no argument has hitherto been devised or brought forward by them which defends their position even slightly.

units.la: Quas Ptolemæus in principio suorum de Astrologia librorum adfert, admodum sunt ridiculæ. Et vehementer miror quomodo inuenire potuerit, qui ei fidem in illa parte habere potuerint. Nō iam vt veras esse ei concedamus, nihilominus de nostra causa nobis decedere poterit. Ere-nim calefaciendo, frigefaciendo, humectando, exiccando, omnia ab ipsis effici sideribus affirmat. Sic Solem hæc permutare notum est. Ipse quoque plerosque planetarum à Solis vicinia calorem, ab eiusdem distantia frigus, à terræ humore humectandi vires mutuatos asserit. Idem tu quoque hactenus sensisse videris in his tuis literis. Quòd si ita res habet, plura prædici ex congressibus astrorum nō poterunt, quàm calefactura terram atque aerem magis minusque, prout plura pauciorauè taha[?] coierint. Eadem de humiditate & cæteris qualitatibus ratio est. Quanquam de humiditate quæstio esse minimè leuis potest. Nō enim videtur aliquid humectari, sine humidi corporis accessione. Frigus & caliditas se ipsas propagant, generando scilicet similem sibi qualitatem in vicinis sibi corporibus. Hoc in caliditate ignis apertissimum est. Etenim quæ in igne caliditas est, dum calefit aqua ab eo, per generationem caliditaris in aqua, calefacit aquam, non verò per trasitionem seu transmigrationem eiusdem illius caliditatis ex igne in aquam. Hoc modo ut exiccari corpora posse concedamus, quod tamen tardè admodum fiet, de humiditate quomodo dici queat, non video. Nisi enim aqua aut humidum aliud corpus arido permisceatur, humectari nunquam videbimus. Sed præstat brevitatis causa te remittere ad lib. 4. Meteororum Arist. ubi hæc diligenter exposita sunt. Ergo si astra quædam humectant aërem, aut ita humectant, ut ignis ceram evocando & solvendo concretam humiditā-tem, aut subitantiam in aërem demittunt humidam, aut denique ex terra & aqua excitant vapores, & in sublime ad se attrahentes aërem humectum reddunt. Priores duo modi inepti sunt. Postremus ipse quoque valde lubricus est & dubius. Etenim non tam humectare ex Ptolemæi sententia aërem tales Planetæ videntur, quàm humectari. Siue igitur ab illis net[?] stel is humidi vapores de terra ele-ventur, per quos ipsæ humiditatem cōcipiunt, siue ab alijs, caloris opus esse semper videbitur[?]. Sed hæc libenter sino, de quibus multa non male dici præterea possent, & ad propositum redeo. Nihil, inquam, aliud prædici posset, quàm terram vel calefaciendam (siue aërem) frigefaciendam, humectandamque esse. Verum hic quoque addere oportebit, modò apta sit, ut vapores tam multos tam facile, tam leuiter inuirata, tam brevi tempusculo irritata, de sese spargat. Qua ratione rursus spe sua frustrari se videnr[?], qui hinc aliquid certi sibi pollicebantur.
units.tr: The things Ptolemy brings forward at the beginning of his books on astrology are very ridiculous. And I wonder greatly how he could have found anyone who could put faith in him on that point. Let us not yet concede that they are true to him; nevertheless, he can yield nothing to our cause. For he affirms that all these things are effected by the stars: heating, cooling, moistening, drying. Thus it is well known that the Sun changes these. He himself also asserts that most of the planets borrow heat from their nearness to the Sun, cold from its distance, and the power of moistening from the moisture of the earth. You too seem hitherto to have held the same view in this letter of yours. If this is so, the stars in their conjunctions will be able to predict no more than that they will make the earth and air warmer or cooler, according as more or fewer of them have come together. The same reasoning holds for moisture and the other qualities. Yet the question concerning moisture can be by no means trivial. For nothing seems to become moist without the addition of a moist body. Cold and heat propagate themselves, namely by generating a similar quality in bodies near them. This is most evident in the heat of fire. For the heat which is in the fire, when water is warmed by it, warms the water by generating heat in the water, not by a transition or transmigration of that same heat from the fire into the water. In this way, although we may grant that bodies can be dried, which nevertheless happens very slowly, I do not see how moisture can be spoken of. For unless water or some other moist body is mixed with a dry one, we shall never see it made moist. But for the sake of brevity it is better to refer you to the fourth book of Aristotle's Meteorology, where these matters are diligently set out. Therefore, if certain stars moisten the air, they either do so by fire, which by evoking and dissolving the moisture or substance thickened into wax, sends it into the air as moisture; or finally they raise vapours from earth and water, and drawing them upwards to themselves, render the air moist. The first two ways are foolish. The last also is itself very slippery and doubtful. For in Ptolemy's opinion such planets seem not so much to moisten the air as to be moistened. Therefore, whether moist vapours are raised from the earth by those stars themselves, through which they receive moisture, or by others, it will always appear that heat is needed. But I willingly let these matters go, about which many things could well be said besides, and return to my point. Nothing else, I say, could be predicted than that the earth (or the air) will be warmed or cooled and moistened. But here too it will be necessary to add that this holds only if the earth is suitable, so that it can give off so many vapours, so easily, so lightly, when stirred up so quickly and in so short a space of time. By this reasoning, those who were promising themselves something certain from this will again see their hope frustrated.

units.la: Verùm enim ut juculentè videas quàm sint falsæ & futiles Astrologorum de tempestatibus prædictiones, sic experiaris rem velim. Nota in libello aliquo, vel ephemeride ad marginem, vel ut aliter libet ac potes, qui singulis totius anni diebus venti spirarint, & quæ ceciderint plu-viæ, nives, grandines, & huius generis omnes aeris tempe-ries bonas pariter ac malas. Anno confecto cura ut habeas prognostica omnium aut plurium [?], qui scripserunt in tuo horizonte aut vicino. Ubi animum negocijs defessum re-laxare & recreare voles, primum considera quos illi Anni Dominos statuerint sive gubernatores, in qua re nunquā aut perraro duos concordes reperies.
