Taceo cætera, quæ non facere quilibet potest. Deinde vide quam tempesta-tem illi diebus singulis.quorum mentionem fecerunt, esse debuisse scripserint, & cum tuis annotatis confer. Si sece-ris, rarissimè eos scopum attigisse deprehendes. Sanè vel hinc eos nō ex arte, sed casu aliquando verum dixisse reip-sa comperies. Discrimen porrò tantum reperies, quantū nemo fuisset credere ausus. In plerisque omnibus, neque ipsos inter se, nec cum veritate conuenire perspicies. Nisi tum forte consonantia dicant, cum frigus circa brumam & nives, calorem verò & siccitatem sub Canis tempus de-nunciant. Quidam prudentiores non dies nominant, sed iuxta quartas Lunæ vocatas vaticinantur de hisce, & ita quidem temperant, ut difficilius errorem hic redarguas. Dum enim generalia quædam dicunt, & pro ratione anni temporum aut ventos aut aliud simile futurum asserunt, vix accusari mendacij possunt. Raro enim non aut ventus aliquis toto illo octiduo, præsertim Vere & Autumno spi-rat, aut pluit semel iterumque. Habebis tamen & hic nō-nunquam illustres occasiones perspiciendi falsitatem prae-dictionum. Possem, liquidem res postularet, quid expertus ego sim narrare. Et facerem etiam, nisi aliquos ita inter-pretaturos vererer, quasi perstringere ipsos in animo habuissem. Proinde finem faciam, ubi unum præterea supra dictis addidero. Id huiusmodi est.
units.tr: But so that you may see playfully how false and worthless the astrologers' predictions of weather are, I would like you to test the matter in this way. Note in some little book, or in a calendar in the margin, or in whatever manner you like and are able, which winds blew on each day of the whole year, and what rains, snows, hails, and every kind of weather, good and bad alike, fell. When the year is over, see to it that you have the prognostics of all, or of most, of those who have written for your horizon or a nearby one. When you wish to relax and refresh your mind, weary from business, first consider which lords or governors of the year they have appointed; in this matter you will never, or very rarely, find two in agreement. I say nothing of the other things that anyone can check. Then look at what weather they wrote that each of the days they mentioned ought to have had, and compare it with your notes. If you do this, you will discover that they very rarely hit the mark. Indeed, from this you will find that they sometimes spoke the truth by chance and not by art. Moreover, you will find such a discrepancy as no one would have dared to believe. In most cases you will see that they agree neither with one another nor with the truth. Unless perhaps they agree when they foretell cold and snow around the winter solstice, and heat and drought in the season of the Dog Star. Some more prudent ones do not name days, but prophesy about these things according to the quarters of the moon, and they so qualify their statements that you will find it more difficult to refute their error here. For while they say certain general things, and, according to the character of the season, assert that winds or something similar will come, they can hardly be accused of lying. For there is rarely a week, especially in spring and autumn, in which some wind does not blow, or it does not rain once or twice. Yet here too you will sometimes have clear opportunities to perceive the falsity of their predictions. I could relate what I have experienced, if the matter required it. And I would do so, were I not afraid that some would interpret it as though I had intended to attack them. Therefore I will make an end, once I have added one more point to what has been said. It is of this kind.

units.la: Etsi Astrologiam utilem esse ad præno-scendas tempesta-tes concedam, non tamen aut utilem aut necessariam pro-pterea Medico fateri me oportebit. Nam cui rei in Medi-cina hæc notitia sit usui, non facile dixeris, nisi vel ad præ-videndos futuros morbos, vel ad instituendam victus rationem prodesse, contendas. At neutri admodum prodes-se, facilè consideranti apparebit. Quod ad victus ratione artinet, sanè nihil prodest, quod vel hinc intelligas, quod neque Galenus neque Hippocrates cum de instituendo victu agunt, nos temporum istam praescientiam docet. Loquor hic de aegris. (Nam in sanis nemo victum iubeat mutare propter suspicionem temporis futuri, quod quale futurum sit certò nequeat sciri. Non enim negant, puto, Astrologi, probabilem tantum esse hanc praesensionem, minimè verò necessariam.) Nam tempus futurum status consiederandū & praenosceudū docent, non vtrū pluuiae, an nebulae, an grādo casura sit spectare nos iubet. Quod si aut vtile hoc aut necessariū iudicassent, praeteriturī nō fuerant.
units.tr: Although I will concede that astrology is useful for foreseeing the weather, I must not therefore admit that it is either useful or necessary for the physician. For, unless you were to contend that this knowledge serves some purpose in medicine, either for foreseeing future diseases or for arranging a regimen of life, you could not easily say to what use it is put. But on careful consideration it will be plain that it is of little use for either. As for the regimen of life, it is certainly of no benefit; you may see this from the fact that neither Galen nor Hippocrates, when they treat of arranging a diet, bring in any foreknowledge of the seasons. I am speaking here of the sick. (For no one, I think, would order a healthy man to change his diet on account of the suspicion of future weather, which cannot be known for certain to be of any particular kind. I do not suppose the astrologers deny that this foreknowledge is only probable, and by no means necessary.) For the teaching is that we should consider and foreknow the present state of the weather, and it does not bid us look to whether rain, or mist, or hail is going to fall. If they had judged this useful or necessary, they would not have passed it over.

units.la: Praeterea non mutauerit vnquam rationem victus praesentibus conuenientem prudens Medicus, quia vel speret vel metuat aëris aliquam mutationem. Primum quidem, quia neque obesse neque prodesse nouit, quod non est, sed futurum expectatur. Victus autem iuuare, & quatenus ratio fert, opponi laedentibus caussis, etiam aëris intemperiei noxiae solet. Quare ei quae adest, si noceat, opponetur, quàdiu adest: vbi adesse desierit, ipse quoque oppugnare eam Medicus desinit. Quis non iudicaturus sit fatuum Ducem, qui ab hoste oppugnatus non se strenuè velit defendere, aut etiam hostem profligare, cum possit propter incertam spem auxilij aduenturi? Quo quisque dux melior est, tanto superat hostem libentius praesentibus copijs, quàm vt incertus expectet auxiliarios, atque interea cum suis periclitetur. At similis imperito huic Duci Medicus est, qui cum praesentis aëris statui opponere se possit victus ratione id facere nolit, quia mutandam post dies aliquot suspicetur aëris temperiem praesentem. Deinde hac etiam de caussa non mouebitur futura spe Medicus, quia nouit certum non esse quod astra promittunt. Nolet igitur propter incertam spem praesente & certa occasione nō uti. Vbi aduenerit expectata tempestas, non antè, victus rationem, re ita postulante mutabit.
units.tr: Moreover, a prudent physician would never change a regimen suited to present conditions merely because he hopes or fears some change in the air. First, because he knows that it does neither harm nor good, since it is not yet, but is only expected. Now a regimen usually helps, and, so far as reason allows, is set against harmful causes, and this includes the harmful intemperance of the air. Therefore, if the present condition is harmful, it will be opposed for as long as it is present; when it has ceased to be present, the physician too ceases to oppose it. Who would not judge a general a fool who, when attacked by the enemy, did not vigorously defend himself, or even rout the enemy, because of the uncertain hope of help that might come? The better a general is, the more willingly he overcomes the enemy with the forces at hand, rather than waiting uncertainly for allies while his own men are in danger in the meantime. But the physician who, though he can oppose the present state of the air by a regimen, does not wish to do so because he suspects that the present temperature will change after some days, is like this incompetent general. Then, too, the physician will not be moved by a future hope for this reason, because he knows that what the stars promise is not certain. He will therefore not wish to forgo a present and certain opportunity for the sake of an uncertain hope. When the expected storm has arrived, and not before, he will change the regimen, as the matter then requires.

units.la: Esto febriat aliquis tempore calido & sicco. Promittat
units.tr: Suppose someone has a fever in hot and dry weather. Let an astrologer promise

units.la: Astrologus frigidum pluuiumque cœlum in diem crastinum, aut inde ad biduum. An hic minus frigidum ac humidum cibum offeret ægro Medicus, quàm ratio morbi flagitat, quia frigus expectat? Insaniat, si id fecerit. Primùm non pugnat aut defendit ægrum contra morbum quantū debet. Deinde cum incertum sit tempus ita[?] mutandum ægroto interim plurimum obfuerit. Ex quibus aperte vides, nihil habere hanc rem, cuius causa laborare Medicus prudens & doctus velit vel unicum diem, ut addiscat.
units.tr: a cold and rainy sky for the following day, or for two days from then. Would the physician offer the patient food less cold and moist than the course of the disease demands, because he expects cold? He would be mad if he did so. First, he would not fight against the disease or defend the patient as much as he ought. Then, since the time of the change is uncertain, the patient would meanwhile suffer very great harm. From these points you clearly see that this matter has nothing for which a prudent and learned physician would wish to labour even for a single day, so that he might learn it.

units.la: Sed neque ad præsciendos morbos vtilis est. Nam aëris temperies non ipsa per se parit morbos, nisi malis succis repleat corpora, aut repleta excipiat. Prius non nisi longo tempore fit, ac facile tum cum incidit mutatio, occurri ei tum cibo ac potu, tum aliis potest. Cum enim longo tempore intemperiem perseuerare videt, satis tempestiuè remedia adhibere poterit. Equidem non aliter antiqui omnes morbos prædixisse feguntur[?], quàm ex præsente vel præterita aëris temperie, non ex futura, quæ & dubia est, nec quàm diu duratura sit sciri potest. Decet autem artifices bonos, non nisi comperta præsagire, ne incontemtum artem trahant falsis prædictionibus. In posteriore casu vtilis certè esse posset tempestatum certa prænotio, vt facilius corpora ad perferendam ipsam præpararentur. Sed hic quoque breuis mutatio non magnum adfert periculum. Vt autem hic vtilis esse posset, ita in plerisque nihil commodi adferret, imò potius incommodaret. Frustra verò de hac re dicam plura, quum falsam, vanam & impossibilem esse constet, ab Astrologis traditam ex astris prædicēdi ratione. Quod qui non credit, perfacile ex experientia certissima discet verum esse, siquidem ita, sicut monui, rem tentare & experiri non grauetur.
units.tr: But nor is it useful for foreseeing diseases. For the temperature of the air does not itself produce diseases by its own nature, unless it fills bodies with bad humours, or finds them already filled. The former happens only over a long time, and when a change occurs, it can easily be met by diet and drink, or by other means. For when he sees the intemperance persisting over a long time, the physician will be able to apply remedies in good time. Indeed, all the ancients are said to have foretold diseases in no other way than from the present or past temperature of the air, not from the future, which is doubtful, and of which one cannot know how long it will last. Good practitioners ought to foretell only what has been ascertained, lest they bring their art into contempt by false predictions. In the latter case, a certain foreknowledge of the weather could certainly be useful, so that bodies might be better prepared to endure it. But here too a brief change does not bring great danger. Yet just as it could be useful here, so in most cases it would bring no advantage, but rather harm. I would say more about this in vain, since it is established that the method of predicting from the stars which the astrologers hand down is false, empty and impossible. Whoever does not believe this will very easily learn from most certain experience that it is true, provided that, as I have advised, he does not scruple to try the matter and test it.

units.la: Vale. Heidelbergæ, Anno 1560.
units.tr: Farewell. Heidelberg, in the year 1560.

units.la: AD EVNDEM.
units.tr: TO THE SAME.

units.la: Epistola IX.
units.tr: Letter IX.

units.la: PLurimum gaudeo, & non immeritò, me tibi viro præstanti doctrina aliqua ex parte, (maluissem omni ex parte) satisfecisse. Nosti quàm variis disparibusq; negociis distrahatur animus, quæ res in primis fecit, vt quæ cogitarem minus commodè explicarem. Hanc ob rem prorsus tibi credo, ideo quædam à te in superioribus literis negligentius scripsisse, quia neque meditandi neque scribendi ocij satis habueris. Est quod gaudeam, quòd me tua rectè intellexisse affirmas. Quæ nunc desideras, tunc scribenti mihi in mente sanè non venerunt. Sed bene habet, cum adijcere nunc potero, quæ antè omissa putas. Tantum certè abest, vt graue mihi hoc futurum sit, vt vehementer tibi pro eo gratificari cupiā. Quatuor sunt quæ declarari tibi planius petis. Primùm, vt Hippocratis mentem non aliam fuisse doceam. Deinde an cœlos siue sidera causas tempestatum arbitrer. Tertiò quomodo eas à sideribus effici putem. Postremò quid ad argumenta autoris illius responderi posse existimē, qui librum conscripsit, cui titulus est, Prognosti-ca de ægrorum decubitu ex mathematica scientia. Ad hæc, (siue tria ex his siue quatuor capita facias, nihil refert) tentabo[?] ita tibi respondere, vt nihil te præterea desideratu-rum confidam.
units.tr: I rejoice greatly, and not undeservedly, that I have satisfied you, a man of outstanding learning, at least in part (I would rather have satisfied you entirely). You know how a mind is pulled apart by various and dissimilar affairs, and this is chiefly why I explained less well what I was thinking. For this reason I truly believe you, and that is why in your earlier letters you wrote some things rather carelessly: you did not have enough leisure for reflection or for writing. It gives me joy that you affirm you understood my meaning. The things you now ask for did not indeed come to my mind when I was writing then. But it is well, since I can now add what you think was omitted before. It is so far from being a burden to me that I greatly wish to oblige you in this. There are four things you ask me to explain more clearly. First, that I should show that Hippocrates' mind was not otherwise. Second, whether I think the heavens or the stars are the causes of weather. Third, how I think these are brought about by the stars. Last, what I believe can be answered to the arguments of that author who wrote the book entitled Prognostics on the Lying Down of the Sick from Mathematical Science. In addition, whether you make three of these or four heads makes no difference; I will try to answer you in such a way that I trust you will want nothing further.

units.la: Quod ad primum caput attinet, minimè erit difficile ostendere, Hippocratem nihil minus aut cogitasse aut do-cuisse, in lib. de Locis aëre & aquis, quàm ex astris tempe-states aëris esse præcogonscēdas, præsertim eo modo, quo Astrologi prægnosci volunt. Ostendam ex ipsis Hippocra-tis verbis tam plane quàm potero. Ergo in primo capite sic statim proponit: Quicunque Medicam artem integrè assequi velit, hæc illi omnino sunt agenda. Mox quæ agenda sint percenset, quæ in 5.capita dispartiri possunt. Primum est, vt norit quam vim & quantam habeat aëris quælibet siue temperies siue intemperies in corpora nostra, & quo-modo anni tempora sint distinguenda. Alterum vt quæ sit ventorum omnium natura & facultas tum communiũ[?] tum propriorum, non ignorer. Tertium est, vt non nesciat aquarum in quolibet loco qualitates, substantiam, & vires. Quartum vt loci situm ad ventos, ad Solis ortum & occasum exploratum habeat, ac terræ siue Soli naturam perspexerit. Postremum est, vt hominum in eo loco vitas[?] rationem perceperit ac obseruauerit vniuersam. Qui hæc quinque probè norit, inquit, quatum[?] scilicet fieri potest, is duo præcipuè commoda maxima inde percipiet. Primum enim non nesciet quibus morbis locus aut vrbs quælibet tum priuatis siue proprijs subiecta sit, tum etiam quinam ex communibus eam inuadere plerunque soleant, ac præterea communium morborum naturam peruidebit. Et hic primus fructus est qui ad dignoscendum maximè pertinet. Alter fructus qui ex prædictorum notitia oritur, hic est, quòd vniuscuiusque temporis anni atque adeò anni futuri constitutionem prædicere poterit.
units.tr: As for the first head, it will be by no means difficult to show that Hippocrates neither thought nor taught anything less than that the weather of the air is to be foreknown from the stars, especially in the way the astrologers wish it to be foreknown, in his book On Airs, Waters and Places. I will show this from Hippocrates' own words as plainly as I can. So in the first chapter he proposes at once: Whoever wishes to master the art of medicine completely, these things must by all means be done by him. Soon afterwards he lists what must be done, which can be divided into five heads. The first is that he should know what power and strength the quality of the air, whether temperate or intemperate, has on our bodies, and how the seasons of the year are to be distinguished. The second is that he should not be ignorant of the nature and property of all the winds, both common and peculiar. The third is that he should not be unaware of the qualities, substance and powers of the waters in any place. The fourth is that he should have examined the position of the place with respect to the winds and the rising and setting of the sun, and should have understood the nature of the land and of the sun. The last is that he should have perceived and observed the whole way of life of the people in that place. He says that whoever knows these five well, as far as that can be done, will gain from them two chief and very great advantages. For first, he will not be ignorant of what diseases any place or city is subject to, both those peculiar and private to it, and also which of the common diseases are accustomed to attack it for the most part; and besides, he will see clearly the nature of common diseases. This is the first fruit, and it pertains most to diagnosis. The second fruit, which arises from knowledge of the aforesaid things, is that he will be able to predict the constitution of each season of the year, and indeed of the coming year.

units.la: Hic iam somniant Astrologi, ipsum de prædictione temperiei temporum siue aëris loqui. At non hoc dicit ac sentit Hippocrates. Hæc est ipsius mens atque sententia, illum qui commemorata cognita habeat, prædicere posse, qui morbi quolibet tempore, scilicet qui æstate, qui hyeme, qui vere & qui autumno, inuasuri sint eam vrbem, non vero, an præter naturam suam vel humidiora vel aridiora tempora anni sint futura. Et vt verissimum esse videas, quod dico, verba quibus semetipsum explicat cõsidera. Sic enim habent: Vniuscuiusque præterea temporis ac anni futuri constitutionem prædicere poterit, qui videlicet morbi communi affectione ciuitatem sint inuasuri tum æstate tum hyeme, &c. Non poterat planius se ipsum exponere quid per constitutionem anni atque temporum vellet intelligi, scilicet non pluuiosam aut squalidam, calidam aut frigidam, sed vel salubrem vel morbosam. Et si non ipse tam diserte se interpretatus fuisset, tamen aliter exponi ista non poterant. Nihil enim aliud ex prædictis consequitur. Astrologi certè pro se facere nunquam fuissent ostensuri. Etenim ne verbum quidem unū de astris ac coelo in quin-que illis capitibus reperias dictum.
units.tr: Here now the astrologers dream that he is speaking of predicting the temperature of the seasons or of the air. But Hippocrates does not say or think this. This is his mind and opinion: that one who has the things mentioned known can predict which diseases are going to attack that city at any time, namely which in summer, which in winter, which in spring and which in autumn, and not whether the seasons of the year are going to be moister or drier than their nature. And so that you may see that what I say is most true, consider the words by which he explains himself. For they run thus: He will be able to predict the constitution of each season and of the coming year, namely which diseases are going to attack the city by their common character, both in summer and in winter, and so on. He could not have set out more plainly what he meant by the constitution of the year and of the seasons, namely not rainy or foul, hot or cold, but either healthy or sickly. And even if he had not interpreted himself so clearly, still those words could not be explained otherwise. For nothing else follows from what has been said. The astrologers would certainly never have wished to show anything in their favour. For you will not find even one word said about the stars or the heavens in those five heads.

units.la: Hæc nisi planè fallor, satis esse poterant ad ostendendū, quod propositum est. Non enim dicit, qui observet quando Mars cum Joue, Sole, Luna aut Venere hoc vel illo modo congrediatur, is pluvia ne sit futura præintelliget. Hoc ait, qui suprà enumerata capita perdidicerit, is, qui morbi quolibet anni tempore regnaturi præcipuè sint, & à quo sibi quisque metuere merito debeat, præsagire poterit. Quomodo autem ex istis capitibus connumeratis morbi tum communes tum privati præuideri queant, in progres-su libri exponitur, ut mox indicabimus.
units.tr: Unless I am greatly mistaken, these things could be enough to show what is proposed. For he does not say that one who observes when Mars joins with Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon or Venus in this or that way will foreknow whether there is going to be rain. He says that one who has learned the aforesaid heads will be able to foretell which diseases are going to reign chiefly in any season of the year, and against which each person ought rightly to be afraid. How the common and private diseases can be foreseen from those listed heads is explained in the course of the book, as we shall point out soon.

units.la: Planius adhuc seipsum exponit in verbis quæ mox sequuntur, quorum sensus hic est. Nam qui anni tempora observaverit, & ortus occasusque siderum, (quibus quaedam circunscribuntur ex anni temporibus & denominantur) adverterit quomodo fiant, an sciiicet[?] cum pluvia vel siccitate, cum frigore vel calore, cum vēris aut sine his oriantur & occidant, is quid futurum sit postea præscicet, hoc est, qui nam morbi exorituri sint præintelliget. Per anni tempora, tempus solstitiorum & æquinoctiorum intelligit, at per sidera ortum Arcturi & Canis & Pleiadum simulque harum occasum. Nam horum siderum ortu & occasu describebant antiqui initia æstatis, hyemis, autūni, atque calidissimam æstatis partem. Et hanc esse mentem Hippocratis ex 6. capitis fine perspici potest. Hic tantum proponit, quæ in processu operis exponit. Suprà dixerat, Medico necessarium esse, ut quam vim aëris mutatio quælibet obtineret corpora nostra permutandi: differre verò tempora inter se atque à seipsis etiam plurimum, propter factas in ipsis mutationes. Quare hic ait, cum qui diligenter ipsa inter se distinguat, & qualia singula sint[?] observet, cum de morbis nascituris facilè judicaturum esse.
units.tr: He explains himself still more plainly in the words that immediately follow, whose sense is this. For one who has observed the seasons of the year, and the risings and settings of the stars (by which certain parts of the year are marked off and named), and has noticed how they happen, whether they rise and set with rain or drought, with cold or heat, or without these, will foreknow what is going to happen afterwards, that is, he will foresee which diseases are going to arise. By the seasons of the year he means the time of the solstices and equinoxes, but by the stars the rising of Arcturus and of the Dog, and of the Pleiades, and likewise their setting. For the ancients marked the beginnings of summer, winter and autumn, and the hottest part of summer, by the rising and setting of these stars. And that this is Hippocrates' mind can be seen from the end of the sixth chapter. There he only proposes what he explains in the course of the work. He had said above that it is necessary for the physician to know what power any change of the air has to alter our bodies, and that the seasons differ among themselves and even from themselves, because of the changes made in them. Therefore here he says that one who distinguishes these carefully among themselves and observes what each is like will judge easily about the diseases that are going to arise.

units.la: Profectò non aliud hic dicere voluit, quàm quod antè dixerat: Quin nec debuit. Non enim aliud probare debet ratio, quàm quod propositum est. Propositum autem erat docere illum Medicum rectè præcogniturum morbos, qui cùm alia recensita, tum tempora anni & horum mutationes quales fierent considerasset, non quales futurae essent. Non ait, Medicum obseruare debere quomodo sidera oritura sint, & ex eo aëris temperiem praedicere: sed iubet eum obseruare qua temperie sit autumnus, hyems, ver, æ-stas, & ex horum temperie iam obseruata, visa, cognita, coniicere de futuris morbis. Perinde est ac si ita dixisset: Medicus qui cùm alia, tum vero anni tempora quomodo ea habeant, scilicet an autumnus, hyems, æstas frigida, pluuio-sa fuerit, ad aliter affecta apparuerit, is qui morbi quouis in loco regnaturi sint peruidebit.
units.tr: Surely he wished to say nothing else here than what he had said before. Nor ought he to. For reason ought to prove nothing other than what is proposed. The proposal, however, was to teach that the physician will correctly foreknow diseases, who, having considered the other things listed, and also the seasons of the year and how their changes came about, not how they are going to be, will do so. He does not say that the physician ought to observe how the stars are going to rise, and from that predict the temperature of the air. Rather he bids him observe what temperature autumn, winter, spring and summer have, namely whether autumn, winter or cold summer was rainy, or appeared otherwise affected, and from the temperature of these now observed, seen and known, to conjecture about future diseases. It is just as if he had said: the physician who has seen how the seasons of the year, along with the other things, stand, namely whether autumn, winter, or cold summer was rainy, or appeared otherwise affected, will foresee which diseases are going to reign in any place.

units.la: Atque hunc esse genuinum Hippocratis sensum, sequentia verba planissimè demonstrant. Quomodo autem singula, inquit, quae diximus, scrutari ac explorare oporteat, deinceps dicam. Si totum opus hoc perlegeris, videbis omnia quae promisit diligentissimè explanata ab ipso esse. At nullo in loco vel unico verbulo docet ex astris iudicare de temperie aëris futura. Quinimò nullo in loco dicit praecognoscendam esse, sed hoc tantum docet, quomodo ex praegressa & visa, aut etiam praesente adhuc aëris temperie sint praeuidendi morbi futuri sequentibus temporibus. Hic tantum, sicut paulò ante quoque monui, proponit capita, quae in sequentibus edisserit. Quamobrem non aliter verba ipsius hoc loco posita intelligi exponique poterunt, quàm ipsemet tum hic, tum in sequentibus declarauit. At verò sic declarauit, vt ego exposui & probaui. Astrologicū nihil interseruit.
units.tr: And that this is Hippocrates' genuine sense, the following words show most clearly. How each of the things we have mentioned ought to be searched and examined, he says, I will explain next. If you read through this whole work, you will see that everything he promised has been most carefully explained by him. But in no place, not even in a single word, does he teach that the future temperature of the air is to be judged from the stars. Indeed, in no place does he say that it must be foreknown; he teaches only how future diseases in the following seasons are to be foreseen from the air's temperature, either past and observed, or even still present. Here he only proposes, as I pointed out a little earlier also, the heads which he will set out in what follows. Therefore his words here cannot be understood or explained in any other way than as he himself declared both here and in what follows. And he has declared them just as I have set out and proved. He has inserted nothing astrological.

units.la: Quod vt perspiciatur planius, particulatim capitum argumenta inspiciemus. Secundo capite declarat, quomodo ex cuiuslibet loci situ ad ventos, de morbis coniiciendum sit, quod vnum erat ex supra propositis. Capite tertio, quarto & quinto de aquarum natura & effectibus diuersis pro earum diuersitate disputat. Sexto demum de morbis, qui ex mutatione temporum anni proueniunt, disserit, vbi sic rem orditur: Caterùm de annis hoc modo consideratione facta quis cognoscere possit, qualis nam annus futurus fit, salubris an morbosus. Supra cum dixisset, illum, qui anni temporum vires pernouisset, ac mutationes eorundem obseruasset, de toto anno & singulis temporibus, qualis eorū constitu-tio futura esset, rectè iudicaturum: hoc est, quinam morbi nascituri essent, intellecturum, ac deinde qua ratione hoc foret cognoscendum, se indicaturum promisisset, idjam præstare incipit. Et quod supra proposuerat, planissimè exponit, videlicet, se per constitutionem, non aeris tempe-riem, sed morbositate[?]n, ut sic dicam, & salubritatem intellexisse. Quare cum nihil hic aliud doceat, quàm quod in 3. Aph. libro quoque docuit, satis[?], imò plus quàm satis, patet, ipsum aliud nihil hic velle, quàm quod supra exposui, nempe si hyemem hoc modo temperatam subsequatur ver ita temperatum, æstate sequente nascituros morbos tales. Statim enim post supra citata verba, anni salubris naturalemque constitutionem qualis ea esse debeat describit. Deinde insalubrium aliquot temporum combinationes, quasi exempla, ut alicubi Galenus monuit, nobis proponit, ut ex illis cætera nos addisceremus. Si verò hyems quidem sicca sit & borealis, inquit Hippocrates, ver autem pluviosum & australe, necesse est, æstatem febriculosam fieri & lippitudines inducere, &c. Si verò hyems australis fiat & pluviosa & clemens, ver autem boreale & siccum & tempestuosum, primùm quidem mulieres, &c. Quisquis nō videt hoc agere Hippocratē, ut ex intēperie duorū siue pluriū anni temporū, siue unius etiam doceat prænoscere morbos, qui sequenti tempore nascituri sint, is parum videt. Qui verò videt, ac nihilominus. Astrologiæ hisce patrocinari Hippocratem voluisse contendit, is rixosus est ac obstinatus. Non enim unica extat litera, quæ vel suspicionem aliquam faciat, quasi ex astris docere voluerit æris mutationes præsagire, aut hinc præsciri posse crediderit. Illud solum & maximè docet ac vrget, quomodo ex præcedente vel præsente anni temporum temperie siue natura, morbi futuri temporis sint prædiscendi. Cui hæc non satisfacient, ei aut nihil satisfaciet, aut sententiam dissimulat. Tibi me confido præclarè hac in re satisfecisse.
units.tr: That this may be seen more clearly, let us examine the arguments of the chapters one by one. In the second chapter he explains how, from the situation of any place with respect to the winds, conclusions may be drawn about diseases, which was one of the points proposed above. In the third, fourth and fifth chapters he discusses the nature of waters and their various effects, according to their variety. In the sixth he treats of the diseases that arise from changes in the seasons of the year, and begins the matter thus: But from consideration of the years in this way, anyone may come to know what sort of year is to come, healthy or diseased. Having said above that one who had thoroughly grasped the powers of the seasons and observed their changes would rightly judge, over the whole year and each season, what their condition would be, that is, which diseases would arise, and having promised to show by what method this could be known, he now begins to do so. And he sets out plainly what he proposed above, namely that he understood by the constitution, not the temperature of the air, but, so to speak, its morbidity and salubrity. Therefore, since he teaches here nothing other than what he also taught in the third book of the Aphorisms, it is clear enough, indeed more than enough, that he wishes nothing else here than what I set out above: namely, that if a winter tempered in this way is followed by a spring tempered thus, the diseases arising in the following summer will be of such kind. Straight after the words cited above, he describes the healthy year and its natural constitution, what it ought to be like. Then, as examples, as Galen somewhere remarked, he sets before us some combinations of unhealthy seasons, so that we may learn the rest from them. But if the winter is dry and northerly, says Hippocrates, and the spring rainy and southerly, it is necessary that the summer become feverish and induce eye inflammations, etc. But if the winter is southerly and rainy and mild, and the spring northerly and dry and stormy, first indeed the women, etc. Whoever does not see that Hippocrates is doing this, namely teaching that from the intemperature of two or more seasons, or even of one, one may foreknow the diseases that will arise in the following time, sees little. But whoever sees this and nevertheless contends that Hippocrates wished to favour these astrological views, is quarrelsome and obstinate. For not a single letter exists that could give any suspicion, as if he had wished to teach from the stars to foretell changes of the air, or believed that they could be foreknown from them. He teaches and urges this alone and above all: how the diseases of a coming time may be foreknown from the preceding or present temperature or nature of the seasons. For whom these things do not satisfy, either nothing will satisfy, or he dissembles his opinion. I trust that I have satisfied you well in this matter.

units.la: Iam ad sequentes duas quæstiones, an purem cœlos caussas esse tempestatum, & quomodo ab ipsis scisciti res arbitrer, descendam. Ad priorem responsio facilis est, ad alteram non æque. Conabor nihilominus ad utranque perspicuè simul & quàm fieri poterit breuissimè respondere. Sentio cum Aristotele, cunctisque rectè philosophantibus cœlestia totius generationis & corruptionis (Illius per se, huius vero per accidens) in hoc inferiore mundo caussas esse iudicarique debere. Per generationem intelligo etiam conseruationem ac gubernationem. Hoc posito, ambigi nequit, quin & aëris constitutionum siue mutationum caussas existimè ac ponam. Etenim ab his & per has universa hæc nostratia, ut sic vocem, potissimum generantur, corrumpunturque. Nihil hîc excipio illorum omnium, quæ ex elementis constant, quatenus scilicet ex his constât. Omnia nanque talia à Sideribus alterari, disponi, regi, persuasissimum habeo. Animos autem nostros, quorum origo non elementaris, sed cœlestis, imò diuinus est, cœlorum viribus minimè subijcio subiectosúe [?] credo. Sed nec Astrologos nostros, quidquid Arabes quidam sensisse putentur, hoc à me postulaturos confido.
units.tr: Now I shall proceed to the two following questions: whether I think the heavens are the causes of weather, and how I hold that things are brought about by them. The answer to the first is easy, to the second not so. Nevertheless I shall try to answer both together, clearly and as briefly as possible. I agree with Aristotle, and with all who philosophize rightly, that the heavenly bodies must be judged to be causes of all generation and corruption in this lower world, of the one through themselves, of the other accidentally. By generation I also understand preservation and governance. Granted this, there can be no doubt that I also hold and affirm that they are causes of the constitutions or changes of the air. For by these and through these all these things of ours, if I may so call them, are chiefly generated and corrupted. I make no exception here of all those things which are composed of the elements, insofar as they are so composed. For I am firmly convinced that all such things are altered, disposed and ruled by the stars. Our souls, however, whose origin is not elemental but heavenly, indeed divine, I do not subject, nor do I believe them subject, to the powers of the heavens. Nor, I trust, will our astrologers demand this of me, whatever some Arabs may be thought to have held.

units.la: Porrò caussas esse aio, non particulares, sed dictorum omnium communes & generales. Non enim ullum per se, sine ope aliarum propinquiorum caussarum, effectum, producunt sidera hîc in terris, sed cum secundis caussis omnibus omnia efficiunt. Si paucioribus me, quod sentio, dicere iubeas, actum & potestatem omnibus rebus cœlitus dari dixerim, per quam singulæ pro sua insita propriaque natura mox agere possint. Est hoc in Sole manifestissimum, in cæteris astris obscurius. Et Luna quidem minus, in reliquis intelligitur potius quàm sensu percipiatur. In caussa fortasse est, quòd Luna nobis vicina admodum est, vel quòd non tam suis proprijs viribus, quàm facultate à Sole accepta huc agit. Etenim lumine ipsius, (quod ex se non habet, sed à Sole mutuatur) augescente, omnia ferè naturali succo abundant: decrescente verò eodem, tantum succi natiui omnibus decedit, quantum ipsa luminis amittit. Equidem quando cum Sole descendit sub horizonte, nec reflexum Solis lumen terris largitur, imbecilliora omnia propemodum videntur. Pleraque certè minus natiui succi obtinent, quantumuis excrementis persæpe redundent. Hæc sententia Galeno minimè displicuit, nec[?] in illo quidem 3. Decreti[?] libro, in quo permulta Astrologica probare visus est. Ipsi quoque Astrologi negare non aut volunt aut possunt rem ita habere, vt dictum est.
units.tr: Moreover I say that they are causes, not particular, but common and general to all the things mentioned. For the stars do not produce any effect here on earth by themselves, without the help of other nearer causes, but with secondary causes they bring about all things. If you bid me speak in fewer words, as I think, I would say that power and action are given to all things from heaven, through which each, by its inborn and proper nature, can immediately act. This is most evident in the Sun, less clear in the other stars. And the Moon indeed less so, and in the rest it is understood rather than perceived by the senses. The cause of this is perhaps that the Moon is very near to us, or that she acts here not so much by her own powers as by the faculty received from the Sun. For when her light (which she does not have of herself but borrows from the Sun) increases, almost everything abounds with natural moisture; but when it decreases, just as much natural moisture leaves everything as the Moon loses of her light. Indeed, when she goes down below the horizon with the Sun and does not bestow the reflected light of the Sun on the earth, nearly everything seems weaker. Most things certainly have less natural moisture, however often they overflow with excrements. This opinion did not displease Galen at all, nor in that third book of his Decrees, in which he seemed to prove many astrological things. The astrologers themselves neither wish nor are able to deny that the matter stands as has been said.

units.la: Toto isto tempore quo cum Sole occidit Luna, destituitur terra viuifico Solis lumine caloreque totis noctibus, donec ab eo digressa lumen à Sole acceptum terris communicet iterum. Quæcunque hoc tempore animalia nascuntur, aut non viuunt, aut imbecillia permanent. Huius rei causa, quia ex iam dictis intelligi poterit, pluribus hic non explicabitur. Hoc sufficiat monuisse in præsenti loco, quantum Solis calor interdiu exiccet, tantum restituere nativi humoris noctu per Lunam. Etenim plurima tantum calorem, quantum Sol terris impertit, ferre nequeunt, tepidiore plurimum ruuantur[?]. Quo fit, vt flosculi[?] ferè noctu dehiscant ante ortum Solis. Diurnus enim calor exiccat magis, nocturnus humectat felicius. Ille calorem & spiritus euocat ac dissipat, hic diffundit augetque magis, nutricationemque plurimum promouet. Quod enim à diurno calore excitatus plantarum calor attraxit ex terra nutrimenti, id dispergit ac distribuit beneficio lunaris caloris. Sunt tamen hic etiam quibus nimia sit Lunæ potētia. Vnde cum alia quædam, tum cepæ felicius germinant, cum Luna lumen suum amittit, quàm cum idem recipit & plena est. Sic alijs hyberni solis potētia talis est, æstiua noxia, plerisque hæc salutaris existit, illa causa interitus euadit.
units.tr: During all that time when the Moon sets with the Sun, the earth is deprived of the life-giving light and heat of the Sun through the whole nights, until, having departed from it, she again imparts to the earth the light received from the Sun. Whatever animals are born at this time either do not live, or remain feeble. The cause of this, since it can be understood from what has already been said, will not be explained here at length. It will suffice to have pointed out in the present place that just as much natural moisture is restored at night by the Moon as the Sun's heat dries up by day. For most things cannot bear as much heat as the Sun imparts to the earth, and are chiefly refreshed by a milder warmth. Hence it comes about that flowers mostly open at night before the rising of the Sun. For the heat of the day dries more, the heat of the night moistens more happily. The former calls forth and dissipates heat and spirits, the latter diffuses and increases them more, and promotes nourishment greatly. For the warmth of the plants, roused by the daytime heat, has drawn nourishment from the earth, and this it spreads and distributes by the benefit of the lunar warmth. There are, however, some here for whom the power of the Moon is excessive. Hence, among other things, onions sprout more happily when the Moon has lost her light than when she receives it again and is full. Thus the power of the winter sun is of one kind, that of the summer sun is harmful; for many it is healthful, for others that very power proves the cause of their death.

units.la: Quæ ideo tam breuibus & tam multis exemplis declaro, vt rectè me dixisse liqueat, causas generales & communes esse sidera. Dum enim omnia ex æquo afficiunt, fit, vt alia commodum, alia incommodum inde percipiant, pro vt vnuquodque aptum à natura factum est ad patiendum ab ipsis. Neque puto tam esse aliquem vel contentiosum vel imperitum, qui concedere nolit, aut non intelligat, eadem esse Solis ac cæterorum siderum rationem, quod ad hoc nostrum institutum pertinet. Etenim quibuscunque viribus astra singula prædita existimentur, res omnes pro suis viribus immutare student. Quòd si non eundem in omnibus effectum pariunt, non ipsorum viribus, sed rerum quas afficiunt, varie tati[?] tribuendum est. Quod quomodo eveniat, duobus illustrare exemplis breviter conabor.
units.tr: I set these things out in such brief terms and with so many examples so that it may be clear that I was right to say that the stars are general and common causes. For since they affect all things alike, it comes about that some things receive benefit from them, others harm, according as each has been made by nature suited to be acted upon by them. Nor do I think there is anyone so contentious or unskilled as to be unwilling to concede, or not to understand, that the relation of the Sun and of the other stars is the same, so far as pertains to this our undertaking. For whatever powers the individual stars are thought to possess, they all strive to change things according to their powers. But if they do not produce the same effect in all, this must be attributed not to their powers but to the variety of the things they affect. How this comes about I shall try to illustrate briefly with two examples.

units.la: Cogita omnis generis animalia pedes habere vinculis compedibusve ligatos aliquo in loco uno, ut nullum incedere queat. Accedat aliquis, qui similiter vincula soluat, quocunque modo id faciat. Hoc facto continuo expedite omnia ingredientur, tardè, celeriter, cursim, saltim, unumquodque pro sua natura & consuetudine. Qui hoc modo vincula, quibus pedes eorum constricti tenebantur, dissoluit, gressum dedisse, aut reddidisse omnibus rectè vereque dicitur. Non tamen is aut pedes aut gradiendi currendiue facultatem contribuit. Nec, quia ab uno eodemque homine similiter soluta sunt, omnia similiter etiam incedunt curruntque, sed unumquodque illum servat incessum, qui suae naturae convenit. Hoc fere modo Sol cunctis rebus, aut plantis saltem penè universis, cum post hyemē ad nos revertitur, hoc largitur, ut pro suae naturae viribus singulae nutriatur, crescant, augeantur, generent. Frigore nanque impeditae, quasi vinculis constrictae forent, nihil agebant, & pleraeque emortuae videbantur. Eo per solis calorem depulso, insitus ipsarum calor alacriter resurgit, humorem sibi convenientem ac familiarem attrahit, attractum concoquit, & in omnes partes distribuit, ac folia, flores, fructus, pro sua natura producit, demumque reliqua officia exercet, ad quae peragenda singulae creatae sunt.
units.tr: Think of all kinds of animals with their feet bound by fetters or shackles in one place, so that none of them can walk. Suppose someone comes along who loosens the bonds in some way or other. At once they will all go free, some slowly, some quickly, some running, some leaping, each according to its own nature and habit. The one who loosed the bonds that held their feet is rightly and truly said to have given them movement, or to have restored it to them all. Yet he has not bestowed either the feet or the faculty of walking or running. Nor, because the same man loosed them all alike, do they all walk and run alike; each keeps the gait that suits its own nature. In much the same way the sun, when it returns to us after winter, grants this to nearly all things, or at least to almost all plants: that each is nourished, grows, increases and reproduces according to the powers of its own nature. For they had been hindered by the cold, as if held fast by chains, and did nothing, and most of them seemed dead. When the cold is driven off by the sun's heat, their innate warmth rises up briskly again, draws in the moisture suited and familiar to it, digests what it has drawn in, and distributes it through every part. It then produces leaves, flowers and fruits according to its nature, and at last performs the remaining functions for which each thing was created.

units.la: Non dat tum Sol plantis naturas suas & admirabiles illas, quas obtinent singulae, dotes. Haec enim omnia iam ante habebant, atque ita habebant, ut uti eam per propagationem ab illis acceperùt, quas Deus ab initio, talibus esse, non alijs, viribus jussit. Hae nanque quomodo agere ac se in omne tempus propagare jussae sunt, ita hodie etiam agunt ac se multiplicant. Ergo sicut qui pedum vincula soluit, nec pedes nec progredien di facultatem dedit, sed impedimentum duntaxat abstulit: ita Sol quoque non vim & potestatem rebus inserit singulis, sed impediens frigus, à quo actiones omnium præpeditæ fuerant, pellit.
units.tr: The sun does not then give plants their natures or those wonderful powers which each possesses. For they already had all these things, and had them in such a way that they received them by propagation from those powers which God at the beginning commanded to be such and not otherwise. For just as they were commanded to act and to propagate themselves for all time, so they still act and multiply today. Therefore, just as one who loosens the bonds of the feet gives neither the feet nor the faculty of moving forward, but merely removes the obstacle, so too the sun does not insert strength and power into individual things, but drives away the cold which had hindered the actions of all.

units.la: Si quid hîc est in similitudine discriminis aut dissimili-tudinis, hoc ferè est, quòd qui vincula soluit, impedimentū incessus solum abstulit, facultati nihil contulit. Astra autem non impedimenta solum actionum tollere, sed insitum calorem etiam fouere, confirmare, augere, alacrioremq; reddere videntur. Hinc est, quòd non modò absentia sua So-lis calor plurima corrumpit, sed præsentia quoque nonnulla (utrunque per accidens) perdit. Etenim, ut qui vincula dissecare volens, penitius nonnunquam penetrans pedes vulnerat: ita Solis calor insitum quarundam rerum calo-rem non erigit tantum ac recreat initiò, sed tandem quo-que euocat ac dissipat, præsertim si imbecillior existat. Sic idem calor multis est beneficus, aliquibus verò noxius, ut suprà quoque monui.
units.tr: If there is any likeness or unlikeness of this kind here, it is chiefly this: the one who loosens the bonds has only removed the hindrance to movement and has contributed nothing to the faculty. But the stars seem not only to remove hindrances to action, but also to foster, strengthen, increase and render more lively the innate heat. Hence it is that the sun's heat not only destroys many things by its absence, but also loses some by its presence (each in an incidental way). For just as one who, wishing to cut through the bonds, sometimes cuts more deeply and wounds the feet, so the sun's heat not only raises up and revives the innate heat of certain things at the start, but in the end also draws it out and dissipates it, especially if it is rather weak. Thus the same heat is beneficial to many things, but harmful to some, as I have also noted above.

units.la: Quare duplici ratione actum largiri videntur sidera ter-renis istis rebus, impedimentorum scilicet remotione, & insiti natiuiqué caloris corroboratione. Posterior hic mo-dus ex prædicta similitudine intelligi minus fortasse com-modè potest. Quanquam si quis accuratè perpendat, v-trunque in ea appareat. Vix enim aliter calor confirmatur à Solis calore, quàm frigoris à quo frenabatur cohibeba-turque ablatione. Quantum enim contrarij frigoris ha-bet res quælibet, tantò est calor ipsius in agendo imbecil-lior. Frigore pulso, nutrimentum attrahit, concoquit, assi-milat, spiritus copiosè procreat, seque ipsum hoc pacto au-get. Attamen ut res minus habeat obscuritatis, sed prorsus fiat plana, exemplo utar alio, rudi quidem illo, sed aperto & valde apposito.
units.tr: Wherefore the stars seem to grant activity to these earthly things in a twofold way: namely by removing hindrances, and by strengthening the innate and natural heat. This second mode may perhaps be understood less readily from the aforesaid likeness. Yet if anyone weighs it carefully, both appear in it. For the heat is strengthened by the sun's heat in much the same way as the cold, by whose restraint it was held back and checked, is taken away. For the more cold a thing contains, the weaker its heat is in acting. When the cold is driven out, it draws in nourishment, digests it, assimilates it, abundantly produces spirits, and in this way increases itself. But so that the matter may have less obscurity and become quite plain, I shall use another example, rough indeed, but clear and very apt.

units.la: Imaginare tibi gallinam ouis diuersi generis, anatum scilicet, anserum, gallinarum, & aliorum animalium incubantem. Non hic propono, quæ non aut videris sæpe, aut certè audieris euenisse. Ex Galeno desumpsi, ex primo vi-delicet libro de Usu part. cap.3. ubi pulcherrimè hanc rem explanat, quemadmodum videre ipse poteris[?] Hæc ova diuersa,non vnum prorsus calorem,sed diuersos,quælibet nī mirum suum, hoc est,suæ tantum naturæ conuenientem in se continent.Qui in anserino ouo inest, nec gallinaceis nec anatum ouis conuenit. Et qui in gallinaceo reperitur, haud commodus fuerit anserinis. Ratio eadem est in cæ-teris.In hoc conueniunt,quòd tam est in singulis calor im becillus,vt nisi ab externo & moderato calore adiuuentur, nullum vnquam sint animal procreaturi. Ergo cum vni-cus idemque gallinæ calor omnia hæc oua fouens, frigus quod in singulis inest superauerit,& hoc modo de poten-tia ad actum perduxerit, temperieque sua confirmauerit, singuli iam agere pro sua natura incipiunt. Sic anseri-ni oui calor, non pro natura recepti à gallina incuban-te caloris, sed pro sua propria, non gallinam, sed anserem fingit ac format: gallinaceus vero,non anserem, sed gallū gallinamúe[?] creat. Ab vnico igitur incubantis & oua fouē-tis gallinæ calore, multi ac natura viribusque diuersi calo-res actum acceperè, hoc eit,impedimento demto hacte-nus confirmati sunt,vt iam quisque animal pro suo inge-nio ex subiecta sibi materia efformare quiuerit. Non enim aliter gallina anserina oua calefecit,quàm reliqua. Neque diuersis caloribus, sed prorsus vno cuncta fouit. Et hic quamuis vnus & idem esset, ac diuersa genere oua simili-ter calefaceret,diuersa tamen anima ia[?] generauit,nō qui-dem per se,sed auxilio diuersorum calorum. Diuersos vo-co,quia non eadem est omnium temperies,nec idem om-nes operantur.
units.tr: Imagine a hen sitting upon eggs of different kinds: those of ducks, geese, hens and other animals. I am not proposing here things that you have not often seen or at least heard of happening. I have taken it from Galen, from the first book of his work On the Use of the Parts, chapter 3, where he explains this matter most beautifully; you can see it for yourself. These different eggs do not contain one and the same heat, but different heats, each of them its own, that is, suited only to its own nature. The heat that is in a goose's egg does not suit hens' eggs or ducks' eggs; and the heat found in a hen's egg would be of little use to geese's eggs. The same reasoning holds for the others. They agree in this: the heat in each is so feeble that unless it is helped by an external and moderate warmth, they will never produce any animal. Therefore, when the single heat of the hen, which broods over all these eggs, has overcome the cold that is in each and has thus brought them from potency to act, and has strengthened them by its own temperature, each one begins to act according to its own nature. Thus the heat of the goose's egg, not received from the brooding hen's heat according to its nature but according to its own, forms and shapes not a hen but a goose; while the hen's egg produces not a goose but a cock or a hen. Therefore, from the single heat of the brooding hen that fosters the eggs, many heats, differing in nature and in powers, have receivedActivity; that is, once the hindrance was removed, they were strengthened so that each could shape an animal according to its own disposition from the matter placed under it. For the hen did not warm the goose's eggs in any different way from the rest; she cherished them all with one and the same warmth. And although this heat was one and the same, and warmed eggs of different kinds alike, it nevertheless produced different living creatures, not by itself, but with the help of the different heats. I call them different because the temperament of all is not the same, and they do not all work in the same way.

units.la: Sic idem hypocausti caloris in quo diuersas genere plan-tas aliqui seruant,diuersissimarum actionum causa com-munis existit. Dum enim calefaciendo insitum in sin-gulis calorem fouet ac conseruat , omnes pro sua natu-ra operantur perinde ac si Soli æstiuo expositæ forent. Proferunt enim folia, flores, fructus,paulò infelicius quā æstate, quæ in temperato loco dicto modo fouentur plantæ.
units.tr: So too the one heat of a hypocaust, in which some keep plants of very different kinds, is the common cause of very diverse actions. For while by warming it fosters and preserves the innate heat in each, all of them work according to their own nature, just as if they had been exposed to the summer sun. They put forth leaves, flowers and fruits, somewhat less happily than in summer, the plants which are cherished in a temperate place in the way described.

units.la: Simili ratione ac modo recipiunt hæc terrena actum ab astris, præcipuè vero à Sole,deinde à Luna. Quo accepto, universa iam, non pro natura à sideribus recepti ca-loris, sed pro insitis sibi à Creatore viribus agunt. Quare tametsi iuxta rutam posita lactuca, ab eodem Solis calore & eodem modo, quo ruta, calefiat: non tamen, ut ruta, amarescit unquam, nec vel folia vel semina similia illis profert. Quæ caussa est? Hæc est, quòd Solaris calor frigus, quod insitum harum plantarum calorem quasi strangulabat, dissipauit, & cognata vi auxit. Quo facto, unusquisque ita incoepit agere, uti à Creatore agere iussus est. Iussus verò est sibi simile generare. Quare non aliud lactuca generat, quàm lactucam, si nihil interueniat quo actio impediatur, aut quasi adulteretur. Hucusque cœlos docui universales caussas me credere rerum sublunarium, atque etiam quomodo intelligi id debeat explanaui.
units.tr: In a similar way and manner these earthly things receive activity from the stars, chiefly from the sun and then from the moon. Once this is received, all things now act not according to the heat received from the stars, but according to the powers implanted in them by the Creator. Hence, although lettuce placed beside rue is warmed by the same heat of the sun and in the same way as the rue, it never becomes bitter like the rue, nor does it put forth leaves or seeds like theirs. What is the cause? It is this: the sun's heat dissipated the cold which was, as it were, strangling the innate heat of these plants, and by its kindred power increased it. Once this was done, each one began to act as it was commanded to act by the Creator. And it was commanded to generate what is like itself. Therefore lettuce generates nothing but lettuce, unless something intervenes by which its action is impeded or, as it were, corrupted. So far I have shown that I believe the heavens to be the universal causes of sublunary things, and I have also explained how this ought to be understood.

units.la: Iam ad tempestatum generationes ista utcunque aptare conabimur. Exactè me hîc omnia dicere posse neque polliceor, nec expectare te iubeo. Nolim quisquam hoc sibi de me persuaderet. Pluvias, nives, grandines, ventos, ex vaporibus exhalationibusúe de terra & aqua sursum elatis generari, confessum est omnibus. Eadem non secus fieri igniqúe posse, quàm ex aqua & terra attenuatis, similiter notum testatumqúe est. Nec minus illud verum est ac certum, à calore attenuari hæc elementa prius oportere, quàm hos de se vapores emittant. Ineptissimè fecerim, ista si pluribus probare velim. Nam argumentis demonstrare id velle, cuius contrarium fieri non potest, insania potius est, quàm sapientia.
units.tr: Now I shall try, in whatever way I can, to apply this to the generation of weather. I neither promise nor ask you to expect that I can say everything here exactly. I would not have anyone persuade himself of this concerning me. That rains, snows, hails and winds are generated from vapours and exhalations lifted up from earth and water is agreed by all. It is likewise well known and attested that the same things can also come about by fire, no less than from water and earth made thin. Nor is it less true and certain that these elements must first be thinned by heat before they send forth such vapours from themselves. I would be most foolish to try to prove these things at length. For to wish to demonstrate by arguments what cannot be otherwise is madness rather than wisdom.

units.la: Porrò calor extenuans & rarefaciens duplex est, subterraneus & aëreus siue cœlestis. Hic à sideribus omnibus, præsertim verò à Sole & Luna promanat. Ille in terræ visceribus hæret, undecunq; eum profectum putes. Nec est in omnibus locis æquè vel potes vel copiosus, sed in aliis parcior, in aliis copiosior invenitur. Nonnullis in locis igneus reperitur.
units.tr: Moreover, heat that thins and rarefies is of two kinds: subterranean, and aerial or celestial. The latter flows from all the stars, especially from the Sun and Moon. The former lies in the bowels of the earth, wherever you may suppose it to have come from. Nor is it equally strong or abundant in all places; in some it is found more sparingly, in others more abundantly. In some places it is found to be fiery.

units.la: Tāta ipsius vis cū sit, nō mirū est, quod & admirabiliū operū est effector, & spiritus siue halitus infinitā pene copiam generat. Hic maximus & potentissimus est, cum aëris ca-lor est minimus, & contrà etiam cum Solis calor imperiū aëris obtinet, exilis admodum imbecillusque existit, si se-cum, qualis in hyeme esse solet, conferatur.
units.tr: Since its power is so great, it is no wonder that it is the author of marvellous works and generates an almost infinite supply of spirits or breath. This heat is greatest and most powerful when the heat of the air is at its least; and conversely, when the heat of the Sun holds sway over the air, it is quite feeble and weak, if compared with the cold that is usual in winter.

units.la: Huius similitudo quædam in corporum nostrorum calore cernitur, qui & ipse hyeme copiosissimus, æstate parcissimus est. In causa est, quòd vterque æstate propter cognationem euocatur ac dispergitur, hyeme verò vnitur ac cogitur in profundo, propter circunstans aëris frigus. Quæ huc vsque dixi, tam planè tamque solerter & solidè ab Aristotele in lib. Meteororum exposita reperiuntur, vt merito ab vberiore vel declaratione, vel probatione abstinere debuerim. Inspicere vel solam disputationem te velim de Ventorum generatione, quæ in 2.[?] libro ab eo perscripta est. Quanta verò sit vis frigoris æstate in terræ cauitate cōclusi, & rursus caloris à frigore hyemali in profundū repulsi, ibidemque coacti, illustri exemplo breuiter exponam.
units.tr: Something similar to this is seen in the heat of our own bodies, which is likewise most abundant in winter and scarcest in summer. The cause is that both are drawn out and dispersed in summer on account of kinship, while in winter they are joined together and driven into the depths by the surrounding cold of the air. What I have said so far is set out so plainly, so skilfully and so soundly by Aristotle in his book of Meteorology that I ought rightly to refrain from a fuller explanation or proof. I would have you look at the discussion alone on the generation of winds, which he wrote out in the second book [?]. But how great the power of cold is in summer, shut up in the hollows of the earth, and conversely of heat driven down into the depths by the winter cold and gathered there, I shall briefly set out by a notable example.

units.la: In ditione illustrissimorum principum Hennenbergē-sium, prope pagum Northeim (cui ab ista re, quam narrare incipio, nomē à frigiditate additū videtur, <bl>Kalt Northeim</bl>) locus est in accliui montis parte, qua meridiem spectat, amplus admodum, qui media æstate densissimam habet glaciē, media verò hyeme, cum omnia sunt altissimis tecta niuibus, & frigore omnia ferè pereunt, neque nix neque glacies vlla cernitur in toto eo spacio. Et quāto æstas est calidior, tanto glacies est crassior. Contrà quanto hyems est frigidior, tanto caret magis niue & glacie. In cæteris temporibus mediocribus, mediocria omnia visuntur.
units.tr: In the territory of the most illustrious princes of Henneberg, near the village of Northeim (which seems to have been given its name from this very thing I am beginning to describe, "Kalt Northeim"), there is a place on the slope of a mountain facing south, quite large, which in mid-summer has very dense ice, while in mid-winter, when everything is covered with the deepest snows and almost everything perishes from the cold, no snow or ice at all is to be seen in the whole of that space. And the warmer the summer, the thicker the ice. Conversely, the colder the winter, the less it lacks snow and ice. In other, moderate seasons, everything appears moderate.

units.la: Caussa huius miraculi minimè obscura est. Etenim terra illo in loco poris meatibusque plena est & caua. Operta est multis lapidibus, inter quos terra quædam rara, porosa & muscosa cernitur. Inter eundum si inter duos lapides pedem aliquis ponat, cedit sub pedibus terra. Ex quibus haud difficulter perspicitur, calorem hyeme ibi potentissimum esse, qui viues decidentes facile dissoluat, colligiqúe[?] ibidem non patiatur. Contrà verò æstate frigus eò repulsum cogi vniriqúe[?] hactenus, vt vapores incidentes terræ atq; pluuias in glacie cogat, quâ neq; Syrij neq; Solis radij soluere queant. Argumento certissimo sit, quòd, cum æ-stas frigida est, glacies aut nulla aut pertenuis & perexigua reperitur. Non potest circumstans calor frigus tunc coge-re satis vnireque, sicut cum vehementior est, potest.
units.tr: The cause of this marvel is by no means obscure. For the earth in that place is full of pores and passages and is hollow. It is covered with many stones, among which a certain loose, porous and mossy earth is seen. If someone, while walking, sets his foot between two stones, the earth gives way beneath his feet. From these things it is not difficult to perceive that the heat in winter is most powerful there, which easily dissolves the falling snows and does not allow them to gather there. On the other hand, in summer the cold, driven in there, is so compressed and gathered together that it turns the vapours and rains falling on the earth into ice, which neither the rays of the Syrian star nor of the Sun can dissolve. A most certain proof of this is that, when the summer is cold, ice is either absent or very thin and very scanty. The surrounding heat cannot gather and unite the cold enough then, as it can when it is more vehement.

units.la: Ex hac narratione satis patet, quanta sit vis caloris sub-terranei, cuius infiniti alij effectus indices existunt. Gene-rat hic magnam, imò incredibilem sub terra spirituum co-piam, ex quibus metalla & metallica omnia, si Aristoteli credendum est, fontes, lapides, &c oriuntur. Ab ijsdem col-le&is, exitumque non inuenientibus terræ motus excitan-tur, quibus non ædificia modò, verum etiam montes ali-quando euulsos legimus. Non male mihi videntur senti-re, qui Gigantum fabulam ad hæc significanda confictam ab antiquis iudicant. Eructant enim sæpe terram, & quasi mótes montib. imponunt. Ergo à duplici isto calore va-pores siue exhalationes suscitatur, ex quibus meteora om-nis generis nascûtur. Et solis quidé calor, tametsi lõgè po-tentissimus est aliquando, vix tamē solus, imò ne vix qui-dem, tantam exhalationum copiam generet, quanta tot nubibus, pluuijs, niuibus, ventis, generandis sufficiat. Nam sæpe nimis est vehemens, consumens potius vapores quā cogens, nonnunquam imbecillior est, quàm vt tantum opus solus perficiat. Hinc æstate pauciores venti ac pluuiæ generari putantur, quia plus discutiat vaporum Solis ca-lor, quam ferè generet. At hyeme inefficaciorem esse, quā vt excitare satis multos possit.
units.tr: From this account it is sufficiently clear how great is the power of subterranean heat, of which countless other effects are signs. It generates a great, indeed an incredible, supply of spirits under the earth, from which metals and all metallic things, springs, stones, etc., arise, if we are to believe Aristotle. When these have been gathered together and find no exit, earthquakes are stirred up, by which we read that not only buildings but even mountains have sometimes been torn up. Those seem to me not wrongly to feel who judge that the fable of the Giants was invented by the ancients to signify these things. For the earth often belches forth, and as it were heaps mountains upon mountains. Therefore vapours or exhalations are raised from this twofold heat, from which meteors of every kind are born. And indeed the heat of the Sun, although at times it is by far the most powerful, yet scarcely by itself, or rather not even scarcely, generates such an abundance of exhalations as suffices for generating so many clouds, rains, snows and winds. For it is often too vehement, consuming vapours rather than gathering them; at other times it is too weak to accomplish so great a work alone. Hence it is thought that fewer winds and rains are generated in summer, because the heat of the Sun dispels more vapour than it generates. But in winter it is too ineffective to be able to stir up enough of them.

units.la: Hæc vt vera sint, non tamen omnia explicant. Quippe æstate calor subterraneus ab aëreo calore euocatus, terram ferè deseruit, pauciores que multò quàm in vere & autúno spiritus halitusue suscitat. Vnde cum & pauciores colli-gantur, & à calore collecti iam magna ex parte dissipen-tur, non immeritò pauci venti tunc regnant, rarioresque pluuiæ decidunt. Hyeme autem etsi calor subterraneus ef-ficacissimus est, & halitus omnino plurimos generat, nec exire tamen facilè, nec à sideribus attrahi aptè possunt. Clausa nâque vndique est terræ superficies, & altissimis praeterea contecta niuibus, vt perpauci ex ea effluant, praeter eos, qui ex fontibus, fluminibus, specubus, & terrae hiatibus siue rimis exhalant.
units.tr: Although these things are true, they do not explain everything. Indeed in summer the subterranean heat, drawn out by the aerial heat, almost abandons the earth, and it stirs up far fewer spirits or breaths than in spring and autumn. Hence, since fewer are gathered together, and those that are gathered are for the most part already dissipated by the heat, it is not unreasonably that few winds then reign and rains fall more rarely. In winter, however, although the subterranean heat is most effective and generates very many vapours, they can neither easily get out nor be drawn aptly by the stars. For the surface of the earth is closed on every side and moreover covered by the deepest snows, so that very few exhale from it, except those that rise from springs, rivers, caves and the gaps or fissures of the earth.

units.la: Non obstat nostrae sententiae, quòd hyeme plerunque aër est crassus, nebulosus, turbidus, obscurus. Non enim hoc fit, quia plures aut æquè multi ascendant ex aqua & terra nostra vapores, ac æstate aliisque anni temporibus eleuari probabile est. In causa hoc est, quòd pauca etiam illae exhalationes, quas in aëre colligi diximus, propter imbecil-lam Solis actionem non discutiuntur. Quapropter in eo permanent, nisi Boreae flatibus dispellantur, alioque propellantur. Tunc enim redditur purior multò aër, vt nemo non videt.
units.tr: It does not stand against our opinion that in winter the air is for the most part thick, misty, turbid and dark. For this does not happen because more vapours, or as many, rise from our water and earth as is likely to be lifted up in summer and other seasons of the year. The cause is that those exhalations, which we said are collected in the air, are not dispelled, because of the feebleness of the Sun's action. Therefore they remain in it, unless they are scattered by the blasts of the North wind and driven elsewhere. For then the air is rendered much purer, as everyone sees.

units.la: Similiter illud mouere neminem debet, quòd crebriores pluuiae videntur hyeme cadere, quàm aliis anni temporibus. Primum quidem, quia non hic necesse est materiam pluuiarum collectam esse, sed aliunde adduci potuit. Ego certè cum vltimam pueritiae meae ætatem memoria mecum repeto, non recordor vllam me pluuiam vidisse, quæ non præcessisset ventus, qui nubes secum, quibus cœlum obtegeret, aliunde adduxisset. Nebulas crassas in aquam solui aliquando tam multam vidi, vt depluere putarem, & terram madefieri cernerem. At pluuiam sine accessu nubium ex regionibus aliis alioue ex cœlo, decidisse non memini.
units.tr: Likewise, that rains seem to fall more often in winter than at other seasons of the year ought not to disturb anyone. First, because it is not necessary here that the matter of the rains be gathered in this place, but it could have been brought from elsewhere. For my own part, when I recall in memory the last age of my boyhood, I do not remember ever seeing any rain that was not preceded by a wind which brought clouds with it from elsewhere, to cover the sky. I have sometimes seen thick mists dissolve into water so abundantly that I thought it was raining and saw the earth being soaked. But I do not remember rain falling without the approach of clouds from other regions, or from some other quarter of the sky.

units.la: Atque haud scio, an ex vaporibus siccis, qui apud nos in aërem ascendunt, ventum hic frequenter generatum, dicere ausim. Quanquam in ea sum sententia, vt putem facilius probabiliusque defendi posse, ventos aliquando etiam hic generari, qui longius progrediantur. Etenim negari nequit, quin certa loca peculiares habeant ventos, quibus alia loca remotiora careant. Experientia probat, atque præter alios autores Hippocrates & Galenus obseruandos Medico tales optimo iure docuerunt. Non raro ventos in montibus obseruaui, quos in planicie nemo percipere potuit. Hippocr. etiam non sine causa dixit, ventos nunquam discedere à montibus. Hic enim spirituum maxima generatur copia.plerique cavitates multas habent,in quas se cōdit calor,cum frigus aëris fugit. Hinc ferè metalla & metallica in montanis locis fœlicius, quā in planis proveniunt. Certè nubes,nebulæ,& omnis generis vapores circa montes plurimi semper colliguntur. Quòd si non generari ex his constet pluvias, quod an de-fendi possit,nescio:certum tamen est,ventos hinc nasci, & pluvias inde augeri plurimum posse. Nihilominus verum erit,plerunque ex aliis locis nubes adduci, ex quibus hye-me pluviæ nivesque ferè nascuntur. Hæc prima est re-sponsio.
units.tr: And I do not know whether I would dare to say that the wind is frequently generated here from dry vapours which rise into the air among us. Still, I am of the opinion that it can be more easily and more probably defended that winds are sometimes generated even here, and that they travel farther. For it cannot be denied that certain places have their own peculiar winds, which other more distant places lack. Experience proves this, and besides other authors, Hippocrates and Galen, who are to be observed, have rightly taught this to physicians. I have often observed winds on mountains which no one could perceive on the plain. Hippocrates also said not without reason that winds never depart from mountains. For here the greatest abundance of spirits is generated. Most of them have many hollows into which the heat retreats when the cold of the air flees. Hence metals and metallic things are for the most part found more happily in mountainous places than on plains. Certainly clouds, mists and vapours of every kind are always gathered in very great numbers around mountains. But if it is established that rains are not generated from these, whether this can be defended I do not know; it is certain, however, that winds are born here and that rains can be greatly increased from them. Nevertheless, it will be true that clouds are for the most part brought from other places, from which the rains and snows of winter are generally produced. This is the first answer.

units.la: Altera est,quòd non hyeme semper tam crebræ decidunt pluviæ nivesque,sed autumno potius & veris initio. Quòd si hyeme accidat,ex aliis locis advenire materiam oportet,& expositum est. Vere autem & autumno etiam hic generari facilè possint, certè plurimū augeri necessa-rium prorsus videtur. Hisce nanque temporibus vapori-bus omnino plurimis aër replctur. Etenim subterraneus calor vere,frigore iam mitescente,prodire,terramque ape-rire incipit. Quo facto,spiritus,qui per hyemem sub terra collecti sunt, erumpunt,aëriqúe se permiscent, Solis verò calor tepidus consumere eos nequit. Quare in nubes co-guntur,ex quibus resolutis in aquam terra madescit. Simi-li ferè ratione autumno calor sese rursus in terræ cava insi-nuans, pręcal factas ab æstiuo calore humidiores terræ partes facile in spiritum convertit, aëriqúe miscet.
units.tr: The second answer is that rains and snows do not always fall so thickly in winter, but rather in autumn and at the beginning of spring. If they do fall in winter, the matter must come from other places, as has been explained. But in spring and autumn they can easily be generated here too, though it certainly seems absolutely necessary that they be greatly increased. For at these seasons the air is filled with very many vapours. In spring, as the cold begins to soften, subterranean heat starts to come forth and open the earth. When this happens, the spirits gathered under the ground during winter burst out and mix with the air, and the mild heat of the sun cannot consume them. So they are gathered into clouds, and when these dissolve into water the earth is soaked. In a similar way in autumn, heat creeps back into the hollows of the earth and easily turns into spirit the parts of the earth made more moist by summer heat, and mixes them with the air.

units.la: Ex cōmemoratis liquet,cur nec æstate media,nec hyeme ad summum frigiditatis perducta,tanta exhalationum co-pia referciatur aër,quanta aliis temporibus impletur. Pa-tet illud etiam,utrunque calorem necessarium esse ad te-pestatum generationem. Quinimò subterraneus calor, si quis rem exactè ponderet, primas in opere isto partes ob-tinent,aut saltem non otiosus est,parumque res istas pro-movet. Quæ quanquam ita habent (Non flagitabis argu-menta plura hoc loco, cum sensus re docere queant vera esse omnia) non tamen accusandus erit ,qui ab astris om-nia hæc solis fieri affirmet,modò quod recte dicitur, recte intelligatur Etenim astra huius quoque caloris, qui sub terram hyeme colligitur, caussæ sunt effectrices, per accidens tamen. Nam à calore aëris augetur, minuitur, cogitur, dispergitur, licet per accidens fiat.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clear why the air is not filled with as great a supply of exhalations in midsummer, nor in winter when cold has reached its height, as it is at other times. It is also plain that both kinds of heat are necessary for the generation of storms. Indeed, if one weighs the matter exactly, subterranean heat holds the first place in this work, or at least is not idle, and it does not a little advance these things. Although this is so (you will not demand more arguments here, since the senses can show that all these things are true), nevertheless he will not be blamed who asserts that all these things are done by the stars alone, provided that what is rightly said is rightly understood. For the stars are also effective causes of this heat which is gathered under the earth in winter, but per accidens. For by the heat of the air it is increased, diminished, condensed and dispersed, although this happens per accidens.

units.la: Nec mirum id videri alicui debet, cum multa per accidens cœlestia tum generent tum interimant animalia quoque, nedum plantas & inanimata. Supra exemplis tota hæc res est declarata copiosius. Equidem Solis ad nos accessu frigus ad profundum terræ pelli, caloremque ibi existentem euocari certum est, quocunque id modo eueniat. Contrà cum à nobis abit, frigoriqve aëris imperium permittit, in causa est, cur calor magno impetu ad profundum refugiat, & frigus inde exire cogat. Neque difficulter hoc aduenienti calore cedit, præsertim cum suo se expetat similî coniungere.
