Quare vt non male dicimus, Solem ortus atque interitus omnium rerum causam esse (Quod de Sole exempli gratia dicimus, de omnibus sideribus intelligi volumus) tametsi diuersorum, imò contrariorum istorum effectuum non eodem modo causa fiat: ita recte etiam asserimus, Solem causam esse, cur subterraneus calor modò augeatur, modò minuatur. Quo fit vt serenitatis etiam atque tempestatum causa recte affirmetur esse, quocunque tandem modo vtraque ista perficiat. Astra ergo aëris tempestates omnes pariunt, partim per accidens, partim vero per se, terram scilicet atque aquam calefaciendo, extenuando, & in vapores ac spiritus conuertendo.
units.tr: Nor should this seem strange to anyone, since many heavenly bodies per accidens both generate and destroy animals, not to mention plants and inanimate things. This whole matter has been explained more fully above with examples. Indeed it is certain that when the sun approaches us, cold is driven into the depths of the earth and the heat existing there is drawn out, however that happens. On the contrary, when the sun departs from us and leaves the rule of the air to cold, this is the reason why heat rushes back with great force into the depths and forces the cold out from there. Nor does it yield with difficulty to the approaching heat, especially since it seeks to join its like. So, as we rightly say that the sun is the cause of the rising and perishing of all things (what we say of the sun for example, we want understood of all the stars), although these opposite effects are not caused in the same way, so we also rightly assert that the sun is the cause why subterranean heat is now increased and now diminished. Hence it is rightly affirmed to be the cause of both clear weather and storms, however each is brought about. Therefore the stars produce all weather in the air, partly per accidens and partly per se, namely by heating and thinning earth and water and turning them into vapours and spirits.

units.la: Iam verò cum manifestum sit, tempestates aliter generari non posse, illud etiam patet, Solem atque Lunam præcipuè tempestates excitare, minus alia sidera. Illorum enim actio sensibilis est ac manifesta, horum nullo percipitur sensu, sed mente duntaxat percipitur. Quocirca si quid illa hîc possunt, attrahere potius sursum genitos iam vapores à Sole atque Luna possunt, quàm eosdem generare. Hinc est, quòd Aristoteles Solis atque Lunæ tantum fere meminit, præsertim verò Solis, cum de meteororum istorum ortu disserit. Quòd si à subterraneo calore solo omni tempore satis suppeditari spiritum putes, sideribus, vt necesse non habeant excitare, sed satis habeant, si attrahe-re eos queant, non parum hic falleris. Quippe hallucina-tus plurimum fuisset Aristoteles cum præstantissimis omnibus omnium ætatum Philosophis, in reddenda causa cur uno tempore pluviæ ac venti nascantur plures, quàm alijs temporibus. Deinde si satis magna suppeteret horum semper copia, necessario semper plueret aut ningeret, quoties sidus aliquod oriretur, quod attrahere eos posset. At possunt omnia, aut certè plurima, eaque singulis 24. horis super horizontem feruntur. Semper igitur aut nocte aut die plueret ningeretúe[?]. Idem de grandine, ventis ac simi-libus intelligi volo.
units.tr: Now since it is clear that storms cannot be generated in any other way, it also follows that the sun and moon chiefly stir up storms, and the other stars less so. For the action of these is sensible and manifest, while that of the others is perceived by no sense, but by the mind alone. Hence, if these can do anything here, they can draw up vapours already generated rather than generate them. This is why Aristotle mentions almost only the sun and moon, and especially the sun, when he discusses the origin of these meteors. But if you think that spirit is always sufficiently supplied by subterranean heat alone, so that the stars need not stir it up but are content if they can draw it, you are not a little mistaken. For Aristotle, together with all the most distinguished philosophers of every age, would have been greatly mistaken in giving the reason why rains and winds arise more at one time than at others. Further, if a sufficiently large supply of these were always present, it would necessarily rain or snow whenever some star rose that could draw them up. But all the stars, or at least very many, can do this, and each of them is carried above the horizon every twenty-four hours. Therefore it would always rain or snow, by night or by day. I want the same understood of hail, winds and the like.

units.la: Neque effugiat Astrologus, si asserat sidera per se vim hanc non obtinere, sed ex certo cum alijs congressu vel aspectu adipisci. Nam ut alia argumenta omnia hic mitta, necessario pluvia fieret, quoties huiusmodi stellarum aspectus contingeret. At hoc non minus manifestè falsum est, quàm prius, id quod ne Astrologos quidem prudentiores negaturos certò scio. Falsum ergo illud est, ex quo ista sequebantur, quòd copia semper exhalationum satis magna præsens sit, ut non nisi attractione opus habeant. Aut certè causa est adferenda, cur non semper attractioni paratos halitus rapere ad se possint. Quod quia multo difficilius ipsis erit ostendere, quàm veritati cedere, libentius qui sapiunt cum Aristotele & cunctis rectè philosophantibus sentiunt: ita sidera tum aquas tum terras semper attenuare, inque halitus vertere, ut apta sit utraque. Quo posito, nihil erit inter nos discriminis aut controversiæ amplius. Iam pridem enim declarauimus, cœlestia sidera terrena hæc universa ita permutare, ut permutari omni tempore apta sunt singula, quod exemplis suprà propositis copiosè satis declaratum fuit. Et hæc ad secundam & tertiam interrogationem dicta sint.
units.tr: Nor will the astrologer escape if he asserts that the stars do not possess this power in themselves, but acquire it from a certain conjunction or aspect with others. For, to pass over all other arguments here, rain would necessarily fall whenever an aspect of such stars occurred. But this is no less manifestly false than the former, and I know for certain that even the more prudent astrologers would not deny it. That from which these consequences followed is therefore false, namely that a sufficiently large supply of exhalations is always present, so that they need only attraction. Or at least a cause must be given why the vapours, ready to be attracted, cannot always be drawn up to them. Since this will be far more difficult for them to show than to yield to the truth, those who are wise prefer, with Aristotle and all who philosophise rightly, to hold that the stars always thin both waters and lands and turn them into vapours, so that each is apt for this. Once this is granted, there will be no further difference or controversy between us. For we have already declared that the heavenly stars so change all these earthly things that each is apt to be changed at every time, which was shown fully enough by the examples proposed above. And let these things have been said in answer to your second and third questions.

units.la: Ad postremam tuam quæstionem haud difficile est re-spondere. Nam certum est, vel te ipso affirmante, librum illum superstitiosis & anilibus fabulis ita esse refertum, vt vix[?] aliud contineat. Nec minus illud etiam constat, quod Medicorum verissimis placitis autor contradicat. Ipsemet autor uno in loco dissimulare nō est ausus, cum sic scribit: Licet hoc dictis Medicorum nonnihil repugnare videatur. Postremo argumentis ipsum uti futilib. & falsis, hoc est, verè Astrologicis, facile ex dicendis apparebit, cui per se id nō patet.
units.tr: Your last question is not hard to answer. For it is certain, even by your own affirmation, that that book is so filled with superstitious and old-wives' fables that it contains hardly anything else. It is equally established that its author contradicts the most true opinions of the physicians. The author himself did not dare to conceal this in one place, when he writes: "Although this seems somewhat to clash with the sayings of the physicians." Lastly, that he uses trifling and false arguments, that is, truly astrological ones, will easily appear from what follows, to anyone for whom it is not plain already.

units.la: Mathematicam scientiam exactæ veritatis esse, quāuis vel ex Stoicorum sententia constare possit, tamē se id probaturum propter duas causas scribit. Prima est, ut ab omnibus Mathematica cognoscatur. Altera, ut plurimi Medici, non tamen omnes intelligant, se artem præsagiēdi Mathematicæ scientiæ debere. Atque hīc cum, quod fuerat pollicitus, præstare debuisset, propositi sui oblitus, transit ad probandum, Astrologiam Medico utilem esse. Quare falsò dixit se Mathematicæ veritatem velle probare.
units.tr: He writes that mathematical science is of exact truth, though this could be established even from the opinion of the Stoics, and he says he will prove it for two reasons. The first is that mathematics may be known by all. The second is that many physicians, though not all, may understand that they ought to owe the art of prognosticating to mathematical science. Here, when he ought to have carried out what he had promised, he forgot his purpose and passed over to proving that astrology is useful to the physician. Therefore he falsely said that he wished to prove the truth of mathematics.

units.la: Quod si per scientiam Mathematicam dicatur Astrologiam intellexisse, longè errauit crassius. Primùm quidem, quia non probat, hanc exactæ veritatis esse, quod recepe-rat. Deinde, quia nullum existimo Astrologum eò demen-tiæ peruenisse, ut prædictiones ex astris exactè veras cēseat. Ptolemæus certè aliter scriptum reliquit. Si quis hactenus insanit, cum eo frustra egero. Præterea si exactæ veritatis eam esse ostensurus fuerat, non tamen inde consectarium erat, ut Medici præsagiendi artem huic acceptam referret. Et si referre eos oportebat huic acceptam, omnes boni Medici id facturi fuissent. Ipse verò, ait, non tamen omnes.
units.tr: But if by mathematical science you say he meant astrology, he erred far more grossly. First, because he does not prove that this is of exact truth, which he had undertaken to do. Then, because I think no astrologer has fallen into such madness as to judge that predictions from the stars are exactly true. Ptolemy certainly left it written otherwise. If anyone still rages on this point, I shall labour in vain with him. Moreover, even if he had been going to show that it is of exact truth, it would not follow from this that physicians should attribute the art of prognosticating to it. And if they ought to attribute it to it, all good physicians would have done so. But he himself says, "not however all."

units.la: Quæro quos intelligat per istos, quos hic excipit. Si Hip-pocratem, Galenum, & qui inter hos duos floruerunt, intellexit illud quod verum est fatetur, hos non debere peritiam præsagiendi Astrologiæ. At hi artem præsagiendi inuenerunt & excoluerunt, ut addi nihil præterea posse videatur: hisce igitur, non Astrologis, artem omnem præsagiendi debebimus.
units.tr: I ask whom he means by those whom he here excepts. If he means Hippocrates, Galen, and those who flourished between these two, he confesses what is true, that these men ought not to have the skill of prognosticating from astrology. But they invented and cultivated the art of prognosis so fully that nothing further seems able to be added. To these men, therefore, and not to the astrologers, we shall owe the whole art of prognosis.

units.la: Postremò quomodo non veritus est Astrologiam Mathematicam facere scientiam? Mathematica versatur circa lineas, superficies, magnitudines, & ut semel dicam, circa ea quæ ἐξ ἀφωρίσεως ὄντα[?] vocarunt Græci. Quamquam enim in subiecto aliquo hæc sunt, attamen ut Mathemaca ea considerat, immutabilia & in mente artificis tantum existunt. At vero Astrologia circa operationes & effectus astrorum versatur, quos naturalis examinat inquiritq; philosophus. Ille certa & immobilia spectat, Astrologus autem contingentia & dubia tractat. Taceo hic, quòd nihil aliud quàm mendacia consarcinat. Si non plus haberent Mathematicæ scientiæ veritatis, quàm habet Astrologia, tar-dè ac serò probare hic autor nobis poterat, Mathematicam scientiam exactæ veritatis esse. Iam ut hoc libenter credi-mus, ita mentiri Astrologos pleraque non nescimus.
units.tr: Lastly, how did he not hesitate to make astrology a mathematical science? Mathematics is concerned with lines, surfaces, magnitudes and, to put it briefly, with those things which the Greeks called ἐξ ἀφωρίσεως [from definition]. For although these things exist in some subject, yet as mathematics considers them they are unchangeable and exist only in the mind of the craftsman. But astrology is concerned with the operations and effects of the stars, which the natural philosopher examines and investigates. The one looks at certain and immovable things; the astrologer deals with contingent and doubtful ones. I pass over here the fact that he merely patches together lies. If the mathematical sciences had no more truth than astrology has, this author could have been slow and late in proving to us that mathematics is a science of exact truth. Now, we gladly believe this, but we are not unaware that astrologers mostly lie.

units.la: Neque ad rem est, quod à nonnullis obijci contra prædi-cta solet, Astrologiam ad Mathematicas scientias pertine-re ideo, quia Astronomiam præsupponat, ut loquuntur. Nam si hoc sit satis, licebit unicuique præstantissimis arti-bus pro libidine aliquid affingere, & sub eiusdem nomine venditare & nobilitare. Constat Astronomiam non astro-rum vires & actiones considerare, sed motum atque mag-nitudinem eorum investigare ac metiri. Quare non erit illa vanitas præstantis huius scientiæ pars aliqua existiman-da. Sed ad rem redeo.
units.tr: Nor is it to the point what is often objected by some against what has been said, that astrology belongs to the mathematical sciences because, as they say, it presupposes astronomy. For if that were enough, anyone may at will attach something to the most excellent arts, and peddle and dignify it under their name. It is agreed that astronomy does not consider the powers and actions of the stars, but investigates and measures their motion and magnitude. Therefore that vanity should not be counted as any part of this excellent science. But I return to the matter.

units.la: Nunquam iste autor suis argumentis probabit Medi-cos bonos artem præsagiendi Astrologiæ debere. Etenim si memineris eorum, quæ in superioribus meis literis à te perlectis, scripsi, facilè recordaberis Galenum affirmasse, nunquam Astrologos aut alios Vates vera de ægris prædixisse. At ipse ex arte præsagiendi Medica nūquam erravit. Quomodo ergo quod verum est, mendacio id, quod est, debebit? Et non pertinere ad Medicam artem Astrologiam planum relatumque omnibus est non stupidis omnino. Hic certè autor, licet obscurè, confitetur. Quo fit, ut magis mirer quomodo non puduerit eum asseuerare, præsagien-di artem nos Astrologiæ debere, cui non plus est cum ea familiaritatis, quàm cum Extispicio vel Augurio vel alia quavis vaticinandi vanitate. Sed argumenta ipsius exami-nare iam tempestiuum est.
units.tr: That author will never prove by his arguments that good physicians ought to owe the art of prognosis to astrology. For if you remember the things I wrote in my earlier letters, which you have read, you will easily recall that Galen affirmed that astrologers and other seers never foretold true things about the sick. Yet he himself never erred in the medical art of prognosis. How then can what is true owe its origin to what is false? And that astrology has nothing to do with the medical art is plain and acknowledged by everyone who is not utterly stupid. This author, though obscurely, admits it himself. Hence I wonder all the more how he was not ashamed to assert that we owe the art of prognosis to astrology, which has no more familiarity with it than with haruspicy, augury, or any other vanity of divination. But it is now time to examine his arguments.

units.la: Duobus utiuntur[?] argumentis, vel unico potius, quod duo-bus comprobat mediis, ad probandum Astrologiam Me[illegible, ~1 letters]icinæ vtilem esse. Præclarissimi inquit, Medici ita censuerunt, ergo verum est. Antecedens probat authoritate Hippocratis & Dioclis. Primum hoc modo. Hippocrates ait illos decipi, qui physiognomoniam ignorant, ergo Astrologiam approbauit. Consecutionem sic ostendit. Hippocrates laudauit partem philosophiæ diuinatoriæ, ergo laudauit totam. Porrò maxima Astrologiæ pars pertinet ad hanc philosophiæ partem, ergo Astrologiam commendauit. Altera confirmatio primæ propositionis argumenti primi, talis est: Diocles non hoc tantum dixit cum Hippocrate, sed præterea affirmauit, veteres Medicos præcognitiones, quæ in morbis fiunt, ex diuersitate luminis & cursus Lunæ, conficere solitos fuisse. Hæc sunt præclara præclari illius autoris firmamenta, quæ quomodo refellenda putè audire cupis?
units.tr: He uses two arguments, or rather one, which he supports by two means, to prove that astrology is useful to medicine. The most distinguished physicians, he says, have judged so; therefore it is true. He proves the antecedent by the authority of Hippocrates and Diocles. First, in this way: Hippocrates says that those are deceived who are ignorant of physiognomy; therefore he approved astrology. He shows the consequence thus: Hippocrates praised a part of divinatory philosophy; therefore he praised the whole. Moreover, the greatest part of astrology belongs to this part of philosophy; therefore he commended astrology. The second confirmation of the first proposition of the first argument is this: Diocles not only said this with Hippocrates, but in addition affirmed that the ancient physicians were accustomed to make prognoses of changes in diseases from the variation of the light and course of the moon. These are the splendid supports of that splendid author; how do you wish to hear that they should be refuted?

units.la: Valde miror, cum conquisiuisse omnia, corrasisseque videatur, quæ aliquo pacto huc inflecteret ac intorquerct, Galeni ipsum non meminisse, & ex 3. Decretoriorum nihil protulisse: Aut non legit illos, aut Galenum nō satis æquū Astrologiæ perspexit. Vt enim post Galeni ætatem vixisse ipsum credam, non prorsus nulla coniectura est. Et certè cum non omnes Medicos artem præsagiendi Mathematicæ acceptam relaturos scribit, in eam suspicionem venio, ipsum non ignorasse quàm nullum inueniret apud Galenum patrocinium aut subsidium.
units.tr: I am much surprised that, although he seems to have searched out and gathered everything which might in some way bend and twist this to his purpose, he does not mention Galen and has brought forward nothing from the third book of the Decretory days. Either he has not read them, or he has not understood Galen's attitude to astrology well enough. For I am not without some conjecture that he lived after Galen's time. And certainly, since he writes that not all physicians will refer the art of prognosis to mathematics, I come to suspect that he was not ignorant how no patronage or support he could find in Galen.

units.la: Sed neque Hippocratis, neq; Dioclis autoritas ei suffragantur. De hoc vt credam id facit, quòd Galenus non de-misse [?] de hoc homine sensit, huiusque testimonio libenter visus est. Quod si in 3. Decretor. potuisset suam sententiam tanti viri authoritate ornare, non prætermissurus fuisse videtur. Adde quòd Galenum mentitum fuisse oporteret, si verum esset, quod hic dicit. Etenim Galenus aperte asseuerat, se primum tetasse caussam motus illius in morbis per quaternarium & septenarium, in Lunæ motum reducere, Medicos omnes qui ante se fuerint, ne conatos quidem aliquid simile fuisse. Locus in 1. com. Prognh. habetur. Quare nec crisis, nec alius in morbis prædictionem mutationis ex Lunæ cursu veteres reddidisse liquet.
units.tr: But neither the authority of Hippocrates nor of Diocles supports him. That I think so is because Galen did not dismiss this man, and seemed to be pleased with his testimony. But if he could have adorned his own opinion with the authority of so great a man in the third book of the Decretory days, he seems not to have omitted it. Add that Galen would have had to be lying if what this author says were true. For Galen plainly asserts that he was the first to attempt to reduce the cause of the motion in diseases, through the quaternary and septenary, to the motion of the moon, and that all the physicians who came before him did not even try anything similar. The passage is in the first commentary on the Prognostics. Therefore it is clear that the ancients did not render any prediction of change in diseases from the course of the moon, nor of a crisis.

units.la: Si quid tale dixit Diocles, proculdubio non de Medicis, sed de Astrologis asseruit. Tentasse nanque Vates morbo-rum cuentus[?] præsagire, vt hodie, ita olim quoque, ex Galeno colligi potest, cum Romæ nunquam Vates vera de ægris prædixisse asseueranter affirmat. Nisi hoc intelligere velis, veteres Medicos in consideratione temporum, etiam Lunæ statum ac lumen considerasse. Omnia nanque cum plena est, tutiora sibi promittere æger potest, quàm cum lumine aut prorsus, aut magna ex parte priuata est. Verū ego pro certo mihi persuadeo, Dioclem tale nihil aut sensisse aut scripsisse. Probabilius esse, quòd dico, tūc videbis, cum quomodo Hippocratis testimonium citet, perspexeris, de quo iam dicendum erit.
units.tr: If Diocles said anything of the kind, he undoubtedly asserted it not of physicians but of astrologers. For from Galen it can be gathered that, today as well as formerly, seers have tried to foretell the outcomes of diseases, since he firmly affirms that seers never foretold true things about the sick at Rome. Unless you wish to understand that the ancient physicians, in considering the seasons, also considered the state and light of the moon. For when it is full, the sick man can promise himself safer things than when it is wholly or for the most part deprived of light. But I am firmly persuaded that Diocles neither thought nor wrote anything of the kind. What I say is more probable, as you will see when you have considered how he quotes the testimony of Hippocrates, which must now be discussed.

units.la: Non sine causa iterum hîc me mirari dixero, quòd non alia ex Hippocrate testimonia protulerit in medium. Sanè nostri temporis Astrologi vix ita inepti sunt, vt hæc prosè adducant, cum verisimiliora se habere putent. Nec potest negari, locū de quo suprà ad-te, & in literis Stathmionis disserui[?], facilius & aptius huc trahi posse, quàm quæ hic autor huc inducit: Suspicor hîc etiam Galeni ipsum interpretationem sibi obstare vidisse. Sed vt vt ista habeant, nihil efficit eorum quæ volebat. Hippocrates, ait, tribuit plu-rimum physiognomoniæ, & decipi Medicum, qui non sit in ea exercitatus, affirmat. Hîc nullam ei moueo litem. Neque superstitiosè percuntari volo, quid per physiognomoniam intellexerit, & quousque credendum ei censuerit. Nemo, puto, Medicus ambigit, quin ex corporis habitu, colore, lineamentis, figura, & similibus, rectè quædam conijciamus. Certè talia cùm in sanis tum in ægris vtiliter obseruari constat, imò sæpe necessarium est.
units.tr: I will say again, not without cause, that I am astonished here that he has brought forth no other testimonies from Hippocrates. Indeed, the astrologers of our time are scarcely so foolish as to adduce these, since they think their own are more plausible. Nor can it be denied that the passage I discussed above, and in my letter on the Stathmion, can be drawn to this point more easily and aptly than those which this author brings in: I suspect that here too he saw that Galen's own interpretation stood in his way. But however these things stand, he achieves nothing of what he wished. Hippocrates, he says, attributes very much to physiognomy, and affirms that a physician who is not trained in it is deceived. I raise no quarrel with him here. Nor do I wish to inquire superstitiously what he understood by physiognomy, and how far he thought it should be believed. No physician, I think, doubts that from bodily habit, colour, features, figure and the like we can rightly conjecture certain things. Certainly it is agreed that such signs are usefully observed both in the healthy and in the sick, indeed it is often necessary.

units.la: Quod mox addit, maximam Astrologiæ partem ad hãc iudicatoriam philosophiam, hoc est, ad physiognomoniā pertinere, vehementer ab eo ostensum velim. Quid, quæso te, simile habent vaticinium ex astrorum coitionibus, digessionibus, quadratis, trigonis aliisque aspectibus vocatis, & ex corporis lineamentis, figura, forma, habitus incessu, locutione,aspectu,& similibus de caussis, à quibus ista orta sunt,conijcere? Hæc omnia,qui,quomodo à temperatura & formatrice facultate fiant, percepit, nonnihil ex ipsis vt ex effectibus de caussis efficientibus colligit. At vero quam habent cœlestes aspectus connexionem cum particularibus morborum mutationibus,aut moribus hominum? Semel dicam omnia, ineptum esse qui Astrologiam partem physiognomoniæ fecit,ineptiorem qui credit,ineptissimum qui defendere studet. Sic enim sapien-tes iudicant,per imprudentiam ei,qui primus inuenire aliquid tentat, falsi aliquid excidere posse,nec tantopere dā-nandum hunc esse,quàm qui postea legit & secum perpendit,nec falsitatem perspicit. Maximè verò reprehensione dignum videri,qui,quod falsum esse perspexit,tanquam verum defendere nititur. Neque verò opus esse iudico,vt sal-sitatem sententiæ istius pluribus coarguam. Ambigitur enim à multis,vter stultior sit dicendus is,qui absurda cogitauit[?],an qui eadem longiore oratione impugnat.
units.tr: What he adds next, that the greatest part of astrology pertains to this judicial philosophy, that is, to physiognomy, I should very much like him to show clearly. What, I ask you, do divinations from conjunctions of the stars, their separations, squares, trines and the other so-called aspects have in common with conjecturing from the features, figure, form, habit, gait, speech, look and similar signs of the body, and from the causes from which these arise? Whoever has grasped how these things come about from temperament and the formative faculty, gathers something from them, as from effects, about their efficient causes. But what connection do celestial aspects have with the particular changes of diseases, or with the characters of men? To say everything in a word: whoever made astrology a part of physiognomy was foolish; more foolish is he who believes it; most foolish of all is he who strives to defend it. For wise men judge thus: that through the imprudence of one who first tries to discover something, something false may slip out, and he is not to be condemned as severely as one who afterwards reads it, weighs it with himself, and does not perceive its falsity. And he seems most worthy of reproof who strives to defend as true what he has perceived to be false. Nor do I judge it necessary to refute the falsity of that opinion at greater length. For it is disputed by many which should be called the more foolish: he who has thought up absurdities, or he who refutes the same things in a longer discourse.

units.la: Quamobrem pessimè iam concludere ipsum liquet, quia partem probarit Hippocrates,totam probasse videri. Non enim aut partem aut particulam vllam huius vanitatis probauit vnquam vir eruditissimus & prudentissimus. Quis non iam cernit Astrologica esse, quæ adduxit argumenta huius libri autor,hoc est,euanida,falsa, & mentita? Iam me tibi[?] præstasse opinor,quod à me petiuisti. In pri-mis tribus capitibus explicandis longior paulò fui, quod non indigna opera illa viderentur. Postremum vix dignum est,de quo tot dicantur,quot tibi vt gratificarer, dixi. Si quid præ-terea desideraberis, meq; ad-monueris,pro virili parte exponam. Vale.
units.tr: Wherefore it is now clear that he has concluded very badly, because Hippocrates proved a part, he seems to have proved the whole. For that most learned and most prudent man never proved any part or particle of this vanity at all. Who does not now see that the arguments which the author of this book has brought forward are astrological, that is, empty, false and fabricated? I think I have now done for you what you asked of me. In explaining the first three chapters I was rather longer, because those labours seemed not unworthy of attention. The last point is hardly worth that many words, but I have said as much as I could to oblige you. If you should miss anything else, and let me know, I will set it out to the best of my ability. Farewell.

units.la: Heidelbergæ.
units.tr: Heidelberg.

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS. EPISTOLA X.
units.tr: BOOK TWO. LETTER X.

units.la: Thomas Erastus viro clarissimo, Domino N. N. Mathematico, amico optimo S. D.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus to the most distinguished man, Lord N. N., mathematician and best of friends, greetings.

units.la: VIX dici potest quā gratæ mihi literæ tuæ fue-rint, quas nuper nobilis ille mihi reddidit, cùm propter alias quasdam causas, tum quòd te cum coniuge rectè valere, meiq; memoriam te retinere demonstrarēt. In præsentia omnibus alijs omis-sis, quæ de Astrologia scribis examinanda putaui. Scribis te opinari, quæ contra Astrologos disputasse me audieris, non tam contra Astrologiam, quàm contra abusum, qui magnus vbiq; sit, dicta scriptaq; mihi fuisse. Ac non alia de causa Romanos aliquot Imperatores Chaldæis imperas-se, vti malam artem relinquerent (sic enim appellas) ac si non paruissent, pœnas penderent, arbitraris. Quinetiam vrbe aliquoties ob hanc rem pulsos iudicas. Veram Astrologiam, quæ ex crebra naturaliū causarum obseruatione orta sit, magnum Dei donum te reputare addis. Eam & naturalem esse & ab homine sciri posse, aliquot argumentis te in opere, quod in manibus habere te scribis, probaturum asseueras. Præterea ad calumnias quorundam ex Patribus & historijs respondere te statuisse asseris.
units.tr: It can hardly be said how welcome your letter was, which that noble gentleman lately delivered to me, both for other reasons and because it showed that you and your wife are well and that you still remember me. Now, setting aside everything else, I have thought it right to examine what you write about astrology. You write that the arguments I am said to have made against the astrologers were aimed not so much at astrology as at its abuse, which is widespread everywhere. You also think that several Roman emperors ordered the Chaldeans to give up their evil art (for so you call it), and that if they did not obey, they paid the penalty. You judge that they were expelled from the city more than once for this reason. You add that you consider true astrology, which arises from careful observation of natural causes, to be a great gift of God. You assert that you will prove in the work you say you are now writing, by several arguments, that it is both natural and knowable by man. Furthermore, you state that you have resolved to answer the charges of certain men drawn from the Fathers and from histories.

units.la: Hæc tua cum legerem, maximè cum Astrologiam quandam verā esse naturalemq; credere videreris, substiti paulisper, & quid tibi velles, diligentius cogitare mecum coepi. Nec videre tamen potui te de alia loqui, quàm de iudiciaria siue diuinatrice, quam ωεγνωστικὴν[?] δὲ ἀστρονομίας appellant. Quo pacto naturalem hanc vocares, multò minus intelligebam. Nam si ita naturalem esse putares, vt diuinationum Cicero aliquas naturales facit, atq; artificiosis opponit, constare sententiā minimè posse præclarè videbam. Quoniam de tali Astrologia nemo vnquā, quod scire potuerim, aut scripsit aut disseruit vnqua[?]. Deinde non fue-rit ars hæc Astrologia, tu autem de arte mihi loqui videbaris,de qua me concertationem suscepisse nō ignorabas.
units.tr: As I read these things of yours, especially since you seemed to believe that there is some true and natural astrology, I paused a little and began to think more carefully with myself about what you meant. Yet I could not see that you were speaking of anything other than judicial or divinatory astronomy, which they call [ωεγνωστικὴν] of astronomy. How you could call this natural I understood even less. For if you thought it natural in the way that Cicero makes some kinds of divination natural and sets them against artificial ones, I saw clearly that your view could hardly hold together. For no one, so far as I know, has ever written or argued about such an astrology. Moreover, this would not be an art, astrology, yet you seemed to me to be speaking of an art, and you knew that I had taken up a dispute about it.

units.la: Quod si propterea naturalē dicere velles, quia insitam nobis vaticinandi facultatem fingeret, exornaret, perficeret,ne sic quidem defensurus opinionem videbaris. Non dubito quidem, quin artibus quibusdam insitas nobis facultates plurimum augere, perpolire, melioresq; reddere valeamus. Vis est hominibus orandi ac differendi ingenita,qua nonnulli sine arte,multò differunt ac orant elegantius meliusq; alijs quibusdam, qui hasce artes perdiderunt. Hanc nihilominus illustriorem perfectioremq; effici posse,si ars accedat,nemo arbitror negat. Ptolemæū quoq; minimè nesciebam alicubi scripsisse, illū solum optimum Vatem Astrologumúe[?] fore, qui ad futurorum præsensionem natus, & quasi numine quodam afflatus esset. Attamen persuadere mihi nō potui, te hoc pacto Astrologiam connasci nobis existimare. Nullus enim vnquam extitit Astrologiæ ignarus, qui pro astrologo haberetur. Nullus etiam ex astris futura præuidere creditus est, qui motum eorum obseruare nunquam didicisset.
units.tr: But if you wished to call it natural for the reason that it would shape, adorn and perfect a faculty of prophesying implanted in us, you did not seem to be going to defend your opinion even in that way. I do not doubt that by certain arts we can greatly increase, refine and make better the faculties implanted in us. There is an innate power of speaking and arguing in men, by which some, without art, speak and argue far more elegantly and better than certain others who have lost these arts. No one, I think, denies that this power can be made more distinguished and more perfect if art is added. I was not unaware that Ptolemy wrote somewhere that only that man would be the best seer and astrologer who was born for foreseeing the future and was, as it were, inspired by some divine power. Nevertheless, I could not persuade myself that you think astrology is innate in us in this way. For no one has ever been regarded as an astrologer who was ignorant of astrology. Nor is anyone believed to have foreseen the future from the stars who had never learned to observe their motions.

units.la: Potest præterea illa doctrina,quę cœlorum & astrorum, (naturalium scilicet corporum,) naturas, causas, facultates, proprias operationes perscrutatur, naturalis Astrologia rectè nominari. At hæc non docet ex astrorum viribus, quasq; huc demittunt qualitatibus hariolari,nec ad vatem vllum pertinet,sed tota philosophiæ naturali subiecta est. Hanc Aristoteles nō exorsus modò est in sua philosophia, sed propemodum perfecit, diuinatricem nusquam approbauit. Quinimò futurorum præscientiam,quam Astrologi sibi arrogant, supra vires captumq; hominis esse demonstrauit. Astra sanè ab ipso non vt particulares & propinquæ siue definitæ causæ (ex quibus tamē solis distincta rerū cognitio oritur) horū inferiorū cōsiderantur, sed maximè tū vniuersales communesq;,tū remotas & interminatas omniū,quæ hic fiūt,causas docuit. Iā vero constat inter has & particulares effectus, qui hic sunt, infinitas & homini incōprehensibiles causas alias interuenire. Quomodo igitur ex illarū inspectione aliquid prædiuinare homines queant?
units.tr: Moreover, that doctrine which investigates the natures, causes, powers and proper operations of the heavens and stars (that is, of natural bodies) may rightly be called natural astrology. But this does not teach us to prophesy from the powers of the stars or from the qualities they send down here, nor does it belong to any seer; it is wholly subject to natural philosophy. Aristotle not only began this in his philosophy but very nearly completed it, and he never approved of divination. Indeed, he showed that the foreknowledge of future events, which the astrologers claim for themselves, lies beyond the powers and grasp of man. Certainly, he did not consider the stars as particular and near or definite causes (from which, however, alone a distinct knowledge of things arises) of these lower things, but chiefly taught that they are universal and common causes, and also remote and unbounded causes of all that happens here. Now it is clear that between these causes and the particular effects that occur here, other causes intervene, which are infinite and incomprehensible to man. How, then, can men foretell anything by inspecting those causes?

units.la: Quæ à sideribus hic fiunt, non nisi opera secundarum causarum producuntur. Quamobrem nō minus per acci-dens ab ipsis particulares euentus efficiuntur, quàm unum idemq; vinum perficere per accidens dicitur, ut inebriato-rum hic quidem ploret, ille rideat, alius irascatur, alius ob-mutescat, atq; pro suæ quisq; naturæ propensione aliud ac aliud agat. Cæterum Aristoteles in hac de cœlo & sideribus tractatione non fortuitas accidentales q; causas, sed pro-prias & per se appellatas tum causas tum facultates inue-stigat. Ex quo liquidò cernitur, Astrologia μαντικὸ[?] sub hac doctrina minimè cōtineri. Quòd si per Astrologiam hanc de sideribus & astris scientiam intelligis, tuæ me sententiæ laudatorem approbatoremq; habebis. Quippe donū Dei esse ac sciri ab homine posse libenter confiteor. At diuina-tricem, quam ego solam vituperò, sciri posse, naturalemq; esse haud probabis. Ne hoc quidē igitur modo naturalem te Astrologiam vocasse facilè cognoscebam.
units.tr: What is done here by the stars is produced only by the work of secondary causes. Therefore the stars produce particular events no more directly than one and the same wine is said to produce, by accident, that one drunkards weep, another laugh, another grow angry, another fall silent, and each act differently according to the inclination of his own nature. But Aristotle, in his treatment of the heavens and stars, investigates not chance and accidental causes but causes and powers that are called proper and essential. From this it is clearly seen that [μαντικὸ] mantic astrology is in no way contained under this doctrine. But if by astrology you mean this science of the stars and heavenly bodies, you will have me as a praiser and approver of your opinion. For I gladly confess that it is a gift of God and can be known by man. But you will not prove that divination, which I alone condemn, can be known, or that it is natural. So I could easily see that you did not call astrology natural even in this way.

units.la: Quare in hanc nonnihil inclinabat sententiam animus, te doctrinam operationum exercitationumq; Astronomicarum accipere me voluisse, præsertim cum non nescirem Aristotelem cū veteribus per Astrologiæ nomē aut astro-nomiā, aut eā, de qua nuper dixi, scientiā intellexisse. In hac sententia me cōfirmabant, primùm quidē, quod nullus alius modus, quo Astrologia rectè naturalis dici posset, restare videretur. (Non enim tā iudicare ineptū te possim, ut naturalem te nūcupare ita crederē, quomodo Ioannes Indagi-nes quandā confinxit nouā, naturalemq; vocauit.) Deinde quòd supradictas significationes tanquā à tuo proposito alienas minimè amplexus putareris. Iā enim annos aliquot non sine laude Mathesin te profiteri scio, & in explicatio-ne usus astrolabij versatum felicissimè compertum habeo.
units.tr: For this reason my mind leaned somewhat toward the view that you meant the doctrine of astronomical operations and exercises, especially since I knew that Aristotle, with the ancients, understood by the name of astrology either astronomy or that science of which I spoke recently. Two things confirmed me in this opinion. First, because no other way seemed open by which astrology could rightly be called natural. (For I could not think you so foolish as to call it natural in the way that John Indagine invented some new thing and called it natural.) Second, because you did not seem to have embraced the meanings mentioned above, as foreign to your purpose. For I know that for some years you have professed mathematics, not without praise, and I have found that you are very skilled in explaining the use of the astrolabe.

units.la: Per astrolabiū concinnè fabricatū, siderū ortus, occasus, cōuersiones, progressus, occursus, cōgressus, retrocessiones, (hæ obseruationes astronomicæ quædā sunt exercitationes) deprehēdi posse notissimū est. At ex illo siderū positu, quē astrolabij auxilio cōprehēdimus, de futuris effectibus, quos nō sine multiplici undiq; cōfluētiū rerū atq; causarū astra hic pariunt, vaticinari velle, quomodo Astrologi solent, id iam non Astronomicū porrò, sed Astrologicum fuerit negotium. In hac opinione propterea libens perstitisse, quòd te Astrologicis fabulis addictum esse non libenter credidi.
units.tr: It is very well known that by a neatly made astrolabe one can determine the risings, settings, conjunctions, progressions, oppositions, meetings, and retrogradations of the stars (these astronomical observations are certain exercises). But to wish to foretell, as the astrologers usually do, future effects from that position of the stars which we grasp with the help of the astrolabe, effects which the stars produce here not without the manifold confluence of things and causes from every side, this is no longer astronomical but astrological business. I remained in this opinion willingly, because I did not readily believe that you were devoted to astrological fables.

units.la: Cæterum duo me aliter sentire propemodum coegerunt. Alterum est, quòd te in explicatione vsus astrolabij ad quorundam calumnias ex Patribus & historijs respon-surum scribis. Alterum, quòd Imperatores, Picum, Manardum, Theologos, non astrologiam damnare, sed abusum duntaxat reprehendere opinaris. Prius interpretabar mollius, ac si eos refutaturus videri velles, qui sententias theologorum, quibus diuinatricem vituperant, ad astronomiæ accusationem male transferre ausi fuissent. Nam etsi neminem scirem hoc fecisse, malebam tamen hoc credere, quàm te astrologiæ fidē adhibere, cogitare. Posterius cum quomodo excusarem non reperirem, diuinatoriam te naturalem putare conieci.
units.tr: But two things almost forced me to think otherwise. One is that in your explanation of the use of the astrolabe you write that you will answer certain charges drawn from the Fathers and from histories. The other is that you think the emperors, Pico, Manardo and the theologians do not condemn astrology but only rebuke its abuse. I interpreted the first more mildly, as if you wished to refute those who had dared to apply wrongly to the accusation of astronomy the opinions of theologians by which they condemn divination. For although I knew no one who had done this, I preferred to believe this rather than to suppose that you give credit to astrology. As for the second, since I could not find how to excuse it, I guessed that you consider divinatory astrology to be natural.

units.la: Picus & Manardus, vt præstantes Philosophi, futurorum præsensionem, quam Astrologi pessimè profitentur, damnarunt, & naturalibus viribus eiusce modi præsciri nō posse demonstrarunt. Theologi non abusum tantum, quod tu te credere simulas, potius quàm verè credas, sed totā Astrologiam detestantur. Equidē si rectè examines, nil tibi aliud tota videbitur esse, quàm abusus & ψ&δολογία[?], pestis animorum, veritati & sacrosanctæ religioni ex diametro opposita superstitio. Imperatores quoq; idem iudicasse, ex eo potest intelligi, quòd explicatis minimeq; ambiguis verbis, non abusum duntaxat (vt tu ais) sed ipsammet artem reiecerunt, eamq; nec disci nec exerceri permiserunt. Sic in Cod.9. tit. de Maleficis & Mathematicis, in l.2. habetur. Artem Geometria discere atque exercere publicè interest: ars autem Mathematica damnabilis tota est & interdicta omnino. Hic certè totā interdictam & omnino interdictam lex dicit, nō abusum duntaxat prohibitum esse, cuius ne mentio quidem facta cernitur. Scire causam cupis? Quia diuinatrix est. Erenim paulo post multis diuinandi modis enumeratis, inter quos Astrologia quoq; nominatim recense-tur, tur, addit lex. Sileat omnis in perpetuum diuinandi curiositas. Et hanc veram esse caussam, non aliam, hinc perspicitur, quòd parem poenam omnibus statuit diuinatoribus.
units.tr: Pico and Manardo, as outstanding philosophers, condemned the foreknowledge of the future, which the astrologers profess very badly, and they demonstrated that such things cannot be known by natural powers. The theologians detest not merely abuse, which you pretend to believe rather than truly believe, but all of astrology. Indeed, if you examine it correctly, the whole of it will seem to you to be nothing other than abuse and pseudology [ψευδολογία], a plague of minds, a superstition diametrically opposed to truth and to sacred religion. That the emperors also judged the same can be understood from the fact that, in clear and wholly unambiguous words, they rejected not merely the abuse (as you say) but the art itself, and did not permit it to be learned or practised. Thus in Cod. 9, title On Malefactors and Mathematicians, law 2, it is written: It is in the public interest to learn and practise the art of geometry; but the mathematical art is wholly damnable and entirely forbidden. Here the law plainly says that the whole art is forbidden and entirely forbidden, and it does not mention any prohibition of abuse alone. Do you want to know the reason? Because it is divinatory. For shortly afterwards, after listing many modes of divination, among which astrology is also named expressly, the law adds: Let all curiosity about divining be silent forever. And that this is the true reason and no other is clear from this, that it imposes the same penalty on all diviners.

units.la: Nec reperies magis damnatum augurium & extispicium, quàm Astrologiam. Quinimò de his nullibi dicitur in lege nominatim, omnino interdictas esse has artes, quod de astrologia expressè dictum audisti. Quamobrem cū nemo ausit vel dicere vel cogitare nō Augurium & Extispicium, sed abusus horum duntaxat vetare legē, ne de Astrologia quidem rectè affirmari hoc poterit. Imò multò minus dici de hac poterit, quia magis est expresse in lege dānata. Lex non aliter Astrologum, si in comitatu Caesaris deprehen-datur, gladio puniri iubet, atq; aruspicem. Pro caussa poni-tur, nō hoc, quia perperam vsus arte putetur: sed quia diui-nator fit. Ideo somniorum quoq; interpretem, si artem oc-cultare diuinandi videatur, lex eadē punire praecipit. Taceo quod Constantinus simpliciter mandauit, vt capite plecte-retur, quisquis aruspicem aut Mathematicum cōsuluissēt.
units.tr: Nor will you find augury and extispicy more condemned than astrology. Indeed, the law nowhere names those arts as altogether forbidden, as you have heard was expressly said of astrology. Therefore, since no one would dare to say or even think that the law forbids augury and extispicy only in their abuse and not in themselves, it cannot rightly be asserted of astrology either. Much less can it be said of astrology, since it is condemned more expressly in the law. The law orders an astrologer caught in Caesar's household to be punished with the sword, just as a haruspex is. The ground for this is not that the art is supposed to be wrongly used, but that the man is a diviner. So too the law commands that an interpreter of dreams, if he seems to be concealing the art of divining, be punished in the same way. I pass over the fact that Constantine simply ordered that anyone who consulted a haruspex or a mathematician be put to death.

units.la: Ex cōmemoratis intelligis ac vides, aperte Astrologiam, Aruspicinam, Extispicium, Somniorum interpretationē, si arte nitatur, ex æquo damnari nō aliam ob caussam, quàm quòd diuinatrices sint. Sic igitur Imperatores statuerunt: Omnis diuinandi modus ex coetu hominum Christianorum ex-terminandus est. Ergo astrologia quoq;. Quippe diuinandi curiositas hæc quoq; existit. Falleris ergo tu plurimum, qui ex vrbe Chaldæos eiectos arbitraris propter artis abusum. Non enim ideo pellebantur, quòd Astrologia abuterentur: sed quòd Astrologi, hoc est, diuinatores essent.
units.tr: From what has been mentioned you understand and see that astrology, haruspicy, extispicy, and the interpretation of dreams, if they rest on art, are condemned alike, and for no other reason than that they are forms of divination. So the emperors laid down: "Every mode of divining is to be driven out of the assembly of Christian men." Therefore astrology too. For this curiosity about divining exists in astrology as well. You are therefore greatly mistaken, you who think the Chaldeans were expelled from the city because of an abuse of their art. They were not driven out because they misused astrology, but because they were astrologers, that is, diviners.

units.la: Igitur cum Imperatores multi Astrologiam sub graui poena prohibeant, elegantiores omnes philosophi futilem esse affirment ac probent, praestantiores omnes theologi execrentur, sacra Scriptura, hoc est, ipsemet Deus deteste-tur: non video ego, quomodo tu vel partium ipsius aliquā, vel totam sis probaturus naturalem veramq; esse. Et quae ad Theologos & Sacras literas pertinet, cùm alibi tum in libello Sauonarolae, atq; in eiusdem apologia contra Chri-stophorum Stathmionem Medicum Coburgensem reperies. Hic philosophica quædam attingere placet, ne dicere nos tantum multa, nihil verò probare, cogitare nobisque obijcere possis.
units.tr: Therefore, although many emperors forbid astrology under heavy penalty, all the more refined philosophers declare and prove it to be worthless, all the most distinguished theologians execrate it, and Holy Scripture, that is, God himself, detests it. I do not see how you could prove that any part of it, or the whole of it, is natural and true. As for what pertains to the theologians and the sacred letters, you will find it both elsewhere and in the little book of Savonarola, and in his apology against Christophorus Stathmion, physician of Coburg. Here I am pleased to touch on some philosophical points, lest you be able to say that we merely assert much and prove nothing, and think and object so to us.

units.la: Astrologorum Vaticinia omnia, nec de rebus necessa-rio euenientibus, nec de rebus naturalibus in genere, sed de particularibus tantum euentibus expetuntur. Ex quo perspicuè sequitur, omnia arte carere. Nemo etenim in bo-nis artibus mediocriter versatus non videt, illiusmodi om-nia incertam & dubiam habere originem, & nõ magis fie-ri, quàm non fieri posse, siue ex eorum esse genere, quæ vsi-tata in scholis voce contingentia nominantur. Hæc autem arte rationeue prædici ante nõ possunt, quàm vel esse iam, vel certè fieri aliquo modo incœperint. Quare necesse est talium præsensiones inartificiosas & fortuitas esse. Præte-rea notum est, nihil nos futurorum præintelligere, quod non in suis caussis præuideamus. Nã cum, quæ futura sunt, intellectum mouere ipsa per se nequeant, (quippe nõ sunt in rerum natura,) consectarium profectò est, talia ne perci-pi quidem in se ipsis posse. Etenim intellectus noster in se illa tantum apprehendit, quæ præsentia habet. Hæc verò præsentia non sunt, quatenus nimirum futura sunt. Si ergo ea tanquam futura percipit, in suis caussis, ex quibus con-secutura peruideriit, ipsa percipere eũ prorsus oportet. Nul-lus est modus reliquus futura prænoscendi arte & ratio-ne, qualem Astrologiam Astrologi esse dictitant quidem, ar non probant.
units.tr: All the prophecies of the astrologers are sought neither about necessarily occurring events, nor about natural things in general, but only about particular events. From this it clearly follows that they lack all art. For no one moderately versed in the good arts fails to see that all such things have an uncertain and doubtful origin, and that they are no more bound to happen than not to happen, being of the kind that the schools call contingent. Moreover, such things cannot be predicted by art or reason before they have already begun to be, or at least to come about in some way. Hence it is necessary that the foreknowledge of such things be unskilled and fortuitous. Further, it is known that we foreknow nothing of the future that we do not foresee in its causes. For since future things cannot of themselves move the intellect (since they do not exist in the nature of things), it is a necessary consequence that such things cannot be perceived in themselves. Indeed, our intellect apprehends in itself only those things that it has present. But future things are not present, precisely in so far as they are future. If therefore it perceives them as future, it must surely perceive them in their causes, from which they will follow, as they have been foreseen. There is no remaining way of knowing the future by art and reason, such as astrology, which the astrologers keep saying exists, but do not prove.

units.la: Quanquam verò in suis caussis futuri quidam effectus contingentes (de talibus semper loquimur in præsentia) præuideantur: non tamen in quibusliber caussis cerni pos-sunt, sed tantum in propinquissimis, definitis & proprijs. Nam in remotis, indefinitis, & communibus, nihil cogno-sci potest, quod sit commemoratione dignum. In causa est, quòd non ab his, sed ab illis res omnes primo & sine me-dio oriuntur: nec ut sint tantum, sed ut tales sint, non alius modi & naturæ, omnino obtinent. Canis non à cœlo, ut ta-le sit animal natum ad latratum, sed à cane generante ac-cipit. Quis dubitet, hominem suam naturam, quatenus ho-mo est, mo est, à suis parentibus adeptum esse? Pronunciatum hoc in tota est philosophia probatissimum, rebus omnibus hoc à natura siue Deo insitum esse, vt se propagare, hoc est, simile sibi generare velint, ac, nisi per accidens aliquod impediantur, possint. De illis loquor, quæ generare possunt ac debent. Hac de causa pulchrè simul ac verè à philosophis dictum est, generans & generatum in omni vniuoca appellata generatione eadem specie existere.
units.tr: Although certain future contingent effects may be foreseen in their causes (we are always speaking of such things here), they can be discerned not in any causes whatever, but only in the nearest, definite, and proper ones. For in remote, indefinite, and common causes, nothing can be known that is worth mentioning. The reason is that all things arise first and without intermediary not from those remote causes but from the nearer ones, and that they acquire not merely their being but also their being of such a kind, of this nature and no other. A dog does not receive its nature from the heavens, so that it is born as an animal fit for barking, but from the dog that begets it. Who would doubt that a man has received his nature, in so far as he is a man, from his parents? This is the most approved proposition in all of philosophy: that it is implanted in all things by nature or God that they wish to propagate themselves, that is, to generate what is like themselves, and, unless they are hindered by some accident, they can. I speak of those things that can and ought to generate. For this reason the philosophers have rightly and neatly said that in every univocal generation the generator and the generated exist in the same species.

units.la: Quare si non in aliis præuideri causis nascituri effectus possunt, quàm in illis à quibus effici generariq; per se, non verò per accidens solent, frustra aliæ considerentur. Equidem vix puto quenquam tam esse inertem, qui se canis generationem in illius causæ actione præuisurum speret, quæ canis naturæ nihil habeat, ideoque nulli eam materiæ communicare possit. Nulla enim res, quod vulgò dicitur, alteri dare poterit, quod ipsa nunquam possedit. Vnde non ex cœlo, aut apris, aut ouibus, expectamus canes, sed ex canibus tantum. Illa enim non habent in se aliquid naturæ canis, quam communicare alteri materiæ valeant. Quæ cum in omnibus causis remotis, interminatis, communibus, & non propriis, locum habeat ratio: efficitur omnino imperitè facere illos, qui ex talibus futurorum effectuum particularium præsensionem venantur. Vt hoc planius perspiciatur verum esse, de singulis paulo pluribus agam.
units.tr: Therefore, if the effects about to be born cannot be foreseen in other causes than those by which they are wont to be produced and generated through themselves, and not through accident, other causes are considered in vain. Indeed I scarcely think anyone is so inert as to hope that he will foresee the generation of a dog in the action of a cause that has nothing of the nature of a dog, and therefore cannot communicate it to any matter. For no thing, as the common saying goes, can give to another what it has never possessed itself. Hence we look for dogs not from the heavens, or from boars, or from sheep, but from dogs alone. For those things do not have within them anything of the nature of a dog that they could communicate to other matter. Since this reasoning holds for all remote, indefinite, common, and non-proper causes, it follows that those who hunt for a prediction of particular future effects from such causes act altogether unskilfully. To make this truth clearer, I shall treat each point at somewhat greater length.

units.la: Et primum quidem, quod ex remotæ causæ notitia[?] nō possimus euentus particulares, quos multis aliis interuenientibus causis producunt, præsagire, non est difficile cognitu. Aut enim mediæ illæ causæ, quæ inter effectum & causam remotam intercidunt, immutabiles & perpetuæ sunt, necessarioque mouentur, cum primum remotior moueri incoeperit, veluti in miraculis illis spontinis & horologiis affabrè compositis cernere licet: aut mu-tabiles sunt, nec statim prima mota ipsæ quoq; perpetuo ordine vnoque semper modo mouentur. Primum asseue-rare nullus, puto, volet Astrologus. Etenim fatalis ista caussarum[?] connexio, siue Stoica necessitas veritati pariter & Aristotelæ philosophiæ, quæ hac in re magno ab omnibus doctis consensu recepta est, repugnat. Sed & Astrologorum placitis plurimum aduersatur. Putant enim & docent, prudentes homines multa cauere illorum posse, quæ ex cœlo sibi impendere præuiderint. Ac nisi ita res haberet, tunc etiam, cum vera probata fuisset, scire eam nemo sapiens vellet. Duplicaretur namq; malum & infinitè maius redderetur, si futurum intelligeretur, declinari autem non posset.
units.tr: And first, that from knowledge of a remote cause we cannot foretell the particular events that they produce through many other intervening causes, is not hard to see. For either those intermediate causes that lie between the effect and the remote cause are unchangeable and perpetual, and are moved of necessity as soon as the more remote cause begins to be moved, as can be seen in those marvellous self-moving devices and skilfully made clocks; or they are changeable, and, even when the first cause is set in motion, they are not moved by a perpetual order and always in one way. No astrologer, I think, will want to assert the first alternative. For that fatal connection of causes, or Stoic necessity, conflicts both with truth and with the philosophy of Aristotle, which on this point is accepted by the consensus of all learned men. But it is also very much opposed to the tenets of the astrologers. For they hold and teach that prudent men can guard against many of those things which they have foreseen to be impending upon them from the heavens. And unless matters were otherwise, then even when the prediction had been proved true, no wise man would wish to know it. For evil would be doubled and made infinitely greater if the future were understood but could not be avoided.

units.la: Deinde tantum abest, vt hoc pacto res omnes necessario accidant, vt ne tum quidem prædictio firma sit, cum effectus iam effici producq; visus est, vt cum Philosophia docet, tum Medicina quotidie comprobat. Non enim, vt, cum posterius est, prius præfuisse oportet: ita cum prius est, posterius quoq; fore oportet. Inter factum atq; factum motus intercedit, habitum non necessario, sed contingenter producens. Quo fit, vt habitus ac finis non semper ad præcedentem motum consequatur. Impediri enim nō potest, antequam ad finē præfinitum opus perduxerit. Quæ res in causa est, vt plurima incipiant fieri ac nasci, non tamen perficiantur omnino, sed semiperfecta, aut vix etiam inchoata relinquantur. Qui in arte nostra versatus est, nō habet opus longiore expositione.
units.tr: Next, it is so far from the case that all things happen of necessity in this way, that even when an effect already seems to be produced and brought about, a prediction is still not firm; as philosophy teaches and medicine confirms every day. For it is not necessary that, because a thing comes later, the earlier thing must have gone before it; and so, when a thing is earlier, the later thing need not follow. Between one act and another there intervenes a motion that produces the habit not of necessity but contingently. From this it comes about that the habit and the end do not always follow the preceding motion. For it can be hindered before it has brought the work to its predetermined end. This is the reason why very many things begin to be made and to be born, yet are not brought to completion at all, but are left half-finished or hardly even begun. Anyone versed in our art has no need of a longer explanation.

units.la: Quamobrem alteram partem approbare, & medias illas causas mutabiles statuere cogimur. Quo posito, necessarium prorsus est, vt operationes earum variè mutari impediriq; concedamus. Ergo qui ex remotæ causæ actione præsagire effectum particularem ex arte volet, cum quot inter hanc & effectum mediæ causæ interuenire possint, necesse est scire. Nec hoc solum modo, sed illud præterea scire debebit, quomodo vnaquæq; moueri ab alijs possit. Demum ignorare eum nō oportebit nihil interuenturum esse, quod alicuius harum actione mutet, impediat, alterue determinet. Cæterum cœlū esse remota causam, quod nō nisi beneficio aliarum propinquiorum causarum hæc terrena producat, non debet à me probari hoc loco.
units.tr: Therefore we are compelled to approve the other alternative and to hold that those intermediate causes are changeable. Once this is granted, it follows that we must also concede that their operations can be varied and impeded in many ways. So whoever wishes to foretell from the action of a remote cause a particular effect according to art must necessarily know how many intermediate causes can come between this cause and the effect. Nor is this enough: he must also know how each of them can be moved by the others. Lastly, he cannot be ignorant that nothing will intervene which might change, impede or determine the action of any of these. For the rest, that the heavens are a remote cause, which produces these earthly things only by the help of other, nearer causes, need not be proved by me in this place.

units.la: Ponatur igitur certa aliqua cœli figura, puerum, qui na-sciturus mox fuerat, aut nascebatur, ingeniosum reddidis-se. Necesse est ut opera aliarum causarum hoc perfecerit. Ipsa enim cū ingenium non habeat, non potest iudicij atq; ingenij causa immediata censeri. Nec potest instrumenta animæ, cerebri scilicet spirituumque substantiam repente permutare, nulla propinquarum ope causarum. Cum igi-tur sciri nequeat, quas, quales, quot numero, interuenire causas alias necesse sit, nec quo pacto inter se coire, con-sentire, temperariq; eas necesse sit, ad hoc, ut nascens reddatur ingeniosus, cū inquâ ista scire nemo queat, nec in cœ-lo descriptum reperiat, quomodo quæso poterit aliquis in-specto cœlo & causa remotissima, de effectu ipsius aliquid coniectare? Cerebrum & spiritus suam tunc, cum nascitur puer, temperaturam obtinent, non à cœlo accipiunt. Qua-re mutari temperiem oportet, si mutatur ingenium. At nō repente hoc fieri potest, sed tempore admodū est ad eam rē longo opus. Nescitur à quibus id causis efficiatur. Neq; an præsentes vel omnes sint, vel aliquæ earum, dicere licet. Postremò quæ impedimenta sint apparitura incertum est. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, non indoctum modò esse, sed omnino dementem, qui ex remotæ causæ notitia velit talia præcognoscere. Loquor de iliis duntaxat, qui rem & intelligunt, & ad trutinam expenderunt, nec persuaderi tamē potuerunt. Plurimi ne cogitarūt quidem, an fieri talia possint nec ne possint, quos ego non vitupero, sed ut consideRent moneo.
units.tr: Let us suppose, then, that some definite configuration of the heavens made the boy who was about to be born, or was being born, ingenious. It must be that the work of other causes brought this about. For since the heavens do not themselves possess intelligence, they cannot be regarded as the immediate cause of intelligence. Nor can they suddenly change the instruments of the soul, namely the brain and the substance of the spirits, without the help of nearby causes. Since, therefore, it cannot be known which causes, of what kind and how many, must necessarily intervene, nor how they must come together, agree and be tempered among themselves, in order that the newborn child should be made ingenious, and since no one can know these things, nor find them described in the heavens, how, I ask, can anyone, by inspecting the heavens and the most remote cause, conjecture anything about its effect? The brain and spirits, when the child is born, already have their temperament; they do not receive it from the heavens. Hence the temperament must change if the intelligence changes. But this cannot happen suddenly; it requires a very long time for that purpose. It is not known by what causes this is brought about. Nor can one say whether they are all present, or only some of them. Finally, it is uncertain what impediments will appear. From all these things it is evident that whoever wishes to foreknow such things from knowledge of a remote cause is not only unlearned but altogether mad. I speak only of those who both understand the matter and have weighed it in the balance, yet could not be persuaded. Most people have not even considered whether such things can happen or not; I do not blame them, but I advise them to consider.

units.la: Jam quòd neque indefinitæ causæ cognitio ad futuro-rum præscientiam utilis sit, non minus promtum est videre. Etenim tales paribus viribus utrumq; contrariorum efficere possunt ex æquo, nisi accessione secundarum causa-rum determinentur in unam partem potius, quàm in alte-ram. Quare non unum magis contrariorum quàm alte-rum effecturam talem causam, ex ipsius naturæ actionisq; notitia colligi potest, nisi à secundis causis circumscripta determinataq; ad certum effectum producendum cognita sit. Quoties hoc scitur, tunc iam fieri effectum oportet. Praevidetur igitur non ex indefinita causa, sed ex definita, & determinata. Exemplum rem illustrans tale sit: Potest homo exire domo, & non exire. Nec poterit quisquam ex natura hominis intelligere, utrum tali die & hora domi sit mansurus an exiturus è domo. Quòd si voluntatem, quae libera est, à certis accidentibus ad exeundum flecti coniecerit, ut quod pecuniam se accepturum speret, probabiliter exiturum ad recipiendam pecuniam praevidet, non ut ex indefinita, sed ut ex definita caussa. Novit enim iam in utram partem inclinauerit voluntas, quae sua natura non huc magis quam alio inclinabat. Et quae determinant voluntatem, fere sunt obiecta sensuum & intellectus. Haec vix aliter quam casu offeruntur. Unde perspicuè patet, arte nulla praescire nos ex huiusmodi caussae cognitione, quae ab infinitis & prorsus fortuito occurrentibus accidentibus in unam magis quam alteram partem inclinatur, particulares effectus ullos posse, de quibus aliquid scire homines desiderent.
units.tr: Now, that knowledge of an indefinite cause is no use for foreseeing future things is no less easy to see. For such causes, with equal powers, can produce either of two contraries equally, unless they are determined by the addition of secondary causes to one side rather than the other. Hence from knowledge of the nature and action of such a cause one cannot gather that it will produce one of the contraries rather than the other, unless it is known to be limited and determined by secondary causes to produce a certain effect. Whenever this is known, the effect must then follow. Thus foresight is had not from an indefinite cause but from a definite and determined one. Let an example illustrate the matter: a man can leave the house, or not leave it. Nor can anyone understand from the nature of man whether he will remain at home or go out of the house on such a day and hour. But if he conjectures that his will, which is free, is bent to going out by certain circumstances, as when he hopes to receive money, he foresees that he will probably go out to receive the money, and this is foresight from a definite, not an indefinite, cause. For he now knows in which direction the will has inclined, although by its nature it inclined no more to this than to that. And the things that determine the will are for the most part objects of the senses and the intellect. These are offered almost only by chance. Whence it is clearly evident that by no art can we, from knowledge of such a cause, which is inclined to one side rather than the other by infinite accidents occurring entirely by chance, foresee any particular effects about which men might wish to know something.

units.la: Eadem atque adeò maior est difficultas in communi caussa. Voco autem communem caussam, quaecunque unica & eadem facultate res multas varie, unamquamque scilicet pro sua natura, substantia, proprietate, aptitudine, potest ac solet afficere, alterare, immutare. Exemplo ignis declarabo breviter. Hic unica potestate, scilicet caliditate, uno eodemque tempore alia liquefacit, alia cogit indurare, quaedam dealbat, nonnulla denigrat, aliqua corrumpit, plurima recreat & confirmat, res certas dulciores, alias amaras, acidas, ingratas, efficit. Haec omnia ut alia infinita praeterea, quia calefaciendo tantum perficere potest, pro naturarum diversitate illarum rerum, quas calefacit, communis omnium horum effectuum caussa est ac dicitur.
units.tr: The difficulty is the same, or even greater, in a common cause. I call a common cause whatever thing can, and customarily does, affect, alter and change many things in various ways by one and the same power, each according to its own nature, substance, property and aptitude. I will explain this briefly by the example of fire. Here, by one single power, namely heat, at one and the same time it melts some things, forces others to harden, whitens some, blackens others, corrupts some, restores and strengthens very many, and makes certain things sweeter, others bitter, sour or unpleasant. All these effects, and countless others besides, are, because fire can produce them only by heating, and because of the diversity of the natures of the things it heats, called the common cause of all these effects.

units.la: Iam vero quis tam sit rerum imperitus, qui se ex confideratione naturæ ignis solius certum effectum prædi-cere posse cogitet aut sperét [?]? Igne conspecto, si plum-bum injici videam, atque ab igne plumbum solui non nesciam, plumbi liquefactionem prævideo. Si verò nullum adijciatur siue apponatur propè ad eum corpus quod liquefieri aptum sit, aut tale admoueatur, quod ab igne solui ego non sciam, ex ignis consideratione nunquam præscire potero, an aliquid tale sit dissoluendum ab eo. Ex quibus patet, præter naturæ ignis notitiam duo me præterea explorata habere oportere, si certi aliquid tale præuidere cupiam. Primum est, vt quid admouendum igni sit perspexerim. Alterum vt, quid ab igne pati queat, quod admouendū præintellexi, compertum habeam. Istis ignora-tis, nihil præsentire futurum, quod quidem ab igne ef-ficiendum sit, vnquam potero ex inspectione ignis. Lo-quor non de effectu ignis primo, videlicet caliditate, sed de particularibus aliis, quos per caliditatem in diuersis natura rebus efficit longè diuersissimos. Hoc enim Ru-stici quoque omnes intelligunt de igne, nimirum ita ip-sum omnia per calorem immutaturum, vt mutari natu-ra possint, quod communis multorum effectuum causæ proprium munus esse præmonuimus.
units.tr: Now, what man is so unskilled in things that he thinks or hopes he can foretell from consideration of the nature of fire alone a certain effect? If I see lead thrown into the fire, and I know that lead is melted by fire, I foresee the melting of the lead. But if no body suited to being melted is added or placed near it, or if something is brought near which I do not know is dissolved by fire, I can never foreknow from consideration of the fire whether anything of that kind will be dissolved by it. From this it is evident that, besides knowledge of the nature of fire, I must have two further things established if I wish to foresee anything certain of this kind. The first is that I have examined what must be brought to the fire. The second is that I have ascertained what can be suffered from the fire by that which I have understood beforehand must be brought near. If these are unknown, I shall never be able, from inspecting the fire, to presage anything future that is to be effected by the fire. I speak not of the primary effect of fire, namely heat, but of the other particular effects which, through heat, it produces in the various natural things, very widely differing. For even all country folk understand this about fire: that it will change all things by heat in such a way that they can be changed in nature, which we have said is the proper office of a common cause of many effects.

units.la: Quod ignis exemplo valde appositò expositum est, de communi qualibet causa, quatenus talis existit, intelligendum est. Non enim ex ipsius notitia particularis aliquis effectus præuideri poterit, nisi in quæ actura sit præcognitum sit, & quomodo singula illorum affecta aptaq; sint perspectum, & quidem certò præcognitum sit. Nam cum, quæ hoc modo à communi causa patiun-tur, mutabilia plerunque sint, & pro varia naturæ suæ permutatione, accidentibusque causis alijs, non vno semper modo patiantur, prædici arte ne tum quidem aliquid rectè poterit, cum prædicta non ignoramus, nisi talia permansura non inanibus conjecturis deprehen-derimus.
units.tr: What has been set out most aptly by the example of fire must be understood of any common cause, so far as it exists as such. For no particular effect can be foreseen from knowledge of the cause itself, unless it is known in what matter it will act, and unless it is perceived how each of those things is affected and suited, and this is certainly known beforehand. For since those things which are suffered from a common cause in this way are for the most part changeable, and do not always suffer in one way, because of the varied change of their nature and the other accidental causes, nothing can be rightly predicted by art even then, when we are not ignorant of the things to be predicted, unless we perceive by no empty conjectures that they will remain such.

units.la: Summa est, quia & infinita sunt quæ à communi cau-sa ex æquo omnia mutantur mutariue possunt, & quia eædem res pro diuersa affectione & aptitudine, quam per accidens adipiscuntur, diuerso modo mutantur, non mutari ea hoc modo potius quàm alio quouis, nisi per accidens. At horum nulla est ars aut ratio. Quare ex communi caussa nihil artificiose præsciri aliud potest, nisi hoc, ipsam in rebus singulis, in quas aget, perfecturam, quod pati ipsæ queant, siue ad quod patiendum aptæ tum sint. Mutata vero aptitudine effectum quoq; mutatum iri.
units.tr: In sum: since there are infinitely many things which are all changed, or can be changed, equally by a common cause, and since the same things are changed in different ways according to the different disposition and aptitude which they acquire by accident, it is not that they are changed in this way rather than in any other, except by accident. But there is no art or reason for these things. Therefore nothing can be artfully foreknown from a common cause except this: that it will bring about its effect in the individual things upon which it acts, namely whatever they are able to suffer, or to what they are then suited to suffer. But if the aptitude changes, the effect too will be changed.

units.la: Ergo si neque ex actione causæ remotæ, neque indefi-nitæ, neque communis, futurum aliquid arte præcognosci potest, quis quæso ex illis caussis se futura, quæ hic fiunt, peruidere confidat, quæ maximè sunt à talibus effectibus remotæ, & omnium communissimæ? Minus sperabit, opinor, vbi præterea maximè indefinitas perspe-xerit esse, vt non nisi ab infinitis accidentibus determi-natæ aliquid tale producere vnquam valeant. Rectè ergo suprà affirmaui, particulares istos euentus, non nisi in propinquissimis & prorsus proprijs caussis cerni. Qui in alijs quærit huiusmodi præsensionem, credere hoc etiam videtur, intercedentes caussas immutabili lege atque nexu inter se cohærere, vt aliter concurrere mutariqué nequeant, sed prima mota, posteriores omnes certa & ineuitabili necessitate similiter semper moueri. Deinde nec sic quidem proderit ei communissimæ istius caussæ notitia, nisi illa etiam duo præsciat, videlicet per quot & quas medias caussas effectus sit producendus, & an, quod actionem recepturum est, adsit, idoneumq; pro tali receptione existat. Quæ cum sint omnia impossibilia, & caprum hominis superent, necessariò sequitur, ex consideratione & inspectione talium caussarum, nihil prædictorum arte præsciri præsagiriq; posse.
units.tr: Therefore, if nothing future can be foreknown by art either from the action of a remote cause, or of an indefinite one, or of a common one, who, I ask, can trust that he foresees by those causes the things that happen here, which are most remote from such effects and the most common of all? He will hope for less, I suppose, when he has seen that they are most indefinite, so that they can produce anything of this kind only when determined by infinite accidents. I was right, therefore, to affirm above that these particular events are discerned only in the nearest and wholly proper causes. Whoever seeks such foresight in other things seems also to believe that intervening causes cohere among themselves by an unchangeable law and bond, so that they cannot concur or change otherwise, but that, once the first is moved, all the later ones are always moved in a like manner by a certain and inevitable necessity. Then, even so, knowledge of that most common cause will not help him, unless he also foreknows two further things: by how many and what intermediate causes the effect is to be produced, and whether that which is to receive the action is present and fit for such reception. Since all these things are impossible, and exceed the capacity of man, it follows necessarily that from consideration and inspection of such causes nothing of the aforesaid can be foreknown or foretold by art.

units.la: Porrò sidera nemo[?] sanæ mentis homo vnquam negabit, caussas horum terrenorum maximè esse remotas interminatas & communes generalesq;. Quare necesse est verum esse, ex inspectione cœli nihil horum prænunciari posse. Omnia à sideribus per accidens, non per se, fiunt; sicut ignis per accidens alia nigra, alia alba, dulcia, amara, facit. Quod ut fiat planius, exponam hoc quoque pluribus, ut quid per se cœli efficiant, cernas, & quid per accidens ab ijsdem perficiatur, videas.
