units.tr: Moreover, no man of sound mind will ever deny that the causes of these earthly things are for the most part remote, indefinite, common and general. Therefore it must be true that nothing of these things can be foretold from the inspection of the heavens. Everything comes from the stars per accidens, not per se; just as fire per accidens makes some things black, others white, sweet, or bitter. So that this may become clearer, I shall set out this point at greater length, so that you may see what the heavens effect per se, and what is brought about per accidens by the same.

units.la: Ignem calefaciendo diversissima opera efficere supra indicaui. Non potest autem vlla causa naturalis unica vi & facultate, (nisi diversis forte utatur instrumentis,) diversa producere opera. Unum etenim unum solum agit ac gignit per se, non autem multa genere naturaq; diversa seu disparata, multò minus contraria. Ignis ergo per se calefacit, accidit autem ei, ut, dum plurima calefacit ex æquo, alia quidem nigriora, alia verò candidiora reddan-tur. Simili ferè modo Sol calorem in aërem spargit vivi-ficum, qui innumerabilium operum longeque diversissi-morum causa existit, quæ certum est ab eo per se non ef-fici. alijs vitam, alijs verò interitum vno eodemq; adfert calore. Alia liquefacit, alia indurat eodem tempore eademque potentia seu virtute. Quæ si Solis per se opera aliquis existimat esse, is plurimum fallitur. Unum ergo per se, ut ignis, facit, scilicet calorem nobis salutarem lar-gitur. Ab hoc alia bene, alia verò pessimè affici cum vi-demus, non in Solem referenda culpa est, quasi per se utrumque efficeret, sed in naturam earum earum, quas calor attingit.
units.tr: I have shown above that fire, by heating, produces very diverse works. But no natural cause can, by a single power and faculty (unless perhaps it uses diverse instruments), produce diverse works. For one thing acts and begets only one thing per se, and not many things differing in kind and nature, or disparate, much less contrary ones. Fire therefore heats per se; it happens to it that, while it heats many things alike, some are rendered blacker and others whiter. In much the same way the Sun spreads life-giving heat into the air, which is the cause of countless works, most diverse of all, and which is certainly not effected by it per se. With one and the same heat it brings life to some things and death to others. It liquefies some things and hardens others at the same time, by the same power or virtue. If anyone thinks these to be the works of the Sun per se, he is greatly mistaken. The Sun therefore, like fire, does one thing per se, namely, it bestows on us the heat that is salutary. When we see that other things are affected well by this and others very badly, the fault is not to be laid to the Sun, as if it effected both per se, but to the nature of those things which the heat reaches.

units.la: Quascunque iam imaginetur aliquis in sideribus sin-gulis inesse vires, (de quo non statui hic disputare,) cum oporteat eas rebus cunctis communes esse, necesse est, ut in omnibus rebus unum aliquid gignant, (ut Sol & ignis calorem,) à quo mox singulæ res, pro sua quælibet natu-ra, ita afficiantur, ut affici apta est illarum quæuis. Hoc quod universis ex æquo infunditur, per se à sideribus ma-nat. Quas autem communis iste effectus in singulis mu-tationes discrepantes & dispares[?] parit, eæ per accidens à sideribus generatæ sunt. Quibus expositis perfacile est videre, quid ex inspectione cœlestium artificiosè prædici possit, & quid non possit. Etenim quæcunque sidera per se absque adminiculo secundarum causarum efficiunt, ex eorum motu præ-dici arte possunt. Quæ secundarum causarum naturam magis, quàm cœli virtutem sequuntur, talia ex cœlo præintelligi nullo modo possunt. Res exemplis patefiet melius.
units.tr: Whatever powers someone may imagine to be present in the individual stars (a matter I have not decided to dispute here), since these must be common to all things, it is necessary that they generate something one in all things (as the Sun and fire generate heat), by which the individual things, each according to its own nature, are then affected in such a way as each of them is fit to be affected. That which is poured out equally upon all comes from the stars per se. But those changes, differing and dissimilar, which this common effect produces in individual things, have been generated by the stars per accidens. With these points set out, it is very easy to see what can be foretold artfully from the inspection of the heavenly bodies, and what cannot. For whatever the stars effect per se, without the aid of secondary causes, can be foretold by art from their motion. Those things which follow the nature of secondary causes more than the power of the heavens cannot in any way be foreknown from the heavens. The matter will be made clearer by examples.

units.la: Sol proprijs viribus generat diem, noctem, æstatem, hyemem aliasque anni consuetas & statas mutationes. Perficit hæc sine ope vllius sublunaris causæ, sed beneficio obliqui circuli, in quo mouetur, radios in terram demittit magis minusque rectos, pro loco quem in suo circulo obtinet. Hanc Solis actionem nec adiuuare & promouere, nec impedire tardareque res aliqua sublunaris potest. Quæ ergo sol hoc modo efficit, ex motu ipsius prævideri & prædici possunt, multò ante quàm fiant. At hæc non ad Astrologiam, sed Astronomiam pertinent. Ergo quo tempore nec incipiat, quo æstas futura sit, præsciri potest ex Solis motus cognitione. At an salutaria hæc tempora futura sint an morbosa, an calidiora vel frigidiora, humidiora, siccio-ra solito, an fructus paritura sint plures an pauciores, item suauiores ne an minus suaues atque maturos productura sint, & quæ his similia sunt, ad diuinationem pertinet quidem, sed ex Solis astrorumq; motu cognosci non amplius hæc talia queunt. In causa est, quòd neque per se neque solus hæc efficit sol, sed vnà cum aliis causis propè infinitis, aut certè homini non compre-hensibilibus. Intelligo per alias causas, causas propin-quiores & proprias.
units.tr: The Sun by its own powers generates day, night, summer, winter, and the other customary and fixed changes of the year. It accomplishes these without the help of any sublunary cause, but by means of the oblique circle in which it moves, it sends its rays down to the earth more or less perpendicularly, according to the place it holds in its circle. No sublunary thing can either aid and promote this action of the Sun, or hinder or delay it. Therefore what the Sun effects in this way can be foreseen and foretold from its motion, long before they happen. But these things pertain not to Astrology but to Astronomy. Therefore, at what time the coming summer will begin can be known from knowledge of the Sun's motion. But whether these seasons will be wholesome or diseased, whether warmer or colder, moister or drier than usual, whether they will bring forth more or fewer fruits, and likewise whether they will produce sweeter or less sweet and ripe ones, and the things like these, pertain indeed to divination, but these things can no longer be known from the motions of the Sun and stars. The reason is that the Sun does not effect these things alone or per se, but together with other causes, nearly infinite, or at least not comprehensible to man. By other causes I mean the nearer and proper causes.

units.la: Per se igitur sol calefacit. At cum ei salubres causæ con-iunguntur vel insalubres, non calefacit tantum, sed salu-briter vel insalubriter calefacit. Exempli gratia: Si cum solis calore coniungatur ventus salubris tempore aliquo annì, non simpliciter sed cum salubritate calefaciet. Si is vel non sit talis, vel frigidus, vel humidus, non tantum calefaciet, tempusque anni certum pariet, sed vel insalubre, vel solito frigidius vel humidius simul vt sit, non per se quidem, sed per accidens efficiet. Accidit enim vt talis ipsi ventus coniungeretur. Cum per se calefacere dico, id volo, calidiorem fieri semper, caeteris paribus, aerem, cum ad nos accedit sol propius. Non nescio quae inter se philosophi de modo, quo sol calefacit aerem, disputant. At haec concertatio huc non pertinet. Hic satis est scire, solem calefacere tantum & semper per se. Quod si iam aliter, quàm alias eodem hoc tempore aerem calefacit, certum est ideo fieri, quia secundas causas aliter sibi habet consociatas, quam alias haberet. Quare cum calefaciat per se tantum, cum aliis atque aliis causis sublunaribus, inter quas subiectorum aptitudinem in praesentia connumerare placet, coniunctus aliter atque aliter calefaciat, ex ipsius motu nullus supra dictorum & similium effectuum praecognosci potest. Ratio eadem est prorsus astrorum omnium, quod ad hanc rem attinet. Omnia namque vniuersaliter siue communiter agunt, hoc est, generales causae sunt eorum, quae hic oriuntur & intereunt. Etenim omnia & singula siue coniunctim siue separatim agere putes, omnia haec nostratia ita mouent, afficiunt, coniungunt, distrahunt, vt pro sua natura varietateque accidentium quibus subijciuntur, moueri, affici, coniungi, distrahi, possunt.
units.tr: The Sun therefore heats per se. But when wholesome or unwholesome causes are joined to it, it does not merely heat, but heats wholesomely or unwholesomely. For example: if a wholesome wind is joined to the heat of the sun at some time of the year, it will heat not simply but with wholesomeness. If the wind is either not such, or is cold or moist, it will not merely heat and bring about a certain season of the year, but will effect, not per se indeed but per accidens, something unwholesome, or colder or moister than usual, as the case may be. For it happens that such a wind is joined to it. When I say that it heats per se, I mean that the air always becomes warmer, other things being equal, as the sun approaches us more closely. I am not unaware of the various things which philosophers dispute among themselves about the manner in which the sun heats the air. But that controversy does not pertain to this matter. Here it is enough to know that the sun heats only, and always, per se. But if it heats the air at this time otherwise than at other times, it is certain that this happens because it is joined with secondary causes otherwise than it would be at other times. Therefore, since it heats per se only, but with other and other sublunary causes, among which I think it fitting to count for the present the aptitude of the subjects, it heats differently when joined differently; and from its motion none of the aforesaid and similar effects can be foreknown. The reasoning is entirely the same for all the stars, as far as this matter is concerned. For they all act universally or commonly, that is, they are general causes of those things which arise and perish here. Indeed, whether you think of all and each of them acting together or separately, all these things of ours they move, affect, join and separate, so that they can be moved, affected, joined and separated according to their own nature and the variety of the accidents to which they are subjected.

units.la: Si quod dico obscurius adhuc est, quàm vt plane intel-ligatur, apertissimo exemplo planissimum faciam, generatione videlicet hominis. Vt enim homo hominem per se generat, pulchrum aut deformem non nisi propter adiunctionem aliarum causarum, qua ipsi per accidens & casu coniunguntur: ita fere sol æstatem, ver, autumnum per se facit, salubre aut insalubre vnumquodque horum temporum non aliter efficit, quàm per accessionem alia-rum caussarum, quæ casu ipsi coniunguntur hoc magis tempore, quàm alio quouis. Quare sicut prædicere pos-sumus, hominem cum generat, hominem generaturum esse, at pulchér ne an deformis futurus sit, qui nascetur, non possumus præuidere: ita hîc quoque res habet. Vt non eadem omnino sunt, hominis generatio, &, huius certi talisque generatio: ita non idem dicit, qui à Solis motu æstatem fieri absolutè ait, & qui talem, salubrem scilicet aut insalubrem, sterilem aut fœcundam asseuerat ab eodem fieri. Illa enim per se ab vtrisque fiunt, hæc ve-rò per accidens, hoc est propter coniunctionem aliarum caussarum accidentalium. Ex dictis huc vsque manife-ste patet, quid astra per se efficiant, & quid per accidens hic generent. Patet illud etiam, astra non esse ex illa-rum caussarum genere, in quibus effectus certus & par-ticularis cognosci queat. Quibus omnibus efficitur, ina-nem esse & ridiculam Astrologiam, quæ ex inspectio-ne talium caussarum futura præsagire docet, ex qui-bus præcognosci nullo modo possunt. Non video quid ad hæc sis responsurus, cum præsertim ipsis sensibus com-probentur.
units.tr: If what I say is still too obscure to be plainly understood, I shall make it very plain by a most evident example, namely the generation of man. For just as man generates man per se, but whether he is beautiful or deformed only on account of the addition of other causes which are joined to him per accidens and by chance, so the sun in much the same way makes summer, spring and autumn per se; whether each of these seasons is wholesome or unwholesome it does not bring about otherwise than by the addition of other causes, which are joined to it by chance, more at this time than at any other. Therefore, just as we can foretell that when a man begets, he will beget a man, but we cannot foresee whether the child that is born will be beautiful or deformed, so the case is here too. Just as the generation of man in general and the generation of this or that particular man are not the same thing, so he who says absolutely that summer comes about from the motion of the Sun does not say the same as he who asserts that such a summer, namely wholesome or unwholesome, barren or fruitful, is produced by the same. For the former are effected per se by both, but the latter per accidens, that is, on account of the conjunction of other accidental causes. From what has been said so far it is plainly clear what the stars effect per se, and what they generate here per accidens. It is clear also that the stars do not belong to the class of causes from which a certain and particular effect can be known. From all these things it follows that Astrology, which teaches that future things are to be foretold from the inspection of such causes, from which they can in no way be foreknown, is empty and ridiculous. I do not see what you will answer to these things, especially since they are confirmed by the very senses.

units.la: Nec minus certum est prius argumentum, cuius hæc summa est: Astrologorum Vaticinia circa particularia contingentia solum versantur. At talia arte futura præ-cognosci nequeunt, antequam fieri iam aliquo pacto visa sunt. Ergo inania sunt & futilia. Furilis igitur ars quæ talia docet. Ac quòd particulares euentus contingen-tes præsciri ab homine per artem nullam possint per se notum est. Concessum etenim testatumque est doctis omnibus, ea quæ per accidens fiunt aut futura sunt, qua-tenus nimirum ita futura sunt, nullam sub artem cade-re. Sed omnes particulares effectus non nisi per acci-dens fiunt, seu futuri cognoscuntur, vt indissolubilibus argu-mentis demonstrare facilè poterit. Quid dico argumentis confirmandum esse? Tam est res per se nota & clara, vt si declaretur alicui, probationem praeterea nullam expectet. Duo igitur haec probanda mihi intelligo, scilicet, Astrologos versari circa particulares effectus, & tales per accidens euenire: His comprobatis, necessario perficietur, Astrologorum conatus atque studia vanissima & salsissima esse.
units.tr: Nor is the first argument less certain, and its substance is this: the prophecies of the astrologers are concerned only with particular contingent events. But such things cannot be foreknown by art before they have in some way been seen to happen. Therefore they are empty and futile, and the art that teaches such things is therefore frivolous. That particular contingent events cannot be foreseen by a human being through any art is known in itself. For it has been granted and attested by all the learned that things which happen or will happen by accident, insofar as they are future in that way, do not fall under any art. But all particular effects come about only by accident, or are known only as future, as can easily be demonstrated by indissoluble arguments. Why do I say it must be confirmed by arguments? The matter is so self-evident and clear that, if it is set out to anyone, it needs no further proof. I understand that two things must therefore be proved: first, that the astrologers are concerned with particular effects, and second, that such effects happen by accident. Once these are established, it will necessarily follow that the endeavours and studies of the astrologers are most vain and most foolish.

units.la: Astrologorum conatus circa particularia solum versari, non longa eget probatione. Etenim artifices & ex arte quadam futura praeuidere videri desiderant. Iam constat artifices omnes non circa necessaria, sed circa contingentia, & particularia occupatos duntaxat esse. Etenim ars omnis habitus esse dicitur cum ratione actiuus aut factiuus. Quo fit, ut artifex omnis (tametsi artes habitus sunt universalium) circa particulare versetur. Nam circa universale neque actio neque factio, vt hoc loco de ipsis disserimus, versatur. Sic videmus omnem Medici actionem non circa hominem, sed circa hunc hominem, Petrum videlicet, versari. Astrologus quoque non hominem, sed hunc certum hominem hoc loco & tali tempore natum, felicè aut infelicem fore pronunciat. Qui consulunt eos, nō quid homini, sed quid sibi aut suis euenturum sit scire cupiunt. Quae cum sint non vera modò, verum etiam ipsismet Astrologis confessa, satis ostensum est, quod primo loco ostē-surum me receperam, Astrologorum praedictiones circa particulares hominum aut urbium aut rerum euentus occupari.
units.tr: That the efforts of the astrologers are concerned only with particulars needs no lengthy proof. For artists, and those who seem to foresee the future by some art, wish to be thought so. It is clear that all artists are occupied not with necessary things but with contingent and particular ones. For every art is said to be a habit of acting or making with reason. Hence every artist, although arts are habits of universals, is concerned with the particular. For neither action nor making, as we are discussing them here, is concerned with the universal. Thus we see that every physician's action is concerned not with man, but with this man, Peter for example. The astrologer too does not pronounce that man, but that this particular man, born here and at such a time, will be happy or unhappy. Those who consult them wish to know not what will happen to man, but what will happen to themselves or their families. Since these things are not only true but have been confessed by the astrologers themselves, it has been sufficiently shown what I had undertaken to show first: that the predictions of the astrologers are concerned with the particular events of men, cities, or things.

units.la: Ex dictis alterum quoque perspici poterit, videlicet, per accidens talia euenire omnia. Unde consectarium est, nec arte nec ratione praesagiri posse. Nemo negare potest, quin particularia artium sint ex genere contingentium. Et ut quarundam artium effecta seu obiecta, talia non essent, quod falsum esse constat: Astrologiae tamen effecta, seu ea, quae praedicere conantur Astrologi, talia negare nequirēt. Ipsimet affirmant, non semper, quae caelestia efficere coeperint, euenire, sed multis modis impediri posse, ut suprà quoque monui. At vero particularia contingentia per accidens fieri quis negabit? Etenim res quaelibet talis fit necessario, qualem ipsam propria proxima & per se causa efficit ac producit. Non enim ipsi sibi ipse dare aliquid potest, cum non sit. Ab effectrice sui causa proxima & vera, non id tantum habet ut fiat, sed illud etiam ut talis fiat.
units.tr: From what has been said, the other point also can be seen, namely that all such things happen by accident. From this it follows that they cannot be foreseen either by art or by reason. No one can deny that the particulars of the arts belong to the class of contingent things. And even if the effects or objects of certain arts were not such, which is known to be false, the effects of astrology, or those which the astrologers try to predict, could not be denied to be such. They themselves affirm that what the heavenly bodies have begun to bring about does not always come to pass, but can be hindered in many ways, as I have also warned above. But who will deny that particular contingent things happen by accident? For any thing whatever comes about of necessity in the way its own proximate and essential cause produces and brings it about. For nothing can give itself what it does not yet have. From its proximate and true effective cause, a thing has not only the fact that it comes to be, but also that it comes to be in this particular way.

units.la: Hoc quoque suprà ostensum est, res omnes, quòd tales sint, proximæ & propinquissimæ suæ causæ debere. Ita nanque hæ causæ suos effectus producunt, ut quasi se ipsas in illos transfundant, & se totas illis communicet, quantum omnino possunt. Non alia ratione se ipsas perpetuare immortalesque reddere queunt, quod facere à creatore, cui fideliter obtemperant, iussæ fuerunt. Quare non multum interfit in proposita nostra causa, sive per effectus causas, sive per causas effectus contingentes & fortuitos esse, probare studeamus. Ut enim causa necessaria non potest producere per se & sola effectum contingentem, ita nec contingens causa unquam produxerit effectum necessarium. Manifestissima & verissima haec esse tunc intelliges, cum me hic non aliter de hisce loqui cogitaveris, quatenus hi tales futuri, illæ verò tales effecturæ sint.
units.tr: This too has been shown above: all things must be such as their nearest and closest causes are. For these causes produce their effects in such a way that they pour themselves, as it were, into them and impart themselves entirely to them, as far as they are able altogether. They cannot perpetuate themselves and make themselves immortal in any other way, which they were commanded to do by the Creator, whom they faithfully obey. Therefore, in our present argument, it matters little whether we undertake to prove that the effects are contingent and fortuitous because of their causes, or that the causes are contingent and fortuitous because of their effects. For just as a necessary cause cannot by itself and alone produce a contingent effect, so a contingent cause never produces a necessary effect. You will understand these things to be most evident and most true when you consider that I am not speaking of these matters in any other way than insofar as these things are to be such, and those causes are to produce such effects.

units.la: Non me latet aliam esse rerum quatenus sunt, & aliam rursus quatenus futuræ sunt rationem. Quæ distinctio in causis etiam locum habet. Alia earum ratio est, cum quatenus sunt: & alia rursus, cum quatenus effecturæ tale aliquid sunt, considerantur. Quæcunque igitur causa necessario agit, determinatione nulla indiget, effectumque necessario pro suis viribus producet. Quæ autem ab accidentibus & fortuitò concurrentibus causis determinatur, antequam agere certi aliquid possit, ab ea effectus contingenter & per accidens talis proficiscitur.
units.tr: I am not unaware that things have one account insofar as they exist, and another insofar as they are about to be. This distinction also applies to causes. They have one account when considered as existing, and another when considered as about to produce something of a certain kind. Therefore, whatever cause acts of necessity needs no determination, and will produce its effect of necessity according to its powers. But whatever cause is determined by accidents and by chance concurrences, before it can act in a definite way, its effect proceeds from it contingently and by accident, and is of such a kind.

units.la: Sed in præsentia satis est monuisse, particulares effectus, si, ut futuri sunt, considerentur, contingentes esse, atque adeò à causis produci talibus, nempe contingenter sic agentibus. Quare cum tales non nisi per accidens suos effectus producant, certo certius est, eos ut tales futuros non ante præcognosci posse, quàm visi sint fieri. Porrò ut nihil desideres, aut obscura hæc nimis esse conquerare, tentabo planissimè alio modo ostendere, particulares omnes effectus, quatenus tales sunt, per accidens tales produci, ideoque præsciri arte nulla posse. Loquar autem de illis præcipuè, de quibus Astrologi vaticinari solent, ex inspectione cœli.
units.tr: But for the present it is enough to have pointed out that particular effects, if they are considered as future, are contingent, and are therefore produced by causes of such a kind, namely causes that act contingently. Hence, since such causes produce their effects only by accident, it is more than certain that these effects, as such future things, cannot be foreknown before they have been seen to come about. Moreover, so that you may not want anything more or complain that these matters are too obscure, I shall try to show quite plainly in another way that all particular effects, insofar as they are such, are produced by accident, and therefore cannot be foreknown by any art. I shall speak chiefly of those things about which the astrologers are accustomed to prophesy from the inspection of the heavens.

units.la: Quęcunque hîc in terris particulatim fiunt, eorum causæ sunt vel Fortuna & Casus, vel Hominis voluntas, vel Natura aliqua particularis. Cœlum vt vniuersalis & remota causa cum omnibus concurrit ad actionem. De cœlestib. postea, iam de prioribus agendum est. Hæ omnes causæ suos effectus solum per accidens efficiunt. Ergo nihil horum præsciri futurum potest. Ac de primis duabus causis nullam mihi tecum controuersiam fore non temerè spero. Equidem Fortunam cæcam hodie quoque omnes fatentur, & ab hac facta dicimus, quorum causam veram nullam inuenimus. Vt Fortuna nil aliudferè sit[?], quàm veræ causæ ignoratio.
units.tr: Whatever happens here on earth in particulars has as its causes either Fortune and Chance, or the will of man, or some particular Nature. The heavens, as a universal and remote cause, concur with all of these in the action. I shall treat of the heavenly bodies afterwards; now the first causes must be dealt with. All these causes produce their effects only by accident. Therefore none of these things can be foreknown as future. And I do not rashly hope that there will be any dispute between us over the first two causes. Indeed, everyone today still confesses that Fortune is blind, and we say that things are done by her when we find no true cause for them. Fortune is scarcely anything other than ignorance of the true causes.

units.la: Hominis etiam voluntatem per accidens vnum magis quàm aliud facere, minimè ambiguum est. Aristoteles causas ratione præditas, vtriusque contrariorum æquè effectrices esse rectè docuit. Nos ex euidentibus & à nobis met edocti sumus vt verum crederemus. Quis etenim nescit, voluntatem nostram indefinitam indeterminataque[?] esse, nec in hanc magis quàm alteram partem inclinare, priusquam ab obiectis quomodocunque occurrentibus in alteram partem flectatur impellaturque? Hoc qui negat, nihil videt, præsertim cum omnes homines in se ipsis, omnibus horis ita rem habere experiantur. Quis enim neget, se & domi manere & non manere æquè & posse & velle, si nulla ei causa occurrat, quæ indicet quòd vel exire ex ædibus, vel non exire præstet? Has autem causas & cogitationes innumerabiles esse, & per accidens incidere, nemo sanus mente dubitare vnquam potuerit.
units.tr: That the will of man does one thing rather than another by accident is in no way doubtful. Aristotle rightly taught that causes endowed with reason are equally able to produce either of two contraries. We have been taught by evident things, and by our own experience, to believe this to be true. For who does not know that our will is undefined and undetermined, and does not incline to one side more than the other until it is turned and pushed to the other side by objects that present themselves in whatever way? Whoever denies this sees nothing, especially since all men experience in themselves that this is how things stand at all hours. For who would deny that, if no cause presents itself that shows it is better to go out of the house or not to go out, he is equally able and willing both to stay at home and not to stay at home? Moreover, that these causes and thoughts are innumerable, and fall in by accident, no sane person could ever doubt.

units.la: Quòd verò Naturales etiam causæ suos effectus per accidens & contingenter producant, in philosophorum scholis mediocriter versatis non est obscurum. Qui ex diētis[?] percipere non potuit, ex dicendis perspiciet. Primùm constat, quæcunque hîc oriuntur & occidunt, hoc est fiùt, singularia esse. Deinde causas quoque earum singulares esse. Impossibile nanque est, causam universalem, quatenus talis permanet, nec adiunctione aliarum contrahitur ad hoc, non aliud agendum, effectum particularem gignere. Præterea certum est, accidentia ab accidentibus nasci. Ad hæc oculi nobis nostri testes sunt certissimi, indiuidua omnia non modò ab aliis, sed etiam à suì generis aut speciei indiuiduis distincta esse. Postremò concedunt omnes, indiuidua, præsertim unius speciei, accidentibus inter se, non verò substantiis, differre.
units.tr: That natural causes also produce their effects by accident and contingently is not obscure to anyone moderately versed in the schools of the philosophers. He who could not perceive it from what has been said will see it from what is to be said. First, it is agreed that whatever arises and perishes here, that is, comes to be, is singular. Next, that their causes too are singular. For it is impossible that a universal cause, insofar as it remains such and is not narrowed down to this or that by the addition of other things, should produce a particular effect rather than another. Moreover, it is certain that accidents arise from accidents. Besides, our own eyes are most certain witnesses that all individuals are distinguished not only from others, but also from the individuals of their own genus or species. Finally, all agree that individuals, especially those of one species, differ from one another in accidents, but not in substance.

units.la: Ex recensitis liquidò apparet, nullam causam inueniri, quæ eodem prorsus modo affecta bis agere, seu duos effectus producere possit. Si nanque nullis in ipsa qualitatib. siue accidentibus mutatis utrunque pariat effectum, proferet eos prorsus similes. Jam enim à causa, cui aliquid acciderit, individuum aliter affectum produci diximus, ut mox copiosius exponetur.
units.tr: From what has been reviewed, it is clear that no cause, when affected in exactly the same way, can act twice or produce two effects. For if, with none of its qualities or accidents changed, it produced both effects, it would produce them entirely alike. We have already said that a cause produces an individual differently affected when something has happened to it, as will be explained more fully shortly.

units.la: Non refert hoc loco siue causas immutatas dicas, siue obiectum in quod illa agit. Satis est accessisse aliquid in hac secunda actione, quod in priore non fuerat. Differt enim quod factum est jam, ab eo quod prius factum fuit. At hoc est accidens, quo inter se duo effectus isti differunt. Sequitur ergo aliter actionem nunc, quàm prius, fuisse affectam. Et nunquam similiter prorsus agere causam vllâ posse hinc perspicuè apparet. At verò causa, quæ non potest agere, ut non aliter atque aliter ab accidentibus quasi informetur & circumscribatur, per accidens effectus suos tales generat. Quod qui ignorat, is quæ dicta jam sunt, præ ruditate non intelligit. Nam si eadem permanens generaret, hoc est, si actio ipsius non aliter ab accidentibus causis & qualitatibus terminaretur, dirigeretur, impediretur, adiuuaretur, & tandem circumscriberetur & coherceretur, effectus suos omnes omnino similes necessariò generet. At hoc est impossibile, falsumque, & manifestæ experientiæ quotidianæ, ut rationem sileam, repugnat Quare dum varios & dissimiles effectus produxit, variè ab accidentibus mutatam, effictam, cohibitam, terminatam fuisse oportuit. Exemplo pulchrè explicabitur propositum negocium.
units.tr: It makes no difference here whether you say the causes are unchanged or the object on which they act is. It is enough that something has been added in this second action which was not in the first. For what has now been done differs from what was done before. But this is an accident, by which the two effects differ. It follows that the action was now affected differently than before. And that a cause can never act in exactly the same way is plainly evident from this. A cause that cannot act unless it is, as it were, shaped and bounded by accidents, now one way and now another, produces its effects in that way by accident. Whoever does not know this does not understand what has been said, through lack of skill. For if the same enduring cause produced them, that is, if its action were not terminated, directed, impeded, aided, and finally bounded and restrained by accidental causes and qualities, it would necessarily produce all its effects wholly alike. But this is impossible and false, and it contradicts everyday experience, not to mention reason. Therefore, since it produced various and dissimilar effects, it must have been varied, shaped, restrained and terminated by being changed by accidents. The matter in hand will be made clear by an example.

units.la: Hominē per se hominis causam esse omnino constat. Huius autem hominis, videlicet Petri, nō homo absolutè, sed certus homo, Paulus, exempli gratia, genitor siue effectrix causa est. Sicut iā Paulus generat non solum quatenus homo est, verum etiā quatenus talis homo est, nimirum crassus, robustus, ingeniosus, callidus, iuuenis, sanus, &c. ita non absolutè homine, sed certis qualitatibus prędītum[?] vestitumq; homine generat: vt marem, aut foeminam, pulchrum, aut deformem, diuitem, aut pauperem, claudum, aut integrum, industriū, aut ignauum. Dico igitur in Petro considerandā, primùm quidem, quòd est homo, deinde quòd est mas, quòd sanus, quòd pulcher, quòd ingeniosus, &c. Hæc quia toto genere & natura inter se differunt, non potuerunt ab vna eademque causa, quatenus vna, per se facta esse.
units.tr: It is wholly agreed that a man is per se the cause of a man. But of this man, namely Peter, the cause or begetter is not man in the abstract but a certain man, Paul, for example. Just as Paul begets not only insofar as he is a man, but also insofar as he is such a man, namely stout, robust, clever, shrewd, young, healthy, and so on, so he begets not man absolutely but a man endowed and clothed with certain qualities: male or female, handsome or ugly, rich or poor, lame or whole, industrious or lazy. I say, therefore, that in Peter we must consider, first, that he is a man; then that he is male, healthy, handsome, clever, and so on. Since these differ from one another in their whole kind and nature, they could not have been made per se by one and the same cause, insofar as it is one.

units.la: Aphabet[?] omnia hæc à Paulo. Quòd homo est, ab ipso tanquam ab homine per se habet, qua ratione ab alijs hominibus non differt. Siquidem neque Paulus generans, quatenus homo est, ab alijs distinctus est hominibus. Quia ergo homo, qua homo est, nunquam mutatur, similem sibi semper effectum producit, scilicet hominem. At quòd pulcher est Petrus, quòd ingeniosus, &c. à plerisque, imò ab omnibus alijs differt. Quæ cum à generante similiter acceperit, constat generantem illis tunc qualitatibus fuisse circumscriptum, quibus talem, non alium, generaret. Atqui per accidens ineraat hæ qualitates Paulo. Accidit enim ei, vt, cum generaret Petrum, tales omnes qualitates & circumstantiæ concurrerēt, per quas posset generare talem hominem, non alium, siue talibus affectum qualitatibus, nō alijs, quibus videlicet differret à cunctis alijs hominibus. Nam si per se ipsi adfuissent, perpetuò adfuissent. Semper ergo aut certè plerunque talem præcisè generasset. Hoc autem falsum. Per accidens igitur generauit Petrum, hoc est, talem hominem qualis est Petrus, non alium. Equidē pulchritudo, deformitas, robur, imbecillitas, &c. accidunt hominibus, non per se insunt cuiquam. Quæ cum non sine causa orta sint, necesse est ab simili, hoc est, accidentali causa effecta esse. Quare accidisse necesse est Paulo generanti talia quædam, propter quæ, qui natus est, hisce potius quàm aliis insigneretur qualitatibus.
units.tr: All these things are from Paul. That he is a man he has from him per se, as a man, and in that respect he does not differ from other men. For Paul, begetting insofar as he is a man, is not distinguished from other men. Therefore, since man as man is never changed, he always produces a like effect, namely a man. But that Peter is handsome, clever, and so on, differs from most others, indeed from all. Since he received these from the begetter in a similar way, it is clear that the begetter was then bounded by those qualities by which he would beget such a man and not another. But these qualities were in Paul by accident. For it happened to him that, when he begot Peter, all such qualities and circumstances came together through which he could beget such a man and not another, or be affected by such qualities and not by others, by which Peter would differ from all other men. For if they had been present to him per se, they would have been present always. He would therefore always, or at least for the most part, have begotten exactly such a man. But this is false. Therefore he begot Peter by accident, that is, a man such as Peter is, and not another. Indeed beauty, deformity, strength, weakness, and so on, happen to men; they do not inhere in anyone per se. Since these have not arisen without cause, they must necessarily have been produced by a like, that is an accidental, cause. Hence it must have happened to Paul, as he begot, that certain things occurred, by reason of which the one born was marked with these qualities rather than others.

units.la: Quòd si iam Paulum iterum generare cogites, non generabit hominem in omnibus priori similem. (De tempore non loquor, sed aliis accidētibus tum corporis tum ani-mi, quatenus ratione caret. Nam de ratione prædita anima hæc[?] vera non sunt, nisi quatenus pro natura tempera-turæ & instrumentorum hoc magis modo quàm alio operatur.) Necessarium igitur est, non iisdem omnino accidentibus vallatum seu circunscriptum ad generandum accessisse, aut certè non eosdem comites habuisse. Supra nanque monui, nostra non referre siue in generante, siue in fœmina matre, siue in utrisque mutatum aliquid existimetur. Eundem sæpius generare si cogitaveris, dissimiles semper filios generare cernes. Non potest hoc in caussam quæ per se ipsi adsit, referri. Nã quod tale est, semper adest. Semper igitur aget, & eodem modo aget. Ergo accidisse aliud atque aliud, quoties ad generandum processit, omnino confiteri nos oportet, cuius causa ista in effectibus dis-similitudo sive disparitas nata sit. Quia non per accidens, sed per se homo est, semper hominem generat. Quia au-tem per accidens talis fuit, cum primò generaret, secundò non similiter omnino generavit. Facilè nanque & frequē-ter mutantur huiusmodi accidentia, quibus fœtus dispa-res gignantur.
units.tr: But if you now think of Paul begetting again, he will not beget a man wholly similar to the first. (I am not speaking of time, but of other accidents, both of body and of mind, insofar as the mind lacks reason. For these things are not true of the rational soul, except insofar as it operates in this way rather than that, according to the nature of the temperament and the instruments.) It is necessary, therefore, that the accidents surrounding or bounding him when he begot were not wholly the same, or at least that he did not have the same companions. For I have said above that it makes no difference to our argument whether something is thought changed in the begetter, in the female mother, or in both. If you think of the same man begetting often, you will always see him begetting dissimilar sons. This cannot be referred to a cause that is present per se. For what is present per se is always present. It would therefore always act, and act in the same way. Therefore we must wholly admit that something different happened each time he proceeded to beget, and it is by this cause that dissimilarity or disparity arose in the effects. Because he is a man per se, he always begets a man; but because he was such-and-such by accident, when he first begot, he did not beget wholly similarly the second time. For such accidents, by which offspring are begotten unlike, change easily and often.

units.la: Ergo cum à tali, non alia, quapiam affectione caussarūq; coitione unusquisq; generetur talis, qualis est, perspicuè apparet, quēlibet, quatenus talis est, per accidens generatū est. Accidit nāq; generanti, dū generaret, ut illo modo non aliter affectus ad generandū progrederetur. Non est satis ut vir fœcūdus mulieri fœcūdę congrediatur, sed cerro modo & tēpore cōiungi ipsos oportet. Præterea sanguinē, seminā, matricē, animos atq; mores, aëris tēperiem[?], aliaq; innu-merabilia merabilia, quæ ne intelligi quidem, nedum verbis exponi possunt, certa quadam ratione, mensura & proportione inter se concurrere oportet. Nisi enim ita, non aliter concurrant, aut non generabunt, aut non tale fœtum generabunt. Nam pro diuerso talium concursu, variari in fœtu accidentia nemo ignorat non rerum naturalium imperitus. Quid vel vnica faciat aëris temperies dilucidè Hippocr. exposuit in lib. de Aëre, aquis & locis, capitib. 10 & 12. Qui de cæteris similiter cogitabit, nihil frustra hîc dictum comperiet.
units.tr: Therefore, since each man is begotten such as he is by a certain affection and coming together of causes, and not by some other, it is clearly apparent that whatever is begotten insofar as it is such is begotten by accident. For it happens to the begetter, while he begets, that he proceeds to begetting not otherwise affected in that way. It is not enough that a fertile man should have intercourse with a fertile woman; they must be joined in a certain manner and at a certain time. Moreover, blood, seed, womb, spirits and morals, the temperature of the air, and countless other things, which cannot even be understood, let alone explained in words, must come together in a certain proportion, measure and reason. For unless they do so, they will either not concur at all, or will not beget, or will not beget such an offspring. For no one who is not ignorant of natural things is unaware that, according to the different concurrence of such things, accidents vary in the offspring. What the temperature of the air alone can do Hippocrates has clearly set out in the book On Airs, Waters and Places, chapters 10 and 12. Whoever considers the others in the same way will find that nothing has been said here in vain.

units.la: Ergo sicut infinitè omnia hæc mutari possunt, ita infinita & incomprehensibilia cernimus indiuiduorum discrimina. Qui de his dubitat, is parum se iudicio valere probat. Nam vt cætera mittam, quis dubiter [?], eundem hominem aliter affectos gignere liberos, cum est ebrius, valetudinarius, tristis, iratus, quàm cū est contrà affectus? Certè, vt ab initio dixi, tā sunt ista cunctis testata & nota hominib. vt non sine reprehensione pluribus probare me posse arbitrer.
units.tr: Therefore, just as all these things can be changed without limit, so we see infinite and incomprehensible differences among individuals. Whoever doubts this shows that he has little judgment. For to pass over other things, who could doubt that the same man begets children differently when he is drunk, sickly, sad or angry than when he is disposed otherwise? Certainly, as I said at the outset, these things are so attested and known to all men that I think I can prove them without being blamed by many.

units.la: Dicebamus suprà, causas naturales & particulares non producere suos effectus particulares aliter posse, quàm per accidens. Causam afferebamus, quia non nisi indiuiduas, hoc est, accidetib. inter se differentes res gignerent. Etenim reperire non est duo vnius eiusdēq; speciei prorsus similia indiuidua, multò minus diuersis in spiciebus similia esse aliqua possunt. At verò si non accidetibus different, similima esse oporteret vnius speciei omnia singularia. Et accidentium diuersitas cum ipsis nascitur. Quocirca necessarium est, vt vel ipsæ causæ mutatæ sint, vel alias atque alias qualitates inter agendum comites habeant, hoc est, in materiam aliter atque aliter affectam agant, vel vtrumque variatum sit. Hæc enim sunt omnis contingentiæ principia. At hæc accidisse ipsis certum est. Quare accidit ipsis vt dispares effectus generarent, sicut exemplo hominis dilucidè declaraui. Generantur igitur talia omnia per accidens. At de talibus solis Astrologi diuinant, de effectibus scilicet per accidens euenturis. Cæterum hæc arte nulla possunt doceri aut comprehendi, vt omnes omnium ætatum docti homines summo consensu semper censuerunt. Quamobrem sapien-tissimè præceperunt, ne talium præsentiam affectemus aut speremus arte nos consecuturos. Qui enim artem se inuenturum sperat, per quam, quæ rebus accidens, possunt, præsentiat?
units.tr: I said above that natural and particular causes cannot produce their particular effects otherwise than by accident. The reason I gave was that they would produce only individuals, that is, things differing from one another in accidents. For one cannot find two wholly similar individuals of one and the same species, much less can any be similar across different species. But if they did not differ in accidents, all the singulars of one species would have to be most alike. And diversity of accidents arises together with the individuals. Hence it is necessary either that the causes themselves be changed, or that they have different qualities as companions in acting, that is, that they act upon matter affected now one way, now another, or that both be varied. For these are the principles of all contingency. But it is certain that these things happen to them. Therefore it happens to them to produce dissimilar effects, as I have clearly shown by the example of man. Such things, then, are produced by accident. But astrologers divine only about such things, namely effects that will occur by accident. Yet such things cannot be taught or grasped by any art, as all learned men of all ages have always held with the highest consensus. Wherefore the wise have very rightly warned us not to aim at, or hope to attain by art, a foreknowledge of such things. For who hopes to find an art by which he could foresee what can happen to things by accident?

units.la: Cæterum quærat hic forte aliquis, si particularia tantū fiant, & præter hæc nihil, hæc autem per accidens omnia fiant, vt expositum est, quomodo non sequuntur omnia per accidens nasci, & nullius rei cognitionem ab homine haberi posse? Ego mehercle non vereor cum optimis quibusque philosophis, & ipsa rerum evidentia affirmare, particularia omnia, quæ sunt eiusmodi, per accidens fieri, vt est declaratum. Verùm hinc non sequi aio, per accidens omnia fieri, multo minus nullius rei nos scientiam aut cognitionem habere. Nam, vt quæ hic aptè dici possent omittam omnia, in particularibus communem quandam esse naturam, quæ non per accidens, sed per se fit, (suprà satis clarè exposui. Homo enim non fit per accidens; sed talis homo videlicet longus, breuis, pulcher, deformis, robustus, crassus, infirmus, gracilis, pauper, dives per accidens generatur. Siquidem parentibus nostris accidit, vt vel diuites vel pauperes essent, deformes & pulchri, russi, pallidi, &c. dum nos generarent. Homo autem ab homine per se ge-neratus est, quia qui generauit nos, non per accidens homo erat. Vnde fit, vt quarenus homines sumus, nullum inter nos discrimen inueniatur. Quare homo per se generatur, talis autem homo per accidens nascitur.
units.tr: Here someone may perhaps ask: if only particulars come to be, and nothing beyond them, and if all these come about by accident, as has been set out, why would it not follow that everything arises by accident, and that man can have no knowledge of anything? By Hercules, I do not hesitate, with all the best philosophers and with the very evidence of things, to affirm that all particulars of this kind come about by accident, as has been declared. But I say it does not follow from this that everything comes about by accident, much less that we have no science or knowledge of anything. For, to omit all the things that could fittingly be said here, among particulars there is a certain common nature which comes about not by accident but per se, as I have explained clearly enough above. Man is not produced by accident; but such a man, tall, short, handsome, ugly, strong, fat, weak, slender, poor or rich, is generated by accident. For it happened to our parents, while they were begetting us, that they were rich or poor, ugly or handsome, ruddy, pale, and so on. But man is generated by man per se, because the one who begot us was not a man by accident. Hence, insofar as we are men, no difference is found among us. So man is generated per se, but such a man is born by accident.

units.la: Quæ tamen ita intelligi oportet, si ad nostram cognitionem, non ad Dei max.optimique consilium referantur. Is enim causas illas, quæ fortuito & casu nobis convenisse cum causis per se vocatis videntur, suo arbitratu & modo nobis ineffabili imperceptibilique sic[?] cogit, aptat, iungit, idoneas reddit, vt talem quempiam, non alium, effectum simul pariant. Si rem ipsam spectemus, non ad nostrum captum referamus, non dubium est, quin pulcher & inge-niosus homo ex causis certo modo inter se iunctis per se, non autem per accidens, producatur. Et si semper eo mo-do, do,non aliter, omnes coirent, certum est semper pulchros & ingeniosos producturas esse, nosq; tales nascituros omnino praedicere possemus. Quia vero ista non pertinent ad hominis substantiam, sed jam accedunt, mox recedunt, neq; naturali aliqua lege colligata sunt, fortuita ratione conue-nire nobis dicuntur. Nobis ergo per accidens eveniunt, ut qui nulla vi mentis praeintelligere quimus, quae aut quot & quomodo inter se concursura sint, quae hoc modo acci-dunt. Quae facta jam sunt, cognoscere saepe possumus, co-gnitis causis ex quibus & a quibus facta sunt. Non enim quatenus sunt jam, per accidens sunt. At eadem, dum futu-ra erant, & ita, quatenus scilicet futura adhuc essent, con-siderarentur, per accidens utique nobis futura esse vere ac recte dicebantur tunc, cum fieri nondum incepissent, aut incepisse fieri nos ignoraremus.
units.tr: Yet this must be understood only if these things are referred to our knowledge, not to the plan of God, most great and best. For he, by his own judgment and in a manner ineffable and imperceptible to us, so drives, fits, joins and renders apt those causes which seem to us to have come together by chance and accident with causes called per se, that together they bring forth just this or that effect and not another. If we look at the thing itself, and do not refer it to our grasp, there is no doubt that a handsome and clever man is produced per se, not by accident, from causes joined together in a certain fixed way. And if they always came together in that same way and never otherwise, it is certain that they would always produce handsome and clever offspring, and we could predict infallibly that such children would be born. But because these things do not pertain to the substance of man, and instead come and go at once, and are not bound by any natural law, they are said to meet us by a fortuitous reason. Therefore they happen to us by accident, since by no power of mind can we foresee beforehand which causes will concur, how many, and in what way, and these things happen in this way. Things that have already come to pass we can often know, once we know the causes from which and by which they were made. For insofar as they now are, they are not by accident. But the same things, while they were still to be, and considered in that way, insofar as they were still future, were rightly and truly said to be future to us by accident, at the time when they had not yet begun to come into being, or when we did not know they had begun.

units.la: Summa igitur est, naturalia, si ut vere particularia, hoc est, suis peculiaribus accidentibus distincta ab aliis, & ut futura considerentur, per accidens omnia fieri ac nasci. Nam ut a certo aliquo causarum concursu effectus quispiam per se efficiatur, per accidens tamen nobis ortum hoc esse, quia syndrome illa causarum quolibet fere temporis momen-to permutetur. Quod si per se omnia sic in principali ge-nerante fuissent, semper in eo permansura etiam fuisse. Sin autem ut communem in se naturam habent sive essentiam, quae accidentibus priuatis subsistunt, aut quatenus jam facta sunt, considerentur, nihil prohibere, quin & per se facta dicamus, & notitiam plurimarum omnino rerum evidentem ac certam habeamus. Praeterea quae nobis fortuita sint ac dicantur, si ad nostram imbecillem intelligentiam refe-rantur, ea certa ratione omnia & per se evenire, si ad im-mensam & inscrutabilem Dei sapientiam reducantur. In quam sententiam scitissimè & planè divinè Hippocrates scribit, ἡμῖν μὲν αὐτόματον[?], τῷ δὲ θεῷ μηδὲν αὐτόματον. Sic philo-sophi elegantiores omnes docuerunt. Tales autem appel-lo, qui nec imperiti, nec ἀξιοί[?] fuerunt.
units.tr: The sum, then, is this: natural things, if they are taken as truly particular, that is, distinguished from others by their own peculiar accidents, and if they are considered as future, all come about and are born by accident. For although some effect is brought about per se from a certain definite concurrence of causes, it is nevertheless an accidental occurrence for us, because that concurrence of causes changes almost every moment of time. But if all things were thus per se in the principal generating cause, they would also have been going to remain always in it. But if they are considered as having a common nature or essence in themselves, which subsists in private accidents, or insofar as they are already made, there is nothing to prevent us from saying that they are also made per se, and that we have an evident and certain knowledge of very many things. Moreover, whatever things seem and are called fortuitous to us, if they are referred to our feeble understanding, all of them come about per se by a certain fixed reason, if they are traced back to the immense and unsearchable wisdom of God. To this effect Hippocrates writes most wisely and quite divinely: "To us, chance; to God, nothing is by chance" [hēmin men automaton, tō de theō mēden automaton]. All the more elegant philosophers have taught in the same way. I call such men notable, who were neither unlearned nor of no account.

units.la: Utrunq; igitur probatum a me jam vides, Astrologos cir-ca particularia praevidenda versari, & eiusmodi, si nostrae cognitioni comparentur. nō nisi per accidens cuenire. An non hinc perficitur concluditurq; necessaria ratione, illa omnia præsciri arte nulla posse, anteaquam fieri iam & esse aliquo pacto incipiant? Dico autem hoc propter Medicos, Nautas, Agricolas, Prudentes viros. Hi enim omnes præsagire futura contingentia recte dicuntur, quantumuis Vates seu diuinatores proprie nec sint, nec nominari possint. Non enim quæ prædicunt, ante futura enunciant, quàm fieri iam obseruarint, vt alibi expositum mihi memini.
units.tr: So you see that I have now proved both points: that the astrologers are concerned with foreseeing particulars, and that such things, if compared with our knowledge, come about only by accident. Does it not follow and is it not concluded, by necessary reasoning, that none of those things can be known in advance by any art before they have already begun to be and to exist in some way? I say this on account of physicians, sailors, farmers and prudent men. For all of these are rightly said to foretell contingent future events, although they are not, and could not properly be called, seers or diviners. For what they predict they do not announce before the future, but only after they have observed it already coming to be, as I remember having explained elsewhere.

units.la: Et si quis Astrologum non prorsus imperitum interroget, qua ratione horum prædictiones præcipuè differat ab Astrologorū vaticinijs, aliud nō poterit respondere, quàm paulo ante enumeratos viros ex actione & inspectione proximarum causarum de illis rebus duntaxat coniectare, quas iam fieri aliquo modo cognouerint, Astrologos autem multo ante quàm fieri inceperint, ex motu siderum prædiui-nare solere. Miror certè eos ne tum quidem sententiæ suæ pudere, cum philosophos audiunt dicentes, harum rerum præsensionem antequam fiant, captum nostrum excedere, omnemq; diuinationem (μαντικήν vocant Græci) inspiratione Deorum (ita illi Dæmones, quos colebat Gentilitas, appellabant) fieri. Ac sunt interim, qui se diuinatores siue μάντεις esse negent, propterea nimirū, quia prædictam vocem ita vsurpatam bonis autoribus perspexerunt, vt iam monebam. Verùm enim verò si diuinator est, qui futura contingentia, non cognitis proximis eorū causis, præscire se posse ex communibus remotis, indefinitis & per accidēs causis, dictitat opinaturq;, non possunt non veri diuinatores esse Astrologi. Nam ex coelorū siderumq; motu, situ, viribus hariolātur, causas proximas, à quibus singulæ res naturam, formā, operationes, proprietates, & deniq; totū hoc qd' sunt, accipiūt, neq; cognoscūt neq; cognoscere studēt.
units.tr: And if one should question an astrologer who is not altogether unskilled, as to the reason by which the predictions of these men differ chiefly from the prophecies of the astrologers, he will be able to answer nothing other than that the men just listed conjecture from the action and observation of proximate causes only about those things which they have already come to know are happening in some way, whereas the astrologers are accustomed to foretell from the motion of the stars long before the things begin to happen. I am certainly amazed that they are not ashamed of their opinion even when they hear the philosophers saying that foreknowledge of these things before they happen exceeds our capacity, and that all divination (the Greeks call it mantikē) comes by the inspiration of the gods (so those demons whom the Gentile world worshipped were called). And there are meanwhile some who deny that they are diviners or diviners [mantis], plainly because they have perceived that this word has been so used by good authors, as I have already warned. But truly, if a diviner is one who claims and holds that he can foreknow contingent future events, without knowing their proximate causes, from common, remote, indefinite and accidental causes, then the astrologers cannot fail to be true diviners. For from the motion, position and powers of the heavens and stars they divine, and they neither know nor seek to know the proximate causes from which each thing receives its nature, form, operations, properties, and finally all that it is.

units.la: Satis iam euidenter ostensum explanatumq; est, etiam proprias & definitas rerum causas hic nihil generare, nisi varie accidentibus formētur & vestiantur, seu circumscribantur ad ta'lem aliquem effectum producēdum. Quanto magis hoc in remotissimis & generalissimis causis fieri oporoportet: Falsum ergo est, quod se ex veris caussis futura præ-dicere gloriatur. Qui namq; causas rerū per accidēs intue-tur, & in illis se, quæ lōgo post tēpore euentura sunt, prospicere inuenireq; credit, is perinde facit, ac si causæ rerū essent, quas ipse esse credidisset, vel esse voluisset. Sed ad rē re-deo. Quia Astrologorum omnes prædictiones inuestigant siue præsagiunt de rebus per accidēs futuris, (horū autē ars nulla est) patet Astrologiā nō esse artē, quæ, quod illi sperāt ac optant, præstare queat. Frustra igitur naturalis dicitur, & donū Dei putatur. Nō à Deo, sed aliunde deliramēta & su-perstitiones istæ profectæ sunt, à curiosis & vanis homini-bus. Tametsi nāq; à Dæmonibus excogitatas nō negemus, opera tamen talium vti pro sua consuetudine voluerunt.
units.tr: It has now been shown and explained quite plainly enough that even the proper and definite causes of things generate nothing here, unless they are shaped and clothed in various accidents, or circumscribed so as to produce some such effect. How much more must this happen in the most remote and most general causes! It is therefore false that the astrologers boast of foretelling the future from true causes. For whoever looks at the causes of things by accident, and believes that he can see and discover in them those things which are going to happen long afterwards, does just the same as if the causes of things were those which he himself had believed, or had wished, them to be. But I return to the matter. Since all the predictions of the astrologers seek out or foretell things that are future by accident, and there is no art of these things, it is clear that astrology is not an art able to achieve what they hope and wish for. Therefore it is called natural in vain, and is thought to be a gift of God. These delusions and superstitions did not proceed from God, but from curious and vain men elsewhere. Although we do not deny that they were devised by demons, nevertheless they chose to use the work of such men for their own customary purposes.

units.la: Hactenus duobus argumentis præcipuis vanū & falsum ostendi Astrologorū conatū. Primùm quia eiusmodi scire, antequā fiant, laboriosè studēt, quæ per accidēs fiunt. Dein-de quia non in suis veris caussis futura quærunt. Summam vtriusq; breuiter iterum repetere libet, quo vel sic dilucida sint omnia, & facilius adhæreant. Ac quod ad prius attinet, tam perspicuè ostendi, tam apertis exēplis declarau, & tam copiosè exposui, omnia quæ hic fiūt particularia, quatenus talia sunt, per accidens fieri, vt non aūsim aliquid repetere. Explanaui illud etiā, quomodo nihilominus quædam, imò plurima per se fiant cognoscíq; possint. Et de talibus nihil hic amplius. Quēadmodū nec de eo quidē, quomodo Nau-tæ, Rustici, Medici, Prudētia præstātes viri, plurima cōtingē-tia particularia rectè tū præuideant, tū prædicāt. Præuident enim in suis caussis veris. Nec hoc modo, sed tūc solum, cū iam fieri quodammodo, aut certè esse perspexerunt.
units.tr: Thus far, by two chief arguments, I have shown the futility and falsity of the astrologers' attempt. First, because they labour to know beforehand those things which come about by accident. Second, because they do not seek the future in its true causes. It is pleasing to repeat briefly the sum of both, so that all things may be clearer even in this way and cling more easily. As to the first, I have shown so plainly, declared with such clear examples, and set out so fully that all the particulars that happen here, insofar as they are such, come about by accident, that I do not dare to repeat anything. I have also explained how, nevertheless, some things, indeed very many, come about and can be known per se. And nothing more here about such things. Nor, indeed, about this either: how sailors, rustics, physicians and men excelling in prudence rightly foresee and foretell many contingent particulars. For they foresee them in their true causes. Nor do they do so in this way, but only then, when they have perceived in some manner that the thing is already coming to be, or at least already is.

units.la: Illud certum est, futura nō esse præsentia intellectui, quatenus futura sunt. Nō enim sine tempore homo intelligit, nec semel omnia comprehendit mēs humana, sed aliud ex alio, vel post aliud intelligit, sicut aliud ex alio fit, aut aliud post aliud consequētia quadā nota cōsequitur. Quamobrē si quid, cum non est, videt intellectus futurum esse necesse est, vt ex eo quod videt tanquā effectum ex causa nasciturum, aut certè necessaria cohæsione secuturum perviderit. Si causam necessario suum effectum producere nouerit, certò futurum praedixerit vtiq;. Si in vtranq; partem æquè inclinet, hoc tantum cognouerit, fieri posse vt sequatur effectus, fieri etiam posse vt non sequatur. Quòd si causam, quæ præsens intellectui est, sciat nō nisi per accidens effectū suum certum proferre, nihil præsciet aliud, quàm varios effectus consequi posse huius causæ actionem, pro vario secundarum causarum siue accidentium confluxu. Talis namq; semper est præscientia, qualis est causa eum producens. At contingentia à contingentibus manare causis controuersia caret. Quo fit vt prædicti artifices ne ex causis quidem illarum rerum, quarum præsensionem inuestigat, ante concludere aliquid possint ac velint, quàm producere iam incepisse eas obseruauerint suos effectus. Alias inepta esset omnis ipsorum praesagitio, sicut Astrologorum inepta est & inartificiosa.
units.tr: It is certain that future things, insofar as they are future, are not present to the intellect. For a human being does not understand without time, nor does the human mind grasp everything at once; rather it understands one thing after another, just as one thing comes about from another, or follows another by some connection of sequence. Therefore, if the intellect sees something as future, which does not yet exist, it must have perceived that it will arise from what it sees as its cause, as an effect from a cause, or at least follow by a necessary connection. If it knows that a cause will necessarily produce its effect, it will surely predict that the effect will come about. If it inclines equally to either side, it will know only this: that the effect may follow, and may also not follow. But if it knows that a cause, which is present to the intellect, produces its effect with certainty only by accident, it will foreknow nothing beyond that this action of the cause can have various effects, according to the varying concurrence of secondary causes or accidents. For foreknowledge is always of the kind that its cause is. But that contingent things arise from contingent causes is beyond dispute. So it is that the aforementioned craftsmen cannot, and do not wish to, conclude anything even from the causes of those things whose foreknowledge they seek, before they have observed that these causes have already begun to produce their effects. Otherwise all their prognostication would be pointless, just as the prognostication of the astrologers is pointless and unskilled.

units.la: Sed quoniam ipsos amplis efflare buccis semper audio, causas se obseruare, illud ostendere volui, ipsos causas illorum, quorum præscientiam sibi falso arrogāt, & quorum causa prædictiones à parum cautis expetuntur, omnino ignorare. Nam si proximæ indiuiduarum rerum causæ, quatenus vtiq; talem aliquem certum productureque[?] sunt effectum, homini sunt incognitæ, nec vlla naturali percipi possunt, antequam vel produxerint vel iam producat suos effectus, quis Astrologos arte cognouisse ipsas credat? Sūt enim homines, nec vlla in re cæteris feliciores, imò plerūq; minus sunt in bonis literis multis aliis versati & exercitati. Nisi enim ita esset, non tanto conatu tantas defendere nugas tentarent. Quare falsum est, quod perpetuò iactitare solent, se ex cœlo prædiscere futura posse arte Astrologiæ.
units.tr: But since I constantly hear them boasting loudly that they observe causes, I wanted to show that they utterly ignore the causes of those things whose foreknowledge they falsely claim for themselves, and for which predictions are sought by the less cautious. For if the proximate causes of individual things, insofar as they are certainly going to produce some such effect, are unknown to men and cannot be perceived by any natural means before they have produced or are producing their effects, who would believe that the astrologers know them by their art? For they are men, and not more fortunate than others in anything; indeed they are often less versed and practised in the good letters than many others. For if this were not so, they would not attempt with such effort to defend such great trifles. Therefore it is false what they constantly boast, that they can foreknow future things from the heavens by the art of astrology.

units.la: Nō nego hic, quod supra declaraui, causas per se & proximas plurimarum in natura rerum, vt canis, hominis, pyri, mali, & similium cognosci. Hoc dico, non cognosci quibus accidentibus circumscriptæ generent, vt talem quempiam, non alium, effectum consecuturum suspicari conijcereq; valeamus. At talia præscire prædicere neque[?] se posse iactitant Astrologi, beneficio Astrologiæ suæ. Hominem ab homine, canem à cane, & quidem venaticum à venatico, pira à piris generari omnes norunt. Nemo certè talia scisciretur ab Astrologo, uti nec an mespilus mespila producat. Hoc desideret aliquis praevidere, & Astrologum percunctetur fortasse, utrum pirus multa sui generis pira hoc anno sit productura an non, magna an parua, bene matura sint futura an nō, an grando illis sit incommodum allatura vel non, & quae huius generis alia dici possunt. At per accidens à piro fieri constat, quod vno anno paucos, bonos, coctos: alio autē multos, malos crudos, &c. fructus produ-cit. Quippe accidit ei causa talis (aut ipsi aut materiae) pro-pter quā multa vel pauca, magna vel parva, &c. profert. Sed haec supra sunt declarata. Ad rem igitur. Concedo, inquies, futura, quae sunt talia, non posse aliter quam in suis causis prospici. At Astrologos causas nescire nego. Norunt enim siderum varios congressus, à quibus talia efficiuntur. Re-spondeo, sidera vniuersalissimas cunctarum rerum com-munes esse causas, ideoque non vnam rem magis quàm aliā quamuis, quod ad ipsa attinet, producere. Vt enim per se sola nihil horum efficiunt, de quibus sermo & disceptatio nobis fuit instituta, ita cum secundis causis quibuslibet, perficiunt ac generant quaelibet. Si in illis causis, quae sunt rei producendae quasi continuatae & proximae, & ad certum determinatumq; effectum producendum à natura factae, praevidere futura nequimus, quomodo quaeso in illis per-spiciemus, quae omnia cum omnibus efficere debent, per se solas nihil talium generant?
units.tr: I do not deny here what I have declared above, that the proximate causes of most things in nature, such as of a dog, a man, a pear tree, an apple tree and the like, are known in themselves. I say only that we do not know with what accidents, when circumscribed, they produce this or that effect rather than another, so that we might suspect or conjecture such a thing. But the astrologers boast that by the benefit of their astrology they can foresee and predict such things. Everyone knows that a man is generated from a man, a dog from a dog, and a hunting dog from a hunting dog, and pears from pears. No one would certainly learn such things from an astrologer, any more than whether a medlar produces a medlar. Someone may wish to foresee this, and perhaps ask the astrologer whether a pear tree will bear many pears of its kind this year or not, large or small, whether they will be well ripened or not, whether hail will bring harm to them or not, and whatever else of this kind can be said. But it is established that a pear tree produces in one year few, good, and ripe fruit, and in another many, bad, and unripe fruit, and so on. For it happens to it by such a cause (either in itself or in its matter), on account of which it bears many or few, large or small, and so on. But these things have been declared above. To the point, then. You will say: I grant that future things of this kind cannot be foreseen except in their causes. But I deny that the astrologers know the causes. For they know the various conjunctions of the stars, from which such things are brought about. I reply: the stars are the most universal common causes of all things, and therefore, so far as they are concerned, they do not produce one thing more than another. For just as by themselves alone they produce none of those things about which our discussion and dispute has been undertaken, so with whatever secondary causes they produce and generate whatever things. If we cannot foresee future things in those causes which are, as it were, continuous and proximate to the thing to be produced, and which are made by nature for producing a certain and determinate effect, how, I ask, shall we perceive them in those causes which must produce all things together with all, and which by themselves alone generate none of these things?

units.la: Res omnes verè ab illis causis profectae generataeq; dicuntur, quae suam cuique essentiam, speciem siue naturam contribuerunt, & seipsas rebus generatis communicarunt. Quae autem omnia aequè mouent, omnibus eadem sunt, & omnia talia efficiūt, quales intermediae sunt causae, quae in agendo concurrunt, illae inquam prorsus per accidens particulariū causae existimandae sunt. Equidem inter actionem siderum, & effectus, qui hic in terra fiunt, causas alias innumerabiles, hominiq; incomprehensibiles per ac-cidens interuenire nemo ignorat. At hae omnes vt effectus vel fiant, vel non fiant, aut certè tales, non alij, fiant, per-ficiunt. Si inter hominem generantem & eum qui gene-ratur tam multæ intercidunt causæ actionem generatis ad-iuuantes, impedientes, terminantes, & huc non aliò diri-gentes, quot putabimus inter hanc generantem atq; coe-lum interuenire? Multò sanè plures quàm quisquam no-strum aut intelligere possit, aut cogitet. Tales igitur cum lege nulla certa naturali inter sese cohæreant, sed fortuitò concurrant, si nostram intelligentiam consulas, sapienter philosophi proximas & per se causas intuendas proposuerunt. Quod si natura cohærerent, nec temerè ita conuenirent, vel semper vel plerunque sic coirent. Quo posito, effectus semper aut plerunq; omni ex parte similes produce-rentur. Quod hoc testimonio mentis, atq; omnium quoq; sensuum judicio falsum sit, ac nunquam aut omnino rarif-simè eveniat, nemo nescit.
units.tr: All things are rightly said to have been truly produced and generated by those causes which contribute to each thing its essence, species or nature, and have communicated themselves to the things generated. But those causes which move all things equally are the same for all, and produce all such things as the intermediate causes that concur in acting are; those, I say, must be regarded as entirely accidental causes of particular things. Indeed, no one is ignorant that between the action of the stars and the effects which occur here on earth, innumerable other causes intervene by accident, incomprehensible to man. But all of these bring it about that the effects either come to be or do not come to be, or certainly that such effects, and not others, come to be. If between a man generating and the one who is generated so many causes intervene, assisting, impeding, terminating the action of generation, and directing it not here or there, how many shall we think intervene between this generating power and the heavens? Far more than any of us can understand or imagine. Since, therefore, such causes cohere by no fixed natural law among themselves, but meet by chance, if you consult our understanding, the philosophers wisely proposed that the proximate and per se causes be considered. But if they cohered by nature, they would not come together by chance in this way; they would always or for the most part unite in this manner. Given this, effects would always or for the most part be produced entirely alike in every respect. That this is false, by the testimony of the mind and the judgment of all the senses, and that it never or very rarely happens, no one is unaware.

units.la: Rectè ergo ijdem sapientes philosophi, divinationem suis Dijs, cum verum Deum ignorarent, adscripserunt. Facilè illi perspexerunt, ab eo tantum præuideri talia posse, qui cōcursum illum causarum accidentalem perspiceret, imò qui hoc non alio modo cogere eas posset. Quod verò non vlla creatura aut videat, aut cogere possit, certum est. Quare reliquum est, vt Deo opt. max. soli hoc tribuamus, cui etiam soli convenit. Huius ergo gloriæ & honori tantum detrahunt tum Astrologi tum alij Divinatores, quantum præscientiæ futurorum sibi arrogant. Ex quibus evidenti & necessaria prorsus ratione concluditur, tam non esse Astrologiam aut Naturalem aut Donum Dei, vt Deo maximè aduerserur. Vale felicissimè.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, these same wise philosophers ascribed divination to their gods, since they did not know the true God. They easily perceived that such things could be foreseen only by one who perceived that accidental concurrence of causes, and who could even compel them in no other way. That no creature either sees or can compel these things is certain. Therefore it remains that we ascribe this to God, the best and greatest, to whom alone it belongs. So much, then, do the astrologers and the other diviners take away from this glory and honour, as much as they arrogate to themselves the foreknowledge of future things. From this it is concluded by a clear and wholly necessary reasoning that astrology is neither natural nor a gift of God, but is most opposed to God. Farewell most happily.

units.la: Anno 58.[?] prid. Palmarum, Fracoforto ex Nundinis.
units.tr: Given the day before Palm Sunday, in the year 58, at Frankfurt during the fair.

units.la: Epistola XI.
units.tr: Epistle XI.

units.la: LITERAS tuas Non. Augusti scriptas, ego hic 18. Calend. Septembris accepi, attenteq; perlegi. Sic enim sentio, quod de Astrologia tu aliter sentis atq; ego, id amicitiæ nostræ, quæ mutua multorum annorum benevolentia plurimum creuit, rationes perturbare non debere. Non enim possumus eadem omnes aut videre aut sentire, sed alijs aliud pulchrum iucundumq; videtur. Spero te eodem in me, quo ego in te animo affectum esse. Id ut crederem, vel hoc mihi persuasit, quòd te apud cõuictores tuos, magna contentione defendere, librum à me editum, conatum fuisse scribis. Pro quo tibi officio gratias merito ago.
units.tr: I received your letter, dated the Nones of August, here on the 18th day before the Kalends of September, and I have read it through carefully. I feel that because you judge Astrology differently from me, our friendship, which has grown greatly through many years of mutual goodwill, ought not to be disturbed by reasoning. We cannot all see or feel the same things; what seems beautiful and pleasing to one seems otherwise to another. I hope you feel towards me as I feel towards you. What persuades me of this, above all, is your report that you have defended my published book with great energy against your fellow-disputants. I thank you rightly for this kindness.

units.la: Scribis deinde, posse te vltra tres significationes huius vocis, Naturalis, à me positas, septem aut octo alias apud viros doctos, imò apud Hippocratem atq; Galenum ostendere. Hic sanè attentionem atq; diligentiam in te requiro. Neq; enim mihi propositum fuit, si non me fallit memoria, in literis illis meis ostendere, quomodo hanc vocem authores vsurparint, sed quot modis de Astrologia diuinatrice rectè dici quiret. In Hippocr. & Galeni lectione aliquot iam annos versor, nec obiter solum obseruaui, quàm multiplex esset horum nominum, Naturæ, & Naturalis, vsus. Illo autem tempore hoc tantum quærebam, quot modis posset Astrologiæ rectè adhiberi.
