Cumq; ex tribus modis, quibus naturalis appellari posse videretur, nullus ei conuenire posset, nec alius tunc mihi modus occurreret, sicut ne nunc quidem occurrit, ignorare me scripsi, quid aut quam artem tu naturalem Astrologiam appellares. Et iam quoq; me non posse (tu malè suspicaris me nolle) intelligere, quid per naturalem Astrologiam tu intelligas, si non sub aliquo enumeratorum modorum continetur, libenter fateor. De quarto namque ne cogitare quidem debui, quasi de eo tu loquereris. Quæ motus obseruat, coniunctiones, oppositiones siderum notat, magnitudines metitur, & huius generis alia considerat, eam nemo cum τῇ μαντικῇ[?] eandem esse putauit. Rogo igitur te pro nostra amicitia proq; tua humanitate & eruditione absq; omni simulatione, à qua me semper alienum fuisse nosti, vt si alium tu modum nouisti, eum vt mihi indices.
units.tr: You next write that you can show seven or eight other meanings of the word "natural," beyond the three I set down, from learned men, indeed from Hippocrates and Galen. Here I certainly require your attention and care. If my memory serves, it was not my purpose in that letter to show how writers have used this word, but how many ways one can rightly speak of divinatory Astrology [τῇ μαντικῇ]. I have spent some years now on Hippocrates and Galen, and I have not merely noticed in passing how manifold the use of the words "nature" and "natural" is. At that time, however, I was asking only in how many ways Astrology could rightly be called natural. Since none of the three ways in which "natural" might be understood fitted it, and no other way came to mind then, as none comes to mind now, I wrote that I did not know what art you meant by "natural Astrology." And I readily confess that, unless what you mean by natural Astrology falls under one of the modes I listed, I cannot understand it (you wrongly suspect me of not wanting to). For I ought not even to have thought of a fourth mode, as if that were what you were speaking of. The art which observes the motions of the stars, notes their conjunctions and oppositions, measures their magnitudes, and considers other things of this kind, no one has ever thought to be the same as divination. I therefore ask you, for the sake of our friendship and your courtesy and learning, and without any pretence (which you know I have always been far from), that if you have discovered another mode, you point it out to me.

units.la: Scribis post haec, quae mihi de Ente per accidens, contingētibus, & caussis propinquis ac remotis scripta sint, à nullo Astrologo, quod quidē tu scias, negata fuisse, nec Astrologiam ea infirmare iudicas. Quî hoc quaeso? An non est vera haec ratiocinatio?
units.tr: After this you write that the things I wrote about what is accidental, about contingent events, and about near and remote causes have not, so far as you know, been denied by any astrologer, and you do not judge that Astrology is weakened by them. How so, I ask? Is not this reasoning sound?

units.la: Quae Astrologi se praescire & praedicere ex arte sua posse credunt, antequam eueniant, per accidens omnia futura sunt.
units.tr: Whatever astrologers believe they can foreknow and foretell from their art, before it happens, is all future by accident.

units.la: At quae per accidens futura sunt, arte nulla praesciri possunt. Eorum etenim quae per accidens fiunt, ars nulla, & ratio nulla esse potest. Ergo,
units.tr: But what is future by accident cannot be foreknown by any art. For there can be no art and no reasoning about what happens by accident.

units.la: Nihil eorum omnium, de quibus Astrologi diuinant, ex arte futurum praesciri potest.
units.tr: Therefore nothing of all those things about which astrologers divine can be foreknown from art as future.

units.la: Non ex his consequetur, Astrologiam vanam & inutilem esse? Quid hic reprehendis, maiorem ne, vt Logici appellant? At ne Scepticus quidem negauerit ipsam. Minorem negare similiter non potes, cum in superioribus literis à me probata sit, ac tu veram illa esse confessus hic sis. Quo pacto ergo suum Astrologia retinet vsum, si tota inutilis, vana & falsa existit? Breuius colligam.
units.tr: Does it not follow from this that Astrology is vain and useless? Why do you object here: to the major premise, as the logicians call it? But not even a Sceptic would deny it. Nor can you deny the minor premise, since it was proved in my earlier letter, and you have here admitted that it is true. How, then, does Astrology keep its practice, if it is wholly useless, vain and false? I shall draw the conclusion more briefly.

units.la: Per accidens futura, nec arte nec ratione praesciri possunt. Astrologicae omnes praedictiones circa effectus per accidens euenientes versantur. Ergo,
units.tr: Things future by accident can be foreknown neither by art nor by reasoning. All astrological predictions are concerned with effects that come about by accident. Therefore,

units.la: Astrologicarum praedictionum ars nulla est, sed inartificiosae omnes sunt & falsae.
units.tr: there is no art of astrological predictions, but all of them are unskilled and false.

units.la: Conuerte iam rationem & à caussis sumito, hoc vel simili modo.
units.tr: Now turn the argument round and take it from causes, in this or a similar way.

units.la: Cœlestia omnes effectus, de quibus Astrologi diuinare solent, per accidens efficiunt siue generant. Per accidens dico, non vt cū dicimus, obstructionem febrem interdum generare per accidens, quia per interuenientem putredinem mediam eam generet, sed ita, ut cum vulneratum ali-quem dicimus, vel quia mane de lecto surrexerit, vel quia domo exierit.
units.tr: Celestial causes produce or generate, by accident, all the effects about which astrologers are accustomed to divine. I say "by accident," not in the sense in which we say that an obstruction sometimes generates a fever by accident, because an intervening putrefaction in the middle generates it, but in the sense in which we say of someone who has been wounded that he was wounded because he rose from bed in the morning, or because he went out of the house.

units.la: At ex talis causæ notitia, nulla eiuscemodi effectuum præscientia artificiosa haberi potest. Quinimò ne cognosci quidem tales causæ, quatenus scilicet certum iam producere aptæ sunt effectum.
units.tr: But from knowledge of such a cause, no skilled foreknowledge of effects of this kind can be had. Indeed, such causes cannot even be recognised, at least insofar as they are fitted to produce a certain effect already.

units.la: Nulla ergo potest ex astris haberi artificiosa præsensio illarum rerū quas ab astris fieri Astrologi fabulātur, Astrologia ergo ars non est. Vana itaq; & putida [?] fabula est.
units.tr: Therefore no skilled foreknowledge of those things which astrologers fable are brought about by the stars can be had from the stars. Astrology, therefore, is not an art. It is a vain and foolish fable.

units.la: In superioribus literis, si rectè memoria teneo, effectus quosdam à cœlestibus per se nasci, non per accidens, ostendi, quos hic excipere non fuit necesse. Tales enim suo semper tempore eoq; statuto & necessario, non autem per accidens eveniunt. Siue hac siue illam rationem magis probes, parum intererit. Utraq; certè quod propositum est, perficit, & in superioribus ambæ sunt perspicuè evidenterq; comprobatæ. Astrologicas fabulas ita evertunt, ut vix alijs sit opus argumentis apud non ignaros veritatisq; amantes. Ex Aristotelis principijs desumtæ sunt, & nullum tu philosophum Astrologiam damnare dicere non es veritus. Sic vides te mea vel non attentè perlegisse, vel non satis quid vellem percepisse.
units.tr: In my earlier letters, if I remember correctly, I showed that certain effects are produced by the celestial bodies through themselves, not by accident, and these I did not need to exclude here. For such effects always happen at their own fixed and necessary time, not by accident. Whether you prefer this argument or that one will make little difference. Each certainly accomplishes what is proposed, and in my earlier letters both were clearly and evidently proved. They overturn astrological fables so thoroughly that there is hardly any need for other arguments among those who are not ignorant and who love the truth. They are drawn from the principles of Aristotle, and you did not hesitate to say that no philosopher condemns Astrology. Thus you see that you have either not read my words carefully, or have not sufficiently grasped what I wished to say.

units.la: Quòd me Astrologos scribis hæreticos, diabolicos, condemnatos appellasse, in eo parum amicè mecū agis. Nam in parte libri, quam ego addidi, nusquam, opinor, hæc reperies. In huius fine, ubi de origine Astrologiæ quædā scripsi, auxilio Dæmonum inventam, promotam, auctam, confirmatam aio, & eosdem Astrologis inspirare interdum futuri aliquid, (opinione hominum, non simpliciter futurum, nisi ipsi hoc facere decrerum habeāt, perficereq;, possint) ex authoritate D. Augustini affirmo. Idem hoc si ex propria dixissem authoritate, convicium tu nominasses? Sic arbitror, at non rectè tamen. Etenim quotidie omnes experimur, callidissimos hostes nostris sensibus se miscere, multa insinuare, ad scelera nos movere, sæpe etiam permovere, & quod maximè est miserandum, divini verbi semen ex animis interdum eripere teste grauissimo ipsomet Chri-sto. Attamen ex his nō conficiatur rectè, nos hereticos, diabolicos, cōdemnatos statim esse. Inanis ergo est hæc ratio-cinatio. Erastus ex Augustino ait, Dæmones nonnunquam Astrologis futura inspirare: ergo habet eos pro condemna-tis, hæreticis, & diabolo deditis hominibus. In priore libri parte, Sauonarolæ sensum expono & verba interpretor.
units.tr: As for your writing that I called the astrologers heretics, diabolical, and condemned, you deal with me rather unkindly in this. For in the part of the book which I added, I think you will find nowhere such things. At the end of it, where I wrote something about the origin of Astrology, saying that it was invented, promoted, increased and confirmed with the aid of demons, and that these same demons sometimes inspire astrologers with something future (not future absolutely, but in the opinion of men, unless they have decided to do this themselves and are able to bring it about), I affirm this on the authority of St Augustine. If I had said the same on my own authority, would you have called it an insult? I think so, but you would be wrong. For every day we all experience how the most cunning enemies mingle with our senses, insinuate many things, move us to crimes, and often even provoke us, and, what is most to be pitied, sometimes snatch the seed of the divine word from our minds, as Christ himself, the most weighty witness, testifies. Yet it does not follow rightly from this that we are at once heretics, diabolical, and condemned. This reasoning is therefore empty. "Erastus, following Augustine, says that demons sometimes inspire astrologers with future things; therefore he regards them as condemned, heretical men given over to the devil." In the earlier part of the book I set out Savonarola's meaning and interpret his words.

units.la: Parem negligentiam arguit, quòd parum habere eruditionis librum asseueras. Si de ea parte intelligi vis, quæ adiecta à me est, facilè tibi assentiar. Nō enim præcipuam mihi eruditionem vnquam arrogaui. Hoc verè de me affir-mare possum, me veritatis amantissimū & studiosissimum semper fuisse. Hac in parte nemini facilè cessero, in alijs cū nemine temerè certauero. Si verò de Sauonarolæ libello ita sentis, vide ne studium tuendæ Astrologiæ, vt hoc dicere-res ac sentires, impulerit. Vtinam hominis eruditionem non dico superare, sed exæquare nos valeamus. Cogitare etiā debebas, vtrumq; idiotis & vulgaribus scripsisse, quos ne illa quidem, quæ ruditer explicata sunt, intelligere satis posse ex eo perspicio, quòd ex illis quoq;, qui operam aliquam bonis literis nauarunt, non omnes firmamenta illius libri percipiunt. Cur igitur tantam in ipso eruditio-nem desideras, in quo nimia potius diligentia reprehendi queat? Vulgaribus scriptus est, non doctis, præsertim cum Picum hi legere possint, quem de præsenti controuersia doctissimè scripsisse, tu quoq;, cum aliter facere non possis, concedis. Hunc si tu aliquando attentè legisses, vt argu-mentorum quæ in eo leuissima videri possint, firmitatem intellexisses, non te patronum absurdissimæ causæ constituere voluisses. Si viri doctissimi scripta, qua oportet diligentia non expendisti, imprudenter sanè aliquid in Astro-logiæ patrocinium scribes, priusquam an ruinosa sint ip-sius fundamenta nec ne, diligentius exploraueris. Quan-quam si vel hunc ipsum libellum, vt Picum seponam, diligenter perpendere voles, videbis talia in ipso argumenta contineri, quæ arte nulla labefactar[?]. ab Astrologis possint, siue doctum putes siue indoctum.
units.tr: You charge me with a similar carelessness in saying that the book shows little learning. If you mean the part that I added, I will readily agree with you. For I have never claimed for myself any outstanding learning. This I can truly affirm of myself: I have always been a most devoted and eager lover of the truth. In this respect I shall readily yield to no one, and in others I shall not rashly contend with anyone. If, however, you think this way about Savonarola's little book, take care that the wish to defend Astrology has not driven you to say and think this. Would that we might be able not to say that we surpass the man's learning, but at least to equal it. You ought also to have considered that both parts were written for the unlearned and the common sort, whom I can tell from this alone could not understand even those things which were explained in a rough way: not all those who have devoted some effort to good letters grasp the foundations of that book. Why, then, do you demand such great learning in it, in which rather an excess of care could be blamed? It was written for common readers, not for the learned, especially since these can read Pico, who, as you yourself concede, since you cannot do otherwise, has written most learnedly on the present controversy. If you had once read him carefully, so as to understand the firmness of the arguments which in him may seem very slight, you would not have wished to set yourself up as the champion of an utterly absurd cause. If you have not weighed with proper diligence the writings of so learned a man, you will certainly be writing something rashly in defence of Astrology before you have examined more carefully whether its foundations are ruinous or not. Yet even if you want to weigh carefully this little book itself, setting Pico aside, you will see that it contains arguments of such a kind that they cannot be overthrown by astrologers by any art, whether you think them learned or unlearned.

units.la: Maiorem modestiam decere Christianos homines in quæstione dubia, nescio cur dicas. Nam nec immodestius quàm hominem Christianum & pium decet, quicquam scripsi, nec dubiam quæstionem tractaui. Nisi dubium id voces, quod non omnes magno animorum consensu comprobant. Hoc pacto vix aliquid in rerum natura non dubium reperias. An tu incertum esse ais, utrum Astrologia falsa sit & impia? At Deus max. opt. damnauit. Prophetæ impiam esse docuerunt. Sacræ scripturæ interpretes à Religione alienam iudicauerūt. Philosophi futilem comprobarunt. Imperatores ex hominū societate exterminandam censuerunt. Ratio inanem & putidam demōnstrat. Sensus falsam esse ostendunt. Quid dici potest amplius? Patet te libellum & meas literas parum diligenter legisse & considerasse. Partem huius, quod dixi, aliquam certè vidisses, si totum peruidere nequiuisses.
units.tr: I do not know why you say that Christian men ought to show greater modesty in a doubtful question. I have written nothing more immodest than befits a Christian and pious man, nor have I treated a doubtful question. Unless you call doubtful whatever not all men approve with great unanimity of minds. In this way you would scarcely find anything in nature that is not doubtful. Do you say it is uncertain whether astrology is false and impious? But God, most good and great, has condemned it. The prophets taught that it is impious. The interpreters of Holy Scripture judged it alien to religion. The philosophers proved it futile. Emperors decreed that it should be banished from human society. Reason shows it to be empty and foul. The senses show it to be false. What more can be said? It is plain that you have not read and considered my book and my letter with sufficient care. You would at least have seen some part of what I said, if you could not perceive the whole.

units.la: Quod mox viros quosdam doctos & claros, imò meum Principem me condemnare addis, te non sine perturbato animo hæc scripsisse ostendit. Quem ego Principem condemnem ipse videris. Ego librum in utriusque principis mei nomine prodire volui in publicum, ipsis ita volentibus. Perlectus illis est antea, quàm in publicum veniret. Quare quid tibi velis non video, nisi de hoc Principe, sub quo nunc ago & viuo, intelligi velis. At cum illum librum ederem, hic mihi Princeps planè erat incognitus, & ne nunc quidem scio quid hac de re sentiat. Quomodo ergo me condemnare scribis, de quorum sensu nihil conijcere potui. In utilitatem & usum vulgi, non in condemnationem editus est. Vnum hoc spectaui, ut idiotas à vanitate superstitiosa abstraherem & præmonerem [?], ne tam facilè sibi ab Astrologis imponi paterentur. Certè plurimum impediunt istæ fabulæ Medicorum consilia & studia, cum rectè mederi volunt.
units.tr: That you add that certain learned and distinguished men, indeed my Prince, condemn me, shows that you wrote these things not without a troubled mind. Whom I condemn you yourself seem to see. I wished the book to go out to the public under the name of both my princes, and they were willing. It was read by them before it came out to the public. So I do not see what you wish, unless you wish it to be understood of this Prince, under whom I now act and live. But when I was publishing that book, this Prince was entirely unknown to me, and even now I do not know what he thinks of this matter. How, then, do you write that I condemn them, whose opinion I could not conjecture at all? The book was published for the benefit and use of the common people, not for condemnation. I aimed at this one thing: to draw the unlearned away from superstitious vanity and to forewarn them, lest they allow themselves to be so easily deceived by astrologers. Certainly those fables greatly hinder the plans and labours of physicians when they wish to heal properly.

units.la: De doctis quos me condemnare similiter scribis, nihil affirmare certi possum. Si aliqua in re, & in hac ipsa quoque, errent, nihil mirum. Homines enim sunt, quos in omnino multis errare omnes constat. Errauit Aristoteles, Augustinus,alij.Erro & ego in plurimis,&admonitus quo-tidie non erubesco errata corrigere. Vtinam verò sint, qui multos mihi meos errores comonstrent. In hac me causa non errare certò scio. Nihil est ab omni parte, vt Horatius recte scripsit, beatum. Ideo autem veritas explicanda non est,quia clarissimi viri eam alicubi non vident, aut nō pro-bant,quamcunq; ob causam id faciāt? Statim ne, qui eam patefacere tentarit,damnare illos existimetur? Quid si er-rare eos nesciat? Sic potius cogitandum est, nullius quan-tumuis clarissimi hominis autoritatem veritati praeiudi-care debere. Certum est illos, qui non argumentis,sed ho-minum praestantium authoritate aduersarios premere stu-dent,aut non satis intelligere concertationem,aut malam defendere causam. Quid opus erat tibi ista mihi obijcere, dum intacta relinquis argumenta quae produxi? Vbi ad illa responderis,non deerit,quod obijciamus praeterea.
units.tr: As to the learned men whom you similarly write that I condemn, I can affirm nothing for certain. If they err in some matter, and in this one too, that is no wonder. For they are men, and it is agreed that all men err in many things. Aristotle erred, Augustine erred, and others. I too err in very many things, and when reminded of it every day I am not ashamed to correct my errors. Would that there were people who might point out many of my errors to me! In this matter I know for certain that I am not in error. Nothing is wholly happy in every respect, as Horace rightly wrote. But is the truth not to be explained because very distinguished men do not see it somewhere, or do not approve it, for whatever reason they do so? Is he who tries to lay it open at once to be thought to condemn them? What if he does not know that they err? Rather we ought to think in this way: the authority of no man, however distinguished, ought to prejudge the truth. It is certain that those who strive to overwhelm their opponents not by arguments but by the authority of eminent men either do not understand the dispute well enough or defend a bad cause. Why was it necessary for you to bring these objections against me, while you leave untouched the arguments I have put forward? When you have answered those, there will be no lack of further things to object.

units.la: Huius generis illud etiam est, quod statim addis: Habes aduersarios, scribas ipsis, vt relinquant artem diabolicam, &c. Neminem aduersarium,quod sciam,habeo, qui non & ve-ritatis,(quam defendendam contra ineptos quosdam,pro-uocatus,sumsi,) quoq; sit hac in parte aduersarius. Intelli-go ergo aduersarium in hac causa esse, qui aduersum me sentit,meaq; oppugnat, quae vera esse reputo,quantumuis in caeteris sit amicus. Ex horum numero tu quoq; vnus es tandem factus,idq; praeter meam opinionem.Inter primos est Christophorus Strathmion, qui publicè priuatimq; no-stra oppugnare parum feliciter & scitè tentauit. Literas Deo volēte cum occasione nactus fuero edam, quo multi videant,quales habeat Astrologia patronos. Ad publicum ciusdem scriptum iam pridem respondi, at propter certas causas nondum edidi.Tunc edam,cum quorundam refu-tatio apparuerit. Nam Princeps meus nuper mihi Schleu-singa scripsit, aliquot Doctores siue doctos quodam in lo-co conuenisse,deq; refutando libello deliberauisse.Scriptū hoc magno sanè desiderio expecto, vt vno labore vtrisque satisfaciam. Qui sint ignoro, nec scire laboro: sed hoc illis ex animo opto, & meliora, quàm Stathmion, promāt, qui-bus vel doceri vel certè exerceri possim.
units.tr: Of this kind also is what you add at once: "You have opponents; write to them that they should give up the diabolical art, etc." I have no opponent, as far as I know, who is not also an opponent of the truth, which I took up, provoked by certain foolish men, to defend against them. I understand, then, that an opponent in this matter is one who thinks against me and attacks my positions, which I hold to be true, however friendly he may be in other respects. Of this number you too have at last become one, and that contrary to my expectation. Among the first is Christopher Strathmion, who has tried, rather unsuccessfully and unskilfully, to attack our views both in public and in private. If I find an occasion, with God willing, I shall publish my letter, so that many may see what sort of patrons astrology has. I answered his public writing long ago, but for certain reasons I have not yet published it. Then I shall publish it, when a refutation of some of them has appeared. For my Prince recently wrote to me from Schleusingen that some doctors, or learned men, have met in a certain place and deliberated about refuting the book. I await that writing with great eagerness, so that I may satisfy both parties with one labour. I do not know who they are, nor do I trouble to find out; but I wish them well from my heart, and that they may produce something better than Strathmion, by which I might either be taught or at least be exercised.

units.la: Quod nullū philosophum Astrologiam damnasse opi-naris, in eo plurimum deciperis. Nullus etenim clarus ex-titit philosophus, quod quidem scire hactenus quiverim, qui ipsam probarit, praeter paucos Platonicos, qui & super-stitiosissimi & summi praeterea daemonum cultores fuère. Inter hos Porphyrius numeratur, qui saepe tamen in diver-sam abijt sententiam, & praedictiones ex coelo mendaces esse affirmauit. Ex Parisiensibus vix unus atq; alter patroci-nium ipsius suscepit. Patres hanc μωνυχλὸ[?] nunquam probarunt, Astronomiam vero merito plurimi commenda-runt. Quo fit ut mirer, quòd tu rem cōtrà habere affirmes. Quanquam negare ita non potuisti, quin asseveraveris, multos ex patribus asseverare à Daemonibus excogitatam tra-ditamue esse. Non abusum, ut tu male iudicas, damnarunt hi omnes cum Imperatoribus, ut nuper exposui, rationi-busq; confirmaui. Non enim temerè aliquid absq; ratione, quod Astrologorum penè proprium est, asseveranter affir-mo. Librum me indignum ais esse, propter cōvicia, & quae-dam in eo male collecta, & quòd parum sit eruditus. Si ve-ra sunt, quae in eo docentur, me dignus est, tametsi inerudi-tus sit. De convicijs iam satis multa.
units.tr: In thinking that no philosopher has condemned astrology, you are greatly mistaken. For no famous philosopher, as far as I have so far been able to know, has approved it, except a few Platonists, who were also most superstitious and, moreover, the greatest worshippers of demons. Among these Porphyry is numbered, who nevertheless often changed to the opposite opinion and affirmed that predictions from the heavens are false. Of the Parisians scarcely one or two have taken up its defence. The Fathers never approved this [...], but they have rightly commended astronomy very highly. So I wonder that you affirm the contrary. Although you could not deny it, you did assert that many of the Fathers asserted that it was devised and handed down by demons. These all condemned not the abuse, as you judge wrongly, but the art itself, together with the emperors, as I have lately set out and confirmed by reasons. For I do not assert anything rashly and without reason, which is almost peculiar to astrologers. You say that the book is unworthy because of insults, and certain things badly gathered in it, and because it is not learned enough. If what is taught in it is true, I am worthy of it, although I am unlearned. Enough has been said about insults.

units.la: Docti quidam, inquis, aegerrimè tulerunt argumentationes & convicia. Qui aegrè ferunt tales argumentationes, hanc nauent operam Reipub. ut falsas esse ostendant. Magnam sanè apud omnes bonos, pios & doctos laudem merebuntur hoc facto, meq; immortali sibi devincient beneficio, quòd me ab errore liberaverint. Si id facere non possunt, me certè non mouere aut ab instituto retrahere debebit, quòd aliqui veritatem publicè proponi graviter ferunt. Si Astrologos alicubi ineptos & imperitos appellaui, optimo iure fecisse censeri possum. Etenim dum dogmata eorum & praeterea argumenta, quibus ea defendere frustra laborant, inepta esse doceo, nō video quomodo nō ipsos quoq; ineptos vere dicam. Qui me mendacium docuisse probauerit, is me illa in parte mentitum aut mendacem fuisse si dicat, non magnopere iniuriam mihi fecisse ceseri[?] poterit.
units.tr: "Learned men," you say, "have taken it very badly that arguments and insults were used." Those who take such arguments badly ought to labour for the commonwealth by showing them to be false. They will certainly earn great praise from all good, pious and learned people by doing so, and will bind me to themselves by an immortal favour, in that they have freed me from error. If they cannot do this, my resolve should certainly not be disturbed or drawn back from my course because some grieve that the truth is publicly put forward. If I have called astrologers in some places foolish and inexperienced, I may rightly be judged to have done so. For while I show that their doctrines, and the arguments by which they vainly labour to defend them, are foolish, I do not see how I should not also truly call the men themselves foolish. Whoever proves that I have taught falsehood will not be able to be thought to have done me any great wrong if he says that I lied or was a liar in that respect.

units.la: Ad extremum iterum te hortor, ne temerè Astrologiam publico præsertim scripto defendere coneris. Illi, de quibus suprà memini, arma iam, copias, omnisq; generis ἀσχολή-μάτων[?] communicatis inter se consilijs, studijs, operibus, expedire dicitur. Horum apparatum, vires, animos, pugnan-di peritiam, & demum ipsius pugnæ euentum obseruare securo tibi licebit. Cumq; operam eos nauare vtilem & bonam conspexeris, prodire, & profligatas iam nostras co-pias ad internecionem delere poteris. Si autem frustra eos tentasse pugnam, infeliciterq; manus conseruisse cogno-ueris, illorum periculo cautior factus, id consilij, quod esse optimum atq; saluberrimum iudicaueris, capies. Non scio an candidè magis tecum agere, tibiq; consulere quisquam aut velit, aut possit. Vale feliciter. Anno 58. Heideibergæ.
units.tr: Finally, I again urge you not to attempt rashly to defend astrology, especially in a public writing. Those of whom I have spoken above are said to be now preparing arms, troops, and every kind of equipment, having shared their plans, zeal and labours. You will be free, in safety, to observe their preparation, their strength, their spirits, their skill in fighting, and finally the outcome of the battle itself. And when you have seen that they are labouring usefully and well, you can come forward and destroy our forces, now routed, to the last man. But if you find that they attempted the battle in vain and joined combat unsuccessfully, having become more cautious through their danger, you will take that counsel which you judge to be best and most wholesome. I do not know whether anyone either wishes or is able to deal more frankly with you and to advise you. Farewell and prosper. In the year 58, at Heidelberg.

units.la: AD EVNDEM. Epistola XII.
units.tr: To the same man. Letter XII.

units.la: AD diem Cal. Octobris literas tuas 20. Septem-bris istic à te scriptas, recepi. Quas cū longiu-sculas cernerem, maiore voluptate simul atq; attentione perlegi. Sperabam me explicatio-nem aliquam illarum rerum, de quibus ad te iam antè verbosius scripsissem, in ipsis inuenturum. Cum nō semel perlegissem, nihil aliud inde percepi, quàm quòd vidi, te mea minus diligenter legisse, nec tua quoq;, qua so-les, industria elaborasse. Rescribā ea tantum, quæ rectè præ-terire nō potero. Sequar verò tuam narrationem, nisi cum diuulsa reperero cognata membra, vt singula singulis con-ferre promtius sit.
units.tr: On the first of October I received your letter, which you wrote there on 20 September. Since I saw that it was rather long, I read it with both greater pleasure and closer attention. I hoped to find in it some explanation of those matters about which I had already written to you at more length earlier. After reading it through more than once, I gathered nothing from it except that you had read my writings less carefully than I could have wished, and that you had not applied your usual diligence to your own. I will answer only those points which I cannot properly pass over. I will follow your narrative, unless I find related parts separated from one another, so that it is easier to compare them piece by piece.

units.la: Ex priuatione & negatione cum me argumentari scri-bis, non te intelligo, nisi id velis, quod postea dicis, me, quia tres significationes vocis, Naturalis, Astrologiæ conuenire nequeant, concludere, nullam ei conuenire. Sed de hoc po-stea suo loco. Excusare quoquo modo cupis quod scripsi, te immeritò me reprehendisse, quia tria tantum significata dictionis, Naturalis, enumaraui, sed frustra. Quocunq; enim modo tu de Astrologia scripseris, verū semper hoc est, me non habuisse in illis literis propositum docere, quomodo ea vox bonis authoribus usurpata sit, sed quot modis Astrologiae tribui posset, investigare voluisse. Vides iam, puto, me non torquere tua in alienā sententiam, duriusq; tua interpretari. Hoc nisi dixisses, praeteriturus haec fueram.
units.tr: You write that I argue from privation and negation. I do not understand you, unless you mean what you say afterwards: that because the three senses of the word "natural" cannot apply to astrology, I conclude that it applies to nothing. But I will deal with that later, in its proper place. You want to excuse, somehow, your having reproached me unjustly for listing only three meanings of the word "natural", but to no avail. However you have written about astrology, the truth is always this: in those letters I had no intention of teaching how that word has been used by good authors. I wished to investigate in how many ways it could be attributed to astrology. I think you now see that I am not twisting your words to another's meaning or interpreting your harsher statements too severely. Had you not said this, I would have passed these matters by.

units.la: Putas me in primis meis literis probare voluisse, Astrologiam non esse naturalem, hoc modo: Tres significationes vocis huius, Naturalis, non conueniunt Astrologiae, ergo non est naturalis. Mihi tum id nō venit in mentem, qui hoc solum inquirere volebam, quid per naturalem Astrologiam intellexisses. Nō enim certò sciebam, an iudicialem illam totam, vel aliquam ipsius partem ita vocares. Non-dum persuasum mihi erat, te Astrologicis fabulis fidè ha-bere. Divinatricem Astrologiam, non ut tu putas, sed his ra-tionibus non naturalem esse probaui, nempe quia sacrae literae ut falsam, impiam & impossibilem damnent, & ratio futurorum praescientiam, qualem ipsa pollicetur, supra captum humanae mentis esse convincat. Rationibus, quas tu refellere nunquam poteris, & veras esse iam ante fassus es, demonstraui. Principia & fundamenta, super quae extructa est, & ex quibus suas deducit conclusiones, ruinosa, falsa & inania esse docui.
units.tr: You think that in my first letters I wanted to prove that astrology is not natural, by this argument: the three senses of this word "natural" do not agree with astrology; therefore astrology is not natural. At that time this did not occur to me, since I wanted to inquire only what you understood by "natural astrology". For I did not know for certain whether you meant the whole of judicial astrology or some part of it. It had not yet been made clear to me that you give faith to astrological fables. I proved that divinatory astrology is not natural, not in the way you suppose, but for these reasons: Holy Scripture condemns it as false, impious and impossible, and reason shows that the foreknowledge of the future which it promises lies beyond the grasp of the human mind. I demonstrated this by arguments which you will never be able to refute, and which you have already admitted to be true. I showed that the principles and foundations on which it is built, and from which it draws its conclusions, are ruinous, false and empty.

units.la: Iam ad ratiocinationis meae refutationem descendo, quae his verbis à me proposita fuit, ut rectè eam tu hic repetis.
units.tr: Now I come to the refutation of my argument, which I put forward in these words, as you rightly repeat them here.

units.la: Quae Astrologi se praescire & praedicere posse ex arte sua credunt, antequam fiant, per accidens omnia futura sunt.
units.tr: Whatever the astrologers believe they can foreknow and foretell from their art, before it happens, all these things are future per accidens.

units.la: At quae per accidens futura sunt, nulla praesciri possunt arte.
units.tr: But things that are future per accidens cannot be foreknown by any art.

units.la: Nihil ergo eorum omnium, de quibus divinant Astrologi, praesciri ex arte futurum potest, antequam fiat. Ad haec tu ita, in nulla esse dispositione hanc ratiocinationem, ad quod cōsectariū sit, vitiosam esse. Probas autè in nulla esse figura, quia medium neq; subijciatur [?] in propositione & in assumtione fiat attributum, neq; sit attributum in propositionibus ambabus,neq;-in vtraq; subijciatur.
units.tr: Therefore nothing of all those things about which the astrologers divine can be known in advance from art, before it happens. To this you reply that the argument has no disposition, to whatever consequence it leads, and that it is faulty. You prove that it has no figure, because the middle term is neither made the subject in the premise and the predicate in the assumption, nor is it the predicate in both premises, nor the subject in either.

units.la: Quid si Medium subijci in propositione & in assumtione attributum fieri tibi commonstrem ? Nō negabis arbitror tunc, in prima dispositione rectè me collegisse. Hæc mea est conclusio.
units.tr: What if I show you that the middle term is made the subject in the proposition and the predicate in the assumption? I do not think you will then deny that I concluded correctly in the first figure. This is my conclusion.

units.la: Nulla prædictio Astrologica est artificiosa, siue ex arte procedit,vel quomodocunq; loqui libet,modò sensus permaneat idem.Voco prædictiones Astrologicas,Astrologorum ex siderum observationibus desumtas hariolationes. In hac conclusione Minor terminus est,Prædictio Astrologica.Maior,Non est artificiosa. Semper enim conclusionis subiectum Minoris termini in omni syllogismo: Prædicatū verò eiusdem, Maioris ratione obtinet. Iam Medium quæramus,qui est,per accidens fieri aut futurum esse.Vbi ergo dico,Quæ per accidens futura sunt, arte nulla præsciri possunt, Medium subijci Maiori termino vides. Erit ergo hîc propositio siue Maior. Deinde in primo loco posita propositione,hac scilicet,Quæ Astrologi se credūt ex arte prædicere posse', omnia per accidens futura sunt : hîc inquam idem medium attributum factum vides Minoris termini. Erit igitur hæc Minor propositio siue assumtio, quantumuis primum locum occupet in meis literis. Quid igitur reprehendis?
units.tr: No astrological prediction is artful, whether it proceeds from art or whatever way one likes to put it, provided the sense remains the same. I call astrological predictions, divinations drawn by the astrologers from observations of the stars, conjectures. In this conclusion the minor term is "astrological prediction" and the major term is "not artful". For in every syllogism the subject of the conclusion holds the position of the minor term, and its predicate that of the major term. Now let us seek the middle term, which is "that which happens or will be per accidens". Where, then, I say "things that are future per accidens cannot be known by any art", you see that the middle term is made the subject of the major term. This, then, will be the major proposition. Next, in the proposition placed first, namely "whatever the astrologers believe they can predict from art, all these things are future per accidens", you see that the same middle term is made the predicate of the minor term. This, then, will be the minor proposition or assumption, although it occupies the first place in my letters. Why, then, do you find fault?

units.la: Ego non ad locum propositionum, cum autores lego, sed ad conclusiones respiciendum mihi didici, vt quo in loco Maior,& quo rursus loco Minor posita sit intelligam. Vbicunq; enim Medius terminus cum Minore, siue conclusionis subiecto reperitur,ibi assumtio est seu Minor propositio. At vbi idem Medium cum Maiore termino, siue cōclusionis prædicato ponitur,ibi ppositio[?] siue Maior posita est, siue primo siue medio siue vltimo loco reperiatur collocata. Nec refert siue prædicetur Medius,siue subijciatur cæteris duobus terminis. Semper enim hoc verum inuenies quod dixi.Cum iam præterea scire volumus,in qua dispositione seu figura syllogismus collocari debeat, considerare oportet, quomodo vel attribuatur vel subijciatur duobus in conclusione inuentis terminis. Perspicis iā,opi-nor,non fuisse tibi opus ut admoneres me,ne in argumentando Dialecticorum & Philosophorum rationes negligā.
units.tr: When I read authors, I have learned to look not at the place of the propositions but at the conclusions, so that I may understand in what place the major is set and in what place the minor. For wherever the middle term is found with the minor term, that is, with the subject of the conclusion, there is the assumption or minor proposition. But where the same middle term is placed with the major term, that is, with the predicate of the conclusion, there the proposition or major is set, whether it is found placed in the first, middle or last place. Nor does it matter whether the middle term is predicated or made subject of the other two terms. For you will always find this true which I have said. Moreover, when we wish to know in what disposition or figure a syllogism ought to be placed, we must consider how the two terms found in the conclusion are either predicated or made subject. I think you now see that there was no need for you to warn me not to neglect the arguments of the dialecticians and philosophers when I argue.

units.la: Quæ hic interseris ut Astrologiam naturalem esse probes,postea examinabuntur, vbi quæ de eadem hac mea ratiocinatione respondes expendero. Melius enim est diuulsas istas partes coniungere,ut res liquidior sic fiat. Sic ergo scribis: Si maiorem ex parte intelligis,ut verba significant, totam ratiocinationem nego, quòd modus iste sit fallax in argumentando. Sin ex toto intelligis, ut sæpe authores solent, nimium tribuis Astrologis, quasi nequeant errare. Asseris enim ea omnia futura esse, quæ ipsi credunt se præscire posse, tanquam semper fiant quæ ipsi prædicunt, aut prædicere posse credunt. Hæc tua sunt. Non ego hic attentione & diligentiam à te requiram? Quam tu Maiorem siue propositionem iudicas, assumtio est siue Minor. Contrà verò quæ tibi assumtio videtur, propositio est.
units.tr: The points you insert here to prove that astrology is natural will be examined later, when I have weighed what you reply about this same argument of mine. For it is better to join these separated parts together, so that the matter may become clearer. So you write: If you understand the major as the words signify, I deny the whole argument, because this mode is fallacious in arguing. But if you understand it as a whole, as authors often do, you grant too much to the astrologers, as though they could not err. For you assert that all those things are future which they believe they can foreknow, as though what they predict, or believe they can predict, always happens. These are your words. Am I not to require attention and diligence from you here? What you judge to be the major premise or proposition is the assumption or minor, and conversely, what seems to you to be the assumption is the proposition.

units.la: Quod ad primam attinet,quæ tibi Maior esse perperam visa est, quæris,an ex toto intelligam. Quid hic dicam? Ita habet propositio ea: Quæ Astrologi præscire se credùt,omnia per accidens eueniunt. Potest ne dubitari,quin vniuersaliter hæc siue ex toto,ut tu loqueris,intelligenda sit? Sensus est, Omnia quæ Astrologi prædicunt, per accidens sunt futura. Certè nomen, Omnia, antecedens est,ut grammatici dicunt,ad quod refertur relatiuum, Quæ. Ita ne Astrologia tibi oculos animi simul & corporis perstrinxit, ut ista non cerneres,quæ tam sunt trita? Quod deinde addis,si ex toto intelligam, nimium me[?] tribuere Astrologis, quasi in prædicendo errare nequirent,simile est iam dictis. Non disertis aliò[?] verbis, talia omnia quæ præscire se Astrologi putent,per accidens euenire? Non ergo euenire ea semper dico,sed eius esse naturæ asserò, ut per accidens fiant, si fiant. Ideo falli ipsos, quòd talium sibi præscientiam stultè arrogent. Qui per accidens aliquid futurum esse ait,is ostendit apertè,non etiā fieri tale posse, imò planè incertū esse,præsciriq; nullo modo posse,utrum futurū sit,an nō futurū sit.
units.tr: As for the first point, which you have wrongly judged to be the major, you ask whether I understand it as a whole. What am I to say here? The proposition reads: whatever the astrologers believe they can foreknow, all these things happen per accidens. Can there be any doubt that this must be understood universally, or as a whole, as you put it? The sense is: all things that the astrologers predict are future per accidens. Certainly the word "all" is the antecedent, as the grammarians say, to which the relative "whatever" refers. Has astrology so dazzled your eyes of mind and body that you did not see these things, which are so commonplace? What you add next, that if I understand it as a whole I attribute too much to the astrologers, as though they could not err in predicting, is similar to what has already been said. Do I not say in plain words that all such things which the astrologers think they can foreknow happen per accidens? I do not therefore say that they always happen, but I assert that they are of such a nature that they come about per accidens, if they come about at all. Hence they err because they foolishly claim for themselves a foreknowledge of such things. Whoever says that something will be future per accidens shows clearly that it cannot even be made to happen in that way, but rather that it is wholly uncertain, and that it cannot in any way be foreknown whether it will be future or not.

units.la: Addis postea, te propter artis certitudinem admittere, omnia futura esse, quæ futura prænunciant Astrologi: at quatuor esse in ratiocinatione terminos, minoremq; cum maiori pugnare. Quod dū probare studes, in eodē semper errore volueris, imò inuoluis te magis magisq;. Spero te ex prædictis perspexisse, quantū ubiq; sis hallucinatus. Tandē vero opinari te rectè scribis, me hoc velle, Omnia Astrologica, hoc est, quæ Astrologi futura prænunciare solēt, non nisi per accidens euenire. Coniectasse id te ex assumtione sequentis argumenti ais, cuius propositio de parte tantum asserat. Est autem hæc illa ratiocinatio.
units.tr: You add afterwards that, on account of the certainty of the art, you admit that all things are future which the astrologers foretell as future, but that there are four terms in the argument, and that the minor fights with the major. While you labour to prove this, you will always remain in the same error, or rather you entangle yourself more and more. I hope that from what has been said you have seen how far you have gone astray everywhere. Finally, you rightly write that you suppose I mean this: that all astrological things, that is, the things which the astrologers are accustomed to foretell as future, come about only per accidens. You say you have gathered this from the assumption of the following argument, whose proposition asserts this only of a part. The argument is this.

units.la: Per accidens futura, nec arte nec ratione aliqua præcognosci possunt.
units.tr: Things that happen by accident cannot be foreknown by any art or reasoning.

units.la: Astrologicæ p[?]dictiões oēs cōtinēr tātū p accidēs futura.
units.tr: All astrological predictions concern only things that happen by accident.

units.la: Astrologiæ ergo prædictiones nec ex arte nec ratione proficiscuntur.
units.tr: Therefore the predictions of astrology proceed neither from art nor from reason.

units.la: Hæc ratiocinatio eadē est cū superiore. Contraxeram in pauca ista, ut clarior esset. Rectè ergo hic ex assumtione collegisti, quod supra voluerim. Hoc merito mirari cogor, quòd, cum hic ordine suo propositiones positas videre potueris, non animaduerteris eam, quæ hic est assumtio, supra quoq; assumtionem fuisse.
units.tr: This argument is the same as the earlier one. I had condensed it into these few words so that it would be clearer. You were right, then, to draw from the minor premise what I had said above. I am compelled to marvel at this: although you could see the propositions laid out in their proper order here, you did not notice that the minor premise here was itself a premise supporting something above.

units.la: Maiore sive propositione tu in hac ratione de parte asserere, nō de toto cur dicas nescio. Certè eadē est cum ista: Nulla res per accidēs futura, arte præcognosci, antequā fiat, poterit. Nescis indefinitas propositiones in necessaria materia universales esse? An non principij universalis rationē obtinet? Quinimò tu idē sentire ac dicere paulo post videris, cū ita scribis, cōtingentia nō sunt artis nec scientiæ: proculdubio id voluisti, Nulla cōtingētia arte cōtineri. At quæ per accidēs fiūt, Contingēter fiūt, seu cōtingētia sunt. Quomodo ergo negare eā potes? Suprà namq; negabas. Hāc, respōdebis, nego, Astrologica omnia per accidēs euenire seu futura esse. At hæc nō est Maior. Ergo Minorē negare voluisti fortasse. Atq; in primis eā literis Fracofordia[?] ad te scriptis pbaui. Et vera esse q attuli tu cōfessus es. Quare nullā à me aliā probationē tantisper petere debes, dū aut nō refutaueris illa, aut non hoc efficere, quod v[?]oluisti, demonstrauueris.
units.tr: Why you say that in this argument the major premise asserts something only of a part, and not of the whole, I do not know. It is certainly the same as this: No thing that happens by accident can be foreknown by art before it happens. Do you not know that indefinite propositions in necessary matter are universal? Or does this not hold the force of a universal principle? Indeed, you seem to think and say the same thing a little later, when you write that contingent things are not the object of art or science. Surely you meant: no contingent thing can be contained by art. But things that come about by accident come about contingently, or are contingent. How, then, can you deny it? For above you were denying it. You will reply, "I deny this: that all astrological things come about by accident, or are future." But this is not the major premise. So perhaps you wished to deny the minor. Yet I have already proved it in my letter written to you from Frankfurt, and you have admitted that the things I brought forward are true. Therefore, for the time being you ought to seek no other proof from me, unless you have refuted those things, or have shown that they do not accomplish what you wished.

units.la: Equidem cum Astrologos de solis cōtingentibus, ut futura sunt, vaticinari negas, qd neges nescis. Quis enim res necessario eventuras prædici sibi velit? Si, quæ nuper Francofordia ad te scripsi, perlegisti attentè, nō potuisti ignorare. Cur igitur tā acerbè me accusas ignorantiæ? Sed quæ huius generis scribis universa, facilè tibi condono, præsertim cū perturbatum & commotū te fuisse inter scribendū ostendant. In secunda ista ratiocinatione si Maiorē universim accipiam (ita accipiendā indicaui) minorē te negare inquis, statimq; addis: Nihil video hic te probare contra Astrologiam, nisi argumentis per accidens longè magis quàm ipsa Astrologia probet. An tibi argumentum prædictum per accidens videtur probare, Astrologorum conatus evanidos esse & inartificiosos? Refelle, si quidem potes, nec nihil te fecisse dicā.
units.tr: Indeed, when you deny that astrologers prophesy only about contingent things as they are future, you do not know what you are denying. For who would wish to have things that will necessarily happen foretold to him? If you had read attentively what I recently wrote to you from Frankfurt, you could not have been ignorant of this. Why then do you accuse me so bitterly of ignorance? But I readily pardon you for everything of this kind that you write, especially since it shows that you were disturbed and agitated while writing. In this second argument, if I take the major premise universally (as I indicated it should be taken), you say you deny the minor, and you immediately add: I see nothing here that you prove against astrology, except arguments that prove the point by accident far more than astrology itself does. Does the argument just stated seem to you to prove that the efforts of the astrologers are empty and unskilled? Refute it, if indeed you can, and I will say you have done nothing.

units.la: Nullus eventus per accidens futurus, potest arte, antequam fiat, futurus præcognosci.
units.tr: No event that will happen by accident can be foreknown by art before it happens.

units.la: Quæ Astrologi futura prædiuinant, omnia per accidens eveniunt, sive futura sunt.
units.tr: Whatever future things the astrologers foretell all come about by accident, or are future.

units.la: Ergo quæ Astrologi se præscire & prædicere posse arbitrantur, præscire futura nequeunt. Frustra igitur laborant. Falsum etiā est Astrologiam, cuius ope se præuidere dictitant talia, artem esse.
units.tr: Therefore, the things which the astrologers think they can foreknow and predict cannot be foreknown as future. Their labour is therefore in vain. It is also false that astrology, by whose help they claim to foresee such things, is an art.

units.la: Quid hic negabis? Maiorem ne? Atqui concessisti eam paulo ante Minorem ne? Minimè gentium. Dicis enim neminem Astrologum, quod quidem tu scias, illa negasse, quibus eam probaui. Et certè nullus negare poterit, ita inquâ, ut falsa esse probet, aut non firmiter efficaciterq; propositum probare ostendat. At conclusio rectè ex præmissis infertur. Necessario ergo sequitur, Astrologiam fabulam esse, deliramentum & superstitionē ociosorum & credulorum hominum. Si æquè firmis argumentis, quod tibi facilè esse asseris, Medicinam vanam, falsam, futilem probaveris, eris mihi magnus Apollo, imò novus Apollo, & in disserendo ipso etiā magistro Aristotele peritior. Nō enim ex astris Medicina prœsagit, nec omnino prædicere præsentireq; futura, quatenus futura sunt, sed quatenus iam fieri & esse incepe-rūt, docet. Sed de hisce in prioribus meis ad te literis plura.
units.tr: What will you deny here? The major premise? But you conceded it a little while ago. The minor? By no means. For you say that no astrologer, so far as you know, has denied those things by which I proved it. And certainly no one will be able to deny it, unless he proves them false or shows that the proposition was not firmly and effectively proved. But the conclusion is rightly inferred from the premises. It necessarily follows, therefore, that astrology is a fable, the delirium and superstition of idle and credulous men. If you were to prove with equally firm arguments, which you assert you can do easily, that medicine is empty, false and trifling, you would be a great Apollo to me, indeed a new Apollo, and more skilled in disputation even than Aristotle, the master himself. For medicine does not foretell from the stars, nor does it teach how to foreknow or predict future things at all, insofar as they are future, but insofar as they have already begun to happen and to be. But I will say more about these matters in my earlier letters to you.

units.la: Astra non particulares & proprias horum inferiorum causas, sed maximè tum generales tum remotas esse dixi, & verè quidem dixi. Harum autem nullam cognitionem & scientiam haberi neq; dixi, neq; cogitaui unquam, multò minus Aristotelem ita scripsisse alicubi affirmaui. Falsò igitur me id dixisse censes, quod ne in mentem quidem mihi aliquando venit. Hoc dixi, tales causas nesciri, aut non cognosci, quatenus effectum certū sint productura. Cum enim per se nequeant, aliæ autem causæ ipsis accidant, cognosci ut tales nequeunt, nisi accidentes omnes cognoscan-tur. At hoc impossibile. Ergo & illud. Hominem cognoscere possum, tametsi huius hominis, Petri scilicet, notitiam nullam habeam, imò ne natum quidē sciam. Eodem modo cœlestium notitiam habere nos nihil vetat, quantum-uis hoc aliquid effectura ignoremus. Hæc quoq; jam antea in literis meis tibi transmissis, licet breviter, exposita sunt.
units.tr: I have said that the stars are not the particular and proper causes of these lower things, but chiefly general and remote ones, and indeed I said this truly. But I have never said or thought that any knowledge or science of these causes is had, much less have I ever affirmed that Aristotle wrote this anywhere. You therefore wrongly think that I said what has never even come into my mind. What I said is that such causes are not known, or are not recognised, insofar as they are going to produce a certain effect. For since they cannot act by themselves, but other causes accompany them, they cannot be known as such unless all the accompanying causes are known. But this is impossible. Therefore that is impossible too. I can know a man, although I have no knowledge of this man, Peter, indeed I do not even know that he has been born. In the same way, nothing prevents us from having knowledge of the heavenly bodies, although we do not know what they are going to bring about. These things too were set out briefly already in my letters sent to you earlier.

units.la: Non hoc quæritur, an universalium causarum cognitio aliqua habeatur, vel, an cœlestium vires percipiamus: sed hoc quæritur, utrum particulares inferiorum causæ sidera censeri debeant. De priore nulla est quæstio, si cùm quæ antè scripsi, tum quæ nuper dixi considerentur. Sidera particulares causas esse horum effectuum, vel te quoq; teste, falsum est. Quæ de Dæmonibus & cōuicijs assuis, libens prætereo, etsi non parum multa hic quoq; haberem, quæ tuis rectè opponerem. Quòd libellum à Sciolo scriptum tibi videri addis, nihil detrahit eruditioni Sauonarolæ.
units.tr: The question is not whether some knowledge of universal causes is had, or whether we perceive the powers of the heavens; but the question is whether the stars ought to be counted as particular causes of lower things. On the former there is no dispute, if both what I wrote before and what I have lately said are considered. That the stars are the particular causes of these effects is false, even on your own testimony. As for what you add about demons and your own invented slanders, I gladly pass over them, although I would have not a little to set against your points here too. As for your saying that the little book was written by a dabbler, this takes nothing away from the learning of Savonarola.

units.la: Picum te legisse & intellexisse, atq; adeò solutiones argumentorum te invenisse, demum Bellantium & Raphaelem (arbitror te Gabrielem voluisse dicere) quendam, qui ipsius argumenta omnia doctissimè refutent, ipsi te opposuisse, scribis quidem: an verè autem scribas, suspicari non immerito mihi licet. An te, qui mea & Sauonarolæ levicula argumenta, (si cum Pici argumentis conferantur,) ut quæ propter vulgum scripta sint, inte ligere non potuisti, (nisi fortasse noluerís [?] intelligere, quod certè libentius credo) Pici viri doctissimi doctissima argumenta peruidisse verisimile sit: Si nō videre potuisti quàm inscitè [?] nulloq; judicio Bellantius[?] argumenta ipsius reprehendat, quàm imperitè & temerariè damnet, quàm absurdè erret, cum se dissoluere ea putat,quàm astutè & malignè eleuet ac dissimulet,nun-quam mihi persuadebis illius te sensum assecutū fuisse. In præsentiarum satis sit monuisse, doctiores Astrologos Bel-lantium nō facilè producere. Putas me Bellantium,& qui-dem maiore multo diligentia, quàm tu meas literas perle-geris,non perlegisse? Falleris plurimum,si credis.
units.tr: You write that you have read and understood Pico, and indeed that you have found solutions to his arguments, and that you have finally set against him Bellanti and a certain Raphael (I suppose you meant Gabriel) who refute all his arguments most learnedly. Whether you write this truthfully, I may not unreasonably suspect. If you could not understand my arguments and those of Savonarola (which are rather slight, if they are compared with Pico's arguments, since they were written for the common people), perhaps you did not grasp it (unless you were unwilling to understand, which I certainly prefer to believe), and it is likely that you saw through the most learned arguments of the most learned Pico. If you could not see how unlearnedly and without judgement Bellanti criticises his arguments, how rashly and foolishly he condemns them, how absurdly he errs while thinking he dissolves them, how cunningly and maliciously he evades and conceals them, you will never persuade me that you grasped his meaning. For the present it is enough to have warned that the more learned astrologers do not readily produce Bellanti. Do you think that I have not read Bellanti, and with much greater care than you have read my letters? You are very much mistaken, if you believe so.

units.la: Fallacibus me & captiosis argumentis vti non rectè sen-tis,dum ita scribis:Nec patronum Astrologæ[?] me constituo. Un-de hoc sumis argumentum ? Ex eodem sophismatis gene-re,quo & prius.Iste non sequitur Picum,ergo non legit,nec intellexit. Mox aliud adducis meum sophisma, his verbis: Iste vult obiter in explicatione usus astrolabij ad aliquorum ca-lumnias respondere,ergo constituit se absurdissimè causæ patro-num. Facilis est ad utrunq; responsio. Nullo enim sophisma-te usus sum vel hic,vel ibi. Prius argumentum tale est: Qui Picum Astrologiam rectè vereq; confutantem legit ac in-tellexit,is aut non probabit vanitatem dogmatis,aut perti-nacia quadam in cōcepta opinione vult persistere. Postre-mum hoc ideo non addidi, quia de te credere nō potui, & ne nunc quidem credo.Hac de causa iam quoq; nō appo-suissem, nisi ita me vt facerem cogisses. Vides nullum hic esse sophisma. Non enim dubitari potest,quin rectè & soli-dè Picus confutarit. Omnes fassi[?] hactenus sunt,& fatebun-tur in posterum,qui argumētorum vim'perspiciunt. Quòd Astrologi non multi cedūt,hinc euenire arbitror,quòd nō intelligunt,aut non legunt. Quotidē studiosè in errore per-manere velle,non probabile tolum[?],sed omnino verum est.
units.tr: You do not rightly perceive that I use fallacious and captious arguments, when you write: Nor do I set myself up as a patron of astrology. From what source do you draw this argument? It comes from the same kind of sophism as the earlier one: "This man does not follow from Pico, therefore he has not read or understood him." Next you bring forward another of my sophisms, in these words: This man wishes, in passing, in the explanation of the use of the astrolabe, to answer some men's calumnies; therefore he has set himself up most absurdly as a patron of the cause. The answer to both is easy. For I have used no sophism either here or there. The earlier argument runs thus: whoever has read and understood Pico refuting astrology rightly and truly will either not prove the vanity of the doctrine, or wishes to persist in some opinion conceived with obstinacy. I did not add the last point because I could not believe it of you, and I do not believe it even now. For this reason I would not even have added it now, had you not forced me to do so. You see there is no sophism here. For it cannot be doubted that Pico refuted it rightly and soundly. All who understand the force of the arguments have so far confessed it, and will confess it in future. I think the reason many astrologers do not yield is that they do not understand or do not read. That someone should wish to remain studiously in error every day is not merely probable but altogether true.

units.la: Alterū tale erat: Hic conabitur hoc anno aliquot argu-mentis probare Astrologiam esse naturalem,& ab homine posse sciri, Deumq; velle hanc ad nominis sui gloriā disci. Item, Si Deus ei concesserit vitam bonam, Deiq; donum esse, certissimis & evidentibus argumentis se probaturum promittit: ergo constituit se patronum Astrologiæ. At hæc absurda est,si modò talia sunt, quæ falsa & mērita sunt. Fal-sam esse ratio, sensus,philosophia,sacræ literæ, huius interpretes probarũt. Si nõ credis, Sauonarolã, (vt Picũ taceam) lege, & vel vnicũ ipsius argumentũ dissoluere tẽtato, minimeq́; ignauũ Astrologiæ expugnatorẽ esse perspicies. Idem hoc magis intelliges, si plura vel omnia cũ ratiõe refellere conari audebis. Sic nullo me sophismate vsum clarẽ docui.
units.tr: The second was of this sort: "Here he will try this year, with several arguments, to prove that Astrology is natural and can be known by man, and that God wishes it to be learned for the glory of his name. Likewise, if God grants him a good life, and it is God's gift, he promises to prove it with the most certain and evident arguments." So he sets himself up as the champion of Astrology. But that is absurd, if such things are false and deserving of contempt. That it is false, reason, the senses, philosophy and the Holy Scriptures, and their interpreters, have proved. If you do not believe me, read Savonarola (not to mention Pico), and try to dissolve even his single argument; you will see that he was no cowardly conqueror of Astrology. You will understand this even better if you dare to try to refute the whole of it, or most of it, by reason. So I clearly showed that I used no sophism at all.

units.la: An verum sit, quod de Pico Bellatius scribit, Sauonarolæ precibus impulsum diuinũ illud opus cõtra Astrologos cõscripsisse, ad caussam nihil facit, dũ quę scriptsit vera sunt, vt rationi, philosophiæ, sanctæq́; Religioni consona. Bellantius nõ asseueranter, vt hoc etiam obiter dicam, scribit, Picum Sauonarolæ precibus adductũ opus illud composuisse: sed verisimile putat, vt ex epist. dedicatoria ad Catharinã Sfortiam, & illis quæ post Præfatione in suas responsiones posuit, videre licet. Quæ ideo dico, vt ne Bellantium quidẽ satis diligenter te legisse videas.
units.tr: Whether it is true, as Bellantius writes about Pico, that he wrote that divine work against the astrologers at the urging of Savonarola, has no bearing on the matter, since what he wrote is true, agreeing with reason, philosophy and holy religion. Bellantius does not write this positively (to say this too in passing), but thinks it probable that Pico composed that work at Savonarola's urging, as you may see from the dedicatory letter to Caterina Sforza and from those things which he placed after the Preface in his replies. I say this so that you may not seem to have read Bellantius quite carefully enough.

units.la: Tu nõ Italo illi seni, à quo te accepisse scribis, magis quã ipsimet Bellatio credere debuisti. Is in principio libri 5. suarũ respons. sic scribit: Nec vnũ tacendũ videtur, cõplures sunt autẽ Florẽtiæ testes fide dignißimi, quibus, inspecta Hieron. Sauo-narolæ genitura, quinq̧ ante eius iacturã menses, dũ florebat, & ipsum Hieron. ad hæresim inclinatũ, & vitã laqueo terminatũ prædixi. Hæc Bellatij sunt, ex quibus perspicis, te vnà cum Italo, cui imprudẽter credidisti, decipi. Nõ Pisis ille Sauonarolæ hoc prædixit. Nõ Sauonarolæ, sed quibusdã Florẽtinis dixit. Nõ comburendũ aut Florẽtiæ aut alibi affirmauit, sed laqueo vitã finiturũ scribit se de eo prænũciasse, quinto ante ipsius mortẽ mẽse. Quomodo me vis credere, te cũ iudicio Bellantiũ Pico opposuisse, qui nihil eorũ, quæ maximè scire te cõueniebat, in ipso animaduertisti? Si minus facilè crederes, ne Astrologiæ quidem fidem adhiberes.
units.tr: You ought to have believed not so much that Italian old man, from whom you write that you had it, as Bellantius himself. In the beginning of the fifth book of his replies he writes thus: "Nor should one thing be passed over: there are several most trustworthy witnesses at Florence, to whom, having examined the nativity of Girolamo Savonarola, I predicted, five months before his downfall, while he was flourishing, and when Girolamo himself was inclined to heresy, that his life would end in a noose." These are the words of Bellantius, from which you perceive that you, together with the Italian whom you rashly believed, are deceived. He did not predict this of Savonarola at Pisa. He said it not to Savonarola but to certain Florentines. He did not affirm that he would be burned at Florence or elsewhere, but he writes that he predicted of him that his life would end by a noose, five months before his death. How do you wish me to believe that you have set Bellantius against Pico in judgement, when you have noticed in him none of those things which it most befitted you to know? If you were less ready to believe, you would not give even faith to Astrology.

units.la: Valde exultat in hoc loco Bellatius, & Astrologos supra vulgarẽ hominũ sortẽ extollit, ac diuinã vocat Astrologiã. Cur faciat quaeris? Quia, inquit, ex magna Iouis & Saturni cõiunctione Astrologi quidã, falsi propheræ[?] aduentũ prædixerũ: quæ res minimè, vt Picus sensit, vana fuit. Sauonarolã namq; sidera significabat. Bellatius Sauonarolæ sæpe, tametsi nõ vbiq; tã explicatè, vt hic facit, falsum propheræ[?] appelappellat. Quam verè, pij omnes & docti viri intelligunt. Sa-nè cum à suæ ætatis theologis discedit, ita ferè sentit, vt ho-die pleriqꝫ omnes boni, & tu quoqꝫ sentis. Et propter hæc falsus propheta dictus est Bellatio. Libelli, quos pij omnes per Germaniam probant, suisqꝫ legēdos proponunt, pieta-tem hominis testatam nobis faciūt. Quare si hæreticus ille fuit, nos quoqꝫ omnes, qui à Pontificis dogmatibus discef-simus, hæreticos esse oportebit. Ob eandem caussam Car-danus Lutherum quoqꝫ à sideribus ad hæresim impulsum opinatus est. Si ætatem nostram ille vidisset, Magnam illam coniunctionem nostri temporis viros sanctos significasse absqꝫ dubio asseueranter affirmauisset.
units.tr: Bellantius rejoices greatly in this passage, and raises the astrologers above the common lot of men, and calls Astrology divine. Why he does so, you ask? Because, he says, some astrologers, from the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, predicted the coming of a false prophet; which thing, as Pico perceived, was by no means in vain. For he signified Savonarola by the stars. Bellantius often calls Savonarola a false prophet, although not so explicitly everywhere as he does here. How truly all pious and learned men understand. Indeed, when he departs from the theologians of his own age, he thinks much as nearly all good men do today, and as you yourself think. And for these reasons he was called a false prophet by Bellantius. The little books which all pious men throughout Germany approve, and propose to be read by their own people, bear witness to us of the man's piety. Therefore if that man was a heretic, we too, all of us who have departed from the dogmas of the Pontiff, shall have to be called heretics. For the same reason Cardanus also thought that Luther was driven to heresy by the stars. If he had seen our age, he would undoubtedly have affirmed positively that that great conjunction of our time signified holy men.

units.la: Sed fac verum esse, quòd hæreticus fuerit: an ideo cœli hoc indicarunt? Ponamus ita credidisse Bellantinm[?], quem ex alijs coniecturis ista coniecisse plus satis constat, an propterea Astrologia vera dicenda putandáue sit? Ego nō ita iudico, & cur non ita iudicem declarabo. Quis neget longè plura, & his multò admirabiliora, Augures, Extispices, Geo-mantes, alios qꝫ diuinatores olim ac hodie etiam diuinare consueuisse[?]? Quòd si propter a[?] quod euentus aliqui vati-cinijs respondent, (siue casu quopiam, siue Dæmonū inspi-ratione eueniat,) ars illa vera iudicanda est, oportebit præ-dictas omnes non veras modo, sed verissimas ponere. At sunt impiæ, futiles, & ex æquo cum Astrologia damnatæ.
units.tr: But grant that he was a heretic: were these things therefore indicated by the heavens? Let us suppose that Bellantius believed so, whom it is quite clear conjectured these things from other conjectures; should Astrology therefore be called or thought true? I do not judge so, and I shall declare why I do not judge so. Who would deny that Augurs, Haruspices, geomancers, and other diviners, both formerly and even today, have been accustomed to divine, and far more numerous and much more wonderful things? But if, because some outcomes correspond to prophecies (whether by some chance, or by the inspiration of demons, it happens), that art must be judged true, it will be necessary to pronounce all the aforesaid diviners not only true, but most true. Yet they are impious, futile, and condemned alike with Astrology.

units.la: Si quo in loco Deus opt. max. Astrologiā damnarit, vbi Prophetæ impiā docuerint, quomodo ratio & philosophia inanem & putidā demonstrent, scire cupis, lege Picū, Sauo-narolam, Philosophos & Theologos omnes, maximè antiquos (de Theologis ipse non negas) lege sacras literas, & abundè quod quæris inuenies. Reperies in meis etiā literis nonnihil, quod certè hactenus refutare nō potuisti. Formā argumēti vitiosam malè credidisti. Assumtionem perperā negasti, quam ego validissimis rationibus, vel te ipso teste, cōfirmaui. Horum cū nihil neges, neqꝫ nō conficere propo-situm ostēdas, immeritò plures à me probationes flagitas.
units.tr: If you wish to know in what place God, best and greatest, has condemned Astrology, where the Prophets taught it to be impious, how reason and philosophy demonstrate it to be empty and rotten, read Pico, Savonarola, all the philosophers and theologians, especially the ancient ones (of the theologians you yourself do not deny), read the holy writings, and you will find abundantly what you seek. You will find in my writings also something which you certainly have not until now been able to refute. You have badly believed the form of the argument to be faulty. You denied the assumption wrongly, which I confirmed by the strongest reasons, even with you yourself as witness. Since you deny none of these things, nor show that the proposition does not follow, you rightly demand more proofs from me than are owed.

units.la: Nō vno tantū argumēto in primis meis literis ad re vsu-sū[?], sed pluribꝰ, p̄cipuè verò duobꝰ. Quā infeliciter cofutareprius tétaris vidimus. Ad alterū ne verbo quidē sigillatim respondisti. Habet aūt, si in forma cupis videre, hoc modo:
units.tr: In my first letters I did not deal with only one argument, but with several, and chiefly with two. How unhappily you tried to refute it, we have seen above. You did not answer the other even in a word, one by one. It runs, if you wish to see it in form, in this way:

units.la: Quæcunq; causa non potest suos effectus absq; ope & auxilio aliarum causarum, quæ ipsi pro generatione illorū effectuum per accidens coniunguntur, producere, huius causæ solius accuratissima etiam cognitio nihil nos iuuat ad præsensionem talium effectuum.
units.tr: Whatever cause cannot produce its effects without the help and assistance of other causes, which are joined to it accidentally for the generation of those effects, the most accurate knowledge of that cause alone does not help us to foresee such effects.

units.la: Sidera à natura ita facta sunt, vt hos effectus, de quibus Astrologi se diuinare posse opinantur, producere nequeant absq; coniunctione aliarum causarum, quæ sideribus per accidens varie coniunguntur. Exempli gratia: Sidera non possunt generare hominem, nisi vir mulieri iungatur, multo minus pulchrum aut deformem, robustum aut valetudinarium, diuitem aut pauperem poterunt generare, nisi robustus cum robusta, diues, pulcher, &c. congrediatur. At hæc omnia sideribus accidere vel cæci peruideant.
units.tr: The stars were so made by nature that they cannot produce those effects, which the astrologers believe they can foretell, without the conjunction of other causes, which are variously joined to the stars accidentally. For example: the stars cannot generate a man unless a man is joined to a woman; much less can they generate a beautiful or deformed, a robust or sickly, a rich or poor person, unless a robust man joins with a robust woman, a rich one with a beautiful one, and so on. But that all these things happen to the stars, even the blind can see.

units.la: Ergo ex perfectissima etiam siderū notitia intelligi non potest, an effectus tales futuri sint nec ne sint. Non enim quales ipsi causæ coniungendæ sint hominis mens comprehendere valet.
units.tr: Therefore from the most perfect knowledge of the stars it cannot be understood whether such effects will be future or not. For the human mind is not able to grasp what sorts of causes are to be joined.

units.la: Iam aliud argumentum tuum recito. Astrologiæ operam dantes, fidem q; habentes Diabolicos censes. At viri quidā docti id faciunt. Ergo, &c. Ad hoc quia in superioribus respondi, paucis me expediam in præsenti loco. Propositionē tuam falsam esse aio, neq; ex scriptis meis, quod tamen tu putas, probari vnquam poterit, si candidè interpretari voles. Hoc modo si ponas, verā esse concedam. Qui Astrologiam colunt, nec eam repudiant, tametsi impiam & Deo aduersariam cognouerint, impij sunt. Hoc pacto si mea intelliges, aio cætera recte sequi, quamdiu non resipiscunt. Scriptura ebrios nō possessuros regnū Dei pronunciat. Nemo est, qui non ita intelligat, si nō eos facti sui pœniteat. Hoc modo omnes loqui solemus. Si ergo impij non sunt absolutè, qui scientes peccant, nisi resipiscere serio nolint, multo minus impij mihi iudicati sunt vnquam, qui nescientes offendunt. Vides quàm facilè me ex laqueo, quo me cōstrictum teneri arbitratus es, explicauerim. Veritate, acutissimo sci-licet licet gladio, semel totum dissecui. Frustra me iubes de quo-rundam sententia exquirere. Non enim censor constitutus sum, vt in aliorum mores inquiram superstitiosius. Ocio-sorum hoc est, & curiosorum hominum, à quorum inge-nio mei mores meaq; vita semper fuit alienissima. Sed hi-sce & similibus aliis relictis, ad ea redeundum iam est quæ supra in hunc locum reieci, ne disputatio de mea ratioci-natione discerperetur.
units.tr: Now I recite your other argument: "Those who practise Astrology and have faith in it you judge to be diabolical. But certain learned men do so. Therefore, etc." Since I answered this in what went before, I shall be brief in the present place. I say that your proposition is false, nor can it ever be proved from my writings, as you think, if you wish to interpret them fairly. If you put it in this way, I shall grant it is true: those who cultivate Astrology, and do not reject it, although they have recognised it as impious and opposed to God, are impious. In this way, if you understand my meaning, I say the rest follows correctly, as long as they do not repent. Scripture declares that drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God. There is no one who does not understand it so, unless they regret their deeds. We are accustomed to speak in this way. If therefore those who sin knowingly are not impious absolutely, unless they are seriously unwilling to repent, much less have those who offend unknowingly ever been judged by me to be impious. You see how easily I have freed myself from the snare by which you thought I was held fast. With the sharpest sword of truth, I have cut through the whole thing at once. You vainly bid me inquire into the opinion of certain persons. For I have not been appointed a censor, to inquire too scrupulously into the morals of others. That belongs to idle and curious men, from whose disposition my morals and my life have always been most alien. But leaving these and similar things aside, we must now return to those matters which I set aside above for this place, lest the discussion of my reasoning be torn apart.

units.la: Postulaui à te, vt, si modum aliū nosses, quo Astrologiam naturalē dici posse constaret, eū mihi indicares. Huic meæ petitioni satisfacturus, naturalem dici scribis, quia sit consideratio de corporibus naturalibus, & eorundē operationibus. Verùm ego hunc modū non ignorabam. Inter alios recensui, & diuinatrici non rectè adhiberi docui. Alium te modum indicaturum putabam, cū tot me significationes vocis, Naturalis, omisisse scriberes. Sed jā tua expendamus. Si Astrologiam naturalem esse solidè probaueris, non tu quidem inter homines infimum, sed summum obtinebis locum. Sex tuas rationes quibus probare tentas, ordine ad veritatis stateram examinabimus.
units.tr: I asked you that, if you knew some other way by which astrology could be shown to be called natural, you would point it out to me.
