To meet this request, you write that it is called natural because it considers natural bodies and their operations. But I was not unaware of this way. I listed it among the others and showed that it is not rightly applied to divinatory astrology. I thought you would indicate a different way, since you wrote that you had left out so many meanings of the word "natural." But let us weigh your arguments. If you prove solidly that astrology is natural, you will win not the lowest but the highest place among men. We will examine your six arguments in order, by the balance of truth.

units.la: 1 Prima huiusmodi est: Omnis ars corporū naturalium, naturalis est. Astrologia est ars corporum naturalium. Ergo est naturalis. Assumptionem vehementer tibi metuo vt verā probaturus sis. Prudenter sanè probare tentasti, Astrologiam esse arrem[?]. Statim enim hoc negaturus fueram. Ergo quo-modo probes consideremus oportet. Astrologiæ accōmodari seu tribui potest artis definitio. Ergo ars est. Etenim præcepta, inquis, multa huius artis extare, vnumq; finem spectare vtile vitæ, nullius hominū recte negare potest, licet aliqui eū nō semper cōsequantur. Paulò post, quid per præcepta intelligas, satis dilucidè declaras, cū Astrologos hoc anno vehementer æstū frequetesq; grandines futuras prædixisse scribis, ob Planetarū positū in trigonis & signis cali-dis[?], ac Martis sitū in Ariete, quo in eundē tepore sol ingres-sus est. Præceptū namq; Astrologicum tale erit: Planetæ & Mars si hac inter sese figura, cū sol arietem attingit, consti-tuti fuerint, æstum & grandinem expectabimus.
units.tr: 1. The first argument is this: Every art of natural bodies is natural. Astrology is an art of natural bodies. Therefore it is natural. I greatly fear that you will not prove the minor premise true. You have certainly tried to prove, prudently enough, that astrology is an art; for I would otherwise have denied it at once. So we must consider how you prove it. A definition of art can be applied to astrology, or assigned to it. Therefore it is an art. You say, indeed, that many precepts of this art exist, all aiming at one end useful to life, and no one can rightly deny this, although some do not always attain it. A little later you make clear enough what you mean by precepts, when you write that astrologers this year predicted a violent heat and frequent hailstorms, on account of the planets' positions in the trines and the hot signs, and the position of Mars in Aries, into which the sun had entered at that time of year. The astrological precept will therefore be this: if the planets and Mars are placed in this relation to one another when the sun reaches Aries, we shall expect heat and hail.

units.la: Talia præcepta (hac iā nominatione dignabor) cōtinere plurima Astrologiam nō nescio. Eadē illa inter se cōspirare ad vnū finē, scilicet ad futurorū præsensionē, minimē nego. Concedo etiā, utile hominibus plurimis videri posse futurorū præscientiā. Sic igitur artē esse ‚pbas: Astrologia est collectio multarū ppositionū[?] cōsensione quadā futurorū præsensione spectatiū. At hæc est ratio seu definitio artis. Quæ cū astrologia cōueniat, arte probatū est esse ipsam. Bona, ut puto, fide ratione tuā deduxi. Ad eā ego ita respondeo, fallacē esse tuā collectionē. Nā caret illis præceptis Astrologia, quæ in definitione artis ponūtur. Quod quō sit verū, iā docere aggredior.
units.tr: I am not unaware that astrology contains very many precepts of this kind (I will now deign to call them so). I do not deny in the least that these precepts agree with one another in aiming at one end, namely the foreknowledge of future events. I also concede that foreknowledge of the future may seem useful to very many people. Thus you prove that astrology is an art: Astrology is a collection of many propositions, aimed by a certain agreement at foreknowledge of the future. But this is the reasoning or definition of an art. Since it fits astrology, it is proved that astrology is an art. I have, I think, set out your reasoning in good faith. To it I answer that your collection is fallacious. For astrology lacks those precepts which are placed in the definition of an art. How this is true I now undertake to show.

units.la: Artē cū dicimus esse comprehensionē multorū præceptorum ad finē utile vitæ conspirantiū, nō quāliber propositionum siue enunciationum collectionē intelligimus, tamētsi mutua cōspiratione utilē hominī vitā quærāt. Veras esse tales propositiones, nō falsas oportet. Argumento nobis sint, Augurium, Extispicium, Geomātia, Onomātia, & huius generis cōplura alia deliramenta. Quis tā est audax, qui nō has quoq; artes (sic enim olim vocabantur) multa præcepta habuisse & habere, quæ aptē inter se consentiant ad intelligēda futura? Equidē, ut de alijs, quas nunquā sciui, nihil dicā, de Geomātia cui olim, dū Astrologica mihi adhuc arrideret, nō impigrā operā nauaui, hoc verè affirmare possū. Sed negari de alijs nullo modo pōt. Cur igitur nō habētur inter artes istæ superstitiones? Quia artis ratio illis cōuenire negat. Vera nāq; nō falsa esse oportet præcepta, ex quibus cōcinnē iūctis ars coalescere pōt. (Loquor de honestis & liberalibus artibus, nhonestę[?] ne nomine quidē hoc dignæ sunt.)
units.tr: When we say that an art is a comprehension of many precepts agreeing to a useful end of life, we do not mean just any collection of propositions or statements, even if by their mutual agreement they seek a life useful to man. Such propositions must be true, not false. Let augury, haruspicy, geomancy, onomancy, and many other follies of this kind serve as examples. Who is so bold as to deny that these arts (for so they were once called) have had, and still have, many precepts which fit together aptly in understanding future events? Indeed, I will say nothing of the others, which I have never known; but of geomancy, to which I once devoted no little effort while astrology still smiled on me, I can truly affirm this. Yet it cannot be denied of the others in any way. Why then are these superstitions not counted among the arts? Because the nature of an art denies that they belong to it. For the precepts from which an art can be properly constructed, when fitted together, must be true, not false. (I speak of honest and liberal arts; the dishonest ones are not even worthy of the name.)

units.la: Unde scitè Galenus tria in omni præcepto requirit, ut sit verum, utile, cōsentiens. Horū si aliquo careat, præcepti nomen pariter & naturam amisit. Quòd si vera esse oportet, ut ostensum iam est, sequitur primùm quidē, ut cum rebus concordent. Veritas enim orationis non aliunde, quàm ex concordia cū rebus æstimatur: deinde aliarū artium principijs nō repugnabunt. Verum etenim vero nunquam adversatur. Postremò propositum finem ut plurimum, si non semper possunt, & per se, non autem per accidens, efficere[?] seu consequi debebunt. Nam eorū quæ per accidens fiunt, nec ars est, nec ratio aliqua. Talia quoq; non plerunq;, sed raro eveniunt. Artes autē plerunq; suos effectus seu fines assequuntur. Ac referuntur artificiosa omnia, quatenus talia, in artem, à qua effecta sunt, tanquam in per se causam. Quare etsi præcepta aliquis complura congerat, itaq; inter se copulet, ut mutua consensione finem unum quærant, illum tamen per se nunquam assequantur, nomen artis non merebuntur. Falsa nāq; talia esse palàm est, nisi vera putentur, quæ eiuscemodi promittūt, qualia præstare nequeunt.
units.tr: Hence Galen rightly requires three things in every precept: that it be true, useful, and consistent. If any of these is lacking, the precept loses both its name and its nature. But if they must be true, as has now been shown, it follows, first, that they must agree with things; for the truth of a statement is judged by nothing other than its agreement with things. Second, they will not conflict with the principles of other arts; for truth never opposes truth. Last, they must be able, if not always then for the most part, to bring about or attain the proposed end through themselves, and not by accident. For things that happen by accident belong neither to art nor to any reasoning. Such things do not happen usually, but rarely. Arts, however, for the most part reach their effects or ends. And all artful things, as such, are referred to the art by which they were produced, as to their cause in itself. Therefore, even if someone heaps up many precepts and so links them that by mutual agreement they seek one end, yet if they never attain that end through themselves, they will not deserve the name of art. For it is plain that such precepts are false, unless they are believed true when they promise things they cannot perform.

units.la: Talia sunt, exempli gratia, Chymistarum præcepta, quibus aurum venantur infelices quidam. Tametsi enim illa concinnè iunguntur, unumq; omnia finem, scilicet auri effectionem, quærant: eum tamen, quia efficere & assequi non possunt, falsa meritissimo cēsenda sunt. Scio & experientia didici, multa & vulgò incredibilia per illa præcepta à peritioribus artificibus effici posse. Ad hæc si referantur, artis nomine dignabimur. At verò cum ad auri argentive effectionem, quam præstare non valent, conferuntur, falsa sunt, & à loco & dignitate præceptorum artis excidunt. Primum, quia non præstat quod promittūt: deinde quia huic principio sive axiomati, Ars naturam imitari potest, eadem quæ natura facit facere non potest repugnant.
units.tr: Such, for example, are the precepts of the alchemists, by which certain unfortunate men hunt for gold. For although these precepts are joined together neatly and all seek one end, namely the making of gold, yet, because they cannot make or attain it, they must rightly be judged false. I know, and have learned by experience, that by those precepts many things, often incredible, can be effected by more skilled practitioners. If they are referred to these, we shall grant them the name of art. But when they are applied to the making of gold or silver, which they cannot achieve, they are false and fall from the place and dignity of artistic precepts. First, because they do not perform what they promise; second, because they conflict with this principle or axiom: Art can imitate nature, but it cannot do what nature does.

units.la: Talis fuit illius conatus, qui se nauem fabricaturum receperat, in qua ita per aërem homines ad certum spacium veherentur, ut in aqua vehi videmus. Præcepta ad nauis fabricam, ut ille animo conceperat, collata, consentientia & vera potuerunt æstimari: at ad verum finē, hoc est, ad usum illius nauis relata, falsa fuerūt. Ex quibus omnibus apparet, quo pacto intelligendū sit, cum artē dicimus comprehensionem esse multorum præceptorum ad finē utilem vitæ producendū cōsentientium. Nihil ergo efficis, cū multa Astrologiæ extare præcepta dicis, quæ finē utilem, videlicet præsensionē futurorum spectent. Nā de Geomatria, Augurio, Extispicio, alijsq; divinandi modis eadē dici possunt nō minus verè, quàm de Astrologia, artes tamē inde eas ꝑbare, nemo sanæ mentis conabitur. Sic igitur ratiocinari te oportuit.
units.tr: Such was the attempt of the man who undertook to build a ship in which men would be carried through the air over a set distance, as we see them carried on water. The precepts for building the ship, as he had conceived them, could be judged consistent and true; but when they are referred to the true end, that is, the use of such a ship, they were false. From all this it appears how we must understand what we mean when we say that an art is a comprehension of many precepts agreeing to produce a useful end of life. Therefore you accomplish nothing when you say that astrology has many precepts which aim at a useful end, namely the foreknowledge of future events. For the same things can be said of geomancy, augury, haruspicy, and the other modes of divination no less truly than of astrology; yet no one of sound mind will try to prove from this that they are arts. So you ought to have reasoned in this way.

units.la: Ars est cōprehensio multorū præceptorū verorū, ad finē vtilē vitæ per se efficiendū cōspirantiū. (Si per se finē, non autē per accidens producant, patet vt plurimū cū attingi.)
units.tr: An art is a comprehension of many true precepts agreeing to bring about through themselves a useful end of life. (If they produce the end through themselves, and not by accident, it is evident that it is attained in most cases.)

units.la: Atqui Astrologia multa habet vera præcepta, quibus futurorū præsensio per se docetur, vt rarò à scopo artifex aberret.
units.tr: But astrology has many true precepts by which the foreknowledge of future events is taught through themselves, so that the practitioner rarely misses the mark.

units.la: Ergo astrologia ars est nominanda & habenda.
units.tr: Therefore astrology is to be named and held an art.

units.la: Hoc modo si fueris ratiocinatus, assumtio siue Minor tibi restat probanda. Quodcū facere incipis, quàm sint omnia vana intelliges, & cui humeros oneri subieceris cōperies. Loquor autē de præceptis Astrologicis, nō Astronomicis aut naturalibus. Nā Planetas certo tēpore tali schemate in cœlo apparituros cū aliis stellis, præceptum Astronomicum est. At talem stellarū dispositionem, talem aliquem certū effectum hic producturā, quales Astrologi se prævidere iactitant, præceptū est Astrologicum. Talia omnia, aut sunt manifestè falsa, aut ita incerta & dubia, vt probabilioribus semper cōfutari, quàm cōfirmari queant. Ergo nondum te probasse Astrologiam artem esse perspicuè vides.
units.tr: If you have reasoned in this way, there remains for you to prove the assumption, or minor premise. As soon as you begin to do so, you will understand how vain all these things are, and you will find what a burden you have put on your shoulders. I am speaking of astrological precepts, not astronomical or natural ones. For that the planets will appear in the heavens at a certain time, in such a configuration with the other stars, is an astronomical precept. But that such an arrangement of the stars will produce here such and such a certain effect, as the astrologers boast they foresee, is an astrological precept. All such precepts are either manifestly false, or so uncertain and doubtful that they can always be refuted more readily than confirmed by probable arguments. Therefore you see that you have not yet proved, clearly, that astrology is an art.

units.la: Miror profectò te credere causas insoliti caloris, fuisse planetarum in trigonis & calidis signis, ac Martis in Ariete constitutionem sub ingressum solis in eundem. Miror illud etiā, quòd torpens & frigore enectus veterator ille Saturnus, Martis æstū, quē ex solis propinquitate cōcepit, reprimere nō potuerit, præsertim cum in Tauro signo secundū vos frigido, (in quo etiā sol defecit,) cōgressus cū eo sit. Ego hoc anno quorundam, qui præcipui habētur, libellos prognosticos legi, nec tamē ab ipsis tale aliquid prædictum adverti. Tardum esse necesse est, qui præteritorum non causas qualescunq; comminiscatur, cum & somnia hoc modo aptent pleriq; præteritis. Sed hic nō est de his locus. Vnum præterire nō debeo, multis annis nunquā infrequentiores grandines in his & vicinis locis visas esse. Nihil etiam apud vulgares magis futilitatē Astrologiæ arguit, quàm de temporum mutationibus infinita mendacia. Lege quæ Bellan-tius in 2. artic.[?] quæstionis hac de re scripsit.
units.tr: I am truly surprised that you believe the cause of the unusual heat was the planets being in trine and in hot signs, and Mars being placed in Aries when the sun entered it. I am also surprised that old Saturn, sluggish and worn out by cold, could not check the heat of Mars, which he got from the sun's proximity, especially since he joined Mars in the sign of Taurus, which you call cold, and in which the sun was also eclipsed. I have read this year the prognostic pamphlets of some who are considered the leading men, yet I found no such thing foretold in them. It must be a slow mind that invents some kind of causes for past events that were not foreseen, since many people fit even dreams to past events in this way. But this is not the place for such matters. There is one thing I must not pass over: for many years, hailstorms have never been less frequent in these and neighbouring regions than they have been this year. Nothing also shows the futility of astrology among ordinary people more than the endless lies about changes in the weather. Read what Bellantius wrote on this subject in the second article of the question.

units.la: Quanquam si his terminis se contineret Astrologia, tolerabilis minusq; impia foret, quantumuis falsa maneret nihinihilominus. Quod ne tu quidem intra hosce cancellos te cōtinere possis, id probat, quod in fine de aduersarijs meis, de quibus ad te scripseram, assuis: Illi, inquis, nihil contra te scribent hoc anno. Astra enim nolunt, nisi mirabile aliquid. Haec cū legerem, risum tenere nō potui, statimq; sic cogitaui. Astra nihil nisi mirabile permittēt. Atqui edere, bibere, ambulare, loqui nō sunt mirabilia. Nihil ergo horū faciēt illi homines. Nulla videbā ratione, cur loq, numerare, currere, legere, si ita placuisset ipsis, possent: scribere aut quae cogitasset, nō possent. Ita ne animi nostri alligati sunt cœlis, vt ne scribere quidem nobis liceat, nisi Astrologica aliqua figura id iubeat aut permittat? Lōgissimè extra terminū procurris, & nisi substiteris, regressum non facilè inuenies.
units.tr: Yet if astrology kept within these limits, it would be more tolerable and less impious, although it would remain just as false. That you cannot keep yourself within these bounds is shown by what you add at the end about my opponents, of whom I had written to you: They, you say, will write nothing against you this year. For the stars do not want them to, unless something marvellous happens. When I read this I could not hold back my laughter, and I immediately thought as follows. The stars will permit nothing except what is marvellous. But eating, drinking, walking and speaking are not marvellous. Therefore those men will do none of these things. I could see no reason why they could talk, count, run and read, if it pleased them, but could not write what they had thought. Are our minds so bound to the heavens that we may not even write, unless some astrological figure commands or permits it? You have run far beyond the boundary, and unless you stop, you will not easily find your way back.

units.la: Tu ne ex astris, quid homines facturi sint particulatim vides? Ab alijs Astrologis negari audio. Si eiusmodi actiones nostrae à coelo pendent, vt eo nolente, nequeamus, quę meditati sumus, scribere, quae porro nobis relicta est libertas? Praeterea videris hoc velle, illos nihil pro Astrologia admiratione dignum posse praestare. Si possunt, & astra mirabilia non prohibent, incitè concludis eos pro Astrologia nihil scripturos. Si nō possunt, ignavos & imperitos Astrologiae patronos facis, nisi hoc pro excusatione adducas, quod ego vt verissimum libenter concedo, nihil praeclari, quod scilicet praecipua laude admiratione dignum sit, (hoc enim te mirabile appellare suspicor) à quoquam pro Astrologia excogitari posse. Si aliud per mirabile intelligis, quid mirabilius illi facere possint, quàm vt pro Astrologia ita, vt tu, pugnent, non perspicio. Quare si ἀστρολογικῶς[?] argumentari velim, maximè scripturos probem. Quod praeterea dicis nihil me physicum arbitrari, quod nō expresse docuerit Aristot. hoc tu nunquā ostendes à me dictū scriptrúmue esse.
units.tr: Do you see from the stars what men will individually do? I hear that other astrologers deny it. If our actions depend on the heavens in such a way that, if it is unwilling, we cannot write what we have planned, what freedom is left to us? Moreover, you seem to want this: that those men cannot offer anything worthy of wonder on behalf of astrology. If they can, and the stars do not forbid marvellous things, you wrongly conclude that they will write nothing for astrology. If they cannot, you make astrology's defenders idle and unskilled, unless you put forward as an excuse what I gladly grant as most true: that nothing outstanding, that is, nothing worthy of special praise and admiration, can be devised by anyone on behalf of astrology (for I suspect you call this marvellous). If by "marvellous" you mean something else, I do not see what more marvellous things they could do than argue for astrology as you do. So if I wished to argue astrologically [ἀστρολογικῶς], I would prove that they will write most of all. Moreover, you say that I think nothing is physical unless Aristotle has expressly taught it. You will never show that I have said or written this.

units.la: Secunda ratio tua haec fere est. Aristoteles non excludit Astrologiā à physica. Quinimò physicę ab Astrologo motū, lumē, influētias ita mutuatur, vt ab arithmetico numeros, à Geometra lineas accipit. Ergo Astrologia est Naturalis.
units.tr: Your second argument is roughly this. Aristotle does not exclude astrology from physics. Indeed, physics borrows motion, light and influences from the astrologer just as it takes numbers from the arithmetician and lines from the geometer. Therefore astrology is natural.

units.la: Hoc primum falsum est, Aristotelē non excludere eam à physiologia. Si [illegible, ~2 letters] faciat interroges, respondeo, ibi, vbi arte nō esse subindicat: ubi ex caussæ Universalis cognitione ar-tificiosa nihil illorum præsciri posse docet, quæ ab ea sine opera secundarum caussarum fortuito cum ea concurren-tium, effici non possunt: ubi contingentium futurorum præ-sensionem impossibilem esse monet: deniq; in tota ipsius physiologia. Quòd si mentionem Astrologiæ ipsum facere obijcies, verè tibi respondebo, ipsum non ita hanc vocem vsurpare, ut nos solemus, id quod & tu cognouisse videris. Si meum argumentum, quod Aristoteleum esse non negabis, considerasses, non hoc modo interrogasses. Primam ergo antecedentis partem nondum probatam vides. Nō ve-rius est, quod physicum proprie dictum, ab Astrologo aut Astronomo influentias & lumen mutuari addis. Nō enim unquam probabis. Motum, si rectè intelligas, siderum, ab Astronomo accipit. At disputatio de operationibus, viri-bus, & qualitatibus siderum, itemq; de luminis natura, & potestate, non ad Astronomum, sed ad philosophum natu-ralem pertinet, si rationi, si philosophorum sententiæ, si Ari-stoteli sides hic habenda est. Quis, quæso te, concedet tibi Physicum accipere motum ab Astronomo, ut iam taceam Astrologos? Ego ideo Astronomiam ex parte Physicæ sub-iectam putaui adhuc, propterea quòd motū ab ea mutuata fuisset. Ad Physicum pertinet disputatio de motu omnis, non ad Astronomum vel Mathematicum. Ubi nam hi do-cent quid sit Motus, quomodo fiat, quæ species, & quę præ-terea ad considerationẽ Motus pertinent? Plurimum cer-tè hic aberras. Proinde vides nunc tam esse falsam secun-dam tuam rationem, quàm falsa est prima.
units.tr: The first point is false: that Aristotle does not exclude it from physics. If you ask where he says it is not an art, I reply: where he indicates that it is not an art; where he teaches that from knowledge of the universal cause none of those things can be foreseen by artificial means, which cannot be brought about by it without the work of secondary causes that chance to concur with it; where he states that the foreseeing of contingent future events is impossible; and finally, throughout his whole physics. But if you object that he himself mentions astrology, I will truly answer you that he does not use this word as we do, as you seem to have recognised too. If you had considered my argument, which you will not deny is Aristotelian, you would not have asked this way. So you see that the first part of your antecedent is not yet proved. Nor is it truer that you add that physics, properly so called, borrows influences and light from the astrologer or astronomer. For you will never prove it. If you understand rightly, it is from the astronomer that physics takes the motion of the stars. But the discussion of the operations, powers and qualities of the stars, and likewise of the nature and power of light, belongs not to the astronomer but to the natural philosopher, if reason, the opinion of philosophers, and Aristotle's authority are to be trusted here. Who, I ask you, will grant that physics takes motion from the astronomer, not to mention astrologers for the moment? I had therefore thought that astronomy was still a subordinate part of physics, because it had borrowed motion from it. The discussion of all motion belongs to the physicist, not to the astronomer or mathematician. Where, pray, do these men teach what motion is, how it comes about, what its kinds are, and what else belongs to the consideration of motion? You are certainly very far wrong here. So you now see that your second argument is as false as the first.

units.la: 3 Tertia talis est. Philosophia distribuitur in Physicè, Lo-gicen, Ethicen. Ergo cū Mathematicæ disciplinæ sub Phy-sica continentur, multò magis huc Astrologia referetur. Naturalis ergo est. Mathematicas disciplinas sub Physica latè dicta (nam si proprie dictam intelligas, falsum est) con-tineri scio. Cur propterea Astrologiam sub eadem cõtineri oporteat, non scio. Nam nihil illa Mathematicum habet. Hæc enim certissima & verissima sunt omnia. Astrologica incerta & probabilia sunt tantum, vel ipsorum Astrologorum iudicio.Si ppterea[?] putes ad naturalē philosophię partē referendā, quia de siderū actionibus & potetijs[?] disserat, negabo tibi facultates in astris inueniri tales, quales Astrologi putāt dicūtq;. Quare cū somnia sint, frustra in diuinis illis corporibus assueueraueris, nisi rationibus demonstres.
units.tr: 3 The third argument is of this kind. Philosophy is divided into physics, logic and ethics. Therefore, since the mathematical disciplines are contained under physics, astrology will much more be referred to it. Therefore it is natural. I know that the mathematical disciplines are contained under physics taken broadly (for if you understand it properly, the claim is false). But why astrology should for that reason be contained under it, I do not know. For astrology has nothing mathematical about it. The mathematical disciplines are all most certain and true. Astrological claims are uncertain and only probable, even by the judgement of the astrologers themselves. If you think it should be referred to the natural part of philosophy because it discusses the actions and powers of the stars, I will deny that such powers are found in the stars as astrologers suppose and claim. Therefore, since these are dreams, you have been wasting your effort on those divine bodies, unless you demonstrate it by reasons.

units.la: Aves,atq; viscera animalium,ex quibus diuinabant omnes fere olim nationes, naturalia erant corpora. Quis pro-pterea species illas vaticinādi naturalis philosophiæ particulas hodie ponat? Quid in causa est? Nihil aliud, quàm quòd in cōmemoratis corporibus naturalibus, vires illæ, quibus talia præsignificētur, nō insunt. Si sæpe tamē eventum præsensioni respondisse dicas, respondebo & ego, vel casu aliquando ita evenisse, vel Dæmonum fuisse ludibria. Quod quia nemo, ut cōsido[?], nunc negat ac nescit, probare pluribus iam nō volo, quantumuis facilis sit ostēsio[?]. Quod augures avium volatu gestibusq; tribuerunt, quod Geomantes appellati punctis, aut ex his concinnatis figuris adscribunt, sed falso, hoc aut simile Astrologi perperam astris inesse affirmant. Non igitur considerat naturales Astrologia siderum vires, sed fictitias. Frustra ergo hinc probabis eam naturalem esse, nisi ante illud demonstratum sit, has potestates insitas ipsis esse, quae res particulares nostrates producant, quomodo producere Astrologi credidisse hactenus videntur, non sine magno errore.
units.tr: Birds and the entrails of animals, by which almost all nations once divined, were natural bodies. Who therefore today counts those kinds of prophecy as parts of natural philosophy? What is the reason? Nothing except that in the natural bodies mentioned there are no such powers by which such things are foreshadowed. If you say that the event often answered to the prediction, I will answer too: either it happened so by chance at some time, or it was the mockery of demons. Since, as I believe, no one now denies or ignores this, I do not wish to prove it at length to many, however easy the demonstration would be. What augurs ascribed to the flight and gestures of birds, what those called geomancers ascribe to dots or figures put together from them, astrologers, wrongly, assert belongs to the stars in the same way; but it is false. Astrology therefore considers not the natural powers of the stars but fictitious ones. You will therefore prove in vain from this that it is natural, unless it is first shown that those powers are inherent in the stars so as to produce our particular affairs in the way that astrologers have hitherto believed they produce them, and not without great error.

units.la: Quae de Thalete Milesio ex Aristotele adfers, causam tuam nihil juvat. Neq; enim Aristoteles eo in loco aliquid affirmat, sed Thaleti hoc adscriptum fuisse scribit, propter sapientiā. Permultum refert scire, cū authoritate alicuius probare aliquid volumus, utrum author, quē pro teste producimus, ex aliorū, an ex propria mente ac sententia loquatur. Equidē universa Aristotelis philosophia satis superq; declarat, nihil ipsum Astrologiæ credidisse. Adde quod ex historijs aperte admodū probari poterit, Thalete Astrologiæ divinatricis imperitū fuisse. Illo nāq; tēpore Græcis Astronomiæ principia incognita fere fuerūt, nedum Astrologicas nugas sciebāt. Thaletē primū Physicū fuisse, & primū inter Græcos cœlestiū motuū causas indagare coepisse referunt. Post hunc annis plus minus 8o. Anaxagoras floruit. Qui cū primus de Lunę defectionis caussa autus fuisset scribere, ab Atheniensibus in carcerem coiectus, vix est Periclis precibus seruatus. Nam sidera putabant Atheniensses esse Deos, nec naturali ratione & lege contorqueri credebant, sed se ipsa pro suo arbitrio circumducere existimabant. Quomodo post totidem fere annos Nicias Atheniensium res afflixerit propter ignoratam caussam deliquij Lunæ, docent Plinius & Plutarchus. Certè ante Platonis tempora, nemo præcipui aliquid inter Græcos in astronomicis percognouisse legitur. Huius amicus Eudoxus Cnidius, cū nō Astronomiā ratūm ab Aegyptijs, verùm etiā Astrologiā didicisset: hāc expressè damnauit, illā summo studio primus inter Græcos diligētius excoluit exornauitq;. Nō legimus vllum ex Græcia tanto studio hisce rebus operā dedisse. Tam studiose omnia apud Aegyptios obseruauit, siderūq; motus notauit ex loco editiore, vt Eudoxi specularū nomen ætate Strabonis adhuc locus ille retineret. Et hūc primum apud Græcos legimus Astrologiam nouisse, quem nihilominus damnasse eandē scribunt authores, propterea quòd fallacem & futilem deprehēdisset. Qui veræ Mathematicæ studiosi sunt aut gnari, hi facilè cum Eudoxo nugas istas reijcient. Sed redeo ad propositum.
units.tr: What you bring from Aristotle about Thales of Miletus does not help your case. For Aristotle does not affirm anything in that passage, but writes that this was ascribed to Thales on account of his wisdom. It matters very much, when we want to prove something by someone's authority, whether the author we cite as a witness speaks from the opinion of others or from his own mind and judgement. Indeed, the whole philosophy of Aristotle declares plainly enough that he never believed anything of astrology. Add that from histories it can very clearly be proved that Thales was ignorant of divinatory astrology. For at that time the principles of astronomy were almost unknown to the Greeks, let alone that they knew the astrological trifles. They report that Thales was the first natural philosopher and the first among the Greeks to begin to investigate the causes of celestial motions. About eighty years after him, Anaxagoras flourished. When he was the first to write about the cause of the eclipse of the moon, he was thrown into prison by the Athenians and was barely saved by the prayers of Pericles. For the Athenians thought the stars were gods, and did not believe they were turned by natural reason and law, but thought they moved themselves at their own pleasure. How Nicias, after nearly as many years, ruined the affairs of the Athenians because of his ignorance of the cause of a lunar eclipse, Pliny and Plutarch teach us. Certainly, before the time of Plato, no outstanding man among the Greeks is read to have known much in astronomy. His friend Eudoxus of Cnidus, who had learned not only astronomy but also astrology from the Egyptians, expressly condemned the latter, while with the greatest zeal he was the first among the Greeks to cultivate and adorn the former more carefully. We do not read that anyone from Greece devoted work to these matters with such eagerness. He observed everything among the Egyptians so diligently and noted the motions of the stars from a higher place that the name of Eudoxus' observatories still kept that place in Strabo's time. And we read that he was the first among the Greeks to know astrology, though the same authors write that he condemned it, because he found it deceptive and futile. Those who are students or experts of true mathematics will readily reject those trifles along with Eudoxus. But I return to my purpose.

units.la: Eudoxum secutus est Aristoteles, qui Callippi Cyziceni (vixit hic cum Polemarcho Cyziceno familiari & amico Eudoxi) familiaritate operaq; vsus, Eudoxi inuentis addere aliquid est conatus. Hunc si Astronomiæ tu non admodum peritum fuisse credis, quem post Thaletem fere 3oc. annis scripsisse ex historijs colligimus, quid de Thalete credes? Merito, ait, de Thalete hoc dictum fuisse, & propter sapientiam ei attributū, hoc ipso significans se nihil certi affirmare de ea re, quam compertam nō haberet. Profecto si quid tale cognouisse Thaletē credidisset, nō voluisset ipse quoq; nō scire. Sane quod hic de Thalete dictū refert, Plinius de Democrito scribit, ita sunt incerta omnia. Taceo quòd post Aristotelē neminē inter Græcos aliquot sæculis Astrologica[?] ꝑbasse[?] legimus. Ptolemęus Aegyptius primus, quod sciam, de hisce Græcè scripsit. Qui ipso antiquiores sunt, Astronomica duntaxat scripserunt. Hæc & huius ge-neris alia te examinasse conueniebat, antequam Thaletem diuinatricis Astrologiæ studiosum & peritum fuisse tibi persuaderes. Aristoteles certè hoc illi propter sapientiam adscriptum scribit ab aliis, ipse Astrologum fuisse non di-xit, nec fuisse cum talem credere potuit.
units.tr: Aristotle followed Eudoxus, who, making use of the familiarity and work of Callippus of Cyzicus (he lived with Polemarchus of Cyzicus, a friend and companion of Eudoxus), tried to add something to the discoveries of Eudoxus. If you believe that Aristotle was not very skilled in astronomy, and we gather from the histories that he wrote about 300 years after Thales, what will you believe about Thales? Rightly, he says, this was said of Thales, and it was attributed to him on account of his wisdom, thereby signifying that he affirmed nothing certain about a matter he did not have ascertained. Indeed, if he had believed that Thales knew anything of the kind, he would not have wished to appear ignorant himself. Certainly what Plinius writes of Democritus, about what is said here of Thales, shows that all these things are uncertain. I say nothing of the fact that after Aristotle we read of no one among the Greeks for some centuries who wrote on astrological matters. Ptolemy the Egyptian was, as far as I know, the first to write about these things in Greek. Those who were earlier than him wrote only on astronomical matters. It would have been fitting for you to examine these and other things of this kind before you persuaded yourself that Thales was a student and expert of divinatory astrology. Aristotle, to be sure, writes that this was ascribed to him by others on account of his wisdom; he did not say that he was an astrologer, nor could he have believed him to be one.

units.la: Ut non te decipiat homonymia vocabuli, sciendum est, Aristotelem nomen Astrologiæ hoc loco ex aliorum sententia ponere, pro obseruatione ortus & occasus siderum, quibus antiqui tempora operarum Rusticarum describebant. Qui vel Plinium vel rerum Rusticarum scriptores perlegit, facilè, quid velim, percipit. Quippe Astrologia ista Diuinatoria, de qua nunc agimus, apud Græcos Thaletis ætate ignota fuit. Quanquam verò per se res est probabilis & nota, non tamen pigebit Plinij verbis atque auctoritate planiorem restatioremque facere.
units.tr: So that the ambiguity of the word does not deceive you, it must be understood that Aristotle here uses the name of astrology, on the opinion of others, for the observation of the rising and setting of the stars, by which the ancients marked the seasons of rural work. Whoever has read through Plinius or the writers on rural matters will easily grasp what I mean. For that divinatory astrology, of which we are now speaking, was unknown among the Greeks in the time of Thales. Although the matter is in itself plausible and well known, I will not hesitate to make it plainer and clearer by the words and authority of Plinius.

units.la: Plinius lib. Nat. hist. 18. cap. 28. hæc habet: Ferunt Democritum, qui primus intellexit ostenditque cum terris cœli societatem, spernentibus hanc curam eius opulentissimis ciuium, præuisa olei caritate ex futuro Vergiliarum ortu, qua diximus ratione, ostendemusque iam plenius, magnam utilitate propter spem oliuae coëmisse in toto tractu omne oleum, &c. Et paulo post: Hoc postea Sextius e Romanis sapientiæ adsectatoribus Athenis fecit eadem ratione.
units.tr: Plinius, Natural History book 18, chapter 28, has these words: "They say that Democritus, who first understood and showed the fellowship of the heavens with the earth, while the wealthiest of the citizens scorned his care, foreseeing the dearness of oil from the future rising of the Pleiades, by the reason we have described, and which we shall show more fully, bought up all the oil in the whole district for the hope of the olive crop, to great profit," and so on. And a little later: "Afterwards Sextius, one of the Romans who pursued wisdom at Athens, did the same by the same method."

units.la: Hic primum dissentit Plinius ab Aristotele in nomine. Ille nanque Democritum, hic Thaletem fecisse hoc scribit. Deinde scribit ille, Democritum olei caritatem præuidisse: Aristoteles autem ait, Thaletem uberem olei prouentum præintellexisse. Quod Aristoteles dicit Thaletem ex Astrologia cognouisse, idque ex aliorum sententia, hoc af-firmat Plinius Democritum ex Vergiliarum ortu conie-ctasse. Et qua ratione præuiderit, explicatis verbis exponit, cum ait: Qua diximus ratione, ostedemusque iam plenius.
units.tr: Here Plinius first differs from Aristotle in the name: the one writes that Democritus did this, the other that Thales did. Then the one writes that Democritus foresaw the dearness of oil, while Aristotle says that Thales foresaw an abundant yield of oil. What Aristotle says Thales knew from astrology, and this on the opinion of others, Plinius affirms that Democritus conjectured from the rising of the Pleiades. And by what reasoning he foresaw it, he sets out in explained words when he says: "by the reason we have described, and which we shall show more fully."

units.la: Cæterum constat, Plinium nullibi docuisse, quomodo more Astrologico, ut hodie Astrologi talia profitentur, olei vel caritas vel ubertas sit præuidenda. At ita præcognoscere docuit, quemadmodum Agricolæ de hoc & aliis fructibus coniectat, & quemadmodum supra monuimus. Inuenies hoc cum alibi, tum in lib. præcedente, cap. 2. lucu-lente expositum. In utroque citato libro multa huiusmodi commemorat, ex quibus, quod dico, facilè intelligi potest, qualia nonnulla in 25. & 26. cap. libri 18. reperies. Huc & illa disputatio referri aliquo modo poterit, quæ de olei perfectione apud Theophrastum cap. 11. libri de plantarum causis sexti habetur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is evident that Plinius nowhere teaches how the cheapness or abundance of oil is to be foreseen in the astrological manner, as astrologers today profess such things. Rather, he teaches that it is to be foreseen in the way that farmers conjecture about this and other crops, and as we noted above. You will find this clearly explained both elsewhere and in the preceding book, chapter 2. In both of the books cited he records many things of this kind, from which what I say can easily be understood; you will find some such things in chapters 25 and 26 of book 18. Theophrastus's discussion on the perfection of oil, in chapter 11 of the sixth book on the causes of plants, may also be referred to in some way here.

units.la: Illud in Plinio & Aristotele primùm apparet, admodum incertam fuisse olim eam historiam. Deinde utrunque ea scribere, quæ apud alios inuenit. Præterea Plinium non in Astrologiam istam hodiernam, sed in antiquam illam referre. Inter alia dissensionis capita hoc etiam unū est, quod Aristoteles Thaletem nō scribit oleum coëmisse, sed arrabone data officinas Olearias pro eo anno conduxisse, id quod Io. Genesius Sepulveda primus, quantum ego scio huius rei, animaduertit, & ex Græco textu manifestū fecit. Hoc obiter, quanquam ad rem nihil admodum faceret, monere quoque placuit.
units.tr: In Plinius and Aristotle this appears first: that the story was in former times very uncertain. Second, that each of them writes what they found in others. Moreover, Plinius refers to not the astrology of today but that ancient kind. Among the other heads of disagreement this is also one: Aristotle does not write that Thales bought up the oil, but that, having given a deposit, he leased the olive presses for that year. Johannes Genesius Sepulveda was, as far as I know, the first to notice this and to make it plain from the Greek text. I have thought it worth noting this in passing, although it does not greatly bear on the matter.

units.la: Non malè fortasse senserit, qui falsò de Thalete hoc scri-ptum ac dictum putauerit. Neque primum fit hoc Græcorum in historia mendacium. Quinimò in eadem re non minus turpiter mentiti sunt, cum Anaxagoram ex A-strologia siue siderum scientia anno secundo 78. Olympia-dis dies prædixisse scripserunt, quibus saxum è Sole casurū esset, quod & cecidisset ad flumen Ægos. Quin & alium casurum prædixisse scripserunt, qui in Abydi gymnasio ea causa cultus postea fit. Vide Plin. lib. 2. cap. 58. Ratio quæ huc Anaxagoram perduxit, ea fuit, quòd Solem iudicauit lapidem ignitum. Quid mirum fuerit, si tam verum illud sit, quàm hoc est? Nisi plurimum fallor, minus posthac robo-risputabis in hoc Arist. et Plinij loco siue testimonio inesse, quàm vt vestram Astrolog. hinc Aristo. probatā ostēdaris.
units.tr: Perhaps he judged rightly who supposed that this was falsely written and said of Thales. Nor is this the first lie of the Greeks in history. Indeed, in the same matter they lied no less shamefully, when they wrote that Anaxagoras, from astrology or knowledge of the stars, predicted in the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad the day on which a stone would fall from the Sun, which indeed fell at the river Aegos. Moreover, they wrote that he also predicted another fall, and that a man who was later worshipped for this reason in the gymnasium at Abydos. See Plinius, book 2, chapter 58. The reason that led Anaxagoras to this was that he judged the Sun to be a fiery stone. What wonder would it be if that story were as true as this one? Unless I am much mistaken, you will show, hereafter, less strength in this passage or testimony of Aristotle and Plinius than is needed to show your astrology approved by Aristotle.

units.la: Quarta ratio hæc est: Verustissimi gentium Theologi, inter quos ultimus Plato fuit, anima mundi omnia per secundas stellas gubernari tradiderunt, ex quarum energia pro diuerso situ motuque omnes mutationes in inferioribus fiant. Ergo Astrologia naturalis est. Nihil hic de consequentia dicam tuae ratiocinationis. Nihil de theologorum illorum gentilitatis mente & opinione. Nihil de Platonis sententia, quam constat non fuisse Astrologicam. Plato certe, sicut post ipsum, Aristoteles, & post utrumque Averroes, nunquam crediderunt planetarum sive stellarum alias esse beneficas, alias maleficas, sed omnes omnino bonas putauerunt. At hoc principiis Astrologiae ita adversatur, ut vix aliquid, hoc non concesso, efficiant. Quomodo Plato animis ex astris descendentibus peculiares inesse dixerit potestates, quas inde acceperint, nō nescio. Sed quàm non sit vera illa sententia, & quàm nihil Astrologiae patrocinetur, similiter non ignoro. Istis omissis, ex quibus iam argumentū solutum est, alio modo apertius ita tibi respondere iam libet. Si omnes inferiorum mutationes à stellis, veluti à causis per se, proprijs & definitis fieri putas, plurimum deceperis. Etenim rationi, evidentiae & sensibus repugnat. Si vero tanquam à causis universalibus & remotis gubernari haec nostratia à stellis opineris, pinatique sint olim veteres illi, vitiosa[?] est tuae ratiocinationis consequentia, ut ratio, sensus, experientia, doctorum omnium consensus, & ipsimet Astrologi (inuiti licet) declarant ac probant.
units.tr: The fourth reason is this: the most ancient theologians of the nations, the last of whom was Plato, handed down that all things are governed by the secondary stars, the soul of the world, and from their energy all changes in lower things come about according to their differing position and motion. Therefore astrology is natural. I will say nothing here about the consequence of your reasoning. Nothing about the mind and opinion of those gentile theologians. Nothing about the view of Plato, which is certainly not astrological. Plato certainly, as also after him Aristotle, and after both of them Averroes, never believed that some planets or stars are beneficent and others maleficent, but thought them all wholly good. But this is so opposed to the principles of astrology that they can scarcely accomplish anything, even if this be granted. How Plato said that particular powers are present in souls descending from the stars, which they received from them, I do not know. But how untrue that opinion is, and how little it supports astrology, I am likewise not unaware. Setting these aside, from which the argument has already been resolved, I now wish to answer you more plainly in another way. If you think that all changes in lower things are caused by the stars as by causes per se, proper and definite, you will be greatly mistaken. For this is contrary to reason, evidence and the senses. But if you suppose that these earthly things are governed by the stars as by universal and remote causes, and those ancient men thought so, the consequence of your reasoning is faulty, as reason, the senses, experience, the agreement of all the learned, and the astrologers themselves (though unwillingly) declare and prove.

units.la: Quintam jam inspiciamus. Si Magia naturalis est, quid prohibet Astrologiam, quae rudior est naturaliorq̃e[?], & ad Aristotelis doctrinam accedit propius, naturalem esse? Si per naturalem Magiam intelligis eam facultatem, quae rerum naturalium omnium coelestium & terrestrium vires, naturas, operationesque perscrutatur, antipatheiam & sympatheiam rerum observat; latentes earum potestates explicat, quae quibus aprè[?] coniungi, quo pacto, quo tempore per quae media debent, perquirit: & ut temel[?] omnia dicam, quae nihil non facit, ut exactam rerum notitiam consequatur: dubium non est, quin eiusmodi ratio naturalis sit. Quinimò naturalium scientiarum omnium quasi complexus quidam summumque fastigium siue extrema perfectio existit. Hanc minus accedere ad Aristotelis doctrinam, cuius est absolutio quædam, quam Astrologiam, tunc[?] probabis, quando verum falsum esse ostenderis, aut contrà falsum verum esse declaraueris. Si quæris cur non vt hæc, Astrologia quoque possit naturalis censeri: respondeo, hoc obstare, quòd Astrologia tota est falsa, ficta, vana. Quòd sideribus tribuit, quæ nunquam habuerunt. Quòd ex fabulosis & fictitijs principijs & imaginibus futurorum præscientiam pollicetur. Quòd sensui ac intellectui notis principijs repugnat. Quòd si per Magiam aliud intelligis, tum respondebo, cum quid intelligas ipse intellexero. Nō enim diabolicam illam Magiam omnibus bonis damna-tam te commendare hic velle credere audeo.
units.tr: Let us now look at the fifth reason. If magic is natural, what prevents astrology, which is ruder and more natural and comes closer to the teaching of Aristotle, from being natural? If by natural magic you mean that faculty which investigates the powers, natures and operations of all natural things, celestial and terrestrial, observes the antipathies and sympathies of things, explains their hidden powers, and inquires which things are fittingly to be joined, in what manner, at what time and by what means, and, to say everything in a word, which does nothing so as to attain an exact knowledge of things: there is no doubt that such a method is natural. Indeed it is a kind of complex and highest summit, or perfection of all the natural sciences. Astrology comes less close to the teaching of Aristotle, of which it is a certain completion; you will prove that it does so when you show that the true is false, or declare that the false is true. If you ask why astrology too cannot be counted natural in the same way: I reply that what stands in the way is that the whole of astrology is false, feigned and vain. It attributes to the stars what they never had. It promises foreknowledge of future things from fabulous and fictitious principles and images. It contradicts principles known to sense and intellect. But if by magic you mean something else, I will answer when you yourself have explained what you mean. For I do not dare to believe that you wish to commend here that diabolical magic condemned by all good men.

units.la: 6 Sexta & postrema ratio similis est cęterarum. Multi appellant Astronomiæ partem naturaliorem, quæ est Astro-logiæ, naturalem. Ergo est Naturalis. Quis amabo te Astrologiam non Astrologus naturalem vnquam appellauit? Si hoc satis est, vt naturalis sit, quia à suis cultoribus ita nominetur: nulla tam impura inuenietur superstitio, quæ non ad minimum velit naturalis censeri. Pleræque non contentæ ista nominatione diuinæ videri volunt. Alia est probatione opus, quàm Astrologorum testimonio. Valde nanque parum integri incorruptique sunt in præsenti causa testes. Scio quidem Aristotelem & antiquos, Astrologiam naturalem appellasse: verùm non iudiciariam siue diuinatricem illi intellexerunt, sed Astronomiam notarunt, quam medium tenere locum inter physicas & veré Mathematicas scientias putauerunt. At hoc quid ad rem nostram? Non propterea vestra illa aut naturalis aut Astronomiæ pars censeri poterit.
units.tr: The sixth and last argument is like the rest. Many call the more natural part of astronomy, which is astrology, "natural." Therefore it is natural. Pray tell me, which astrologer has ever called judicial astrology natural? If it is enough to be natural that its own practitioners call it so, no superstition, however impure, will be found that does not wish at least to be considered natural. Most of them, not content with that label, want to seem divine. Proof of this must come from something other than the testimony of astrologers, for witnesses in this case are very far from honest and impartial. I know that Aristotle and the ancients called astrology natural, but they did not understand it as judicial or divinatory. They meant astronomy, which they thought held a middle place between the physical and the truly mathematical sciences. But what does this have to do with our question? Your astrology cannot for that reason be counted either as natural or as a part of astronomy.

units.la: Quemadmodum neque Onomantia illa rectè pars Arithmetices dicatur, quæ ex numeris præcipuè de cuiusque hominis natura, moribus, ingenio,felicitate, infortunio,liberis,exoribus vaticinatur[?]. Non enim quia numeris perperam vtitur, statim ad Arithmeticam pertinet. Sic neque Astrologia,quia sideribus abutitur, inter Astronomiæ partes reponi debet. Astronomiam veram esse, om-nes libenter docti confitentur. Astrologiam falsam esse, cũ alij multi, tum Deus ipse docuit in Sacris literis. Tu igitur incertissimum certi, contingens necessarij, per accidens contingens eius quod per se euenit, falsum: & quod esse nequit, veri ac necessario veri partem arbitraris? Non si sapis. Mathematica sunt certissima, Astrologica vobismet testi-bus maximè incerta & dubia. Quare veram te antè pro-bare Astrologiam oportet, quàm Astronomiæ partem facias.
units.tr: In the same way, that divination by numbers is not rightly called a part of arithmetic, the kind that prophesies from numbers about each person's nature, morals, talent, fortune, misfortune, children and wives. Using numbers wrongly does not make it belong to arithmetic at once. Likewise astrology, since it abuses the stars, must not be placed among the parts of astronomy. All learned men gladly admit that true astronomy exists. That astrology is false, many others have taught, and God himself has taught it in the Sacred Writings. So do you judge the most uncertain to be certain, the contingent to be necessary, the accidental contingency of what happens by chance to be what happens of itself, the false to be a part of the true, and what cannot exist to be a part of what is true and necessarily true? Not if you are wise. Mathematics is most certain, while astrology, by your own witnesses, is most uncertain and doubtful. So you must first prove astrology to be true before you make it a part of astronomy.

units.la: Sex tuas rationes omnino Astrologicas, hoc est, euani-das, elumbes, friuolas esse omnino perspicis, si non te cæ-cum reddidit Astrologia. Meas autem rationes ita suo lo-co persistere intelligis, ut ne pilum unum dimoueri ab omnibus tuis arietibus quiuerint. Prima tua ex commemo-ratis sola speciem aliquam habebat, quam tamen ita per-spicuè ostendi vanam esse nihilq; probare, ut nihil te de-sideraturum merito confidam. Cæterae vix dignæ responsione videbantur. Tam malè cohærent, tamque infelici-ter confutæ sunt, ut hiatum nemo non palpet.
units.tr: You clearly see that your six arguments are wholly astrological, that is, empty, feeble and trivial, unless astrology has blinded you. You understand that my arguments stand so firmly in their place that all your rams together cannot move them by a single hair. Your first argument, of those you have mentioned, alone had some appearance, yet I showed so clearly that it is empty and proves nothing that I am confident you will rightly have nothing more to ask on it. The rest hardly seemed worth an answer. They hang together so badly, and have been refuted so unhappily, that anyone at all can feel the gap.

units.la: In fine tuarum literarum hæc scribis: Rogo[?] ne ægrè feras, quòd durius aliquande[?] te appellem. Feci, ut stylus appareret vehementior. Hæc tua sunt. Quæso te, putabas me vehementiore oratione permotum stationem veritatemq; deserere, & in Astrologorum castra transfugere velle? Non ista metuo, nec minas & conuicia pertimesco. Solis argumen-tis terga do. Quòd si ignosci tibi cupis, propter ea quòd stylum hoc modo acuere placuisset, æquissimo iure me vicissim feres, cum à me durius aliquid dictum videris. Quippe nō vt stylum acuerem, sed vt partim tuas accusationes depellerem, partim veritatem strenuè defenderem, quæ duri-usculà vel acerbiusculè dicta videantur, dixi. Puto me, si tu-as literas cum meis contuleris, modestissimè scripsisse. Nō opus erat ista deprecatione. Nam, vt alias monui, non tam alios sine perturbatione & odio refellere, quā ab alijs quo-ties à vero discedere videor, sine dolore refelli paratus sum. Vale felicis. Non. Octob. Anno 1558. Heidelbergæ.
units.tr: At the end of your letter you write this: I ask you not to take it badly that I call you rather harshly at times. I did it so that my style would appear more vehement. These are your words. I ask you, did you think that I, moved by a more vehement manner of speech, would abandon my post and the truth and desert to the camp of the astrologers? I do not fear such things, nor do I dread threats and abuse. I turn my back only on arguments. But if you wish to be pardoned because you chose to sharpen your pen in this way, you will with the fairest justice bear with me in turn, since you see I have said something rather harsh. Indeed I did not write to sharpen my pen, but to refute your accusations in part and to defend the truth vigorously; what I have said, which may seem somewhat harsh or bitter, I said for those reasons. I think that if you compare your letter with mine, you will find that I wrote most moderately. That apology was unnecessary. For, as I have warned on other occasions, I am ready to refute others not so much without disturbance and hatred as I am to be refuted by others, without resentment, whenever I seem to depart from the truth. Farewell, happy one. Nones of October, 1558, Heidelberg.

units.la: EPISTOLA XIII. Thom. Erastus viro clariss.D. Petro Lothichio S. Medico, S. D.
units.tr: LETTER XIII. Thomas Erastus to the most distinguished Peter Lothichius, physician, greetings.

units.la: DIsceptationis quam nuper, vir ornatissime & clarissime de ortu, natura, motu, viribus Cometarū inter nos habuimus, adeò non memineram am-plius, ut nunquam recordaturus viderer, si non missò ad me libro in memoriā[?] revocasses. Nō enim ex professo in eā dissertatione, sed casu quodā incideramus. Nec eo studio ego tū quicquā asserebā, quo, cū cōsulto aliquid ago, asserere soleo. Ubi vero librū misisses, ac locum consignatū inspicere iussisses, minimè fuit difficile cunctorū reminisci, præsertim cū recens adhuc res esset. Cæteris autem omnibus, de quibus nō admodū discordantes habebamus sententias, omissis, de motu Cometarum, in quo plurimum dissentiebamus, & illis quæ præterea exponi tibi volebas, tunc, in præsentia quantum res postulare videbitur, dicam. Non aliud à me petere iam videris, cum de hac re duntaxat legere me, commonstrato per puerum loco, librum iubes. Quo res clarior fit, & nihil me falsi dixisse magis perspiciatur, rem totam ut gesta est, breviter repetam.
units.tr: The discussion we recently had together, most distinguished and illustrious sir, on the origin, nature, motion and powers of comets, had so completely slipped my mind that I would have seemed never to recall it, had you not revived it by sending me a book. In that discussion we had not set out to treat the subject formally but had stumbled upon it by chance. Nor did I then assert anything with the care I usually take when I deliberately set out to assert something. But once you had sent the book and asked me to look at the marked passage, it was not at all hard to recall everything, especially since the matter was still fresh. Leaving aside all the other points on which we did not greatly disagree, and those you also wanted explained to you, I will now, as far as the matter seems to require, speak about the motion of comets, where we differed greatly, and about the other points you wished to have set out. You seem now to ask nothing else of me, since you bid me read only this one matter, having the boy show me the passage in the book. So that the matter may be clearer, and so that it may be more evident that I said nothing false, I will briefly repeat the whole affair as it happened.

units.la: Cum amicis quibusdā & discipulis obiter insoliti caloris causas reddere tētaremus, & in ea narratione mentionē Cometæ, qui illis diebus apparuerat, fecissem, signū ipsum esse affirmavi, multitudine & copia siccarū exhalationū aërem crassiorē redditū fuisse, atq; ideo impressum à Solis radijs calorē pertinacius retinere. Quia vero neq; magnus, neq; vehementer ardens, neq; diu apparuisset, indicia nobis ea esse, nō tam multos in ipso vapores sive halitus potuisse contineri, quot sæpe in alijs animadvertissemus. Hæc tu cum audires, respondebas causam, quòd minus fuisset splendidus obscureque palluisset, non in materiæ qualitatem & copiam, sed multò magis in Saturnum, à quo esset accensus & ductus, referri debere. Nullū enim nasci, qui non à planetarū aliquo succenderetur ac moueretur. Hoc ego cum mihi verisimile fieri non posse dice-rem, propterea quod frequenter extra Zodiacum apparerent, nullaq; certa lege sæpe iam huc iam illuc inclinarēt, iā tardè, mox celerrimè[?] moueretur, & deniq; nullius planetæ motum seruarent: tu contrà, demonstrari posse rem ita habere, & iam pridem demonstratum fuisse, demūqúe omnes Astrologos ita semper sensisse aiebas. Omnium namq; sæculorum obseruationem ita rem habere demon-strasse.
units.tr: When I was trying, in passing, to give the causes of unusual heat to some friends and pupils, I mentioned in that account the comet which had appeared in those days. I affirmed that this very sign had been caused by the multitude and abundance of dry exhalations, which made the air thicker, and that therefore it held the heat impressed on it by the rays of the sun more stubbornly. But since it had been neither large, nor burning fiercely, nor visible for long, I said that these were signs that it could not contain as many vapours or breaths as we had often observed in others. When you heard this, you replied that the reason it had been less bright and had turned a dim pallor should be referred not to the quality and quantity of the matter but much more to Saturn, by whom it had been kindled and drawn; for no comet arises that is not kindled and moved by one of the planets. When I said that this could not be probable, because comets often appeared outside the zodiac, and often inclined now here, now there, without any fixed law, moving now slowly, soon very swiftly, and finally kept to no planet's motion, you on the contrary said that it could be demonstrated that the matter was so, and that it had been demonstrated long ago, and that all astrologers had always thought so; for the observation of all ages, you said, had shown that this is how things stand.

units.la: Quomodo, inquam ego, demonstrari potuit, cuius causa propria & proxima ignoratur? Vbi reperietur causa huius affectionis in Cometis, quod motu planetæ potius sequi eos oporteat, quàm stellæ alius cuiuslibet? Non enim videre me potuisse hanc apud vllum probatum authorem causam. Cometas ita ab exhalationibus generari, vt reliquæ traiectiones, eàdemq; materiam vtrorūq; esse. Quod si illi non nisi à planeta ducantur & attrahantur, consectarium videri, vt hæ quoq; ab ijsdem ducantur. Non generari eos certo & statuto tempore, vt eclypses, non ab vna eademq; causa, non ex vna semper & æquali materia. Deniq; tam esse in his, quàm in cæteris meteoris incerta omnia, ortum motumq; eorum tum solum sciri, cum præsentia fuissent aut essent. Formis differre, effectricem causam & materiam eadem esse.
units.tr: "How," I said, "could it be demonstrated, when its proximate and proper cause is unknown? Where will the cause of this property of comets be found, namely that they must follow the motion of a planet rather than that of any other star? For I could not see that any approved author gives this cause: that comets are generated from exhalations in the same way as the other meteors, and that the matter of both is the same. But if comets are led and drawn only by a planet, it would seem to follow that these meteors too are led by the same. Comets are not generated at a certain and fixed time, as eclipses are; they do not arise from one and the same cause, nor always from one and the same uniform matter. Finally, in them, as in the other meteors, everything is uncertain; their origin and motion are known only once they have been present or are present. They differ in form, but the efficient cause and the matter are the same."

units.la: Durare Cometas longiore tempore, moueriq; non tam celeriter, sed magis accedere ad stellarum motus. Causam dissimilitudinis quæri à philosophis & inueniri etiam in materię caliditate, siccitate, raritate, densitate, lentore, grauitate, leuitate, multitudine, crassitudine, paucitate, distractione, coagulatione, inclinatione, agitatione, impulsione ventorum, & similibus materiæ qualitatibus.
units.tr: Comets endure for a longer time and move not so swiftly, but rather approach the motions of the stars. The cause of this dissimilarity is sought by the philosophers and is found in the heat, dryness, rarity, density, viscosity, weight, lightness, quantity, thickness, scantiness, dispersion, coagulation, inclination and agitation of the matter, the impulse of the winds, and similar qualities of matter.

units.la: Ratiocinationem hanc tuam, Astrologi ita cuncti senti-unt, ergo verum est, nec veram nec necessariam mihi videri. Omnibus hoc sæculis ita obseruatum non posse dici, cum Aristoteles dicat, obseruatum inerrantes stellas aliquando materiam attraxisse, suoque motu circumduxisse. Talem etiam cometam Olympiodorum à se visum scriAd hæc tu, vehementer te admirari meam imprudentiā, imò potius temeritatem, quòd certa & confessa omnibus in dubium & controuersiam vocare nihil vererer. Facile esse omnia negare, at cum eiusmodi ne disputandum quidem esse, sapientes rectè prudenterq; præcepisse. Hic me nihil affirmare dixi, quod non à clarissimis ante viris com-probatum certò scirem. Itaque ex Aristotele eiusdemq; in-terpretibus, quæ memoria tenebam, (Tenebam autē ple-raq; adhuc, quod sub apparitionem Cometæ, de hac re di-sputationes eorum attentè perlegissem) attuli.
units.tr: You say that astrologers all think this way, and so it is true; but this reasoning of yours does not seem to me either true or necessary. It cannot be said that this has been observed in all ages, since Aristotle says that it has been observed that fixed stars sometimes drew matter to themselves and carried it around in their own motion. Olympiodorus also wrote that he himself saw such a comet. To this you replied that you marvelled greatly at my lack of caution, or rather my rashness, in not fearing to call into doubt and controversy things that are certain and admitted by all. It is easy, you said, to deny everything, but the wise have rightly and prudently taught that such things ought not even to be disputed. Here I said that I affirmed nothing that I did not know for certain to have been previously confirmed by the most distinguished men. So I brought forward from Aristotle and his interpreters what I remembered (and I did still remember much of it, since, at the time the comet appeared, I had read their disputations on this matter attentively).

units.la: Tandem non esse opus authorum testimonio dixi, ubi sensus controuersiam dirimere possent. Iudicare autem et videre nos oculis motus ipsorum ἀνωμαλίαν, nec posse eos ad ullius sæpe Planetæ motū aptari. Tametsi enim Planetæ errarent, & alij alijs motibus cierentur, esse tamen singulorūm motus certos & regulares. At cometas iam tardè, mox celerrimè progredi, paulò post subsistere videri, & repentè aliquando cursum incœptum inflectere, atq; aut ad latus declinare, aut retrorsum contendere.
units.tr: Finally I said that there was no need for the testimony of authors where the senses could settle the controversy. We judge, and see with our own eyes, that their motion is irregularity [ἀνωμαλίαν], and that they cannot be fitted to the motion of any one planet. For although the planets wander, and are moved by different motions, yet each has its own motion, fixed and regular. Comets, however, are seen now to advance slowly, soon very swiftly, shortly afterwards to stand still, and suddenly at times to bend the course they had begun, and either to swerve aside or to head backwards.

units.la: Hanc tu conuersionem ad retrogradationem Planetarum vocatam pertinere aiebas. Ego verò Planetas nō retrogredi, sed nobis ita nonnunquam videri, cum inter cætera hūc dicerem, seuerè monebas, ne Mathematicorū dogmata subuertere tentarem, magno meo malo. Non esse de eo dubitandum, quod summo ab omnibus doctis consensu esset semper approbatum. Ego quid hic dicerem aliud, quàm ut Mathematicos consuleres super hac re, siq; aliter illi rem habere te docerent, errorem me meum libenter cōfessurum. Multò magis mirabar, te Astrologię patrocinari voluisse sine causa, nec tamen principia eorum, quę huc pertinerent, perdidicisse. Quia consilium secutus es, eosq; consuluisti, & verè id à me dictum fuisse, te intelle-xisse mihi significasti, nulla nobis porrò hac de re controuersia erit.
units.tr: You said that this turning back belongs to what is called the retrogradation of the planets. I, however, said that the planets do not retrograde, but only sometimes seem so to us; and while I was saying this among other things, you sternly warned me not to try to overturn the doctrines of the mathematicians, to my great harm. There was no doubt about that, you said, since it had always been approved by the universal agreement of all learned men. What else, I said, could I say on this matter than that you should consult the mathematicians, and that if they taught you that the matter was otherwise, I would gladly confess my error? I wondered much more that you had wished to defend astrology without cause, and yet had not learned its principles, which bear on this matter. Since you followed my advice and consulted them, and have told me that you understood that what I said was true, there will be no further controversy between us on this matter.

units.la: Hoc te permouisse, ais, quòd ex falsis suppositis, non videres, quomodo vera demonstrarentur. In philosophia nō semel impossibilia, ut sic appellem, supponuntur, ut ex illi veritas propositarum rerum inuestigetur. Quod cum faci-mus, nec alios, nec nos ipsos fallimus. Ponimus substãtiam corporatam aliquando à quantitate & qualitate separatim considerandam. Ponimus materiam primam omnibus carere formis. Ponimus Aethyopem candidissimum esse, & huius generis infinita alia, ex quibus alia deinde rectè concludimus. Non enim philosophi ex his positis ita ratiocinantur vt Astrologi, sed verum hoc modo indagare solent. Sic Astronomi quae non sunt, esse ponunt, vt quae sunt hinc inueniant.
units.tr: You say that what moved you was that from false suppositions you could not see how true things were demonstrated. In philosophy, I reply, impossibilities, as I may call them, are not supposed only once, so that from them the truth of the propositions in question may be investigated. When we do this, we deceive neither others nor ourselves. We posit a corporeal substance that is to be considered at one time apart from quantity and quality. We posit that prime matter lacks all forms. We posit that an Ethiopian is very white, and infinitely many other things of this kind, from which other things are then rightly concluded. For philosophers do not reason from these suppositions as the astrologers do, but are accustomed to investigate the truth in this way. Thus the astronomers posit things that are not, in order to find from them the things that are.

units.la: Tota Mathematica disciplina constat ex talibus principijs, mente scilicet separatis rebus intentibus. Quòd si philosophus aliquis ita argumentetur, ponimus substantiam aliquā corporatam carere omnibus qualitatibus: ergo talis aliqua in rerū natura extat. Vel sic: Materia ponitur carere omnibus formis & qualitatibus, ergo reperitur alicubi talis. Si, inquam, aliquis ita argumentetur, an nō rideatur ab omnibus doctis? Similiter non valet, Lineæ Mathematicæ ponuntur extra subiectum, ergo re vera inueniuntur abstractæ. Fuit qui Mathematicas disciplinas falsas existimaret, propterea quòd non prorsus eandem reperiret rationem in Mathematicis lineis ac superficiebus, & in illis quæ in subiectis corporibus insunt. Quamobrem nō rectè argumentabuntur Astrologi, Planetæ ponuntur retrogradi, ergo verè retrogrediuntur.
units.tr: The whole mathematical discipline consists of such principles, namely of things considered in the mind as separated. But if some philosopher should argue thus: we posit that some corporeal substance lacks all qualities; therefore such a thing exists in the nature of things; or thus: matter is posited to lack all forms and qualities, therefore such matter is found somewhere; if, I say, someone should argue in this way, would he not be laughed at by all learned men? Likewise it does not follow that mathematical lines are posited outside a subject, and therefore are really found abstracted. There was a man who thought the mathematical disciplines false, because he did not find exactly the same account of mathematical lines and surfaces as of those that inhere in bodies as subjects. Therefore the astrologers do not argue correctly: the planets are posited to retrograde, therefore they really do retrograde.

units.la: Quòd si aliquis mihi hîc obijciat, Astrologos non ita ratiocinari, respondeo ipsos re vera ita argumentari. Dum enim ita colligunt, cum Planeta retrogreditur, Cometam qui prorsum antea mouebatur, retrorsum ire cogit, siue retrahit ab instituto cursu, & in contrariam partem impellit, nihil aliud prope affirmat. Argumentū certè vim roburq;, si valeat, inde habere oportebit, quod retrocedere verè ponatur. Si namq; hoc non sit verum, quomodo aliquid efficiet? Quod enim non est in rerum natura, id ne agere quidem aliquid poterit, vt omnes homines nō amentes libenter fatentur & præclarè intelligunt. Non verius est bis quatuor octo facere, quàm hoc est. Quò fit, vt ratio tua valere nullo modo possit, nec retrogressio Cometarum à Plane-tarum retrogradatione tanquam ab efficiente causa per-ficiatur, ut quæ in rerum natura non extet.
units.tr: But if someone here objects that Astrologers do not reason in this way, I reply that they in fact do argue this way. For when they conclude that, while a planet retrogrades, it compels a comet that was previously moving forward to go backward, or draws it back from its course and pushes it in the opposite direction, they are affirming almost exactly this. Their argument can only have force and strength, if it has any, if it is taken for granted that the planet really retrogrades. For if this is not true, how could it produce any effect? What is not in the nature of things cannot act at all, as all sane people readily admit and clearly understand. It is no more true that twice four makes eight than this is true. So your argument cannot possibly hold, and the backward movement of comets cannot be brought about by the retrogradation of the planets as by an efficient cause, since that retrogradation does not exist in the nature of things.

units.la: Quanquam si ea extet, nihil admodum Astrologos iu-vet, præsertim si Heliodorus recte docuit, retrogredientes Planetas nō aliter agere, quàm cū progrediūtur. Efficacius autē agere, cum propiores sunt, imbecillius cū plus absunt. Iam propinquiores terræ sunt, cum retrogredi videntur.
units.tr: Yet even if it did exist, it would do the Astrologers scarcely any good, especially if Heliodorus taught correctly that retrograde planets act no differently than when they advance, but act more effectively when they are nearer and more weakly when they are further away. Now they are nearer the earth when they appear to retrograde.

units.la: Quare Cometam qui prorsum ante ferebatur, nō retrahet, sed magis quàm ante impellet. Virtus enim Planetæ non mutata, sed efficacior est reddita, cum retrorsum ferri videtur, iuxta Heliodori opinionē, magni nominis Astrologi. Sed frustra hæc tā multis apud te expono, qui ab Astronomis & Mathematicis persuasus iam es, nullas esse Planetarum retrogradationes, sed apparere tantùm. Etenim inter φαινόμενα, non inter ea, quæ verè extant, numeratur Planetarum retrocessio.
units.tr: Therefore a comet that was previously carried forward will not be drawn back, but will rather be pushed more strongly than before. For the power of the planet is not changed, but is made more efficacious when it seems to be carried backward, according to the opinion of Heliodorus, an Astrologer of great repute. But I expound these things in vain to you, who have been persuaded by Astronomers and Mathematicians that there are no retrogradations of the planets, but that they only appear to be so. For the retrocession of the planets is counted among the phenomena [φαινόμενα], not among those things that truly exist.

units.la: In libro, quem mihi misisti, opinionem tuam probatam nō rectè credis. Aduersatur enim author tuæ sententiæ omnino plurimum. In 2. & 3. argumento, quibus probat, cometas non esse stellas, ita scribit: Cometa non apparent ullis statis temporibus, & cum fulgent, motus habent dissimilimos. Et mox: Deinde nec regulari motu aut certo feruntur. In 4. argumento: Et varietas ac dissimilitudo motus, non obscurè significat, materiam esse halitū in aere. Non uno aliquo loco, non spacio certo oriuntur aut vehitur, sed aliàs alibi incenduntur, & variè agitantur, propemodum ut aliæ traiectiones. Hisce iam, si libet, adde: sed Planetæ habēt motus certos. Concludes inde, non semper motu Planetarum moueri.
units.tr: In the book you sent me, you do not rightly believe that your opinion is approved. For your author is entirely and very much opposed to your view. In the second and third arguments, by which he proves that comets are not stars, he writes: Comets do not appear at any fixed times, and when they shine they have most dissimilar motions. And soon after: Furthermore, they are not carried by a regular or certain motion. In the fourth argument: And the variety and dissimilarity of their motion does not obscurely signify that their matter is a vapour in the air. They do not arise in any one place or at any fixed space, but are kindled now here, now there, and are variously driven, very much like other meteors [traiectiones]. Now add to these, if you like: but the planets have fixed motions. You will conclude from this that comets are not always moved by the motion of the planets.

units.la: Velim hîc obiter illud etiam notes, non posse ortum eorū prædici, nisi fortasse casu aliquādo euentus & forte fortuna respondeat prædictioni. Si namq; nec loco nec tempore nec cœli spacio certo oriuntur, sed instar traiectionum nascuntur & propemodum agitantur: facilè apparet, incertum esse eorum ortum, nullaq; præsciri eum arte posse.
units.tr: I would like you also to note in passing that their rising cannot be predicted, except perhaps when some event happens by chance and luck responds to the prediction. For if they rise neither at a fixed place, nor at a fixed time, nor in a fixed space of the heavens, but are born like meteors and are driven almost at random, it is easily apparent that their rising is uncertain and cannot be foreseen by any art.

units.la: Verum enimuerò respōdebis hîc mihi fortasse, nihil ad-ducta testimonia probare. Nā authorem diuersitatem seu dissimilitudinem motus Cometarum in diuersis conside-rare. Jam nihil prohibere, quin motum nihilominus singuli alicuius Planetæ sequantur, cum etiam Planetæ diuersissimis moueantur motibus, quantumuis singuli suos habeant peculiares & certos. Non difficile mihi foret ostendere, verba authoris ita esse intelligenda, vt ego intelligo, præsertim cum falsum sit Cometas irregulari motu cieri, si Planetæ alicuius motum imitentur, quos regulares esse constat. Cōparatione tantum dicuntur motus habere magis minusq; regulares. Deinde fatetur idem author, materiam Cometarum nō semper à Planetis eleuari atq; attrahi, sicut nuper tibi ex Aristot. & Olympiodori observatione probaui. Si ab alia stella attrahitur, ab eadem etiam duci valde est probabile.
