units.tr: But indeed you will perhaps reply to me here that the testimonies I have adduced prove nothing, because the author considers the diversity or dissimilarity of the motion of comets in different respects. Nothing prevents, you will say, comets from nonetheless following the motion of some single planet, since the planets too move by very diverse motions, however regular and fixed each may have its own peculiar motion. It would not be difficult for me to show that the author's words must be understood as I understand them, especially since it is false that comets are moved by an irregular motion if they imitate the motion of some planet, which is known to be regular. Their motions are said to be more or less regular only by comparison. Next, the same author admits that the matter of comets is not always raised and attracted by the planets, as I recently proved to you from Aristotle and the observation of Olympiodorus. If a comet is attracted by one star, it is very probable that it is also led by the same star.

units.la: Sed cōcedam hoc loco, (quia de huius duntaxat authoris sententia concertatio est) te prædicta verba interpretari vt voles, cū apertissimis ipsius verbis aliis ostendere propositum queam. Nam cum ad 1. argumentum Senecæ respondet, sic scribit: Antecedens non est perpetuò verum. Sæpe enim prorsus irregulari motu vagantur extra Zodiacum. (Hoc est, non sequūtur signorum ordinem, nec aliùm quoq; vllum, ut ponebat in antecedente Seneca) deinde etiam cum vehuntur iuxta signorum ordinē, id fit prorsus per accidens. Rapitur enim materia alicuius Planetæ viribus, à quo inflammata est. Non hic aperte dicit, Cometarum motus interdum prorsus esse irregulares? Regulares autem tum fieri, cum à Planeta materia illa rapiatur? Ergo aliquando nō feruntur Planetarū motibus. Idem sensus docet, quod hic author dixit. Nullus autē sensilium melior est certiorq; iudex, quàm sensus. Idē Aristotelem atq; Olympiodorum censuisse, supra indicaui.
units.tr: But let me concede at this point (since the dispute concerns only this author's opinion) that you may interpret the aforesaid words as you wish; I can show from the author's own most open words that the contrary is the case. For when he replies to Seneca's first argument, he writes thus: The antecedent is not always true. For they often wander outside the Zodiac with a wholly irregular motion. (That is, they do not follow the order of the signs, nor any other order, as Seneca assumed in his antecedent.) Then also, when they are carried along in the order of the signs, this happens wholly by accident. For the matter is seized by the powers of some planet by which it has been set alight. Does he not here plainly say that the motions of comets are at times wholly irregular? And that they become regular only when that matter is seized by a planet? Therefore at times they are not carried by the motions of the planets. The same meaning shows what this author said. Now no judgement of sensible things is better or more certain than the senses. I have already pointed out above that Aristotle and Olympiodorus held the same view.

units.la: Certum est inerrantes stellas nō moueri Planetarū motibus. Quare ne Cometæ quidē, qui harū stellarū motibus cientur, Planetarū motus imitātur. Nō minus certū est, tra-jectiones siue impressiones igneas planetarū motus nō semper, imò raro admodū, sequi. Materiæ motū sequūtur magis quàm stellarum. Porrò Cometas ex eadem gigni materia, & eodem propè modo, vel hic tuus author confitetur. Sententia eadem est Aristotelis, qui non nisi materiæ den-sitate, duratione & similibus qualitatibus differre arbitratus est Cometas & traiectiones. Nec dubitare videtur quin à traiectione Cometæ aliquando incendantur. Cum enim materia in loco aliquo conglobata est, & pars tenuior instar radij cuiusdam longius extenditur, ignemq; concipit, ignis per tenuiorem materiæ partem celerrimè discurres, vbi in crassiorem deuenerit, sistitur.
units.tr: It is certain that the fixed stars are not moved by the motions of the planets. Therefore not even comets, which are driven by the motions of these stars, imitate the motions of the planets. It is no less certain that the meteors or fiery impressions do not always follow the motions of the planets, indeed very rarely. They follow the motions of matter more than those of the stars. Moreover, even your author admits that comets are generated from the same matter and in almost the same way. This is Aristotle's opinion too, who thought that comets and meteors differ only in the density, duration and similar qualities of their matter. Nor does he seem to doubt that a comet is sometimes kindled from a meteor. For when matter has gathered together in some place, and its thinner part extends farther like a kind of ray, it catches fire, and the fire runs very swiftly through the thinner part of the matter, and when it reaches the thicker part, it stops.

units.la: Ex quibus liquet, non moueri eos semper aut necessario motu Planetarum, quemadmodum neq; traiectiones. Hinc illud etiam intelligi poterit, cur modo huc, modo illuc inclinent moueanturq;. Sequitur enim materia instar ignis, quæ iam in hanc, iam in illam partem exporrecta est, prout collecta in uno loco magis est, quàm in alio. Sæpe à vento in unum aliquem locum cogitur. Certè ex motu traiectionum ventos spiraturos præuidemus ab illa parte, vnde ipsos moueri conspeximus. Huc etiam facit loci consideratio, ex quo continuè halitus isti ascendunt. Confirmat hæc omnia, quod Philoponus scribit, Ammonium Cometam vidisse, cuius una pars magis quàm aliæ splendesceret. Pars una extinguebatur, dum alia quæpiam magis accendebatur, sicut in facibus quibusdam contingere aliquando solet.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that they are not always, or necessarily, moved by the motion of the planets, any more than meteors are. From this it can also be understood why they now incline here, now there, and are moved. For the matter, like fire, follows whichever way it is extended, now this way, now that, according as it is more gathered together in one place than in another. Often it is driven by the wind into one particular place. Certainly from the motion of meteors we foresee winds blowing from that quarter from which we have seen them move. The consideration of the place from which these vapours constantly rise also bears on this. Everything here is confirmed by what Philoponus writes: that he saw the comet of Ammonius, one part of which shone more brightly than the others. One part was going out while another was kindled more strongly, as often happens with certain torches.

units.la: Cæterùm motu primi mobilis circumducuntur Cometæ, sed plurimùm [illegible, ~9 letters], vt & aer, in quo est, propter materiæ ineptitudinem. Quòd si casu propter nuper commemoratas & alias similes causas prope Zodiacum materia constiterit, & deinde à motu primi mobilis magis magisq; relinquitur, mirum non est, quod instar stellæ certo videatur motu per Zodiacum ferri. Motum Planetarum tunc solum sequuntur, cum ab aliquo ex ipsis materia est attracta, vt comæ ei fecisse videatur. Vnde patescit, non esse verum quod Astrologi nugantur, à certa solum constellatione materia pro Cometa[?] attrahi, de qua re alibi firmiora diximus. Et vt verum esset, falsum nihilominus foret, præ-uideri eorum ortum posse. Nam qui in actione qualibet vel agens solum, vel patiens solum consideratur, necessario plerunq; fallitur. Sed nec philosophi aut prudentis intelligentisq;[?] hominis est, ex agetis natura velle de effectibus igno-rata passi natura & aptitudine, cōiectare. Caeterum de istis hoc loco disserere non fuit propositum. Quare finem fa-ciam, praesertim cum mihi persuadeam, me, quod probare debebam, validissimè probasse, Cometas non semper mo-tu Planetarū moueri. Iam quod præterea ex me scire de-sideras, quomodo Cometas negè principum mortes signi-ficare, & pestem mortalibus adferre, breuiter quidem, sed aperte tamen edisseram. Cometas significare aerem, quo tempore ipsi apparent, halitibus refertum esse, concedi ab omnibus scio. Quanto maiores sunt, longioreq; tempore apparet, tanto maiorem in aere halituum copiam collectā esse necessarium prorsus est. Etenim ex tali materia ipsi con-stant, imò nil sunt aliud, quàm exhalatio conglobata & in-censa. Quare necesse est, si magni sint, magnā etiam exha-lationum copiam de terra ascendisse.
units.tr: Moreover, comets are carried around by the motion of the first mover, but for the most part [illegible], just as the air in which they are is too, because of the unsuitability of their matter. But if, by chance, on account of the causes just mentioned and other similar ones, the matter has stopped near the Zodiac, and then is more and more left behind by the motion of the first mover, it is no wonder that it seems to be carried through the Zodiac with a fixed motion, like a star. They follow the motion of the planets only when the matter has been attracted by one of them, as a comet seems to have done for it. Hence it is evident that it is not true, as the Astrologers trifle, that matter is drawn to become a comet only by a certain constellation, a matter on which I have said firmer things elsewhere. And even if it were true, it would nonetheless be false that their rising can be foreseen. For whoever considers in any action either the agent alone or the patient alone will very often be deceived. But it is not the part of a philosopher or of a prudent and intelligent man to want to conjecture about effects from the nature of the agent while ignoring the nature and aptitude of the patient. But to discuss these matters here was not my purpose. So I will make an end, especially since I persuade myself that I have very forcefully proved what I ought to prove: that comets are not always moved by the motion of the planets. Now, as to what else you wish to know from me, how comets signify the deaths of princes and bring plague to mortals, I shall set it out briefly, but nevertheless plainly. I know that all admit that comets signify that the air, at the time they appear, is filled with vapours. The greater they are, and the longer they appear, the more necessarily there must have been gathered in the air a greater quantity of vapours. For they are made of such matter, indeed they are nothing other than an exhalation gathered together and set alight. Therefore, if they are large, it is necessary that a large quantity of exhalations has risen from the earth.

units.la: Quòd si longo tempore ardeant, præterquā quòd crassiorem indicant esse materiam densioremq;, necesse est, vt inferne continuè alimentum accedat, quo foueantur. Ne cogitari quidem aut fingi potest, quomodo vapor siue exhalatio tot diebus & septimanis, interdum etiam mensibus ignem sustineat, si non recens materia semper succedat. Quàm celeriter materia talem, præsertim tenuiorem ignis devoret ac absumat, cū alia meteora ignita, tum[?] stellæ cadentes nominatæ perspicuè demonstrant, quemadmodum fulgura quoq;. Celerrimè namq; ignis per eam discurrit, illo fere modo, quo per puluerem illum tormentarium discurrit. Dubium non est, Cometæ materiam densiorem, crassiorem, magisq; lentam esse, quàm aliorum ignitorum meteororum, quæ celeriter postquam orta sunt, iterum disparent ac dissipantur. At quantumcunq; lentam, crassam, densam imagineris, igni tanto tempore nunquam resistet, nisi continuè renouetur. Etenim ne densissima quidem ligna vim actionemq; ignis tam diu sufferat siue perferant. Quæ idcirco commemoro, vt rectè me posuisse liqueat, argumentum ipsos esse referti aëris crassis lentisq; vaporibus. Certum illud etiam est, ignem in ea materia accesum, ad se non ex vicina tantum, sed etiam remotiore aeris par-te exhalationes omnis generis attrahere, quantum omni-no attrahere potest. Quod non de illis tantum intelligi de-bet, quae inferne ascendunt, sed etiam de illis, quae per ae-rem antea sparsae fuerant.
units.tr: But if they burn for a long time, then, apart from showing that the matter is thicker and denser, there must be a continual supply of fuel from below to keep them alight. One cannot even imagine or conceive how a vapour or exhalation could sustain fire for many days and weeks, sometimes even months, unless fresh matter always came in to replace it. How quickly fire devours and consumes such matter, especially when it is thinner, is clearly shown both by other fiery meteors and by the so-called falling stars, as well as by lightning. For fire runs through such matter very swiftly, much as it runs through gunpowder. There is no doubt that the matter of a comet is denser, thicker and slower than that of other fiery meteors, which quickly vanish and disperse soon after they arise. Yet however slow, thick and dense you imagine it, it could never withstand fire for so long unless it were continually renewed. Indeed, even the most dense woods cannot endure the force and action of fire for so long. I mention these things so that it may be clear that I was right to lay down that comets are a sign of air full of thick, sluggish vapours. It is also certain that fire kindled in such matter draws to itself exhalations of every kind, not only from the neighbouring part of the air but also from a more distant part, as far as it possibly can. And this must be understood not only of those exhalations that rise from below, but also of those that had been previously dispersed through the air.

units.la: His ita positis, quae negari à nemine possunt, alterum ex duobus consequatur oportet, nempe, ut vel consumi hanç materiae maximam partem contingat, vel in aere relinqui. Non de illa tantum halituum parte, quae accesa est loquor (hac enim cōsumi aut semper, aut ferè semper, nemo, puto, ambigit) sed de omnibus per aerem vicinum dispersis, deq; terra eleuatis. Ab his si aer repurgatus fuerit, necesse est, ut qui relicti sunt, rariores, tenuiores, aridioresq; effecti sint, a lentorem maxima ex parte exverint. Unde necessum est, ventos & siccitatem aeris consequi, id quod plerunq; eve-nire tum nos videmus, tum antiqui observarunt. Aristote-lem eiusdemq; interpretes hic consulas moneo, qui hanc rem, ut cætera propemodum omnia, pulcherrimè accura-tissimeq; explanant.
units.tr: Since these points are granted, which no one can deny, one of two things must follow: either the greater part of this matter is consumed, or it is left behind in the air. I am speaking not only of that part of the vapours which is kindled (for that, I think, no one doubts, is consumed always, or nearly always) but of all those dispersed through the neighbouring air and raised from the earth. If the air is cleansed of these, then those that remain must become rarer, thinner and drier, having mostly lost their thickness. Hence it must follow that winds and dryness of the air result, which we see happen quite often, and which the ancients also observed. I advise you to consult Aristotle and his interpreters here, who explain this matter, as they do nearly everything else, most beautifully and accurately.

units.la: Si verò certa occasione eueniat, ut aer non expurgetur ab halitibus crassis ac lentis, & sequens aeris cōstitutio eos-dem vel non dispulerit, vel etiam auxerit: facilè putrescent, præsertim si vel venti humidi & pluviæ accedant, vel multi de terra vapores certa de causa eleuentur. Non enim om-nibus temporibus aut supra aut infra terram æqualis va-porum exhalationumúc copia suscitatur: id quod neminē negaturum cōfido. Nec ego sum, qui primus id dico. Dixit ante me Aristoteles sæpe, & longa admodum oratione in 2. Meteororū exposuit. Præterea non sunt vnius semper natu-ræ vapores, qui tolluntur de terra in aerē. Ex quo fit, ut nunc ventosus, nunc pluvius, nunc aliter affectus sit annus. Siqui-dē igitur nō expurgetur ab expirationibus aer, & aliæ eius-dem generis præterea accedat, pestē generari nō est mirū.
units.tr: But if by some particular occasion it happens that the air is not cleansed of the thick and sluggish vapours, and the following condition of the air either does not disperse them or even increases them, they will easily putrefy, especially if damp winds and rains come on, or many vapours are raised from the earth for some particular reason. For the quantity of vapours and exhalations raised either above or below the earth is not equal at all times; I am confident that no one will deny this. Nor am I the first to say so. Aristotle said it before me, and set it out at length in the second book of the Meteorology. Moreover, the vapours that are lifted from the earth into the air are not always of one nature. Hence it comes about that the year is now windy, now rainy, now affected otherwise. If therefore the air is not cleansed of these exhalations, and others of the same kind are added besides, it is no wonder that plague is generated.

units.la: An verò post extinctionem Comeræ, in aere exhalatio-nū magna vis remanserit, ex aliis est quàm ex Cometa con-iectandum. Quanquam nō negem, ex magnitudine ipsius, ex duratione, ex augmento, ex decremento, ex motu & in-clinaclinatione, deniq; ex ipsius extinctione cōiecturas nō omnino leues sumi posse. Hoc tamē certū est, rarò ita euenire, vt nō post Cometā purior sit aer multo quàm ante fuerit.
units.tr: Whether, however, after the extinction of a comet a great quantity of exhalations has remained in the air, is to be conjectured from other evidence rather than from the comet itself. Yet I would not deny that conjectures, not altogether slight, may be drawn from its magnitude, its duration, its increase and decrease, its motion and inclination, and finally from its extinction. This is certain, however: it rarely happens that the air is not much purer after a comet than it was before.

units.la: Neq; ego Cometam adferre pestem inter concertandū dixi, sed fieri posse, vt aliquando ipsius extinctionem pestis consequatur, affirmaui. Huius pestis nō Cometa causa fuerit, sed illa, quæ Cometam generauit. Hāc enim pestem generasse rectius veriusq; dixeris, quàm Cometam. Hic enim aliud nihil est, quàm accensus vapor, qui ab igne plerunq; consumitur. Et qui non absumitur, ita saltem attenuatur & disijcitur, vt altius ascendat, & in suprema aeris regione totus pereat. Quę autē causa hunc vaporem extulit, & in aere conglobauit, eadem etiam pesti materiam suppeditat, si nō maxima ex parte consumatur.
units.tr: Nor did I say that a comet brings plague while it is contending, but I affirmed that it can sometimes happen that plague follows its extinction. The cause of this plague was not the comet, but that which generated the comet. For you would speak more correctly and truly if you said that this vapour generated the plague rather than the comet. For the comet is nothing other than a kindled vapour, which is for the most part consumed by the fire. And that which is not consumed is at least so thinned and scattered that it rises higher and perishes entirely in the uppermost region of the air. But whatever cause drew up this vapour and gathered it together in the air, the same also supplies matter to the plague, unless it is for the most part consumed.

units.la: Si ante extinguatur, quàm halituum maximam partem dissoluerit, quacunq; tandē ratione accidisse intelligatur, non dicetur proprie causa esse, tametsi per accidens causa dici queat. Quomodo enim aliquid effecerit, cum est extinctus? Quæ causa eum extinxit, ea propius accedit, vt pestis causa existimetur, tametsi hic quoq; per accidēs id sequatur. Sed hac de re nimis multa.
units.tr: If it is extinguished before it has dissolved the greater part of the vapours, by whatever chance it is understood to have happened, it will not properly be said to be a cause, although it may be called a cause by accident. For how could it bring anything about when it has been extinguished? That cause which extinguished it comes closer to being thought the cause of the plague, although here too this follows only by accident. But enough on this matter.

units.la: Frequentius accidit, vt post Cometā aer nō tā multis vaporibus repletus existat, sed q[?] humidiores fuerat, pluuijsq; generādis apti, exiccetur, & flatuū ventorūq; apta materia fiat, siccitateq; pariat. Superiore anno 1556. qualis quātusq; per hyemē Cometa apparuerit, vidisti. Quāta siccitas eū secuta sit, præclarè omnes meminimus. Is quē pxime aliquot noctibus diligēter contemplatus nobiscū es, citò extinctus est, & non magnus fuit. Nihilominus calor eū solito maior & exoptatissima siccitas cum ventis siccis cōsecuta statim est, quæ iam tertium ferè perdurat mensem.
units.tr: More often it happens that after a comet the air is not filled with so many vapours, but, having been more humid before, it is dried out, so that it becomes unfit for generating rains and becomes a suitable matter for blasts and winds, and brings about drought. In the year 1556 you saw what sort of comet appeared during the winter, and how great. We all remember clearly how great a drought followed it. The one which you observed carefully with us for some nights just before was quickly extinguished, and was not large. Nevertheless, a heat greater than usual and a most desired drought followed immediately, with dry winds, and it has now lasted almost three months.

units.la: Prioris generis cometæ, vix rectè ab aliquo dicātur credantúrue occidere Principes. Etsi nāq; pestis eos sequatur, eo modo quo diximus, plures tamē ex vulgo pereūt, quàm ex nobilibus & opulentis, nisi omnino sæua sit latissimeq[?]; regnet. Diriores enim aut remedijs opportunis arcent, aut loco idoneo sibi cauent, infecta loca deserentes.
units.tr: Of the first kind of comets, it can scarcely be rightly said, or believed, that princes die because of them. For although plague follows them in the way we have described, more of the common people perish than of nobles and the wealthy, unless it is utterly savage and reigns very widely. For the rich either ward it off with suitable remedies, or guard themselves by a suitable place, abandoning infected places.

units.la: De posterioribus quid dicam nō habeo. Nec; unquā, po-stea quàm has res utcūq; intelligere coepi, credidi Come-tas aut signū aut caussā mortis Principū esse. Nā quomodo sint, nec Astrologi quidē exponere poterūt. Sed nō ideo non ess: eos aut signa aut causas dico, quia quomodo aut alte-rutrum aut utrūq; sint nō video: sed quia multi apparēt, cū nullus Princeps moritur: & multi occumbūt Principes, cū nullus illis præluceat Cometa. Quæ sit materia Cometarū, si perpēdere volemus, quomodo generētur, quæ forma, fa-cilè apparebit, tam nō esse eos aut signa aut causas interi-tus Principum, quàm nō sunt alterutrū cæterę omnes tra-iectiones. Ut uno me verbo expediā, & rationi & euidentiæ siue experiētiæ non cōsentire certò scio. Multo plures sum-mi Principes & Monarchæ moriuntur sine præcedēte Co-meta, quàm cū Cometis. Sępenumero insignes apparuerūt Cometę, post quos longo tēpore nullus Princeps mortuus fuit. Si quādo accidit, satis apparet casu ita cōtigisse, ut tum aliquis obiret mortem, cum Cometa nuper apparuisset.
units.tr: About the latter kind I have nothing to say. Nor, since I began to understand these matters in some measure, have I ever believed that comets are either a sign or a cause of the deaths of princes. For how they could be such, not even the astrologers will be able to explain. Yet I do not say that they are not signs or causes because I do not see how they could be either one or the other, or both; but because many comets appear when no prince dies, and many princes die when no comet shines upon them. If we wish to weigh carefully what the matter of comets is, how they are generated and what their form is, it will easily appear that they are no more signs or causes of the death of princes than all the other transits are one or the other. To put it in one word: I know for certain that it does not agree with reason and with evidence or experience. Far more of the highest princes and monarchs die without a preceding comet than with comets. Often remarkable comets have appeared, after which no prince died for a long time. If it happens at some time, it is clear enough that it has come about by chance, that someone died just when a comet had lately appeared.

units.la: Videtur hęc opinio inde nata esse, qd' inter aëreos ignes ita pene excellit Cometa, ut inter mortales hic Principes illustriores sunt, magisq; celebres. Sed quàm vanè hoc ad hanc rem aptetur, nemini non videre licet.
units.tr: This opinion seems to have arisen from the fact that a comet stands out among the fiery meteors as princes are more illustrious and more famous among mortals. But how vainly this is applied to the matter, anyone may see.

units.la: Nō nescio interim, qd Aristotelis aliqui expositores hïc cōmenti sint. Cum ex Aristotele didicissent, Ventorū & sic-citatis indicia & caussas modo exposito ipsos esse, sic ratio-cinati sunt quidam: Constitutione sicca & calida aeris lædi corpora necesse est, præsertim verò imbecilliora & delica-tiora. Taliaserè sunt Principum, quippe qui nec laboribus, nec perferēdæ aeris iniuriæ satis assuefacti sunt, & præterea delicatè uiuunt, in ocio degunt, corpus vitiosis humoribus replent. Quare promtius ab aeris intemperie tales lædun-tur, atq; vitam cum morte frequenter commutant.
units.tr: I am not unaware, meanwhile, what some expositors of Aristotle have devised here. Having learned from Aristotle that comets are signs and causes of winds and dryness in the manner just set out, certain men reasoned thus: bodies must be harmed by a dry and hot constitution of the air, especially the weaker and more delicate ones. Such are, for the most part, the bodies of princes, who are neither sufficiently accustomed to labours nor to enduring the injuries of the air, and moreover live delicately, pass their time in idleness, and fill their bodies with vicious humours. Therefore such men are more readily harmed by the intemperance of the air, and frequently exchange their life for death.

units.la: Quòd si hoc modo & caussæ & signa perhibeantur esse interitus Principum, nō repugno, modò longissimè petita ista cogites. Equidem per accidēs omnino & signa & caussæ erunt mortis Principum. Nā si multos alios Principum more viuere contingat, necesse est, ut non minus his, quàm principibus exitium minitentur & creent. Quod illi ipsi huius authores sententiae concedunt: quare non magis principibus, quàm aliis ominosi sunt hoc pacto Cometae. Si probare hanc sententiam potes, facilepatior.At hac ratione omnis, à quacunq; causa orta sit, aëris calida siccaq; intemperies, non minus quàm Cometae, exitiosa principibus dicenda erit.
units.tr: But if in this way both causes and signs of the death of princes are alleged, I do not object, provided you consider these things as drawn from far off. Indeed, signs and causes of the death of princes would be such only by accident. For if it should happen that many others live in the manner of princes, it is necessary that they threaten and bring about ruin for these no less than for princes. The very authors of this opinion concede this; therefore comets are no more ominous to princes in this way than to others. If you can prove this opinion, I shall gladly put up with it. But by this reasoning, any hot and dry intemperance of the air, from whatever cause it arises, will have to be called no less deadly to princes than comets are.

units.la: Quod de Porphyrij sententia in praesenti causa legimus, nihil aliud probat, quàm incerta esse omnia, quae Astrologi vaticinati sunt de Cometarum effectionibus. Nō enim non volunt hinc etiam suae vanitati commendationem aucupari, quamuis ad Astrologiam haec res non proprie pertineat. Est enim Cometa non in coelo, sed in aëre. Sic ergo Porphyrius: Si ad Austrum deferantur, pluvias dabunt. Si ad Boreales cœli plagas tendant, siccitates denotant. Si ad occasum praecipitentur, egregiam anni constitutionem futuram significant. Sin ad ortum vergant, pestes noxios q; alios morbos, quibus nequicquam manum Medicam admoveas, pranunciant. Haec Porphyrij, si juxta modum supra à nobis expositum accipiantur, non carebunt ratione. Sin aliter interpreteris, satis constat, rationi ea non consentire, nec even-tus semper respondere. Certè videtur ita intellexisse, uti jam demonstravi. Ad Austrum inclinantes indicium faciunt plurimarum exhalationum. Sed de his supra satis.
units.tr: What we read of Porphyry's opinion in the present matter proves nothing other than that all the things which the astrologers have prophesied about the effects of comets are uncertain. For they do not want to win from this a commendation for their folly as well, although this matter does not properly belong to astrology. For the comet is not in the heavens but in the air. So Porphyry: "If they are carried towards the south, they will give rains. If they tend towards the northern regions of the sky, they signify droughts. If they are hurled towards the west, they signify an excellent constitution of the year to come. But if they incline towards the east, they foretell pestilences and harmful and other diseases, against which you may apply the physician's hand in vain." If these words of Porphyry are taken according to the method I have set out above, they will not lack reason. But if you interpret them otherwise, it is clear enough that they do not agree with reason, nor do the outcomes always correspond. Certainly he seems to have understood them as I have now demonstrated. Those inclining towards the south give a sign of very many exhalations. But enough on these matters above.

units.la: Hactenus perspicuè, ut arbitror, & meam sententiam veram esse ostendi de motu Cometarum, & quomodo Principum interitus ac pestis vel signa vel caussæ dici posse videantur, exposui. Obiter etiam naruram[?], generationem, causam motus ipsorum juxta signorum ordinem, si aliquando ita moveantur, declaravi. Omnia verò satis, puto, copiose, brevius tamen quàm res poscere videretur tra-ctavi, propterea quòd negocijs impeditus aliter non pos-sem.
units.tr: Thus far I have shown clearly, as I think, that my opinion on the motion of comets is true, and I have set out how the deaths of princes and plague can seem to be either signs or causes. Incidentally I have also explained the nature, the generation, and the cause of their motion, according to the order of the signs, if they ever move in that way. I believe I have treated everything fully enough, yet more briefly than the matter seemed to demand, because I am hindered by business and could not otherwise do it.

units.la: Festinationi igitur nostræ ignosces, spero, cum quod desiderabis addi semper a nobis queat.
units.tr: I hope, therefore, you will pardon our haste, since whatever you may desire to have added can always be supplied by us.

units.la: Vale felicis. Ex nostro Museo.
units.tr: Farewell, and be happy. From our Museum.

units.la: Anno 58.
units.tr: In the year 58.

units.la: EPISTOLA XIIII.
units.tr: EPISTLE XIV.

units.la: Thomas Erastus D. I. C. Medico, & Mathematico S. D.
units.tr: Thomas Erastus, Doctor (D. I. C.), to the physician and mathematician, greetings.

units.la: QUod in fine literarum tuarũ à me petis, ne ægrè fera te hac in re à me dissentire, vir ornatissime, & omni mihi officiorũ genere colendissime, antea quã peteres impetrasti. Debet enim libera esse hominum iudicia, nõ ex alieno arbitrio pendere. Quare nõ modò nõ grauiter fero, sed vehementer etiã iudiciũ ingeniũq; probo, ꝙ[?] nõ temere à tua sententia recedes, in alienam pedibus discedas. Sapientissimè namq; Galenus monuit, ne temere cuiuis assentiremur, sed rationum momenta prius diligenter ponderemus. Ego ex te vehementer discere cupio, qua in re potissimum errasse censeri possim. Vbi docueris, instar Doctoris & præceptoris merito te colam, gratiasq; publicè priuatimq; agam vti debebo. Quod ad illa quinq; capita attinet, quæ in me reprehendis, culpa me omni vacare arbitror.
units.tr: You ask me, at the end of your letter, not to take it badly that I differ from you on this matter, most distinguished sir and most devoted to me in every kind of service. You obtained that before you asked, for a person's judgments ought to be free and not hang on another's decision. So I not only do not take it badly, but I warmly approve your judgment and talent, since you will not lightly depart from your own opinion to follow another's. Galen wisely warned us not to assent to anyone without thought, but first to weigh the force of the arguments carefully. I earnestly wish to learn from you in what matter I may be judged to have gone most wrong. When you have taught me, I will honour you as a teacher and master, and I will give you the thanks, public and private, that I owe. As for the five points you criticise in me, I believe I am free of fault in every one.

units.la: Nam quod ad primũ attinet, mihi vereor affirmare, me doctorũ hominũ de siderib. obseruationes veras, & ratione nitētes nõ contenere, sed omnino magni facere. Non hoc quæro, quomodo sidera suos effectus producant: sed illud inqro[?], an ratione aliqua probari possit, à siderib. talia effici. Alia quæstio est, cum, quomodo Rhabarbarum bilem pur-get, inquiritur, & cum, an probari possit bilè à Rhabarbaro educi, quæritur. Certè nemo facilè dicenti, Rhabarbarum bilè expurgare, credet, nisi vel ratione vel experientia verum esse doceri posse cognoscit.
units.tr: First, as regards your first point, I am reluctant to claim that I do not hold the true observations of learned men about the stars, which rest on reason, but rather that I think them of the highest value. I am not asking how the stars produce their effects, but whether it can be proved by some reason that such things are produced by the stars. This is a different question from asking how rhubarb purges bile, and whether it can be proved that bile is drawn out by rhubarb. Surely no one will readily believe someone who says that rhubarb purges bile unless he knows, from reason or experience, that this can be shown to be true.

units.la: Hoc scire velimus, an ratione vel experientia probari queat, illos effectus, de quibus vaticinantur Astrologi, à siderib. veluti à causis per se, & nõ accidens proficisci. Quod si experientia id ostendi possēt[?], credere nos vtiq; oportéret in sideribus potestatem inesse, qua hæc perficerent. Si vero nec ratione nec experientia demonstrari possit, nemo certè doctus credet, talia à sideribus effici, præsertim cum veræ & proximæ causæ notæ sunt. Si quis recte confutet rationes, quas attuli paucas ad probandum, Astrologos nō posse experientia probare, quòd tales effectus à sideribus efficiantur, fortasse credam aliquid huic vestræ experientiæ. Non sequitur, Astrologi prædicunt interdum aliqd, qp[?] ita fere vsuuenit: ergo Astrologia vera simul & ars est. Non enim vlla est tam inepta diuinādi ratio, quā nō arte esse, & quidem veram sis probaturus, si hæc ratio valeat.
units.tr: We want to know whether it can be proved by reason or experience that those effects which the astrologers predict proceed from the stars as their own causes, and not merely by accident. If experience could show this, we would certainly have to believe that the stars have a power by which they bring these things about. But if it cannot be shown either by reason or by experience, no learned person will believe that such things are produced by the stars, especially since the true and nearer causes are known. If someone refutes properly the few arguments I have offered to show that the astrologers cannot prove by experience that such effects are produced by the stars, perhaps I will believe something of this experience of yours. It does not follow that, because the astrologers sometimes predict something and it usually happens that way, therefore astrology is both a true thing and an art. For there is no method of divination so absurd that it could not be called an art by this argument, and you would be able to prove that it is a true one, if this argument held.

units.la: Non satis est, vt aliquid, quod Astrologus euenturum prædixerit, acciderit, sed à siderum tali positu effectum su-isse probare oportet. Plurima eorum ita euenerunt, vt Aruspices euentura dixerunt: at probari non poterit, aues ista naturaliter significasse. Plurima hodie, cuius rei testis esse certissimus possum, Geomantes prædiuinant ex punctis suis, vt ipsi quidē opinantur, quę sic euenniunt fere postea: at hinc non dices cōsequi, vt vel ars sit dicenda Geomātria, vel vera existimanda. Rhabarbarum probare facilè possumus bilem extra corpus exigere, quo fit vt nemo dubitet, quantumuis causam huius effectus ignorent. Docet namque experientia ita rem habere, quæcunque tandem eius rei causa ponatur. Ergo non nego experientiam, sed hoc ne-go, experientia ostendi probariq; posse, tales effectus à side-ribus, vt per se causa, effici.
units.tr: It is not enough that something which an astrologer foretold has come to pass; one must prove that it was brought about by such a position of the stars. Very many of the things that the diviners of entrails foretold have happened, yet it cannot be shown that the birds signified them by nature. Today, of which I can be a most certain witness, geomancers foretell many things from their points, as they themselves think, and these things often happen afterwards; yet you will not say from this that geomancy should be called an art or regarded as true. We can easily prove that rhubarb drives bile out of the body, so that no one doubts it, even though they do not know the cause of this effect. For experience teaches that the matter stands thus, whatever cause is finally assigned to it. So I do not deny experience; what I deny is that it can be shown and proved that such effects are produced by the stars as their own cause.

units.la: Alterum caput accusationis est, me perpetuò ridere e-ruditas doctorum hominum de his rebus coniecturas. Pu-to te intelligere, me de Astrologicis, non alijs vllis obseruationibus loqui, in quibus nihil eruditi reperiri posse existimo. Quare non eruditas, sed Astrologicas, hoc est, vanas & friuolas coniecturas despicio.
units.tr: The second charge is that I constantly laugh at the learned conjectures of learned men about these things. I think you understand that I am speaking of astrological observations and of no others, in which I believe nothing learned can be found. So I scorn not learned conjectures but astrological ones, that is, vain and frivolous ones.

units.la: Tertio illud tibi displicet, quòd non videam, quam sideralium effectuum notitia pulchritudinem habeat in natura. Ego non solum, quam pulchritudinem habeat mediocriter video, sed etiā quàm sit necessaria omnibus bus eorum virtus, præclarè intelligo. Illos autem effectus, de quibus Astrologi diuinant, à sideribus non nisi per accidens euenire certissimum est. Quare non est, vt eos valdè admirer, tanquam arte præcognosci in sideribus possin[?]:
units.tr: Third, you dislike that I do not see what beauty the knowledge of stellar effects has in nature. I not only see moderately well what beauty it has, but I also clearly understand how necessary its power is to everyone. Yet it is quite certain that those effects which the astrologers divine come from the stars only by accident. So there is no reason for me to admire them greatly, as if they could be foreknown by art from the stars.

units.la: Quarto loco damnas, quòd putem nullam esse homini cum cœlo cognationem, & non esse in temperamentorū varietate interdum ad cœlestes causas respiciendum. Primus nemo ex me vnquam audiuit. Sol & homo, inquit Magister Aristoteles, generat hominem. Non vbiq; ego & doceo & expono, cœlos esse generales horum inferiorū causas? Quomodo vero in varietate temperamentorum ad cœlestes causas me respicere velis, non intelligo. Non enim magis temperamenta per se efficiunt sidera, quā quid vis aliud, & quàm nos ipsos. Sidera cum homine generant hominem, nō absq; eo. Et cum ita temperatis hominibus, ita nō aliter temperatos generant, cum aliter temperatis, aliter etiam temperatos gignūt. Si ergo hæc ita intelligis, nihil repugno, sed tecum sentio. Si vero vt Astrologi accipiunt, tu quoq; intelligas, optima ratione dico non tantū non vtilem esse Medico eam consideratione: sed etiam perniciosam, idq; ex omnium doctorum Medicorum sententia asseuero.
units.tr: Fourth, you condemn me for thinking that man has no kinship with heaven, and that in the variety of temperaments one should sometimes not look to celestial causes. First, no one has ever heard this from me. "The sun and man," says Master Aristotle, "generate man." Do I not everywhere both teach and explain that the heavens are the general causes of these lower things? But how you wish me to look to celestial causes in the variety of temperaments, I do not understand. For temperaments do not produce the stars by themselves any more than anything else does, nor do we ourselves. The stars generate man together with man, not without him. And when they generate men of one temperament, they generate men of a different temperament from men of another temperament. So if you understand these things in this way, I do not oppose anything, but I agree with you. But if you understand them as the astrologers do, I say, for the best reason, that such consideration is not only not useful to the physician but even harmful, and I affirm this in accordance with the opinion of all learned physicians.

units.la: Quod postremò in me vituperas, id quoque nec dixi, nec credidi vnquam, scilicet omnium naturalium actionū rationes methodo ex corporū temperaturis desumi posse. Scio permultas esse occultas rerum vires, quæ ex crasi nō proprie pendent, tametsi absq; certa crasi esse nequeunt. Scio formas rerum suas in subiectis rebus exercere operationes, quas nemo temperaturæ effectus existimarit. Astro-logos rideo, & merito quidem, qui cum in veras & proximas causas referre tales recte possunt, in generalissimas & remotissimas causas, siderum videlicet mistiones, dedu-cunt. Qui in philosophia mediocriter versatus est, non ig-norat quamlibet stellarum figuram, quomodocunq; sese mutuo intueri dicantur, facultate vniuersali hæc nostratia permutare, ita nimirum, vt singula perperi apta sunt[?]. Nec refert, quòd non omnium eadem esse vis & potentia exi-stimatur.
units.tr: As for the last thing you blame me for, I have never said or believed it either: namely, that the reasons for all natural actions can be drawn by method from the temperaments of bodies. I know that there are very many hidden powers of things which do not properly depend on the mixture, although they cannot exist without a definite mixture. I know that the forms of things exercise in their subjects operations which no one would think to be effects of temperament. I laugh at the astrologers, and rightly so, who, though they could rightly refer such things to true and nearer causes, derive them instead from the most general and remote causes, namely the mixtures of the stars. Anyone moderately versed in philosophy knows that whatever the figure of the stars, however they are said to look at one another, they change these lower things by a universal power, so that each is aptly suited to its own purpose. Nor does it matter that the power and force of them all is not thought to be the same.

units.la: Non igitur negamus magnam esse cœli vim in hæc inferiora. Nec illud etiam omnino inficias, si ita velint Astrologi, cœlestium vires differre, non tantum vt Solis & Lunæ lu [?]men differunt, sed alia etiam ratione. Quanquam si accu-rate & ex Aristotelis sententia loqui velimus, non nisi maioris minorisque discrimen statuemus. Sed ex omnibus istis confici pernegamus, coelestia particulares & propinquas horum, quae hic fiunt, & quorum praenotionem profiten-tur Astrologi, causas existere. Non enim haec efficiunt coelestia, sed secundae, propriae, proximae, & per se causae, om-nia talia generant & producunt, actu a coelestibus recepto, ut in libello exposui, quorum à te iam refutationem ex-pecto.
units.tr: So we do not deny that the heavens have great power over these lower things. Nor do we altogether deny, if the astrologers wish it so, that the powers of the heavenly bodies differ, not only as the light of the Sun and Moon differs, but also in other respects. Yet if we wish to speak precisely and according to the opinion of Aristotle, we shall establish only a difference of greater and less. But from all these things we flatly deny that the heavenly bodies are the particular and proximate causes of the things that happen here below, and of which the astrologers profess foreknowledge. For the heavenly bodies do not produce these things; the secondary, proper, proximate and per se causes generate and bring forth all such things, by the action received from the heavenly bodies, as I set out in my little book, and whose refutation I now await from you.

units.la: Non tibi concedo Astrologiam à doctis partim bonam, partim vero malam iudicari. Totam enim, quanta quanta est, friuolam existimant, ac rationi, sensibus, philosophiae, pietati, aduersari maximè affirmant. Nunquam probabis ideo ipsam à D. Basilio & Augustino repudiatam & damnatam esse, quia pars ipsius aliqua tantum sacrarum literarum authoritatem imminuat. Totam, totam, inquam, friuolam, vanam, falsam, impiam, asseuerarunt, quatenus de contingentibus futuris diuinat. Hactenus enim iudiciaria & diuinatrix est. Quod in ea praeterea quiddam inesse aiunt, non ad hanc, sed ad Astronomiam pertinet.
units.tr: I do not grant you that astrology is judged by learned men partly good and partly bad. For they think the whole of it, however large it is, to be frivolous, and they strongly assert that it is wholly opposed to reason, the senses, philosophy and piety. You will never prove that it was therefore rejected and condemned by Basil and Augustine, because some part of it diminishes the authority of the holy Scriptures. They affirmed the whole of it, I say the whole, to be frivolous, vain, false and impious, insofar as it divines contingent future things. For so far it is judicial and divinatory. That it contains some other element, as they say, pertains not to this but to astronomy.

units.la: Auium naturam, motum, & huius causam considerat Philosophus naturalis. At quid futurum sit, si in hac vel alia coeli regione volet vel considerat, praedicere ad Augurij superstitionem pertinet. Valde miror, quomodo nō sis veritus hoc de Basilio & Augustino affirmare. De Basilio legere potes, quae in Genesim scripsit. Augustinus theologiae studiosum ne Astronomiam quidem, (quam tamen vtilem concedit, ad loca quaedam scripturae intelligenda,) perdiscere permittit, hac de causa duntaxat, quod Astrologiae finitima est. Quomodo igitur partem Astrologiae bo-nam seu veram concedat?
units.tr: The natural philosopher considers the nature and motion of birds and the cause of these things. But to predict what will happen if they fly in this or that region of the sky belongs to the superstition of augury. I am greatly surprised that you were not afraid to assert this about Basil and Augustine. You may read about Basil in what he wrote on Genesis. Augustine does not even permit a student of theology to learn astronomy thoroughly (though he concedes that it is useful for understanding certain passages of Scripture), and he does so for this reason alone, that it borders on astrology. How then could he grant that some part of astrology is good or true?

units.la: Non hi solum, sed alij omnes antiqui Theologi pariter & philosophi, eandem vituperarunt & condemnarunt, Hie-ronymus, Ambrosius, Athanasius, Origenes, Eusebius, Mar-tyr Cyprianus, Chrysostomus, Lactantius, Gregorius, Seue-rianus, Nemesius. Similiter philosophi Gentilium, quicūq; alicuius nominis & authoritatis fuerunt, ipsam deriserunt & repudiarunt.
units.tr: Not only these men, but all the other ancient theologians and philosophers alike, condemned and censured it: Jerome, Ambrose, Athanasius, Origen, Eusebius, the martyr Cyprian, Chrysostom, Lactantius, Gregory, Severian, and Nemesius. Likewise the philosophers of the Gentiles, all who were of any name and authority, scorned and rejected it.

units.la: Iureconsulti quoq; Christiani nō partem aliquā huius vanitatis, sed totam prohibuerunt. Constantinus capitis poena afficit Mathematicum, hoc est, Astrologum cōsulē-tem. Non addit is exceptionem hanc, si de talibus reb. cō-sulat, quæ sacrarum literarum authoritatem imminuant: sed absolutè occidi iubet omnes, qui Mathematicos de su-turis rebus consuluerint. In lege. 2. dicit Imperator, artem Geometriæ interesse Reipub. vt discatur, Mathematicam autem (ita tunc vocabant Astrologiam) damnalibem esse & omnino interdictam. Eodem fere loco, ita argumenta-tur Imperator, siue lex.
units.tr: Christian jurists too have forbidden not some part of this vanity but the whole of it. Constantine punishes the mathematician, that is, the astrologer who is consulted, with capital punishment. He does not add the exception, "if one consults about such matters as diminish the authority of Holy Scripture"; rather, he orders absolutely that all who consult mathematicians about future events be put to death. In the second law the Emperor says that the art of geometry is useful to the commonwealth and should be taught, but that mathematics (for so they then called astrology) is damnable and utterly forbidden. In nearly the same place the Emperor, or the law, argues thus:

units.la: Omnis diuinatio punienda est gladio.
units.tr: Every divination is to be punished by the sword.

units.la: Astrologia est diuinandi species.
units.tr: Astrology is a species of divination.

units.la: Astrologia igitur capitali supplicio prohibenda est.
units.tr: Therefore astrology is to be prohibited under pain of capital punishment.

units.la: Execrari te dicis, quæ sacræ scripturæ authoritate minu-unt, qp merito probo. Si ergo quę huius authoritatē quo-cūq; modo eleuāt ac diminuūt, verè detestaris, tota te diui-natricē Astrologiā detestari oportet. An tu credere potes, oēs Theologos veteres, quos & doctissimos & summos fuisse Philosophos constat, tanto consensu Astrologiam dā-naturos fuisse, si non perspexissent, ipsam pietati & sacrarum literarum veritati maximè aduersari?
units.tr: You say that you detest those things which diminish the authority of Holy Scripture, and rightly so, I approve. If therefore you truly detest whatever in any way raises up or diminishes its authority, you ought to detest the whole of astrology, which is divinatory. Can you believe that all the ancient theologians, who are known to have been both most learned and the greatest philosophers, would have condemned astrology with such unanimous agreement, had they not perceived that it is especially opposed to piety and to the truth of Holy Scripture?

units.la: Liber hic argumētum Pici obiter adducere. Argumētū est extra caussam, & ad hominē, scilicet Astrologos, hoc est, leue quidē, quod tamē eos perurgeat. Cum ostēdimus Theologos (taceo iam Philosophos & Imperatores) uniuersam Astrologiā, excipere Astrologi solent, ut tu quoq; hic facis, abusum duntaxat siue partē ipsos dānare, nō totā Astrologiā. Rationē esse putatis, quia quędā in ea viderint nō-satis pia & religioni consona esse. Sic ergo ex Pico arguo: Aut pie, sapienter & rectè fecerunt Theologi, quòd propter ab-usum siue partem Astrologiæ, totam damnarunt, aut non rectè fecerunt. Posterius hoc dici nequit. Non enim errasse uniuersos unà cum præclarissimis Philosophis et piis Imperatoribus rectè credi potest. Nō inficior oēs errasse in multis:at oēs errasse in ea re,in qua cōsenserunt, hoc est quod pernego. Nā si aliqua in re una ipsorum aliquis erravit, alij errorē correxerunt ac indicarūt. Ubi inter se cōsentiūt,nō facilè ipsos errasse demōstraveris. At hac in re cōsentiunt omnino. Malè igitur putaveris eos hīc aberrasse. Rectè ergo & piè fecerunt. Cur igitur nō & vos eā abijcitis, & rectè factū sanctissimorū hominum imitamini? Nullā illi honestā artē spreuerunt. At Astrologiam modis omnib. lacerarunt. Quòd si tot ac tanti viri Astrologiā ideo vituperārunt, ac ut discereturvetuerunt, quia aliquid solū in se haberet vitij, ut tu ais, vel quia multi ea perperam uterentur, ut alij quidā affirmānt: quid existimaturos fuisse cogitas, si totā vanā cognouissent? Ac re vera vanā illi totā esse peruiderunt,ideoq; execrati eam sunt. Hæc respondere ad tuam accusationem volui, expectans interim quomodo argumētis sis confutaturus, quæ te refutare posse aiebas. Vale feliciter. 16. Januarij. Anno 59.
units.tr: I have briefly brought this book's argument, that of Pico, into the matter. It is an argument beside the point and addressed to the man, namely to astrologers; it is a light one, yet it presses them hard. When we show that the theologians (I say nothing yet of the philosophers and emperors) condemned the whole of astrology, astrologers are accustomed to make an exception, as you also do here: they condemn only the abuse, or a part, and not the whole of astrology. You think the reason is that they saw some things in it that were not sufficiently pious and consonant with religion. So I argue from Pico as follows: either the theologians acted piously, wisely and rightly in condemning the whole of astrology on account of its abuse or part, or they did not act rightly. The latter cannot be said. For it cannot be credited that all of them, together with the most distinguished philosophers and pious emperors, were wrong. I do not deny that all of them erred in many things; but that they all erred in the matter in which they agreed, this I flatly deny. For if one of them erred in some point, the others corrected and pointed out the error. Where they agree among themselves, you will not easily demonstrate that they were in error. But in this matter they agree entirely. Therefore you will have thought wrongly that they went astray here. Rightly, then, and piously did they act. Why, then, do you not also reject it, and imitate the right action of these most holy men? They spurned no honourable art. But they tore astrology apart in every way. And if so many great men condemned astrology, and forbade it to be learned, because it contained only some fault in itself, as you say, or because many used it wrongly, as others maintain, what do you think they would have judged had they known it to be wholly vain? And indeed they saw clearly that it was wholly vain, and therefore they execrated it. I have wished to answer thus to your accusation, meanwhile awaiting how you will refute the arguments which you said you could overturn. Farewell happily. 16 January, in the year 59.

units.la: AD EUNDEM
units.tr: AD EUNDEM

units.la: Epistola XV.
units.tr: Epistle XV.

units.la: DVo tantū te attingere velle, vir colendissime, ex illis, quę in meis literis cōtinentur, scribis. Primū est, quòd scripsi, cœlum universalē caussam esse effectuum, de quibus Astrologi vaticinantur. Alterum, quòd per experientiā cognosci posse negaui, an effectus eiusmodi à sideribus producti effectiq; sint. Hæc duo leviter te attingere velle scribis. Maluissem te graviter tractasse. Deinde vehementer cupiebā, ut argumēta edi ti libelli confutasses, sicut nō esse tibi difficile affirmabas. Neq; te excusat, quòd jam nō omnia te perlustrasse dicis. Illorum nāq; refutatione tantū ex te discere desiderabam, quæ perlegisses, & refellere posse videri volebas. Sed quia aliter tibi visum est, libet hæc ipsa ordine expendere, quæ pro Astrologia adduxisti.
units.tr: You write, most honoured sir, that you wish to touch on only two points from what is contained in my letter. The first is that I wrote that the heavens are the universal cause of the effects which the astrologers prophesy. The second is that I denied that it can be known by experience whether effects of that kind are really produced by the stars. You say you wish to touch on these two points only lightly. I would have preferred you to treat them seriously. I was also eager for you to refute the arguments of my published little book, as you claimed would not be difficult for you. Nor does your saying that you have not yet gone through everything excuse you. I only wished to learn from you the refutation of those arguments which you had read through and which you wanted to seem able to refute. But since you have decided otherwise, I am pleased to weigh in order the very points you have advanced for astrology.

units.la: Principiō rectè colligis, me in ea opinione esse, ut putē, astra cōcurrere ad generationē & effectionem omnium, quæ hīc fiunt à Natura. Rectè illud etiam me respondere asseris, ut generales causas duntaxat concurrere, at effectus nequaquam distinguere. Non rectè autem illud addis, Sauonarolam hac responsione prognostarū de morte sua sententiam eludere voluisse. Nam suum hunc librum anno 1497. conscripsit, quo tempore neminem illi morte praedixisse legi. Equidem hostis ipsius Bellantius, quicquid vel à se vel ab aliis praedictum cognouit, quod de illo quo vis modo intelligi exponiq; posse iudicaretur, comme-morat, sed tale nihil recitat. Narrat Episcopum quendam ex magna Saturni & Iouis coiunctione, quae ante aliquot annos apparuerat, de aduentu falsi prophetæ, in genere ta-men, praediuinasse. Hanc Episcopi hariolationem iniquis-simè pariter ac imperitissimè in Sauonarolam detorquet. Refert idem se quinq; ante ipsius obitum mensibus inspecta ipsius genitura, praedixisse, ipsum ad haeresim propen-sum, vitamq; laqueo finiturum esse. At cōbustus est anno 1499. Ante ergo ediderat suum libellum, quàm Bellantius de ipsius morte vaticinatus fuisset. Sed quid hic dixit Sauonarola, quod non ante eum Picus rectè verisimeq; dixisset? Num & hunc ideo dixisse dices, vt prognostas eluderet? Mirari magis debemus, quòd praeuidere propria calamitatem non potuit Bellantius, tantus scilicet vates, & tam oculatus in cognoscenda aliena Astrologus.
units.tr: First, you rightly infer that I hold the opinion that the stars concur in the generation and production of all the things that nature brings about here. You also rightly say that I reply that they concur only as general causes, and do not determine particular effects. But you wrongly add that by this reply Savonarola wished to evade the sentence of his prognosticators concerning his death. For he wrote this book of his in the year 1497, at which time I have read that no one had predicted his death to him. Indeed Bellanti, his enemy, recounts whatever he knew to have been predicted, either by himself or by others, that could be judged to be explained or interpreted in some way as referring to Savonarola, but he reports nothing of that kind. He relates that a certain bishop, from the great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter which had appeared some years earlier, foretold in general terms the coming of a false prophet. Bellanti twists this bishop's guess against Savonarola most unjustly and most ignorantly. The same man reports that five months before Savonarola's death, having examined his horoscope, he predicted that Savonarola, being inclined to heresy, would end his life by a noose. But Savonarola was burned in the year 1499. So he had published his little book before Bellanti made his prophecy about his death. But what did Savonarola say here that Picus had not said earlier, rightly and more truly? Will you say that he too said it for this reason, to evade the prognosticators? We ought rather to marvel that Bellanti, so great a seer and so keen-sighted an astrologer in reading others' fortunes, could not foresee his own calamity.

units.la: Sed praestiterit videre quàm docta fuerit Bellantij hariolatio. Multo iam tempore publicè priuatimq; docue-rat Florentiæ Sauonarola.
units.tr: But it is worth seeing how learned Bellanti's prophecy was. For a long time Savonarola had been teaching publicly and privately at Florence:

units.la: Communionem sub vtraque specie percipiendam.
units.tr: That the Communion is to be received under both kinds.

units.la: Indulgentias esse Paparum aucupia.
units.tr: That indulgences are the Pope's fowling-snares.

units.la: Primatum Papæ non esse iuris Diuini.
units.tr: That the primacy of the Pope is not of divine right.

units.la: Claues non vni Petro, sed toti Ecclesiæ traditas.
units.tr: That the keys were given not to Peter alone, but to the whole Church.

units.la: Papam suas traditiones pluris facere, quàm Christi me-ritum, atque Antichristum esse.
units.tr: That the Pope values his own traditions more than the merit of Christ, and that he is Antichrist.

units.la: Excommunicationes Pontificias non metuendas esse, & huius generis alia plurima. An erat Bellantio hæcaudienti (exulabat enim tunc Florentiæ) difficile prædicere, quòd ad hæresim inclinaret, occidendusq; à Pontifice esset? Qui illis temporibus talia docebat, pro hæretico ab omnibus habebatur. Rusticii inter Papicolas nunc etiam tantum habent ingenij,eruditionis,Astrologiæ.
units.tr: That papal excommunications are not to be feared, and many other things of this kind. Was it difficult for Bellanti, hearing these things (for he was then living in exile at Florence), to predict that Savonarola was inclining to heresy and would be killed by the Pope? Whoever taught such things in those times was regarded by everyone as a heretic. Even now the simple folk among the Papists have as much wit, learning and astrology as that.

units.la: Iam alterum consideremus, vt Astrologorum inceptias propius videas. Occidendum prædixit. Cur quaso? Quia hæreticus erat,respondebit. Cur hęreticus,rogo,erat? Quia Papam vocauit Antichristum,& cætera illa,quæ suprà con-numeraui docuit. Omnes igitur nos hæretici cōburendiq; Astrologorū iudicio sumus. Vehementer velim scire,quo-modo stellæ falsos faciāt prophetas. Bellantius intemperatas stellas fures,homicidas efficere ait,corrumpendo spiritus,humores,& elemēta natorum. Tale quid ergo efficiendo,falsos prophetas generabunt. Non enim animum per se afficere mutareq;, ex omnium etiā Astrologorum sententia,stellæ possunt. Sed friuola est, à ratione & philosophia alienissima ista imaginario.
units.tr: Now let us consider the second point, so that you may see more closely the follies of the astrologers. Bellanti predicted that Savonarola would be killed. Why, I ask? Because he was a heretic, you will reply. And why, I ask, was he a heretic? Because he called the Pope Antichrist, and taught those other things which I listed above. Therefore by the judgment of the astrologers all of us are heretics and deserve to be burned. I very much want to know how the stars make false prophets. Bellanti says that the stars, when unrestrained, make thieves and murderers by corrupting the spirits, humours and elements of those born. If they bring about such things, they will generate false prophets in the same way. For, by the judgment of all astrologers too, the stars cannot in themselves affect or change the mind. But this imagining is frivolous and utterly alien to reason and philosophy.

units.la: Impiam esse vident omnes, qui nō prorsus nihil vident. Quomodo enim pulcherrima Dei opera, à suì creatoris iussu nusquam discedentia (carent enim ratione & voluntate,qua resistere Dei præcepto queant) impellere ad scelera,imò ad hæresim sine impietate credemus? Deum certè authorem huius rei faciunt, quicunq; stellis hanc potestatem stultrè[?] tribuunt. Nihil enim cū agant aliud,quàm quod agere à Deo,cuius voluntati repugnare non possunt, iussæ sunt,& homicidas,adulteros,fures generent, patet ipsas ita à Deo iussas fuisse. Porrò qui alius mandata exequitur, per se & ex sua natura ac sententia nihil agit,non nisi instrumentum est effectoris. Sicut igitur non calamus, sed homo calamum ducēs,scripturæ author effectorq; rectè dicitur cogitaturq; ita[?] necesse est,vt Astrologi confiteantur,Deum esse scelerum authorem & effectorem. Vel ex uno isto perspicitur dogmatis impietas.
units.tr: Everyone who sees at least something sees that it is impious. For how can we believe, without impiety, that the most beautiful works of God, which never depart from the command of their Creator (for they lack the reason and will by which they could resist God's precept), can be driven to crimes, indeed to heresy? Whoever ascribes this power to the stars in such a way certainly makes God the author of the thing. For since the stars do nothing other than what they were ordered by God to do, and whose will they cannot resist, and since they generate murderers, adulterers and thieves, it is clear that they were so ordered by God. Moreover, whoever carries out another's commands does nothing through himself, from his own nature and judgment; he is merely the instrument of the agent. Just as it is not the reed but the man wielding the reed who is rightly called and thought to be the author and maker of the writing, so the astrologers must confess that God is the author and maker of crimes. From this one point alone the impiety of the doctrine is evident.

units.la: Sed Astrologorum etiam nostri sæculi præceptionibus idem repugnat. Sauonarolam intemperatæ stellæ falsum prophetā reddiderunt, corruptis videlicet spiritibus & humoribus ipsius,vnde occidendū ipsum præuiderūt Astrologi. At fuit vir sanctus & bonus Propheta factus,talisq; ad finem usq; permansit, ac propter veritatis doctrinam, non propter ullum scelus,tandē occisus est. Ergo intemperatæ stellæ dū corruperūt spiritus Sauonarolę,ut falsū prophetā crearēt,verū ipsum Prophetā,sanctū,& religiosum hominē effecerūt. Intēpatæ igitur stellę nōnunquā corrūpendo spi-ritus,humores, & elementa natorū,per se reddūt homines sanctos. An potest aliqd magis falsum ineptūq; excogitari?
units.tr: The same thing is also contrary to the teachings of the astrologers of our own age. The unrestrained stars made Savonarola a false prophet, namely by corrupting his spirits and humours; for this reason the astrologers foresaw that he would be killed. But he became a holy man and a true prophet, remained such to the end, and was finally killed not for any crime but on account of the teaching of truth. Therefore the unrestrained stars, while they corrupted Savonarola's spirits in order to create a false prophet, actually made him a true prophet, a holy and religious man. So unrestrained stars sometimes, by corrupting the spirits, humours and elements of those born, make men holy by their own power. Can anything more false or more foolish be devised?

units.la: Bellātius alibi negat,cœlū indicare posse,quis religiosus aut irreligiosus futurus sit,hīc nefariē asserit. Sed & Carda-nus hoc pacto quaeda scripsit,quę valde erasa cupiūt nostri Astrologi. Mirū certē est,eos tāto veritatis odio flagrare,ut quiduis admittāt potius,quàm vanitatē suā ꝑsiteantur. Tu quoq; pturbatē & iracūdē hęc scripsisse videris,cū Sauona-rolā exustū appellas Monachū. Quod gloriæ ducūt oēs bo-ni,id tu acerbē tanquā malū carpis. Multo meliore possem ego iure,si qd ad rē faceret patrono vestro Bellātio iugula-to insultare. Ille nāq; ꝑpter Christū cōbustus est: hic ꝑpter facinus ab hostibus suis foedē trucidatus est. Nec ꝑfuit illi diligentissima cœli inspectio. Quāuis enim domo nunquā egress° dicitur,qn[?] fausta cœli ominari videretur,decept° ta-mē in sua sapiētia fuit. Quis miretur infaustas stellas bona, & faustas mala facere? Iā enim audiuim° intēpatas sanctita-tē creare in Sauonarola potuisse. Sed ad rem redeundū est.
units.tr: Bellanti elsewhere denies that the heavens can indicate who will be religious or irreligious, yet here he asserts it wickedly. Cardan too wrote certain things in this way, which our astrologers very much wish to be erased. It is certainly astonishing that they burn with such hatred of truth that they will admit anything rather than be shown to be vain. You too seem to have written these things in a troubled and angry mood, when you call Savonarola a monk burned at the stake. What all good men count as glory, you bitterly carp at as an evil. I could with much better right, if it had any bearing on the matter, insult your patron Bellanti, who was strangled. For Savonarola was burned on account of Christ; Bellanti was foully butchered by his enemies for a crime. Nor did his most diligent inspection of the heavens help him. For although he is said never to have gone out of doors when the heavens seemed to portend fortunate things, he was nonetheless deceived in his own wisdom. Who would wonder that unlucky stars produce good things, and lucky ones produce evil? For we have already heard that unrestrained stars could create holiness in Savonarola. But we must return to the matter.

units.la: Cœlū & cœlestia uniuersa, cū uniuersales sublunarium caussas negare te nō posse vides, interpretādo sententiā le-nire,ut argumentū effugias,conaris,cū sic scribis: Verū euē-tus liquido ostēdit, cœli lumina locáue posse habere caussa etiam particularis rationem, aut omnino talis in natura caussa, cuius aspectio cōducit nōnihil ad preuideda futura, quod cōtra experientia cū Pico tu negas,&c. Hęccine tua est,quam nobis promittrebas, ingeniosa & docta argumentorū nostrorū cōfutatio? Rationū mearū dissolutionē expectabā, tu vero negas,ne una quidē ratione prolata. Non te principiū petere, siue quod in cōtrouersia est sumere intelligis? Ego particularem caussam cœlū aut sidera esse posse nego, & rationibus certis cōfirmo. Tu istis pręteritis,particularis caussæ rationē habere posse affirmas,& ratione nulla comprobas.
units.tr: Since you see that you cannot deny the universal causes of things below the moon, you try to escape the argument by softening the opinion through interpretation, when you write thus: But the events clearly show that the lights and places of the heavens can have a particular cause as well, or altogether such a cause in nature, whose observation contributes somewhat to foreseeing future things, which, contrary to experience, you deny with Pico, etc. Is this the ingenious and learned refutation of our arguments which you promised us? I was expecting a dissolving of my reasons, but you deny them without putting forward even one reason. Do you not understand that you are begging the question, assuming what is in dispute? I deny that the heavens or the stars can be a particular cause, and I confirm this with certain reasons. You pass over those and affirm that they can have the character of a particular cause, and prove it by no reason at all.

units.la: Cæterūm quia res huc perducta est,& tu,si cœlū uniuersalis tantum caussa sit,consequi vides, Astrologia esse vanā, non fuerit præter rem exponere vniversalis causæ actionē aliquot exemplis. Nam ex ista declaratione apparebit, nun-quam cœlestia particulares causas ita fieri, ut ex ipsis futura prænosci queant. Utar autē Medicis primùm apud Medi-cum, deinde etiam alio rudi quidem illo, sed valde apto.
units.tr: But since the matter has been brought to this point, and you see that if the heavens are only a universal cause, astrology is vain, it will not be beside the point to set out the action of a universal cause by a few examples. For this explanation will make clear that the heavenly bodies never produce particular effects in such a way that the future can be known from them. I shall first use an example from medicine, addressed to a physician, and then another, rude indeed but very apt.

units.la: Cor unica facultate unā eādēq; vim, vitā scilicet, ꝑ spiritū omnibus corporis partibus largitur. Hāc ubi accepit, suū quēq; officiū facit, cui à natura ꝑficiēdo destinata est. Vēter cibos conficit. Hepar sanguine generat. Oculus videt. Auris ꝑcipit sonos. Lingua saporū discrimina indicat. Fecē sanguinis attrahit ad se lien. Renes inutile serū. Musculi ꝑ motu animalis explicātur & cōtrahuntur, & facit quælibet particula, quod ꝑ sua natura facere debet ac potest. Nemo igno-rat, si vim istā, quæ unica est, & omnibus ex æquo communicatur, pars aliqua amiserit, omnē ipsam mox actionē amit-tere. Quam ratione hic cor habet ad reliquas corporis parti-culas, talem propè cœlum habet ad res sublunares.
units.tr: The heart, by one single faculty, pours one and the same force, namely life, through the spirit, into all parts of the body. When these receive it, each performs its own office, for which nature has destined it by making it so. The stomach digests food. The liver generates blood. The eye sees. The ear perceives sounds. The tongue distinguishes the differences of tastes. The spleen draws the dregs of the blood to itself. The kidneys expel useless serum. The muscles are extended and contracted by animal motion, and each part does what by its nature it ought and is able to do. No one is ignorant that if any part should lose that force, which is one and is communicated equally to all, it will soon lose all its action. The heart stands to the remaining particles of the body in the same way that the heavens stand to things below the moon.

units.la: Si qs jā Medicꝰ ex cordis eiusq; facultatis notitia ꝑscire se posse diceret, quā rectè unaqlibet corporis pars suū parti-culatim officiū faciat, aut quā natiuā habeat tempiem, nō tu eū rideres? At nō magis ex cœli viriū cognitioē sciri pōt, quō hæc sublunaria sint actura seu futura. Non sequitur, Cor egregiè valet, vitāq; largiter de se spargit, ergo vētriculꝰ be-ne tēpatus est aut male, bene maleue cōcoqt. Pōt enim hic optimè tēpatus esse, corde parū bene valēte: & cōtrà corde rectissimè affecto, pessimè tēpatꝰ esse pōt. Ratio eadē est oculorū, hepatis & omnino partiū cunctarū totius corporis.
units.tr: If some physician were to claim that from knowledge of the heart and its faculty he could know exactly how each part of the body performs its own function, or what natural temperament it has, would you not laugh at him? Yet the powers of the heavens can be known no more by knowledge of them than these sublunary things can be known in advance as to what they will do or what will happen to them. It does not follow that, because the heart is very strong and pours life abundantly from itself, the stomach is therefore well or badly tempered, or digests well or badly. For here the stomach may be very well tempered while the heart is only moderately healthy; and conversely, with the heart in the best condition, the stomach may be very badly tempered. The reasoning is the same for the eyes, the liver, and indeed all the parts of the whole body.

units.la: Si cur ita res habeat qris, in prōtu est verissima respōsio. Quia facultas cordis nō dat partibꝰ, ut sint quæ[?] sunt, sed actū omnibus eodē modo eadēq; potestate cōtribuit solū. Hoc accepto oculus videt, auris audit, nō videt, quātumuis eandem quam oculus vitā, non aliam à corde receperit. Suam quælibet pars actionem, nō à corde accipit, sed à sua insita natura habet. Hoc solum à corde accipit, ut pro sua natura in actum exeat. Simili modo cœlum idem præcisē dat vni homini, quod alij cuiuis in vno loco existēti, idem robusto quod imbecillo, idē bono quod malo, idē ægro quod sano.
units.tr: If you ask why things are so, the most true answer lies ready to hand. Because the faculty of the heart does not give the parts their being, what they are, but only contributes action to all alike, with the same power. Having received this, the eye sees and the ear hears; the eye does not see because it has received from the heart the same life as the ear, and no other. Each part receives its own action not from the heart but has it from its own inborn nature. The heart gives only this: that each part goes forth into action according to its nature. In a similar way the heavens give exactly the same thing to one man as to any other who is in the same place: the same to the strong as to the weak, the same to the good as to the bad, the same to the sick as to the healthy.

units.la: Non magis dat vt sis bonus, quàm vt sis malus. Neutrum enim dat, sed actum solum tribuit, vt cor omnibus ex ęquo vitalem calorem de se mittit.
units.tr: It gives no more that you should be good than that you should be evil. For it gives neither, but only imparts action, just as the heart sends its vital heat from itself equally to all.

units.la: Sed dices fortasse magnum esse discrimē. Cordis namq; facultatem eandem permanere, coelestium vires variè huc demitti, pro varijs ipsorum motibus. Ad hoc respondeo, ni-hil hoc rationes nostras turbare. Satis nobis est ex hoc exe-plo rei naturam intelligere, quomodo scilicet vniuersalis causa nō distinguat particulares effectus. Quomodocūq; coelū mutari cogites, semper tamen vniuersalis causa ma-net. Aspectus siue contuitus Planetarū aliquis triangularis, etiāsi aliud posse atq; efficere cōcedatur, quàm quadratus aut ipsorū coniunctio, non tamē illius effectus minus erit vniuersalis, quàm horū. Recte igitur quadrat exemplum.
units.tr: But you will perhaps say that there is a great difference: that the faculty of the heart remains the same, while the powers of the heavenly bodies are sent down here in varying ways according to their varying motions. To this I reply that this does nothing to disturb our arguments. It is enough for us to understand the nature of the matter from this example, namely how a universal cause does not distinguish particular effects. However you imagine the heavens to change, the universal cause nevertheless remains. Suppose some aspect or sight of the planets is triangular: even if it is granted that it can do and produce something other than a square aspect or their conjunction, its effect will be no less universal than theirs. Rightly, then, does the example fit.

units.la: Quanquam si accurate examines, non minus varie cor permutari quàm coelum videbis. Certum est ipsum bene & male, melius ac deterius valere, & perpetuae subiectū esse mutationi. Quomodocunq; vero permutetur, semper vniuersalis causae rationem possidet, particularis nunquā acquirit. Quae causa est? Quia semper communis est virtus illius membris omnibus, itaq; singula afficit, vt affici quouis tempore apta sunt. Siue igitur valeat, siue aegrotet, semper suam vim, quantum in ipso est, omnibus aequaliter communi-cat, licet non similiter vitam operetur in ipsis, cum valet & cum aegrotat. Pariter coelestia quoq;, vt vt varie coueniant, ac à se mutuo abeant, atq; ideo varie res subiectas afficiat, nunquā tamen particulares causae fiunt. Sol aliter hyeme quàm aestate subiectas terras aspicit. At non minus aut magis communis est potestas eius hyeme quàm aestate, tamersi [?] imbecillior huc descēdat. Inscitè igitur & contra tū ratione tum euidentia Astrologi coelū particulare causam faciūt.
units.tr: Yet if you examine it carefully, you will see that the heart changes no less variously than the heavens. It is certain that it is well and ill, healthier and less healthy, and always subject to constant change. However it may be changed, it always keeps the character of a universal cause and never acquires that of a particular one. What is the reason? Because its virtue is always common to all its members, and so it affects each one in whatever way they are fit to be affected at any time. Whether it is healthy or sick, it always communicates its power, as far as lies in it, equally to all; although it does not work life in them in the same way when it is healthy and when it is sick. Likewise the heavenly bodies, however they are arranged and however they move away from one another, and therefore affect the things beneath them in various ways, never become particular causes. The sun looks upon the lands beneath it differently in winter than in summer. But its power is no less, or rather is just as common, in winter as in summer, although it descends here weaker. Therefore astrologers foolishly and against both reason and evidence make the heavens a particular cause.

units.la: Secundū exemplum hoc sit. Rhabarbarum, Agaricum, Helleborumq; nigrum misce, ac homini devoranda exhi-be. Calor innatus vnicus eodem modo in omnia tria agen-do, vnica virtute sua ad actum similiter perducet. Actu ac-cepto, nō vnum trahent humorem, quia vnum actum spe-cie ab vno calore receperūt, sed omnino diuersos.
