Rhabarbarum flauam bile, Agaricus pituitam, Helleborus melan-cholia expurgabit, unūquodq; scilicet suae naturae familiarem. Nō enim naturā suam à calore innato accipiūt, sed actū pro sua natura agēdi. Eodē modo quaelibet coeli figuratio, unā eandēq; facultatē rebus cūctis infundit, qua rece-pta, singulae pro suae naturae modo aliter atq; aliter agunt.
units.tr: Let this be a second example. Mix rhubarb, agaric and black hellebore, and offer them to a man to be swallowed. The one innate heat, acting in the same way on all three, will bring each to action in the same way by its single power. Once they are set in action, they do not draw one and the same humour, because they have received from one heat a single kind of action, but entirely different ones. Rhubarb will purge yellow bile, agaric phlegm, hellebore black bile, each its own familiar humour according to its nature. For they do not receive their nature from the innate heat, but only the action of acting according to their nature. In the same way, every configuration of the heavens pours one and the same faculty into all things, and once it is received, each thing acts differently according to the mode of its own nature.

units.la: Tune speres ex solius insiti caloris notitia quenquam praeintelligere posse, quomodo aut quid medicamenta, quae certo homini offerenda oblataue sint, perfectura sint? Non tantum, arbitror, de te nobis polliceri audebis. Quin potius impossibile dices, ac medicamentorum exacta cognitione singulorum opus esse fateberis ei, qui praedicere ista rectè velit. At nō minus impossibile est ex inspectione & notitia motus siderū praeintelligere, quid & quomodo hic omnia actura sint, nisi pbe[?] singulorū natura cognita sit. Caeterum si haec sint accuratè cognita, ne opus quidē erit, nisi generali quadā cognitione coelestiū. Intelligi, ꝙ dixi, ex his potest.
units.tr: Would you hope that anyone could foresee, from knowledge of the innate heat alone, how or what the medicines offered or to be offered to a certain man will bring about? You would not dare, I think, to promise us so much. Rather you would call it impossible, and you would admit that a precise knowledge of each medicine is needed by anyone who wishes to predict these things correctly. But it is no less impossible to foresee from observation and knowledge of the motion of the stars what all things here will do and how, unless the nature of each individual thing is known. Yet if these natures are known exactly, there will be no need even for more than a general knowledge of the heavenly bodies. This, as I have said, can be understood from these things.

units.la: Qui naturam Rhabarbari exactè percepit, is quid in corpus hominis possit agere, cū ab insito calore ad actum perductum est, tametsi caloris naturā & modū, quo in actum ab eo perducitur ignoret. Qui nouit aliquē possidere ventriculum rectè apteq; temperarum[?], rectè cōcoctūrum oblatos cibos intelligit, tantisper dum ipsius temperies nō labefit, & à corde vitā recipit. Sic qui nouit equum vim habere generandi equum, non opus habet ad huius rei notiam siderum aspectione, ut quando & quid generaturus sit praeuideat. Sanè Rhabarbarum omni tēpore bilem purgat, cum à natiuo calore est in actum perductum, quocūq; tandem sidere obtuleris, modò in corpore bilem quae educi possit offendat.
units.tr: He who has perceived the nature of rhubarb exactly knows what it can do in the human body, once it has been brought into action by the innate heat, even though he is ignorant of the nature of that heat and the manner in which it brings the rhubarb into action. He who knows that someone has a stomach well and aptly tempered understands that it will digest the food offered to it correctly, so long as its temperament is not weakened and it receives its life from the heart. So too he who knows that a horse has the power of begetting a horse does not need the observation of the stars to foresee when and what it will beget. Certainly rhubarb always purges bile, whenever it has been brought into action by the natural heat, whatever star you may offer it under, provided that it finds in the body some bile that can be drawn off.

units.la: Iam verò quis nescit Astrologos temperaturas, naturas, vires, proprietates illarum rerum, de quarū mutationibus nugantur in suis vaticinijs, prorsus ignorare, quinetiam nō inquirere? Supponūt, authore Bellantio, materias. An possit aliquid magis ridiculum fingi? Sic ratiocinantur:
units.tr: Now who does not know that the astrologers are utterly ignorant of, and indeed do not even inquire into, the temperaments, natures, powers and properties of those things whose changes they babble about in their prophecies? They assume, following Bellantio, certain matters. Could anything more ridiculous be imagined? They reason like this:

units.la: Hic natus est, cum talis quidam in coelo appareret sidē-rum positus & aspectus. At quicunq; sub tali sidere nascitur, propesum gerit ani-mum ad latrocinia vel homicidia.
units.tr: This man was born when such-and-such a position and aspect of the stars appeared in the sky. But whoever is born under such a star has a propensity of mind towards robbery or homicide.

units.la: Ergo hic homo ꝑcliuē[?] possidet animū ad ꝑdicta scelera.
units.tr: Therefore this man possesses a mind inclined to such wicked deeds.

units.la: Vitiū ratiocinationis ꝑculdubio cernis: Si cœlū rē quā-libet ita afficit, ut affici apta est, falsa erit cōplexio apud il-los etiā, qui talibus cœlestia viribus prædita esse stultè credunt. (Plato, Aristoteles, Auerroes, ac verè Docti omnes aliter sentiunt.) Nō enim cōstat, utrū qui nascebatur aptus ef-set[?], ut à cœlo huc impelli posset. Si dū cōciperetur præpara-tam materiā cū Astrologis dicas, rursus respōdebo, tam nō cōstare utrū ea materia apta esset ad recipiendū tūc talem præparationē, quàm est incertū, an, cū prodiret ex utero in lucem, aptus idoneusq; ad peculiares istos cœli impulsus fuisset. Si omnes aptos respōdeat Astrologus, sic percuncta-bor: Cur non omnes homines, quos illi sīderū latētes radij attingebāt, huc perpulerūt? Cur solius nati pueruli animū figura cœli flexit? An hic solus erat aptus? Aliud respōderi non pōt. Sed ponebātur oēs esse idonei. Et hoc nisi ponere-tur, nō posse ostēdi, utrū is, q in lucē exijt, aptē esset. Quis qso Astrologos docuit, hūc nascētē magis, quā reliquos idoneū existere? An cœlū aptū reddidit? Redibit mox quæstio prima, cur non etiā alios reddiderit aptos. Quid hīc respondebis? Si ad cōceptionē refugias, eadē hīc quoq; interrogabo.
units.tr: You clearly see the fault in this reasoning. If the heavens affect each thing in the way it is apt to be affected, the conclusion will be false even for those who foolishly believe that the heavenly bodies are endowed with such powers. (Plato, Aristotle, Averroes, and truly all the learned think otherwise.) For it is not established whether the one who was being born was apt to be impelled hither by the heavens. If you say that the matter was prepared at the time of conception, according to the astrologers, I will again reply that it is no more established whether that matter was then apt to receive such a preparation, than it is uncertain whether, when he came forth from the womb into the light, he was fit and suited to those particular impulses of the heavens. If the astrologer answers that all are apt, I will question him thus: why did not the rays of the stars that touched all men drive all of them hither? Why did the shape of the heavens bend the mind of this one newborn child alone? Was he the only one who was apt? No other answer can be given. But it was assumed that all were suited. And unless this were assumed, it could not be shown whether he who came out into the light was aptly suited. Who has taught the astrologers, I ask, that this child, being born, was more suited to it than the rest? Did the heaven render him apt? The first question will soon return: why did it not render the others apt as well? What will you answer here? If you take refuge in conception, I will put the same questions here too.

units.la: Addamus iam & tertium exemplū, ex lib 1. Galeni de usu part.cap.3. desumptum. Ova diversi generis, anatis scilicet, anseris, testudinis, columborum, gallinarum uni supposito gallinæ, ut calore suo foveat. Calor quo omnia hæc ova fovet, unicus & simplex est. Nec aliud facit, quā quod ęquo omnia calefacit. Nō enim alio calore, siue alio modo gallinacea, alio anserina, alio rursus anatum ova calefacit ac fovet: sed unico & simplici omnia æqualiter calefacit, eodēq; modo, ut disparitatis ne fingere quidem aliquid hīc possis. Calefaciendo ergo ac fovendo excludentur diversi generis pulli, gallinacei, anserini, columbini, anatum, &c.
units.tr: Let us now add a third example, taken from Galen, On the Use of the Parts, book 1, chapter 3. Eggs of different kinds, namely of ducks, geese, tortoises, pigeons and hens, are placed under a single hen so that she may warm them with her own heat. The heat with which she warms all these eggs is one and simple. It does nothing else than warm them all equally. For she does not warm and cherish the hen's eggs with one heat, the goose's with another, and the duck's with yet another; rather, she warms them all equally with one and the same simple heat, in the same way, so that you cannot even imagine any difference here. Therefore, by warming and cherishing them, chicks of different kinds are hatched: hens', geese's, pigeons', ducks', and so on.

units.la: Quæ nam dicetur causa diversitatis animaliū istorum esse: Nō calor incubantis gallinæ, qui unicus ac simplex est. Unicū igitur quid per se, non distincta genere facit, nempe teperepefacit oua. Non ergo calor,sed ouorum natura in causa est,cur non unius naturæ pulli ex omnibus prodeant,sed ex alijs alij. Quid igitur ouis cōtulit gallinæ calor? Vitalem vim in ouis potentia existentem excitauit,confirmauit,auxit,ad actum perduxit. Hoc facto, qui in singulis inerat calor diuersus, ex subiecta sibi materia animal tale efformauit atq; finxit, quale fingere poterat. Nihil ergo aliud omnibus quàm calorem contribuit,à quo congeniti ouorum calores de potentia ad actum perducti sunt.
units.tr: What, then, will be said to be the cause of the diversity of these animals? Not the heat of the sitting hen, which is one and simple. What is one and simple by itself, and does not make distinctions of kind, namely warmth, warms the eggs. So the cause is not the heat but the nature of the eggs, why chicks of one nature do not come forth from all, but different chicks from different eggs. What, then, does the hen's heat contribute to the eggs? It stirs up, strengthens, increases and brings to act the vital power existing in the eggs as a potency. Once this is done, the heat that was in each one, being diverse, forms and fashions from the matter placed under it an animal of such a kind as it was able to fashion. Therefore the heat contributes nothing to all of them except warmth, by which the innate heats of the eggs are brought from potency to act.

units.la: Non puto iam quenquā hominē inueniri tam fatuum, qui speret, se ex notitia caloris gallinacei, siue ex eo, quod gallinam intelligit desiderare ouis incubare (intelligi hoc potest ex ipsarum voce, scilicet cū glocitant) præintelligere cuiusmodi animalia fotu suo ex ouis fit generatura. Nõ minus vel difficile vel impossibile est, ex inspectione cœlorū cognoscere, quid hic particulatim fit euenturū. Sicut enim gallinæ calor per se nec gallinam, nec anserem, nec anatem generat, sed cū calore ingenito anserini oui anserem, cū eo qui in anatum ouis inest, anatem, & cum gallinacei oui calore, gallinaceum pullū generat: ita cœlū per se nihil sigillatim efficit, sed cum secūdis caussis omnia. Et ut insiti ouorum calores, nisi caloris externi fotu, gallinæ, exēpli gratia, quasi de somno excitarentur, siue adiuuarentur, non poterant in actum exire, ac pullos sui generis excitare: ita propemodum terrena ista sine salutari & vivifica siderum potētia iacēt nec in actum exeunt. Adiuta autem pro sua natura omnia alacriter agunt, ut in ouis inclusi natiui calores. Præterea ut à valido gallinæ calore felicius oua excluduntur quàm ab imbecillo, & à reperato melius quàm intemperato: ita cœlum quoq; felicius & melius quædam æstate, quædā verò hyeme afficit, quatenus videlicet uniuscuiusq; natura valido aut imbecillo indiget calore.
units.tr: I do not think anyone can now be found so foolish as to hope that from knowledge of the heat of a hen, or from the fact that he understands that the hen wishes to sit on the eggs (this can be understood from her voice, namely when she clucks), he could foreknow what kinds of animals will be generated from the eggs by her warming. It is no less difficult, or rather impossible, to know from inspecting the heavens what will happen here in particular. For just as the heat of the hen by itself generates neither hen, goose nor duck, but with the innate heat of a goose's egg it generates a goose, with that which is in a duck's egg a duck, and with the heat of a hen's egg a chick, so the heaven by itself effects nothing in particular, but all things together with secondary causes. And just as the innate heats of the eggs, unless they were roused, as it were from sleep, or aided by the warming of an external heat (of the hen, for example), could not come into act and bring forth chicks of their own kind, so these earthly things lie almost inert and do not come into act without the saving and life-giving power of the stars. Being aided, however, all things act vigorously according to their nature, as the innate heats enclosed in the eggs do. Moreover, just as the eggs are hatched more happily by the vigorous heat of a hen than by a feeble one, and better by a moderate heat than by an intemperate one, so the heaven also affects some things more happily and better in summer and others in winter, inasmuch as the nature of each thing needs a strong or weak heat.

units.la: Eadē ratio est omniū cœli virtutū, quod ad hanc rē attinet. Hæc enim nostratia mouētur, quia illa mouētur. Quòd autē hoc modores [?] qlibet magis mouetur, quā alio quouis, hoc à sua natura singulæ habēt, non à cœlo p se acceperūt.
units.tr: The same reasoning holds for all the powers of the heaven, as far as this matter is concerned. For these lower things are moved because those are moved. But that each thing is moved more by one than by any other, each has this from its own nature, not from the heaven, which it did not receive from it by itself.

units.la: Calores in ouis mouēt, ꝗa calor incubātis gallinæ mouet. [?] Quòd autē hīc anserem, ille anatem, alius gallinam ex subiecta sibi materia fabricatur, hoc ex sua natura singuli habent, non ab incubantis gallinæ calore nanciscuntur.
units.tr: The heats in the eggs are moved because the heat of the sitting hen moves them. But that here one fashions a goose, there one a duck, and another a hen, from the matter placed under it, each has from its own nature; they do not obtain it from the heat of the sitting hen.

units.la: Ex omnibus istis exēplis pulcherrimè intelligis, vniuersalem caussam, nunquam posse particularem caussam fieri, ratione & comparatione illorum, quorū causa vniuersalis existit. Quod commune aliquibus rebus est, non potest alicuius illarum esse proprium, vt nemo non intelligit. Cæterum coelum & coelestia vniuersales caussas esse particularium effectuum huius mundi, alibi satis probatum est, hīc non eget probatione apud te, qui non negas.
units.tr: From all these examples you understand very clearly that a universal cause can never become a particular cause, in reason and comparison with those things of which it is the universal cause. What is common to some things cannot be the proper property of any one of them, as everyone understands. Moreover, that the heaven and heavenly bodies are universal causes of the particular effects of this world has been sufficiently proved elsewhere; here it needs no proof before you, who do not deny it.

units.la: Quod cum dico, nō nego sidera particulares caussas fieri, quoties cum particulari causa iunguntur, cumq; ea effectum particularem producunt. Sic virtus cordis cū ventriculi potestate coniuncta, particularis causa concoctionis, quæ in ventre fit, aliquo modo existimari potest. Sic eadem cordis potestas, cum hepate sanguinem generat, cum liene eundem à sece purgat, cū oculo (vt sic dicam) videt, cum auribus audit, & cū omnibus partibus omnia efficit. Sic etiam coelum cum homine generat hominē, cum herbæ semine herbam, cum lepore leporem, & cum re qualibet rem quamlibet, vt iam expositū est. Nō aliud tu quoq; dicis, cum vniuersalem causam per aduentū secundarum causarum contrahi scribis. Vt autē res tota explicetur, nec scrupus tibi relinquatur, libet quæ Bellantius hac de re affert, confutare. Facio vel ob eam causam libentius, quòd prorsus idem tu quoq; sentis in his literis.
units.tr: When I say this, I do not deny that the stars become particular causes whenever they are joined with a particular cause and produce a particular effect together with it. Thus the power of the heart, joined with the power of the stomach, can in some way be considered the particular cause of the digestion that takes place in the belly. Likewise the same power of the heart, together with the liver, generates blood; together with the spleen it purges the same of its dregs; together with the eye it sees (so to speak), with the ears it hears, and with all the parts it effects all things. So too the heaven together with a man generates a man, together with the seed of an herb an herb, together with a hare a hare, and together with any thing whatever any thing whatever, as has now been explained. You too say nothing different when you write that the universal cause is restricted by the arrival of secondary causes. But so that the whole matter may be explained and no doubt be left for you, I am pleased to refute what Bellantius brings forward on this subject. I do so the more willingly because you too think exactly the same in this letter.

units.la: Verborum Bellantij in 2.quæst.artic.6. vbi particularem causam trifariā dici monuisset, hæc ferè sententia est. Cœlū etsi ratione plurimorū effectuū vniuersalis causa sit, in quibusdā tamē particularis causæ ratione habere posse, scilicet in generatione muriū, ranarū, & aliorū animaliū, quæ nō ex semine, sed ex putredine & limonascūtur. Quæ mox de Ioue addit, ineptissimè adscribuntur ab ipso, cū aliud nihil sint q; principij petitio. Audio Bellantiū dicere coelū particulare causā esse illorū, quæ sine manifesta causa propria[?] semē conferēte, ex putredine generātur. At probatione[?] nullā audio. Si asseuerasse satis est, omnia probari ab omnibus poterunt Sed age expendamus accuratius.
units.tr: The sense of Bellantius's words, in the second question, article 6, where he had pointed out that a particular cause is spoken of in three ways, is roughly this: although the heaven, by reason of very many effects, is a universal cause, yet in some cases it can have the nature of a particular cause, namely in the generation of mice, frogs and other animals which arise not from seed but from putrefaction and mud. What he adds immediately about Jupiter is most foolishly ascribed to him by himself, since it is nothing but a begging of the question. I hear Bellantius say that the heaven is the particular cause of those things which are generated from putrefaction without a manifest proper cause conferring seed. But I hear no proof. If it is enough to assert, all things can be proved by all men. But come, let us weigh this more carefully.

units.la: Dum Sol in limum agit, ranasq; ex eo generat, virtute illa sua ranarum generatrice non solum putrefactum limum, sed alia omnia, arbores, herbas, animalia, &c. attingit & afficit. Quare ergo non ex omnibus his ranas generat? Dices ne hanc Solis βατραχοποιητικὴν δύναμιν (hanc enim pro exemplo posui) duntaxat limum alterare posse? At hoc est sensui, rationi, omnium doctorum hominum sententiae contrarium. Constat enim omnia omnibus coeli viribus subiecta esse, omniaq; ab ipsis affici, mutari, moveriq; posse. Nam sicut corporis nostri partes, aptae sunt pro recipienda à cordis viribus vita, ita naturalia cuncta apta sunt pro recipiendo à coelestibus actu. Quid igitur ad praedictam quaestionem responderi aliud possit, quàm non esse omnium eandem naturam & dispositionem recipiendi, ego certè videre nequeo. Caeterum quaecunq; causa res diversas una eademq; potestate afficiens, unamquaq; ita movet, ut moueri idonea est, ac res omni tempore diversissimas, pro diversitate patientium, efficit, communis generalisq; causa est, ac dici debet. Sic vitalis in homine calor ex quibusdam humoribus putrefactis vermes generat, ex aliter vel temperatis vel affectis nō generat, quantumuis eodem utrosq; modo afficiat.
units.tr: While the Sun acts upon the mud and generates frogs from it, by that power of his which generates frogs he touches and affects not only the putrefied mud but all other things as well: trees, herbs, animals, and so on. Why, then, does he not generate frogs from all of these? Will you say that this frog-making power of the Sun (for I have taken this as an example) can alter only the mud? But this is contrary to sense, to reason, and to the opinion of all learned men. For it is agreed that all things are subject to the powers of the heaven, and that all can be affected, changed and moved by them. For just as the parts of our body are apt to receive life from the powers of the heart, so all natural things are apt to receive actual influence from the heavenly bodies. What else could be answered to the aforesaid question, than that not all things have the same nature and disposition for receiving, I certainly cannot see. Moreover, whatever cause, by one and the same power, affects diverse things and moves each one in such a way as it is fit to be moved, and produces the most diverse things at all times according to the diversity of the things affected, is a common and general cause, and ought to be called so. Thus the vital heat in a man generates worms from certain putrefied humours, but does not generate them from humours differently tempered or disposed, although it affects both in the same way.

units.la: Quid ad hæc respondebit Astrologus? Dicet ne Solem disponere limum, nō vero alia, pro tali receptione? (Ratio prorsus eadem est, à quocunq; siue qualicunque cœlestiu positu fieri cogites. Ego namq; claritatis gratia Solem ista facere pono, ut plerique omnes censent.) At redibit prior quaestio, cur, cum ad alias res plurimas pertingat, nō easdem illas similiter sic disponat siue præparet, ut præparare limū putridum creditur? Respondere Astrologi nihil aliud poterunt, quocunque se vertant, quàm non omnia idonea fuisse, quæ ita præpararetur. Ex quo conficitur, cœlū rem quālibet ita afficere, ut affici potest. At hoc universalis causæ munus est & officium, à qua particulares effectus non distinguuntur, ut ex suprà enumeratis exemplis liquidò apparet. Ergo ideo ex limo putrido ranas generat, quia apti-tudinē et præparationē ad hęc habebat. Si cętera eandē ha-buissent, ex omnibus ranas produxisset. Eadē ista cœli vis, quæ ex disposito luto ranas gignit, ex apta materia mures generat, uel alia consimilia animalia.
units.tr: What will the astrologer reply to this? Will he say that the Sun disposes the mud but not other things, for such reception? (The reasoning is entirely the same, whatever the position of the heavenly bodies by which you think it is done. For I supposed the Sun to do these things for the sake of clarity, as most people think.) But the former question will return: why, since it reaches many other things, does it not dispose or prepare those same things in the same way as it is believed to prepare putrid mud? The astrologers will be able to reply nothing else, whichever way they turn, than that not all things were apt to be so prepared. From this it follows that the heaven affects any thing in such a way as it can be affected. But this is the office and function of a universal cause, from which particular effects are not distinguished, as is clearly apparent from the examples listed above. Therefore it generates frogs from putrid mud because it had the aptitude and preparation for this. If the other things had had the same, it would have produced frogs from all of them. This same power of the heaven, which generates frogs from prepared mud, generates mice from apt matter, or other similar animals.

units.la: Quod si nondū rectè percipis quæ dicta hactenus sunt, exēplum de ouis in memoriā reuocato. Certū est ingenitū in singulis ouis calore, effectore esse pulli q generatur. Et hic nulla est cōtrouersia. Nō minus certū est, hunc cōgeni-tū ouis calore imbecilliore esse, quā vt pullū generet un-quā, nisi ab externo calore corroboretur. Æqueè notū cō-fessum q; cunctis est hominibus, externū illū calore, (gallinæ scilicet aut huic aliū simile) ex ouis nū quā pullū genera-re, si non coniungatur cum innato ouorum calore.
units.tr: If you do not yet rightly grasp what has been said so far, call to mind the example of eggs. It is certain that in each egg there is an innate heat, which is the effective cause of the chick that is generated. Here there is no controversy. It is no less certain that this innate heat of the egg is too weak to produce a chick at any time, unless it is strengthened by an external heat. And it is equally well known and admitted by everyone that this external heat (namely of the hen, or something similar to her) never generates a chick from eggs unless it is joined with the innate heat of the eggs.

units.la: Si non omniū ætatū certa experientia id nos fateri co-geret, ex eo saltē cognosci posset, quòd cū subuātaneis ouis incubant gallinæ, putredinē pro pullo generant. Cur non hic etiam generant pullos? Quia calor pulli effector, qui cuilibet ouo suus est & proprius, in talibus[?] ouis nullus adest. Sicut gallinæ calor absq; ouorum calore tali corrumpit potius ouā, quā pullos ex ipsis generet: ita cœlestis figura quælibet siue. Sol in limum agens, si non calorem in eo inueniat formandis ranis & muribus aptum atq; idoneū, tantum abest, vt talia tunc animalia ex luto generet, vt multo magis putrefaciat aliterue corrumpat. Non magis caret lutum pro generatione murium aut ranarum dispositum calore suæ naturæ accommodato, quàm fe-mina, licet non perinde nos intelligamus, vnde ipsum ac-ceperit, aut quomodo paulatim in eo generatus sit.
units.tr: Even if certain experience of all ages did not compel us to confess this, it could at least be recognised from the fact that when hens sit on addled eggs, they produce putrefaction instead of a chick. Why do they not generate chicks here too? Because the heat of the chick, which is the maker and is proper to each egg, is absent from such eggs. Just as the hen's heat without the heat of the eggs corrupts the eggs rather than producing chicks from them, so any heavenly figure whatever, or the sun acting on mud, if it does not find in it heat suited and fit for forming frogs and mice, is so far from generating such animals from the mud that it rather putrefies or otherwise corrupts it. The mud disposed for the generation of mice or frogs lacks heat suited to its nature no more than a female lacks... although we do not understand in the same way whence it received it, or how it was gradually generated in it.

units.la: Cogita carnes putrefactas asini, equi, bouis seu vituli soli eodem modo expositas esse, & ab eadem. Solis aut cœli calore cōfoueri, & vespas, apes, crabrones, vermes, muscas diuersi omnino generis animalia nasci conspicaberis. An diuersa ista animalia absque ope & auxilio diuersorum ca-lorum, qui in singulis carnibus inerat, generasse cœlum credes? Non arbitror, quemadmodum neque gallinæ calo-rem pullum excludere ex ouis apto calore destitutis audisti. Quomodo ergo vel Bellantius, vel tu potes credere, coelestia particularis causae rationem inducere, cum ex putrida terra aut fimo generantur animalia quædā? Non sicco indiget calore, qui in re putrida inest, coq; certo: Nemo sanæ mentis dubitabit vnquam.
units.tr: Consider that the putrefied flesh of an ass, a horse, an ox or a calf, exposed alone in the same way and cherished by the same heat of the sun or sky, you will see wasps, bees, hornets, worms and flies, animals of entirely different kinds, being born. Do you think the sky generated these different animals without the help and aid of the different heats that were in each flesh? I do not think so, just as you have not heard of a hen's heat hatching a chick from eggs deprived of suitable heat. How then can Bellantius, or you, believe that heavenly things act as a particular cause, when certain animals are generated from putrid earth or dung? The heat that is in putrid matter is not dry, and of that there is certainly no doubt; no one of sound mind will ever doubt it.

units.la: Hactenus exposui quæ esset vniuersalis causæ natura & proprietas. Declaraui etiam, quomodo particularis causa fieri nequeat, nisi per coiunctionem particularium causarum. Talis autem particularitas, vt sic vocem, Astrologos nihil omnino iuuat. Bellantij præterea sententia, quæ eadē cum tua est, falsam esse planissimè docui. Coelum vniuer-salè causam esse, hic non probaui ex professo. Hoc enim alibi feci, & quomodo ad ea tu respondeas, etiam nunc expecto. Deinde non fuit opus, vt pluribus ostenderē, cum præsertim te negare non posse ex tuis literis appareret. Quan-quam si attētè omnia obseruabis, hic etiam ratione simul atque experientia conprobatum perspicies. Ex quibus omnibus liquet, falsum esse quod scribis, euentus liquidò ostendere, aëtra interdum particularis causæ rationem habere. Si verum est superiora quolibet tempore hunc inferiorem mundum, & in eo res singulas ita mouere, vt moueri singulæ aptæ sunt, ac sine secundis causis nihil parti-culatim efficiunt: manifestum est rectè me cum Pico ne-gare, quod perperam tu cum Bellantio affirmas.
units.tr: Hitherto I have set out what the nature and property of a universal cause is. I have also declared how a particular cause cannot come about except through the conjunction of particular causes. Such particularity, if I may so call it, does not help the astrologers at all. Moreover, I have very plainly shown that the opinion of Bellantius, which is the same as yours, is false. That the heavens are a universal cause I have not here proved expressly; for I did this elsewhere, and I am still waiting to see how you answer those arguments. Then there was no need to show it at length, especially since it was evident from your letters that you cannot deny it. Yet if you observe everything carefully, you will see that here too it is proved by reason as well as by experience. From all these things it is clear that what you write is false, namely that events plainly show that the heavens sometimes have the character of a particular cause. If it is true that the superior bodies at all times move this lower world, and move the individual things in it in the way each is apt to be moved, and that they effect nothing particularly without secondary causes, then it is manifest that I rightly deny with Pico what you wrongly affirm with Bellantius.

units.la: Malè illud etiam dicis, me viris doctis & prudentibus multis sensum communem adimere malle, quàm admit-tere aliquas esse demonstrationes ex effectibus sumtas. Ego hoc nè dixi nec scripsi vnquam. Hoc autè dixi, & nunc quoque dico, Astrologos non posse aut ratione aut experientia docere, particulares huius mundi mutationes à sideribus per se fieri. Nō est verū quod tu putas, præcepta Astrologica ex effectibus, vt Medicinæ & Nauticæ orta esse. Quos enim putatis siderum effectus esse, non sunt ab ipsis, vt à proprijs & per se causis profecti, sicut iam ccpioses[?] & planè explicasse[?] me puto. At Medicina & Nautica effectuum, de quibus præsagiunt, proximas & per se causas considerant[?], & ex his siue ex harum actionibus diuinant. Quinetiam quia varie actiones earum mutari, impediri, tardari, impelli ab accidentibus aliis caussis intel-ligunt Medici & Nautæ, non ante prædicunt aliquid futu-rum, quàm iam produci aliquo modo perspexerint. Sed nec causas duntaxat proprias & finitimas inspiciunt, verum obiecta quoque contemplantur. Ex mutua horum actione & perpessione cognita præsagiunt. Ex effectibus talibus, quorum causas proximas, proprias, determinatas, veras peruiderant, sua præcepta collegerunt.
units.tr: You also say wrongly that I would rather take away common sense from learned and prudent men than admit that there are some demonstrations drawn from effects. I never said or wrote this. But I did say, and I still say, that astrologers cannot teach, either by reason or by experience, that the particular changes of this world are brought about by the stars of themselves. It is not true, as you think, that astrological precepts arose from effects, as medicine and navigation did. For the effects you suppose to come from the stars do not proceed from them as from their own and per se causes, as I believe I have already begun to explain and made plain. But medicine and navigation consider the proximate and per se causes of the effects they predict, and divine from these, or from their actions. Moreover, because physicians and sailors understand that their actions can be changed, hindered, delayed, or driven by other accidental causes, they do not foretell anything as future before they have seen that it is in some way already being produced. Nor do they look only at the proper and neighbouring causes, but also contemplate the objects. From the mutual action and reaction of these they foretell what is known. From such effects, whose proximate, proper, determinate and true causes they had clearly seen, they gathered their precepts.

units.la: Astrologi contrà, quæ in alias causas veras & proximas referre debebant, in remotissimas, communissimas & in contractas retulerunt. Et nunc in diuinando non alias contuentur, quas tamen per accidens producere talia certissimum est. Materiam nec considerant, nec considerare possunt, sed supponunt. Non secus faciunt, ac si tota natura id tantum facere posset ac vellet, quod illi præmentiri (volui dicere prænunciare) statuissent. Jactitant etiam se loco ante tempore quàm eueniant omnia prævidere posse. Quo fit, vt ex omni parte Nautarum & Medicorum præsagiis contraria sint Astrologorum vaticinia. Quis non rideret Medicum particulares crises ex solius nativi caloris consideratione prædicere tentantem? Quid si respondeat, se humorem aptum expulsioni supponere? Perinde is faciat, ac is, qui ex incubatione gallinæ prædicere velit, quos pullos exclusura sit, cum ignoret quibus ovis insideat. Talis illius etiam conatus fuerit, qui ex contactu arteriarum, hoc est, virtute cordis cognoscere studeat partium omnium corporis naturam, actionem, temperiem, robur, sanitatem, morbos, & quæ his similia sunt. An non merito dicerentur insanire, qui talia stultè tentarent? At vero non aliud faciunt Astrologi, cum ex cœlo hariolantur, suppositâ materia recte præparata.
units.tr: Astrologers, on the contrary, referred to remote, most common and contracted causes what they ought to have referred to other true and proximate causes. And now in divining they look at no other causes, though it is most certain that these produce such things only by accident. They neither consider nor can consider matter, but suppose it. They act no differently than if the whole of nature could do and wished only what they had determined to foretell (I meant to say, to announce beforehand). They also boast that they can foresee in place and time before all things come to pass. The result is that in every respect the prophecies of astrologers are contrary to the presages of sailors and physicians. Who would not laugh at a physician who tried to predict particular crises from the consideration of the native heat alone? What if he answered that he supposes a humour apt for expulsion? He would be acting just like one who wished to foretell from a hen's sitting which chicks she will hatch, since he does not know which eggs she sits on. Such was the attempt of one who, from the touch of the arteries, that is, from the power of the heart, seeks to know the nature, action, temperament, strength, health, diseases of all parts of the body, and things like these. Would they not rightly be called mad who foolishly attempted such things? Yet astrologers do nothing different when they divine from the sky, supposing matter rightly prepared.

units.la: Valde scire velim, cur tibi Picus oscitanter expendisse videatur sententiam Aristot. in l. Meteor. quà hunc mundum à superiore gubernari asserit. An tu aliud Aristot. illo loco per inferiorem mundum intellexisse censes, quàm elementarem hanc machinam? Equidem nullius rei quam elemetorum affectiones, illis in libris tractat. Taceo quòd verba, quæ antecedunt, & mox sequuntur, hanc expositionē requirunt, imò nobis extorquēt. An vt illa scriberet, illo in loco caussa ei fuit alia? Certè omnes boni Philosophi ita semper interpretati sunt. Tibi plus videtur dicere voluis-se. Verùm non quod tibi aut mihi videtur, dixit Aristote-les, sed quod verum iudicauit. Verba diligenter ponderan-da primùm sunt. Deinde est intelligentia eorum ex dicen-dorum caussis, ex ipsa rei de qua dicuntur natura, ex ante-gressis & consequentibus eruenda. Tu vide ne locum parum diligenter inspexeris, & magis quid Astrologi contra mentem authoris ex coelo particularem caussam facientes, ip-sum dixisse cupiant, quàm quid dicere voluerit, spectaris. Quanquam non tecum litigem, si hac eum sententia illud significasse asseueres, Omnia huius mundi à coelestiibus vniuersali & communi ratione gubernari. Idem nos & dicimus & sentimus. Et quid amplius ex propositis verbis elici possit, ego sanè non video.
units.tr: I would very much like to know why Pico seems to you to have weighed carelessly the opinion of Aristotle in the book Meteorologica, where he asserts that this world is governed from above. Do you think Aristotle meant by the lower world anything other than this elemental machine? Indeed he treats in those books of nothing but the affections of the elements. I say nothing of the fact that the words which precede and immediately follow require this explanation, and indeed force it upon us. Was there another reason for him to write those things in that place? Certainly all good philosophers have always interpreted it so. It seems to you that he said more; but Aristotle did not say what seems to you or to me, but what he judged to be true. The words must first be weighed carefully. Then their meaning must be drawn out from the causes of what is said, from the very nature of the thing of which they are spoken, and from what goes before and after. Take care that you have not looked at the passage too carelessly, and that you are looking more at what the astrologers, making a particular cause from the heavens against the mind of the author, want him to have said, than at what he meant to say. Yet I would not quarrel with you if you maintained that by this opinion he meant this: that all things of this world are governed by the heavenly bodies by a universal and common reason. We both say and think the same. And what more can be drawn from the words proposed, I for my part certainly do not see.

units.la: Cum me dicis negare caussas naturales contrahi posse ad indiuidua, quid dicas ignoro. Iam exposui, astra cū homine generare hominē, cū equo equū, cū herbę cuiuslibet semine talē herbā, cum diuersarum formarum indiuiduis, diuersa speciei indiuidua, cū vnius speciei indiuiduis diuer-sis, vnius speciei indiuidua diuersa. Explanaui exemplis, præsertim verò gallinæ calore fouentis oua diuersa. Quæ si non intelligis, quid dicere possim clarius non scio. Possum ex tuismet verbis hoc loco positis probare, coelestia vniuersales causas esse.
units.tr: When you say that I deny that natural causes can be restricted to individuals, I do not know what you mean. I have already explained that the stars generate man along with man, horse along with horse, and any herb with the seed of that same herb; that with individuals of different forms there are different individuals of one species, and with different individuals of one species there are different individuals of one species. I illustrated this with examples, especially the hen that hatches different eggs by her warmth. If you do not understand these, I do not know what I could say more clearly. From your own words quoted here I can prove that the heavenly bodies are universal causes.

units.la: Coelestium vires lōgè latè q; patet, nihil certi efficiunt, nisi ab aliis caussis determinētur, inq; angustū cōtrahātur, hoc est, ad certum effectum producēdum dirigātur & circum-scribātur. At tales causę vniuersales, cōmunes, interminatę sunt, neq; effectus distinguunt. Ergo sidera vniuersales causę sunt, effectus nō distinguūt, ideoq; ad diuinādū inutiles existūt, siue particulares eiuscemodi effectus ex ip-sis prænosci nequeūt. Rectè tu fateris amplum, hoc est, vni-uersale ꝑ[?] particulare cōtrahi, sicut nup declaraui. Quæ vt merito mirer, cur interroges causam, quòd Aristoteles vniuersalem causam particulari copulauit. Sed profecto verum est, quod Galenus dixit, falsa dogmata caecos et surdos reddere, quorum animos occuparūt, vt nec videre nec audire possint, quæ alij vident audiuntq;.
units.tr: The powers of the heavenly bodies extend far and wide and produce nothing certain unless they are determined by other causes and narrowed, that is, directed and limited to produce a definite effect. But such causes are universal, common and unbounded, and they do not distinguish their effects. Therefore the stars are universal causes, they do not distinguish effects, and for that reason they are useless for divination, since particular effects of this kind cannot be foreknown from them. You rightly admit that the broad, that is, the universal, is restricted to the particular, as I declared just now. So I am rightly surprised why you ask about the cause, since Aristotle joined the universal cause to the particular. But it is certainly true what Galen said, that false doctrines make blind and deaf those whose minds they have seized, so that they cannot see or hear what others see and hear.

units.la: Nisi ita esset, iam dicta intellexisses, & praeterea vidisses, cur Cicero sui dissimillimum generarit filium. Nō ex eodē semine, nō eodē loco generatus ē filius, ex quo et in quo pater natus fuit. Nō eādē habuere matrē. nō ex simili vterq; nutritus est sanguine. nō codē vterq; modo educatus fuit. Lege Cic. filij epistolam, quę in 16. lib. Fam. epistolarum extat. Huic adiunge Plutarchum in vita Ciceronis, & intelliges quę res corruperint adolescentis mores. Nō ita multò an-tè vel ex tuis verbis ostendi, sidera cū diuerso semine & sanguine, cum diuersis indiuiduis diuersos seu dispares fœtus procreare. Quid igitur miri accidit, q; filius nō eisdem mo-ribus praeditus fuit, nō eadem vsus est fortuna, nō idem cū patre ingenium & iudicium nactus est. Dispares causæ di-spares pariunt effectus. Sed haec satis.
units.tr: If this were not so, you would have understood what I have said, and you would also have seen why Cicero begot a son very unlike himself. The son was not generated from the same seed, nor in the same place, from which and in which the father was born. They did not have the same mother; neither was nourished by the same blood; neither was brought up in the same way. Read the letter of the son of Cicero, which is found in the sixteenth book of the Letters to Friends, and join to it Plutarch in the Life of Cicero, and you will understand what things corrupted the young man's morals. Not long ago, even from your own words, I showed that the stars with different seed and blood produce different or unlike offspring from different individuals. Why then is it surprising that the son was not endowed with the same morals, did not have the same fortune, and did not acquire the same character and judgement as his father? Unlike causes produce unlike effects. But enough of this.

units.la: Non nego diuersos astrorum positus diuersè & dissimi-liter huc agere, scilicet efficacius & minus efficaciter. Ali-ter namq; Sol oriens & occidēs, aliter in medio cœlo hæ-rens calefacit. Aliter, dico, non alia vi aliōue calore, sed po-tentius, & imbecillius. Sic & Lunæ motus hoc abundè ar-guit & demonstrat. Nec illud etiā negaui vnquam, homini cum cœlo esse cognationem, quæ rebus naturalibus omnibus est. Hoc negabam, cœlos particulares causas esse effectuum, quorum prœuisionem [?] sibi falsò arrogant Astro-logi. Huius rei probationē ex te auditurū me sperabā, aut saltem, quia facilius est docere cur aliquid falsum sit, quā cur verū sit, nostra te cōfuraturū [?], sicuti pollicitus fueras, suspicabar. Tu verò horum nihil adfers, sed tantum fingis me dicere & scribere, quæ per omnem vitā nunquā cogitaui. q; scia. Tale illud etiā est, q; me existimare ais, causarum vniuersaliū indagationē impossibilem & inutilē esse. Item quòd sensibus neglectis, te rationes meas sequi iubeam. Certè quod scripsi haętenus, non vllis magis testibus, quàm sensibus iudicari cupio. Tu, si potes, non cōsona sen-suum iudicio doceto.
units.tr: I do not deny that the different positions of the stars act here in different and dissimilar ways, namely more and less effectively. For the sun rising and setting acts otherwise than when it stands in mid-heaven. Otherwise, I say, not by a different power or a different heat, but more strongly or more weakly. So the motion of the moon also abundantly proves and demonstrates this. Nor have I ever denied that man has a kinship with the heaven, which all natural things have. I denied only that the heavenly bodies are particular causes of effects, whose foreknowledge the astrologers falsely claim for themselves. I hoped to hear the proof of this from you, or at least, since it is easier to teach why something is false than why it is true, I supposed you would refute my arguments as you had promised. But you bring nothing of this, and only pretend that I say and write things that I never thought in my whole life, as I know. Of the same kind is what you say, that I think the investigation of universal causes is impossible and useless. Likewise that I bid you to follow my arguments with the senses neglected. Certainly, I wish what I have written so far to be judged not so much by any witnesses as by the senses. If you can, teach something that does not agree with the judgement of the senses.

units.la: Post multa huius generis haec demum scribis: Quae haec est consequentia, Aristoteles primos stimulos dixit esse stellas, nec longius est progressus, ergo nemo mortalium aliquid certi divinare potest ex primis & communibus illis impulsibus. Haec tua est ratiocinatio, quam mihi tribuis, sed frustra. Neque enim sic ego argumentatus sum. Praeclarè intelligo, non propterea non posse mortales divinare ex astris, quia non potuit Aristoteles. Ergo quod ad antecedens attinet, verum esse concedo, tibique probari gaudeo. Dum non aliud quàm consequentiam negas, Aristotelem Astrologica nō consectatum fuisse aperte satis te credere ostendis. Consequens non minus est verum, tametsi consequentiam non esse firmam & bonam, aperto, ut dicitur, ore fatear. Ex supra commemoratis patet, me non ita fuisse ratiocinatum. Ideo non possunt ex siderum motibus futura praevideri, quia rerum natura id non patitur, ut cùm alibi, tum hīc etiam, quantum res postulabat, probaui.
units.tr: After many things of this kind you finally write these words: What kind of consequence is this: Aristotle said that the stars are the first impulses, and did not go further; therefore no mortal can divine anything certain from those first and common impulses? This is your reasoning, which you attribute to me, but in vain. For I did not argue in this way. I understand perfectly well that mortals cannot divine from the stars not because Aristotle could not. So as far as the antecedent is concerned, I concede that it is true, and I am glad that you prove it to me. Since you deny only the consequence, you show clearly enough that you believe Aristotle did not pursue astrological matters. The consequent is no less true, although I would openly admit, as they say, that the consequence is not firm and sound. From what was mentioned above it is clear that I did not reason in this way. Therefore the future cannot be foreseen from the motions of the stars, because the nature of things does not allow it, as I proved both elsewhere and here, as far as the matter required.

units.la: Vter nostrum in schola viuat, in qua αὐτὸς ἔφα [?] valeat, is intelliget, qui nostra cum iudicio leget [?]. Ego argumenta plurima attuli. Tu nullum ex his confutare potuisti hactenus, imò me rentasti [?] quidem. At absque probatione complura scripsisti. Quo argumento, ut praeterea alia, confirmare conatus es, quod confidenter supra asseuerabas, cœlos particularis causæ rationem habere posse? Certè nos rem non nuda asseueratione, ut tu, gessimus, sed firmamenta nostræ causæ minimè leuia attulimus. Ea cū tu loco mouere, sicut te facere posse nuper iactitabas in aliorum præsentia, huc usque nequiueris, quomodo sola affirmatione pugnare tecum tibi videar?
units.tr: Whichever of us lives in the school in which ipse dixit [αὐτὸς ἔφα] has force, he will understand this, who reads our arguments with judgement. I have brought forward many arguments. You have so far been unable to refute any of them, and indeed you have only mocked me. Yet you have written many things without proof. With what argument, as with others, have you tried to confirm what you asserted so confidently above, that the heavenly bodies can have the nature of a particular cause? Certainly we did not handle the matter with a bare assertion, as you did, but we brought forward firm supports for our case, not at all slight ones. Since you have not been able to move them from their place, as you lately boasted you could do in the presence of others, how can it seem to you that I am contending with you by affirmation alone?

units.la: Si vidisset, ais, apotelesmata Ptolemaei Aristoteles, probaturus credo fuisset. Bene est quod credis. At ego non quid tu credas, sed quid probes specto. Nisi vniuersam abijcere dānareq; suā voluisset philosophiā, probare nō potuisset. Nā ex diametro hæc cū Astrologicis fabulis pugnat. Quę de Democrito scribis, nihil ad rem nostram. Hippocrates, inquis, Ptolemai de siderū potestatibus sobriam (rectius dixisse ebriam) inquisitionem non fuisset, credo, refutaturus. At ego non credo. Plus enim habuit iudicij & ingenij, quàm ut talibus nugis fidem adhiberet. Atqui iussit, inquies, obseruari ortum & occasum certorum siderū, Arcturi, Pleia-dum, Canis, &c. Si vel ipsum Hippocratem hæc scribentem accuratè consideraueris, vel Galenum hæc interpretantem attentè perlegeris, in primo scilicet comm. in. 1. Epid. Hip-pocratis, nihil Astrologiæ ea patrocinari aptissimè co-gnosces.
units.tr: You say that if Aristotle had seen the apotelesmata of Ptolemy, he would have approved them, I think. Good that you think so. But I do not look at what you believe, but at what you prove. Unless he had wished to cast off and condemn his whole philosophy, he could not have approved them. For this contradicts the astrological fables diametrically. What you write about Democritus has nothing to do with our question. Hippocrates, you say, would have refuted, I think, Ptolemy's sober (or rather drunken) inquiry into the powers of the stars. But I do not think so. For he had more judgement and ability than to give credence to such trifles. But, you will say, he ordered the rising and setting of certain stars to be observed, Arcturus, the Pleiades, the Dog, and so on. If you consider carefully Hippocrates himself writing these things, or read attentively Galen interpreting them, namely in his first commentary on the first book of Hippocrates' Epidemics, you will know that these things support astrology very little indeed.

units.la: Vinum, ais, plus trudit ad arma scio, quàm Martium sidus, & Satyriones ad aphrodysia potetius incitāt, ergo Veneris influxus nihil est. Falsa est consequentia. Sed hæc ἀτοπώτερα, verba tua sunt. Miror te tales producere nugas, quales à me nunquā audisti. Argumenta potius mea sicut receperas, proferre, & in illis dissoluendis desudare te decebat. Quæ hactenus attulisti, non ἀτοπώτερα, sed planè ἀτοπώτατα sunt. Quòd si hoc ipso fuissem argumento, te concedente, usus, multum certè effecissem. Si namq; plus vinū trudit ad arma, quàm Martium sidus, non quidem sequitur, Martij sideris vim nihil esse: at hoc sequitur, ex sidere Martis bellū prædici præscisse nullum unquam posse. Nam si ex vini viribus & actione in corpora nostra prædiuinare ex arte hoc nemo potest, multò minus ex actione huius sideris quisquam poterit. Prius verum esse nemo sanus negabit. At maiorem vini vim hic esse tu ipse fateris. Concedes ergo prorsus, quod inde sequi dixi.
units.tr: Wine, you say, drives men to arms more than the star of Mars does, and satyrs urge them to love more powerfully; therefore the influence of Venus is nothing. The consequence is false. But these are your words, and they are more absurd [ἀτοπώτερα]. I am surprised that you bring forward such trifles, of the kind you never heard from me. It would have befitted you rather to set out my arguments, as you had received them, and to sweat over refuting them. What you have brought forward so far is not merely absurd [ἀτοπώτερα] but altogether most absurd [ἀτοπώτατα]. But if I had used this very argument, with your concession, I would certainly have achieved a great deal. For if wine drives men to arms more than the star of Mars does, it does not indeed follow that the power of the star of Mars is nothing; but this does follow, that no one could ever foresee from the star of Mars that war would be foretold. For if no one can foretell from the powers of wine and its action on our bodies by art, much less can anyone foretell from the action of this star. No sane man will deny the first point to be true. But you yourself admit that wine has a greater power here. You will therefore fully concede what I said follows from it.

units.la: Frigidè primam te disputationis tuæ partem defendis-se, omnino vides. Iam an felicius alteram, tueris, videndum nobis erit. Argumentum primum tale est: Ptolemæus, Cardanus, Trapezuntius, experimenta sua narrant, ergo de siderum operationibus experientia potest haberi. Si talibus ipse uterer argumentis, quid non tu diceres? Sed facilè patior mihi nō licere ἀστρολογίζειν. Nego tibi hos viros probare posse, quod aliquid eorum, de quibus nostra disputatio est, à sideribus per se, non per accidens, effectum sit. Rationes & argumenta flagito,non Astrologorum testimonia. Nunquam dubi-taui eos pro sua vanitate absq; argumentis testimonium dicturos.Miror tamen te Cardani authoritate hac in re ni-ti,quem impiè Astrologum esse, & de Christo mentiri non erubescere,non potes ignorare. An talibus tu me in hac re & caussa fidem adhibere iubes?De Trapezuntio nihil affir-mare aut negare possum,vtrū tale aliquid dixerit.De Ptole-meo frustra respondeam.Si huius apud me plus valeret au-thoritas quàm veritas,tecū de his rebus nō concertarem.
units.tr: You clearly see that you defend the first part of your argument feebly. Now we shall have to see whether you defend the second more happily. The first argument is this: Ptolemy, Cardan, and Trapezuntius relate their experiments; therefore experience of the workings of the stars can be had. If I used such arguments myself, what would you not say? But I readily allow that I may not play the astrologer. I deny that these men can prove that anything of the things with which our disputation is concerned has been effected by the stars per se, not per accidens. I demand reasons and arguments, not the testimonies of astrologers. I have never doubted that they, for all their vanity, would give testimony without arguments. Yet I am surprised that you rely on the authority of Cardan in this matter, whom you cannot be unaware is an impious astrologer, who is not ashamed to lie about Christ. Or do you bid me give credence in this matter and cause to such men? Concerning Trapezuntius I can affirm or deny nothing, whether he said any such thing. As for Ptolemy, it would be vain for me to answer. If his authority counted for more with me than the truth, I would not contend with you about these matters.

units.la: Quæ de Mauritij Ducis Astrologo narras,audisti tātum. Falsa esse potuēre.Scis quā coactè[?] Astrologi suas prędictio-nes ad facta aptent, cū ante ne somniassent quidē aliquid simile. Similiter ac illi faciūt,qui somniū vident. Hi namq; tunc nihil intelligunt, cum somniauerunt. Postridie quic-quid illis accidit, hoc à somnio præsignificatum rentur, & sæpe violenter & ineptissimè facto accommodant.Sed sin-ge vera fuisse,quę de ipso audisti,scilicet prænunciasse eum talia,antequam euenirent. Non potuit alia fraude, vt ple-runq; faciunt Astrologi,vti? Si & hoc neges,esto ita.Verum ne continuò erit,à sideribus effecta fuisse,quæ ille prædixe-rat? Minimè gentium.
units.tr: What you relate about the astrologer of Duke Maurice, you have only heard. It may well be false. You know how cleverly astrologers fit their predictions to events, even when beforehand they had not dreamed anything like them. They behave just as people do who have a dream: they understand nothing at the time of dreaming. The next day, they take whatever happens to them to have been foreshadowed by the dream, and often they force it to fit violently and most absurdly. But suppose what you heard about him is true, namely that he foretold such things before they came about. Could he not have used some other trick, as astrologers very often do? If you deny even this, so be it. But will it follow at once that what he predicted was brought about by the stars? By no means.

units.la: At in sideribus hæc vidit,respondebis.Ponamus ita ipsum credidisse.Attamen non est consectarium,sidera illa aut ef-fecisse aut significasse.Nam si consequi cōtendas,concede-re hoc etiam velis nolis cogeris, Aues præsignificasse vola-tu & gestibus, quæ ex his Augures se præuidere putabant. Huius certè vanitatis impiæ, sicut Extispicij,& Geomantiæ plura & illustriora exempla ex omnibus historijs adferre & ex quotidiana exercitatione Geomanticorum poterimus, quàm Astrologiæ. Non nescis Romanos (vt gentes alias ta-ceam) nihil inauspicato domi forisq; inchoasse ac gessisse. An infinita propemodum euenisse,quę futura prædixerant augures,dubitas ? Falsi crebrò sunt isti diuinatores omnes, scio. At crebrius aberrant Astrologi,quod omnes homines fateri coguntur,qui obseruant.
units.tr: "But," you will reply, "he saw these things in the stars." Let us grant that he believed so. Still, it does not follow that those stars either caused or signified them. For if you insist on this inference, you will be forced, whether you like it or not, to concede that birds foretold by their flight and gestures what augurs thought they foresaw from them. Of this impious vanity, as of haruspicy and geomancy, we can bring more and more striking examples from all histories and from the daily practice of geomancers than we can for astrology. You are not unaware that the Romans (to say nothing of other nations) began and carried out nothing at home or abroad without taking the auspices. Do you doubt that almost countless events happened which the augurs had predicted? All these diviners are often false, I know. But astrologers go wrong more often, as everyone who observes them is compelled to admit.

units.la: Quod si artificum, non artis (sic enim iam nomino) vi-tio cōtingere dicas,idem Augures, Aruspices, Geomantes, cum universa divinatorū turba respondebūt. Quid ipsis respōdebis? Si dicas experientiā ipsorū fallacē esse, nec fuisse talia ab avibus & extis & pūctis pindicata [?], sensum cōmunē te doctis & prudētibus omniū ætatum viris adimere velle vociferabūt, & experientiā identidē urgebūt, ita nimirū evenisse dictitates, sicut euētura in avium volatu vel garritu & similibus præuisa fuerint. Nō tu hic ratione ab ipsis petes, quæ ab avibus talia præsignificari potuisse doceat ac ꝑbet? Cur nō idē nobis in vos liceat? Ecqd tandē interrogati hoc modo, respōdebitis? Augures à Dijs suis ita cōmotas aves ut hæc p̄mōstraret fortasse dixerint. Vos autem qd habebitis? Naturale hāc siderū [?] vim esse dicitis. Nos verò id negam⁹, & ut ꝑbetis petim⁹, p̄sertim cū validissimè nos ꝑbem⁹ falsū esse qd dicitis, nec argumēta vos dissolvere cōfutareq; possitis.
units.tr: If you say the fault lies with the practitioners and not with the art (for so I now name it), the augurs, haruspices, geomancers and the whole crowd of diviners will give the same answer. What will you say to them? If you say that their experience is deceptive, and that such things were not foretold by birds, entrails and points, they will cry out that you want to strip learned and wise men of every age of common sense. They will press their experience again and again, insisting that events happened just as they had foreseen from the flight or chirping of birds and similar signs. Will you not here ask them for a reason that teaches and proves that such things could have been foreshadowed by birds? Why should it not be equally permitted to us against you? Well then, when questioned in this way, what will you answer? The augurs may perhaps have said that their gods so moved the birds that they would show these things. But what have you to offer? You say it is a natural power of the stars. We deny it, and we ask you to prove it, especially since we can strongly prove that what you say is false, and you cannot refute or dissolve our arguments.

units.la: Augurium multo illustrius verū esse probauit Accius Na-vius Tarquinio Prisco regi Romanorū, quā omnes Astrologi suā Astrologiā. Historiā reperies apud Liviū lib.1.decadis primæ, apud Dionysiū Halyc. sub finē libri tertij, apud Lactant.li.2.instit. cap.8. Tametsi hæc ita habent, nihil tamē aliud sunt oēs istę species vaticinādi, quàm indoctę, ineptæ, falsæ & impiæ gentilitatis superstitiones, rationi ac sensui repugnātes. Quod si ex eventis hic ꝑbari nihil pōt, vides facilè te quoq; nihil ꝑbaturū, etiāsi aliquid ita accidisse cōstet, ut eventurū p̄dixit Astrologus, nisi pariter cōmonstres sidera talia p se efficere posse. Cōueniebat instituto tuo argumēta mea & Savonarolæ refellere, qbus ꝑbatur, nullā experientiā taliū haberi posse, quod scilicet à sideribus, ut per se caussis, nata profectaq; sint. Sed præstiterit fortasse hanc rē verbo-sius explicare hoc loco, ut minus dubitare posthac possis.
units.tr: Accius Navius proved an augury to be true, for King Tarquinius Priscus of the Romans, far more convincingly than all astrologers prove their astrology. You will find the story in Livy, book 1 of the first decade; in Dionysius of Halicarnassus near the end of book 3; and in Lactantius, Institutes, book 2, chapter 8. Yet although these things stand as they do, all these kinds of prophesying are nothing but the unlearned, foolish, false and impious superstitions of paganism, opposed to reason and sense. And if nothing can be proved here from events, you see easily that you too will prove nothing, even if it is established that something happened just as the astrologer predicted, unless you equally demonstrate that the stars can produce such things by themselves. It would have suited your plan to refute my arguments and those of Savonarola, by which it was proved that no experience of such things can be had, because they arise and proceed from the stars as causes in their own right. But perhaps it will be better to explain this matter more fully here, so that you may have less doubt hereafter.

units.la: Experientia est eiusdem rei sæpe eodemq; modo factæ obseruatio. Ergo non poterit quisquam rectè affirmare, se per experientiam cognouisse, hoc ab illo factum, nisi ab eo-dem sæpe eodemq; factum modo percognouerit. Dico necesse esse, ut ab eodem factum sciat per se, nō per accidens. Deinde ut caussa nulla præsens fuerit alia, à qua idē effectus potuerit produci. Postremò ut neq; sensui neq; rationi repugnet, illum effectum ab illa caussa produci. Nemo ergo rectè gloriabitur de experientia, nisi eandem rem saepe fieri obseruarit. Deinde vt eodem modo siue ab eadē causa saepe produci cognorit. Hoc autē scire nunquam poterit, nisi duo ista explorata habeat. Primum, nullam adfuisse aliam causam, dum fieret, in quam rectè referri effectus potuerit. Postea vt non repugnet rei naturae, si ab illa causa generatus talis effectus ponatur. Haec iam examinabimus, vt ea necessariò requiri liqueat.
units.tr: Experience is the observation of the same thing often done in the same way. Therefore no one can rightly claim to have learned by experience that this was done by that unless he has often observed it done by the same thing in the same way. I say it is necessary that he know it was done by that thing of itself, not by accident. Next, that no other cause was present by which the same effect could have been produced. Lastly, that it contradicts neither sense nor reason that this effect should be produced by that cause. No one therefore may rightly boast of experience unless he has observed the same thing happen often. Then he must know that it is produced often by the same cause in the same way. But he can never know this unless he has these two things established. First, that no other cause was present at the time to which the effect could rightly be referred. Second, that it is not contrary to the nature of things that such an effect should be posited as generated by that cause. We shall now examine these points, so that it is clear they are required.

units.la: Primùm quod saepe ita euenisse oporteat, ipsa notio experientiae indicat. Non enim satis est, vt re aliqua praesente, quippiâ fiat, ad hoc, vt ab ea re factù credi debeat. Nō enim quod precedit aut adest, causa semper est eius, quod fit aut sequitur. Sic enim solis ortus causa ꝑ se foret omniū illorū dicēda, quae post ipsius ortū homines faciūt. Saepe tonitru facto, aut dū fieret, aliquis forte in febre incidit, nec tamen tonitru ꝑ se causa fuerat illius febris. Sic aliquādo causam certi effectus putat homines esse, cuius causa nullo modo est, nisi ꝑ accidēs. Quia ergo q ꝑ accidēs eueniūt, fermè rarò eueniūt, oportet nos scire, idē eodē modo saepe euenisse.
units.tr: First, that it must often have happened in this way, the very notion of experience shows. For it is not enough that, with something present, something else happens for it to be believed to have been made by that present thing. What precedes or is present is not always the cause of what happens or follows. Thus the rising of the sun would have to be called the cause of all the things men do after it rises. Often thunder has occurred, or while it was occurring someone happens to fall into a fever, yet thunder was not in itself the cause of that fever. So sometimes men think something is the cause of a certain effect when it is not the cause in any way except accidentally. Since things that happen accidentally happen rarely, we must know that the same thing has often happened in the same way.

units.la: Sed hoc nondū satis est. Multa namq; saepe fiunt eodem fere modo, praesente aut praecedente causa aliqua, quae tamen effectuū illorū causa non est. Omnibus aliqui diebus scribūt, studet, &c. Nec tamē solis exortus & dies causae harū rerū propriae existimari debēt. Scire ergo praeterea oportet, nullā aliam adesse causam, quae apte rectèq; dici queat effectū pduxisse. Quàm difficile sit iudiciū, cū in plures praesentes causas ꝑbabiliter effectas aliqs referri valet, ipsa res satis declarat. Potes quę de hac re Galenus in cōm.1.aphor.1. cōscripsit plegere. Qui Medicā artē exercēt, nimis frequenter experiūtur. Quare nō satis est scire, eandē causā aliquā praesentē fuisse, cū vnus idēq; effectus saepe fieret, sed nullā praeterea adfuisse oportet, in quā, vt verā causam, effectus ille referri potuerit. Sol semp est in coeli medio, aut certè plerunq;, cū horologiū duodecies pulsat, exēpli gratia: sed ista pulsatio ab aliis causis fieri potuit, vel cōmodius vel æquè cōmodè, ac à sole. Ex hoc exēplo cætera cognosci facilimè poterunt. Ideo enim rudi vti placuit, vt dilucidior res esset.
units.tr: But this is still not enough. For many things often happen in nearly the same way, with some cause present or preceding, which nonetheless is not the cause of those effects. People write and study every day, and so on. Yet neither the rising of the sun nor the day should be thought the proper causes of these things. Therefore one must further know that no other cause is present which could aptly and rightly be said to have produced the effect. How difficult such judgement is, when an effect can probably be referred to several present causes, the matter itself makes plain enough. You may read what Galen wrote on this in his commentary on the first aphorism. Those who practise the medical art experience it too often. Hence it is not enough to know that some one present cause was there when one and the same effect often happened; there must also be no other cause present to which that effect could be referred as the true cause. The sun is always in the middle of the sky, or at least usually, when a clock strikes twelve, for example; but that striking could have been caused by other things, as conveniently as, or equally conveniently with, the sun. From this example the rest can be understood very easily. I chose a crude example so that the matter would be clearer.

units.la: Verumenimuerò ne hoc quidem satis est. Potest enim quæ verè causa effectus est latère, & quæ nō verè causa est, apparere, ac ita vsuuenire, vt quæ causa non est, causla[?] putetur fuisse. Et contrà, quę causa verè est, effectum q; produxit, causa esse nesciatur, vt quæ latuerit, ea interim apparente, quæ causa effectus non fuit. Quare hoc quoq; considerare oportet, vtrum pugnet cum sensu, cum ratione, cum ipsa rerum natura, vt illum effectum ab ea, quæ nobis occurrebat tunc caussa, productum afferamus.
units.tr: But even this is not enough. For what is truly the cause of an effect may lie hidden, while what is not truly a cause may appear; so it may happen that what is not the cause is thought to have been the cause. Conversely, what truly is the cause, and has produced the effect, may not be recognised as the cause, since while it lay hidden, something else that was not the cause of the effect was in view. Therefore one must also consider whether it contradicts sense, reason, or the very nature of things to attribute that effect to the cause which then presented itself to us.

units.la: Hæc iam ad rem nostrã accommodaturi exemplo prius declarabimus Rhabarbari. Hac radicem purgare bilem dicimus. Et si quis roget, quomodo aut vnde sciamus, respondemus, experientia id nos docuisse. Etenim cũ homini aliquando exhibitum fuisset, bilemq; multam eduxisset, orta suspicio fuit, Rhabarbarum hac vi præditum esse. Cum idè postea plurimis saturis, famelicis, calefactis, perfrigeratis, ociosis, exercitatis mulieribus, viris, adolescentibus, pueris, propinatum fuisset, semperq; bilis deiectio consecuta fuisset, Rhabarbarum virtutem in se bilem purgãdi habere cognouerunt per experientiam. Si tu id neges, respondebunt tibi, qui huius rei periculum fecerunt, hoc modo: Quoties Rhabarbarum homini exhibetur, siue calidus, siue frigidus is sit factus, siue æger sit siue sanus, expurgat semper bilem, tunc etiam cum causa nulla fingi posset alia præsens, quæ idem hoc efficere potuerit. Ambigi hac de causa non potest, quin huius effectus per se causa sit Rhabarbarũ, si non aliter, certè vt instrumentum idoneum naturæ corporis. Ergo recte bilis ista deiectio in Rhabarbarũ tanquã causam refertur. Nõ aduersatur autẽ rerũ naturæ, si fungus aut radix aliqua pituitam detrahit, aliquã esse quæ bilẽ ducat. Recte ergo dicetur, experientia cognitũ esse, quod Rhabarbarum bilẽ trahat. Omnes enim cõditiones cõmemoraræ adsunt.
units.tr: Now, to apply this to our matter, we shall first explain it with an example: rhubarb. We say that rhubarb purges bile. And if someone asks how or whence we know this, we reply that experience has taught us. For when rhubarb had at some time been given to a man and had drawn off a great deal of bile, a suspicion arose that rhubarb had this power. Afterwards, when it had been administered to very many people (the sated and the hungry, the heated and the chilled, the idle and the exercised, women, men, young people, boys), and the discharge of bile always followed, they came to know by experience that rhubarb has in itself the power of purging bile. If you deny this, those who have tested the matter will answer you thus: whenever rhubarb is given to a man, whether he has become hot or cold, whether he is sick or well, it always purges bile, even when no other present cause can be imagined that could have produced this same effect. There can be no doubt that rhubarb is by itself the cause of this effect, if not in some other way, then at least as a suitable instrument of the nature of the body. Therefore that discharge of bile is rightly referred to rhubarb as its cause. Nor is it contrary to the nature of things that some fungus or root draws off phlegm while another draws off bile. Therefore it will rightly be said that it is known by experience that rhubarb draws bile, for all the conditions mentioned are present.

units.la: Jã,an Astrologi possint effectus, quos prescire cupiũt, imò videri prescire volũt, sic aptare sideribus, dispiciamus. Equidem cõditiones omnes repugnãt. Nã nec eundẽ effectum sæpe obseruarũt ab eadẽ causa puenisse. Nec possunt negare, quin ijdem effectus, quos à sideribus profectos conten-dunt, dunt, in alias propiores & veriores caussas referri queant. Quod postremò ipsorū positio, euidētiæ, rationi ac naturæ aduersetur, ex suprà declaratis patet, vbi dilucidè expositū est, qua ratione fieri nequeat, vt vniuersalis cōmunisq; caussa, particularis fiat. Artamē[?] vt res illustrior sit & clarior, exēplum adferā Astrologicū, nō parū aptū proposito nostro.
units.tr: Now let us examine whether the Astrologers can fit effects, which they want to foresee, or even want to seem to foresee, to the stars in this way. Indeed all the conditions are against them. For they neither observe that the same effect has often arisen from the same cause, nor can they deny that the very effects which they claim proceed from the stars can be referred to other, nearer and truer causes. Lastly, that their position is opposed to evidence, reason and nature is plain from what has been declared above, where it has been clearly explained how it cannot come about that a universal and common cause becomes a particular one. Nevertheless, so that the matter may be clearer and more evident, I will offer an astrological example, not a little apt for our purpose.

units.la: Ponamus certā solis eclipsim bellum ciere posse, vt tu in tuis literis affirmas. Si quomodo id cognoueris percūcter, experiētia te cognouisse respōdebis. Quęro ergo ex te iam, vtrū eandē speciē solis eclipsim sæpe bellū suscitasse obseruaueris? Quæro deinde, an belli cuiuslibet, quod eclipsim eam secutū ponitur, nō veriores hīc inuenire licuerit caussas? Quæro tertiò, an nō rerum euidentiæ contrarium credat, qui eclipsim excitare per se bellum credit?
units.tr: Let us suppose that a certain eclipse of the sun can stir up war, as you affirm in your letter. If you are asked how you came to know this, you will reply that you know it from experience. I ask you then: have you observed that an eclipse of this same kind has often stirred up war? I ask next: when some war is said to have followed that eclipse, could you not find truer causes for it here? I ask thirdly: does not he who believes that an eclipse of itself stirs up war believe something contrary to the evidence of things?

units.la: Quid ad primum respōsurus sis ignoro, quid verum sit probè scio. Certū est eandē prorsus speciē eclipsīm, aut aliā quamuis siderū figurationē redire nunquā posse: aliqua ex parte simile posse, at nō nisi post longū tēpus. Non id dico, quod aliquibus placuit, mihi placere nisi rectè intelligatur, nō poterit, totius cœli sidera concurrere ad effectū quēlibet particulare producendū. Nihil tamē isti quoq; dicūt, quod, qui cādidè interpretatur, facilè dānare possit. Hoc certū est, maximā partē hæmisphęrij siue dimidij cœli vires sibi mutuo secundū Astrologorū dogma cōmunicare. Radij nāq; omniū suo modo vniūtur, pro diuersitate tamē positus, diuersē. Iā constat hoc etiā, sidera siue stellas perpaucas notas esse Astrologis. Nō enim omniū, imò ne plurimarū quidē se vires cognoscere affirmare audēt. Quare cū diuerso positu aliæ aliarū vires augeāt, promoueant, retardēt, impediāt, mutēt: sciri non pōt, quatenus singularū figurationū potestates pmutaræ sint, nisi omniū vires explorātē cognitas habeāt, & quantū ex figurę mutatione qualibet, viriū vel accedat vel detrahatur, perspexerint. Nā vt sol in eodē signo similiter deficiat, nō tamē cæterę oēs stellæ eū in cœlo situ habēt, quem cū antea in hoc signo deficiebat, obtinebant. Quantū igitur nuper promouerāt efficacitatē eclipsīs, tantum fortasse iam impediūt. Hoc autē ignorare eos necesse[?] est tantisper, dum singularū vires perdidicerint. Quod cum fieri nequeat, quis quæso non videt, prima statim conditione Astrologorum experientiam privatam esse?
units.tr: What you will answer to the first question I do not know; what is true I know well. It is certain that exactly the same kind of eclipse, or any other configuration of the stars, can never return; it may be similar in some respect, but only after a long time. I do not say what has pleased some, that all the stars of the whole heaven concur to produce any particular effect; yet they say nothing which an impartial interpreter could not easily condemn. This is certain: that according to the doctrine of the Astrologers the greater part of the hemisphere, or half of the heaven, mutually communicates its powers to itself. For the rays of all of them unite in their own way, yet differently according to the diversity of position. It is also agreed that the stars, or very few of them, are known to the Astrologers. For they do not dare to affirm that they know the powers of all, nor even of most. Therefore, since with differing position some strengthen, promote, retard, hinder or change the powers of others, it cannot be known how far the powers of the individual configurations have been altered, unless they have the powers of all thoroughly known and have perceived how much of the power is added or taken away by any change of figure. For although the sun eclipses in the same sign in similar fashion, the other stars do not hold the same position in the heavens which they held when it eclipsed in this sign before. So as much as they previously increased the efficacy of the eclipse, perhaps they now hinder it just as much. But they must be ignorant of this for as long as they have not learned the powers of the individual stars. Since this cannot be done, who, I ask, does not see that the first condition of astrological experience is wholly lacking?

units.la: Respondet hoc loco ineptissimus Astrologus ineptissimè. Medici, ait, etsi herbarū omnium vires non explorarunt, multarū tamen facultates p experientiā cognouerunt. Quid igitur ꝓ-hibet idem de Astrologis sentire? Nō opus est, arbitror, multis declarare qd ꝓhibeat. Iam enim expositum est.
