Herbę singulę p se adhiberi corporibus, vel intra corpora sumi solet ac possunt, cū qua potestate ꝑditę sint, inuestigatur. Quare singularum p se actione obseruare sigillatim Medici possunt. Nam quę nec admouentur nec sumuntur, eę admotarum vim nec augere nec impedire possunt. Si eodem modo singularum stellarum potentia, ab aliarum viribus separata ostendere mihi aliqs possit, credā tunc Astrologis eos aliqd interdum scire amplius posse. Iam cum omnia sidera eodem tempore semp vires communicet, ac radios seorsum nullū solū agat: certum est mutatę figurę potestatē ignorari, dū nescitur quantum singulę stellę, propositus diuersitate, figurę cuiuslibet actione vel ꝓmouere vel retardare valeat. Etenim nullius sideris vires tantæ (exceptis solis atq; lunæ potestatibus) ad nos perveniunt, ut sensibiliter ab aliorum viribus discernere possimus. Possunt ergo Medici plantarum vires quarundā cognoscere, tametsi lōgę plurimarum virtutes ignorent, Astrologi stellarum hoc modo non possunt. Taceo qd ꝑter experientiā sensu ac ratione variarum vires dijudicare possumus, illarum si possemus, nō nisi ꝑ experientiā possem notare & discernere. Putidā ergo, impiā, & verè Astrologicā cōsirat hāc esse responsione, & primā conditione Astrologicę experientię prorsus deesse magis elucet.
units.tr: At this point the most foolish Astrologer answers most foolishly. Physicians, he says, although they have not explored the powers of all herbs, have nevertheless learned the faculties of many by experience. What then forbids the same opinion about the Astrologers? There is no need, I think, to explain at length what forbids it; it has already been set out. Individual herbs are, by themselves, applied to bodies or taken into bodies, and their power is investigated along with the effect they produce. So physicians can observe each one's action separately. For those which are neither applied nor taken cannot either increase or hinder the force of those applied. If someone could show me that the power of each star, separated from the powers of the others, is of the same kind, I would then believe that the Astrologers might sometimes know something more. But since all the stars at the same time always communicate their powers, and no single ray acts alone, it is certain that the power of a changed figure remains unknown, as long as it is not known how much each star, according to its position and diversity, can either promote or retard the action of any figure. For indeed the powers of no star (except those of the sun and moon) reach us so strongly that we can distinguish them sensibly from the powers of others. Physicians, then, can know the powers of some plants, although they are ignorant of the virtues of very many; Astrologers cannot know those of the stars in this way. I say nothing of the fact that, apart from experience, we can judge the powers of various things by sense and reason; if we could do so for the stars, we could note and distinguish them only by experience. Therefore this answer is foul, impious and truly astrological, and it becomes even clearer that the first condition of astrological experience is wholly absent.

units.la: Videamus ergo nunc, an secunda conditio adsit, utrū bella quæ post dictas eclipseis secuta sunt, nō potuerint rectè, aptè, prudēter, verè in alias causas ꝓpiores referri, in Principum & Regum odium, auaritiam, regnandi libidinē, ambitionem, vanæ gloriæ studium, opes amplificandi cupiditate, & quæ huius generis alia Principes extimulant, ut bonis alij aliorum inhient? Si neges ab his nasci bella, siue appareant siue nō appareat in cœlo eclipseis, verè de te dici potest, test, quod de me falso dicis, te doctis & prudentibus communem sensum adimere, imo te ex hominibus plus quam bruta facere conari. Si affirmes, non ideo bellum exortum esse vides, quia eclipsis apparuit: sed quia haec adfuerunt, & praeterea arma, vires, copiae, pecuniae, occasio. Non dubito quin credas absque his bellum neminem suscipere.
units.tr: Let us now see whether the second condition holds: whether the wars which followed the said eclipses could not rightly, aptly, prudently and truly be referred to other, nearer causes, namely the hatred, avarice, lust for rule, ambition, the pursuit of empty glory, the desire to increase wealth, and the other things of this kind which spur on princes so that they covet each other's goods? If you deny that wars arise from these, whether or not an eclipse appears in the heavens, then truly it can be said of you, as you falsely say of me, that you rob learned and prudent men of common sense, and indeed try to make yourself more than brutes out of men. If you affirm that war has broken out not because an eclipse appeared, but because these causes were present, and besides them arms, forces, troops, money and opportunity, I do not doubt that you believe no one undertakes war without these things.

units.la: Si ergo haec adsunt, nec ab eclipsi dari potuerint, frustra nobis narras eclipsim suscitasse bellum. Sane qui aliena invadere cupit, & suis adjicere satagit, atque iam commemorata habet in promtu, bellum vicino inferet, sive eclipsis in coelo visa sit, sive non sit visa. Unde plurima bella nulla eclipsi praecedente exorta sunt, ac multas eclipseis etiam nulla bella secuta sunt. Atqui, respondeat forte Astrologus, eclipsis Principum animos qui ad bellum parata omnia habent, excitat? Respondeo, falsum esse. Nam nec animos coeli permouere possunt, nec corpora aliter afficere quam affici idonea sunt, sicut supra ostendimus. Et quomodocunque cogitetur hoc perficere eclipsis, semper tamen rectius in praedictas causas propinquas referretur bellum, quam in coelum, ex omnium non infatuatorum hominum sententia. Ruit ergo hac quoque in parte experientia vestra, cum quae a coelo effecta dicitis, aptius & verius in proximas causas referuntur. Eclipseis certe non nisi prorsus per accidens causae vocari possunt.
units.tr: If then these things are present, and could not have been given by the eclipse, you tell us in vain that the eclipse stirred up war. Certainly a man who desires to invade the possessions of others and is eager to add them to his own, and who already has the aforesaid causes ready to hand, will make war on his neighbour whether or not an eclipse was seen in the sky. Hence many wars have arisen with no eclipse preceding them, and many eclipses have been followed by no war. But perhaps the Astrologer will reply: does the eclipse stir up the minds of princes who have everything ready for war? I answer: that is false. For eclipses can neither move the minds of the heavens, nor affect bodies otherwise than they are fitted to be affected, as we showed above. And however one may imagine that an eclipse brings this about, war would always be more rightly and truly referred to the proximate causes named, than to the heavens, in the judgement of all men who are not infatuated. So in this part too your experience collapses, since what you say is done by the heavens is more fittingly and truly referred to proximate causes. Eclipses, certainly, can be called causes only in the way of an accident.

units.la: De tertia conditione, quod illa etiam absit, non opus est longa disputatione. Tu ab eclipsibus bella cieri asseueras, & nihil probas. Ego nego, & illis argumentis demonstro, quae tu refellere non potes. Non possum mihi persuadere te nolle, cum praesertim in his literis aliquo modo tentaris. Quam feliciter, ex iam dictis perspicies. Perinde facit qui eclipsim bellum suscitaturam affirmat, ac si quis glocientem gallinam anseres exclusuram narret, cum, an subiicienda anserina ova illi sint, prorsus & simpliciter ignorat. Si etiam eclipsis aliqua permouere ad bellum Principis animum posset alicuius, non tamen constaret cuius. Nam omnium dici nequit. Sic enim omnium hominum permoueret, quod perspicue falsum, & absurdorum absurdissimum est. Deinde si hoc etiā cognitū foret, quod impossibile esse tu ipse vides, nondum tamen cōstaret, an vires, milites idoneos, pecunias, & occasionē obtineret. Nisi fortasse ei thesaurū ostēdat latentē alicubi eclipsis, & exercitū ei conscribat, ac animos eorum, qui à cōsilijs ipsi sunt, ita flectat, vt à proposito Principem nō dehortētur suum. Nō satis est eclipsim in cœlo apparere, alijs præterea opus est. Si quia illa præcessit, hæc sequi oportet, caussa eorum vt sit, & quidem per se caussa, est necesse. Sed hoc falsum tu quoq;, credo, fateberis. Quòd si sæpe post eclipsim bellū secutum responderis, nihil dixeris. Nō enim quod precedit, semper est caussa eius quod sequitur. Fortasse caussa vera effectus latuit, & quæ caussa non erat præcessit. Nisi ita sit, Cometa siue eclipsis proxima te impulit, vt tam præclarè Astrologiam tuis argumentis defenderes.
units.tr: As for the third condition, that it too is lacking, there is no need for a long dispute. You assert that wars are stirred up by eclipses, and you prove nothing. I deny it, and I demonstrate it by arguments which you cannot refute. I cannot persuade myself that you are unwilling, especially since you are in some way attempting this in these letters. How happily you will see from what has already been said. The man who affirms that an eclipse will stir up war acts just as if someone should tell of a brooding hen that she will hatch geese, when he is wholly and simply ignorant whether goose eggs are to be placed under her. Even if some eclipse could move the mind of some prince to war, it would still not be settled whose. For it cannot be said of all: in that case it would move all men, which is plainly false, and the most absurd of absurdities. Next, even if this too were known, which you yourself see to be impossible, it would still not be settled whether he would obtain forces, suitable soldiers, money and opportunity. Unless perhaps an eclipse should show him a treasure hidden somewhere, and enlist an army for him, and so bend the minds of those who are his counsellors that they do not dissuade the prince from his purpose. It is not enough for an eclipse to appear in the heavens; other things are also needed. If it must follow that because one thing preceded, another follows, then that thing must be the cause of the other, and indeed a cause per se. But you too, I think, will admit that this is false. And if you answer that war has often followed an eclipse, you will have said nothing. For what goes before is not always the cause of what follows. Perhaps the true cause of the effect lay hidden, and what was not the cause went before. Unless it is so, it was a comet or a nearby eclipse that drove you to defend astrology so brilliantly with your arguments.

units.la: Sed hæc satis multa sunt ad ostendendum, nulla vos experientia probare posse à cœlo fieri[?], quæ ab eo effici vos somniatis. Generali modo à cœlo ista proficisci non nego, sed ita, vt vos putatis, inde manare nego, ac rectè me negare probo. Proinde nō verè de me scribis, me experientiam negare, cum vos nulla experientia didicisse affirmo, quod à cœlo eiusmodi facta sint. Experientia id præstare non potestis, ratione caretis. Nos contrà, rationes ac sensus habemus testes nostræ sententiæ, experientiam q; iudicem pro nobis sententiam ferentem. Vtra ergo pars veriorē caussam tueatur, valde considerare te velim.
units.tr: But these points are enough to show that no experience you could cite proves that the things you dream of being produced by the heavens are in fact produced by them. I do not deny that these things come from the heavens in a general way, but that they flow from them in the way you think, I deny; and I prove that I deny it rightly. So you are not correctly writing about me when you say that I deny experience, since I affirm that you have learned from no experience that such things are done by the heavens. Experience cannot give you that; you lack reason. We, on the other hand, have reason and the senses as witnesses to our view, and experience as the judge who gives its verdict in our favour. I would very much like you to consider carefully which side defends the truer cause.

units.la: Ad eclipseis tuas facile iam quid respondendū sit vides. Eclipsim solis anno 1540 æstū effecisse aut significasse scribis. Signum quomodo potuerit esse æstus non video. Cœlestia caussas poni ab Astrologis scio. Quare de signis hîc disputare nolo, apud Medicum præsertim & philosophum, quem signorum omnium ortum & proprietates ignorare non decet. Caussa igitur fuit etiam tibi. At hoc anno non fuit minor æstus (quemadmodum & 1556, cuius æstum nemo Astrologus præsensit) nulla tali præcedente eclipsi. Nam quæ hoc anno minima fuit, eam nihil aut perparum ad nos pertinere, cū cæteris Astrologis omnibus, quorum iudicia vidi,tu quoq; in Ephemeride, nisi vehementer sal-lor,affirmasti.
units.tr: You can now see easily what should be answered to your eclipses. You write that the solar eclipse of 1540 caused or signified the heat of that summer. I do not see how it could have been a sign of the summer's heat. I know that Astrologers posit heavenly bodies as causes. But I do not wish to dispute here about signs, especially with a physician and philosopher, who ought not to be ignorant of the origin and properties of all signs. So the cause, you say, was also present for you. But this year the heat was no less (as was also the case in 1556, whose heat no astrologer foresaw), with no such eclipse preceding it. For the eclipse of this year, which was the smallest, you yourself, unless I am greatly mistaken, have affirmed in your Ephemeris, along with all the other astrologers whose judgments I have seen, that it had little or nothing to do with us.

units.la: Quęso te,cum eclipsis solis aliud nihil sit,quàm ereptio luminis & caloris per interiectionem Lunæ, quo pacto æ-stum creabit? Tale est hoc,ac si dicam,cæcum acutius visu-rum, aut qui clausos habet oculos,aut absentē magis esse præsentem. Aristoteles in 12. sect. probl.2. cum de Iride loquitur, quam aliqui odoris causam ponebant, sic air[?]: τὸ δ᾽ ἐκλεῖπον κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς τῇ ἰρίδι ἀποδοτέον, ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν τε ᾖ εἰ μὴ ἐστὶς φύσις ἡ ἴρις, ἀλλὰ τῆς ὄψεως πάθος ἀνακλωμένης. Sane minus est revera aliquid eclipsis,quàm Iris,aut certè simi-liter,ut considerantì utriusq; naturam patet. Multò ergo magis erit per accidens causa, quemadmodum suprà dixi, quàm iris: aut saltem non magis erit causa belli, quam Iris causa odoris. Est enim mera & simplex privatio,atq; ita belli causa, ut absens Nauta submersionis nauis. Fortè per ec-lipsim putas Solis vim augeri, ut in oculis clausis spiritus multiplicari solent. Sed malè hoc putas. Soli nec accedit nec decedit aliquid ex ista Lunæ interpositione. Nobis hoc accedit,quod interea lumine ipsius caremus. Cum re-dit,non aliud nec aliter,reditquàm antè nobis adfuisset.
units.tr: I ask you: since a solar eclipse is nothing other than the taking away of light and heat by the interposition of the Moon, how will it create heat? This is as if I said that a blind man will see more sharply, or that one with closed eyes, or that an absent man is more present. Aristotle, in the twelfth section of the Problems, number 2, when he speaks of the rainbow, which some held to be the cause of a smell, says: "What is eclipsed is to be attributed to the rainbow incidentally, but whenever the rainbow is not a nature but an affection of sight refracted..." [τὸ δ᾽ ἐκλεῖπον κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς τῇ ἰρίδι ἀποδοτέον, ἀλλ᾽ ὅταν τε ᾖ εἰ μὴ ἐστὶς φύσις ἡ ἴρις, ἀλλὰ τῆς ὄψεως πάθος ἀνακλωμένης.] Indeed, an eclipse is really less of something than the rainbow is, or at least similar, as is clear to anyone who considers the nature of each. Therefore it will be a cause only incidentally, as I said above, much more than the rainbow; or at least it will be no more a cause of war than the rainbow is a cause of smell. For it is a mere and simple privation, and so it is a cause of war in the way an absent sailor is a cause of a ship's sinking. Perhaps you think that through an eclipse the power of the Sun is increased, as spirits are commonly multiplied in closed eyes. But you think this wrongly. Nothing is added to or taken from the Sun by this interposition of the Moon. What happens is that for us, meanwhile, we lack its light. When it returns, it returns no different and in no different way than it was present to us before.

units.la: Illud magis miror,quòd eclipsim Solis anno 44. visam belli Germanici, quod biennio post erupit, causam fuisse scribis. Bellū tantū quatū. Germania multis retrò annis nō vidit,ab eclipsi, quæ tanto antè tèpore euanuerat, excitatū credam? Perinde hoc est,ac si dicam te biennio post morte tuam, artem Medicam maiore vi & doctrina publicè do-cturum viua voce,quàm vivus docueris. An tu naturalem causam agere aliquid posse censes, cum non est in rerum natura amplius? Si Bellantium hanc tem[?] explicantem legisti,& extremam absurditatè nō animaduertisti,est quod merito admirer. Nemo ferè est,qui non huius belli causas multò veriores norit,quàm coelum illud vestrum Astrologicum. Tu ipse,puto,non ignoras hoc bellum multis retrò annis, atq; adeò ante eclipsim cogitatum, consultatum, institutumq; fuisse. Occasio rei iam antè cogitatæ non ante se obtulit. Hanc ab eclipsi datam non dices, ne si plumbeus quidē sis. Non puto te veras & proximas caussas, atq; ipsos etiam authores ante eclipsim nesciuisse. Saltē remota à memoria nostra adducere debebas, si minus vanitatem conspici desiderabas. Hæc ad ea, quæ ad duos meos articulos (sic vocas tu) respondisti, refellenda satis esse iudicaui. Ad tertium venio, de quo ita scribis.
units.tr: I am more astonished at this: that you write that the solar eclipse seen in 1544 was the cause of the German war, which broke out two years later. Do you think Germany was stirred up by an eclipse that had vanished so long before, after so many years had gone by? It is just as if I said that you, two years after your death, will teach the art of medicine publicly with a greater force and learning by a living voice than you did while alive. Or do you think a natural cause can act when it no longer exists in the nature of things? If you have read this explanation of the wars and failed to notice its extreme absurdity, there is good reason for me to marvel. Almost no one fails to know that the causes of this war were far truer than that heaven of yours, the astrological one. I suppose you yourself are not unaware that this war had been contemplated, deliberated and planned many years earlier, and so before the eclipse. The occasion of a thing already contemplated did not present itself before. You would not say it was given by the eclipse, not even if you were made of lead. I do not think you were ignorant of the true and immediate causes, and of the very authors, before the eclipse. At least you ought to have adduced things far from our memory, if you did not wish your vanity to be seen. I have judged these remarks sufficient for refuting what you replied to my two articles (as you call them). I come now to the third, about which you write thus.

units.la: Super tertio, quo nos etiam terrefacis, dicam, Astrologos ni-hil habere, in quo sibi metuant à theologis & Imperatoribus ma-gis, quā Medici habet, qui vitiosas inclinationes referūt ad in-felicia temperamenta. Nec laedere possunt religione magis quā re-liquæ Physicæ partes. Hactenus [?]tua recensui. Tu in prioribus literis dixeras Basilium, Augustinum, & Imperatores quosdam ideo damnasse Astrologos, quod propter abusus aliquos, sive quia aliqua ex parte visa ipsis Astrologia fuisset sacrarum literarum dignitate imminuere. Ego contrà ostendi, non parte aliquâ solum, sed omnino totâ eos damnasse Astrologiam. Quod si propter abusum totam ipsos damnasse concederes, ut concedere videbaris, ex Pico argumentabor hoc pacto: Aut rectè fecerunt, quod totâ propter partē sive abusum reiecerūt, aut non rectè. Si prius, decet vos exemplum sequi, & totâ negligere. Si posterius, probandum id vobis erit. Non faci-lè autē in ea re errasse omnes vetustos Theologos probari poterit, in qua omnes consensum habuere.
units.tr: "On the third point, with which you also terrify us, I say that Astrologers have nothing for which they should fear theologians and emperors more than physicians have, who refer vicious inclinations to unhappy temperaments. Nor can they harm religion more than the other parts of physics can." So far I have recounted your words. In your earlier letter you had said that Basil, Augustine and certain emperors condemned the Astrologers because of some abuses, or because astrology seemed to them in some part to diminish the dignity of Holy Scripture. I, on the contrary, showed that they condemned astrology not in some part only but altogether, entirely. But if you were to concede that they condemned the whole on account of abuse, as you seemed to concede, I will argue from Pico in this way: either they acted rightly, in rejecting the whole on account of the part or abuse, or they did not act rightly. If the former, it is fitting for us to follow their example and neglect the whole. If the latter, that will have to be proved to you. Nor will it easily be proved that all the ancient theologians erred in a matter in which they all agreed.

units.la: Ad hæc tu ne verbū quidem respondes, sed ad priora ali-quid dicere conatus es. Ut autem videas antiquos totā dam-nare, Tertullianī tibi, quē, cum hæc describerem, præ manibus habebā, audi sic scribētē: Quas artes (loquitur de Astro-logia, Aruspicina, Augurio & Magia) ut ab angelis desertorib. proditas, & à Deo interdictas, ne suis quidem caussis adhibent Christiani. Tantum abesse, ait, ut de Imperatoris eventu per has artes aliquid præscire desiderent Christiani, ut ne in suis quidem privatis rebus prænoscendis illis urantur? Causam manifestam addit, quia sunt à Dæmonibus proditæ, & à Deo interdictæ. Locum invenies in Apologet. adversus gentes, cap.36. Si illustriora testimonia videre cupis, Augustinum atque alios lege, quos hoc loco citare non est opus. Savonarola quædam produxit. Qui plura cupit, apud ipsos autores inueniet. Non adduxi autem haec vt terrerem quenquam, sed vt non recte affirmare te ostenderem, Basilium, Augustinum, Imperatores totam propter partem siue propter abusum execratos fuisse.
units.tr: To these things you do not reply a word, but have tried to say something about the earlier points. So that you may see that the ancients condemned it entirely, hear Tertullian, whom I had before my hands while writing these things, writing thus: "These arts" (he speaks of astrology, haruspicy, augury and magic) "since they were revealed by fallen angels and forbidden by God, Christians do not use even for their own purposes." So far is it, he says, that Christians desire to foreknow anything about the emperor's fate through these arts, that they do not use them even to foreknow their own private affairs. He adds the manifest reason: because they were revealed by demons and forbidden by God. You will find the passage in the Apology against the Gentiles, chapter 36. If you wish to see more illustrious testimonies, read Augustine and others, whom there is no need to cite here. Savonarola also produced some. Whoever wants more will find it in the authors themselves. I have not adduced these things to terrify anyone, but to show that you are wrong to affirm that Basil, Augustine and the emperors condemned it wholly on account of a part, or on account of abuse.

units.la: Ad rua[?] redeo, in quibus argumenti vim non volo exa-minare, sed rem expendere. Videris autem hoc velle, si A-strologia damnata sit, quia doceat coelum hos ad peccandum flectere. Medicinam eadem ratione damnandam, quae temperamenta nos huc impellere docear. Consequentia falsa est, quia nihil similitudinis inuenitur inter Medicorum & Astrologorum sententias. Qui medio-criter Sacras literas vel inspexit solum, infinitum discri-men cernit. Quis nescit hominem, cum liber esset, sua sponte peccasse, & peccado peccati seruum fuisse factum? Vix iam vestigium pristini & diuini splendoris in eo reli-quum cernitur. Et haec omnia merito suo patitur, quod Dæmoni magis, quam creatoris sui voci praeceptoque pa-rere voluit. Flectitur & impellitur ergo iam homo a sua na-tura, quia serua facta est peccati. Talis autem a Deo facta nequaquam fuit, sed a peccato quod sponte admisit, huc miseriae deducta est. Poena est peccati ista ad peccandum propensio inclinatioq;.
units.tr: I return to your arguments, whose force I do not wish to examine, but whose matter I will weigh. You seem to wish this: if astrology is condemned because it teaches that the heavens bend us to sin, then medicine should be condemned by the same reasoning, since it teaches that temperaments drive us here. The consequence is false, because no likeness is found between the opinions of physicians and of astrologers. Anyone who has even moderately looked into Holy Scripture sees an infinite difference. Who does not know that man, when he was free, sinned of his own accord, and by sin became the slave of sin? Hardly any trace of his former and divine splendour is now seen remaining in him. And all this he suffers by his own merit, because he chose to obey the demon rather than the voice and precept of his Creator. Man is therefore now bent and impelled by his nature, because it has been made the slave of sin. But he was by no means made such by God; he was brought to this misery by the sin that he admitted of his own will. This propensity and inclination to sin is the punishment of sin.

units.la: Quòd si Deus ne naturam quidem nostram talem fecit, vt nos ad praeuaricandum impelleret, quomodo coelum ita factum esse ab eo recte cogitemus, vt nos ne-scientes incitet aduersus pietatem & honestatem? Me-dicina ergo nihil a Sacris literis alienum docet, cum pro temperamentorum ratione inclinatam hominis natu-ram ad scelera exponit, quantumuis huius infelicitatis causam non norit. Sed ne pertinet quidem ad ipsam huius rei & causae inquisitio. Philosophorum potius munus fuerit, qui peruidere natura duce nunquam ori-ginem tanti mali potuerunt. Antea quàm primi paren-tes nostri peccassent, natura non erat, sicut iam est ad peccata prona & facilis. Nec à coelo etiam impelle-batur ad transgressionem. Postquam vero peccarunt, & ingenium naturamq; hanc in nos transfuderunt, propendemus huc toti, non aliunde, quàm ab innata nobis malicia impulsi. Cœlum per pecca-tum hominis mutatum nō legimus. Quare sicut ante pec-catum iussa creatoris faciebat, nec ad peccandum tamen hominem inclinabat, ita ne nunc quidē inclinat. Et posset sanè homo excusare se Deo, si à cœlo ad flagitiosè facien-dum incitaretur. De sua carne queri naturaq; non potest, propterea quòd hanc sibi pestem vltrò contra Dei præce-ptum accersiuit. Hoc Basilius voluit, ad cuius argumentū tu respexisse videri potes, cum hæc scribebas. Puto te iam intelligere, quàm non sit argumentum solutum tua ista euanida responsione de Medicina & Physica: Siue hoc, siue aliud spectaris, parū refert, modò quod res est intelligas.
units.tr: But if God did not make our nature itself such that it should drive us to transgress, how can we rightly think that the heavens were so made by him that they incite us, unknowing, against piety and honesty? Therefore medicine teaches nothing alien to Holy Scripture when, according to the reasoning of temperaments, it sets out the human nature inclined to crimes, although it does not know the cause of this unhappiness. Yet the inquiry into this matter and its cause does not even belong to medicine. It would rather be the task of the philosophers, who, guided by nature, could never perceive the origin of so great an evil. Before our first parents sinned, nature was not, as it now is, prone and easy toward sins. Nor was man then impelled to transgression even by the heavens. But after they sinned, and transfused this nature and disposition into us, we are all inclined toward it, impelled by nothing else than the malice innate in us. We do not read that the heaven was changed by man's sin. Therefore, just as before the sin it carried out the commands of the Creator, yet did not incline man to sin, so it does not incline him even now. And man could certainly excuse himself to God if he were incited by the heavens to commit shameful deeds. He cannot complain about his flesh or his nature, because he brought this plague upon himself of his own accord, contrary to God's precept. This is what Basil meant, and you may seem to have looked to his argument when you wrote these things. I think you now understand how far your empty reply about medicine and physics is from being a solid argument. Whether you look at this or at something else matters little, provided you understand what the matter is.

units.la: Verbosius ista exposui, quàm forte conueniret, non ta-men quàm res apud Astrologos flagitaret, qui ne illa qui-dem intelligunt, quæ satis dilucida aliis videntur. Præcipuè me monuit, quòd te id quod maximè cupiebam, & tibi faci-le fore aiebas, non præstaturum suspicor ac metuo. Argu-menta suspicionis nō leuia in hisce mihi literis præbuisti. Cœlum quomodo vniuersalis causa sit, & quòd particula-ris fieri non possit aliter, quàm per cōiunctionē particula-ris causæ, perspicuè exposui. Deinde etiam quæ & quot requirantur, vt experientia nos aliquid cognouisse rectè af-firmemus, similiter ostendi. Postremò Medicos nihil dis-sonum à sacris literis & Philosophia docere declaraui, adeoq; demonstraui malè te hac in parte has scientias Astrologiæ comparasse, quæ tota falsa, impossibilis, impia, & à Deo interdicta est, vt cùm Lex, rū Tertullianus loquū-tur: Tuum erit ista legere, ponderare, & quæ vera esse perspexeris, amplecti. Vale. Febr. mense,
units.tr: I have set these things out at more length than was perhaps fitting, though not as much as the matter demands from Astrologers, who do not understand even those points that seem clear enough to others. What most prompted me was that you say you will easily do what I most wanted, and I suspect and fear you will not. In this letter you have given me no slight grounds for that suspicion. I have set out clearly how the heavens are a universal cause, and why a particular effect cannot come about except through the conjunction of a particular cause. I have likewise shown what and how many things are required before we can rightly affirm that experience has taught us something. Lastly, I have declared that the physicians teach nothing discordant with Holy Scripture or with philosophy, and so I have demonstrated that you have badly matched these sciences with Astrology, which is wholly false, impossible, and impious, and forbidden by God, as both the Law and Tertullian put it. It will be for you to read these things, weigh them, and embrace whatever you find to be true. Farewell. In the month of February,
